units.la: THESAVRI in sacris literis, siue homines, siue Deum spectemus, multiplex occurrit mentio. Seruatoris nostri vocem, de thesauro, qui tibi, Lector, offertur, repetimus, Recondite vobis (inquit) thesauros in cœlo, vbi neque tinea neque erosio corrumpit, & vbi fures non perfodiunt, nec furantur. Nam vbi est thesaurus vester, illic erit etiam cor vestrum. Rerum incorruptibilium thesaurus congerendus qui non deficiat, nobis non deest, & sartus tectus perpetuò maneat, ex quo quod bonum, vtile, iucundum, necessarium est in promptu depromere, aliis proponere ad animæ tranquillitatem conciliandam facile possis. In Christo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ ac cognitionis absconditi. Sed Deus qui edixit vt è tenebris lux splendesceret, is est qui splenduit in cordibus nostris ad prabendum lumen cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Iesu Christi: is est qui thesaurum illum immensum ostendit in verbo scripto, librisque Propheticis & Apostolicis, vasculis quidem testaceis, incluso: vt eius virtutis præstantia sit Dei, & non ex hominibus, quantumuis Dei seruis, per quos preciosissimas misericordia sua diuitias nobis largitus est. Scripturarum Sacrarum equidem tanta est vbertas, tanta diuinarum opum congeries, tantaq; in Dei cognitione tradenda facultas, vt earum splendore perfusi, copia ditati, consilio ducti, gloriam Domini retecta facie, vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformemur ex gloria in gloriam. Atque quod in eo thesauro magis mirere, non locupletes tantùm locupletiores & latiores efficit, sed inopem accedentem sublevat & vndequaque diuitem, beatum, nouaq; sua sorte contentum comitatur. Paulus Apostolus diuersis verbis, sed eodem sensu, discipulum charissimum Timotheum compellans, Permane (ait) in his quæ didicisti, & quæ tibi concredita sunt, sciens à quo didiceris. téque à puero sacras literas nouisse, quæ te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem, per fidem quæ est in Christo Iesu. At tibi, Lector, occi-nimus, Accipe hilari mente Thesaurum veritatis diuinæ, tibi in li-bris Canonicis Veteris nouiq; fœderis oblatum, tibi concreditum conserua fideliter, is enim te diuitiis æternis locupletabit, & beabit pace cœlesti. Quid terrena semper meditamur, caduca, instabilia, relinquenda breui? Cur longum vale sæpius æternum permansuris bonis & diuitiis dicimus? Si tanti vitrum facimus, quid margari-tum? Totus ille Scriptura diuinitus inspirata thesaurus, abyssius di-uitiarum cœlestium apparet, ex quo quacunque sunt utilia ad do-ctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem quæ est in iustitia, ut perfectus sis ad omne opus bonum, aliósque tecum serues, perfectéque instructos eruere possis. Nouum & mirabile pror-sus diuitiarum genus sit oportet, quod ut largiretur Ecclesiæ, qui Deus erat factus est homo, qui immortalis mortalis, qui in sinu pa-tris se in terras demisit. Magnum quiddam, & haudquaquam vulgare sit oportet, quicquid illud est, quod ille tam admirandus author, post tot excellentium Philosophorum familias, demonstra-turus nobis aduenit. Cur non hic pia curiositate, singula in tot ca-psulis & arculis sacris latentia cognoscimus, disquirimus, excuti-mus? præsertim cùm hoc diuitiarum genus, tam eximium, precio-sissimum, immensum, numero innumero, semel & simul pauperri-mas reddiderit vniuersas huius mundi facultates? Cœlestes thesau-ros ex paucis thecis, sed altissimis, & tutissimo loco repositis, desume-re licet, nemine repellente, vel exprobrante, sed inuitante, compellâte, donante Christo, longè minore negotio, quàm ex tot falsò nominata scientia mundana spinosis voluminibus. Nihil hic necesse est, ut tot argutiis instructus ad pecuniam colligendam accedas. Simplex & cuius paratum est donum illum cœleste, modò promptam fidei vera manum adferas, aurémque docilem: tunc aberit à tuo corde formidabilis hæc exprobratio Summi Iudicis ad Ecclesiæ Laodicen-sis ministrum, Noui opera tua, te neque frigidum esse, neque feruì-dum: vtinam frigidus esses, aut feruidus! Itaque quoniam tepidus es, nec frigidus, nec feruidus, futurum est ut te euomam ex ore meo. Nam dicis, Diues sum & ditatus sum, & nullius egeo. Neque nosti te esse æruminosum, & miserabilem, & pauperem, & cæcum, & nu-dum. Suadeo tibi vt emas à me aurum igni exploratum, ut diues fias, & vestimenta alba, ut induaris, nec appareat dedecus nuditatis tuæ, & collyrio inungas oculos tuos, vt videas. Hæc nobis dicta pute-mus, Lector: hæ sint collyria chartæ, hic aurum & vestimenta qua-ramus, vocationi, tenuitati, meditationi nostræ conuenientia, & ad regis regis nostri palatium his vocibus inuitemur, vt ingentes diuitias eiusdem deuotis contemplemur fidei oculis, vt sciamus quæ sit spes illa vocationis ipsius, quæ opes hereditatis populo Dei per Christū acquisitæ, & quanta sit excellens magnitudo potentiæ Dei in nobis qui credimus, ita vt in charitate radicati, tantarum diuitiarum latitudinem, longitudinem, profunditatem, sublimitatem assequi valeamus. Diuitiæ diuinæ omnibus ex æquo sese accommodant, exigua manu præditis & pusillis se submittunt, illorum captum respiciunt, quæ nobis idonea sunt curantes, donec adolescamus in Christo. Grandioribus & cœlesti ætate proueētis, thesaurus hic admirabilis appa- ret, qui vt rerum periti, & sensibus exercitatis præditi, preciosum à vili discernunt. Et certè quo longius Dei opes tractaueris, eò longius illarum maiestate moueberis. Prauis prauæ, parvus pusillæ, magnis magnæ sunt, vt excelsa mente donatis excelsæ. Sed nullam ætatem, nullum sexum, nullam conditionem reiciunt. Sed hic non perinde communis & expositus est omnibus, atque Christi doctrina ex sacris fontibus abundè fluens. Non arcet omnino quenquam, nisi quis semet arceat, ipse sibi inuidens. Vehementer enim istos improbamus, qui thesaurum Sacræ Scripturæ idiotis (quos vocant) suffurantur, & diuitias cœlestes, rubigine deformes, vel ab interpretationum variarum tinea corrosas esse vociferantur: vt nos à domo patris nostri cœlestis abductos, seductos, ad humanarum traditionum sœdissimas, sœtidissimas & lethales cloacas deducant. Regum opes attingere fortasse non satis tutum. at Christus suas quàm maximè cupit euulgari. has lubens suis concedit: præsertim verò harum cupidissimis. Ex quorum numero Theologiæ candidatos esse conuenit. Sed quia ratio alia est Thesauri expositi, & exponendi, factum est vt in Ecclesia, quæ est Dei domus, cui fruendus totus conceditur, non vno tantùm ordine dispositus appareat: sed pro donorum Spiritus Sancti mensura, familiæ sanctæ œconomi, dispensatores diuinarum diuitiarum, harum distribuendarum methodum sibi nec non aliis consignauerint. Inter quos laudabilem operam nauauit fidelis ser- uus, scriba edoctus in regno cœlorum, noua vetera è scrinio sui pe- ctoris olim proferens, D. AVGVSTINVS MARLORATVS, Rho- tomagensis Ecclesiæ pastor vigilantissimus, & Christi martyr inuincitus: cuius opus ex sacris thesauris congestum, dein in arcam suis arculis distinctum, studio D. GVLIELMI FEVGVEREII laborum piorum socij & successoris, variis locis editum, tandem in enchyridij formam contractum, & nunc multis diuitiis vltra priores editiones omnes auctum atque illustratum, tibi offerimus. In ea tria occurrerunt capita pro Alphabeti serie collocata, Rerum, Dogmatum & Phraseon, quibus Exempla admixta sunt. Qua quum uberius a Theologis exponantur, & quis sit omnium usus ex praxi quotidiana percipiatur, in iis fusius declarandis immorari haud necesse est. Ex Apocryphis olim collecta reiecimus: in quorum locum multa praetermissa, praesertim ad voces theologicas pertinentia, per totum volumen, à principio ad calcem sparsa, adiecimus. Nonnulla emendavimus, Exempla omnia, Dogmata item, & quae ab aduersariis pro errorum suorum confirmatione torquentur pridem indicata, reliquimus, vulgatam editionem Latinam post Marloratum, ab initio ad finem sequuti. Huic postremae editioni accesserunt, 1. Locorum ferè omnium, qui à Collectore citantur, necessaria cum suis fontibus collatio. 2. Plaraque virorum, urbium & similium rerum nomina, observatione digna, cum sua breui designatione, adscripta. 3. Qua in hocce Thesauro extabant paucis insertis, pariter illustrata. 4. Tituli etiam nominum, propriorum, appellativorum & rerum, locupletiores redditi, aliique perutiles non pauci commodè adiecti. quorum nonnulli notulis istis [ ] inclusi, alij verò praetermissi, sed in vocum Indice designati sunt. 5. Definitiones quoque quamplurimae seu descriptiones studiosis pergratae. 6. Dictionum Hebr. & Grec. plaraque significationes. Habes, Lector, instituti nostri rationem: tu verò thesauro, in tuum commodum noua editione parato, fruere utere, fretus clementia Christi, quem tibi ex animo vouemus propitium. Calend. Mart. anno MDXCIII.
units.tr: Whether we look at men or at God, the word "treasure" occurs in many places in Holy Scripture. We repeat to you, reader, the Saviour's own saying about the treasure that is offered to you: "Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust corrupts, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." A store of incorruptible things, which will never run out, is not lacking to us. It remains safe and sealed for ever, and from it you can easily bring out whatever is good, useful, pleasant and necessary, and set it before others to win them peace of soul. In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. But God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, is the one who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. He is the one who displayed that vast treasure in the written Word, in the books of the Prophets and Apostles, enclosed in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of its power might be seen to be God's and not men's, even though they were servants of God, through whom he has bestowed on us the riches of his most precious mercy. Indeed, the Scriptures are so abundant, so full of divine riches, and so able to convey the knowledge of God, that, filled with their brightness, enriched with their abundance, and guided by their counsel, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face as in a mirror, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory. And what you may wonder at more in that treasure is that it does not merely make the rich richer and more abundant, but also raises up the needy who come to it and accompanies those who are wealthy in every way, blessed, and content with their new lot. The Apostle Paul, addressing his dearest disciple Timothy in different words but with the same meaning, said: "Continue in what you have learned and what has been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned it, and that from childhood you have known the holy writings, which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus." And to you, reader, I say: receive with a cheerful mind the treasure of divine truth offered to you in the canonical books of the Old and New Covenant, and keep faithfully what has been entrusted to you. For it will enrich you with eternal riches and bless you with heavenly peace. Why do we always think of earthly things, which are perishable and unstable and must soon be left behind? Why do we so often say a long farewell to goods and riches that will last for ever? If we value glass so highly, what shall we make of a pearl? That whole treasure of Scripture, divinely inspired, appears as an abyss of heavenly riches, from which whatever is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness can be drawn, so that you may be perfect and equipped for every good work, and so that you may keep others with you and bring them out thoroughly instructed. It must be a new and truly wonderful kind of riches that God, who was made man, came to bestow on the Church. He who was immortal became mortal and let himself down from the bosom of the Father to the earth. It must be something great and by no means ordinary, whatever it is, that this most admirable author came to show us after so many families of excellent philosophers. Why should we not with pious curiosity examine, search out and explore each thing hidden in so many sacred capsules and chests? Especially since this kind of riches, so rare, so precious, so vast, in countless number, has at once made all the resources of this world utterly poor. From a few chests, but very high and placed in the safest spot, we may take heavenly treasures, with no one turning us away or reproaching us, but with Christ inviting, calling and giving, with far less trouble than from the many thorny volumes of so-called worldly learning, falsely named science. Here there is no need for you to approach to gather money equipped with many subtleties. Only be simple, and let the heavenly gift, which is prepared for the one whose hand is ready, bring the true hand of faith and an ready ear. Then that terrible rebuke of the Supreme Judge to the minister of the Church of Laodicea will be far from your heart: "I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were either cold or hot! So then, because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spew you out of my mouth. For you say, 'I am rich and have prospered, and I need nothing.' You do not know that you are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked. I advise you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so that you may become rich, and white garments, so that you may be clothed and the shame of your nakedness may not appear, and to anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see." Let us take these words as spoken to us, reader. Let these be the eye-salve of the page; let us seek here the gold and garments suited to our calling, our poverty and our meditation, and let us be invited by these words to the palace of our King, so that with the eyes of devout faith we may contemplate his immense riches, that we may know what is the hope of his calling, what the wealth of the inheritance acquired through Christ for the people of God, and how excellent is the greatness of the power of God in us who believe, so that, rooted in love, we may be able to grasp the breadth, length, depth and height of such great riches. The divine riches adapt themselves equally to all; they humble themselves before those who have small hands and little ones, they regard their capacity, caring for what is fitting for us until we grow up in Christ. To those who have advanced in age and heavenly maturity, this admirable treasure appears, which, like men skilled in things and trained by experience, they distinguish the precious from the worthless. And indeed, the further you handle the riches of God, the further you will be moved by their majesty. To the wicked they are wicked, to the small they are small, to the great they are great, so that to those endowed with a lofty mind they are lofty. But they reject no age, no sex, no condition. Yet this treasure is not so common and open to all as the teaching of Christ, flowing abundantly from the sacred fountains. It shuts out no one at all, unless a man shuts himself out, envying himself. For we strongly condemn those who steal the treasure of Holy Scripture from the so-called simple folk, and who cry out that the heavenly riches are disfigured by rust, or eaten away by the moth of various interpretations, in order to lead us, drawn away and seduced from the house of our heavenly Father, down into the most foul, stinking and deadly sewers of human traditions. It is perhaps not altogether safe to touch the riches of kings, but Christ most earnestly desires that his own be made known. He willingly gives these to his own, and especially to those who most eagerly desire them. It is fitting that the candidates for theology should be among their number. But because the reason for setting out the treasure and for setting it out is different, it has come about that in the Church, which is the house of God, to which the whole enjoyment of it is granted, it does not appear arranged in one order only. Rather, according to the measure of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the holy household's stewards, the dispensers of divine riches, have assigned to themselves and to others the method of distributing them. Among these a faithful servant, a scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, who brings forth from the store of his heart things new and old, has laboured commendably: Master AUGUSTINE MARLORAT, most watchful minister of the Church of Rouen and unconquered martyr of Christ. His work, gathered from the sacred treasuries, then arranged into chests in a chest, published in various places through the zeal of Master GUILLAUME FEUGUEREI, companion and successor in pious labours, at last drawn together into the form of a handbook, and now enlarged and illustrated with many riches beyond all earlier editions, we offer to you. In it three heads occur, arranged in alphabetical order: Things, Doctrines and Phrases, with examples mixed in. Since these are explained more fully by the theologians, and since the use of them all is perceived from daily practice, there is no need to dwell at length on explaining them. Those things once collected from the Apocrypha we have rejected; in their place we have added many things that were omitted, especially those pertaining to theological terms, scattered throughout the whole volume from beginning to end. Some things we have corrected. All the examples, likewise the doctrines, and those passages which the opponents twist to confirm their errors, which had been indicated earlier, we have left in place, following the common Latin edition after Marlorat from beginning to end. To this last edition have been added: 1. A necessary comparison of almost all the passages cited by the Compiler with their sources. 2. Most of the names of men, cities and similar things that are worthy of note, with a brief description of each added. 3. Those things which were in this Treasury, with a few additions inserted, likewise explained. 4. The titles of proper and common names and of things have also been made fuller, and not a few other very useful items have been conveniently added. Some of these are enclosed in these little brackets [ ], others have been omitted but are indicated in the Index of Words. 5. Also very many definitions or descriptions, most welcome to students. 6. Many meanings of Hebrew and Greek words. You have, reader, the plan of our undertaking. Use and enjoy the treasure, prepared for your advantage in this new edition, relying on the mercy of Christ, whom we devoutly pray will be gracious to you. Calends of March, in the year 1593.

units.tr: ABARIM, Mount Nebo: [Num. 33:47, 48.] Moses is commanded to look from here upon the land of Canaan, Num. 27:12; Deut. 32:49; there Moses dies, Deut. 34:1, etc.

units.la: ABBA, vocabulum Syriacum, ter inuenitur in noúo Testamento, Marc. 14.36. Rom. 8.15. Gal. 4.6. & vbique explanandi gratia additur ὁ πατὴρ pater. Abba (Syriacè) patrem appellat Christus, Marc. 14.36. Abba Patrem Deum vocant fideles, Rom. 8.15. Gal. 4.6.
units.tr: ABBA, a Syriac word, found three times in the New Testament, Mark 14:36; Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6; and everywhere ὁ πατὴρ [the father] is added to explain it. Christ calls the Father Abba (in Syriac), Mark 14:36. The faithful call God Abba, Father, Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6.

units.la: ABDEMELECH, Eunuchus Æthiops orat pro liberatione Ieremiæ. Ier. 38.v.8.9. eam impetrat, v.10. procurat & præstat, v.11.12.13. liberatur à gladio Chaldæorum, 39.v.16.17. (i. Seruus Regis.)
units.tr: ABDEMELECH, an Ethiopian eunuch, prays for the release of Jeremiah. Jer. 38:8, 9. He obtains it, v. 10; he procures and secures it, vv. 11, 12, 13; he is freed from the sword of the Chaldeans, Jer. 39:16, 17. (that is, servant of the king.)

units.la: ABDENAGO, (i. Seruiens taceo.) appellatur Azarias, & instituitur in disciplina Chal. Dan. 1.7. mittitur in fornacé 3.21.
units.tr: ABDENAGO, (that is, serving, I keep silent.) He is called Azariah and trained in Chaldean learning, Dan. 1:7; he is cast into the furnace, Dan. 3:21.

units.tr: ABDIAS, (that is, servant of the Lord.) Steward of the house of Ahab, 1 Kings 18:3; his piety in fearing God and in hiding the prophets of God, vv. 3, 4, 13. Another, a Zebulunite, 1 Chr. 27:19; and a Levite, 2 Chr. 34:12.

units.la: ABDIAS Propheta: eius de Idumæorum excidio vaticinium, Abd. 1.1. [Alius Abdias, 1. Par. 27.19. & 2. Par. 34.12.] Abdiel, (i. Seruus Dei) 1. Par. 5.15.)

Sam.20.15. liberatur mulieris prudentis consilio,v.22.à copiis Ben-adad feritur. 1.Reg.15.20 2. Paral.16.4. vastatur a Thiglat-Phulassar,2.Reg.15.29.[Abel-Main oppidū Nephthali,2. Chr. 16.4. Abel-mehula, locus in tribu Ephraim, Iudic.7.22.1.Reg.4 12.&19.16.
units.tr: ABEL, otherwise ABEL-MAIM or ABELA (that is, mourning, a name perhaps taken from that slaughter by which the Ammonites were afflicted, Judg. 11:33), a city of the Manassites, besieged by Joab, 2 Sam. 20:15; freed by the counsel of a wise woman, v. 22; struck by the forces of Ben-hadad, 1 Kings 15:20; 2 Chr. 16:4; laid waste by Tiglath-pileser, 2 Kings 15:29. [Abel-maim, a town of Naphtali, 2 Chr. 16:4. Abel-meholah, a place in the tribe of Ephraim, Judg. 7:22; 1 Kings 4:12 and 19:16.]

units.tr: ABIJAH or ABIAM, son of Rehoboam, set up as king over Judah, 1 Kings 14:31; 15:1, 2; 2 Chr. 12:16. Trusting in the Lord and in prayer, he strikes Israel, 2 Chr. 13:14, 15, etc. He dies, 1 Kings 15:8; 2 Chr. 14:1. He left Asa as successor to the kingdom, ib.; Matt. 1:7. (Abia, that is, my father is the Lord.)

units.la: ABIATHAR (i.pater excellens)Sacerdos,ad Dauidem fugit, 1.Sam.22.20.est in Ceila cum Dauide, 23.6. sequitur Adoniam regnum occupare conantem,1. Reg.1.7. ideò priuatur sacerdotio,2.27.iuxta illud,1.Sam.2.v.30.32.
units.tr: ABIATHAR (that is, excellent father), priest, fled to David, 1 Sam. 22:20; was in Keilah with David, 23:6; followed Adonijah, who was trying to seize the kingdom, 1 Kings 1:7; therefore deprived of the priesthood, 1 Kings 2:27, in accordance with that saying, 1 Sam. 2:30, 32.

units.la: ABIATHAR Summus sacerdos, Marc.2.26.qui & Abimelec, 1.Sam.21.8.dat panes propositionis Dauidi fugienti,v.6.
units.tr: ABIATHAR, high priest, Mark 2:26; who is also called Abimelech, 1 Sam. 21:8; he gave the showbread to David as he fled, v. 6.

units.la: ABIB. Vide MENSIS.
units.tr: ABIB. See MONTH.

units.la: ABIDAM(pater meus iudex)Princeps Tribus Beniamin,Nu. 1.11.&10.24.numerus exercitus eius.2.23.eius oblatio,Nu. 7.v.61.62.63. Ahiel(pater meus Deus)auus Saulis,1.Sam.9. 1.&14.51 Heros,1.Par.11.32. Abiezer, Heros, 2. Sam.23.27. Manassis nepos,1.Par.7.18.(Patris mei auxilium.)
units.tr: ABIDAM (my father is judge), prince of the tribe of Benjamin, Num. 1:11; 10:24; the number of his army, Num. 2:23; his offering, Num. 7:61, 62, 63. Ahiel (my father is God), grandfather of Saul, 1 Sam. 9:1; 14:51. A hero, 1 Chr. 11:32. Abiezer, a hero, 2 Sam. 23:27; grandson of Manasseh, 1 Chr. 7:18. (help of my father.)

units.la: ABIGAIL, (i.Patris mei exultatio)vxor Nabal,prudentissima & speciosa,1.Sam.25.3.Dauidem placat,v 35.post mortem Nabal Dauidi nubit,v.42.captiua abducitur ab Amalecitis,30.5.[à Dauide liberatur,ib.18.] [ABI-
units.tr: ABIGAIL (that is, exultation of my father), wife of Nabal, very prudent and beautiful, 1 Sam. 25:3; she appeases David, v. 35; after Nabal's death she marries David, v. 42; carried off captive by the Amalekites, 1 Sam. 30:5; [freed by David, ib. 18.] [ABI-

units.la: [ABIGAIL, neptis Dauidis ex fratre, 2. Chr. 11.18. alij matrem Dauidis fuisse existimant, 1. Chron. 2. 6. 17. alij sororem 2. Sam. 17.25.
units.tr: [ABIGAIL, niece of David through his brother, 2 Chr. 11:18. Others think she was David's mother, 1 Chr. 2:6, 17; others that she was his sister, 2 Sam. 17:25.]

units.la: ABIHAIL, eā duxit vxorē Roboam, 2. Par. 11.18. eius filij v. 19.
units.tr: ABIHAIL, Rehoboam married her, 2 Chr. 11:18; her sons, v. 19.

units.la: ABIHAIL, pater Estherae, Esth. 2.15. & 9.29.
units.tr: ABIHAIL, father of Esther, Esth. 2:15; 9:29.

units.la: ABIHV & Nadab, Filij Aaron, igne absumuntur, Leui. 10.2. Num. 3.4. (pater ipse, siue pater meus est.)
units.tr: ABIHU and Nadab, sons of Aaron, consumed by fire, Lev. 10:2; Num. 3:4. (Father himself, or my father is he.)

units.la: ABILENE, regiuncula inter Libanum & Antilibanum, cui Lysanias præerat. Luc. 3.1.
units.tr: ABILENE, a small region between Lebanon and Antilebanon, over which Lysanias was ruler. Luke 3:1.

units.la: ABIMELECH, 1. pater meus rex, Regum Gerar nomen, Gen. 20.2. & 26.8. Aufert Abrahæ Saram, Gen. 20.2. init pactum cum Abrahamo, 21.23. cum Isaaco 26.31.
units.tr: ABIMELECH, 1. (my father is king), a name of the kings of Gerar, Gen. 20:2; 26:8. He takes Sarah from Abraham, Gen. 20:2; makes a covenant with Abraham, Gen. 21:23; and with Isaac, Gen. 26:31.

units.la: ABIMELECH, filius Gedeonis, Iudic. 8.31. fratribus suis septuaginta occisis, regnat super Israelem, Iudic. 9. v. 5. 6. Sichimitæ ab eo deficiunt, v. 23. Gaal exercitum fugat, v. 40. Sichē omnino cuertit, v. 45. à fœmina læsus, vt ipsum confodiat armigero iubet, v. 53. 54. 2. Sam. 11.21.
units.tr: ABIMELECH, son of Gideon, Judg. 8:31. After his seventy brothers were slain, he reigns over Israel, Judg. 9:5, 6. The Shechemites revolt from him, v. 23; he puts Gaal's army to flight, v. 40; he utterly overthrows Shechem, v. 45; injured by a woman, he orders his armour-bearer to run him through, vv. 53, 54; 2 Sam. 11:21.

units.la: [ABIMELECH, rex Philist. nomine Achis, Dauidis tempore, Psal. 34.1.]
units.tr: [ABIMELECH, king of the Philistines, named Achish, in David's time, Psalm 34:1.]

units.la: ABINADAB, ab eius ædibus Arca fœderis transfertur, 2. Sam. 6.3. [Filius Isai, frater Dauidis, 1. Sam. 16.8. & 17.13. Saulis F. 1. Sam. 31.2.1. Chr. 9.39.]. i. pater magnificus.
units.tr: ABINADAB, from whose house the ark of the covenant was carried, 2 Sam. 6:3. [Son of Jesse, brother of David, 1 Sam. 16:8; 17:13. Son of Saul, 1 Sam. 31:2; 1 Chr. 9:39.] i.e. my father is noble.

units.la: ABINOHAM (patris mei decor) pater Baraki ducis exercitus populi Iudæorum. Iud. 4.6.
units.tr: ABINOAM (the beauty of my father), father of Barak, the commander of the army of the Jewish people, Judg. 4:6.

units.la: ABIRAM, primogenitus Hiel, 1. Reg. 16.34. (pater meus excelsus.)
units.tr: ABIRAM, firstborn of Hiel, 1 Kings 16:34. (my father is exalted.)

units.la: ABIRE, Abire in voluntatibus suis, pro, sequi consilia sua, Ier. 7.24. Abire in viam gentium, pro, ad exteras & profanas gentes, Ier. 2.18. Matt. 10.5. Nam alioqui vias gentium vocant Prophetæ, profanos & impios illarum mores, Ier. 10. 2. Abire in viam Cain, Iudæ, v. 11. [Abire in suum locum. i. æternum perire, Act. 1.25.] Abire per viam vniuersæ carnis, pro mori. Vide INGREDI viam vniuersæ carnis.
units.tr: ABIRE: to go in one's own wills, that is, to follow one's own counsels, Jer. 7:24. To go in the way of the nations, that is, to foreign and profane nations, Jer. 2:18; Matt. 10:5. For otherwise the prophets call the ways of the nations the profane and impious customs of those peoples, Jer. 10:2. To go in the way of Cain, Jude 11. [To go to one's own place, that is, to perish eternally, Acts 1:25.] To go the way of all flesh, that is, to die. See INGREDI viam vniuersæ carnis.

units.la: [ABIRE, Recedere à Deo, 1. Reg. 9.6. & 16.31. 2. Chr. 7.19. Abire post carnem alienam.]
units.tr: [ABIRE: to depart from God, 1 Kings 9:6; 16:31; 2 Chr. 7:19. To go after strange flesh.]

units.la: ABIRON, socius Core & Dathan, insurgit in Mosen, Nu. 16. v. 1. a terra absorbetur. v. 31.32. & 26.10. Deu. 11.6. Ps. 106.17.
units.tr: ABIRAM, companion of Korah and Dathan, rises up against Moses, Num. 16:1; is swallowed up by the earth, vv. 31, 32; Num. 26:10; Deut. 11:6; Ps. 106:17.

units.la: ABISAG, Sunamitis puella, Dauidi senì datur, 1. Reg. 1. v. 3.4. petitur ab Adonia in vxorem, 2.17. (i. pater meus errans.)
units.tr: ABISHAG, a Shunammite girl, given to the aged David, 1 Kings 1:3, 4; sought in marriage by Adonijah, 1 Kings 2:17. (that is, my father is wandering.)

units.la: ABISAI, filius Saruiæ, 2. Sam. 2.18. & 16.9. & 19.21. & 20.6. & 23.18. Dauidem comitatur, 1. Sam. 26.6. Sebam persequitur, 2. Sam 20.6. inter fortes Dauidis censetur, 23.18. (i. patris mei oblatio.
units.tr: ABISHAI, son of Zeruiah, 2 Sam. 2:18; 16:9; 19:21; 20:6; 23:18. He accompanies David, 1 Sam. 26:6; pursues Sheba, 2 Sam. 20:6; is counted among David's mighty men, 2 Sam. 23:18. (that is, my father's offering.)

units.la: ABIV, vide ABIHV.
units.tr: ABIV, see ABIHU.

units.la: ABIVD, filius Zorobabel, Matth.1.13. appellatur Anania, 1. Paral.3 19. (Patris robur.)
units.tr: ABIUD, son of Zerubbabel, Matt. 1.13. He is called Hananiah, 1 Chron. 3.19. (Strength of the father.)

units.la: ABLACTATIO: Ablactationis Isaaci die celebrat conuiuium Abraham, Gen.21.8.
units.tr: ABLACTATION: Abraham holds a feast on the day Isaac is weaned, Gen. 21.8.

units.la: [ABLVTIO peccatorum, Zach.13.1. Act.22.16. 1. Corint.6.11. Hebr.10.22.]
units.tr: [WASHING AWAY of sins, Zech. 13.1. Acts 22.16. 1 Cor. 6.11. Heb. 10.22.]

units.la: ABNEGATIO nostri est, cum nos totos Deo regendos permittimus, & omnem voluntatis nostrae sensum motum & cogitationem eius imperio subiicimus, vt in omnibus illi obsequamur libenter & promptè.
units.tr: SELF-DENIAL is when we allow ourselves to be wholly governed by God, and subject every feeling, movement and thought of our will to his command, so that we obey him in all things willingly and promptly.

units.la: ABNEGATIO nostri, seu mortificatio & viuificatio, siue sanctificatio, altera regenerationis pars, praecipitur, Matth. 16.24. Marc.8.34. Luc 9.23. & 14.26. Rom. 6.4.2. Cor.4.10. & 5.17. Gal.5.16. Eph.4.22. & 2.v.5.4.24. 4.v.1.1. Tit.2.12. Heb.4.10. & 12.16 1. Pet.1.22. & 2.v.5. & 24. & 4. v.1. 1.Ioh. 5.19. Abnegationis sui ipsius & bonorum seu facultatum exempla: Abraham, Genef.12.v.1.4. & 22.v.1.9. Hebr.11.8. Moses, Exodi 2.11. Actor.7.23. Hebr.11.24. Leui, Deuter.33.v.8.9. Ruth, Ruth 2.11. Elisaeus, 1.Reg.19.20. Amasias, 2.Paralip. 25.v.9.10. Apostoli, Matth. 4.v.20. & 19.27. Petrus & Andreas, Matth.4. verf.20. & 19.27. Marc.1.v.17.18. & 10.28. Luc. 5.11. Christi sectatores, Luc.14.26. & 18.22. Zachaeus, 19.8. Pij, Ioh.12.25.1. Corinth. 7.v.29.30.31. Paulus & Barnabas. Act.15.26. & 20.24. & 21.13. Prisca & Aquila, Rom. 16.4. Paulus, Gal.6.14. Dauid, 2. Sam.15.25.26.
units.tr: SELF-DENIAL, or mortification and vivification, or sanctification, the other part of regeneration, is commanded: Matt. 16.24; Mark 8.34; Luke 9.23 and 14.26; Rom. 6.4; 2 Cor. 4.10 and 5.17; Gal. 5.16; Eph. 4.22 and 2.5; 4.24; 4.1; Titus 2.12; Heb. 4.10 and 12.16; 1 Pet. 1.22; 2.5 and 2.24; 4.1; 1 John 5.19. Examples of denying oneself and one's goods or possessions: Abraham, Gen. 12.1, 4 and 22.1, 9; Heb. 11.8. Moses, Exod. 2.11; Acts 7.23; Heb. 11.24. Levi, Deut. 33.8, 9. Ruth, Ruth 2.11. Elisha, 1 Kings 19.20. Amaziah, 2 Chron. 25.9, 10. The apostles, Matt. 4.20 and 19.27. Peter and Andrew, Matt. 4.20 and 19.27; Mark 1.17, 18 and 10.28; Luke 5.11. The followers of Christ, Luke 14.26 and 18.22. Zacchaeus, 19.8. The godly, John 12.25; 1 Cor. 7.29, 30, 31. Paul and Barnabas, Acts 15.26; 20.24; 21.13. Priscilla and Aquila, Rom. 16.4. Paul, Gal. 6.14. David, 2 Sam. 15.25, 26.

units.la: ABNEGATIO veritatis destinata, est peccatum, cùm quis abnegat veritatem certò cognitam, nullo subito & inopinato metu victus & coactus, sed sponte, & consilio vel retinendae dignitatis & vitae causa, vel spe adipiscendorum honorum & diuitiarum. 1.Ioh.2.19.
units.tr: Deliberate DENIAL OF THE TRUTH is sin, when someone denies a truth he knows for certain, not overcome or compelled by any sudden and unexpected fear, but willingly and deliberately, either to keep his dignity and life, or in hope of gaining honours and riches. 1 John 2.19.

units.la: ABNEGATIO Christi quàm noxia, Mat.10.v.33. & 26.v.23.59. 70.Marc.8.38. Luc.9.26. & 12 9. Ioh.9.20. & 12.43. Act.3.17. & 5.v.20.40. & 9.3. & 15.38. & 27.11. Rom.6.7.v.cap.10. 2. Thess.1.5.2. Tim.2.12. & 3.12. Tit.1.16. Phil.v.13. Heb.10.28. 2.Petr.2.1. 1. Ioh.2.22. Iudae v. 4. Abnegationis Christi exempla. Petrus, Matt.26.v.70 72.74. Marc.14.v.68 69.71. Luc. 22.v.57.58.60. Ioh.18.v.17.25.27. Abnegatio gratiae Christi. Vide CHRISTVS.
units.tr: How harmful is the DENIAL OF CHRIST: Matt. 10.33; 26.23, 59, 70; Mark 8.38; Luke 9.26 and 12.9; John 9.20 and 12.43; Acts 3.17; 5.20, 40; 9.3; 15.38; 27.11; Rom. 6.7 and ch. 10; 2 Thess. 1.5; 2 Tim. 2.12 and 3.12; Titus 1.16; Phil. 3.13; Heb. 10.28; 2 Pet. 2.1; 1 John 2.22; Jude v. 4. Examples of denying Christ. Peter, Matt. 26.70, 72, 74; Mark 14.68, 69, 71; Luke 22.57, 58, 60; John 18.17, 25, 27. Denial of the grace of Christ: see CHRIST.

units.la: ABNER, princeps militiae Saulis 1.Sam.14.50. constituit Isboseth Regem in Israel, 2. Sam. 2. 8. admonitionem Domini sui proterue respuit, 3. 8. nuntios in Ebron ad Dauidé mittit. V. tit,v.12. hortatur Israelitas, vt relicto Isboseth, Dauidem suscipiant,v.17. interficit Asaelem fratrem Ioab,2.23. à Ioab dolo occiditur,3.27. sepelitur in Hebrò,v. 32.1. patris lapas.
units.tr: ABNER, commander of Saul's army, 1 Sam. 14.50. He sets up Ishbosheth as king over Israel, 2 Sam. 2.8. He stubbornly rejects the admonition of his lord, 3.8. He sends messengers to David in Hebron, v. 12. He urges the Israelites to abandon Ishbosheth and accept David, v. 17. He kills Asahel, brother of Joab, 2.23. He is killed by Joab's treachery, 3.27. He is buried in Hebron, v. 32. (Lamp of the father.)

units.la: ABOMINATIO: Abominatio desolationis in templo,Dan.9.v. 26.27.Matt.24.15 Marc.13.14. pro, abominanda desolatione. Hebraismus. Abominatio est coram Deo omnis idololatria, Deut.7.25.& 27.15. Abominationes gentium non imitandæ, Leuit.20.23. Abominationes gentium. Vide GENTES.
units.tr: ABOMINATION: The abomination of desolation in the temple, Dan. 9.26, 27; Matt. 24.15; Mark 13.14, put for "the abominable desolation." A Hebraism. Every idolatry is an abomination before God, Deut. 7.25 and 27.15. The abominations of the nations are not to be imitated, Lev. 20.23. The abominations of the nations: see NATIONS.

units.la: [Abominatio coram Deo dicuntur omnia impia,vt illusor, cor prauum,iniusta mensura,labium mendax, via iniquitatis, superbus, &c.tum apud Salomonem, ac passim alibi,praesertim apud Prophetas,qui diuersis verbis idola,falsam religionem,& idololatriam hoc nomine perstringunt. Abominatio Ammonitarum,1.idolum,1.Reg.11.5. & 2. Reg.23.13. Abominationes super aliquem proicere, i. eum reddere turpem,foetidum &c. Nahum.3.6. Abominationem facere,i.inducere nouos & impios cultus,1. Reg.14.24. Apoc. 21.27. Abominatio Antichristi. Apoc.17.4.5.]
units.tr: [Abomination before God is the term for all wicked things, such as a mocker, a perverse heart, a false measure, a lying lip, a way of iniquity, a proud man, etc., both in Solomon and passim elsewhere, especially in the Prophets, who by various words brand idols, false religion and idolatry with this name. Abomination of the Ammonites, 1 Kings 11.5, an idol; 2 Kings 23.13. To cast abominations upon someone, that is, to make him vile, foul, etc., Nahum 3.6. To do abomination, that is, to introduce new and impious worship, 1 Kings 14.24; Rev. 21.27. Abomination of the Antichrist, Rev. 17.4, 5.]

units.la: ABORTIVVS: Poena eius, cuius culpa mulier abortiuum facit,Exod.21.22.
units.tr: ABORTION: The penalty for the one whose fault causes a woman to miscarry, Exod. 21.22.

units.la: [ABSCONDITA Dei, Dan.2.22.Ps.27.5.& 31.24.&81.8.Mat.13. 35. Hominus,Ezech.8.12.Habac.3.14.Matth.6.4.6.18.Luc.11. 33.Rom.2 29.Tenebrarum, 1.Cor.4.5.]
units.tr: [HIDDEN THINGS OF GOD, Dan. 2.22; Ps. 27.5; 31.24; 81.8; Matt. 13.35. Of men, Ezek. 8.12; Hab. 3.14; Matt. 6.4, 6, 18; Luke 11.33; Rom. 2.29. Of darkness, 1 Cor. 4.5.]

units.la: ABRAM,(pater sublimis)filius Thare. Gen.11.26.ducit Sarai in vxorem,v.29.patria migrare iubetur,12.1. Act.7.3. descendit in Ægyptum propter famem.Gen.12.10. vir ditissimus est,13.2.& 24.35.altare Deo erigit,13.18.vincit quinque Reges,14.15.ab auaritia longè alienus est, v.23. quondam idololatra fuit,idolisque seruiuit,Ioh.24.2.fide iustificatus est, Gen.15.6.Rom.4.3. Gal.3.6.accipit signum foederis,appellatur Abraham,(Pater multitudinis.) & quare Gen.17.2.5.se & Ismaelem, & omnes domesticos circumcidit,v.23.promissionem seminis accepit, 15.4.&17.16. & 18.10. Angelos hospitio excipit,18.3.orat pro Sodomitis,v. 24.peregrinatur in Gerar, 20.1. Propheta est, v.7. amicus Dei est,2.Paral.20.7.Esa.41.8.Iac.2.23.haeres mundi dicitur,Rom.4.13. hoc est, Dominus, & quidem paternitatis iure omnium orbis populorum, quod certè non carnali, sed spirituali demum ratione fieri potest. Haeredem ergo esse mundi(nam hereditas Hebraeis dicitur etiam id,quod alicui gratis cedit in possessionem,ac nominatim quidem filij dicuntur haereditas,quę patri à Deo datur,Psal.127.3.) Hebraico more declarat, totum mundum habere pro filiis,& hac ratione quasi vniuerso mundo potiri.Sic dicitur Christus totius mundi hæres constitutus,in quo videlicet & ipsemet pater Abraham cũ toto mundo adoptatus benedicitur, Heb. 1.2. sic dicimur Dei hæredes correlatiue, Rom.8.17.quia iumus hereditas cũ Christo:cùm alioquin Græcis & Latinis,Alicuius esse hæredem,declaret, In alicuius bona post morte succedere. Vnde apparet, Ro.4.13. &aliis plurimis in locis hæredis vocabulũ nõ accipi,pprie.
units.tr: ABRAM (exalted father), son of Terah, Gen. 11.26. He takes Sarai as his wife, v. 29. He is commanded to leave his homeland, 12.1; Acts 7.3. He goes down into Egypt because of famine, Gen. 12.10. He is a very wealthy man, 13.2 and 24.35. He builds an altar to God, 13.18. He defeats five kings, 14.15. He is far removed from greed, v. 23. He was once an idolater and served idols, Josh. 24.2. He is justified by faith, Gen. 15.6; Rom. 4.3; Gal. 3.6. He receives the sign of the covenant and is called Abraham (father of a multitude), and why, Gen. 17.2, 5. He circumcises himself, Ishmael and all his household, v. 23. He receives the promise of a seed, 15.4; 17.16; 18.10. He receives angels into his hospitality, 18.3. He prays for the Sodomites, v. 24. He sojourns in Gerar, 20.1. He is a prophet, v. 7. He is a friend of God, 2 Chron. 20.7; Isa. 41.8; James 2.23. He is called heir of the world, Rom. 4.13; that is, the Lord, and indeed by the right of fatherhood, of all the peoples of the world, which certainly cannot happen by a carnal but only by a spiritual reckoning. So to be heir of the world (for among the Hebrews "inheritance" also means whatever is given freely into someone's possession; and sons are specifically called an inheritance, which is given to the father by God, Ps. 127.3) is, in Hebrew manner, to declare that he regards the whole world as his sons, and in this way to possess, as it were, the entire world. So Christ is called appointed heir of the whole world, in whom indeed the father Abraham himself is blessed together with the whole world, Heb. 1.2. So we are called God's heirs correlatively, Rom. 8.17, because we are heirs together with Christ; whereas in Greek and Latin "to be someone's heir" means to succeed to someone's goods after death. From this it is clear that in Rom. 4.13 and in many other places the word "heir" is not taken properly.

units.la: ABRAHAM seruus Dei dicitur, Deut.9. 27.Ps.105.6. nascitur ei Isaac ex Sara,Gen.21.2 eiicit Agar ancillam cum Ismaele filio,v.14.plantat nemus in Beersabe,v.33.tétatur à Deo 22.1 offert arietem in holocaustum loco filij, v.13. emit agrum à filiisHeth,in quo sepel t Saram,23.v.16.19.seruum mittit ad quærendam vxorem filio Isaac, 24.4. Ceturam ducit vxorem,& plurimos,ex ea suscipit liberos, 25. v.12. promissiones adeptus,Heb.6.15.moritur,Gen.25.8.sepelitur in duplici spelunca, v.9. Abrahæ cor fidele,Nehem.9.8.fides, Gen.12.4.& 15.6.Ioh.8.56. Act.7.4.Rom.4.18.Heb.11.8.16. vidit diem Christi, Ioh.8.56. eminus fidei oculis, Heb. 11.13. semen eius,non autem angelos assumsit Dei filius,Heb.2.16.de Abrahamo & semine eius,vide Iosuæ 24.3.Esa.41.8.&51.2.Ezec.33.24. Nehem.9.7.Matth.8.11.Act.7.2.&c. Heb.11.17. pater multarum gentium, & omnium credentium vocatur,Gen.17.5.Esa.51.2.Matt.3.9.Luc.19.9. Ioh.8.39. Rom.4.v.11.12.16 17.& 9.v.7.8. Gal.3.7.ex operibus iustificatus dicitur,& quomodo, Iac.2.21. hoc est,ex operibus compertus est fuisse iustificatus. Neque enim de causis,sed de effectis iustificationis eo loci agitur, ex quib. intelligi potuit,ipsũ fuisse iustificatũ. VideIVSTIFICARE.
units.tr: ABRAHAM is called the servant of God, Deut. 9.27; Ps. 105.6. Isaac is born to him of Sarah, Gen. 21.2. He casts out the maidservant Hagar with her son Ishmael, v. 14. He plants a grove at Beersheba, v. 33. He is tested by God, 22.1. He offers a ram as a burnt offering in place of his son, v. 13. He buys a field from the sons of Heth, in which he buries Sarah, 23.16, 19. He sends a servant to seek a wife for his son Isaac, 24.4. He takes Keturah as wife, and has many more; by her he has children, 25.12. He obtains the promises, Heb. 6.15. He dies, Gen. 25.8, and is buried in the double cave, v. 9. Abraham's faithful heart, Neh. 9.8. Faith, Gen. 12.4 and 15.6; John 8.56; Acts 7.4; Rom. 4.18; Heb. 11.8, 16. He saw the day of Christ, John 8.56, afar off with the eyes of faith, Heb. 11.13. The Son of God took on the seed of Abraham, not the angels, Heb. 2.16. On Abraham and his seed see Josh. 24.3; Isa. 41.8 and 51.2; Ezek. 33.24; Neh. 9.7; Matt. 8.11; Acts 7.2, etc.; Heb. 11.17. He is called the father of many nations and of all believers, Gen. 17.5; Isa. 51.2; Matt. 3.9; Luke 19.9; John 8.39; Rom. 4.11, 12, 16, 17 and 9.7, 8; Gal. 3.7. He is said to be justified by works, and how, James 2.21; that is, he was found by his works to have been justified. For the passage there deals not with the causes but with the effects of justification, by which it could be understood that he himself had been justified. See JUSTIFY.

units.la: ABRAHAE filij duplices,Matt.3.9.Luc.3.8. &9 9.Ioh.8.v.33. 37.39.Act.13 26.Rom.4.v.11 16.17.&9.7. Gal.3.v.7.29.hospitalitas,Gen.18.3.obedientia, Gen.12.4.&22.18.&26,5. Heb.11.8.pietas,Gen.12.v.7.8.&18 19. Abrahæ sinus, Luc. 16.22. Abraham emortuus dicitur viuente Sara, Rom.4.19. Heb.11,12. cum alioqui ea mortua plurimos filios generarit,Gen.25.v.1.2.sed sensus est: Abrahamum cum suscieperet filium promissionis Isaacum ex Sara,ita non tantum effœtum fuisse,sed etiam non magis ad generandum habilem,quàm si prorsus mortuus esset. Vestigiis fidei Abrahæ incedere, Rom.4 12.est credere sicut & Abraham credidit. Neque enim id de fructibus fidei,sed de ipsa fide acciaccipiendū est. Filij Abrahæ, qui censendi sint, Rom.4.12. & 9.8. Abraham nescit nos, Esa.63.16.
units.tr: The SONS OF ABRAHAM are of two kinds: Matt. 3.9; Luke 3.8 and 9.9; John 8.33, 37, 39; Acts 13.26; Rom. 4.11, 16, 17 and 9.7; Gal. 3.7, 29. Hospitality, Gen. 18.3. Obedience, Gen. 12.4; 22.18; 26.5; Heb. 11.8. Piety, Gen. 12.7, 8 and 18, 19. The bosom of Abraham, Luke 16.22. Abraham is said to be dead while Sarah lived, Rom. 4.19; Heb. 11.12, although she had otherwise borne many sons, Gen. 25.1, 2. But the sense is this: when he received Isaac, the son of promise, born of Sarah, he was not only worn out but also no more fit for begetting than if he had been altogether dead. To walk in the footsteps of Abraham's faith, Rom. 4.12, is to believe as Abraham believed. For this is to be understood not of the fruits of faith but of faith itself. Which of Abraham's sons are to be reckoned as such, Rom. 4.12 and 9.8. Abraham does not know us, Isa. 63.16.

units.la: Absalom, i. Pater pacis, filius Dauidis, 2.Sam.3.3. iubet fratrem suum Ammon interfici propter stupratam sororem Thamar, 13.v.28.29. fugit, v.34. Revocatur Ioab & mulieris Thecuitidis revocatur, 14.23. erat pulcher & formosus, v.25. messem Ioab succendit, & quare, v.30. domum reuersus recipitur, & osculatur à patre, v.33. animos populi sibi conciliat, vt aduersus patrem insurgat, 15.v.6.10.12. ingreditur Ierusalem absente Dauide, v.37. abutitur concubinis patris sui, 16.22. de quercu pendens confoditur à Ioab, 18.v.14.15. in foueam proiicitur, v.17. lugetur à patre, v.33.
units.tr: Absalom, that is, father of peace, son of David, 2 Sam. 3.3. He orders his brother Amnon to be killed on account of the ravished sister Tamar, 13.28, 29. He flees, v. 34. Joab recalls him, and the Tekoite woman does too, 14.23. He was beautiful and handsome, v. 25. He sets fire to Joab's field, and why, v. 30. He returns home and is received, and his father kisses him, v. 33. He wins over the hearts of the people so as to rise up against his father, 15.6, 10, 12. He enters Jerusalem while David is away, v. 37. He defiles his father's concubines, 16.22. Hanging from an oak, he is stabbed by Joab, 18.14, 15. He is thrown into a pit, v. 17. He is mourned by his father, v. 33.

units.la: Abscessionis, vel repudij libellus, V. Libellus.
units.tr: Bill of separation or of divorce: see LIBELLUS.

units.la: [Absit, i. ne fiat, absit vt cogitemus vel dicamus, id fieri posse. Formula loquendi frequens in negando, & detestationis habens significationem, qua obiectionis consequens, tanquam blasphemum pij detestantur. Vide Gen.18.25. Iob. 34.10. Rom.3.4.6.31 & 6.2 & 7.7.13. & 9.14. & 11.1.11. 1.Cor. 6.15. Gal.2.17. & 3.21. Absit mihi gloriari nisi in cruce Christi, Galat.6.24.]
units.tr: [Far be it, that is, may it not happen: far be it that we should think or say that this can happen. A frequent form of speech in denying, having the sense of detestation, by which the godly abhor the consequence of an objection as blasphemous. See Gen. 18.25; Job 34.10; Rom. 3.4, 6; 6.2; 7.7, 13; 9.14; 11.1, 11; 1 Cor. 6.15; Gal. 2.17 and 3.21. "God forbid that I should glory except in the cross of Christ," Gal. 6.14.]

units.la: Absolvere, pro æquo animo ferre, & condonare iniurias; Luc.6.37. pro soluere simplici, 13.12.
units.tr: To absolve: to bear with an even mind and to forgive injuries, Luke 6.37; in the sense of simply paying a debt, Luke 13.12.

units.la: Absolvtvm veri Pastoris exemplar proponitur, 1.Tim.3.v. 1.2 &c. [epist. item 2.& 1.Thess.2.a.2.v.ad 13.& epist. ad Tit.]
units.tr: The perfect pattern of a true minister is set forth, 1 Tim. 3.1, 2, etc.; [likewise in the second epistle, in 1 Thess. 2 from v. 2 to v. 13, and in the epistle to Titus].

units.la: Abstemivs ne sit Timotheus hortatur Apostolus, 1. Tim. 5.23.
units.tr: The Apostle urges Timothy not to be too abstemious, 1 Tim. 5.23.

units.la: Abstinentia, ἐγκράτεια, est cibi, vel somni ordinarij substractio, ad Dei gloriam, & carnis nostræ mortificationem necessaria, & à nobis facta. Vel, est cohibitio gulæ, luxuriæ, cupiditatis, auaritiæ, ambitionisque, & superbiæ, 1.Pet.2. 11. precor, vt tanquam aduenæ ac peregrini, abstineatis à carnis cupiditatibus, quæ militant aduersus animam. Vide Rom.8.13. Ecclesiastic.37.32. Vide simile, & exemplum in Paulo, 1.Cor.9.25 26.27.
units.tr: Abstinence [ἐγκράτεια] is the withholding of ordinary food or sleep, necessary for the glory of God and the mortification of our flesh, and practised by us. Or it is the restraint of gluttony, lust, covetousness, avarice, ambition and pride: 1 Pet. 2.11, "I beg you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which war against the soul." See Rom. 8.13; Ecclus. 37.32. See a similar case and example in Paul, 1 Cor. 9.25, 26, 27.

units.la: Abstinentia, à quibusdam cibis, hisce testimoniis probatur. Gen.1.29. & 2.17. & 3.11. & 9.4. Exo.12.9. & 13.6. & 22.13. &29.34. Leu.6.23. & 7.18. &c.11.4. &c.19.7. & 22.28. & 23.14. Num.6.3. & 18.10. Deut.12.16. & 14 3 &c. Dan.1.8.12. Matt. 12.4. Marc.2.23. Luc.6.1. Actor. 15.9. Abstinentiæ ciborum exempla: Adam, Genes.2. vers.16.17. Moses, Exod.24.18. Manue vxor, Iudic. 13.4. Israelitæ, 20.26.1.Samuel.14.26. Dauid, 2. Sam. 16. Achab, 1. Regum 21.27. Rechabitæ, Ierem.35.v.6.14. Ezechiel,Ezec.4.9. Esdras,Esd. 8.21. Nehemias,Neh.1.4. Israelitæ,9.1. Daniel,Dan.1.8.& 9.3. Iosaph. 2.Paral.20.3. Esther,Esth.4.16. Iohannes Baptista, Matt.3.4.& 11.18. Anna Prophetissa filia Phanuel Luc.2.37. Iesus Christus,Matth.4.2. Luc.4.2. (Apostoli, Luc.10.7. & 24.42.Ioh.21.13.) Paulus & Barnabas.Actor.14.23. Abstinentia commendatur.Luc.1.15.Rom.13.14. Col.2.16.1. Thess.5.6. 1.Tim.3 2.2.Tim.4.5.Tit.1.8.& 2.v.2.3.5.& 1.Pet.5.8. Vide Ieivnii & sobrietatis exempla. Abstinentia a vino,Leuit.10.8.& 11.34 Num.6.3.Iudic.13.v.4.13.Ier.35.6. Ezech.44.21.Luc.1.15.Vide Vinum.
units.tr: Abstinence from certain foods is proved by these testimonies: Gen. 1.29; 2.17; 3.11; 9.4; Exod. 12.9; 13.6; 22.13; 29.34; Lev. 6.23; 7.18; etc.; 11.4; etc.; 19.7; 22.28; 23.14; Num. 6.3; 18.10; Deut. 12.16; 14.3 etc.; Dan. 1.8, 12; Matt. 12.4; Mark 2.23; Luke 6.1; Acts 15.9. Examples of abstinence from food: Adam, Gen. 2.16-17; Moses, Exod. 24.18; Manoah's wife, Judg. 13.4; the Israelites, Judg. 20.26; 1 Sam. 14.26; David, 2 Sam. 16; Ahab, 1 Kings 21.27; the Rechabites, Jer. 35.6, 14; Ezekiel, Ezek. 4.9; Ezra, Ezra 8.21; Nehemiah, Neh. 1.4; the Israelites, Neh. 9.1; Daniel, Dan. 1.8 and 9.3; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20.3; Esther, Esth. 4.16; John the Baptist, Matt. 3.4 and 11.18; Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, Luke 2.37; Jesus Christ, Matt. 4.2; Luke 4.2; (the apostles, Luke 10.7; 24.42; John 21.13); Paul and Barnabas, Acts 14.23. Abstinence is commended at Luke 1.15; Rom. 13.14; Col. 2.16; 1 Thess. 5.6; 1 Tim. 3.2; 2 Tim. 4.5; Titus 1.8 and 2.2-3, 5; 1 Pet. 5.8. See examples of fasting and sobriety. Abstinence from wine: Lev. 10.8 and 11.34; Num. 6.3; Judg. 13.4, 13; Jer. 35.6; Ezek. 44.21; Luke 1.15. See Wine.

units.la: ABSTINENDVM a cibo & potu etiam licito, propter scandalum alterius,Matth.6.16. Rom.14.21.1.Cor.8.13. Abstinentia praeceptum violare nolentium exempla: Rechabitæ, Ierem.35.6.
units.tr: To be abstained from food and drink, even lawful ones, for the sake of another's offence: Matt. 6.16; Rom. 14.21; 1 Cor. 8.13. Examples of those who refused to violate an abstinence commanded: the Rechabites, Jer. 35.6.

units.la: [ABSYNTHIVM herba, Prou.5.4. figuratè significat grauiss. calamitates, Ier.9.15.& 25.15. Thren.3.15.19. Iniustitiam Amos 5.7.& 6.12. Steliæ cognomen,Apoc.8.11.]
units.tr: ABSINTHE, an herb: Prov. 5.4; figuratively it signifies very grievous calamities, Jer. 9.15 and 25.15; Lam. 3.15, 19; injustice, Amos 5.7 and 6.12; a name of a star, Rev. 8.11.

units.la: ABVNDANTIA rerum omnium à Deo,Deut.8.18. Abundantia omnium bonorum Dei pactum seruantibus promittitur, Leuit. 26.v.3.4.Deut.8.v.1.2 4.Abundantia bonorum temporalium vitam homini minimè confert, Luc.12.20. [beneplacitum,Deut.33.23.Bonitas, Psal.145.7. Emolumentum,Prou.14.23.& 21.5.Sordes,Iac.1.21.Iuramentum, Gen.26.Prosperitas,Psal.30.7.& 122.6.7. Pro.1.33.Ierem.22.21.]
units.tr: ABUNDANCE of all things comes from God, Deut. 8.18. Abundance of all good things is promised by God to those who keep the covenant, Lev. 26.3-4; Deut. 8.1-2, 4. The abundance of temporal goods does little to give a man life, Luke 12.20. [Good pleasure, Deut. 33.23; goodness, Ps. 145.7; profit, Prov. 14.23 and 21.5; filth, James 1.21; oath, Gen. 26; prosperity, Ps. 30.7 and 122.6-7; Prov. 1.33; Jer. 22.21.]

units.la: ABVSVS Christianæ libertatis coercetur, Rom.14.3. &c.1. Cor.8.9.Nominis diuini,1.Sam 23.21.
units.tr: The use of Christian liberty is restrained, Rom. 14.3 etc.; 1 Cor. 8.9. Of the divine name, 1 Sam. 23.21.

units.la: ABVSVS vestium notatur,Esa.3.18.Ezec.7.20.Matt.11.8.Mar.12.38.Luc.7.25.& 16.19.& 20.45.1.Tim.2.9.1.Pet.3.3.
units.tr: The use of clothing is noted: Isa. 3.18; Ezek. 7.20; Matt. 11.8; Mark 12.38; Luke 7.25; 16.19; 20.45; 1 Tim. 2.9; 1 Pet. 3.3.

units.la: ABVSVS donorum Dei est,quando ad ignominiam Dei, vel non ad gloriā eius,referuntur:Matt.25.26. Serue male &c.
units.tr: The abuse of God's gifts occurs when they are referred to God's dishonour or not to his glory: Matt. 25.26, "Wicked servant" etc.

units.la: Abuti prosperitate:Solomon,1.Regum 4.21. Vide Dei donorum abusus,& Prosperitas.
units.tr: To abuse prosperity: Solomon, 1 Kings 4.21. See Abuses of God's gifts, and Prosperity.

units.la: [ABYSSVS, sumitur primò, pro aquarum terræ initio, nempe prima die creationis,supernatantium mole,Gen.1.2.Psal.104.6.Prou.8.24.27. Secundò,pro aquarum terram circumcingentium voragine, Gen.7.11. & 8.2.Iob.28.14.& 38.16.30.& 41.23.Psal.33.7.& 107.26.& 135.6.& 148.7.Ion.2.6. Tertiò,pro aquis dulcibus, fontibus, & riuis abundè fluentibus, Gen.49.25.Deu.8.7.&33.13.Psal.78.15.Pro.3.20. Quartò,pro aquis maris rubri, Ex.15.5.8.Psal.77.17.& 106.9.Esa.51.10.& 63.13. Quintò,pro rubri maris & Iordanis fluctib. Habac.3.10. Sextò xtò calamitates grauissimas denotat, Psal.42.8. & 71. 20. Ezech.26.19. Septimò, deiectionis & humiliationis infimum gradum, Rom.10.7. Octauò, Prosperitatem, Ezech.31.4. Nonò, Terrarum ingentem tractum, Amos 7.4. Decimò, Carcerem seu locum damnatorum, nempe Angelorum & hominum reproborum, Luc.8.31. Apoc.9.1.2.11.& 11.7.& 17.8.& 20.1.3. Carcer ille vero non est angustus, sed immensa quaedam profunditatis vorago ignis æterni.]
units.tr: ABYSS is taken first for the beginning of the waters of the earth, namely on the first day of creation, with the mass of the waters floating above: Gen. 1.2; Ps. 104.6; Prov. 8.24, 27. Second, for the chasm surrounding the waters of the earth: Gen. 7.11 and 8.2; Job 28.14; 38.16, 30; 41.23; Ps. 33.7; 107.26; 135.6; 148.7; Jonah 2.6. Third, for sweet waters, springs and streams flowing abundantly: Gen. 49.25; Deut. 8.7 and 33.13; Ps. 78.15; Prov. 3.20. Fourth, for the waters of the Red Sea: Exod. 15.5, 8; Ps. 77.17 and 106.9; Isa. 51.10 and 63.13. Fifth, for the waves of the Red Sea and the Jordan: Hab. 3.10. Sixth, it denotes the most grievous calamities: Ps. 42.8 and 71.20; Ezek. 26.19. Seventh, the lowest degree of dejection and humiliation: Rom. 10.7. Eighth, prosperity: Ezek. 31.4. Ninth, a vast tract of lands: Amos 7.4. Tenth, a prison or place of the damned, namely of the angels and reprobate men: Luke 8.31; Rev. 9.1-2, 11; 11.7; 17.8; 20.1, 3. That prison, however, is not narrow, but a certain immense chasm of the eternal fire.

units.la: ACADEMIA. Vide SCHOLAE. Academica ἀκαδημαϊκὴ προσαγορεύεται à Pontificiis, vt doctrinam ex verbo Dei scripto haustam incertam esse obtineant, ex 1. Cor.13.9.2.Pet.1.16.
units.tr: ACADEMY. See SCHOOLS. The term "academic" [ἀκαδημαϊκή] is applied by the Papists, so that they may maintain that doctrine drawn from the written Word of God is uncertain, from 1 Cor. 13.9; 2 Pet. 1.16.

units.la: ACARON vrbs Philistæorum, à filiis Iuda capitur, Iudi.1.18. Accaronitæ arcam Dei eiiciunt è finibus suis, 1. Sam. 5. 11. Accaronitæ adorarunt Beelzebub, seu dominum muscæ, 2.Reg.1.v.2.3.6.16.]
units.tr: ACCARON, a city of the Philistines, is captured by the sons of Judah, Judg. 1.18. The Accaronites expel the ark of God from their borders, 1 Sam. 5.11. The Accaronites worshipped Beelzebub, or the lord of the fly, 2 Kings 1.2-3, 6, 16.

units.la: ACCEPTIO PERSONARVM, προσωπολημψια, est earum qualitatum, siue verarum siue fictarum, & ad tempus quæsitarum, quæ nihil ad negotium conferunt, consideratio & æstimatio. Contrarium, ἀπροσωπολημψια, 1. Pet.1.17. v.1.Tim.5.21.
units.tr: ACCEPTANCE OF PERSONS [προσωπολημψία] is the consideration and estimation of those qualities, whether true or feigned and sought for the occasion, which contribute nothing to the matter in hand. The opposite is non-acceptance of persons [ἀπροσωπολημψία], 1 Pet. 1.17; 1 Tim. 5.21.

units.la: Acceptio personarum damnatur, Leuit.19.15.& 24.22. Deut.1.17.& 16.19. Psal.82.2. Proverb.18.5.& 24.23. & 28.21. Malach.2.9. Ioan.7.24. 1. Tim.5.21. Iac.2.1. discrepat à fide Christi, Iac.1.v.1.9. Acceptio personarum nulla est apud Deum. (Vide DEVS acceptor personarum non est. Vide persona. Acceptio munerum. Vide MVNVS.)
units.tr: Acceptance of persons is condemned: Lev. 19.15 and 24.22; Deut. 1.17 and 16.19; Ps. 82.2; Prov. 18.5, 24.23, 28.21; Mal. 2.9; John 7.24; 1 Tim. 5.21; James 2.1. It is inconsistent with the faith of Christ, James 1.1, 9. There is no acceptance of persons with God. (See GOD, not an acceptor of persons. See Person. Acceptance of gifts. See GIFT.)

units.la: Accedere ad Deum, & coram Deo, Exod.19.22.& 1.Sam.14.36. Ezech.43.19.& 44.15. Hebr.10.22.& 11.6. Accedere ad Christum in Iudæa versantem multi visi sunt, vt ex Euangelistis constat, nempe varij, hostes, amici, familiares, angeli, discipuli, pauperes, diuites morbis afflicti, corde contriti, Matt.4.3.11.& 5.1.& 8.5.19.25.& 9.14.18.20.28. &c. Accedere ad Christum glorificatum, 1.Petr.2.4. Accedere ad hominem quempiam, Genes.27.22. & passim in scriptura. Accedere ad mulierem, Leuitic.18.14.19.1. Cum ea congredi. Accedere ad mensam, ad altare Dei, &c.
units.tr: To approach God, and before God, Exod. 19.22; 1 Sam. 14.36; Ezek. 43.19 and 44.15; Heb. 10.22 and 11.6. Many are seen to approach Christ while he dwelt in Judea, as is clear from the Evangelists: various people, enemies, friends, family, angels, disciples, the poor, the rich afflicted with disease, the contrite in heart: Matt. 4.3, 11; 5.1; 8.5, 19, 25; 9.14, 18, 20, 28, etc. To approach Christ glorified, 1 Pet. 2.4. To approach some man, Gen. 27.22, and often in Scripture. To approach a woman, Lev. 18.14; 19.1: to have intercourse with her. To approach the table, the altar of God, etc.

units.la: Accessus Dei ad hom. Malach. 3.5.
units.tr: God's approach to man: Mal. 3.5.

units.la: Accessus ad patrem cœlest. Rom.5.2.Ephes.2.12.16. & 3.12.]
units.tr: Approach to the heavenly Father: Rom. 5.2; Eph. 2.12, 16; 3.12.

units.la: ACCESSVS: Accessus ad Deum per Christum. Vide CHRISTVS Mediator.
units.tr: APPROACH: Approach to God through Christ. See CHRIST the Mediator.

units.la: ACCIPITER, avis immunda, Levit. 11. 16. Deuter. 14. Dei sapientiâ volat, Iob. 39. 16. sc. Struthio camelus 4.
units.tr: HAWK, an unclean bird: Lev. 11.16; Deut. 14. It flies by the wisdom of God, Job 39.26, i.e. the ostrich, camel, etc.

units.la: ACCVBITVS primi notantur, Luc.14.8. Accumbere cum Abrahamo in regno cœlorum, Matth.8.11. est, eiusdem Abrahamo æternæ felicitatis fore participem: Metaphorâ à conuiuiis sumta, quibus sæpe solet vitæ æternæ felicitas comparari.
units.tr: The first places at a feast are noted, Luke 14.8. To recline with Abraham in the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 8.11, means to be a sharer in the eternal blessedness of Abraham himself. The metaphor is taken from banquets, to which eternal life's happiness is often compared.

units.la: ACCVSATIO: Accusatio aduersus Presbyterum quomodo ... mittenda, 1. Tim 5.19.
units.tr: ACCUSATION: How an accusation against an elder is to be received, 1 Tim. 5.19.

units.la: ACCVSATIO falsa. Vide CALVMNIA. Falsò accusatorum exempla: Ioseph, Genef. 39. 14. Achimelech, 1. Sam. 22. 9. Miphibosheth, 2. Sam. 16. 3. & 19. 26. Naboth, 1. Reg. 21. 6. Amos mos 7. 10. Christus, Mat. 26. 61. Marc. 14 58. & 15. 7. Luc. 23. Stephanus protomartyr, Act. 6. 11. Paulus & Silas, 16. Iason, 17. 7. Paulus, 18. 13. & 21. v. 21. 28. & 24. 5. & 25. 7. Accusationis falsæ poena: Exempla: Aman. Esth. 7. 10. & 8. 7. Senes, Dan. 13 6. accusatores Danielis. Dan. 6. 23. & 14. Alcimus cum iniquis, 1. Machab. 7. v. 5. 6. Simon, 2. Machab. v. 5. 6 (Accusator fratrum, Apoc. 12. 10. Accusatores, Act. 23. 30. 35 & 24. 8. & 25. 16 18.)
units.tr: FALSE ACCUSATION. See SLANDER. Examples of those falsely accused: Joseph, Gen. 39.14; Ahimelech, 1 Sam. 22.9; Mephibosheth, 2 Sam. 16.3 and 19.26; Naboth, 1 Kings 21.6; Amos, Amos 7.10; Christ, Matt. 26.61; Mark 14.58 and 15.7; Luke 23; Stephen the first martyr, Acts 6.11; Paul and Silas, Acts 16; Jason, Acts 17.7; Paul, Acts 18.13, 21.28 and 24.5, 25.7. The penalty for false accusation: examples: Haman, Esth. 7.10 and 8.7; the elders, Dan. 13.6; the accusers of Daniel, Dan. 6.23 and 14; Alcimus with the wicked, 1 Macc. 7.5-6; Simon, 2 Macc. 5.5-6. (The accuser of the brethren, Rev. 12.10; accusers, Acts 23.30, 35; 24.8; 25.16, 18.)

units.la: ACEDIA est, pigritia & inertia, & fatigatio animi, qua quasi bonum inchoatum fastidit.
units.tr: ACEDIA is idleness, sloth and weariness of mind, by which a man disdains a good thing he has begun, as if it were tiresome.

units.la: ACEDIA mala est, 2. Sam. 11. 1. &c. Prou. 6. 6. & 10. v. 4. 26. & 11. & 13. 4. & 18. 8. & 19. 15. &c. 20. 4. &c. 21. 25. & 24. 30. & 13. & 28 19. Ezech. 16. 49. Eccles. 33. 26. Roman. 12. 11. Acediæ exempla, Vide NEGLIGENTIAE exempla.
units.tr: ACEDIA is an evil: 2 Sam. 11.1, etc.; Prov. 6.6; 10.4, 26; 11.13; 13.4; 18.8; 19.15, etc.; 20.4, etc.; 21.25; 24.30; 13 and 28.19; Ezek. 16.49; Ecclus. 33.26; Rom. 12.11. Examples of acedia: see Examples of NEGLIGENCE.

units.la: ACETVM: Acetum Christo sitienti in cruce offertur. Matth. 27. 48. Marc. 15. 36. Luc. 23. 38. Ioan. 19. 29. Psal. 69 22.
units.tr: VINEGAR: Vinegar is offered to Christ while thirsting on the cross, Matt. 27.48; Mark 15.36; Luke 23.36; John 19.29; Ps. 69.22.

units.la: ACHAB, (frater patris) filius Amri, Rex super Israël constituitur, 1. Regum 16. 29. idololatra fit, v. 31. vincit Syros, 2. v. 20. 29. init, fœdus cum Benadad contra Dei mandatum v 34. petit vineam Naboth, 21. 2. eam occupat, Naboth eius mandato occisus, v. 16. valde impius est, v. 25. Pseudoprophetas consulit, 22. v. 5. 6. 2. Paral. 18, 5. odit Micheam verû Dei Prophetam, 1. Reg. 22. 8. 2. Paral. 18. 7. vulneratur in prælio moritur, 1. Reg. 22. v. 35. 40. 2. Paral. 18. 34. sanguis eius canes lâbunt, 1. Reg. 22. v. 38. filij eius occidûtur. 2. Reg. 10. 7. iuxta illud, 1. Reg. 21. 21. 2. Reg. 9. 7. domus eius malorum dicta, 1. Reg. 21. 22. deleta per Iehu, 2. Reg. 10. v. 11. 17.
units.tr: AHAB, (brother of his father) son of Omri, is established as king over Israel, 1 Kings 16.29. He becomes an idolater, v. 31. He conquers the Syrians, 1 Kings 20.29. He makes a covenant with Ben-hadad against God's command, v. 34. He seeks Naboth's vineyard, 1 Kings 21.2; he seizes it; Naboth is killed on his command, v. 16. He is very wicked, v. 25. He consults false prophets, 1 Kings 22.5-6; 2 Chron. 18.5. He hates Micaiah, the true prophet of God, 1 Kings 22.8; 2 Chron. 18.7. He is wounded in battle and dies, 1 Kings 22.35, 40; 2 Chron. 18.34. His blood is licked by dogs, 1 Kings 22.38. His sons are killed, 2 Kings 10.7, according to that saying, 1 Kings 21.21; 2 Kings 9.7. His house is called evil, 1 Kings 21.22, and is destroyed by Jehu, 2 Kings 10.11, 17.

units.la: ACHAR, filius Colaiæ, Ierem. 29. 21. fuit tostus à Rege B
units.tr: ACHAR, son of Kolaiah, Jer. 29.21, was roasted by the king of Babylon, and therefore a formula of cursing exists, v. 22.

units.la: lonio,& ob id maledicendi formula est,v.22.

units.tr: Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigns over Judah, 2 Kings 15; 2 Chron. 27; Isa. 7; Matt. 1. He is called Eliezer, uc. 3.29. He becomes an idolater and makes his sons pass through the fire, 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Chron. 28:3. He seeks help from the Assyrians, v. 16. He builds altars in Jerusalem, v. 24. He rejects the sign offered him, Isa. 7:12. He dies, 2 Kings 16:20; 2 Chron. 28:27. His son Hezekiah succeeds him, ibid.; Matt. 1:10.

units.tr: Adam is created by God, Gen. 1:27, and placed in Paradise. He gives names to the other living creatures, v. 20. He breaks the command of God, 3:6; Hos. 6:7. He transfers the blame to his wife, Gen. 3:12. He was not seduced, but the woman was seduced, 1 Tim. 2:14; that is, she was seduced immediately by the Devil, but mediately through the serpent. He is cast out of Paradise, Gen. 3:23, 24. His age and death: the death of Adam is a type of Christ, and how, Rom. 5:14; 1 Cor. 15:49. See MAN. The comparison of Adam and Christ, Rom. 5:14; 1 Cor. 15:21, 22, 45. Two Adams are set forth, and the latter (that is, Christ) is called the type and example of the former (Rom. 5:14 and 1 Cor. 15:21, etc.). The Apostle pursues the comparison at length in both cases, not as if both were proposed on equal terms, but because of the power inherent in each, which is in some measure present in both: in the former indeed, destruction propagated to his posterity; in the latter, that is Christ, justification to his own. Adam, the last, is Christ, 1 Cor. 15:45. Adam, a name meaning man, Gen. 11:5; John 14:15; 2 Sam. 7:19; Eccl. 3:21; Jer. 20; Hos. 6:7; Zech. 13:7. Adam, a city, John 3:16.

units.tr: Admah, a royal city, one of the five cities of Sodom, Gen. 14:2. It was overthrown with Sodom and Gomorrah, Deut. 29:23. It is set forth as an example of the wrath of God, Hos. 11:8 (earthly or terrestrial).

units.la: ADIURARE, est cũ obtestatione diuini nominis, aliquem ad aliquid inducere. Alij sic: Adiurare, est interposito iureiurando, & Dei auctoritate præcipere, vt intelligas te coram Deo consistere, & velut à Deo ipso rogari. Græcis tamen scriptoribus significat iureiurando aliquem adstringere. Ac etiam à Theologis accipi consueuit, pro eo quod conjurare dicunt, id est, per Dei nomen adhibitum præcipere. Vnde & Exorcistæ in illis primis Ecclesiæ incunabulis sancti, qui miraculorum dono pollentes, inuocato Christi nomine Diabolos eiiiciebant. Vide EXORCISTAE. Adiurare ergo primò significat iusiurandum ab aliquo exigere, vt ibi caueas, Marc.5.7. secundò imperare aliquid diuini nominis auctoritate interposita, Act.19.13.1.Thess. 5.27. quæ posterior significatio ex illa priore fluxit.
units.tr: To adjure is, with an invocation of the divine name, to induce someone to something. Others put it thus: to adjure is, by interposing an oath and by the authority of God, to command, so that you understand that you stand before God and are, as it were, asked by God himself. Among Greek writers, however, it means to bind someone by oath. Theologians also customarily use it for what they call to conjure, that is, to command by the name of God invoked. Hence also the exorcists of those first holy beginnings of the Church, who, endowed with the gift of miracles, drove out devils by invoking the name of Christ. See EXORCISTS. So to adjure first means to demand an oath from someone, as at Mark 5.7; secondly, to command something by interposing the authority of the divine name, Acts 19.13; 1 Thess. 5.27; and this latter meaning flowed from the former.

units.la: ADIUTOR Deus sępissimè nominatur, præsertim in psalmis, Psal.10.18.19.27. &c. & quidem immediatè. Adiutor, homo sicitur, idque Dei adiutoris beneficio, tũ in Ecclesia tum in variis vitæ nostræ casibus, Iob. 26.2. & 29.12. & 31.35. Genef.2.20. Psalm.72.12. & 109.12. Rom.16.3.9.21.2. Cor.1. 4. & 8.23. Philip.1 24.3. & 4.3. Coloss.4.11. Philem.1.2. Adiutores Dei, 1. Cor. 3.9. Adiutor infirmitatum nostrarū Spiritus. Rom.8.26.
units.tr: God is very often named as helper, especially in the Psalms, Ps. 10.18, 19, 27, etc., and indeed directly. A man is called a helper, and that by the benefit of God the helper, both in the Church and in the various circumstances of our life: Job 26.2; 29.12; 31.35; Gen. 2.20; Ps. 72.12; 109.12; Rom. 16.3, 9, 21; 1 Cor. 1.4; 8.23; Phil. 1.24; 3.3; 4.3; Col. 4.11; Philem. 1.2. "Helpers of God," 1 Cor. 3.9. "The Spirit, the helper of our infirmities," Rom. 8.26.

Adolescentulae quales debeant, v.4.5.] ADONAI, unum ex nominibus Dei, id est, Dominus. ADONIAS, Dominus Dominator, Filius Dauidis regnu uadere nititur, 1.Reg. 1.5. fugit audiens Salomone vnct esse Regem, v.50. petit Abisag in vxorem, 2. 17. iussu Sa monis interficitur, v.25. [Adonias Lenita, 2.Chr.17.8.] ADONIBEZEC Chananaeorum rex, capitur, ac sumis manibus pedibus truncatur, Iudic. 1. 6. idem septuaginta Regibu fecisse fatetur, v.7. i. Domini fulgur. ) [ADONICAM. Eldr. 2.13. & 8.13. ADONIRAM, Dominus excelsus. 1.Reg.4.6. & 5.14. ADONIS, Ezech.8.14.] ADOPT
units.tr: [ADMONITION, fraternal, Νουθεσία (nouthesia), is a reproof of someone with words, given face to face, out of our pious and Christian affection towards our neighbour, for the glory of God and the good of the neighbour. It is necessary: 2 Pet. 1.13. Free people are to be admonished: Eph. 4; Col. 3.16. The disorderly, 1 Thess. 5.14. Those disobedient to the word, 2 Thess. 3.15. We are admonished by the examples of judgments, 1 Cor. 10.11. Admonishers are to be highly esteemed: 1 Thess. 5.12. Whoever admonishes, Col. 1.28. The Corinthians, 1 Cor. 4; the Ephesian elders, Acts 20.28, etc. See CORRECTION. ADOLESCENT. See Ps. 119.9; Eccles. 12; 11.1. Reverence of the young towards elders, 1 Pet. 5.5; they are also stirred up towards the heart of the world, 1 John 2.14–15. Duties of young women and of young men, Titus 2.4–6. What young women ought to be like, vv. 4–5.] ADONAI, one of the names of God, that is, Lord. ADONIAH, "Lord and ruler," son of David, strives to seize the kingdom, 1 Kings 1.5; flees on hearing that Solomon has been anointed king, v. 50; asks for Abishag as a wife, 2.17; is put to death at Solomon's command, v. 25. [Adonijah the Levite, 2 Chron. 17.8.] ADONIBEZEK, king of the Canaanites, is captured and has his thumbs and big toes cut off, Judg. 1.6; he confesses that he had done the same to seventy kings, v. 7. (That is, "the lightning of the Lord.") [ADONICAM, Ezra 2.13; 8.13. ADONIRAM, "exalted Lord," 1 Kings 4.6; 5.14. ADONIS, Ezek. 8.14.]
