units.tr: FLESH, in the Hebrew manner: I. for the whole man, Gen. 6.3, by synecdoche. II. for all and the whole of the human race, Ps. 78.39; Isa. 40.6; Joel 2.28; Matt. 24.22; Luke 3.6; John 1.14; 17.2; Acts 2.17; Rom. 3.20; 1 Cor. 1.29; Gal. 2.16, because by this word human weakness is signified; for this reason the name "flesh" is given also to horses, Isa. 31. III. for human nature, 1 Tim. 3.16. IV. for the human nature of Christ, John 6.51; Acts 2.30; Rom. 1.3; 1 Pet. 3.18; 4.1. Spirit is opposed to it as the divine nature, Rom. 1.3. V. for the gross and impure nature of man: that is, not the fleshly bulk of the body, but the nature of the soul and body of man, given over to sin and death, John 1.13; 3.6; Rom. 7.5; Eph. 2.3. This is everywhere opposed to Spirit in Scripture, especially John 3.6. That the word flesh is used in this way, to comprehend not only the body but also the nature of the human soul given over to sin and death, is clear even from the fact that Paul ascribes to the flesh a mind (φρόνημα), Rom. 8.7, and a mind (νοῦς), Col. 2.18. Flesh is also put for the carnal man, in the Hebrew manner, just as in Latin "crime" is said for "criminal." It designates the wretched condition of man, Ps. 56.5; 78.39, as said above. VI. for the part of man not regenerate, [Ezek. 11.19; 36.26; John 1.13; 3.6], Rom. 7.18; 8.3; Gal. 5.17, 19, 24; Col. 2.11; 2 Cor. 12.7; 1 John 2.16. VII. for the vice that reigns among men, 1 Pet. 4.6. VIII. for the disposition or inclination of nature, Eph. 2.3. IX. for corrupt men, Rom. 7.14. X. for the weakness of human nature, [Gen. 6.9; Ps. 78.39; Isa. 40.6; Jer. 17.5], 2 Cor. 10.2; 1 Pet. 1.24. XI. for the state of this present life, Phil. 1.24. XII. for the mortal body, 2 Cor. 7.1; Gal. 2.20. XIII. for the present life and all that pertains to it, 1 Cor. 7.28. XIV. for the outward appearance [or external form, John 8.15; Rom. 9.8; 2 Cor. 5.16; 11.18], Gal. 4.13. XV. for the ordinary course of nature, v. 29. XVI. for bodily life, Gal. 2.20; Heb. 5.7; 1 Pet. 4.2. XVII. for external ceremonies, Gal. 6.12, and external ceremonial works, to which spirit is opposed, Gal. 3.3. XVIII. for everything that is outside Christ, Phil. 3.3. XIX. for the bond of blood relationship, Rom. 9.3. Flesh is taken in a good sense in 2 Cor. 3.3; [for the male organ, Gen. 17.11, 13, 14; Rom. 2.28; Eph. 2.11; Col. 2.13]. XX. for that part of the animal body which is simple, soft, reddish, and encloses the fibres of the muscles, Gen. 2.21; 9.4; Exod. 4.7; Lev. 4.11; Num. 8.7; Deut. 12.15, 20; 3.27; Judg. 6.19, 20, 21; Ps. 50.13; 109.21; Luke 24.39. XXI. for kinship, Isa. 9.20; 58.7; Zech. 11.9. It is also taken for the skin, Ps. 102.6. It designates the Jews, Rom. 9.8; 1 Cor. 10.18. It is a type of our restoration, Ezek. 39.6, 8. It designates a horrible pollution, 2 Pet. 2.10; Jude 7, 8.

units.la: Caro & sanguis,in Nouo Testamento aliquoties totam humanam naturam σωμικὰ χωρὶς significant: eamque interdum ita vt est corrupta & infirma, Matthæi 16. 17.1. Cor. 15.50. vel simpliciter qualis est in sese, vt à spirituali videlicet & excellentiore natura distinguatur, Gal.1.16.Eph.6. Præterea nomine carnis (Rom.7.5. Eph.2.3.membrorum,Col.3.5.exterioris hominis,Rom.7.23.& alibi sæpe) intelligit Paulus,quicquid est in homine,vel intus vel foris, à capite ad calcem, quatenus quidem homo non est regeneratus: id quod vel ex eo liquet,quòd dicerte Apostolus inter corruptissimas partes mentem numerat,Rom.1.28.1.Tim.6.5.2.Tim.3.8. Tit.1.15.Item Eph. 4.23.vult renouationem ad spiritum usque mentis pertin tingere. Unde illud quoque liquet, quid vocabulum spiritus carni oppositum, seu interior ac nouus homo declarent. Cum carne & sanguine, Gal.1.16. pro, cum quoquam mortalium: ut Eph.6.12. Huc pertinent illæ phrases: Secundum carnem esse, Rom.8.8. de iis dicitur, qui cùm nondum sint Spiritu donati, sese cupiditatibus carnis immergunt. Viuere autem in carne, Phil.1.22. vel ambulare in carne, Cor.10.3. nihil aliud declarat, quàm in hoc caduco corpore vitam degere, tantisper dum cœlesti & æterna vita potiamur, ut Gal.2.20. 1.Pet.4.1. Carni seruere, Gal.6.8. pro iis istis & caducis bonis accumulandis opes impendere.
units.tr: Flesh and blood, in the New Testament, sometimes signify the whole human nature, [carnal, σωμικὰ χωρὶς]: sometimes as it is corrupt and weak, Matt. 16.17; 1 Cor. 15.50; or simply as it is in itself, that is, to be distinguished from the spiritual and more excellent nature, Gal. 1.16; Eph. 6.12. Moreover, under the name of flesh (Rom. 7.5; Eph. 2.3; members, Col. 3.5; the outward man, Rom. 7.23, and often elsewhere) Paul understands whatever is in man, whether within or without, from head to heel, insofar as man is not regenerate. This is clear from the fact that the Apostle expressly counts the mind among the most corrupt parts, Rom. 1.28; 1 Tim. 6.5; 2 Tim. 3.8; Titus 1.15. Likewise, Eph. 4.23 wills that renewal should reach even to the spirit of the mind. Hence it is also clear what the word spirit, opposed to flesh, or the inner and new man, signifies. "With flesh and blood," Gal. 1.16, means "with any mortal." Eph. 6.12 is similar. To these belong the phrases: "to be according to the flesh," Rom. 8.8, said of those who, not yet endowed with the Spirit, plunge themselves into the desires of the flesh. "To live in the flesh," Phil. 1.22, or "to walk in the flesh," 2 Cor. 10.3, declares nothing other than to live in this perishing body, for as long as we enjoy heavenly and eternal life, as in Gal. 2.20; 1 Pet. 4.1. "To serve the flesh," Gal. 6.8, means to spend one's resources on accumulating these fleeting and perishable goods.

units.la: In carne esse, Rom.7.5. & 8.8. significat prioris coniugij conditionem, quæ,7.v.6. vetustas literæ. Carnem igitur appellat hominem ψυχικόν[?], id est, qualis ex Adamo procreatur natura peccato omni ex parte penitus obnoxia, cui opponitur esse in spiritu, 8.9 Secundum carnem nasci, Gal.4.23.29. est consueto hominum more nasci. Damnatur carne, 1.Pet.4.6. dicitur is, in cuius carne damnatum est hoc est, abditum & extinctum est peccatum: quæ pars est sanctificationis, ut diserte loquitur Paulus, Rom.3. adeò ut locus ille Petri, non possit planius explicari quàm ex 1.Cor 5.5. vbi dicit Paulus: Ad interitum carnem suam crucifigere quomodo quisque debeat, Rom.6.12.&8.v.12.13.14. Gal.5.16. Ephes.4.22.&5.3. Tit.2. 1.Pet.2.1.&4.v.2.6. Heb.2.1. Vide SPIRITVS. caro sanguis, pro naturali homine, Matt.16.17. Galat.1.16. Eph.6.12. pro corpore hoc animali ita ut nunc est, 1. Corinth.15.50.
units.tr: "To be in the flesh," Rom. 7.5; 8.8, signifies the condition of the former marriage, which, Rom. 7.6, is the oldness of the letter. Therefore Paul calls man psychical [ψυχικόν], that is, such a nature as is born from Adam, wholly subject to sin in every respect, to which is opposed "to be in the Spirit," Rom. 8.9. "To be born according to the flesh," Gal. 4.23, 29, is to be born in the customary manner of men. "Condemned in the flesh," 1 Pet. 4.6, is said of one in whose flesh sin has been condemned, that is, hidden and extinguished; this is the part of sanctification, as Paul plainly says, Rom. 3. So that Peter's passage cannot be explained more plainly than from 1 Cor. 5.5, where Paul says that one must crucify his flesh to destruction, Rom. 6.12; 8.12, 13, 14; Gal. 5.16; Eph. 4.22; 5.3; Titus 2; 1 Pet. 2.1; 4.2, 6; Heb. 2.1. See SPIRIT. Flesh and blood, for the natural man, Matt. 16.17; Gal. 1.16; Eph. 6.12; for this animal body as it now is, 1 Cor. 15.50.

units.la: CARO una, vir & vxor, Gen.2.24. Matt.19.5. Mar.10.8.1.Cor.6.16. Eph.5.31. Hebraismus, hoc est, unum corpus. Caro non prodest quicquam, Ioan.6.63. Caro spiritui contraria, Rom.7.23. Galat.5.17. Caro cum sanguine non edenda, Gen.9.4. Leuit.19.26. Caro à bestiis laniata non comedenda Iudæis, Exodi 22.31. Carnis cura quatenus habenda, Rom.13.14. Carnis gloriatio vana, 1.Cor.1.29. Carnis infirmitas magna, Matth.26.41. Rom.8.7. Carnis & spiritus lucta, Rom.7.21. Carnis opera Galat.5.19.&c. Prudentia carnis damnatur, Rom.8.6. & 12.16. Carnis resurrectio (Vide RESVRRECTIO) Carnis sapientia damnatur, Pro.3.v.5.7.&14.7.&16.25, Rom.8.7. Iac.3.15. Carnis stimulus Paulo datus, 2. Cor.12.7. Carnes attatim pluunt popu- murmuranti, Num.11.18. ISLEV, mensis nomen, Nehem. I.1.
units.tr: FLESH: one flesh, husband and wife, Gen. 2.24; Matt. 19.5; Mark 10.8; 1 Cor. 6.16; Eph. 5.31. A Hebraism, that is, one body. The flesh profits nothing, John 6.63. The flesh is contrary to the spirit, Rom. 7.23; Gal. 5.17. Flesh with its blood is not to be eaten, Gen. 9.4; Lev. 19.26. Flesh torn by beasts is not to be eaten by the Jews, Exod. 22.31. How far the care of the flesh is to be taken, Rom. 13.14. The boasting of the flesh is vain, 1 Cor. 1.29. The weakness of the flesh is great, Matt. 26.41; Rom. 8.7. The struggle of the flesh and the spirit, Rom. 7.21. The works of the flesh, Gal. 5.19, etc. The prudence of the flesh is condemned, Rom. 8.6; 12.16. The resurrection of the flesh (see RESURRECTION). The wisdom of the flesh is condemned, Prov. 3.5, 7; 14.7; 16.25; Rom. 8.7; James 3.15. The thorn in the flesh given to Paul, 2 Cor. 12.7. Quails rain down on the murmuring people, Num. 11.18. CHISLEV, the name of a month, Neh. 1.1.

units.la: CASTITAS, est integritas tum animi, tum corporis nostri, & ab omni coitu illegitimo puritas: denique ab omni commixtione, quæ præter vel fidem à nobis datam, vel Dei præceptum fieret, integritas & conservatio.
units.tr: CHASTITY is integrity both of mind and of body, and purity from every illegitimate union: in short, the integrity and preservation of ourselves from every mixing that would be contrary either to a pledge given by us or to the command of God.

units.la: CASTITAS vera & Deo accepta commendatur, 1. Cor. 7. 1. Galat. 5. 22. 1. Thess. 5. 23. 1. Tim. 5. 22. Tit. 2. 2. Castitas spiritualis, 2. Cor. 11. v. 2. 3. 1. Pet. 1. 22. Castitas anuū, 1. Cor. 7. v. 4. 5. nuptarum, 1. Tim. 2. v. 9. 15. Vide MULIERUM castitas. Castitatis exempla: Abimelech, Gen. 26. 10. filij Iacob, Genes. 34. v. 7. 25. 26. 27. Ioseph. 39. v. 8. 9. 12. Iuda, qui etsi castus non esset, detestatus tamen est fornicationem Thamar, Genes. 38. 24. Moses, Num. 31. v. 17. 18. Booz, Ruth 3. v. 7. 8. Achimelech Sacerdos, 1. Sam. 21. 4. Iob, Iob 31. 1. Ioseph Mariæ Deiparæ vir, Matth. 1. 19. Deipara virgo Maria, Luc. 1. 34.
units.tr: True chastity, acceptable to God, is commended: 1 Cor. 7.1; Gal. 5.22; 1 Thess. 5.23; 1 Tim. 5.22; Titus 2.2. Spiritual chastity, 2 Cor. 11.2–3; 1 Pet. 1.22. The chastity of virgins, 1 Cor. 7.4–5; of married women, 1 Tim. 2.9, 15. See the chastity of women. Examples of chastity: Abimelech, Gen. 26.10; the sons of Jacob, Gen. 34.7, 25–27; Joseph, Gen. 39.8–9, 12; Judah, who, though not chaste himself, nevertheless abhorred the fornication of Tamar, Gen. 38.24; Moses, Num. 31.17–18; Boaz, Ruth 3.7–8; the priest Ahimelech, 1 Sam. 21.4; Job, Job 31.1; Joseph, the husband of Mary the Mother of God, Matt. 1.19; the virgin Mary, the Mother of God, Luke 1.34.

units.la: Castitatem cœlibum, ut perfectionem Euangelicam, consilii, his Scripturæ testimoniis afferunt Pontificij, Matth. 19. 12. 1. Corin. 7. 25. eamque præstare castitati coniugali. Matth. 19. 12. & 22. 30. 1. Cor. 7. v. 25. 32. 34. 38. Apoc. 14. 4. Castitatis laus, 1. Sam. 21. 5. Ps. 45. 15. Prov. 22. 11. Esai. 7. & 56. v. 3. 4. 5. Zach. 9. 17. 2. Machab. 14. 38. Matt. 5. v. 8. 48. Luc. 1. 27. 30. 34. Act. 24. 25. Rom. 2. 1. Cor. 7. 25. 2. Cor. 6. 5. & 11. 2. 1. Tim. 2. 2. & 3. 2. & 4. 12. & 2. Tit. 1. 8. & 2. 5. Apoc. 14. 4.
units.tr: The Papists cite these testimonies of Scripture for celibacy as an evangelical perfection, a matter of counsel, and claim that it surpasses conjugal chastity: Matt. 19.12; 1 Cor. 7.25. Praise of chastity: 1 Sam. 21.5; Ps. 45.15; Prov. 22.11; Isa. 7; 56.3–5; Zech. 9.17; 2 Macc. 14.38; Matt. 5.8, 48; Luke 1.27, 30, 34; Acts 24.25; Rom. 2; 1 Cor. 7.25; 2 Cor. 6.5; 11.2; 1 Tim. 2.2; 3.2; 4.12; Titus 1.8; 2.5; Rev. 14.4.

units.la: ASTOR, Act. 28. 11.
units.tr: CASTOR, Acts 28.11.

units.la: ABSTINERE se propter regnum Dei, Matt. 19. 12. est à contrario abstinere & continentiam seruare, ex dono Dei videlicet, ut Deo liberius seruiant ac si partibus illis careant, quibus sunt viri: Qualis est etiam amputatio manus, pedis, & exoculatio, Matt. 5. 29. & 18. v. 8. 9.
units.tr: To abstain oneself for the sake of the kingdom of God, Matt. 19.12, is, conversely, to abstain and keep continence, by God's gift, that is, so that they may serve God more freely, as if they lacked those parts by which they are men. Such is also the cutting off of a hand or foot and the plucking out of an eye, Matt. 5.29; 18.8–9.

units.la: CATENA. Catenæ duæ intra vincos, Exodi 28. 14. Catenæ pectorali impositæ, vers. 22. 24. Catenæ mittuntur à Ieremia ad varios Reges iussu Domini, Ier. 27. v. 3 4.
units.tr: CHAIN. Two chains within the settings, Exod. 28.14. Chains placed upon the breastpiece, v. 22, 24. Chains are sent by Jeremiah to various kings at the command of the Lord, Jer. 27.3–4.

units.la: CATHEDRA, thronus [1. Sam. 20. 25. 2. Sam. 23. 8. Ezech. 28. 39. & 23. 6. Cathedra, confessus, Ps. 1. 1. & 107. 32. Cathedra, doctrina Mosis, Matth. 23. 2. Cathedra, scamnum, sedile, Matt. 21. 12.]
units.tr: CHAIR: a throne [1 Sam. 20.25; 2 Sam. 23.8; Ezek. 28.39; 23.6]. Chair, assembly, Ps. 1.1; 107.32. Chair, the teaching of Moses, Matt. 23.2. Chair, a bench, seat, Matt. 21.12.

units.la: CATHOLICAS, id est, vniuersales Epistolæ dicuntur, 1. Pet. 1. Iac. 1. 1. Ioan. 1. quòd vni alicui vel homini, vel ciuitati, aut regioni non sint scriptæ.
units.tr: The Catholic Epistles are so called, that is, universal epistles: 1 Pet. 1; James 1.1; 1 John 1, because they were not written to any one person, or city, or region.

units.la: [CAVDA, pars nota quadrupedum. 2. metaphoricè sumitur pro ignobili, infirmo, vili, Deu. 28. v. 13. 44. Esai. 7. 4. & 9. 14. 15. & 19. 15. 3. pro formidabili potentia satellitum Antichristi, quorum (vt scorpionum, &c. caudæ mysticæ describuntur, Apoc. 9. v. 10. 19. 4. pro cauda stellæ mysticæ, Apoc. 12. 4.
units.tr: [TAIL, the well-known part of quadrupeds. (2) Used metaphorically for what is ignoble, weak, or base: Deut. 28.13, 44; Isa. 7.4; 9.14–15; 19.15. (3) For the formidable power of the satellites of Antichrist, whose tails are described as mystical, like those of scorpions, Rev. 9.10, 19. (4) For the tail of the mystical star, Rev. 12.4.]

units.la: CAVERNA in rupib. & in terra, 1. Sam. 14. 11. Esai. 2. 21. & 7. 19. 11 8. Ier. 16. 16. & 49. 16. Heb. 11. 38. Cauerna, i. Abraham & Sara; allegoricè dictum, Esai. 51. 1. Cauerna mystica, Cant. 2. 14.]
units.tr: CAVE, in rocks and in the earth, 1 Sam. 14.11; Isa. 2.21; 7.19; 8.8; Jer. 16.16; 49.16; Heb. 11.38. Cave, that is, Abraham and Sarah, said allegorically, Isa. 51.1. Mystical cave, Song 2.14.]

units.la: CAVSA, vt plurimum idem est ac controuersia, disceptatius, Exod. 22. 9. Num. 35. 12. Deut. 17. 8. Esa. 1. 23. & 10. 2. Ier. 28. Mich. 7. 9. Matt. 19. 10. 2. Petitio, Num. 27. 5. 3. Ratio, Rpartim & frequentissimè occurrit in Scripturis. 4. Sumitetiam pro culpa siue reatu, Luc. 23. v. 4. 14. 22. Ioh. 18. v. 38. 19. v 4. 6. Act. 13. 28. 18. &c.] Causa est quadruplex; Efficiens, à qua aliquid fit: Materialis, ex qua aliquid fit: Formalis, per quam aliquid tale fit: Finalis, cuius gratia aliquid fit. Vide Tit. Ul. Aitia, & Electionis causæ.
units.tr: CAUSE, for the most part the same as controversy or dispute, Exod. 22.9; Num. 35.12; Deut. 17.8; Isa. 1.23; 10.2; Jer. 28; Mic. 7.9; Matt. 19.10. (2) A petition, Num. 27.5. (3) A reason, which occurs very frequently in Scripture. (4) It is also taken for guilt or culpability, Luke 23.4, 14, 22; John 18.38; 19.4, 6; Acts 13.28; 18, etc.] A cause is fourfold: efficient, that by which something is made; material, that from which something is made; formal, through which something is made such; final, for the sake of which something is made. See the title "Aitia" [αἰτία], and the causes of election.

units.la: CAVTIO, pro obligationis instrumento, Luc. 16. 6.
units.tr: BOND, for the instrument of an obligation, Luke 16.6.

units.la: CEDAR: excidium eius prædicitur, Ier. 49. 28. Est autem regio, in eremo Sarracenorum, à Cedar filio secundo Ismaelis ita cognominata, 1. Chr. 1. 29. Gen. 25. 13. (Kedar tenebræ, tristitia.)
units.tr: KEDAR: its destruction is foretold, Jer. 49.28. It is a region in the desert of the Saracens, so named after Kedar, the second son of Ishmael, 1 Chron. 1.29; Gen. 25.13. (Kedar: darkness, sadness.)

units.la: CEDRI: eorum copia Ierosolymis, Salomonis seculo, 1. Reg. 10. 27. 2. Par. 9. 27.
units.tr: CEDARS: their abundance at Jerusalem in the age of Solomon, 1 Kings 10.27; 2 Chron. 9.27.

units.la: CEDRON, vallis & fluuius inter montem oliuarum & Hierosolymam: Illac transiit Christus mortem petens: Ioh. 18. & Dauid Absalonem fugiens, 2. Sam. 15. 23. Ibi Rex Asa combussit statuam Mahacæ: 1. Reg. 15. 13. Et Iosias vasa Baalis, 2. Reg. 23. 4.
units.tr: KIDRON, a valley and stream between the Mount of Olives and Jerusalem. Christ passed over it seeking death, John 18; and David fleeing Absalom, 2 Sam. 15.23. There King Asa burned the idol of Maachah, 1 Kings 15.13; and Josiah the vessels of Baal, 2 Kings 23.4.

units.la: CEILA, ciuitas in tribu Iuda, liberatur manu Dauidis à Philistæis, 1. Sam. 23. 5. Ceilanorum ingratitudo, v. 11. 12.
units.tr: KEILAH, a city in the tribe of Judah, delivered by David's hand from the Philistines, 1 Sam. 23.5. The ingratitude of the men of Keilah, v. 11–12.

units.la: CENSVS annuus Salomonis. 1. Reg. 10. 14. Census dandus Cæsari. Vide CAESAR, & TRIBVTVM.
units.tr: The annual tribute of Solomon, 1 Kings 10.14. Tribute to be given to Caesar. See CAESAR and TRIBUTE.

units.la: CENTVM, Numerus certus, Gen. 5. v. 3. 6. 18. & variis locis. liquoties pro indefinito numero sumitur, Leu. 26. 8. Pro 17. 10. Eccl. 6 3. Esai. 65. 20. Amos 5. 3.]
units.tr: A HUNDRED, a fixed number, Gen. 5.3, 6, 18, and in various places. Yet it is often taken for an indefinite number: Lev. 26.8; Prov. 17.10; Eccl. 6.3; Isa. 65.20; Amos 5.3.]

units.la: CENTVRIO (qui centum peditibus præest) eius fides, Matth. 8. 8. Luc. 7. v. 6. 7. 9. eius puer sanatur à Christo, Matth. 8. Luc. 7. 10. Centurionis & eius militum de Christo opinio. Matth. 27. 54. Marc. 15. 39. centuriones Israelitis à Mo[ysi] præficiuntur, Exodi 18.25. Deut.1.15. V. Cornelius, & Iulius centur.
units.tr: CENTURION (who commands a hundred foot soldiers): his faith, Matt. 8.8; Luke 7.6–7, 9. His servant is healed by Christ, Matt. 8; Luke 7.10. The opinion of the centurion and his soldiers about Christ, Matt. 27.54; Mark 15.39. Centurions are set over the Israelites by Moses, Exod. 18.25; Deut. 1.15. See Cornelius and Julius the centurion.

units.la: SEPHAS, nomen à Christo Simoni impositū, Ioan.1.42. sonat idem quod Petrus, id est, rupes, vel lapis. Ioan.1.42. 1. Cor.1. & 3.22. & 9.5. & 15.5. Gal.2.9.14. Vide PETRUS.
units.tr: CEPHAS, a name given to Simon by Christ, John 1.42. It means the same as Peter, that is, rock or stone: John 1.42; 1 Cor. 1; 3.22; 9.5; 15.5; Gal. 2.9, 14. See PETER.

units.la: CEREMONIAE
units.tr: CEREMONIES

units.la: Ceremoniae citra Dei timorem observatae reputantur, Psalm.50.v.8.9. & 51.18. Esai. 1.11. & 66.3. Amos v.21.26. Mich. 6.7. Ceremoniae seu ritus certi in orando observati, 1.Reg.8.v.22.54. & 17.21. & 18.42. 2. Para.5.v.12.13. Matth.2.11. & 26.39. Marci 14.35. Luc.22.41.1. Corinth.11.4. 6.1. Timoth.2.8. Ceremoniae umbris similes, Col. 2.17: Hebr.1.1. & 8.5. & 10.1. Vmbras autem intellige dici legales ceremonias, non ut res vacuas & inanes, qualis est corporum umbra (erant enim vera & pro ratione ac modo Sacramentorum efficacia σκιαὶ, id est signa, ac etiam σφραγίδες, hoc est sigilla, in recto ipsorum usu spirituali per fidem in Christum venturum) sed cum ipso Christo iam exhibito comparatas, qui dicitur earum umbrarum corpus, Coloss. 17. quòd illum, velut umbra corpus, à quo efformatur sacramentaliter adumbrarent.
units.tr: Ceremonies performed without the fear of God count for nothing (Ps. 50:8–9; Ps. 51:18; Isa. 1:11; Isa. 66:3; Amos 5:21, 26; Mic. 6:7). There are fixed ceremonies or rites observed in prayer (1 Kings 8:22, 54; 1 Kings 17:21; 1 Kings 18:42; 2 Chron. 5:12–13; Matt. 2:11; Matt. 26:39; Mark 14:35; Luke 22:41; 1 Cor. 11:4; 1 Cor. 6:1; 1 Tim. 2:8). Ceremonies are like shadows (Col. 2:17; Heb. 1:1; Heb. 8:5; Heb. 10:1). By "shadows" understand the legal ceremonies, not as empty and vain things, as the shadow of a body is, for they were, according to their nature and manner, truly effective sacraments, shadows [σκιαί], that is signs, and also seals [σφραγίδες], that is sigils, which in their spiritual use through faith pointed to Christ who was to come. Yet they are compared with Christ himself, now revealed, who is called the body of those shadows (Col. 2:17), because they foreshadowed him, as a shadow foreshadows the body from which it is sacramentally formed.

units.la: Ceremoniae legales, vocantur Mortis chirographum, Col. 2.14. eò quòd illis tanquam chirographo quodam ipsi nostra manu reatum nostrum aduersum nos obsignabamus. Sunt enim ceremoniales, quatenus erant non Euangelii sacramenta, sed Legis nos arguentis appendices, quid aliud quam publica miserae hominum conditionis profissio, & solennis quaedam obligatio? Circumcisio quidem usurpata, naturalem pollutionem: Ablutiones peccatorum & Victimae denique, capitalem reatum publicè testantur. Lex ceremonialis vocatur ab Apostolo pædagogus, Galat.3.24. non quatenus opponitur ea Christo, ut Chirographum mortis, sed quatenus Christum expectatum adumbrabat. Ceremoniae per Christum abolitae, Galat.5.verf.1. Eph.2.15. Colo.2.14. Hebr.8.13. Vide CHIROGRAPHVM.
units.tr: The legal ceremonies are called "the handwriting of death" (Col. 2:14), because by them, as by a kind of signed bond, we ourselves sealed our guilt against ourselves with our own hand. For they are ceremonial in so far as they were not the sacraments of the Gospel but appendages of the Law that accuses us. What else are they than a public profession of the wretched condition of men, and a solemn kind of obligation? Circumcision, used indeed, publicly testifies to natural corruption; the ablutions for sins and, finally, the sacrifices publicly testify to capital guilt. The ceremonial law is called by the Apostle "our schoolmaster" (Gal. 3:24), not in so far as it is opposed to Christ, like the handwriting of death, but in so far as it foreshadowed the expected Christ. The ceremonies were abolished through Christ (Gal. 5:1; Eph. 2:15; Col. 2:14; Heb. 8:13). See CHIROGRAPHUM.

units.la: CEREORVM & lampadum in Templis usum, ut eum hoc tempore reuocare, & usurpare possint, probant Pontif. ex 2.Par.4.20.
units.tr: The Papists prove from 2 Chron. 4:20 that it is lawful to recall and use the custom of candles and lamps in churches at this time.

units.la: CERTAMEN hominis, 1.Sa.17.8.10.20. Certamen Dei, Zac.14. Certamen fidei, 1.Tim.6.11. Certamen fidelium, Philip.1. Heb.10.32. & 13.1. Certamen Pauli, 2.Tim.4.7.
units.tr: THE CONFLICT of man (1 Sam. 17:8, 10, 20). The conflict of God (Zech. 14). The conflict of faith (1 Tim. 6:11). The conflict of the faithful (Phil. 1; Heb. 10:32; Heb. 13:1). The conflict of Paul (2 Tim. 4:7).

units.la: ERTOS non esse nos de accepta peccatorum remissione, vita æterna consequenda, sed dubitandum esse de ea, his G Scripturæ locis nituntur probare Papistæ, Eccl. 9.v.1. Eccl.5.5. Roman.8.17. & 11.20.1.Corinth.4.v.3.4.5.& 9.2. & 10.12.Philipp.2.12.& 3.v.11.13.1.Timoth.1.19.2.Petr.3.1. Hebr.3.14.& 4.1. Vide Dvbitare,& Forte:& Salus.
units.tr: That we are not certain of the forgiveness of sins received and of obtaining eternal life, but ought to doubt it, the Papists try to prove from these passages of Scripture: Eccl. 9:1; Eccl. 5:5; Rom. 8:17; Rom. 11:20; 1 Cor. 4:3–5; 1 Cor. 9:2; 1 Cor. 10:12; Phil. 2:12; Phil. 3:11, 13; 1 Tim. 1:19; 2 Pet. 3:1; Heb. 3:14; Heb. 4:1. See DOUBT, PERHAPS, and SALVATION.

units.tr: THE STAG, the hind. The Hebrews were permitted to eat stags (Deut. 12:22; Deut. 14:5). The love of a stag for a hind (Prov. 5:19). At what time the hinds bring forth their young (Job 39:1–4). They bring forth at the thunder (Ps. 29:9). Naphtali is compared to a hind let loose (Gen. 49:21), and David (2 Sam. 22:34; Ps. 18:33), and the stag in Habakkuk (Hab. 3:19), on account of its speed. (David's soul too is compared to a hind for thirst after the Lord, Ps. 42:1–2.) The lame man leaps like a hart at the coming of Christ (Isa. 35:6). Stags were an ordinary food for Solomon (1 Kings 4:23). See Jer. 14:5.

units.tr: THE CANAANITES, from whom they were descended (Gen. 9:18; Gen. 10:18; 1 Chron. 8:16). They were made tributaries in the midst of Ephraim (Josh. 16:10), to the Israelites (Josh. 17:13; Judg. 1:28), and to Solomon (1 Kings 9:21). God commands that they be slain (Num. 33:52; Deut. 7:2, 16). Why the Canaanites and the other peoples were cast out of the land (Deut. 9:4; Deut. 18:12; Deut. 20:17). Why they were overthrown gradually and not all at once (Exod. 23:29; Deut. 7:22; Judg. 2:23; Judg. 3:1). Why not all the Canaanites were destroyed by God (Judg. 2:2–3, 21; Judg. 3:1, 4). The Canaanites were terrified at the arrival of the Israelites (Josh. 5:1).

Charity, the mutual union of believers, is the work of the Holy Spirit (Rom. 15:30).] (Lev. 19:18; Deut. 22:1; Prov. 10:12; Prov. 15:17; Prov. 24:1; Prov. 31:8; Isa. 1:17; Isa. 58:6; Matt. 5:42; Matt. 19:19; Matt. 22:39; Mark 12:31; Luke 11:42; John 13:34; John 14:28, 31; John 15:12, 17; Rom. 12:9–10, 13; Rom. 13:8; 1 Cor. 13:1; 1 Cor. 14:1, 16; 2 Cor. 2:8; 2 Cor. 6:6; Gal. 5:6, 13–14, 22; Gal. 6:2; Eph. 3:17; Eph. 4:2, 15–16, 32; Eph. 5:2; Eph. 6:23; Phil. 1:9, 16; Phil. 2:1–2; Col. 2:2; Col. 3:13–14; 1 Thess. 3:12; 1 Thess. 4:9; 1 Thess. 5:8; 1 Tim. 1:5; 1 Tim. 2:15; 1 Tim. 4:12; 1 Tim. 6:11; 2 Tim. 1:13; 2 Tim. 2:22; 2 Tim. 3:10; Titus 2:2; Heb. 10:24; Heb. 13:1; James 1:27; 1 Pet. 1:22; 1 Pet. 2:17; 1 Pet. 3:8; 1 Pet. 4:8; 1 Pet. 5:14; 2 Pet. 1:7; 1 John 2:10; 1 John 3:11, 14, 16, 18, 23; 1 John 4:7, 11, 21; 2 John 5; Jude 21; Rev. 2:4, 19.) Quare apud Lucam etiam, iustificationis non causa, sed effectum est, Luc.7.47. eo enim loci non ostenditur causa efficiens, sed potius ex consequenti colligitur antecedens. Deus. n. prior nos dilexit, cū adhuc inimici & peccatores essemus, Rom.5.v.6.8.Vide & Rom.11. 35. Exercitium est fidelium, 1.Cor.16.14.Gal.5.6.Ephes.5. 2. finis praecepti, Rom. 13. 8. Deinde quia in nemine mortalium perfecta eius idea elucet,praeter Christum, ideóque suo exemplo hortatur ad eam colendam,Ioan.13.34. &c.
units.tr: Charity builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). It is a gift of God (Eph. 1:15–16; Eph. 6:23; Phil. 1:9; Col. 1:3–4; 1 Thess. 1:2–3; 1 Thess. 3:12; 2 Thess. 1:3; 2 Tim. 1:7; 1 John 4:7). It is an effect of faith (1 John 3:18–19). For it does not beget that faith and full assurance of which the passage there speaks; rather, it is begotten by faith, which is nonetheless confirmed more and more by it, because from effects we infer the cause. (See 1 John 4:17; 2 Pet. 1:10.) Thus in Luke too it is an effect, not a cause, of justification (Luke 7:47); for in that place the efficient cause is not shown, but rather the antecedent is inferred from the consequent. For God loved us first, when we were still enemies and sinners (Rom. 5:6, 8). See also Rom. 11:35. It is the exercise of the faithful (1 Cor. 16:14; Gal. 5:6; Eph. 5:2). It is the aim of the commandment (Rom. 13:8; Gal. 5:14; 1 Tim. 1:5), the fulfilling of the Law (Rom. 13:8). In that passage it is not a matter of perfect or imperfect observance of the Law, but charity is commended as the sum of the Law, as is clear from the reason given after it and from the conclusion that follows. It is the mark of faith (2 Cor. 9:13). It is the law of Christ (John 13:15, 34–35; Gal. 6:2). Mutual charity is called the law of Christ because it is understood and practised by the one Spirit of Christ breathing in us. Then, because the perfect idea of it shines in no mortal except Christ, he therefore urges us to cultivate it by his example (John 13:34, etc.).

units.la: Charitas fide & spe maior,1.Corint.13.13.quatenus scilicet fructus ipsius longius progreditur, quàm fructus fidei & spei,nempe ad proximum: cùm fides & spes non egrediantur credentis & sperantis personam.Deinde maior dicitur,quòd nobis promissionum,quibus credimus, & quas sperαmus, plenam adeptis possessionem, certè neque fide iam,neque spe opus erit. Charitas in Deũ, quo tunc fruemur,& in salutis nostrae socios, quibus arctissimè coniuncti fuerimus,tunc maxime vigebit. Quocunque autem modo intelligas charitatem dici maximam,non sequetur, nos per eam iustificari coram Deo,sicut nec fide ipsa iustificamur, nisi quatenus Christum iustitiam apprehendimus. Haec autem Christi apprehensio soli fidei tribuitur, quoniam sub hac conditione, si crediderimus, offertur Christus,licet illam etiam conditionem Deus in nobis impleat. Charitas verò quomodo efficeret iustificationem in nobis,cùm sit ipsius iustificationis consequens? Charitas suspicax non est, 1.Cor.13.5.peccata regit, Proverb. 10.12.1. Petr. 4. 8. Charitas perfecta timorem pellit, 1. Ioann.4.18. τὸν μικρὸν vitae aeternae,non causa,1.Ioann.3.14.nó enim dicit Apo-
units.tr: Charity is greater than faith and hope (1 Cor. 13:13), in so far as its fruit reaches further than the fruit of faith and hope, namely to our neighbour; for faith and hope do not extend beyond the person of the one who believes and hopes. It is called greater also because, once we have full possession of the promises in which we believe and which we hope for, there will certainly be no more need of faith or hope. Charity towards God, in which we will then rejoice, and towards the companions of our salvation, with whom we shall have been most closely joined, will then especially flourish. However you understand charity to be called greatest, it does not follow that we are justified before God by it, just as we are not justified by faith itself, except in so far as we apprehend Christ as our righteousness. But this apprehension of Christ is ascribed to faith alone, since under this condition, if we believe, Christ is offered, although God himself also fulfils that condition in us. But how could charity effect justification in us, when it is a consequence of justification itself? Charity is not suspicious (1 Cor. 13:5); it rules over sins (Prov. 10:12; 1 Pet. 4:8). Perfect charity drives out fear (1 John 4:18). [The love of the brethren is a sign of eternal life, not its cause (1 John 3:14)], for the Apostle does not say that we have been translated from death to life through the fact that we love the brethren (for eternal life is the gift of God through Christ, Rom. 6:23), but that from the fact that we love the brethren we know that we have been translated from death into life. A testimony of election (Rom. 8:14; 2 Pet. 1:10).

units.la: Apostolus, Nos per id quòd fratres diligimus, translatos esse ex morte in vitam (est enim vita æterna Donum Dei per Christum, Rom.6.23.) sed nos ex eo, quòd fratres diligamus, scire nos esse ex morte translatos in vitam. Testimonium electionis, Rom.8.14.2.Pet.1.10. Heb.6.11. Vinculum perfectionis, Coloss.3.14. hoc est, vinculum, quo omnia hominum inter se officia continentur, & cohærent.
units.tr: The Apostle: "We know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brothers" (for eternal life is the gift of God through Christ, Rom. 6.23). But we know from our love for the brothers that we have passed from death into life. A testimony of election: Rom. 8.14; 2 Pet. 1.10; Heb. 6.11. The bond of perfection: Col. 3.14, that is, the bond by which all the duties of men toward one another are held together and cohere.

units.tr: What the charity of believers is like: 1 Cor. 13.4. Charity in the elderly: Titus 2.2. God is called charity: 1 John 4.8, that is, he loves us in Christ supremely and so infinitely; but that is far more exceedingly [ὑπερτικῶς]. The charity of Christ: Eph. 3.19, that is, the charity which God showed us in Christ: John 3.16; Rom. 5.6; or that by which Christ, the Son of God, embraced us: John 15.13. The charity of Christ: 2 Cor. 5.14, that is, that love by which Christ pursued us, or by which we in turn love him again. The charity of God, in the passive sense: Rom. 5.5, by which we are loved, is the foundation of our election: Eph. 1.4, to which the Apostle everywhere recalls us, as in Eph. 1.4 and elsewhere throughout. The charity of God in the active sense: 1 John 2.5; 4.15, by which we love God. The charity of the Spirit: Rom. 15.30, is that mutual bond by which the Holy Spirit has joined souls together; Phil. 2.1 calls it the communion of the Spirit; hence that Christian sympathy [συμπαθεία], which produces Christian charity, by which all the members are governed by one Spirit.

units.tr: CARMEL, the name of a mountain: 1 Kings 18.19, 20, 42; Amos 1.2; 9.3. Sometimes it is taken for a pleasant or fertile place: 2 Kings 19.23; Isa. 10.18; Jer. 2.7; Mic. 7.14. It is also the name of a town: Josh. 12.21. (That is, a tender ear of grain.)

units.la: CHERVB, Angelus Iehouæ, Ezech. 9.3, & 10.v.4. 7. 9.14. Effigies pueri in sanctuario & templo, Exod. 25. 19. & 37.8. 1. Reg. 6.v,24.&c. Rex, quod in morem Cherub alas suas (i. ditionem) proferat, Ezech. 28.14.16.]
units.tr: CHERUB: the angel of Jehovah, Ezek. 9.3; 10.4, 7, 9; 9.14. The image of a boy in the sanctuary and the temple, Exod. 25.19; 37.8; 1 Kings 6.24 and following. A king, because he spreads his wings (that is, his dominion) like a cherub, Ezek. 28.14, 16.]

units.la: CHERVBIM: Cherubin collocantur ante terrestrem Paradisum, Gen. 3.24. Cherubim propitiatorij, Exodi 25. 18. Cherubim in medio Templi, 1. Reg. 6.27. Cherubim super Arcam 2. Paral. 5.8.
units.tr: CHERUBIM: Cherubim are placed before the earthly Paradise, Gen. 3.24. Cherubim of the mercy seat, Exod. 25.18. Cherubim in the middle of the Temple, 1 Kings 6.27. Cherubim over the Ark, 2 Chr. 5.8.

units.la: CHIROGRAPHVM, quo obligabamur, deleuit Christus, Col. 2.14. dum nos sanguine suo redemit, & repurgauit, nostrumque debitum totum in ara crucis ad extremum usque quadrantem semel persoluit. Cur enim, persoluto ad vltimum usque quadrantem ære nostro alieno, maneat chirographum? aut manente integro chirographo apud bonæ fidei creditorem, qualis Deus est, idque ex debitoris consensu, imo vero ipso debitore ita postulante, quis persolutum æs alienum dixerit? Quid sit autem chirographi nomine eo loci intelligendum. Vide CEREMONIAE legales quatenus dicatur motus chirographum. CHIVN idolum, Vide IDOLORVM catalogus. CHOREAE, Vide SALTATIO.
units.tr: Christ blotted out the bond that held us, Col. 2.14, when he redeemed and cleansed us with his blood, and once for all paid our whole debt on the altar of the cross, down to the last farthing. For why should the bond remain once our debt has been paid to the last farthing? Or, with the bond still intact in the hands of a creditor who acts in good faith, as God does, and that with the debtor's consent, indeed with the debtor himself asking it, who would say the debt has been paid? What is to be understood here by the name of the bond: see LEGAL CEREMONIES, as far as they are called a bond of motion. CHIVN, an idol: see the list of IDOLS. CHOREAE: see DANCING.

units.tr: CHORAZIN, a town opposite Capernaum: Matt. 11.21; Luke 10.13. (Here are mysteries.)

units.la: CHORE, pronepos Leui, seditiosus in Mosen, e terra absorbetur: Num. 16.31. (Korah, i. calvities) Ex hoc orti sunt Choritæ, 1. Par. 9.19.
units.tr: KORAH, great-grandson of Levi, who rose in rebellion against Moses and was swallowed up by the earth: Num. 16.31. (Korah, that is, baldness.) The Korahites are descended from him: 1 Chr. 9.19.

units.la: [CHORVS, chorea, Exo. 15.20. & 32.19. pro tibia, instrumento musico sumitur, Psal. 149.3.& 150.4. pro turma, Nehem. 12.v. 31, 38.39. Cantic. 6.13.] CHRISTUS, est θεάνθρωπος, (ut breuissimè definiunt Scripturæ) sermo caro factus, seu Deus in carne conspicuus factus, i. persona in cuius singularitate duæ Naturæ, saluis manentibus earum proprietatibus, unitæ sunt, ad humani generis redemptionem.
units.tr: [CHORUS: a dance, Exod. 15.20; 32.19; for a pipe, a musical instrument, Ps. 149.3; 150.4; for a troop, Neh. 12.31, 38, 39; Song 6.13.] CHRIST is God-man [θεάνθρωπος] (as the Scriptures define him very briefly): the Word made flesh, or God made visible in the flesh, that is, a person in whose singular being two natures are united, their properties remaining intact, for the redemption of the human race.

units.la: CHRISTUS, DEUS. Quinque sunt præcipui fontes demonstrationum, quibus vera & æterna Christi Deitas aduersus blasphemos & impuros hæreticos asserenda est.
units.tr: CHRIST, GOD. There are five principal sources of proof by which the true and eternal deity of Christ is to be affirmed against blasphemous and impure heretics.

units.tr: First, from the plain testimonies of Scripture, in which Christ is called GOD and JEHOVAH: not a God in name only (as the heretics blasphemously babble), but truly and by nature God. Christ is therefore God. First, because he is plainly called God: Gen. 32.28; Ps. 45.5; Heb. 1.8; Isa. 7.14; 9.8; 25.9; 35.4-5; 43.11-12; Matt. 1.23; 11.4-5; 15.30; Isa. 40.3; Matt. 3.3; Mark 1.3; Luke 3.4; John 1.23; Isa. 45.15, 21-24; Rom. 14.11; Matt. 1.21, 23; Acts 4.12; Jer. 33.15-16; Hos. 1.7; Zech. 2.8-9; Mal. 3.1, 5; Luke 1.16-17; Acts 20.28; Rom. 9.5; 1 Cor. 2.8; Gal. 1.12; Phil. 2.6; Col. 1.15, 19; 2.9; 1 Tim. 3.16; Titus 1.3-4; 2.13; 2 Pet. 1.3; 1 John 5.20; Rev. 21.7, 22; because he is and is called JEHOVAH: Isa. 45.24-25; Hos. 1.7; Zech. 2.8-9; Mal. 3.1; and often elsewhere, as is clear from a careful comparison, and [syzygia, συζυσία] of these passages of the Old and New Testaments, which explain one another. Jer. 9.23-24; Gal. 6.14. Jer. 23.6; 1 Cor. 1.30. Ezek. 16.60-62; Heb. 9.15-16. In Hosea it is said that Jehovah will save the house of Judah in Jehovah their God (Hos. 1.7). Yet no one is saved except in Christ, through Christ: Matt. 1.21; John 4.42; Acts 12; Titus 1.3; 1 John 4.14; 2 Pet. 1.1. Hos. 2.19; John 3.29; 2 Cor. 11.2; Eph. 5.32; Rev. 19.7; 21.9. See Ps. 43.11-12; Ezek. 16.8; Matt. 9.15. Hos. 6.1; Eph. 2.6; Col. 3.1. Hos. 13.4, 14; John 5.21; 1 Cor. 15.55-57; 1 Tim. 2.6; 2 Tim. 1.10; Heb. 2.14. Hos. 14.2-3; John 1.29. Mic. 7.18; John 1.29; Isa. 53.6; 1 Pet. 2.24. Hag. 2.7; Heb. 1.25-26. Thirdly, Zech. 2.15: two are introduced under the name of Jehovah, the one who sends and the one who is sent, and each of them is called Jehovah. Yet there are not two Jehovahs, but one (Deut. 6). There are therefore several persons in God. Such also is Gen. 19.24; Hos. 1.7; Zech. 3.2, where it is said: "Jehovah said to Satan, Jehovah rebuke you." If anyone, abusing the name Jehovah, applies it to the archangel Michael in v. 9 of the same passage, as if it were a mistake for Judah, he will do violence both to the thing and to the history. For Jude speaks there of another matter, namely, when Michael himself contended with Satan over the body of Moses; but Zechariah speaks of the accusation of Satan, when in a vision Satan accused Joshua the priest. Hence Jude is not the interpreter of this place. I readily grant that the archangel Michael used the same words that Jehovah uses in Zechariah; but it does not follow that this Michael is the same as this Jehovah, for the histories are different. Zech. 12.10; John 19.36-37; Rev. 1.7; John 15.26; Acts 2.2-3. Mal. 3.1; Matt. 11.10; Mark 1.2; Luke 1.17; 7.27. Lev. 26.12; 2 Cor. 6.16; Eph. 3.17. Let these testimonies also be added to those above: Gen. 32.24 and following; Isa. 25.9; 43.11; Jer. 33.11; Hos. 1.7; 12.3, 5; Zech. 2.8-9. Indeed, even in the New Testament the Apostles served Christ himself and taught others to serve him, and professed themselves servants, that is, worshippers of him: Rom. 1.1; Phil. 1.1; Titus 1.1; Jas. 1.1; 1 Pet. 1.1; Jude 1; Rev. 1.1; 3; 19.10. Since, therefore, from these testimonies and sayings of the Old Testament, which are either plainly applied to Christ in the New Testament or are shown without obscurity to belong to him, it must be believed that Christ is the true and eternal Jehovah. Secondly, from what is related of him: he is the only-begotten [μονογενής], that is, the unique Son of God, John 1.18; 3.14, 16, 18; 1 John 4.9. We confess the same in the Apostles' Creed. See also Rom. 1.3-4. He is the image of the Father: John 14.7-9; 2 Cor. 4.4; Col. 1.15; Heb. 1.3. But an image or likeness is not of things that differ among themselves, but of things that are similar and equal.
