Tit.1.v.3.4. & 2.13. Atqui hoc non nisi vere Iehouæ competit, Esa.44.11. & 45.22. Quòd autem hæc appellatio Ministris etiam verbi tribuitur, Abd.v.21. 1. Tim. 4.16. Iac.5.20. eò fit, quia illi sunt administri salutis per Evangelicam doctrinam, 1. Corin.3.9. & 4.11. Quia Evangelium, quod testimonium Dei dicitur, 1. Cor.2.1. dicitur Christi testimonium, 1. Cor.1.6. Quia sperare dicuntur gentes in eo, Esai.11.10. Paulo interprete, Rom.15.12. & beati dicuntur, qui sperant in eum, Psal.2.12. Atqui maledictus, qui spem suam locat in homine, Ier.17.v.57. beatus contra, qui fidit Deo, Psal.84.13. Quia suscitauit seipsum, Rom.1.4. Ioan. 10.18. Quia Spiritum S. mittit, Zach 12.10. Ioan.16.7. & 20. 22. Quia virtus eius diuinos effectus habet, Rom.15.v.18.19. 2. Cor.12.9. Hebr.1.3. Quia vita fuisse in Christo dicitur Ioan.1.4. Atqui in solo Deo viuunt, mouentur, & subsistunt omnia, Actor.17.28. Rom.11.36. 1. Cor.8.6. Quia vnu essentia cum Patre, Ioan.1.18. & 5.18. & 8.38. & 14.v.10.20. Philip.2.6.
units.tr: THIRDLY, from the epithets that belong only to the divine nature: because he is equal to God the Father, Phil. 2.6. Because he is eternal, Prov. 8.22; Mic. 5.2; John 1.1; 8.58; Col. 1.17-18; 1 John 1.1; 2.13; Rev. 1.8, 17; 21.6; 22.13. Because he is the author of election, John 13.18. Because he knows all things, even the secrets of the heart, Matt. 9.4-5; 12.15, 25; 16.8; 17.17; 22.18; Mark 2.8; 14.13; Luke 5.22; 6.8; 9.47; 11.17, 39; 22.10; John 1.48; 2.24-25; 5.42; 6.15, 61, 64; 11.14; 13.11, 19; 14.29; 16.4, 19, 30; 18.4; Rev. 2.9, 13, 19, 23; 3.1, 15, which belongs to God alone, 1 Kings 8.39; 2 Chron. 6.20. Because we are to believe in him as in God, John 14.1. Because he gives eternal rewards, John 5.24; 6.40. Because he led the people of Israel out of Egypt, and they tempted him in the wilderness, 1 Cor. 10.4, 9 (see Exod. 23.20-22). But the leading out of the people is attributed to the true and eternal God, Exod. 20.1-2, and elsewhere throughout. Because he hears those who call upon him, John 14.14. Because he is in the form of God, Phil. 2.6-7; to be a true man is one thing, and to be in the form of God is to be the true God. Because his glory is eternal, John 17.5. Because the glory which Isaiah saw, Isa. 6.1, was the glory of Christ, John 12.41. Because he is the giver of grace and peace, as is clear from the prayers of Paul, in which he joins the Son with the Father, Rom. 1.7; 1 Cor. 1.3; 16.24; 2 Cor. 1.2; 13.13; Gal. 1.3; Eph. 1.2; Phil. 1.2; Col. 1.2; 1 Thess. 1.1; 2 Thess. 1.2; 1 Tim. 1.2; 2 Tim. 1.2; Titus 1.4. Because he enlightens, John 1.9, which is the proper work of God alone, Exod. 4.11. Because he judges the living and the dead, John 5.22, 27, which we are also bound to confess in the Apostles' Creed. Because he is the object of faith, Isa. 8.14; Luke 2.34; Rom. 9.33; 1 Pet. 2.8; Isa. 28.16; Ps. 2.12; Matt. 28.19; Mark 16.16; John 2.11; 3.36; 6.29, 35, 40, 47; 14.1, 6; 17.3; Acts 16.31; 22.19; 24.24; Gal. 2.16; Eph. 1.15; Col. 1.4; 2.5; 1 Tim. 3.13; 2 Tim. 3.15. Because he is almighty, John 5.31; 10.18; 14.14; Phil. 3.21; Heb. 1.3; Rev. 1.8; 3.7; 4.8; 17.14; 19.15-16. Because he has authority to forgive sins, Matt. 9.6; Mark 2.5, 7, 9; Luke 5.20; 7.48. But to forgive sins belongs to God alone, Isa. 43.25; Mark 2.7; Luke 5.21. Ministers also forgive sins, but as heralds and instruments of God, and they hold this authority as received from Christ, Matt. 16.19; John 20.23. Because he fills several places at the same time, Matt. 18.20; 28.20; John 1.18; 3.13; 14.23. But this belongs to God alone, 1 Kings 8.27; 2 Chron. 2.5; 6.18; Job 11.8; Ps. 139.7-10; Isa. 6.3; 66.1; Jer. 23.24; Amos 9.2; Wisd. 1.7; Matt. 5.35; Acts 7.48; 17.24. Because he possesses the same power as the Father, John 5.17, 19; 16.15. Because he confers the power of working miracles, Matt. 10.8; Mark 6.7; 16.17; Luke 10.19; John 14.12; Acts 3.6, 12, 16; 14.3. Because he is the author of the resurrection, John 5.21, 25; 6.39-40, 44, 54; 11.25; 1 Cor. 15.21. Because he is King of kings and Lord of lords, Rev. 19.16, which Paul ascribes to the Father, 1 Tim. 6.15. Therefore Christ shares the same power with the Father. Because he is and is called the Saviour, Matt. 1.21; Acts 4.12; John 4.14; Titus 1.3-4; 2.13. But this belongs only to the true Jehovah, Isa. 44.11; 45.22. That this title is also given to ministers of the Word, Obad. 21; 1 Tim. 4.16; James 5.20, happens because they are the administrators of salvation through the evangelical doctrine, 1 Cor. 3.9; 4.1. Because the Gospel, which is called the testimony of God, 1 Cor. 2.1, is called the testimony of Christ, 1 Cor. 1.6. Because the nations are said to hope in him, Isa. 11.10, as Paul interprets it, Rom. 15.12; and those are called blessed who hope in him, Ps. 2.12. But cursed is he who places his hope in man, Jer. 17.5, and blessed, on the contrary, he who trusts in God, Ps. 84.12. Because he raised himself, Rom. 1.4; John 10.18. Because he sends the Holy Spirit, Zech. 12.10; John 16.7; 20.22. Because his power has divine effects, Rom. 15.18-19; 2 Cor. 12.9; Heb. 1.3. Because life is said to be in Christ, John 1.4. But all things live, move, and subsist in God alone, Acts 17.28; Rom. 11.36; 1 Cor. 8.6. Because he has one essence with the Father, John 1.18; 5.18; 8.38; 14.10, 20; Phil. 2.6.

units.la: Quarto, ab effectu vniuersali, videlicet ὃς ἐκ πάσης κτίσεως ἡ δημιουργίας, à creatione & conseruatione rerum omnium: quia creator, Ioan.1.3. & 5.17. Col.1.16. Heb.1.v.2. 10. Apoc.3.14.
units.tr: Fourthly, from the universal effect, namely that he is the one "through whom [ὃς ἐκ πάσης κτίσεως ἡ δημιουργίας]" all creation and all creating comes, that is, from the creation and preservation of all things: because he is the creator, John 1.3; 5.17; Col. 1.16; Heb. 1.2, 10; Rev. 3.14.

units.la: Quinto, à cultu, quem omnes fideles inde vsque ab orbe condito Filio Dei Christo, vt vero & natura Deo exhibuerunt: Quia adorandus, Psal.97.7. Heb.1.6. Luc.24.52. Ioan.23. Phil.2.10. Apoc.4.v.8.9.10.11. Atqui Deus solus est adorandus, Deut.6.13. & 10.20. Matt.4.10. Luc.4.8. Actor.14. poc.14.7. Quia baptizandum in nomine Christi, Mat.28. Quia idem cultus & honor debetur Filio, qui & Patri, Ioan.5.23.1.Ioan.2.v.22.23. Atqui clamat Deus, Esai.42.8. se noriam suam alteri non daturum. Ergo Filius cum Patre sit idem in essentia Deus. Quia curuabitur ipsi omne genu, Rom.14.11. Philip.2.10. Atqui id est solius veri Iehouæ, E-45.23. Quia inuocandus, Esa.11.10. Rom.15.12. Matth.18. Luc.24.54. Act.7.59. & 9.v.13.14.& 22.16. Rō.1 7.1.Cor. 2.Cor.1.2. Gal.1 3. Eph.1.2. Phil.1.2. Col.1.2 1.Thess.1.1. 3 11.2.Thess.2.16.1. Tim.1.2.2. Tim.1.2. Tit.1.4.Philem.v. 25. 1.Pet.5.14. Apoc.22.v.20.21. Quia iuratur in eius nomine, Esa.45.23.Rom.14.11.Philip.2.v.10.11.
units.tr: Fifthly, from the worship which all the faithful, from the beginning of the world, have offered to the Son of God Christ as to the true God by nature: because he is to be adored, Ps. 97.7; Heb. 1.6; Luke 24.52; John 5.23; Phil. 2.10; Rev. 4.8-11. But God alone is to be adored, Deut. 6.13; 10.20; Matt. 4.10; Luke 4.8; Acts 14; Rev. 14.7. Because he is to be baptized in the name of Christ, Matt. 28. Because the same worship and honour is due to the Son as to the Father, John 5.23; 1 John 2.22-23. But God declares, Isa. 42.8, that he will not give his glory to another. Therefore the Son is the same God as the Father in essence. Because every knee shall bow to him, Rom. 14.11; Phil. 2.10. But this belongs to the true Jehovah alone, Isa. 45.23. Because he is to be invoked, Isa. 11.10; Rom. 15.12; Matt. 18; Luke 24.52; Acts 7.59; 9.13-14; 22.16; Rom. 1.7; 1 Cor. 1.2; 2 Cor. 1.2; Gal. 1.3; Eph. 1.2; Phil. 1.2; Col. 1.2; 1 Thess. 1.1; 3.11; 2 Thess. 2.16; 1 Tim. 1.2; 2 Tim. 1.2; Titus 1.4; Philem. 25; 1 Pet. 5.14; Rev. 22.20-21. Because oaths are sworn in his name, Isa. 45.23; Rom. 14.11; Phil. 2.10-11.

units.la: Porrò, quemadmodum salus æterna nemini mortalium contingit, nisi firma fide credat Christum IESVM Dei Filium verum illum Messiam, verum & natura Deum esse, vt iam unde demonstratum est: ita certo statuat oportet quicumque saluari cupit, eundem Dei Filium, statim post lapsum Paradiso promissum, Sanctis Patriarchis identidem pro-mulgatum & repetitum, promissionibus certis confirma-tum, sacrificiis Mosaicis præfiguratum, & certissimo Prophe-tarum præconio prænuntiatum & prædictum, tandem ve-ro in temporis plenitudine verè exhibitum, esse verum ho-minem, carnem de carne nostra, os ex ossibus nostris, iisdem infirmitatibus, quibus nos, excepto peccato, obnoxium.
units.tr: Moreover, just as eternal salvation falls to no mortal unless he believes with firm faith that Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is the true Messiah and true God by nature, as has already been shown, so whoever desires to be saved must firmly hold that this same Son of God, promised to Paradise immediately after the fall, repeatedly proclaimed and repeated to the holy patriarchs, confirmed by certain promises, prefigured by the Mosaic sacrifices, foretold and predicted by the most certain proclamation of the prophets, and at last truly exhibited in the fullness of time, is a true man, flesh of our flesh and bone of our bones, subject to the same infirmities as we are, apart from sin.

units.la: Sed antequam solida & aperta de vera & minimè phan-tastica humanitate Christi adducantur testimonia, vt fides vestra in Christo IESV, quem verum Messiam agnosci-mus, ac in ipso omnes Dei promissiones Etiam & Amen persuasum habemus, 2.Cor.1.20. magis confirmetur, & cæcitatis apertæque blasphemiæ rei teneantur, duodecim quæstiones ad hanc doctrinam, in qua salus nostra fundata est, solidius & exactius intelligendam multum momenti allaturas pertractabimus, idque ex fontibus Israelis.
units.tr: But before the solid and open testimonies concerning the true and by no means phantasmal humanity of Christ are brought forward, so that your faith in Christ Jesus, whom we acknowledge as the true Messiah, and in whom we are persuaded that all the promises of God are Yea and Amen (2 Cor. 1.20), may be further confirmed, and so that those who are guilty of blindness and of manifest blasphemy may be convicted, we shall treat twelve questions which bear much weight for understanding more firmly and exactly this doctrine on which our salvation is founded, and we shall do so from the sources of Israel.

units.la: I. Quæ sint promissiones divinæ de nascituro & exhibendo Messia, per totam sacram Scripturam passim prodite & promulgatæ? Genesis 3.15. & 12.3. & 26.4. & 49.10. Immolatio Isaaci, Genesis 22.9. exaltatio ænei Serpentis, Numer.21.8. (Ioh.3.14.) omnia denique sacrificia Mosaica, Levit.1.2.3. &c. capitibus: Ionas item tribus diebus in ventre piscis delitescens, Ionæ 2.1. (Matth.16.4. Lucæ 11.29.) fuerunt typus sacrificij, passionis mortis, & resurrectionis Messiæ. Eodem spectant, Deu.18.18.2. Sam.7.12. Psal.2.v.12. & 19.6. & 72.11. & 110.v.1.2.4. & 118.22. (Matthæi.21.4. Marc.12.10. Luc.20.17. Act.4.11. Rom.9.33. 1.Pet.2.7.) Esa.2.v.2.3. & 7.14. & 9.v.6.7. & 11.v.1.10. & 25.v.6.7.8.9. & 35.v.4.5.6. & 40.v.9.10. & 53.v.1.2.3. &c. Ier.23.v.5.6. & 31.v.32. &c. & 33.v.14.15.16. Ezech.34.v.23.24. & 37.26. Dan.9.24.26. Ose.1.11. & 13.14. & Ioel.2.23. & 3.18. Amos 9.11. Abdiæ, v.17. Mich.4.v.1.2.7. & 5.2. Nahum.1.15. Abac.2.3. & v.18.19. Sophon.3.v.14.15. Agg.2 v.7.8. Zach.9.v.9.10.11. 13.v.1.2. Malach.1.11. & 3.v.1.2. & 4.5. (Matth.11.14. Marc. 9.11. Luc.1.16. Vide infra, Christus ante mundum conditum, &c. promissus.
units.tr: I. What are the divine promises concerning the Messiah who was to be born and revealed, published and proclaimed everywhere throughout all Holy Scripture? Gen. 3.15; 12.3; 26.4; 49.10. The sacrifice of Isaac, Gen. 22.9; the lifting up of the bronze serpent, Num. 21.8 (John 3.14); and finally all the Mosaic sacrifices, Lev. 1.2-3, etc., chapters; also Jonah hidden for three days in the belly of the fish, Jonah 2.1 (Matt. 12.40; Luke 11.29), were types of the sacrifice, passion, death, and resurrection of the Messiah. To the same purpose look Deut. 18.18; 2 Sam. 7.12; Ps. 2.12; 19.6; 72.11; 110.1-2, 4; 118.22 (Matt. 21.42; Mark 12.10; Luke 20.17; Acts 4.11; Rom. 9.33; 1 Pet. 2.7); Isa. 2.2-3; 7.14; 9.6-7; 11.1, 10; 25.6-9; 35.4-6; 40.9-10; 53.1-3, etc.; Jer. 23.5-6; 31.32, etc.; 33.14-16; Ezek. 34.23-24; 37.26; Dan. 9.24, 26; Hos. 1.11; 13.14; Joel 2.23; 3.18; Amos 9.11; Obad. 17; Mic. 4.1-2, 7; 5.2; Nah. 1.15; Hab. 2.3; 3.18-19; Zeph. 3.14-15; Hag. 2.7-8; Zech. 9.9-11; 13.1-2; Mal. 1.11; 3.1-2; 4.5 (Matt. 11.14; Mark 9.11; Luke 1.16). See below: Christ promised before the world was made, etc.

units.la: II. Qualis Messias à Deo promissus? qui nimirum pro peccatis nostris sufficiens λυτρον esse, & iram Dei patris nulli mortalium ferendam contra peccatum accensam sustinere posset, id quod solius Dei & naturæ Omnipotentis est, Psal.2.6. & 72.11. & 89.v.27.28. & 110.1. &c. Esaiæ 7.14. & 25.9. & 35.v.4.5.6. & 40.v.5.9.10. Ier.23.6. Mich.5. Abac.3.18. Zach.14.16. Addantur his illa quoque testimonia, quæ ad probandam Christi Deitatem supra sunt allata.
units.tr: II. What sort of Messiah was promised by God? Namely one who could be a sufficient ransom [λύτρον] for our sins and could bear the wrath of God the Father, kindled against sin, which no mortal could endure. This belongs to God alone and to Omnipotent Nature: Psal. 2.6; 72.11; 89.27-28; 110.1; Isa. 7.14; 25.9; 35.4-6; 40.5, 9-10; Jer. 23.6; Mic. 5; Hab. 3.18; Zech. 14.16. To these may be added the testimonies cited above to prove the deity of Christ.

units.la: III. Ex qua gente oriundus Messias? nempe ex gente Iudaica, quam hanc potissimum ob causam, ut est custos divinarum promissionum, & quasi bibliotheca, certis ritibus, legum & ceremoniarum generibus ab aliis gentibus segregari voluit, Deut.18.18. Psal.2.6. & 132.v.13.14.17. Esa.2.v.2. & 25.v.6.8. & 28.16. & 40.v.9.10. Oseæ 1.11. Ioel.2.23. Abdiæ v.17. Mich.4.7. Nahum.1.15. Sophon.3.14. Zachar.9.v.9.10. & 13.v.12.
units.tr: III. From what nation was the Messiah to descend? Namely from the Jewish nation, which God chose to set apart from other nations by certain rites and kinds of laws and ceremonies, chiefly for this reason: that it might be the guardian of the divine promises and, as it were, their library. Deut. 18.18; Psal. 2.6; 132.13-14, 17; Isa. 2.2; 25.6, 8; 28.16; 40.9-10; Hos. 1.11; Joel 2.23; Obad. 17; Mic. 4.7; Nah. 1.15; Zeph. 3.14; Zech. 9.9-10; 13.12.

units.la: IV. Ex qua familia Iudaici populi nascituros Messias nempe empe ex semine Abrahæ & Dauidis. Nam non certam gentem præsciri voluit Deus, ex qua nasciturus esset Saluator mundi Christus, sed ob rei certitudinem & eandem confirmandam, certam etiam eius gentis stirpem familiam prædixit, Abrahæ nimirum & Dauidis, Genesis 12.3. & 26.4. & 28.14. 2.Sam.7.12. Psal.89.v.4.5. & 132.11. Esa. 9.v.6.7. & 11.v.1.2.10. Ier.23.v.5.6. Ezec.34.v.23.24. Amos 9.11. Zac.13.v.1.2.
units.tr: IV. From what family of the Jewish people was the Messiah to be born? Namely from the seed of Abraham and David. For God did not wish a particular nation to be foreknown from which the Saviour of the world, Christ, was to be born. Rather, so that the matter might be certain and the certainty confirmed, he also foretold the exact stock and family of that nation, namely of Abraham and David: Gen. 12.3; 26.4; 28.14; 2 Sam. 7.12; Psal. 89.4-5; 132.11; Isa. 9.6-7; 11.1-2, 10; Jer. 23.5-6; Ezek. 34.23-24; Amos 9.11; Zech. 13.1-2.

units.la: V. Vbi, & quo in loco Iudæ nasci debuerit Messias?
units.tr: V. Where, and in what place, was the Messiah to be born?

units.la: empe in Bethlehem Iudæ ciuitate, quæ huic salutifero artui diuinitus assignata & destinata fuit, Mich.5.2. Matt.2.5.
units.tr: Namely in Bethlehem of Judah, the city divinely assigned and designated for this saving birth: Mic. 5.2; Matt. 2.5.

units.la: VI. Qualis natiuitas Messiæ futura? miraculosa videlicet, & prorsus stupenda, Esai.7.14. non ex commixtione virilis seminis & ex natura immunda, peccatique labe infecta, qualis omnium hominum est, Psal.51.7. Eph.2.3. sed ex sanctificata superuentu Spiritus Sancti, & obumbratione altissimi, sanguinis Mariæ massa, Lucæ 1.35. VII. Quo tempore Messias in mundum venturus? Genes.49.10. Esai.2.2. & 11. 1.Dan.2.v.44.45. & 9.v.24.26. Mich.7.v.7.8. Agg.2.v.7.8.9.10. Ex quorum locorum circumstantiis probe expensis, quòd nimirum Messias, stante adhuc politia Mosaica, & nondum sublato Tribus Iehudæ discrimine, regnoque Dei nondum ab aliis Tribubus deriuato, quòd nouissimis diebus, hoc est, in temporibus Patrum, aut Regum, aut Prophetarum, ad postrema mundi parte, qua Deus per Prophetas loqui assuerat: quòd ex radice Iesse, hoc est, stante quidem ac Mosis politia, sed regio trunco quasi emortuo & derelicto in terris: quòd post septuaginta hebdomadas, hoc est, (computando singulos annos pro singulis hebdomadis, non secus ac Num. 14.34. Ezech.4.6.) post annos quadringentos nonaginta (490) à captiuitate Babylonica, in quarta & postrema mundi Monarchia, quam Romanorum: quòd denique ante vastationem & euersionem Iudaici populi & subuersam politiam Mosaicam, adhuc Templo secundo, gloriosiore quàm priùs, ob spiritualem videlicet ornatum, pacem nempe, æternam prosperitatem (vt ibidem explicatur) futuro, Messias mundum sit venturus, & nasciturus: Ex his, inquam, circumstantiis diligenter confideratis, & rite expensis, ci iam & Tiibuum facta inter sese sit confusio, & radix Ie nunc ignoretur, & leptuaginta hebdomadæ ante mille vltra annos expletæ sint, & miserabilis illa populi Iuda vastatio facta si, & denique Templum secundum dirutu & vastatū penitus sit, atque omnes quotquot sunt fa& Dei promissiones in Christo sint Etiam & Amen, 2. Co 1.20. manifestè euincitur, Messiam iam venisse, nec a plius, vt faciunt cæci Iudæi expectandum esse, nisi ad dicium illud terribile, Matt. 25.v.30 31. Luc.21.v.27.28 Thess.4.v.15.16.Heb.9.28.
units.tr: VI. What sort of birth was the Messiah to have? Clearly a miraculous one, utterly astonishing: Isa. 7.14. Not from the mingling of male seed and from an unclean nature, stained by the taint of sin, as is the case with all men: Psal. 51.7; Eph. 2.3. But from the blood-mass of Mary, sanctified by the coming of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of the Most High: Luke 1.35. VII. At what time was the Messiah to come into the world? Gen. 49.10; Isa. 2.2; 11.1; Dan. 2.44-45; 9.24, 26; Mic. 7.7-8; Hag. 2.7-10. From the circumstances of these passages, carefully weighed, it is clearly shown that the Messiah has already come, and is not to be awaited any longer, as the blind Jews do, except for that terrible day of judgment: Matt. 25.30-31; Luke 21.27-28; 1 Thess. 4.15-16; Heb. 9.28. For the Messiah was to come and be born while the Mosaic polity was still standing and the distinction of the tribe of Judah had not yet been removed, and the kingdom of God had not yet been taken from the other tribes; in the last days, that is, in the times of the Patriarchs, Kings or Prophets, at the last part of the world through which God had been accustomed to speak by the Prophets; from the root of Jesse, that is, while indeed the polity of Moses still stood, but the royal trunk was as it were dead and abandoned on earth; after seventy weeks, that is (reckoning one year for each week, just as in Num. 14.34 and Ezek. 4.6), after four hundred and ninety years (490) from the Babylonian captivity, in the fourth and last monarchy of the world, that of the Romans; and finally, before the devastation and overthrow of the Jewish people and the subversion of the Mosaic polity, while the Second Temple still stood, more glorious than before, on account of its spiritual adornment, namely peace and eternal prosperity, as is explained in the same place. In these circumstances, I say, carefully considered and rightly weighed, the tribes have now been thrown into confusion among themselves, the root of Jesse is now unknown, the seventy weeks were fulfilled more than a thousand years ago, that wretched devastation of the people of Judah has taken place, and finally the Second Temple has been utterly thrown down and laid waste. And all the promises of God, however many there are, are in Christ "Yes and Amen": 2 Cor. 1.20. From this it is plainly demonstrated that the Messiah has already come, and that he is no longer to be expected, as the blind Jews expect him, except at that terrible judgment: Matt. 25.30-31; Luke 21.27-28; 1 Thess. 4.15-16; Heb. 9.28.

units.la: IIX. Quod officium Messiæ futurum, contra blasph mos Iudæos, qui eum mundano more regnaturum, & p steros Abrahæ amplissimis cumulaturum opibus & vol ptatibus somniant, qua in crassa opinione Apostolos e olim fuisse, ex Act.1.6. aliisque locis plurimis cöstat. Co tra hunc, inquam, errorem, notentur hi loci, qui officii Messiæ quale fuerit, ad viuum depingunt, Gen.3.15. & 3.& 4.9.Ps.2.12.Esai.6.v.6.7.& 25.8 & 35.10.& 40.v.10.11 53.v.4.5.Ier.23.6.& 31.v.31.32.& 33.8.& 50.20. Ezech.34 23.24.& 37.26. Dan.9.24. Oseæ 13 14. Abd.v.17.Mich.5 Nah.1.15. Abac.3.v.18.19. Agg.2.8.Zach.9.v.9.10.11.& 13 1.2.Malac. 3. 1. Vide CHRISTVS ante mundum conditu præordinatus, &c. à Deo missus, & quorsum.
units.tr: VIII. What was the office of the Messiah to be? This is contrary to the blasphemous Jews, who dream that he will reign in a worldly manner and will load the descendants of Abraham with the amplest riches and pleasures. That the Apostles too were once in this gross opinion is clear from Acts 1.6 and many other passages. Against this error, I say, let those passages be noted which depict vividly what the office of the Messiah was to be: Gen. 3.15; 4.9; Psal. 2.12; Isa. 6.6-7; 25.8; 35.10; 40.10-11; 53.4-5; Jer. 23.6; 31.31-32; 33.8; 50.20; Ezek. 34.23-24; 37.26; Dan. 9.24; Hos. 13.14; Obad. 17; Mic. 5; Nah. 1.15; Hab. 3.18-19; Hag. 2.8; Zech. 9.9-11; 13.1-2; Mal. 3.1. See CHRIST, foreordained before the foundation of the world, sent by God, and to what end.

units.la: IX. Quibus promissus & exhib tus Messias ? nem quòd ad participationem gratiæ, seu æternæ liberatio per Messiam consequendæ, non vni aut familiæ aut gen sed omnibus nationibus & gentibus, quæ sub cœlo su tam Iudæis, quàm Gentibus, Genef.3.15.& 12.3.& 26. 4. & 28.14.& 49.10.Ps.2.12.& 72.11. Esai.11.v.1.10. Aggæi 2 Malach. 1.11. quamuis hanc Iudæi præ reliquis gentib habuerint prærogatiuam, quòd apud ipsos depositæ su rint singulariter Dei promissiones de Semine benedić inter ipsos instituta sit politia pulcherrima, promissio bus seruiens, & ex ipsorum familia ortus sit Messias secu dùm carnem, vt explicat Apostolus, Rom.9.v.4.5.
units.tr: IX. To whom was the Messiah promised and exhibited? Namely, to the participation of grace, or of the eternal liberation to be obtained through the Messiah: not to one family or one nation only, but to all nations and peoples under heaven, both Jews and Gentiles: Gen. 3.15; 12.3; 26.4; 28.14; 49.10; Psal. 2.12; 72.11; Isa. 11.1-10; Hag. 2; Mal. 1.11. Although the Jews have had this prerogative above the other nations, that the promises concerning the Blessed Seed were deposited singularly among them, and a most beautiful polity was established among them, serving the promises, and the Messiah was born of their family according to the flesh, as the Apostle explains: Rom. 9.4-5.

units.la: X. Quo pacto Messias, antequam venit, promulgat nempe primùm ipsius Dei voce immediatè, Gen.3.15. De de per sanctos Patriarchas, qui ante & post diluuium su runt longo tempore & ordine custodes & propagato promissionis diuinæ de venturo Messia. Tertiò, constitu iam regno in populo Dei, per Prophetas Spiritu Dei flat latos, 2.Pet.1.21. Quarto, postquam Deus nullos amplius mitteret Prophetas, ob maximam sui populi ingratitudinem, praeconum suorum necem, idololatriam, &c. vt praedictum fuerat, Esaiæ 3.v.1.2. Amos 8.11. per pios quosdam viros, custodes ac Doctores Legis, ac veræ doctrinæ usque ad Messiæ aduentum in carne, quales fuerunt Esras, Nehemias, Iesus Syrach, Mathathias, Heli, Simeon, Zacharias, & alij multi. Quinto, & postremo, laus Deo, illuxit felicissimum illud Noui Testamenti seculum, in quo præmisso Ioanne Baptista præcursore, Elia in spiritu, Malachiæ 4.5. Matth.11.14. Lucæ 1.17. non autem in persona, Ioannis 1.21 statim apparuit Filius Dei, Malachiæ 3.1. Dominus noster Iesus Christus, Concionator dulcissimus, Mediator, Redemtor, Iustificator, & Saluator generis humani. Ac peracto sacrificio propitiatorio, emisit Apostolos in vniuersum terrarum Orbem ad prædicandum pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in nomine suo, Matth. 28, v.19.20. Marc.16.15. Luc.24.47. ascendensque in cœlos Luc.21.51. Eph.4.8. Pf.68.19. regnat in cœlestibus coeruans ministerium in hac vita, dona dans hominibus, Euangelistas, Pastores, Doctores, Diaconos, ad instaurationem Sanctorum, donec veniat in nouissimo die Iudex viuorum & mortuorum, Eph.4.v.10.11,12.
units.tr: X. In what way was the Messiah promulgated before he came? First, indeed, by the immediate voice of God himself: Gen. 3.15. Second, through the holy Patriarchs, who before and after the flood were, for a long time and in succession, guardians and propagators of the divine promise concerning the coming Messiah. Third, once the kingdom had been established among the people of God, through Prophets moved by the Spirit of God: 2 Pet. 1.21. Fourth, after God, because of the very great ingratitude of his people, the murder of his heralds, idolatry, and so on, no longer sent Prophets, as had been foretold: Isa. 3.1-2; Amos 8.11. He raised up certain pious men, guardians and Teachers of the Law and of true doctrine, right up to the coming of the Messiah in the flesh, such as Ezra, Nehemiah, Jesus the son of Sirach, Mattathias, Heli, Simeon, Zechariah, and many others. Fifth and last, thanks be to God, that most happy age of the New Testament dawned, in which, with John the Baptist as forerunner, Elijah in spirit (Mal. 4.5; Matt. 11.14; Luke 1.17, not in person, John 1.21), the Son of God, Malachi 3.1, our Lord Jesus Christ, the sweetest Preacher, Mediator, Redeemer, Justifier and Saviour of the human race, immediately appeared. And, when the propitiatory sacrifice was completed, he sent out the Apostles into the whole circuit of the earth to preach repentance and the remission of sins in his name: Matt. 28.19-20; Mark 16.15; Luke 24.47. Ascending into the heavens, Luke 24.51; Eph. 4.8; Psal. 68.19, he reigns in heavenly things, sustaining the ministry in this life and giving gifts to men: Evangelists, Ministers, Teachers, Deacons, for the building up of the saints, until on the last day he comes as Judge of the living and the dead: Eph. 4.10-12.

units.la: XI. Quomodo à mundo & in mundo excipiendus & tractandus? Gen.3.15. Num.21.8. (Ioan.3.14. eôdem spectat & Isaaci immolatio, Gen.22.9.) Pf.22.17 & 89.39. & 118.22. Matt.21.42. Marc.12.10. Luc.20.17. Esai.28.16. Actor.4.11. Rom.9 33.1.Pet.2.7. Vide & Ioan.1.v.10.11.) Esai.53.v.4.8. & Zach.11.12. Matth.26.15. Dan.9 26.
units.tr: XI. How is the Messiah to be received and treated by the world and in the world? Gen. 3.15; Num. 21.8 (John 3.14; the sacrifice of Isaac also looks to the same thing, Gen. 22.9); Psal. 22.17; 89.39; 118.22; Matt. 21.42; Mark 12.10; Luke 20.17; Isa. 28.16; Acts 4.11; Rom. 9.33; 1 Pet. 2.7. See also John 1.10-11; Isa. 53.4, 8; Zech. 11.12; Matt. 26.15; Dan. 9.26.

units.la: XII. An,& in quo impleta sit veritas promissionis? Im-metam eam esse, & quidem in Domino nostro Iesu Christo, nato & exhibito in carne, septem præcipua Noui Testamenti testimonia conuincunt. Primum testimonium de saluatore mundi, Messia, est Angelorum, quorum ministerio placuit primùm Deo vti ad reuelandum & deprædicandum hoc immensum reparationis generis humani opus, Ante conceptionem Messiæ, Luc.1.v.17.30.31. &c. Immægnata iam Maria matre Messiæ, Matth.1.v.20.21 Nato iam Messia, Luc. 2.v.10.11. λὐτρω in Ara crucis peccatis nostris debito persoluto, & tertia die resuscitato à mortuis, Matth. 28.v.5.6. Marc.16.v.5.6. Luc.24.v.4.5. Ioan.20.12. & in cœlos ad dexteram Patris elevato, Actor. 1.verf.10.11.
units.tr: XII. Whether, and in whom, was the truth of the promise fulfilled? That it has been fulfilled, and indeed in our Lord Jesus Christ, born and exhibited in the flesh, seven principal testimonies of the New Testament prove. The first testimony concerning the Saviour of the world, the Messiah, is that of the Angels, through whose ministry God was pleased first to use the revelation and proclamation of this immense work of the restoration of the human race: before the conception of the Messiah, Luke 1.17, 30-31, etc.; when Mary was already pregnant with the mother of the Messiah, Matt. 1.20-21; when the Messiah was already born, Luke 2.10-11; when the ransom [λύτρον] had been paid on the cross for our sins, and he had risen from the dead on the third day, Matt. 28.5-6; Mark 16.5-6; Luke 24.4-5; John 20.12; and when he had been raised into heaven to the right hand of the Father, Acts 1.10-11.

units.la: Secundum, est multorum piorum & sanctorum hominum quales fuerunt Zacharias, Luc.1.v.67.68. Elizabeth,v.4.5.43.44. Maria virgo, v.46.47. & Ioseph vir eius: Pastores Luc,2.v.15.&c.Simeon, v.28.29.Anna prophetissa,v.36.37.38.Magi,Matth.2.v.1.2. Martha Lazari soror, Iohan.11.2. Tertium,Ioannis Baptistæ,Iohan.1.29. Quartum,gravissimum,& veneratione dignissimum, omnique exceptionem malus est ipsiusmet Dei Patris testimonium, coelitus receditum, Matth. 3.17.& 17.5. Marc.9.7. Lucæ 9.35. Quintum sunt inusitata & stupenda facta & miracula à Christo edita, quæ per Messiam venturum edenda Prophetæ prædixerant, ad quæ ipse quoque Christus remittit, Ioh.10.25.&5.36.Matt.11.v.4.5.6. & alibi sæpe, iuxta vaticinium Esaiæ 35.v.5.6.Vide MIRACULA. Sextum est Euangelistarum & Apostolorum Christi:Petri,Matt.16.16.Act.2.36.&3.v.18.&4.v.11.12.&10.43. 1.Pet.1.v.19.20. Stephani Protomartyris, Act.7.52.Philippi, Act.8.32.ex Esaia 53.7. Pauli Act.9.22.&13.v.23.32.Rom.15.8.2.Cor.1.20.2.Timot.2.8. Ioannis Apostoli,1.Ioh.2.22.&5.v.2.15.
units.tr: Second, there are many pious and holy men, such as Zacharias (Luke 1.67, 68), Elizabeth (vv. 4, 5, 43, 44), the virgin Mary (vv. 46, 47) and her husband Joseph; the shepherds (Luke 2.15, etc.), Simeon (vv. 28, 29), the prophetess Anna (vv. 36, 37, 38), the Magi (Matt. 2.1, 2), and Martha, the sister of Lazarus (John 11.2). Third, there is the testimony of John the Baptist (John 1.29). Fourth, and most weighty and worthy of reverence, free from any exception, is the testimony of God the Father himself, given from heaven (Matt. 3.17; 17.5; Mark 9.7; Luke 9.35). Fifth, there are the unusual and wonderful deeds and miracles performed by Christ, which the prophets foretold would be performed by the coming Messiah, and to which Christ himself also points (John 10.25; 5.36; Matt. 11.4, 5, 6, and often elsewhere), in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah 35.5, 6. See MIRACLES. Sixth, there is the testimony of the evangelists and apostles of Christ: of Peter (Matt. 16.16; Acts 2.36; 3.18; 4.11, 12; 10.43; 1 Pet. 1.19, 20); of Stephen, the first martyr (Acts 7.52); of Philip (Acts 8.32, from Isaiah 53.7); of Paul (Acts 9.22; 13.23, 32; Rom. 15.8; 2 Cor. 1.20; 2 Tim. 2.8); and of the apostle John (1 John 2.22; 5.2, 15).

units.la: Addantur his alij etiam infiniti loci,in quibus Euangelistæ & Apostoli omnes Prophetias earumque circumstantias in Christo verè impletas esse, nec desiderari iam quicquam,abundè explicant. Primum enim affirmant,hunc IESVM Christum non tantùm verum & naturalem hominem pro nobis factum,conceptum & natum,sicut alij homines excepta originali labe: sed etiam esse in vna persona Deum, & Dei Patris verum & æternum Filium, Luc.1.v.31.32.33.Matth.3.17.Ioan.1.v 1.18.30.&3.16. Actor.3.13. Ioan.1.7.&5.5.Rom.1.3.&8.3.Galat.4.4.Hebr.13.8. Vide CHRISTVS Deus.Deinde affirmant, hunc Christum Messiam Dei Filium, natum esse verum ac naturalem hominem ex gente Iudaica, & quidem ex familia Abrahæ & Dauidis,secundùm promissionem,Luc.1.v.32.33.68. Matt.1.v.1.16.&2.2.Marc.10.47.Rom.1.3.Act.v.30.&c.2. Tim.2.8.Faciunt praeterea mentionem loci, in quo hic Messias IESUS Christus natus sit: in Bethlehem Iudææ scilicet, secundùm Scripturam,Mich.5.2.Matt 2.v.5.9.10.11. Luc.2.v.6.10.16.Quarto, Messiæ natiuitate non communi seu naturali,sed mirando modo factam esse describunt, Matt.1.20. de Spiritu Sancto, 1.18. priusquam conuenirent,ex Maria tantummodò desponsata natum esse, Luc.2.15. quam non cognouerit vir eius Ioseph, Matt.1.25.ideoque Ioseph pu tatiuus itiuus tantum pater Christi dicitur, Lucæ 3.23. Quinto, adunt & tempus natiuitatis Messiæ, Lucæ 2.v.1.2.4 6.7. quo gnificatur Christum Messiam exactis sepuaginta hebdomadibus, Dan. 9.24. in quarta Monarchia Romanorum, cum populus iam seruituti subiiceretur, natum esse. Sexto, officium etiam Messiæ adeo luculenter explicant, secundum omnia sacrarum literarum vaticinia: item quomodo populo suo, & mundo peruersissimo exceptus fuerit, vt non sit opus hic pluribus repetere. Vide CHRISTVS ratione triplicis officij, &c.
units.tr: Add to these the many other passages in which the evangelists and apostles fully explain that all the prophecies and their circumstances have truly been fulfilled in Christ, so that nothing is any longer lacking. First, they affirm that this Jesus Christ was made, conceived and born for us not merely as a true and natural man, like other men except in respect of original sin, but that he is also, in one person, God, the true and eternal Son of God the Father (Luke 1.31, 32, 33; Matt. 3.17; John 1.1, 18, 30; 3.16; Acts 3.13; John 1.7; 5.5; Rom. 1.3; 8.3; Gal. 4.4; Heb. 13.8). See CHRIST as God. Next, they affirm that this Christ, the Messiah, the Son of God, was born a true and natural man of the Jewish nation, and indeed of the family of Abraham and David, according to the promise (Luke 1.32, 33, 68; Matt. 1.1, 16; 2.2; Mark 10.47; Rom. 1.3; Acts 3.30, etc.; 2 Tim. 2.8). They also name the place where this Messiah, Jesus Christ, was born: Bethlehem of Judea, namely, according to Scripture (Mic. 5.2; Matt. 2.5, 9, 10, 11; Luke 2.6, 10, 16). Fourth, they describe the Messiah's birth as not common or natural but brought about in a wondrous manner: by the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1.20); (Matt. 1.18) before they came together, he was born of Mary, who was only betrothed (Luke 2.15); whom her husband Joseph did not know (Matt. 1.25); and therefore Joseph is called only the supposed father of Christ (Luke 3.23). Fifth, they also tell of the time of the Messiah's birth (Luke 2.1, 2, 4, 6, 7), by which it is signified that Christ the Messiah was born after the seventy weeks had been completed (Dan. 9.24), in the fourth monarchy of the Romans, when the people was already subject to servitude. Sixth, they explain the office of the Messiah so clearly, according to all the prophecies of the Holy Scriptures, and likewise how he was received by his own people and by a most perverse world, that there is no need to repeat more here. See CHRIST in respect of his threefold office, etc.

units.la: Septimum testimonium est pius veræ & catholicæ Ecclesiæ consensus inde ab Apostolorum & omnium sanctorum Patrum & Doctorum temporibus, qui singulis ætatibus à Messiæ natiuitate vixerunt. Item omnium orthodoxorum Conciliorum, sicut tria Symbola Ecclesiæ, Apostolicum, Nicænum & Athanasianum istud probè testantur. Et constat ex Historiis Ecclesiasticis, propter confessionem huius de Filio Dei Messia doctrinæ, multas myriadas Martyrum cum lætissimo beatissimóque vitæ exitu mortem pertulisse. Hæc testimonia breuiter cōmemorata adeò firma & certa sunt, vt eis portæ inferorum non præualeant. Conuincunt etiam indubiè cæcos & blasphemos deos, alium Messiam, hoc Christo Iesv reiecto, adhuc expectantes: pios verò, cùm euentum prophetiis planè consuere vident, corroborant, vt hunc Christum Iesvm, verum Messiam diuinitus missum agnoscant & amplectantur, ideóque pro tanto beneficio Saluatoris exhibiti grati sint: eum in aduentu suo altero glorioso, secundùm Scripturas iam instante, firma fide cum gaudio & lætitia Iudicem viuorum & mortuorum expectent.
units.tr: Seventh, the testimony is the pious consensus of the true and catholic Church from the times of the Apostles and of all the holy Fathers and teachers, who lived in every age since the birth of the Messiah. Likewise, the testimony is that of all orthodox councils, as the three creeds of the Church, the Apostles', the Nicene and the Athanasian, bear witness. And it is established by ecclesiastical histories that, on account of their confession of this doctrine concerning the Son of God the Messiah, many myriads of martyrs endured death with the most joyful and blessed end of life. These testimonies, briefly recalled, are so firm and certain that the gates of hell will not prevail against them. They also indubitably convict the blind and blasphemous Jews, who, having rejected this Christ Jesus, still await another Messiah. They strengthen the pious, when they see the event plainly corresponding to the prophecies, so that they acknowledge and embrace this Christ Jesus as the true Messiah sent by God, and are therefore thankful for so great a benefit of the Saviour revealed; and with firm faith, joy and gladness they await him as Judge of the living and the dead at his second, glorious coming, which according to the Scriptures is now at hand.

units.la: Nunc sequitur, vt de altera Messiæ & Saluatoris nostri Iesv Christi natura, nempe humana, dicatur.
units.tr: Now follows what must be said of the other, human nature of our Messiah and Saviour Jesus Christ.

units.la: CHRISTVS verus homo dicitur, Lucæ 23.47. Ioan. 1.14. Rom. 1.3.& 9.5. Colos. 1.22.1. Timoth. 2.5. & 3.16. Hebr. 2.v.11.14.15. Ioan. 4.2. Christus verus homo, quia filius Abrahæ, & semen eius, Matth. 1.1. Gal. 3.16. Heb. 2.16. Quia ex Tribu Iuda, Genes. 49.10. Hebr. 7.14. Apoc. 5.5. Quia filius & fructus Dauidis, 2. Sam. 7.12. Psalm. 89. versic. 36.37. & 132. 11. Matth. 1.1. Luc. 1.32. & 20.41. Act. 13.23. Roman. 1.3.2. Tim. 2. Apoc. 5.5. & 22.16. Quia radix Iesse, Esaiæ 11. v.1.10. Rom. 15.12. Quia ex Iudæis, 9.5. Quia semen mulieris, Genes. 3.15. Quia Filius Virginis Mariæ, & ex ea genitus. Esa.7.14.Matth.1.v.16 20.21 23. 25. & 2. v.11.20.21.& 12.46. Luc.1.31.& 2.48.& 8.20 Ioan.2.3 & 19.25. Act.1.14. Gal.4.4. Quia anima rationali & vero corpore constat : Anima Christi, Matth 26.38 & 27.50.Marc.14.34. Luc.23.v. 43.46. Quia corpore vero & nostris, excepto peccato, per omnia simili,Luc.24.39.Heb.2 v.14.17. Quia nostris infirmitatibus, secundum carnem obnoxius, Esaiae 53. 4. Hebr. 4.15. Quia natus est,Matth.2 2.Luc.2.7. Quia circuit,v.52. Quia parentibus subditus fuit,v.51.Quia esuriit,Matth.4.2.& 2. 18.Marc.11. 12. Quia fatigatus est, Ioann.4.6. Quia fleuit Lucae 19.41.Ioan.11.35.Quia loco certo &definito continetur,Matth.28.6.Luc.24.6. Act.3.21.Quia mortuus est,Matt 27.50.Luc.23.46.Quia a mortuis excitatus est, Matth 28.5.6.Marc.16.6.Lucae 24.6.Ioan.21.14.Actor.2. v.24.32. & v.15.26.1.Corinth.15.v.4.20.1.Petr.3.21. Quia ut ad coelum ascendei et,eum locum mutare oportuit,Ioann. 12.8.& 14.28.ut re ipsa fecit,Luc.24.51. Act.1.9.
units.tr: Christ is called a true man: Luke 23.47; John 1.14; Rom. 1.3 and 9.5; Col. 1.22; 1 Tim. 2.5 and 3.16; Heb. 2.11, 14, 15; John 4.2. Christ is a true man because he is a son of Abraham and his seed (Matt. 1.1; Gal. 3.16; Heb. 2.16); because he is of the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49.10; Heb. 7.14; Rev. 5.5); because he is the son and fruit of David (2 Sam. 7.12; Ps. 89.36, 37; Ps. 132.11; Matt. 1.1; Luke 1.32; 20.41; Acts 13.23; Rom. 1.3; 2 Tim. 2; Rev. 5.5; 22.16); because he is the root of Jesse (Isa. 11.1, 10; Rom. 15.12); because he is of the Jews (Rom. 9.5); because he is the seed of the woman (Gen. 3.15); because he is the Son of the virgin Mary and was begotten of her (Isa. 7.14; Matt. 1.16, 20, 21, 23, 25; 2.11, 20, 21; 12.46; Luke 1.31; 2.48; 8.20; John 2.3; 19.25; Acts 1.14; Gal. 4.4); because he consists of a rational soul and a true body, the soul of Christ (Matt. 26.38; 27.50; Mark 14.34; Luke 23.43, 46); because he has a true body, like ours in all things except sin (Luke 24.39; Heb. 2.14, 17); because he was subject to our infirmities according to the flesh (Isa. 53.4; Heb. 4.15); because he was born (Matt. 2.2; Luke 2.7); because he went about (Luke 2.52); because he was subject to his parents (Luke 2.51); because he hungered (Matt. 4.2; 21.18; Mark 11.12); because he was wearied (John 4.6); because he wept (Luke 19.41; John 11.35); because he is contained in a certain and defined place (Matt. 28.6; Luke 24.6; Acts 3.21); because he died (Matt. 27.50; Luke 23.46); because he was raised from the dead (Matt. 28.5, 6; Mark 16.6; Luke 24.6; John 21.14; Acts 2.24, 32; 5.15, 26; 1 Cor. 15.4, 20; 1 Pet. 3.21); because, to ascend to heaven, he had to change place, as he indeed did (John 12.8; 14.28; Luke 24.51; Acts 1.9).

units.la: CHRISTI diuinitas & humanitas in una Christi persona coniunctae, stituenda uniuntur,& coalescunt,Esai.7.14.& 9. 6. Matth. 1.23.Ioann.1.14.Roman.9.5.Phil.2.v. 6.7.1. Tim.3. 16. non confunduntur,Ioan.1.18.& 2.19.Rom.1.v 3.4 5. Col.1.19. 2.9.1.Tim.3.16.Heb.9.14.ad unionem earum demonstrandam, uni in persona, alterius proprietas, per idiomatum communicationem tribuitur,Ioan.3.13. Act.20.28.1. Co. 2.8.1.Ioann.1.1.& 3.16. Christi persona una est, a Patre distincta,Ioan.8.v.16.18.1. Cor.8.6.1. Tim. 2. 6. Christus Messias idem, Ioan.1.41.
units.tr: The divinity and humanity of Christ are joined and unite in the one person of Christ, and coalesce (Isa. 7.14; 9.6; Matt. 1.23; John 1.14; Rom. 9.5; Phil. 2.6, 7; 1 Tim. 3.16); they are not confounded (John 1.18; 2.19; Rom. 1.3, 4, 5; Col. 1.19; 2.9; 1 Tim. 3.16; Heb. 9.14). To show their union in the one person, the property of the one nature is attributed to the other by the communication of idioms (John 3.13; Acts 20.28; 1 Cor. 2.8; John 1.1; 3.16). The person of Christ is one and distinct from the Father (John 8.16, 18; 1 Cor. 8.6; 1 Tim. 2.5, 6). Christ and Messiah are the same (John 1.41).

units.la: CHRISTI personae attributa, officia significant,Ioann. 4.2.
units.tr: The attributes of Christ's person signify his offices, John 4:2.

units.la: Hoc titulo,tria filij Dei officia significantur.
units.tr: By this title three offices of the Son of God are signified.

units.la: Primo Regnum,cui inauguratur a Deo Psalm.2 6.& 4. v.7.8.Hebr.10.9. & ob id appellatur Rex, Iere, 23.5.Ezech. 21.v.26.27. Zachar.9.9.Matth.21.5.& 25 34. Luc.1.32.Ioan. 18.36.1. Cor.15.25. Rex aeternus,1.Paral.17.v.12.14.Psal.45. & 89.v.5.35.36.37.38.Esa.9.7.Dan.2.44. Luc.1.33. Hebr.1. Rex Israel & Iudaeorum, Matth.2.2.& 27.37. Marc.15.v. 26.Lice 23.3.Ioan.1.49.& 19.14.Rex iustitiae,Heb.7.2.Magnus,Apoc.12,5.Pacificus,Esa.9.7.& 11.6.& 65.25.Ezech.4 25. & 37. 26.Hebr. 7. 2.Rex Regum,Apocal.1.5.& 17.14. 19.16.
units.tr: First, the kingdom, to which he is anointed by God (Ps. 2:6; 4:7-8; Heb. 10:9), and for which he is called King (Jer. 23:5; Ezek. 21:26-27; Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:5; 25:34; Luke 1:32; John 18:36; 1 Cor. 15:25). He is the eternal King (1 Chron. 17:12, 14; Ps. 45; 89:5, 35-38; Isa. 9:7; Dan. 2:44; Luke 1:33; Heb. 1), the King of Israel and of the Jews (Matt. 2:2; 27:37; Mark 15:26; Luke 23:3; John 1:49; 19:14), the King of righteousness (Heb. 7:2), the Great (Rev. 12:5), the Peaceable (Isa. 9:7; 11:6; 65:25; Ezek. 4:25; 37:26; Heb. 7:2), and the King of kings (Rev. 1:5; 17:14; 19:16).

units.tr: Second, the Son of God is called Christ because he is anointed as the Teacher of the prophets (Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38). His prophetic office is described (Deut. 18:15; Matt. 21:11, 46; Luke 7:16; 24:19; John 4:19; 6:14; 7:40; 9:17; Acts 3:22; 7:37). To this belongs the fact that he acts as Teacher of his Church (Ps. 2:6-7; 22:23; 40:11; Isa. 55:4; Matt. 1:29; 17:5; 22:16; 23:8-10; Mark 13:14; Luke 6:40; 9:35; 10:22; 17:13; 21:15; 22:11; 24:32; John 3:2, 18, 38-39; 4:25; 11:28; 13:13; 17:6; 20:16). He is called Shepherd (Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34:23; Mic. 5:2; Zech. 13:7; Matt. 26:31; John 10:14; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 2:25), herald of the gospel (Isa. 60:1; 61:1; Matt. 15:5; Luke 4:18; Eph. 2:17; Heb. 2:3), announcer of peace (Zech. 9:10; Eph. 2:17), and the faithful witness of God (John 3:32; Rev. 1:5; 3:14).

units.tr: Third, the Son of God is called Christ because he is ordained as Priest (Ps. 110:4; Zech. 6:13; Heb. 2:17; 3:1; 4:14; 5:1, 5-6; 6:20; 7:17, 21, 26; 8:1; 9:24, 26; 10:1, 14, 21). Christ offers himself as the one sacrifice for us (Ps. 40:7-8; Matt. 20:28; Rom. 4:25; Gal. 2:20; Eph. 5:2; 1 Tim. 2:6; Tit. 2:14; Heb. 1:3; 7:27; 9:14, 26, 28; 10:3, 5-7, 10, 12, 14). For this reason he is called the Lamb. See below.

units.tr: Christ, by reason of his threefold office, kingly, prophetic and priestly (this threefold office is expressed in Heb. 2:10: the prophetic function is indicated by the word "bringing", the kingly by "Prince", and the priestly by "consecrating"), is the Mediator, that is, the Intercessor (Gen. 28:12; Hab. 3:3; Matt. 1:23; 21:22; Mark 11:24; Luke 22:32; John 1:52; 14:2, 6, 13-14; 16:23, 26; 17:9; 20:31; Acts 2:33; 4:12; 10:43; Rom. 3:25; 8:34; 2 Cor. 5:18-19; Gal. 3:20; Eph. 2:13-16, 18; 3:12; Col. 1:20, 22; 1 Tim. 2:5; Tit. 3:6; Heb. 4:15-16; 5:1, 5; 7:22, 25; 8:6; 9:14-15, 24; 13:15; 1 Pet. 1:3, 21; 2:5; 4:11; 1 John 2:1-2; 4:10). He is the Redeemer (Matt. 20:28; 1 Cor. 1:30; Gal. 3:13; 4:5; 1 Tim. 2:6; Tit. 2:14; 1 Pet. 1:19; Rev. 5:9). To this belongs the fact that he is called Saviour (Isa. 25:8-9; 62:11; Zech. 9:9; John 3:17; 4:42; 12:47; Acts 5:31; 13:23; Phil. 3:20; 1 Tim. 1:15; 2 Tim. 1:10; Tit. 1:3-4; 2:13; 3:6; Heb. 2:10; 5:9; 7:25). He is Saviour because he bore our sins (Isa. 53:4-6; 1 Pet. 2:24), and for this reason he is called the Lamb (Isa. 53:7; John 1:29, 36; Acts 8:32; 1 Pet. 1:19; Rev. 5:6, 12; 6:1; 7:9, 14, 17; 13:8; 14:1; 15:3; 17:14; 19:7, 9; 21:14, 22-23; 22:1, 3, 14). See LAMB.

units.tr: CHRIST was foreordained before the foundation of the world (1 Pet. 1:20), was slain (Rev. 13:8), and was promised to the Church (Gen. 3:15; 12:3; 18:18; 22:18-19; 26:4; 28:14; 49:10; Num. 24:17; Deut. 18:15; 2 Sam. 7:12, 14; Ps. 2:7; 72:17; 89:4-5; 132:11; Isa. 4:2; 7:14; 9:6-7, 10; 40:10; 49:1; 53:1-2; Jer. 23:5; Dan. 9:24; Mic. 5:2; Hag. 2:8; Zech. 3:8; 6:12; 9:9; Mal. 3:1; 4:2). See above the first of the twelve questions, "What are the divine promises," etc., placed under the heading "CHRIST with respect to substance," etc.

units.la: Officium Christi generatim definitur, Munus Mediatoris filio demandatum a Patre, a filio autem voluntarie receptum, & in utraque natura perfecte adimpletum, ut nos Deo, Deum nobis uniret & reconciliaret in aeternum.
units.tr: The office of Christ is generally defined as the mediatorial function committed to the Son by the Father, received voluntarily by the Son, and perfectly accomplished in both natures, so that he might unite us to God and reconcile God to us for ever.

units.tr: Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:18, 20; Luke 1:35) and born of the Virgin (Matt. 1:16, 23, 25; Luke 1:30-31; 2:7), in Bethlehem (Mic. 5:2; Matt. 2:1, 6; Luke 2:4-6). See above the questions, the fifth, sixth and seventh. He was circumcised (Luke 2:21) and presented to the Lord (2:22-23); he was adored by the Magi (Matt. 2:11); he was baptized by John (Matt. 3:15-16; Mark 1:9; Luke 3:21); he fasted in the wilderness for forty days and nights, and there was tempted by Satan (Matt. 4:2-3; Mark 1:13; Luke 4:2). He proclaimed the kingdom of God (Matt. 4:17, 23; 5:2; 9:35; 11:1; 13:54; 21:23; Mark 1:14-15, 21, 39; 2:2, 13; 4:1; 6:2, 6; 9:31; 10:1; 12:35; Luke 4:15, 31, 44; 5:3, 17; 13:10, 22; 19:47; 20:1, 21, 37; John 6:59; 7:14, 28; 8:2, 20). He baptized (John 3:22; 4:1-2). He was considered the son of Joseph (Matt. 13:55; Luke 3:23; 4:22; John 6:42). He fled from the honours of this world (John 6:15). He swore (Matt. 5:18, 26; 6:2). He washed the feet of the disciples (John 13:5). He read in the synagogue (Luke 4:16). He spoke in parables, and why (Matt. 13:3, 13; 23:37; Mark 4:11, 33-34; John 16:25). He cursed the fig tree (Matt. 21:19; Mark 11:14). He prayed to the Father (Isa. 53:12; Matt. 14:23; 26:39; Mark 1:35; 6:46; 14:35; Luke 3:21; 5:16; 6:12; 9:18; 11:1; 22:42; 23:34; John 11:41; 17:1, 9, 20). He paid tribute to Caesar (Matt. 17:27).

units.tr: He foretells his afflictions to his own from the beginning, and why: John 16:4; his death and resurrection: Matt. 12:40; 16:21; 17:9, 23; 20:19; 26:2, 32; Mark 8:31; 9:9, 12, 31; 10:33-34; 14:28; Luke 9:22, 44; 17:25; 18:33; John 2:19; 3:14; 8:28; 12:24, 32. He sits on a colt of an ass: Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:7; Mark 11:7; Luke 19:35; John 12:14. He is generously received by the people: Matt. 21:8-9; Mark 11:8-9; Luke 19:37-38; John 12:13. He is transfigured before three disciples: Matt. 17:2; Mark 9:2; Luke 9:28-29. He troubles himself: John 11:33; 13:21. He overcomes his enemies by his word: Isa. 11:4; 2 Thess. 2:8. Examples: he overcomes Satan: Matt. 4:4, 7, 10; the scribes and Pharisees: Matt. 22:20-23, 29-32; Mark 12:12; Luke 20:24-26; the Sadducees: Luke 20:37; the Pharisees: John 10:34; Matt. 22:42-44; Mark 12:18, etc.; Luke 20:27, etc.; the chief priests and elders of the people: Matt. 21:42. He is also said to destroy Antichrist by the breath of his mouth: 2 Thess. 2:8. See the reading of Holy Scripture, etc. He avoids the fury of his enemies: Matt. 12:15; Mark 3:7; Luke 4:30; 6:12; John 8:59; 11:54.

units.tr: Then he girds himself for death: Isa. 53:7; Matt. 20:28; 26:46; Mark 10:45; 14:42; Luke 18:32; John 10:12, 18; 12:27; 13:27; 18:4. He is valued at thirty pieces of silver and sold: Zech. 11:12; Matt. 27:3. He comes into the hands of his enemies: Matt. 26:50; Mark 14:46; Luke 22:54; John 18:12. Led to Annas, he is sent back to Caiaphas: John 18:13. He is questioned about his teaching: John 18:19. He is struck by a servant of the high priest: John 18:22. He confesses that he is the Son of God: Matt. 26:64; Mark 14:62; Luke 22:70. For this he is spat upon and mocked: Matt. 26:67; Mark 14:65; Luke 22:63-64. He is taken from Caiaphas to the Praetorium: John 18:28. He is brought before Pilate: Matt. 27:2; Mark 15:1; Luke 23:1. He is silent before him: Matt. 27:12; John 19:9. By his order he is scourged and condemned to death: Matt. 27:26; Mark 15:15; Luke 23:24-25; John 19:1-18. He bears his cross: John 19:17. He is crucified outside the gate between thieves: Matt. 27:38; Mark 15:27; Luke 23:33; John 19:18; 2 Cor. 13:4; Heb. 13:12; Isa. 53:12. Why he complains that he has been forsaken by God: Ps. 22:1; Matt. 27:46; Mark 15:34. He is given gall and vinegar to drink: Ps. 69:12; Matt. 27:34, 48; Mark 15:23, 36; Luke 23:36; John 19:29. He commends his spirit to the Father: Luke 23:46. Crying out with a loud voice, he expires: Matt. 27:50; Mark 15:37; Luke 23:46; John 19:30.

units.tr: <bl>Christ</bl>, why he died: Isa. 53:12; Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; John 11:52; 12:24, 32; Acts 20:28; Rom. 4:25; 5:8; 14:9, 15; 1 Cor. 5:7; 15:3; 2 Cor. 5:14-15; Gal. 1:4; 2:20; 3:13; Eph. 2:16; 5:25; Col. 2:13; 1 Thess. 5:10; 1 Tim. 2:6; Titus 2:14; Heb. 2:9, 14; 5:8; 9:26, 28; 1 Pet. 2:24; 1 John 1:7; 2:2; 3:16; Rev. 1:5; 5:9; 7:14. He is said to have died to sin: Rom. 6:10, not so that he might cease to sin, but so that he might destroy sin. "For no deceit was found in his mouth": Isa. 53:9. Offered as a sacrifice: Rom. 6:10; Heb. 7:27; 6:12, 26; 4:6; 10:5, 12, 14; 1 Pet. 3:18. He is buried: Matt. 27:59-60; Mark 15:46; Luke 23:53; John 19:41-42; Acts 13:29; 1 Cor. 15:4. He rose again: Matt. 28:5-6; Mark 16:6; Luke 24:6, 34, 46; John 21:14; Acts 2:24, 32; 3:15, 26; 4:10; 5:30; 10:40; 13:30, 33-34, 37; 17:31; Rom. 1:4; 4:24-25; 6:4; 8:11; 10:9; 1 Cor. 16:14; 5:20; 2 Cor. 4:14; 5:15; Gal. 1:1; Eph. 1:20; Phil. 2:9; Col. 2:12; 3:1; 1 Thess. 1:10; 4:14; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 1:21; by his own power: John 2:19; 10:17-18.

units.tr: After the resurrection he appears to the disciples: Matt. 28:9, 17-18; Mark 16:9, 12, 14; Luke 24:15, 34, 36; John 20:19, 26; 21:1, 14; Acts 1:2; 10:40-41; 13:31; 1 Cor. 15:5-7. See Ascension. Received into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father: Ps. 68:19; 110:1; Matt. 22:44; Mark 12:36; 16:19; Luke 20:42; 22:69; 24:51; John 6:62; 14:2; Acts 1:9; 2:33-34; 3:21; 5:31; 7:55; Rom. 8:34; Eph. 1:20; 2:6; 4:10; Col. 3:1; 1 Tim. 3:16; Heb. 1:3, 13; 4:14; 9:24; 10:12; 12:2; 1 Pet. 3:22. Christ is to be sought in heaven: Col. 3:1. Christ is absent from us in body: Matt. 26:11; Mark 14:7; John 12:8; 14:2-3, 28; 16:5, 7, 16; 17:11-12; 2 Cor. 5:8-9; Phil. 1:23; 1 Pet. 1:8. His absence is not unprofitable: John 16:7. He will be present with his Church forever by the presence of his Spirit, and with the body as a whole and with each member privately: Matt. 18:20; 28:20; John 6:65; 14:3, 18, 20, 23; 15:4; 17:23; Rom. 8:10-11; Gal. 2:20; Eph. 3:17; 4:10.

units.tr: Christ lives forever: Rom. 6:9-10; Heb. 7:25. He quickens the Church as the head quickens the members: Rev. 1:11; Eph. 1:22; 4:15; 5:23; Col. 1:18; 2:10, 19; Heb. 3:6. He is called the Paraclete [Παρακλητος], but in a quite different sense from the Holy Spirit. See Paraclete [Παρακλητος].

units.la: [Christus pro principe & liberatore populi sumitur, nempe Cyro, Esai. 45. 1. pro seruis Dei, 1. Paral. 16. 22. Psalm. 105, 15. Cyrus nominatur Christus Iehoua, i. consecratus a Deo in eum finem vt Iudaeos liberaret. Serui Dei sunt Christi iuncti & ordinati vt Deo seruiant in sanctitate & iustitia.]
units.tr: [Christ is taken for the prince and liberator of the people, namely Cyrus: Isa. 45:1; for the servants of God: 1 Chron. 16:22; Ps. 105:15. Cyrus is called the Christ of Jehovah, that is, anointed by God for the purpose of freeing the Jews. The servants of God are joined and ordained to Christ so that they may serve God in holiness and righteousness.]

units.tr: The coming of Christ is twofold. The first is in the flesh: Isa. 11:10; John 1:14; Rom. 1:3; 9:5; 15:12; Gal. 3:16; Eph. 4:10; Heb. 1:5; 10:5; 1 Pet. 1:20; 2 Pet. 1:16; 1 John 1:2; 4:2; 2 John 7. This first coming was humble, lowly and marked by the shame of the cross: Isa. 53:2-3, 7; 62:11; Zech. 9:9; Matt. 2:13; 8:20; 20:28; Mark 3:2; Luke 9:5, 8; 22:27; John 6:51; 7:10; 10:11; 13:3; Acts 8:32; Rom. 5:6; Phil. 2:7-8; Heb. 2:9.

Love towards his own (Matt. 8:14, 15; 9:36; 14:14; 15:32; 23:37; Mark 8:2, 3; Luke 13:34; John 10:15; 13:1; Rom. 8:37; Gal. 2:20; Eph. 3:19; 5:2, 25; Rev. 1:5). Baptism (Matt. 3:11; Luke 3:16; John 1:33). Kindness (Titus 3:4). Flesh as spiritual food (John 6:51, 53, 54, 55). Flesh as a veil (Heb. 10:20). Knowledge (Matt. 16:17; Eph. 1:17), how necessary it is (John 17:3). See KNOWLEDGE. Good confession (1 Tim. 6:13). Contempt (Isa. 53:3; Matt. 13:55, 56; Mark 6:3; Luke 4:22; 23:11; John 3:32; 6:42). How destructive is contempt of Christ (John 13:48; Heb. 6:5, 6; 10:29; 11:25; 1 Pet. 2:4, 8). See Denial of Christ. Christ's body is called a temple (John 2:21). It could not be corrupted (Ps. 16:10; Acts 2:27; 13:35, 37). Christ's body stands for the whole Church (Eph. 4:12).

His dignity and excellence (Matt. 3:11; 4:11; 12:6; 21:41, 42; 16:27; 26:53; Mark 1:7, 22; 3:12; 12:36; Luke 11:31, 42; 22:43; John 1:26; Col. 1:18; Heb. 1:4, 9; 3:3; 7:27). Love, and where it lies (John 14:15, 21, 23; 15:10, 21, 15, 16, 17). The disciples, who they are (Luke 14:26, 33; John 6:45; 8:31; 13:35; 15:8; Eph. 4:20, 21). Christ's divine power is not confined to his person but poured out through the whole body of the Church (John 14:12). The riches contained in the Gospel (Eph. 3:8). His doctrine, plainly divine and heavenly (Matt. 7:28; Mark 1:22; 11:18; John 3:34; 7:16; 8:38; 10:30; 14:10, 24; 17:14). It is common to all (Matt. 10:27; 13:37). It is irreproachable (John 8:46; 18:20, 21).

Victory distinguished over enemies (Ps. 110:2, 5; Isa. 11:4; Dan. 2:44; Matt. 24:44; John 16:33; Eph. 4:8; Col. 2:15; Rev. 17:14). Therefore zeal for the Church of Christ (Ps. 69:10; John 2:17).

units.la: CHRISTO omnia postponenda,Matt.10.37. Lucæ 9.verf.25.60.61.Christo nullus similis,Mar.2.12.Ioan.7.46. Christum iterum crucifigere, Heb 6.6.est Christum quasi rursus crucifixum ludibrio exponere. Cum Christo crucifigi vetus homo dicitur, Rom.6.6.hoc est, mori cum Christo, ipsi peccato, aut peccatum esse mortuum, nisi quis priori phrasi mortis genus explicatur. Christum induere, Rom. 13.14. Galat. c.27.metaphora sumta ex Hebræorum idi [illegible, ~2 letters]otismo, dicuntur fideles, eò quòd Ecclesiam Christo quàm quàm veste quadam operiri oportear, & sub eo delitescere, vt sancta sit prorsus & irreprehensibilis, Ephes.5.27. Ideoque Apostolus, Gal.3.16. semen Abrahæ vno Christi nomine significauit, quod idem explicatur, v.28. Christum induere, Philipp.3.8. est Christum loco omnium nan-ciscì, eoque potiri. Christum mori oportuit, Vide CHRI-STI mors.
units.tr: Everything must be put after Christ (Matt. 10:37; Luke 9:25, 60, 61). No one is like Christ (Mark 2:12; John 7:46). To crucify Christ again (Heb. 6:6) is to expose Christ, as it were, crucified anew, to mockery. To be crucified with Christ is said of the old man (Rom. 6:6), that is, to die with Christ, to sin itself, or for sin to be dead, unless the kind of death is explained by the former phrase. To put on Christ (Rom. 13:14; Gal. 3:27), a metaphor taken from the Hebrew custom of dressing, is said of the faithful, because the Church ought to be covered by Christ as with a certain garment and hidden under him, so that it may be wholly holy and irreproachable (Eph. 5:27). Hence the Apostle (Gal. 3:16) signified the seed of Abraham by the single name of Christ, which is explained in v. 28. To put on Christ (Phil. 3:8) is to gain Christ in place of everything and to possess him. It was necessary for Christ to die. See the death of CHRIST.

units.la: Cum Christo mori & resurgere, Rom.6.8. Col.3.1. est mortificari peccato, mundo, Legi denique elementis, atque adeò toti Legi: & resurrectio Christi participatione viuificari Deo, vt pluribus explicatur, Rom. 6. cap. Christum negare coram hominibus, quàm exitiale, Matt.10.33. Marc.8.38. Luc.9.26.& 12.9. 1.Tim.2.12.1.Ioan.2.23. Vide ABNEGATIO Christi. Christum nobis exéplar proponere debemus, Mat.20.28.Marc.10.45. Ioan.13.v.14.15. Rom.15.v.3.7. 2.Cor.8.9. Eph.4.32. Ephes.5.2. Philipp.2.5. Col.3.13. Heb.12.2.1.Pet.2.21.& 4.v.1.2. Ioan.2.6.& 3.16. Christum recipere honorificum, Ioan. 12.& 13.20. Iequi, vtile, Matt.8.22.& 19.v.21.28. Marc.10. Luc.9.v.59.60.& 18.22.Ioan.8.12.& 10.v.4.28.Heb.13.13. exempla. Petrus & Andreas, Mat.4.v.19.20. Iudæi & Ierosolymitani, Marc.1.5. Iacobus & Ioannes, Matth.4.v.21.22. turbæ, v.25. Discipuli, 8.23. Matthæus, Matt.9.9. Marc.2. Petrus, Matt.19.27.Luc.18.28.
units.tr: To die with Christ and rise again (Rom. 6:8; Col. 3:1) is to be mortified to sin, to the world, to the Law, finally to the elements, and so to the whole Law; and the resurrection of Christ is to be quickened to God by participation, as is explained at length in Rom. 6. To deny Christ before men, how destructive it is (Matt. 10:33; Mark 8:38; Luke 9:26; 12:9; 1 Tim. 2:12; 1 John 2:23). See Denial of Christ. We ought to set Christ before us as an example (Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45; John 13:14, 15; Rom. 15:3, 7; 2 Cor. 8:9; Eph. 4:32; 5:2; Phil. 2:5; Col. 3:13; Heb. 12:2; 1 Pet. 2:21; 4:1, 2; 1 John 2:6; 3:16). To receive Christ is honourable (John 12; 13:20). To follow him is useful (Matt. 8:22; 19:21, 28; Mark 10; Luke 9:59, 60; 18:22; John 8:12; 10:4, 28; Heb. 13:13). Examples: Peter and Andrew (Matt. 4:19, 20); the Jews and Jerusalemites (Mark 1:5); James and John (Matt. 4:21, 22); the crowds (v. 25); the disciples (8:23); Matthew (Matt. 9:9; Mark 2); Peter (Matt. 19:27; Luke 18:28).

units.la: Christo συμπάσχειν, & reliquias afflictionum eius replere in carne nostra dicimur, Col.1.24. hoc est, Christum habere socium afrumnarum nostrarum socium, ac proinde vindicam, Matt.9.4. Reliquiæ autem afflictionum Christi non sic accipi debent, quasi non plenè pro nobis satisfecisset, & poenam peccatis nostris debitam non abundè luisset & exhaustiet, sed membrorum Christi respectu id dicitur, vt sit inus. Reliquias afflictionum, &c. hoc est, quod superest afflictionum Christi. Christo autem passo in se (cuius vnius plagæ sanati sumus, Esai.53.5.) superest vt in suis etiam membris affligatur, non vt Ecclesiam redimat, quam sanguine suo iam acquisiuit, Act.20.28. & semel vna oblatione in æternum sanctificauit, Heb.10.14. sed vt virtutem suam in quotidiana suorum infirmitate exerat; denique totius corporis consolatione ac salute, vt mox ibidem subditur. Quod autem dicit Apostolus, Pro corpore, &c. quomodo sit accipiendum, ipsemet explicat, 2.Cor.1. v.5.6.& 4.v.8 9 10.&c.
units.tr: We are said to suffer with Christ [συμπάσχειν] and to fill up the remnants of his afflictions in our flesh (Col. 1.24). That is, Christ has us as partners in our hardships, and in turn we share his suffering, Matt. 9.4. Yet the remnants of Christ's afflictions must not be understood as if he had not fully satisfied for us, or had not paid in full and exhausted the punishment owed for our sins. The phrase refers to the members of Christ's body, so that the sense is: the remnants of his afflictions, that is, what remains of the afflictions of Christ. Since Christ suffered once in himself (by whose one wound we have been healed, Isa. 53.5), what remains is that he is afflicted also in his own members. This is not so that he might redeem the Church, which he has already acquired with his own blood (Acts 20.28) and has sanctified for ever by one offering (Heb. 10.14). Rather, he displays his power in the daily weakness of his people, and in the comfort and salvation of the whole body, as is added immediately afterwards. How the Apostle's words "for the body" are to be understood he himself explains (2 Cor. 1.5, 6; 4.8, 9, 10, etc.).

units.la: Christum tentare,1.Cor.10.9.est Christum velut ad tamen prouocare, vt ibidem explicatur, v.22. In Christo esse,Rom.16.7.est Christo per fidem insitum esse,idem clarat phrasis,In Christo inueniri,Philipp.3.9.
units.tr: To tempt Christ (1 Cor. 10.9) is to provoke Christ, as it is explained in the same place (v. 22). To be in Christ (Rom. 16.7) is to be grafted into Christ by faith. The same meaning is made clear by the phrase "to be found in Christ" (Phil. 3.9).

units.la: à CHRISTO multa sunt præter scopum eius ad nos aduenientia impiorum culpa, & eorum rebellionis occasione: sic addititia dissidiorum causa dicitur, Matt.10.34.Luc.12.9. Sic casum & ruinam multorum positus dicitur, Luc.2.34. lapis offensionis,Esa.8.14.Rom.9.v.32.33.1.Pet.2.v.7.8.
units.tr: Many things that come from Christ, beyond his purpose, come to us through the guilt of the ungodly and by the occasion of their rebellion. Thus discord is said to be an added cause of division (Matt. 10.34; Luke 12.51). Thus he is said to be appointed for the fall and ruin of many (Luke 2.34), a stone of stumbling (Isa. 8.14; Rom. 9.32, 33; 1 Pet. 2.7, 8).

units.la: à CHRISTO multa præter eius naturam suscepta, vnà cum vadis generis humani persona sunt: Quale est illud, quod maledictio,Gal.3.13 & peccatum dicitur,Rom.8.3.2.Cor.21.Sic vermis & opprobrium hominum,Psal.22.6.
units.tr: Many things taken up by Christ, beyond his nature, belong to his person together with the sins of the human race that he took upon himself as surety. Such is what is called a curse (Gal. 3.13) and sin (Rom. 8.3; 2 Cor. 5.21). So also he is called a worm and the reproach of men (Ps. 22.6).

units.la: à CHRISTO eadem ratione Deus Pater ipso maior agnoscitur,Ioan.14.28.eò referendum est, quòd Christus dicitur Angelus Testamenti, Malach.3.1. & Apostolus, Hebr.3. quòd Deus Pater,Deus Christi vocatur, Ioh.20.17.1.Cor.3.23.Eph.1.17. Sic obedientiam didicisse dicitur Christus Heb 5.8. Sic minister Circumcisionis, Rom.15.8.& sertus Patris,Esai.42.1.& 53.11.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, Christ is acknowledged to be less than God the Father (John 14.28). This must be referred to the fact that Christ is called the Angel of the covenant (Mal. 3.1), and the Apostle (Heb. 3.1). It also must be referred to the fact that God the Father is called the God of Christ (John 20.17; 1 Cor. 3.23; Eph. 1.17). So too Christ is said to have learned obedience (Heb. 5.8), to be the minister of the circumcision (Rom. 15.8), and the servant of the Father (Isa. 42.1; 53.11).

units.la: [CHRISTVS, Quæcunque de Christo dicta occurrunt in Scripturis Canonicis, ad hæc duo capita referri possunt: I. Aut enim dicuntur de Christi persona, II. aut de Officiis eius.
units.tr: [CHRIST] Whatever is said about Christ in the canonical Scriptures can be referred to two heads: I. for they are said either of the person of Christ, II. or of his offices.

units.la: In Christi persona sunt duæ naturæ, distinctæ, sed non separatæ, neque confusæ: Diuina,scilicet & humana. Est igitur Christus, Verus DEVS,quod sequentibus demonstrationibus probatur.
units.tr: In the person of Christ there are two natures, distinct but not separated, and not confused: namely, the divine and the human. Therefore, Christ is true God, which is proved by the following demonstrations.

units.la: II. Est Deus,quia cultu diuino adorandus, Psal.97.7.Heb.1.6. Ioan,5.23.Philip.2.10.Apoc.4.v.8.9.10.11.
units.tr: II. He is God, because he is to be worshipped with divine worship (Ps. 97.7; Heb. 1.6; John 5.23; Phil. 2.10; Rev. 4.8, 9, 10, 11).
III. Because he is eternal (Prov. 8.22; Mic. 5.2; John 1.1; 8.58; Col. 1.17, 18; 1 John 1.1; 2.13; Rev. 1.8, 17; 21.6; 22.17).

Resurrectionis est author, Ioan. 6.v.39.44.54.& 11.25. 1. 15.21.& Suscitauit seipsum, Rom.1.4. [?]. Spiritum Sanctum mittit, Ioan 16.7.& 20.20. Virtus eius plane diuinos effectus habet, Rom.15.v.18.19. Cor.12.9. Heb.1.3. Vnus est essentia cum Patre, Ioan.1.18.& 5.18.& 8.38.& 14. Philip.2.6.
units.tr: IV. He knows all things, even the secrets of the heart (Matt. 9.4, 26; 12.25; 15.8; 16.8; 17.17; 22.18; 14.13; Luke 5.22; 6.8; 7.47; 11.17, 39; 22.10; John 1.47; 2.24, 25; 5.42; 6.15, 61, 64; 11.14; 13.11, 19; 14.29; 16.4, 19; Rev. 2.2, 9, 13, 19; 3.1, 15). He is Creator (John 1.2; Col. 1.16; Heb. 1.2, 3; Rev. 3.14). He is the image of the Father (John 14.7, 8, 9; 2 Cor. 4.4; Col. 1.15; Heb. 1.3). He is to be invoked, and is invoked by the godly (Isa. 11; Matt. 18; Acts 7.59; 9.13, 14; 22.16; Rom. 1.7; 15.12; 1 Cor. 1.2; 2 Cor. 1.2, 3; Eph. 1.2; Gal. 1.3; Phil. 1.2; Col. 1.2; 1 Thess. 1.1; 3.11; 2 Thess. 2.16; 1 Tim. 1.2; 2 Tim. 1.2; Titus 1.4; Philem. 3; 1 Pet. 5.14; Rev. 22.20, 21). He is the object of faith (Isa. 8.14; 28.16; Matt. 28.19; John 2; 3.16, 36; 6.29, 35, 40, 47; 9.35; 14.1, 6; 17.3; Acts 16.31; 22.19; 24.24; Rom. 9.33; Gal. 2.16; Eph. 1.16; 1 Tim. 1.4; 2.5; 2 Tim. 2.3; 3.15). He is Almighty (John 3.31; 18.18; Rev. 1.8; 3.7; 4.8; 7.14; 19.15, 16). He has authority to forgive sins (Matt. 9.6; Mark 2.9; Luke 5.20; 7.48). He occupies places at the same time by his ubiquity (Matt. 18.20; 28.10; John 3; 3.13; 14.23). He is mighty with the same power as the Father (John 5.17, 19; 16.15). He bestows the power of working miracles (Matt. 10.8; Mark 6.7; 16.17; Luke 10.19; John 14.12; Acts 3.6, 12; 16; 14.3). He is the author of the resurrection (John 6.39, 44, 54; 11.25; 1 Cor. 15.21). He raised himself (Rom. 1.4). He sends the Holy Spirit (John 16.7; 20.20). His power has plainly divine effects (Rom. 15.18, 19; 2 Cor. 12.9; Heb. 1.3). He is of one essence with the Father (John 1.18; 5.18; 8.38; 14; Phil. 2.6).

units.la: [?]ristus verus Deus est, ita etiam aeterni Patris aeternus Fi- lius est agnoscendus, sicut ex sequentibus testimoniis col-ligimus. Ratione substantiae cum Patre idem, maiestatis aequalitate par, filiationis respectu a Patre reipsa distin-guitur. 2.Sam.7.14.1.Par.17.13.Psal.2.7.& 89 v.27.28. Ex Nouo Testamento, Matt.3.17.& 14.33.& 16.16.& 17.5.& 26.64.& 27.54.Marc.1.v.1.11.& 3.11.& 14.62.& 15.39. Luc.1.v.32.35.& 4.41.& 9.35. Ioan.1.v.14 18.34.49.& 3.v.16.17.18.& 8.18.& 10.36.& 11.4.27.& 17 v.1.20 31. Actor.3.13.& 8.37.& 9.20.& 13.33. Rom.1.v.3.4.9.Rom.8.v.3.29.32. 2.Cor.1.19. Gal.4.4. Eph.1.6.1.Thess.1.10. Heb.1.v.2.5.6.& 3.6.& 4.14.& 5.v.5.8. 6.& 7.28. & 10.29.2.Pet.1.17.1.Ioh.1.v.3.7.& 3.8.& 4.v. 9.14.15. & 5.v.5.9.10.11.12.Ioan.13.20. 2.Ioann.3. Apoc. 1.6.&2.v.18.28.
units.tr: As Christ is true God, so also he is to be acknowledged as the eternal Son of the eternal Father, as we gather from the following testimonies. In respect of substance he is the same as the Father, equal in the equality of majesty, and in respect of sonship he is really distinguished from the Father (2 Sam. 7.14; 1 Chr. 17.13; Ps. 2.7; 89.27, 28). From the New Testament: Matt. 3.17; 14.33; 16.16; 17.5; 26.64; 27.54; Mark 1.1, 11; 3.11; 14.62; 15.39; Luke 1.32, 35; 4.41; 9.35; John 1.14, 18, 34, 49; 3.16, 17, 18; 8.18; 10.36; 11.4, 27; 17.1, 20, 31; Acts 3.13; 8.37; 9.20; 13.33; Rom. 1.3, 4, 9; 8.3, 29, 32; 2 Cor. 1.19; Gal. 4.4; Eph. 1.6; 1 Thess. 1.10; Heb. 1.2, 5, 6; 3.6; 4.14; 5.5, 8; 6; 7.28; 10.29; 2 Pet. 1.17; 1 John 1.3, 7; 3.8; 4.9, 14, 15; 5.5, 9, 10, 11, 12; John 13.20; 2 John 3; Rev. 1.6; 2.18, 28.

units.la: Est etiam Christus verus Homo, vero corpore, & vera ama rationali constans: conceptus de Spiritu Sancto, Natus Maria virgine, sine labe peccati, tota vita iustus, sanctus, incens, obediens Patri usque ad mortem crucis, quod ita demonstratur.
units.tr: Christ is also a true man, consisting of a true body and a true rational soul, conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, without the stain of sin, wholly just, holy, innocent, obedient to the Father even to the death of the cross. This is shown as follows.

units.la: I. Nominatur & est verus homo, Luc.23.47. Ioann.1. Roman.1.3.&9.5. Coloss.1,22. 1.Timo.2.5.&3.16. Hebr.11.14. 1.Ioann.4.2. Ratio 1. est Filius & semen Abrahae Matthaei 1,1.Gal,3.16. Heb.2.16. Ex tribu Iuda, Gen.49. Heb.7.14. Apoc.5.5. Fructus ventris & Filius Davidis, 2.Samuel,7.12. Ps.89.v.36.37.&132.11. Luc.1.32. &20.41. Act.2.30. Rom.1.3.2.Tim.2.8. Apoc.5.6.&22.16. radix Iesse, Esa.11.10. Rom.15.12. Ex Iudaeis, Rom.9.5. semen mulieris, Gen.3.15. Filius mulieris virginis, Esai.7.14. Matth.1.v.16.20.21. &2. ver.11.21.23.&12.46. Lucae 1.31. &2.48. Ioann.3. &19.25. Act.1.14. Galat.4.4. Ratio 2. Anima rationali & vero corpore constat. Anima, Matthaei 26,38.&50. Luc.23.43.46. Corpore, Luc.24.39. Hebr.2. versic.17. nostris infirmitatibus secundum carnem obnoxius Esai.53.4.Hebr.4.15. Natus est, Matth.2.2. Luc.2.7. Crevit, Luc.2.52. parentibus fuit subditus, Luc.2.51. Esuriit Matth.4.2.&21.18.Marc.11.12. fatigatus est, Ioan.4. fleuit, Luc.14.41. Ioan.11.35. loco certo & definito continetur, Matth.28.6. Luc.24.6. Actor.3.21. Mortuus est Matth.27.50,Luc.23.46. Resurrexit a mortuis, Matth.28.v.5.6. Marc.16.6. Luc.24.6. Ioann.21.14. Actor.2.vic.24.32.&3.vers.15.26.1. Corinth.15, versic.4.1.Pet.3.21. Ascendit ad coelos, Ioan.12.8.&16.28. Luc.24.51. Act.1.9.
units.tr: I. He is named and is a true man (Luke 23.47; John 1; Rom. 1.3; 9.5; Col. 1.22; 1 Tim. 2.5; 3.16; Heb. 11.14; 1 John 4.2). Reason 1: he is the Son and seed of Abraham (Matt. 1.1; Gal. 3.16; Heb. 2.16); of the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49; Heb. 7.14; Rev. 5.5); the fruit of the womb and Son of David (2 Sam. 7.12; Ps. 89.36, 37; 132.11; Luke 1.32; 20.41; Acts 2.30; Rom. 1.3; 2 Tim. 2.8; Rev. 5.6; 22.16); the root of Jesse (Isa. 11.10; Rom. 15.12); of the Jews (Rom. 9.5); the seed of the woman (Gen. 3.15); the Son of the virgin woman (Isa. 7.14; Matt. 1.16, 20, 21; 2.11, 21, 23; 12.46; Luke 1.31; 2.48; John 3; 19.25; Acts 1.14; Gal. 4.4). Reason 2: he consists of a rational soul and a true body. Soul (Matt. 26.38, 50; Luke 23.43, 46). Body (Luke 24.39; Heb. 2.17). He was made subject to our infirmities according to the flesh (Isa. 53.4; Heb. 4.15). He was born (Matt. 2.2; Luke 2.7); he grew (Luke 2.52); he was subject to his parents (Luke 2.51); he hungered (Matt. 4.2; 21.18; Mark 11.12); he was weary (John 4); he wept (Luke 19.41; John 11.35); he is contained in a certain and defined place (Matt. 28.6; Luke 24.6; Acts 3.21); he died (Matt. 27.50; Luke 23.46); he rose again from the dead (Matt. 28.5, 6; Mark 16.6; Luke 24.6; John 21.14; Acts 2.24, 32; 3.15, 26; 1 Cor. 15.4; 1 Pet. 3.21); he ascended into heaven (John 12.8; 16.28; Luke 24.51; Acts 1.9).

units.la: Hactenus de duabus Christi Naturis, de Persona vero naturis constante agendum. Naturarum unio & distinctio demonstratur in una persona, Esai.7.14.&9.6. Matth.1. Ioan.1.14. Roman.9.5. Philip.2. vers.6.7. 1. Timoth.3.16. Non confunduntur naturae, Ioann.1.18.&2,19. Rom.1.ver.3.4.5. Coloss.1.19.&2.9. 1.Timoth.3.16. Hebr.9.14. unionem illam demonstrandam toti personae alterius naturae proprietas, per idiomatum communicationem tribuitur, Ioann.3.13. Actor.20.28. 1.Corint.2.8.1. Ioann.1.&3.16.
units.tr: Thus far concerning the two natures of Christ; now the person, consisting of the two natures, must be treated. The union and distinction of the natures is shown in one person (Isa. 7.14; 9.6; Matt. 1; John 1.14; Rom. 9.5; Phil. 2.6, 7; 1 Tim. 3.16). The natures are not confused (John 1.18; 2.19; Rom. 1.3, 4, 5; Col. 1.19; 2.9; 1 Tim. 3.16; Heb. 9.14). That union is shown by the communication of idioms, whereby a property of the other nature is attributed to the whole person (John 3.13; Acts 20.28; 1 Cor. 2.8; 1 John 1; 3.16).

units.la: Nunc agendum est de Christi Officiis, nempe Regio, Prophetico & Sacerdotali.
units.tr: Now we must treat of the offices of Christ, namely the kingly, the prophetic and the priestly.

units.la: I. De regno Christi.
units.tr: I. On the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: 1. Inauguratur Rex à Deo Patre, Psal.2.6. & 45.v.5.9. Heb.1.9. Ob id Rex appellatur, Ier.23.25. Ezech. 21.v.26. Zach.9.9. Matt.21,5.& 25.34. Luc.1.32. Ioan.18.36.1.Cor.15.25. Rex æternus, 1. Paral.17.v.12.14.& 45.8.& 89. v.35.36.37. Esai. 9. 7. Daniel, 2.44. Luc. 1. 33. Hebr. 1.8. Rex Israel & Iudæorum, Matth.2.2.& 27.37. Luc.23 3. Iohann. 1.39. & 19.16. Rex iustitiæ, Heb. 7.2. Magnus, Pacificus, Esai. 9.7.& 11.6. & 65.25. Ezech.34. & 37.26. Hebr.7.2. Rex regum, Apocal. 1.5.& 17.14..& 16.
units.tr: 1. The King is anointed by God the Father: Ps. 2:6; 45:5, 9; Heb. 1:9. For this reason he is called King: Jer. 23:25; Ezek. 21:26; Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:5; 25:34; Luke 1:32; John 18:36; 1 Cor. 15:25. He is the eternal King: 1 Chron. 17:12, 14; Ps. 45:8; 89:35–37; Isa. 9:7; Dan. 2:44; Luke 1:33; Heb. 1:8. He is King of Israel and of the Jews: Matt. 2:2; 27:37; Luke 23:3; John 1:49; 19:16. He is the King of righteousness: Heb. 7:2. Great and Peaceful: Isa. 9:7; 11:6; 65:25; Ezek. 34; 37:26; Heb. 7:2. He is King of kings: Rev. 1:5; 17:14; 19:16.

units.la: 2. De Prophetia Christi.
units.tr: 2. On the prophecy of Christ.

units.la: Propheta & Doctor vngitur, Esai.61.1. Luc.4.18. Act.10. Describitur eius prophetia, Deut.18.15. Matt.21.11.46. Luc.3.16. & 24.9. Ioan.4.19.& 6.14.& 7.4.& 9.17. Actor.3.22.& 7.37. Eo pertinet quod Ecclesiæ suæ Doctorem a-quem Ps.2.6.& 22.23.& 40.12.& 55.4. Matth.11.2.& 17.5.& 22.23. v.8.10. Marc.13.14. Luc. 10.22. & 17.13.& 21.15.& 24.32. Ioan.1.v.18.38.& 3.2.& 4.25.&11.28.& 13.13. 17.6.& 20.16. Pastor dicitur, Esai.40. 11. Ezech. 34. 23. Anch. 5. 2. Matthæi, 2,7. Zachar. 13. 7. Matth. 26.31. Iohann. 10. verf.11. 14. Hebr. 13. 20. 1. Petr. 2. 25. & 5. Euangelij præco, Matthæi 11.5. Lucæ 4.18. Ephes. 2. Hebr. 2. 3. Pacis annunciator, Zachar. 9. 10. Ephes. 7. Dei fidelissimus testis, Ioann. 3 32. Apocalyp.1.5.& 4.
units.tr: The Prophet and Teacher is anointed: Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18; Acts 10. His prophetic office is described: Deut. 18:15; Matt. 21:11, 46; Luke 3:16; 24:19; John 4:19; 6:14; 7:40; 9:17; Acts 3:22; 7:37. To this belongs the fact that he is the Teacher of his Church: Ps. 2:6; 22:23; 40:12; 55:4; Matt. 11:2; 17:5; 22:23; Mark 13:14; Luke 10:22; 17:13; 21:15; 24:32; John 1:18, 38; 3:2; 4:25; 11:28; 13:13; 17:6; 20:16. He is called the Minister (Shepherd): Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34:23; Amos 5:2; Matt. 2:7; Zech. 13:7; Matt. 26:31; John 10:11, 14; Heb. 13:20; 1 Pet. 2:25; 5. He is the herald of the gospel: Matt. 11:5; Luke 4:18; Eph. 2; Heb. 2:3. He is the announcer of peace: Zech. 9:10; Eph. 2:7. He is the most faithful witness of God: John 3:32; Rev. 1:5; 4.

units.la: 3. De Sacerdotio Christi.
units.tr: 3. On the priesthood of Christ.

units.la: Sacerdos æternus ordinatur, Psalm.110.5. Zachar. 6.13. Tit. 2.v.6. Heb.2.17. & 3.1.& 4.14 & 5.v.1.5.6.& 6.20. & 7.17.21.26.& 8.1 & 9.v.11 14.26.28.& 10 21. Vnicum pro vobis sacrificium, nempe seipsum, offert. Psalm.40.10. Matth. 20,24. Rom.4.25. Galat.2.20. Ephes.5.2.1.Timot. 1.Tit.2.14.Heb.1.3.& 7.27.& 9. v.14.26.28.& 10.verf.3. 7. 10. 14. Ob id Agnus (nempe Dei, mysticus) vocitur, Esai.53.7.Ioann.1.verfic.29.36. Actor.8.32, 1.Petr. 1.19. Apocalyp. 5. v. 6. 12. & 6. 1. & 7. v. 9, 12. 17. & 14. 1. 15.3.& 17. 14. & 19. verf. 7. 9. & 21. v. 14. 22. 23. & 22. 1.1.3.
Ratione autem triplicis huius Officij Christus est Dei & hominum MEDIATOR Redemtionis & Intercessionis.
units.tr: Christ is therefore the Mediator between God and men, by reason of this threefold office, of redemption and of intercession.

units.la: De duplici Statu Christi, nempe Humiliationis & Exaltationis.
units.tr: On the Twofold State of Christ, namely of Humiliation and of Exaltation.

units.la: I. Christi Officium Sacerdotale in statu humiliationis fuit tum satisfaciendo, tum intercedendo pro Ecclesia De Satisfaciendo, videlicet ab articulo conceptionis & nativitatis vsque ad mortem crucis: Intercedendo, Ioan.17.& Luc.22.32.&c.
units.tr: I. Christ's priestly office in the state of humiliation consisted both in making satisfaction and in interceding for the Church. Satisfaction ran from the moment of his conception and birth to his death on the cross. Intercession is shown in John 17 and Luke 22:32, etc.

units.la: II. Officium Propheticum in eodem humiliationis statu executus est, dum ipse voce sua docuit, quantum quid docere & scire fas erat,& praesenti statui conueniebat. Itaque de die extremo secundum humanam naturam nescivit, nec docuit, Marc.13.32. quia vt sciret & doceret non postulabat praesens status & officij executio. Docuit autem primum extraordinarie, deinde ordinarie. Extraordinarie in adolescentia ante solemnem inaugurationem, anno aetatis 12. vt futuri ministerij quoddam esset quasi praeludium, Luc. 2.17. Ordinarie, postquam caelitus a Patre inauguratus est, Matt.3.17. anno aetatis tricesimo, Luc.3.23. Ascic docuit annis quatuor, cum authoritate, non vt scribae Matt.7.29.& Luc.4.32. docuit legem, ita vt eam interpretaretur, & a corruptelis purgaret, Mat.5.v.21.22.&c. Euangelium docuit ita, nempe vt de opere redemtionis, de beneficiis Messiæ in genus humanum, & omnibus rebus ad salutem necessariis explicaret, ac non solùm promiscuè auditorum sensus feriret, sed etiam animos electorum peculiariter illuminaret. Ita docuit Euangelium in ministerio verbi & Sacramentorum. In ministerio verbi, sicut passim in historia Euangelica commemoratur. In ministerio sacramentorum, vt quod corpus suum panem vitæ, & panem mysticum corpus suum appellauit, Ioann. 6. v. 48. 50. 51. &c. Matth. 26. 26.
units.tr: II. In the same state of humiliation he discharged his prophetic office, since he taught by his own voice as much as it was right to teach and to know, and as his present condition required. Accordingly, as a man, he did not know the last day and did not teach it (Mark 13:32), because his present state and the discharge of his office did not call for him to know and teach it. He taught first in an extraordinary way and then in an ordinary way. He taught extraordinarily in his youth, before his solemn inauguration, in his twelfth year, so that his teaching would be a kind of prelude to his future ministry (Luke 2:17). He taught ordinarily after he was inaugurated from heaven by the Father (Matt. 3:17), in his thirtieth year (Luke 3:23).
