Afterwards he taught for four years, with authority and not as the scribes (Matt. 7:29; Luke 4:32). He taught the law in such a way that he interpreted it and purged it of corruptions (Matt. 5:21–22, etc.). He taught the gospel in such a way that he explained the work of redemption, the benefits of the Messiah for the human race, and all things necessary for salvation. He did not merely strike the hearing of his hearers in a general way, but also specially illuminated the minds of the elect. Thus he taught the gospel in the ministry of the Word and of the sacraments. He taught it in the ministry of the Word, as is recorded everywhere in the gospel history. He taught it in the ministry of the sacraments, when he called his body the bread of life, and the mystical bread his body (John 6:48, 50, 51, etc.; Matt. 26:26).

units.la: III. Officium Regium in statu humiliationis executus est modicè, dum gloriam suam, quantum temporis illius & muneris sacerdotalis humiliter obeúdi ratio ferebat, patefecit.
units.tr: III. In the state of humiliation he exercised his kingly office only sparingly, in that he revealed his glory only as far as the time and the duty of his priestly office, carried out in humility, allowed.

units.la: Nam officium regium hîc cedere officio sacerdotali debuit: quia officium sacerdotale plenè in his terris exequendum erat. Hanc obedientiam & satisfactionem Christi officium eius Regium minimè impedire debuit: impeiuisseт autem si plenè perfectéque, vt nunc officium illud administratum fuisset. Nam si Dominum gloriæ cognouissent, nunquam crucifixissent, 1. Corinth. 2. 8. Itaque sic vtrunque officium Sacerdotale & Regium Christus administrauit, & sic veluti temperauit, vt & Sacerdotis partes perfectè implerer in his terris, & se non hominem tantùm, sed simul verum Deum, & dominum omnium, ac regem esse, satis pro isto tempore ostenderet, præsertim in miraculis, atque adeò id faceret, quod tum electis ad cognoscendum Messiam satis esset, tum reprobos inexcusabiles redderet. Atque hæc causa fuit, cur publicari interdum miracula à se edita vetuerit, ne si ante tempus innotesceret, officij sacerdotalis executio hoc modo impediretur. Hinc etiam est, quòd Christus formam serui accepisse dicitur, Philip. 2. 7. quia cùm doriam & maiestatem suam diuinam exerere à momento natiuitatis plenè perfectéque potuisset, tamen non exiit vsque ad tempus exaltationis, sed magis vt seruum se gessit.
units.tr: For the kingly office had to give way here to the priestly office, because the priestly office had to be fully carried out on this earth. The kingly office ought not to have hindered this obedience and satisfaction of Christ; it would have hindered it had it been exercised fully and perfectly, as it is now exercised. For if they had known the Lord of glory, they would never have crucified him (1 Cor. 2:8). So Christ administered both the priestly and the kingly office in such a way, and so tempered them, that he fully fulfilled the part of the priest on earth, and sufficiently showed, for that time, that he was not only a man but at the same time the true God, and lord and king of all. This he did especially through miracles, and did so in such a way as to be enough for the elect to recognise the Messiah, and yet to render the reprobate inexcusable. This was also the reason why he sometimes forbade the miracles he performed to be made public, lest, if they became known before the proper time, the execution of his priestly office should be hindered in this way. Hence it is also said that Christ took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), because, although he could have displayed his glory and divine majesty fully and perfectly from the moment of his birth, he did not put them forth until the time of his exaltation, but rather conducted himself as a servant.

units.la: Porrò Officij regij opera, quæ fecit Christus in hoc statu, fecit secundùm diuinam quidem naturam, vt iam gloriam ac maiestatem diuinam in humana natura quamuis infirmitatibus adhuc obnoxia, patefaceret: secundùm humanam verò naturam, vt sicut à Deitate illuminabatur & ducebatur, & sicut statui isti conueniebat, aperet. Ipsi enim secundùm diuinam naturam semper operatus est vnà cum Patre in rerum omnium conseruatione & gubernatione, sicut ipse de se testatur, Ioann.5.17. tamen in humana assumta natura non semper nec plene exeru maiestatem suam diuinam, sed modicè, prout statui il conueniebat. Itaque multa supernaturaliter sciebat, quae do volebat, & officij ratio postulabat, Ioann. 2.25. & 6.6. At rursus vt non semper, nec plene, sed modice faciebat opera huius officij regij, ita non omnia sciebat, sed quaedam naturaliter ignorabat, secundùm humanam naturam quae, si voluisset, vt Deitatis suae scire sanè potuisset, Mar. 11.13. Ioan.11.34.
units.tr: Moreover, the works of the kingly office that Christ performed in this state he performed, indeed, according to the divine nature, so as to reveal the divine glory and majesty in a human nature still subject to infirmities. But according to the human nature he performed them so as to disclose them as he was illuminated and led by the Godhead, and as was fitting for that state. For according to the divine nature he always worked together with the Father in the preservation and government of all things, as he himself testifies (John 5:17). Yet in the human nature he assumed, he did not always nor fully put forth his divine majesty, but only sparingly, as that state required. Thus he knew many things supernaturally, which he was willing to teach and which the reason of his office demanded (John 2:25; 6:6). But again, just as he did not always nor fully, but only sparingly, perform the works of this kingly office, so he did not know all things; in his human nature he naturally did not know some things, which, had he willed it, he could certainly have known by virtue of his Godhead (Mark 11:13; John 11:34).

units.la: Opera autem officij regij fecit, alia externa, alia interna. Externa, nempe miracula, ea quae tum in vita, tum in morte sua. In vita, vt quod aquam in vinum converti, quòd ambulauit super aquis, quòd subitò transfigurat us est in monte, quòd sanauit aegrotos, excitauit mortuos, &c. In morte sua, vt quod velum templi à summo ad imum diruptt, terram concussit, eclipsin solem & tenebras super vniuersam terram induxit, non in coniunctione Solis & Lunae, seu in nouilunio, quod naturale est: sed in oppositione Solis & Lunae, id est, in plenilunio, quod est contra omnem naturam, denique mortuos e sepulcris excitauit. Quae omnia prolixè ab Euangelistis describuntur.
units.tr: He performed works of the kingly office, some external and some internal. External works were miracles, both those in his life and those in his death. In his life, such as turning water into wine, walking upon the waters, being suddenly transfigured on the mountain, healing the sick, raising the dead, etc. In his death, such as the tearing of the temple veil from top to bottom, the shaking of the earth, the eclipse of the sun and the darkness that covered the whole earth, not at a conjunction of the sun and moon, that is at the new moon, which is natural, but at an opposition of the sun and moon, that is at the full moon, which is against all nature; and finally the raising of the dead from their graves. All these things are described at length by the evangelists.

units.la: Interna opera officij regij fecit, vt quod Apostolos & alios efficaciter vocauit, vt relictis omnibus vocantem sequerentur, Ioan.1.41. Matt.4.17. quòd in ministerio verbi magis ac magis in eis efficax fuit, & sibi ceu viti palmites vniuit, Ioan.15.5. quòd generatim omnes qui crederent iustificauit voce sua: qui non crederent damnauit, Ioann. 3. 18.36. quòd latronem conuersum in paradisum transtulit, & salute aeterna donauit, Luc.23. 43. quòd Phariseos, Scribas, & alios, propter antecedentem ingratitudinem, incredulitatem, & contumaciam, vt iusto suo iudicio excaecauit & induravit, Ioann. 12. 40. quòd Iudam proditorem, vt iustus iudex grauiter puniret & à se desertum Satanae tradidit, Ioann.13.2. & 17.12. Matt. 27.5. Act.1.16.
units.tr: He performed internal works of the kingly office, such as effectually calling the apostles and others, so that, having left everything, they followed him who called them (John 1:41; Matt. 4:17). Such as becoming more and more effective in them through the ministry of the Word, and uniting them to himself as the branches to the vine (John 15:5). Such as justifying by his voice all who believed in general, and condemning those who did not believe (John 3:18, 36). Such as transferring the converted thief into paradise and granting him eternal salvation (Luke 23:43). Such as blinding and hardening the Pharisees, scribes and others, on account of their prior ingratitude, unbelief and obstinacy, by his just judgment (John 12:40). Such as delivering Judas the traitor over to Satan, after he had been deserted by him, so that the just judge might punish him severely (John 13:2; 17:12; Matt. 27:5; Acts 1:16).

units.la: Gradus humiliationis Christi sunt 1. Obedientia à conceptione doloribus grauissimis ad mortem crucis usque comitata. 2. Sepultura. 3. Descensus ad inferos. De his supra item in voc. OBEDIENTIA, SEPVLTVRA, DESCENSVS Nunc de altero statu, nempe Exaltationis, agendum. Hic autem tres gradus oppositos continet.
units.tr: The degrees of Christ's humiliation are: (1) obedience, accompanied from his conception through the most grievous sufferings to the death of the cross; (2) burial; (3) descent into hell. These have been treated above, likewise under the headings OBEDIENCE, BURIAL, DESCENT. Now we must treat of the other state, namely of exaltation. This state contains three opposite degrees.

units.la: 1. Primus gradus exaltationis Christi est Resurrectio a mortuis & mansio 40. dierum in his terris. Hoc gradu, secundum humanam naturam, virtute Deitatis ipse reunius-cens, tertia die, victor mortis gloriosè exiit è sepulchro testibus Euangelistis, Matt. 28. Marc. 6. Luc. 24. Ioan. 20. Rom. 1. 4. 1 Cor. 15. v. 1. 2. &c. 1. Pet 3. 18. Tribus personis tribuitur haec resuscitatio, Rom. 6. 4. Col. 2. 12. Ephes. 2. 0. Filio nempe ut intelligatur eum propria virtute non aliena resurrexisse, Ioan. 2. 19 & 10. 18. Nam illud mortuum & etiam ab anima separatum corpus, filio Dei vnitum manebat, & filij Dei corpus erat. Patri & Spiritui Sancto etiam tribuitur, quia potentia illa & virtus, qua resuscitatus est Christus, tribus personis essentialiter est communis. Vide Act. 2. v. 24. 36. & 3. v. 13. 15. 26. & 5. v. 30. 31. & 13. v. 30. 33. 37.
units.tr: 1. The first degree of Christ's exaltation is his resurrection from the dead and his stay of forty days on this earth. In this degree, according to his human nature, reuniting himself by the power of the Godhead, on the third day he gloriously came forth from the sepulchre as victor over death, as the evangelists witness (Matt. 28; Mark 16; Luke 24; John 20; Rom. 1:4; 1 Cor. 15:1–2, etc.; 1 Pet. 3:18). This resurrection is attributed to all three persons (Rom. 6:4; Col. 2:12; Eph. 1:20). To the Son, so that it may be understood that he rose by his own power and not by another's (John 2:19; 10:18). For that dead body, separated also from the soul, remained united to the Son of God, and was the body of the Son of God. It is also attributed to the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the power and virtue by which Christ was raised is essentially common to the three persons. See Acts 2:24, 36; 3:13, 15, 26; 5:30–31; 13:30, 33, 37.

units.la: In resurrectione igitur vtriusque naturae actiones vnitè quidem, sed tamen distinctè, concurrebant ad vnum effectum commune producendum. Nam secundum diuinam naturam Christus effecit resurrectionem, id est resuscitauit: secundum humanam naturam proprie resurrexit, Deo corpus resuscitanti obsequens, & pro eius voluntate & virtute sese mouens: vnde effectum commune extitit, nempe victoria, 1. Cor. 15, 54.
units.tr: In the resurrection, therefore, the actions of both natures concurred, indeed united yet distinctly, to produce one common effect. For according to the divine nature Christ effected the resurrection, that is, he raised himself up; according to the human nature he properly rose again, obeying God who raises the body and moving himself according to his will and power. Hence there resulted one common effect, namely victory (1 Cor. 15:54).

units.la: Tempus resurrectionis passim in Scriptura notatur, nempe tertius à morte & sepultura dies, Matth. 27. 57. & 28. Marc. 16. 9. 1. Cor. 5. 1. &c. Partes duae sunt: vivificatio & exitus è sepulchro: illa morti, haec sepulturae opponitur & respondet. Viuificatio est, qua Christus, anima ad corpus redeunte, reuniuit: vel est animae & corporis quae antea per mortem disiuncta fuerant, à deitate iterum facta coniunctio. Atque hic Christus non tantùm secundum diuinam naturam sciens & volens effecit hanc animae & corporis coniunctionem, sed etiam anima ipsa ad corpus, à quo aliquandiu seiuncta fuerat, sciens & volens rediit, imò cum corpore iterum coniungi gestiuit, Ioan. 2. 19. & 10, 18 Exitus è sepulcro, est, quo Christus iam rediuiuus lapide & obstaculis omnibus ad nutum & imperium ipsius cedentibus, secundum humanam naturam gloriosè è sepulcro prodiit, Matt. 28. 1. &c.
units.tr: The time of the resurrection is noted in many places in Scripture, namely the third day after death and burial (Matt. 27:57; 28; Mark 16:9; 1 Cor. 5:1, etc.). It has two parts: the quickening and the coming forth from the tomb. The first corresponds to death, and the second to burial. The quickening is the reunion by which Christ, when the soul returned to the body, was made alive again. Or it is the reconjoining, effected by the deity, of the soul and body that had been separated by death. Here Christ not only effected this union of soul and body knowingly and willingly according to his divine nature, but the soul itself, which had been separated from the body for a time, knowingly and willingly returned to it. Indeed, it eagerly desired to be joined to the body again (John 2:19; 10:18). The coming forth from the sepulchre is when Christ, now restored to life, went out gloriously from the tomb according to his human nature, with the stone and all obstacles yielding to his nod and command (Matt. 28:1, etc.).

units.la: Haec de resurrectione. Mansio illa 40. dierum est, qua Christus à resurrectione sua 40. diebus in his terris, repressi adhuc radiis claritatis & fulgoris sui, cum fidelib[?] conuersatus est. Conuersatio illa fuit tum in apparitionibus, quibus se rediuiuum discipulis suis & aliis fidelibus ostendit, tum in repressione radiorum maiestatis gloriae suae. Ipso die resurrectionis quinquies apparu[?]t 1.Mariae Magdalenae, Marc. 16. 9. 2.Eidem & alteri Mariae in via, Ioann.20.14. Matth.28.9. 3.Duobus discipulis, Luc. 24.v.13.31. 4.Simoni Petro soli, Luc.24.34. 5.Apostolis omnibus collectis in Ierusalem, Marc. 16. 14. Luc.24. 26.Ioann. 20.19. &c. Octauo die à resurrectione apparuit 1. Discipulis, Thoma praesente, Ioann. 20.26. 2. Septem discipulis piscantibus. Ioann. 21.1.2.3. Vndecim similiter discipulis in monte quodam Galileae, Matth. 28. 1. Plusquam quingentis fratribus simul, 1.Corint.15.64. 5.Iacobo seorsim, ibid.ver.7.46. Ipso ascensionis die, in monte Oliueti, Luc.24.50. Act.1.v.6.12. Variis modis autem resurrectionem suam illis testatam fecit, Luc.24.v.40.41.& Ioan.20.27 & 21.12. Act.10.41.
units.tr: So much for the resurrection. The forty days were the period in which Christ, for forty days after his resurrection, lived with the faithful on this earth, with the rays of his brightness and splendour still held back. This life together consisted both in the appearances by which he showed himself risen to his disciples and other faithful people, and in the restraint of the rays of his majestic glory. On the very day of the resurrection he appeared five times: (1) to Mary Magdalene (Mark 16:9); (2) to her and another Mary on the way (John 20:14; Matt. 28:9); (3) to two disciples (Luke 24:13, 31); (4) to Simon Peter alone (Luke 24:34); (5) to the apostles gathered together in Jerusalem (Mark 16:14; Luke 24:26; John 20:19, etc.). On the eighth day after the resurrection he appeared: (1) to the disciples, with Thomas present (John 20:26); (2) to seven disciples fishing (John 21:1, 2, 3). Likewise to the eleven disciples on a certain mountain in Galilee (Matt. 28:16). To more than five hundred brethren at once (1 Cor. 15:6). To James alone (ibid., v. 7). On the very day of the ascension, on the Mount of Olives (Luke 24:50; Acts 1:6, 12). He also gave them proof of his resurrection in various ways (Luke 24:40, 41; John 20:27; 21:12; Acts 10:41).

units.la: Repressio radiorum talis fuit, ut non plene manifestaret gloriam suam, sed radios fulgoris sui, quo iam splendere poterat, ad tempus quasi cohiberet, ut discipulorum infirmitati inseruiret. Nam si statim omnem fulgorem gloriae corporis sui in his terris exhibuisset, cuius in monte a quem gustum praebuit, Mat.17. Discipuli nec ferre hanc lucem & claritatem, nec per eam videre veritatem corporis & certitudinem resurrectionis potuissent. Itaque hic quasi medius status inter mortalis vitae cursum & caelestis vitae metam fuit, quod Christus significat, Ioh.20.17.
units.tr: The restraint of the rays was such that he did not fully manifest his glory, but for a time held back, as it were, the rays of his splendour, which he was already able to shine with, in order to serve the weakness of the disciples. For if he had at once displayed in this earth the full brightness of the glory of his body, of which he gave a taste on the mountain (Matt. 17), the disciples could neither have borne this light and brilliance, nor, through it, seen the truth of his body and the certainty of the resurrection. So this was a kind of middle state between the course of mortal life and the goal of heavenly life, as Christ signifies (John 20:17).

units.la: 2. Ascensio in caelum est qua Christus secundum humanam naturam 40. die è terris sursum in tertium illum caelum virtute diuinitatis suae vere euectus, ut victor mortis & inferni triumphum egit, & caelestis regni possessionem adiit, Marc.16.24. Actor.1.9.&c. Ephes.4.9. Locus è quo ascendit, in Iudaea, prope Bethaniam, in monte Oliueti, Luc.24.50. Act.1.12. Locus in quem, est supremum caelum, variis nominibus designatum, nempe tertium caelum 2.Cor.12.2. Caelum caelorum, & excelsum caelorum habitaculum, quia est supra alios omnes caelos, 1.Reg.8.27. Psal. 148.1.&68.5.19. Luc.2.14. Ephes.4.8. Paradisus, Luc.23.43. 2.Cor.12.2. Domus Dei Patris, Ioh.14.2. Habitaculum Dei, Psal. 68.6.20. Apoc.13.6. Sedes Dei, Esa.66.1. Psal.11.4.&115.16. 123.1. Mat.5.34.&23.22. Act.7.47. Domicilium & sedes beatorum rurum Angelorum & hominū, & cœlestis patria sanctorum, item sinus Abrahæ, Luc.16.23. Phil.3.20. Heb.11.v.10 14.16. & 13 14.Ioann.14.2.& 17.24.2.Cor.5.1 2.1.Thel.4. v. 14. 17. Ioan.12.32 Apoc. 14.4.
units.tr: 2. The ascension into heaven is that by which Christ, according to his human nature, was truly carried up from the earth into that third heaven on the fortieth day, by the power of his divinity. As conqueror of death and hell he celebrated his triumph and entered into possession of the heavenly kingdom (Mark 16:24; Acts 1:9; Eph. 4:9, etc.). The place from which he ascended was in Judaea, near Bethany, on the Mount of Olives (Luke 24:50; Acts 1:12). The place into which he ascended is the highest heaven, designated by various names: the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2); the heaven of heavens and the high dwelling-place of heaven, because it is above all the other heavens (1 Kings 8:27; Ps. 148:1; 68:5, 19; Luke 2:14; Eph. 4:8); Paradise (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:2); the house of God the Father (John 14:2); the habitation of God (Ps. 68:6, 20; Rev. 13:6); the throne of God (Isa. 66:1; Ps. 11:4; 115:16; 123:1; Matt. 5:34; 23:22; Acts 7:47); the dwelling and seat of the blessed angels and men, and the heavenly fatherland of the saints; likewise the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:23; Phil. 3:20; Heb. 11:10, 14, 16; 13:14; John 14:2; 17:24; 2 Cor. 5:1; 1 Thess. 4:14, 17; John 12:32; Rev. 14:4).

units.la: Porrò, ita Christus ascendit è terra in cœlum, vt secundum diuinam quidem naturam seu omnipotentem sua virtute efficeret hanc ascensionem seu migrationem humanæ naturæ in cœlum, i. humanam naturam eueheret & cœlo inferret. Quæ causa est, cur eueētio illa & translatio Christi in cœlum Patri tribuitur: quia videlicet vna diuina potentia est Patris & Filij, qua hæc translatio Christi in cœlum, vt & resuscitatio à mortuis, facta est, Act. 2. v.32. 33. & 5.31. Secundùm humanam vero naturam, ad Deitatis nutum sese moués sursum proficisceretur, ac proprie veréqs ascenderet, idque tum localiter, tum visibiliter, Luc.24.51. Mar.16,19. Act.1.v.9.11. Eph.4.8. Heb.4.14. E cœlis dein suo tempore descendet & apparebit, 1. Thess 4 16.&c.
units.tr: Furthermore, Christ ascended from earth into heaven in such a way that, according to his divine nature, or as omnipotent, he effected by his power this ascension or passage of the human nature into heaven, that is, he lifted up the human nature and brought it into heaven. This is why that elevation and translation of Christ into heaven is attributed to the Father: namely, because there is one divine power of the Father and the Son, by which this translation of Christ into heaven, as also his resurrection from the dead, was accomplished (Acts 2:32, 33; 5:31). But according to his human nature, moving himself upward at the nod of the Deity, he set out aloft and truly and properly ascended, and this both locally and visibly (Luke 24:51; Mark 16:19; Acts 1:9, 11; Eph. 4:8; Heb. 4:14). Then, in his own time, he will descend from the heavens and appear (1 Thess. 4:16, etc.).

units.la: 3. Sessio Christi ad dexteram Patris est supremus exaltationis gradus. Dextra, vt & sinistra, proprie est hominum: non Dei, qui est incorporeus. Vide Sessio & Dextra. Ad dextram Dei Patris, & ad dextram throni Dei Christus esse, sedere, stare dicitur. Ps.110.1. Marc.16.19. Act. 7.55. Rom.8.34. Col.3.1. Heb.1.3.& 2.7. Matth. 28.18. Act.2.34.36. Eph.1 22. Phil.2.9. Tempus sessionis, post resurrectionem & ascensionem, Mar.16.19. Luc.24.26. Eph.1.v.20.22. Hebr. 1.3 & 12.22. Apo.3.21. Manebit in tertio illo cœlo in quo liberè versatur, víque ad extremum iudiciũ, Act. 3. 21. Eph. 1.20.1. Pet.3.22. Heb.1.3.& 7.26. & 8.1. &c. Col. 3.1. Veniet è cœlo ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos, visibiliter in nubibus, Matth.24 30.& 26.64. Act.1. 11. Phil.3 20.1 Thess. 1. 4.10.16.2. Thess.1.7. Post vniuersale iudicium iterum in cœlo redibit, 1. Thes. 4.17. Ioan. 17. 24.vbi ipsum sedentem ad dextram Patris in omnem æternitatem videbimus, quia cum ipso semper erimus, Ioan.14.3. & 17 24. 1.Thessal.4.17.
units.tr: 3. The sitting of Christ at the right hand of the Father is the highest degree of exaltation. The right hand, like the left, properly belongs to men, not to God, who is incorporeal. See Sessio and Dextra. Christ is said to be, to sit, or to stand at the right hand of God the Father, and at the right hand of the throne of God (Ps. 110:1; Mark 16:19; Acts 7:55; Rom. 8:34; Col. 3:1; Heb. 1:3; 2:7; Matt. 28:18; Acts 2:34, 36; Eph. 1:22; Phil. 2:9). The time of the sitting is after the resurrection and ascension (Mark 16:19; Luke 24:26; Eph. 1:20, 22; Heb. 1:3; 12:22; Rev. 3:21). He will remain in that third heaven, in which he dwells freely, until the last judgment (Acts 3:21; Eph. 1:20; 1 Pet. 3:22; Heb. 1:3; 7:26; 8:1, etc.; Col. 3:1). He will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead, visibly, in the clouds (Matt. 24:30; 26:64; Acts 1:11; Phil. 3:20; 1 Thess. 1:4, 10; 4:16; 2 Thess. 1:7). After the general judgment he will return again to heaven (1 Thess. 4:17; John 17:24), where we shall see him sitting at the right hand of the Father to all eternity, because we shall always be with him (John 14:3; 17:24; 1 Thess. 4:17).

units.la: Sedere igitur ad dextram Patris significat diuina & humana gloria refulgere perfecte, vt regem & dominum ius & potestatemin res omnes habentem, Actor. 7. v. 55.56. Matt.26.64. Ps.110.1. Matt.28.18.1. Cor.15 25 Act.2.34. Eph. 1.20. Heb.1.13.1.Petr.3.22. Talis sessio Christi ad dexteram Patris solius Christi θεανθρώπυς sic est propria, vt nulli merae creaturae sit propria. Nullí enim preterquam Christo Domino nostro dictum est à Patre, sede à dextris meis.
units.tr: To sit, then, at the right hand of the Father signifies that the divine and human glory shine forth perfectly, as of a king and lord who has right and power over all things (Acts 7:55, 56; Matt. 26:64; Ps. 110:1; Matt. 28:18; 1 Cor. 15:25; Acts 2:34; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 1:13; 1 Pet. 3:22). Such a sitting of Christ at the right hand of the Father is so proper to Christ alone, the God-man, that it belongs to no mere creature. For to none other than Christ our Lord has it been said by the Father, "Sit at my right hand."

units.la: 1. Officium Propheticum in statu Exaltationis exer-citus est Christus, primùm in illa 4. dierum schola, quæ post resurrectionem suam habuit, priusquàm cœlum ascenderet, vt quod de veritate resurrectionis suæ, & de si-bus ad regnum Dei pertinentibus voce sua docuit, Matt. 28. 18. Marc. 16. Luc. 24. v. 44. 45. &c. Act. 1. 3. Et quod instituit ministerium verbi, id est ablegauit discipulos ad docendum Euangelium in toto orbe terrarum, Matth. 28. 19. Marc. 16. Ioan. 20. v. 22. 23. Deinde, post ascensionem in cœlum, misso Spiritu S. vt necessariis donis Apostolos ornaret ad ecclesiæ ædificationem, Act. 2. 3. &c. tum quòd mentes electorum illustrauit & adhuc illustrat per ministerium verbi, vt ea quæ docentur intelligant, Act. 16. 14.
units.tr: 1. The Prophetic office was exercised by Christ in the state of Exaltation. First, in that school of forty days which he held after his resurrection, before he ascended into heaven, in which he taught by his voice concerning the truth of his resurrection and the things pertaining to the kingdom of God (Matt. 28:18; Mark 16; Luke 24:44, 45, etc.; Acts 1:3). And in that he instituted the ministry of the Word, that is, he sent the disciples away to teach the Gospel in the whole world (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16; John 20:22, 23). Then, after his ascension into heaven, by sending the Holy Spirit, so that he might adorn the apostles with the necessary gifts for the building up of the Church (Acts 2:3, etc.). Then, in that he enlightened, and still enlightens, the minds of the elect through the ministry of the Word, so that they understand what is taught (Acts 16:14).

units.la: 2. Officium Sacerdotale exequitur nunc in cœlo, non quidem semetipsum offerens amplius: id enim fecit semel, Hebr. 7. 27. & 10. 4. sed apparens pro nobis in conspectu Dei cum perfecta sua obedientia usque ad mortem crucis & suiipsius oblatione, pro nobis apud Patrem interpellans, vt aduocatus noster & obedientia illa sua, quæ viget, valetque perpetuò, nos gratos & acceptos Deo Patri faciens, Rom. 8. 34. Hebr. 7. v. 25. 26. & 9. 24. 1. Ioan. 2. v. 1. 1. Tim. 2. 5.
units.tr: 2. The Priestly office he now carries out in heaven. He does not indeed offer himself again, for he did that once (Heb. 7:27; 10:4). But he appears before God on our behalf, with his perfect obedience, even unto the death of the cross, and with the offering of himself. He intercedes for us with the Father as our advocate, and by that obedience of his, which lives and prevails forever, he makes us pleasing and acceptable to God the Father (Rom. 8:34; Heb. 7:25, 26; 9:24; 1 John 2:1; 1 Tim. 2:5).

units.la: 3. Officium Regium executus est primùm in resurrectio-ne à mortuis, dum obstaculis omnibus ad nutum ipsius cedentibus, propria virtute resurrexit, 1. Petr. 3. 18. Deinde in conuersatione illa 40. dierum cum discipulis, cùm ad eos ianuis clausis ingressus est, Luc. 24. 26. Ioann. 20, 19. Tertio in ascensione, dum propria virtute sursum in cœlum profectus, locum nobis parauit. Ioann. 14. 2. & 16, 10. Actor. 1. Denique in sessione ad dextram, officium regium executus est, & etiamnum exequitur, dum summè gloriosus, seu diuina & humana gloria perfectè refulgens, implet omnia, Ephes. 4. 10. id est, in toto mundo, atque in primis in Ecclesia regnat & potenter omnia administrat. Quæ officii regij executio etiam sessio ad dextram Patris quandoque nominatur.
units.tr: 3. He discharged the kingly office first in his resurrection from the dead, when, with all obstacles yielding at his nod, he rose by his own power (1 Pet. 3:18). Then in that conversation with the disciples over forty days, when he entered to them with the doors shut (Luke 24:26; John 20:19). Third, in the ascension, when by his own power he went up into heaven and prepared a place for us (John 14:2; 16:10; Acts 1). Finally, in sitting at the right hand, he has discharged the kingly office and still discharges it, as he, most gloriously, shining with divine and human glory perfectly, fills all things (Eph. 4:10), that is, throughout the whole world, and above all reigns in the Church and powerfully governs all things. This execution of the kingly office is also sometimes called the sitting at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: Rursus officium regium hic exequitur & omnia potenter administrat, tum in hoc, tum in futuro seculo. In hoc seculo, tum in collectione, tum in gubernatione Ecclesiæ. Colligit Ecclesiam per ministerium verbi & Sacramentorum, operans in electis & efficaciter eos vocãs, id est voluntates eorum mouens, vt iis, quæ ipso docente discerunt, credant. cerunt & intelligunt, assentiantur & obtéperent, vt speci-tim in Paulo & Lydia purpuraria apparet, Act.9.& 16.cap.
units.tr: Again, he here discharges the kingly office and powerfully administers all things, both in this age and in the age to come. In this age he does so both in gathering and in governing the Church. He gathers the Church through the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments, working in the elect and effectually calling them, that is, moving their wills so that they believe, learn, understand, assent and obey the things they learn under his teaching. This appears especially in Paul and in Lydia the seller of purple (Acts 9 and 16).

units.la: In gubernatione Ecclesiæ, tum interna & spirituali, tum externa & corporali. In gubernatione spirituali & interna, quòd fideles sibi magis ac magis vnit, secundùm vtrangue naturam, sciens & volens: secundum diuinam autem naturam, vt est immensus, ad omnes fideles vbiuis locorum existentes in toto terrarum orbe pertingens, & in eis per gratiam suam specialiter inhabitans, & efficaciter agés atque operans, & per hanc Deitatem suam in humana natura personaliter, & in eis ἐνεργητικῶς effectiue inhabitan-tem, eos humanæ suæ naturæ, seu corpori suo, membra capiti & palmites viti coniungens, inserens atque conformans: vt cum ipso communionem habeant, id est, vt eo ad vitam & æternam salutem perfruantur, Ioann.15.1.& Ioan.34.quia videlicet Deitatis propria est omniprælentia & omnipotentia, qua Pater, Filius, Spiritus sanctus, vbique sunt & agunt. Ac similiter in baptismo & mensa domini præsens est Christus, videlicet iis qui sacramentis legitimè vtuntur, & corpus ac sanguinem ipsius in verbo promissionis oblatum fide apprehendunt, vt benignus Rex per gratiam suam clementer operans, eòsque operante & mediante Deitate sua corporis suo, iam olim in mortem tradito, & nunc in cœlo visibiliter existenti, tanquam memora vniens, sicut dicitur, Gal.3.27.& 1.Cor.10.16. In iis audem, qui sacramentis abutuntur, vt rex & iudex iratus, abum grauiter puniens, vt in Simone Mago, Act.8.cap.20.21. & in Corinthiis, 1.Cor.11.v.29.30.&c.
units.tr: In the governing of the Church, both internal and spiritual and external and bodily. In the spiritual and internal governance, he unites the faithful to himself more and more, according to each nature, knowingly and willingly. According to the divine nature, since he is immense, he reaches all the faithful wherever they exist in the whole world, dwells in them specially through his grace, and acts and works effectually in them; and through this his Deity he dwells personally in the human nature and effectively [ἐνεργητικῶς] in them, joining, inserting and conforming them to his human nature, or his body, as members to the head and branches to the vine, so that they have communion with him, that is, so that they enjoy him for life and eternal salvation (John 15:1; John 3:4). This is because omnipresence and omnipotence are proper to Deity, by which Father, Son and Holy Spirit are everywhere and act. Likewise Christ is present in baptism and at the table of the Lord, namely to those who use the sacraments lawfully and receive by faith the body and blood of Christ offered in the word of promise. As a kind king, mercifully working by his grace, he unites them, by his Deity working and mediating, to his body, which was once delivered to death and now exists visibly in heaven, as if they were members, as it is said (Gal. 3:27; 1 Cor. 10:16). But in those who abuse the sacraments, he punishes them severely as an angry king and judge, as in Simon Magus (Acts 8:20, 21) and in the Corinthians (1 Cor. 11:29, 30, etc.).

units.la: In gubernatione Ecclesiæ externa, tum quòd conseruat ministerium verbi & Ecclesiam, dans ei hospitia, atque eam in periculis conseruans & consolans. Apertis cœlis Stephanum martyrem erigit, Act.7.v.55.56. In visione Paulo apparuit, & cum eo locutus est, Act. 22.17. ei adsistit in cartris, Act.23.11. tum etiam quòd hostes Ecclesiæ debellat, & onatus eorum infringens, Psal.2.9.& 110.v.1.5.6. Apoc.2.2.& 12.5.& 17.14.
units.tr: In the external governance of the Church, in that he preserves the ministry of the Word and the Church, giving it shelter, and preserving and comforting it in dangers. With the heavens opened he raised up Stephen the martyr (Acts 7:55, 56). He appeared to Paul in a vision and spoke with him (Acts 22:17), stood by him in prison (Acts 23:11), and also in that he overcomes the enemies of the Church and breaks their rage (Ps. 2:9; 110:1, 5, 6; Rev. 2:2; 12:5; 17:14).

units.la: In futuro seculo officium regium exequetur, in extremo illo die, & postea in æternitatem, dum videlicet è cœlo visibiliter & localiter rediturus, sicut antea ascenderat, iudicium vniuersale secundum vtramque naturam sciens & volens exercebit, id est, homines vniuersos vocaut ad tribunal citauit, de omnibus cognoscet, & sententiam simul feret, latámque statim exequetur, ac fideles quidem in cœlum traductos glorificabit, infideles autem in infernum detrusos ignominia & pœnis afficiet in æternum, Act.17. v.24.25.31. Luc.21.27. & 22.69. Mat.24.30. & v.31 41 46.
units.tr: In the age to come he will exercise the kingly office on that last day and afterwards forever, when he, about to return visibly and locally from heaven just as he had ascended, will exercise universal judgment knowingly and willingly according to both natures. That is, he will call all men to the tribunal, summon them, examine everything, and at the same time pronounce sentence and immediately execute it. He will glorify the faithful, taken up into heaven, but will afflict the unbelievers, thrust down into hell, with shame and punishments forever (Acts 17:24, 25, 31; Luke 21:27; 22:69; Matt. 24:30; 25:31, 41, 46).

units.la: CHRISTIANI appellantur fideles Antiocheni, Actor.11.26. 26.28.2. Corint.10.7. Sancti dicuntur, quia sanctitati studio & profitentur, professionemque suam vitæ sanctimoniam nare contendunt, & sanctificati à Deo sunt, Actor.9.41. Roman.1.7. & 12.13. & 15.26. & 16.ver.2.15. 1.Corinth.1.2. & 14.33. 2.Corinth.1.1. & 9.v.1.12. & 13.12. Ephes.1. v.1. 3.v.8.18. & 4.12. & 6.18. Philip.1.1. & 4.21. Col.1.v.2.4.1. Thess. 5.27.1.Tim.5.10. Hebr.6.10. & 13.14. Christianis viuendum sicut Christus vixit, Galat.2.20.1.Ioann.1.7. & 2.6. & 3.5. Erunt cum Christo, Ioan.12.26. & 14.3. & 17.10. Christiani per contemptum Nazareni dicti, Act.24.5. pro Christiano afflīgi bonum, 1.Petr.4.16.
units.tr: CHRISTIANS are the faithful of Antioch (Acts 11:26; 26:28; 2 Cor. 10:7). They are called holy because they make it their aim to pursue holiness and to strive for sanctity of life befitting their profession, and because they have been sanctified by God (Acts 9:41; Rom. 1:7; 12:13; 15:26; 16:2, 15; 1 Cor. 1:2; 14:33; 2 Cor. 1:1; 9:1, 12; 13:12; Eph. 1:1; 3:8, 18; 4:12; 6:18; Phil. 1:1; 4:21; Col. 1:2, 4; 1 Thess. 5:27; 1 Tim. 5:10; Heb. 6:10; 13:14). Christians must live as Christ lived (Gal. 2:20; 1 John 1:7; 2:6; 3:5). They will be with Christ (John 12:26; 14:3; 17:10). Christians were called Nazarenes by way of contempt (Acts 24:5). It is good to suffer as a Christian (1 Pet. 4:16).

units.la: CHRYSOLITHVS, lapis pr. Exod.26.26. & 39.13. Ezech.10.9. 28 13. Dan.10.6. Apoc.21.20. CHRYSOPRASVS, Apoc.21. CHRYSTALLVM, Apoc.4.6. & 22.1.
units.tr: CHRYSOLITE, a stone. See Exod. 26:26; 39:13; Ezek. 10:9; 28:13; Dan. 10:6; Rev. 21:20. CHRYSOPRASE, Rev. 21. CRYSTAL, Rev. 4:6; 22:1.

units.la: CHVS, filius Cham, Genes.10.6.1. Paral.1.8. à quo Æthiopes. CHVSAI, amicus Dauidis, 2.Sam.15.37. & 18.32. 1. Paral. 27. CHVSCI, pater Sophoniæ Prophetæ, c.1.v.1, (i.Æthiops.) [CHVSSI 1.2.Sam.18.v.21.&c.
units.tr: CUSH, son of Ham, Gen. 10:6; 1 Chron. 1:8, from whom the Ethiopians (come). CUSHAI, friend of David, 2 Sam. 15:37; 16:32; 1 Chron. 27. CUSHI, father of the prophet Zephaniah, ch. 1:1 (i.e., an Ethiopian). [CUSHI] 2 Sam. 18:21, etc.

units.la: CHVSAN Rasathaim, Rex Syriæ, regnat super Israel octo annos, Iudic.3.8.10. (i.migredo iniquitatum)
units.tr: CUSHAN-RISHATHAIM, king of Syria, reigned over Israel eight years (Judg. 3:8, 10). (i.e., the going astray of iniquities.)

units.la: [CHVZA procurator Herodis, vxorem piam & Christi assecla habuit Iohannam. Luc.8.3. Vide v.2.)
units.tr: [CHUZA, the steward of Herod, had a pious wife and follower of Christ, Joanna (Luke 8:3). See v. 2.]

units.la: IBVS est alimentum à Deo, homini ordinatum (a) cum gratiarum actione (b) ad vitæ eius conseruationem (c) a.Gen.1.29. Deut.8.10. Hos.2.8.1. Corinth.10.25. c. Act.14.17. Ps.104. &c. V. Act.27.35.
units.tr: FOOD is nourishment appointed by God for man (a) with thanksgiving (b) for the preservation of his life (c). (a) Gen. 1:29; Deut. 8:10; Hos. 2:8; 1 Cor. 10:25. (c) Acts 14:17; Ps. 104, etc. See Acts 27:35.

units.la: CIBVS à Deo datur omnibus animantibus tempore opportuno, Psalm.145.15. Cibus immundus, Leuit.11.31. Cibus quomodo sanctificatur, 1.Timot.4.4. Ciborum delectus, adventu Christi sublatus, Coloss.2.v.16.17.1. Timoth.4.3. cibis versati, Hebr.13.9. dicuntur qui eorum discrimen perstitiose retinuerunt. Cibus Iudæis vetitus, Exodi 21.22. & 22.31. Leui.3.17. & 7.23. & 11.4. & 17.v.10.13. & 19.26. Deut.12.v.16.23. & 14. versi.7.10. 1. Sam.14.32. Ciborum & potus in conuiuiis luxus, Esaiæ 5.12. Ezech.16.49. Lucæ 16.19. & 21.34. Roman.13.13. Vide EBRIETAS. Cibus anima quam mi quærendus, Ioann. 6. 27. Cibus Christi quis, Ioann. 4.32. Fide parandus, Ioh. 6 27. & 35. A Christo petendus, Ioh.6.34.& 4.15. Quibus detur, Matt.5.6. Esa.55.1. Luc.1.53. Iohan.6.37. Hinc sitietas & vita æterna. Ioh.4.14.& 6.35. Regeneratio, Ioh. 7.37.38. de Ciborum abstinentia, Coloss.2.16. ¶Ciborum delectum habendum etiamnum esse, quibus testimonii probent Pontificij. V. ABSTINENTIA. CONIA, auis piissima, quæ parentes senio confectos alit, quos in viridaria & prata propriis alis deuehit, vt illic pascantur: deinde pullos in nidum reuehit. Est nobis pietas exemplum. Hinc ἀντιπελαργεῖν, beneficium rependere. Tempora sua novit, Hier.8.7. Nidulatur in proceris abietibus, Ps.104.17. ea vesci Iudæis non licuit, Levit.11.9. Deut.14.18. LICIA, regio minoris Asiæ: Act.15.23. Gal.1.21. INIS, homo ex cinere & pulvere, figuratè dictus, Genes.18.7. Iob.34.15.]
units.tr: FOOD is given by God to all living things in due time (Ps. 145:15). Unclean food (Lev. 11:31). How food is sanctified (1 Tim. 4:4). The distinction of foods was abolished at the coming of Christ (Col. 2:16, 17; 1 Tim. 4:3). Those who superstitiously retained the distinction of foods are called "occupied with foods" (Heb. 13:9). Food forbidden to the Jews (Exod. 21:22; 22:31; Lev. 3:17; 7:23; 11:4; 17:10, 13; 19:26; Deut. 12:16, 23; 14:7, 10; 1 Sam. 14:32). Luxury in food and drink at feasts (Isa. 5:12; Ezek. 16:49; Luke 16:19; 21:34; Rom. 13:13). See DRUNKENNESS. Food for the soul is to be sought more than for the body (John 6:27). What the food of Christ is (John 4:32). To be obtained by faith (John 6:27, 35). To be asked from Christ (John 6:34; 4:15). To whom it is given (Matt. 5:6; Isa. 55:1; Luke 1:53; John 6:37). Hence satiety and eternal life (John 4:14; 6:35). Regeneration (John 7:37, 38). On abstinence from food (Col. 2:16). ¶ The Papists prove by testimonies that the distinction of foods is still to be observed. See ABSTINENCE. STORK, a most dutiful bird, which feeds its parents when they are worn out with age, carrying them on its own wings to meadows and pastures so that they may feed there; then it carries its chicks back to the nest. It is an example of piety to us. Hence antipelargein, to repay a kindness. It knows its seasons (Jer. 8:7). It nests in tall fir trees (Ps. 104:17). Jews were not permitted to eat it (Lev. 11:19; Deut. 14:18). CILICIA, a region of Asia Minor (Acts 15:23; Gal. 1:21). CINIS, man made of ashes and dust, figuratively (Gen. 18:27; Job 34:15).

units.la: CIRCVLVS pro annulo, Exod.25.12.&c. pro circuitu temporis seu anni revolutione & complemento, Levit.25.30. Iudic.11.34.1.Sam.1.20.&c. pro hamo, 2.Reg.19.28. pro muri, Prou.11.22. Ezech.16.12. pro iunco, Iob.40.21. Esai.58. pro rotatione.1.Sam.25.29.]
units.tr: CIRCLE: for a ring (Exod. 25:12, etc.); for the circuit of time or the completion of a year's revolution (Lev. 25:30; Judg. 11:34; 1 Sam. 1:20, etc.); for a hook (2 Kings 19:28); for a wall (Prov. 11:22; Ezek. 16:12); for a rush (Job 40:21); Isa. 58; for rotation (1 Sam. 25:29).

units.la: CIRCVNCISIO, est sacramentum V. T. à Deo institutum, (A) in masculis tantum præputiũ carnis amputans, (B) ad significandam hominis regenerationem, (C) & confirmas promissiones de fœdere Dei, (D) ad certum tempus duraturum, (E) A.Gen.17.10.Ios.5.2. B. Gen.17.12. Exod.2.48. C. Deut.30.8. Rom.2.28.29. Coloss.2.11. Ier.44. D. Gen.17.7.&22.18. E. Gal.5.2.&6.15. Cui Christus Baptismum subrogauit: Matt.28. Christus circuncisus fuit, Luc.2.21. non quasi egens, cùm iustus esset, Luc.1.35. Sed vtconfirmaret eum verè lemen esse Abrahæ, in quo nationes omnes benedicerentur, Gen.12.3. Vt confirmaret circuncisionem quam Patribus dederat, iuste hactenus inseruisse, quam sanctificare voluit, vt & Bapt.nostrum, Matt.3.16 vt Legi subiectus nos ab eius maledictione redimeret: Gal.4.4. vt spiritualem cordium nostrorum circuncisionem in se sanctificaret: Col.2.11.
units.tr: CIRCUMCISION is a sacrament of the Old Testament instituted by God, (A) cutting off the foreskin of the flesh in males only, (B) to signify the regeneration of man, (C) and confirming the promises of God's covenant, (D) to last for a set time, (E). (A) Gen. 17:10; Josh. 5:2. (B) Gen. 17:12; Exod. 2:4 [4:25]. (C) Deut. 30:8; Rom. 2:28, 29; Col. 2:11; Jer. 4:4. (D) Gen. 17:7; 22:18. (E) Gal. 5:2; 6:15. Christ substituted baptism for it (Matt. 28). Christ was circumcised (Luke 2:21), not as one in need, since he was righteous (Luke 1:35), but so that he might confirm that he was truly the seed of Abraham, in whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3); so that he might confirm the circumcision which he had given to the fathers, as having rightly been introduced until then, which he wished to sanctify, as also our baptism (Matt. 3:16); so that, being subject to the Law, he might redeem us from its curse (Gal. 4:4); so that he might himself sanctify the spiritual circumcision of our hearts (Col. 2:11).

units.la: CIRCVNCISIO συμπεδοχμως pro tota Lege, Gal.5.2 μετωνυμ- ως pro Iudæis circumcisis, Tit.1.10. Circūcisio sacramentum Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ præcipitur, Gen.17.v.10.11. pactum, seu fœdus appellatur, v.7.10. signum, v.11. iteratur Iosuæ ministerio, iubente Domino, Ios.5.2. ex Patribus est, Ioan. 7.22.fidei sigillum est,Roman. 4. 11. ea signo,id est coris,& re significata,id est cordis circumcisione constat: gnum citra rem signatam nihil prodest, Rom. 2. v.28. Res vero citra signum vtilis est,Coloss.2. 11. ideo lunn pere commendatur, Deuter. 10. 16. & 30.6 Ierem.4.4 9. 25.
units.tr: CIRCUMCISION: synecdochically [συνεκδοχικῶς] for the whole Law, Gal. 5.2; metonymically [μετωνυμικῶς] for circumcised Jews, Tit. 1.10. Circumcision is prescribed as the sacrament of the Jewish Church, Gen. 17.10-11. It is called a covenant or pact, v. 7, 10, and a sign, v. 11. It was repeated under Joshua's ministry at the Lord's command, Josh. 5.2. It comes from the Fathers, John 7.22. It is a seal of faith, Rom. 4.11. It consists of the sign, that is, the circumcision of the flesh, and the thing signified, that is, the circumcision of the heart. A sign without the thing signified profits nothing, Rom. 2.28. The thing itself without the sign is useful, Col. 2.11. Therefore it is especially commended, Deut. 10.16; 30.6; Jer. 4.4; 9.25.

units.la: Hinc circumcisio duplex est:Carnalis,seu externa præp tij carnis,Genesis 17.v.10.25 & 21.4.& 34.24. Exodi 4.25 12.44.Lei i.12.3.Ios.5.v. 2. 7.Ierem.9 25.Luc. 1 59.& 2. Ioann.7.22.Act.7.8 & 15.v.1,24.& 16. 3. Rom. 2.v.25.& & 4.10.1 Corinth,7.19.Galat. 2.3.& 5.2. & 6.12. Ephes. 2 Phil.3.2. Coloss.3. 11. & erat initar solennis obligation qua Iudæi ad integram moralis legis præstationem stringebantur,Rom.2.25.Galat.5.3. propositá ipsis ob o- los Circumcisionis ritu excisionis poena,si vel minimum in legem peccassent,quo respectu Apostolus Col.2.14. legem ceremonialem vocat damnationis chirographum Spiritualis, seu, interior, præputij cordis, cuius illa exte symbolum erat, Deut.10.16.& 30 6.Ier.4.4. & 6.10. Rom 2 29.Col.2.11. Inde factum est,vt Paulus duas Iudæorum species constitueret,Rom.2.v.28 29.Eph.2 11.Col.2.11.
units.tr: Hence circumcision is twofold. Carnal, or external, is the cutting away of the foreskin of the flesh, Gen. 17.10, 25; 21.4; 34.24; Exod. 4.25; 12.44; Lev. 12.3; Josh. 5.2, 7; Jer. 9.25; Luke 1.59; 2.21; John 7.22; Acts 7.8; 15.1, 24; 16.3; Rom. 2.25; 4.10; 1 Cor. 7.19; Gal. 2.3; 5.2; 6.12; Eph. 2.11; Phil. 3.2; Col. 3.11. It was the solemn initiation by which the Jews were bound to the complete performance of the moral law, Rom. 2.25; Gal. 5.3, with the penalty of excision set before them under the rite of circumcision if they sinned in the smallest point of the Law. With respect to this, the Apostle calls the ceremonial law the handwriting of condemnation, Col. 2.14. Spiritual, or inward, is the circumcision of the foreskin of the heart, of which the outward rite was the symbol, Deut. 10.16; 30.6; Jer. 4.4; 6.10; Rom. 2.29; Col. 2.11. From this it came about that Paul established two kinds of Jews, Rom. 2.28-29; Eph. 2.11; Col. 2.11.

units.la: Circúcisionis pactum Abrahæ datum,Act.7.8.Circumcisionis Doctores, 15.v.15.Circumcisionis minister Christus,Rom.15.8. hoc est, Iudæorum, intra quorum fines continuit,quamdiu inter homines versatus est,vt testatur de se,Mar.15.24. Vide Act.13.46. Alioquin dici non potest Circumcisionis Minister,. Legis,quam suo aduentu abrogauit,aut potius complevit. Sic autem fuit minister Iudæorum Christus,vt Euangelium quoque voluerit gentibus annuntiari,vt diserte testatur,Ioan.10.16.Circumcisi Christi, Col.2.11.dicitur qua Christus ipse nos intus su Spiritu circuncidit.
units.tr: The covenant of circumcision was given to Abraham, Acts 7.8. The teachers of circumcision, Acts 15.5. Christ was the minister of circumcision, Rom. 15.8, that is, of the Jews, within whose borders he remained as long as he lived among men, as he testifies of himself, Matt. 15.24. See Acts 13.46. Otherwise he cannot be called the minister of circumcision, of the Law, which by his coming he abrogated, or rather fulfilled. Christ was in this way a minister to the Jews, yet he also willed that the Gospel be proclaimed to the Gentiles, as he plainly testifies, John 10.16. The circumcision of Christ, Col. 2.11, is so called because Christ himself circumcises us inwardly by his Spirit.

units.la: Circumcisio per literam siue carnis,Rom.2.27.est pe liculæ abscissio.Circumcisio autem per Spiritum,siue cor dis,v.28.est spiritualis finis illius ceremoniæ : vera nempe pietas, iustitia, cæterèqué virtutes, quibus verè demum populus Dei à profanis gentibus discernitur:vel, quod dem est, Circumcisio per Spiritum siue cordis est, cuius interior est,& in animo, siue qua circumcisi sunt affectus.Literam enim eo loco vocat Paulus,externum signi ab ipsius signi fine, siue à virtute seiunctum, quam voc Spiritum:quoniam externa ceremonia est res per se mo tu ua,& inutilis,nisi coniungatur veritas quasi illius vita.
units.tr: Circumcision by the letter, or of the flesh, Rom. 2.27, is the cutting away of the skin. Circumcision by the Spirit, or of the heart, v. 28, is the spiritual end of that ceremony: namely true piety, righteousness, and the other virtues by which at last the people of God is truly distinguished from the profane nations. Or, which is the same thing, circumcision by the Spirit, or of the heart, is that which is inward, in the mind, or in which the affections are circumcised. For Paul in that place calls the letter the outward sign, separated from the end of the sign, or from its power, which he calls the Spirit; because an outward ceremony is in itself a lifeless and useless thing unless truth is joined to it as its life.

units.la: Hoc etiam respectu dicitur, Circumcisionem nihil esse, Cor.7.19. seiunctam videlicet ab ipsa Circumcisionis re, ut (quod convenientius illi loco est) habita temporis ratione, quo Circumcisio iam desierat esse fidei Sacramentum: tum etiam personarum respectu, id est, eorum, qui mysterium Christi intelligebant, hoc est, neque Circumcisione, neque praeputio fieri nos sanctiores. Circumcisionis signum, Roman.4.11. pro ipsa Circumcisione, quae signum est. Sic Sacramentum Baptismi dicitur, pro, Baptismus, qui est Sacramentum.
units.tr: In this same sense it is said that circumcision is nothing, 1 Cor. 7.19; namely separated from the very reality of circumcision. This is to be understood (which fits that place better) with regard to the time, when circumcision had already ceased to be a sacrament of faith, and also with regard to persons, that is, those who understood the mystery of Christ, for whom neither circumcision nor uncircumcision makes us holier. "The sign of circumcision," Rom. 4.11, stands for circumcision itself, which is the sign. Thus the sacrament of baptism is spoken of for baptism, which is the sacrament.

units.la: [Circumcisio, pro Christianis, Philipp. 3.3. pro Iudaeis, Act.11.2. Rom.3 30.& 4.12 & 15 8. Gal.2.v.8.12. Col.4.11. Tit.1.10.] CIRENE. V. Cyrenae.
units.tr: [Circumcision: for Christians, Phil. 3.3; for Jews, Acts 11.2; Rom. 3.30; 4.12; 15.8; Gal. 2.8, 12; Col. 4.11; Tit. 1.10.] CYRENE. See Cyrenae.

units.la: Pater Saulis e Tribu Beniamin, 1.Sam.9.1.(Act.13 21.) misit Saul filium asinas perditas quaesitum, v.3.
units.tr: The father of Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin, 1 Sam. 9.1 (Acts 13.21), sent his son Saul to seek the lost asses, v. 3.

units.la: [Cis Mardochaei auus, Esth.2.5. Merarita, 1.Par.23 v.21. ]Cis.i.durus.
units.tr: [Cis, the grandfather of Mordecai, Esth. 2.5; a Merarite, 1 Chr. 23.21.] Cis means "hard."
SON, a torrent, Judg. 4.7, 13; 5.21; 1 Kings 18.40; Ps. 83.10.

units.la: THARA, instrumentum musicum: Eo laudandus Deus: Ps. 2.& 81.3.& 147.7.& 149 3.& 150.3.
units.tr: THARA, a musical instrument, by which God is to be praised: Ps. 2 and 81.3; 147.7; 149.3; 150.3.

units.la: Exemplum: Dauid, Psal.43.4. autor & inventor eius Iubal ius Lamech, filii Cain, Gen.4.21.
units.tr: Example: David, Ps. 43.4. Its author and inventor was Jubal, son of Lamech, son of Cain, Gen. 4.21.

units.la: ES Regni coelestis quales, Ps. 15 v.2.3.4.& 34.v.13.14.15. deles concives Sanctorum in coelestibus, Eph. 2.19.Phi-p.3.20.
units.tr: CITIZENS of the heavenly kingdom, what sort they should be, Ps. 15.2-4; 34.13-15. Fellow citizens of the saints in heaven, Eph. 2.19; Phil. 3.20.

units.la: IVIS. ciuitate donatus, Act.22.26.29. Conciuis, Ephes.2. Eiusdem loci & regionis incola, Iudic.14.11.1.Reg.21.1. ic.15.15.& 19.14. Popularis, leu.19.18.& 21.1.&c.]
units.tr: CIVIS: a man granted citizenship of a city, Acts 22.26, 29. Fellow citizen, Eph. 2. An inhabitant of the same place and region, Judg. 14.11; 1 Sam. 21.1; etc. 15.15; 19.14. A fellow countryman, Lev. 19.18; 21.1, etc.

units.la: ITAS prima a quo condita, Gen.4.17. Ciuitas a Deo abducta, delenda, Deut.13.v.15 16. Ciuitas Dauidis dicta arx onis, 2.Sam.5.v.7.9.1.Paral.11.7. Bethlehem, Luc.2.4. Ciuitas coelestis a Deo fundata, Heb.11.10.16.& 12.22.& 13.14. ooc.3 12.& 21.2. Huius fundamentum: Eph.2.19.&c. Quae eius ciues esse deceat, Phil.3.20.Ps.15.1.&c. Benedictione sanctorum effertur vrbs: ore autem improborum destruitur, Pro.11.11 [Ciuitas refugii, Num.35.6. Deu.4.42.& 19.v.3. Iosue 20.9. Ciuitas a Deo seruatur, Psal.46.v.5 6.7.& 7.1.Esa.37.35. Ciuitatem hic sitam non habemus, Heb.13. Vide 2.Cor.5.6 Heb.11.v.13.14.
units.tr: CITY: first founded by whom, Gen. 4.17. A city taken away from God is to be destroyed, Deut. 13.15-16. The City of David, called the stronghold of Zion, 2 Sam. 5.7, 9; 1 Chr. 11.7. Bethlehem, Luke 2.4. The heavenly city founded by God, Heb. 11.10, 16; 12.22; 13.14; Rev. 3.12; 21.2. Its foundation: Eph. 2.19, etc. What its citizens should be like, Phil. 3.20; Ps. 15.1, etc. The city is exalted by the blessing of the saints, but destroyed by the mouth of the wicked, Prov. 11.11. [City of refuge, Num. 35.6; Deut. 4.42; 19.3; Josh. 20.9. A city kept by God, Ps. 46.5-7; 48.1; Isa. 37.35. "We have no lasting city here," Heb. 13.14. See 2 Cor. 5.6; Heb. 11.13-14.]

units.la: [Ciuitas pro ciuitatis incolis, 1.Sam.4.13.1.Reg.1.v.41.45. Par.15.15. Esth.8.15. Esai.1.21. Ier 4.29. Nahum.3.1. Matt.8. Act.13.44.& 20.30.]
units.tr: City for the inhabitants of the city: 1 Sam. 4.13; 1 Kings 1.41, 45; 1 Chr. 15.15; Esth. 8.15; Isa. 1.21; Jer. 4.29; Nahum 3.1; Matt. 8; Acts 13.44; 20.30.

units.la: [Ciuitas, Ecclesia militans, Apoc.11.2. Ecclesia triumphans,Heb.11.v.11.16. & 12.22.Apoc.3 12.& 20.9.& 21.10.14.15.16.&c.]
units.tr: City: the militant Church, Rev. 11.2. The triumphant Church, Heb. 11.11, 16; 12.22; Rev. 3.12; 20.9; 21.10, 14-16, etc.

units.la: [Ciuitas,Sodoma & Ægyptus spiritualis, Apoc.11.v.8. Babylon mystica, Apoc.14.20. & 16.19.& 17.18.& 18.v.16.18.19.20.]
units.tr: City: Sodom and spiritual Egypt, Rev. 11.8. Mystical Babylon, Rev. 14.8; 16.19; 17.18; 18.16, 18-20.

units.la: CLAMOR, x ἐφωνὴ, ex contentione nascitur : & est vocis humanæ præter modum & decorum tumultuosa eleuatio: Exod.14.31. Clamantes pij ad Deum, exaudiuntur: ut Dauid, Psal.5. Israelitæ, Exod.2.23. Moses, 14.15. Orphani & viduæ, 22.23. Samson, Iudic.15.18. Samuel, 1.Sam.12.17. Ionas, 2.3. Christus, Heb.5.7. V. Apoc.21.4. Impij, Non, ut Ægyptij, Ex.11.6.& 12.30. Hostes Dauidis, 2.Sam.22.42. V. Ebr. Heb.12.16.17.
units.tr: OUTCRY [κραυγή], which arises out of strife, is a tumultuous raising of the human voice beyond measure and propriety, Exod. 14.31. The godly cry out to God and are heard, as David, Ps. 5; the Israelites, Exod. 2.23; Moses, 14.15; orphans and widows, 22.23; Samson, Judg. 15.18; Samuel, 1 Sam. 12.17; Jonah, 2.3; Christ, Heb. 5.7. See Rev. 21.4. The wicked: not as the Egyptians, Exod. 11.6; 12.30; the enemies of David, 2 Sam. 22.42. See Heb. 12.16-17.

units.la: CLAMOR damnatur, Ephes. 4. 31. Clamor Sodomitarum Gen.18.20.& 19.13.Philistinorum, 1.Sam.5.12.Israelis, 9. Mercenariorum, Deut.24.15. Iac.5.4. Sanguinis Abel, Gen. 4.10.Heb.12.24. Vide PECCATVM clamans.
units.tr: OUTCRY is condemned, Eph. 4.31. The outcry of the Sodomites, Gen. 18.20; 19.13; of the Philistines, 1 Sam. 5.12; of Israel, 9; of hired workers, Deut. 24.15; James 5.4; the blood of Abel, Gen. 4.10; Heb. 12.24. See SIN that cries out.

units.la: CLAVDA, Insula vicina Cretæ, Act.27.16.
units.tr: CLAUDA, an island near Crete, Acts 27.16.

units.la: CLAVDIA, pia mulier, 2.Tim.4.21.
units.tr: CLAUDIA, a godly woman, 2 Tim. 4.21.

units.la: [CLAVDICANS, imbecillis in fide, Mich.4.6.7. Sophon.3. Hebr.12.13. Inconstans animo, 1.Reg.18.21. Vacillans metu, Psal.18.46.]
units.tr: [LAME, weak in faith, Mic. 4.6-7; Zeph. 3; Heb. 12.13. Inconstant in mind, 1 Kings 18.21. Wavering in fear, Ps. 18.46.]

units.la: CLAVDIVS Cæsar omnes Iudæos Roma exire iubet, Act. 18.2. eius tempore magna erat in orbe annonæ caritas. Apoc.11.28.
units.tr: CLAUDIUS Caesar orders all the Jews to leave Rome, Acts 18.2. In his time there was great scarcity of grain in the world, Acts 11.28.

units.la: CLAVDIVS Lysias mittit Paulum ad Felicem Præfectum Cæsareæ, Act.23.v.23.30.
units.tr: CLAUDIUS Lysias sends Paul to Felix, the governor of Caesarea, Acts 23.23-30.

units.la: CLAVDVS sanatur, Vide MIRACVLA. Iacob claudicans, Gen.32.31. Claudicantes vtrinque damnantur, 1. Reg.18. Heb.12.13.V.2.Cor.6.15.Apoc.3.15.
units.tr: CLAUDUS is healed; see MIRACLES. Jacob limping, Gen. 32.31. Limping on both sides is condemned, 1 Kings 18; Heb. 12.13; 2 Cor. 6.15; Rev. 3.15.

units.la: CLAVIS Dauid, Esai.22.22. Claues Regni cælorum, Matt.16.19.& 18.18. Ioan.20.23. Clauium nomine metaphorice potestas œconomi significatur (vt apparet ex Esaiæ 22.2 qua funguntur omnes Ministri in Ecclesia Dei, Matth.16.19.vt apparet ex Matth. 18.18. Ministerium enim Euangelicum recte dici potest Clauis Regni cœlorum, Matth.16.19.& 18.18. Ioan.20.23. Cùm Euangelium sit virtus Dei in salutem cuiuis credenti, Rom.1 16.& rursus, Odor mortis ad mortem cuiuis non credenti, 2.Cor.2.16. Vide EXCOMVNICATIO. Clauis scientiæ, Luc.11.52. [Clauis mystica Apoc.1.18.& 3.7. Clauis abyssi, Apoc.9.1.&
units.tr: KEY of David, Isa. 22.22. The keys of the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 16.19; 18.18; John 20.23. By the name of keys the authority of a steward is metaphorically signified (as appears from Isa. 22.22), which all ministers in the Church of God exercise (Matt. 16.19, as appears from Matt. 18.18). For the Gospel ministry can rightly be called the key of the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 16.19; 18.18; John 20.23, since the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, Rom. 1.16; and again, the odour of death unto death for everyone who does not believe, 2 Cor. 2.16. See EXCOMMUNICATION. The key of knowledge, Luke 11.52. [Mystical key, Rev. 1.18; 3.7. Key of the abyss, Rev. 9.1.]

units.la: CLAVSVS, i.captiuus, Esai.61.1. Ierem.32.verf.2.3.&36.5.&39.15.]
units.tr: CLOSED, i.e. captive, Isa. 61.1; Jer. 32.2-3; 36.5; 39.15.

units.la: CLEMENTIA, est virtus animi, quæ magistratum aut etiam hominem priuatum ita mouet, vt leuiorem in peccato ignoscendo pœnam, iusta tamen de causa, sequatur, non aut seueriorem, Pro.20.28. Clementia & fides custodiunt regem, & sustentat clementia solium suum, 2.Paral.30.9. Clemens & misericors est Iehoua Deus vester: neque auertet faciem à vobis, si conuertamini, Vide Deus Clemens.
units.tr: CLEMENCY is a virtue of the mind which moves a magistrate, or even a private man, so that in pardoning a lighter offence he inflicts a punishment that is lighter, though for a just cause, and not a harsher one, Prov. 20.28. "Mercy and faithfulness preserve the king, and his throne is upheld by mercy," 2 Chr. 30.9. "The Lord your God is gracious and merciful, and will not turn his face from you, if you return." See God, Gracious.

units.la: CLEMENS, Pauli commilito, Philip.4.3.
units.tr: CLEMENS, a fellow soldier of Paul, Phil. 4.3.

units.la: CLEOPAS (Gr. i. omnimoda gloria) & alter Discipulus euntes in Emaus, Luc.24.v.13.18. ex fractione panis agnoscunt Christum, v.30. Vir Mariæ sororis matris Christi, Ioh.19.25.
units.tr: CLEOPAS (Greek: "wholly glorious") and another disciple going to Emmaus, Luke 24.13-18; they recognise Christ from the breaking of bread, v. 30. The husband of Mary, the sister of Christ's mother, John 19.25.

units.la: CLERVS, sors & hæreditas Domini, nempe Ecclesia, 1.Pet.5.3. Cleri, i. tripodes, Pf.68.23.]
units.tr: CLERGY: the lot and inheritance of the Lord, namely the Church, 1 Pet. 5.3. Of the clergy, i.e. tripods, Ps. 68.23.

units.la: CLYPEVS, belli instrumentum notissimum, Ios.5.18.&c. Miles armatus qui clypeum gestat: 2.Reg.19.32. Elai.37.33. Protectio inuicta, 2.Sam.22.35. Pf.18.3. Pro.30.5.]
units.tr: SHIELD, a very well-known instrument of war, Josh. 5.18, etc. An armed soldier who carries a shield, 2 Kings 19.32; Isa. 37.33. An invincible protection, 2 Sam. 22.35; Ps. 18.3; Prov. 30.5.

units.la: COCCINVM, Gen.38.28.30.2. Sam.1.24. Esai.1.18. Apoc.17.4. Inde Coccineus color.]
units.tr: SCARLET, Gen. 38.28, 30; 2 Sam. 1.24; Isa. 1.18; Rev. 17.4. Hence the colour scarlet.

units.la: COCCVS, bis tinctus, Exod.25.&seq.capp. Apoc.18.12.16.
units.tr: COCCUS, dyed twice, Exod. 25 and following chapters; Rev. 18.12, 16.

units.la: COECVS, COECITAS, Vide CAECVS, CAECITAS.
units.tr: BLIND, BLINDNESS: see BLIND, BLINDNESS.

units.la: CELIBATVS. Vide CASTITAS. Ad cœlibatum inclinat Paulus, 1.Cor.7. non simpliciter, nec quòd in eo collocet Dei cultum magis quàm in matrimonio, sed propter ea commoda, quibus, si fieri posset, cuperet omnes eximi, vt vni Deo vacarent, vt patet ex v.26.28.&c. 1.Cor.7.34. Virgo quæ est innupta, &c. sit sancta cum corpore, tum spiritu. Vide Ier.5.8. Eccl.36.27.28.
units.tr: CELIBACY. See CHASTITY. Paul inclines towards celibacy, 1 Cor. 7; not simply, nor because he places the worship of God in it more than in marriage, but because of the advantages, from which he would wish, if it were possible, that all be freed, so that they might be free for the one God alone, as is clear from v. 26-28, etc. 1 Cor. 7.34: the virgin who is unmarried, etc., may be holy both in body and in spirit. See Jer. 5.8; Eccl. 36.27-28.

units.la: CELVM, à Deo creatur, Gen.1.1.6. Pf.33.6.&102.26.&136. Act.4.24. sedes Dei est, Esai.66.1. Matt.5.34.&23.22. Act.7.49. instar pellis extensum, Pf.104.2. Cœlum pro quauis maxima altitudine, hyperbole, Gen.14.4. Deut.1.28. pro Deo ex Syrorum idiotismo, Matt.21.25. quod & antithesis declarat. Pro cœlitibus, Iob.15.15. Metonymia. Pro aere, Matth.6.26. Cœlum æreum & ferreum peccatoribus, Leu.26.19. Deut.28.23. Cœlum nouum, 2.Pet.3.13. Apoc.21.1. Cœli militiam adorantes lapidandi, Deut.17.3.5. per cœlum non iurandum, Iac.5.12. Matth.5.34. Cœli coram Deo immundi, Iob.15.15. Cœli aperti Christo baptizato, Matth.3.16.Marc.1.10. Lucæ 3.21.Ioan.1.51.Stephano mar[?]turo,Act.7.56.
units.tr: Heaven is created by God (Gen. 1.1, 6; Ps. 33.6; 102.26; 136; Acts 4.24). It is God's throne (Isa. 66.1; Matt. 5.34; 23.22; Acts 7.49). It is stretched out like a skin (Ps. 104.2). "Heaven" is used for any great height, by hyperbole (Gen. 14.4; Deut. 1.28). It stands for God, by the idiom of the Syrians (Matt. 21.25), which the antithesis also shows. It stands for the heavenly beings (Job 15.15), by metonymy. It stands for the air (Matt. 6.26). Heaven is brass and iron to sinners (Lev. 26.19; Deut. 28.23). A new heaven (2 Pet. 3.13; Rev. 21.1). Those who worship the host of heaven are to be stoned (Deut. 17.3, 5). One must not swear by heaven (James 5.12; Matt. 5.34). The heavens are unclean before God (Job 15.15). The heavens were opened to Christ at his baptism (Matt. 3.16; Mark 1.10; Luke 3.21; John 1.51) and to Stephen as he was dying (Acts 7.56).

units.la: Cœli gloriam Dei prædicant, Psal.8.4.& 19.1.& 89.6. [illegible, ~2 letters] tationi obnoxij sint, Psal.102.27.Matt.24.35.Marc.13.31. [?] cæ 21.33.Rom.8.20.Heb.1.11 1.Pet.1.25.2.Pet.3.v.7.12. [?] poc.6.14.& 21.1. Cœlum & terra donec transeant, Matth.5.18.periphrasis est perpetuitatis, non dissimilis illi, [?] habetur Gen.49.26.Psal.72.v.5.7.17.& 87.v.37.38. Cœlum terrámque Moses testatur, Deut.30.19.& 31.28. Elaias [?] Cœli tertij nomine, 2.Cor.12.2. intelligendum est summum coelum, quasi dicat, in cœlum sublimissimum. [?] autem in sacris literis mentio trium cœlorum, aeris, [?] stellarum orbium, & beatarum sedium, in quas Christus ascendit, inde etiam venturus, vt cum ipso ibi simus in æternum. Cœli exercitus, Vide EXERCITVS cœli. Cœlorum potestates, Matth.24.29. pro potentes cœli, Hebræus. Vide cælum.
units.tr: The heavens declare the glory of God (Ps. 8.4; 19.1; 89.6). They are subject to change (Ps. 102.27; Matt. 24.35; Mark 13.31; Luke 21.33; Rom. 8.20; Heb. 1.11; 1 Pet. 1.25; 2 Pet. 3.7, 12; Rev. 6.14; 21.1). "Until heaven and earth pass away" (Matt. 5.18) is a periphrasis for perpetuity, like the expression found at Gen. 49.26; Ps. 72.5, 7, 17; 87.37-38. Moses calls heaven and earth to witness (Deut. 30.19; 31.28). The third heaven (2 Cor. 12.2) is to be understood as the highest heaven, as if he said, "into the most exalted heaven." In Scripture there is mention of three heavens: the air, the orbits of the stars, and the blessed seats, into which Christ ascended and from which he will also come, so that we may be with him there for ever. The hosts of heaven: see HOST OF HEAVEN. The powers of the heavens (Matt. 24.29) stands for the powerful ones of heaven, a Hebraism. See HEAVEN.

units.la: COELESTIA quærenda, Col.3.1.
units.tr: Heavenly things are to be sought (Col. 3.1).

units.la: COENA Domini, Est noui fœderis sacramentum, à Christo institutum, ex analogis signo & signato, & analogica ratione ipsorum inter se, & actione constans, quo ad Christi & Ecclesiæ ipsius membra, in legitimo visibilium signorum vsu instituuntur, de vera & spirituali communicatione corporis & sanguinis Christi, ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: The Lord's Supper is a sacrament of the New Covenant, instituted by Christ. It consists of an analogy between sign and thing signified, and of the analogical relation of the two to each other, together with the action itself. It is instituted for Christ's members and for the Church itself, in the lawful use of the visible signs, for the true and spiritual communication of the body and blood of Christ, unto eternal life.

units.la: COENA Domini instituitur, Matt.26.v.26.27.28.29. Marc.14.v.22.23.24. Luc.22.19.1.Cor.11.v.23.24.25. eius vius tripartitus primus, 1.Cor.10.16. secundus, v.17. tertius, 1.Corint.11. commédatur, Luc.22.19.1.Cor.11,v.24.25. celebratur, Act.2.42.& 20.7. Signis (quibus fractio & benedictio adiuncta sunt) id est, pane & vino & rebus quæ communicantur, corpore & sanguine Christi, constat, 1.Cor.10.16. sanguis eius, 11.v.20.21.27. præparatio ad eam necessaria, V[?]
units.tr: The Lord's Supper was instituted (Matt. 26.26-29; Mark 14.22-24; Luke 22.19; 1 Cor. 11.23-25). Its use is threefold: the first is 1 Cor. 10.16; the second, v. 17; the third, 1 Cor. 11. It is commended (Luke 22.19; 1 Cor. 11.24-25). It is celebrated (Acts 2.42; 20.7). It consists of signs (to which breaking and blessing are added), that is, bread and wine, and of the things communicated, the body and blood of Christ (1 Cor. 10.16; the blood of Christ, 11.20-21, 27). Preparation necessary for it: V...

units.la: COENÆ magnæ parabola, Luc.14.16. (Vide PARABOLA) dicantur merito excludi regno Dei qui cœlestibus terrenis præferunt.
units.tr: The parable of the great supper (Luke 14.16; see PARABLE). Those who prefer earthly things to heavenly things are rightly said to be shut out of the kingdom of God.

units.la: COENA Agni ad quam vocati beati prædicantur, Apoc.19.9.V.Matt.22.2.&c. Cœna, i.vindicta Dei, Apoc.19.19.
units.tr: The Lamb's supper, to which the called are pronounced blessed (Rev. 19.9; cf. Matt. 22.2 etc.). Supper, that is, the vengeance of God (Rev. 19.19).

units.la: COGITATIO, pro ratione, Ephes.2.3. Cogitationes bonæ Deo,2.Cor.3.5. Pro.16.3.& 29.11.Phil.4.8. malæ hominum infiiciunt, Matt.15.v.19.20. damnantur, Zach.8.v.10.17. Ier.6.14. Matt.15.19. Marc.7.21. à malo sunt: Ioh.13.2. Act.5.3. 1.Tim.4.1. Ab ipso homine: Gen.8.21. Matt.15.19. Remedium [?] Matth.22.37. Act.8.22. Pro.30.32. Ab omni specie mali abstinendum. 1. Thess.5.22. Pro.15.22.26. Cogitationes cordis novit Deus, 1. Reg.8.39. 2. Paral.6.30. Ioan.2.25. & nulla est creatura quae non sit manifesta eius conspectui, Iob 42.2. Esai.29.15. Matt.9.4. Hebr.4.12. Vide DEVS scrutator cordium. Cogitationes impiorum peruersæ, Iob 5.35. Psal.10. v.7.13.15. & 14.1. & 36.4. & 53. & 74.8. & 83.4. & 40.2. Prov.15.3. & 24. 9. Esai.59.7. Ier.6.19. & 18.18. Mich.2. Zach. 1. 4. Cogitationum peruersarum exempla: Fratres Ioseph, Gen.50.20. Scribæ & Pharisæi, Matth.9.3 & 12.14. Marc.2.6. Luc.5.21. & 7.30. Pharisæus quidam, Luc.11.38. Coloni, 20.14. Principes Sacerdotum, Ioan.11.10. Sacerdotes Iudaici, Act.5.33. Simon Magus, 8.22.
units.tr: Thought, for reasoning (Eph. 2.3). Good thoughts are of God (2 Cor. 3.5; Prov. 16.3; 29.11; Phil. 4.8). Evil thoughts of men defile (Matt. 15.19-20). They are condemned (Zech. 8.10, 17; Jer. 6.14; Matt. 15.19; Mark 7.21). They come from evil (John 13.2; Acts 5.3; 1 Tim. 4.1). They come from man himself (Gen. 8.21; Matt. 15.19). The remedy (Matt. 22.37; Acts 8.22; Prov. 30.32). One must abstain from every appearance of evil (1 Thess. 5.22; Prov. 15.22, 26). God knows the thoughts of the heart (1 Kings 8.39; 2 Chron. 6.30; John 2.25), and there is no creature that is not manifest to his sight (Job 42.2; Isa. 29.15; Matt. 9.4; Heb. 4.12). See GOD, searcher of hearts. Wicked thoughts of the impious (Job 5.35; Ps. 10.7, 13, 15; 14.1; 36.4; 53; 74.8; 83.4; 40.2; Prov. 15.3; 24.9; Isa. 59.7; Jer. 6.19; 18.18; Mic. 2; Zech. 1.4). Examples of wicked thoughts: the brothers of Joseph (Gen. 50.20); the scribes and Pharisees (Matt. 9.3; 12.14; Mark 2.6; Luke 5.21; 7.30); a certain Pharisee (Luke 11.38); the tenants (Luke 20.14); the chief priests (John 11.10); the Jewish priests (Acts 5.33); Simon Magus (Acts 8.22).

units.la: COGNATIO [i. familia, generatio, Gen.10.v.20.30. Exod.1.6. etc. Cognatio] spiritualis, Matt.12.50. Marc.3.35. Luc.8.21. 1. Cor.4.15. Gal 4.19. Eph.3.15.1. Tim.1.2.2. Tim.1.2. Tit.1.4. Philem.v.10.1. Pet.1.23.1. Ioan.2.1.
units.tr: KINSHIP [that is, family, generation, Gen. 10.20, 30; Exod. 1.6, etc. Kinship] spiritual (Matt. 12.50; Mark 3.35; Luke 8.21; 1 Cor. 4.15; Gal. 4.19; Eph. 3.15; 1 Tim. 1.2; 2 Tim. 1.2; Titus 1.4; Philem. 10; 1 Pet. 1.23; 1 John 2.1).

units.la: COGNATUS, pro consanguineo, Num.35.v.12.21. Luc.1.v.36. 2.3. & 2.44. Act.10.24. Rom.9.3. pro fratre, Numer.27.v.4. pro socero, Exod.18.v.1.5.6. &c. Num.10.29. Iudic.1. 6. & 11.]
units.tr: KINSMAN, for blood relation (Num. 35.12, 21; Luke 1.36; 2.3, 44; Acts 10.24; Rom. 9.3). For brother (Num. 27.4). For father-in-law (Exod. 18.1, 5, 6, etc.; Num. 10.29; Judg. 1.6; 11.).

units.la: COGNITIO Dei. Cognoscitur Deus a nobis ut Creator, Act.15.16.17. & 17.24. ad 32. Rom.1.19. Ut Redemptor, Ioh.3. & 3.16.
units.tr: KNOWLEDGE of God. God is known by us as Creator (Acts 14.16-17; 17.24-32; Rom. 1.19), and as Redeemer (John 3.16).

units.la: Idque per considerationem rerum creatarum, Psal.19.1. Rom.1.per Verbum: Psal.19.8. Heb.1.1. Per Spiritum S. Matt.25. Ier.31.31. Heb.8.10. Haec cognitio in electis efficit ut eum quaerant, & rite colant, Matth.7.7.1. Ioh.2 3. Ioh.4. Ut voluntatem eius de se seruandis norint, Ioh.3.16. ut vita aeterna certi sint, Ioh.17.3. Rom.8.38. Ut Deum in rem inuocent, Gal.4.6. Psal.50.15. ut sancte viuat, Deum celebrent, 1. Pet.2.9. Col.1 9.
units.tr: This comes through consideration of created things (Ps. 19.1; Rom. 1), through the Word (Ps. 19.8; Heb. 1.1), and through the Holy Spirit (Matt. 25; Jer. 31.31; Heb. 8.10). This knowledge, in the elect, brings it about that they seek him and worship him aright (Matt. 7.7; 1 John 2.3; John 4). That they may know his will concerning their own preservation (John 3.16); that they may be certain of eternal life (John 17.3; Rom. 8.38); that they may call upon God as their Father (Gal. 4.6; Ps. 50.15); that they may live holily and celebrate God (1 Pet. 2.9; Col. 1.9).

units.la: In hac cognitione in dies proficiendum.
units.tr: In this knowledge we must make progress day by day.

units.la: Cor.13.11.12. Eph.4.18. Col.1.9. Non definimus pro vobis ut impleamini omni agnitione voluntatis eius, in omni sapientia & intelligentia spirituali: ut incedatis digne Domino dignum est.
units.tr: (1 Cor. 13.11-12; Eph. 4.18; Col. 1.9.) "We do not cease to pray for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, that you may walk worthily of the Lord."

units.la: COGNITIO: Cognitio dilectionis Christi quam necessaria, Eph.3.19. Cognitio Christi quam necessaria, Ioan.17.3. non secundum carnem, 2. Cor.5.16. donum caeleste est, Matt. 7. Eph.1.17. Col.1.v.26.27. in quo sita, Ioan.7.17. & 14.7. quibus concessa, Matth.11. suos progressus habet, Actor. 8.35. Ephes.4.v.11.12.13.
units.tr: KNOWLEDGE: how necessary is the knowledge of the love of Christ (Eph. 3.19), and the knowledge of Christ (John 17.3). Not according to the flesh (2 Cor. 5.16). It is a heavenly gift (Matt. 7; Eph. 1.17; Col. 1.26-27). Where it lies (John 7.17; 14.7). To whom it is granted (Matt. 11). It has its progress (Acts 8.35; Eph. 4.11-13).

units.la: Cognitio Dei & dona Spiritus Sancti aquis assimilantur. Vide AQVAE. Cognitio Dei mentibus hominum insculpta est, Rom.1.21. quàm necessaria, Ierem.9.v.23.24.1.Cor.1.31.2.Cor.10.17. Oleæ 6.6. Ioan.17.3.Eph.4.18.in quo ea sub regno Christi amplissima, Esa.11.9. Ioan.2.3. Ioan.14.v.7.9. 2.Cor.4.6.Heb.1.3. quibus cessa, Matt.11.27.&13.11.1. Ioan.5.20. humilitatem parit. Cor.8.13.&14.25. fructus eius, 2.Pet.1.3.
units.tr: The knowledge of God and the gifts of the Holy Spirit are compared to waters. See WATERS. The knowledge of God is engraved on the minds of men (Rom. 1.21). How necessary it is (Jer. 9.23-24; 1 Cor. 1.31; 2 Cor. 10.17; Hos. 6.6; John 17.3; Eph. 4.18). In it, under the kingdom of Christ, the knowledge is most abundant (Isa. 11.9; John 2.3; John 14.7, 9; 2 Cor. 4.6; Heb. 1.3). To whom it is granted (Matt. 11.27; 13.11; 1 John 5.20). It brings forth humility (1 Cor. 8.13; 14.25). Its fruit (2 Pet. 1.3).

units.la: COGNOSCI Deus humana sapientia non potest, nisi ipse uelit paruulis & humilibus, Matt.11.27.&16.17.Luc.10. Ioan. 7.28.&8.v.19.27.&10.14.&14.4.&15.1.&17.6. 17.23.1.Cor.1.v.17.18 &2.v.6 1c.&3.19.Col.2.16.
units.tr: God cannot be known by human wisdom, unless he himself wishes it, to the little ones and the humble (Matt. 11.27; 16.17; Luke 10; John 7.28; 8.19, 27; 10.14; 14.4; 15.1; 17.6, 23; 1 Cor. 1.17-18; 2.6; 3.19; Col. 2.16).

units.la: COGNOSCERE licet subinde homines ex verbis & factis. Eccl.19 27.&27.7. Matth.7.16.&12.33.Luc.6.44.
units.tr: Men may sometimes be known from their words and deeds (Ecclus. 19.27; 27.7; Matt. 7.16; 12.33; Luke 6.44).

units.la: COGNOSCERE, Hebraeis honeste significat congressum cum muliere, Gen.4.v.1.17.25.&38.26 1.Reg.1.4.Luc.34. dicitur & de masculorum concubitoribus, Genes. Vide INGREDI.
units.tr: KNOW, among the Hebrews, honourably means intercourse with a woman (Gen. 4.1, 17, 25; 38.26; 1 Kings 1.4; Luke 1.34). It is also said of male lovers (Gen. 19.5). See GO IN.

units.la: COITVS illiciti, Leu.18.v.6.7.8.& seqq. Coitus illiciti supplicium, Leu.20.v.10.11.& seqq. Vide Immunditia.
units.tr: Illicit intercourse (Lev. 18.6-8, and following). The punishment for illicit intercourse (Lev. 20.10-11, and following). See UNCLEANNESS.

units.la: COLLECTAE, inscio Magistratu pro pauperibus sanctis in Ecclesia licitae & commendatae, 1. Corinth.16.1.2.Cor. v.1.2.5. Exempla: Antiochenses, Actor.11.29. Macedones, Rom.15.26.
units.tr: Collections, made without the knowledge of the magistrate, for the holy poor in the Church, are lawful and commended (1 Cor. 16.1-2; 2 Cor. 8.1-2, 5). Examples: the Antiochenes (Acts 11.29); the Macedonians (Rom. 15.26).

units.la: COLLOQVIA praua fugienda, 1.Cor.15.33. V.Matt.12.36.
units.tr: Wicked conversations are to be shunned (1 Cor. 15.33). See Matt. 12.36.

units.la: COLLYBISTAE, Ioan.2.15. Latinis Argentarij, vel Numularij dicti: vocantur ij, qui collybo quaestum faciunt.
units.tr: Moneychangers (John 2.15), called in Latin argentarii or nummularii: those who make gain by trading in coins.

units.la: COLOSSAE oppidum Phrygiae vicinum Laodiceae: Col.1.
units.tr: Colossae, a town of Phrygia near Laodicea (Col. 1).

units.la: COLONIA, gens ad habitandam terram missa, Vide Act. 16.12.
units.tr: A colony, a people sent to inhabit a land. See Acts 16.12.

units.la: COLVMBA, emittitur ex Arca, Gen.8.8. Columba sacrame tale Spiritus Dei symbolum, Matth.3.16. Marc.1.10. Luc. 22 Columbinum stercus comeditur in Samaria vrgeto me, 2. Reg. 6. 25. Estote innocentes ut columbae: Mat. 10.16.
units.tr: A dove is sent out from the ark (Gen. 8.8). The dove is the sacramental symbol of the Spirit of God (Matt. 3.16; Mark 1.10; Luke 3.22). Dove's dung is eaten in Samaria while they besiege me (2 Kings 6.25). Be innocent as doves (Matt. 10.16).

units.la: [COLVMBA mystica, i. Ecclesia, Cantic.2.v.14.&5.2.&6.
units.tr: [The mystical dove, that is, the Church (Song 2.14; 5.2; 6).

units.la: COLVMNA, pro praesentiae Dei signo: nam Deus in columna nubis interdiu, ignis vero noctu, Israelitis itineris fuit, Exod.13.21. [Figurate pro doctoribus Ecclesiae, Ier. 1.18. Prou.9.1. Galat.2.9. Apoc.3.12. pro fundamentis, Iob, 9.6: pro montibus qui coelum fulcire videntur, Iob. b.26.11. pro potentia Christi, Cant. 5 15. pro legibus & gni statu, Psal.75 4.]
units.tr: A pillar, as a sign of God's presence: for God was in the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, as a guide to the Israelites on their journey (Exod. 13.21). [Figuratively for the teachers of the Church (Jer. 1.18; Prov. 9.1; Gal. 2.9; Rev. 3.12); for foundations (Job 9.6); for mountains which seem to prop up heaven (Job 26.11); for the power of Christ (Song 5.15); for laws and the state of government (Ps. 75.4).]

units.la: COLVMNA veritatis, Ecclesia dicitur 1.Tim.3.15. id est custos, testis verbi illius, in quo salutis nostrę veritas perfectè continetur, siue columna, ad quam verbum Dei scriptum velut adfixum, piis omnibus proflat palam propositum, quod perlegant & meditentur. Vide ECCLESIA.]
units.tr: The Church is called the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim. 3.15), that is, the guardian and witness of that Word in which the truth of our salvation is fully contained; or a pillar on which the written Word of God is, as it were, fixed and publicly set forth to all the pious, that they may read it through and meditate on it. See CHURCH.]

units.la: [?]IA viri & mulieris quomodo ornanda, 1.Cor.11.ver.14.15. Tim.2.9.1.Petr.3.3. in rotundum non attondenda, Leuit.19.27.
units.tr: [?]The adornment of man and woman, how it is to be done (1 Cor. 11.14-15; 1 Tim. 2.9; 1 Pet. 3.3). The hair is not to be cut round (Lev. 19.27).

units.la: MBVSTORVM & igne devoratorum exempla: Sodomitę & Gomorritæ, Genes.19.v.24.25. Nadab & Abihu, Leuit.10.1.2. ducenti quinquaginta viri, Numer.16.v.35. Thamnatæus, & vxor Samsonis Iudic.15.6. Saul mortuus & filij eius, 1.Sam.31.12. Quinquagenarij duo cum quinquaginta filij & filiæ Israelitarum, 2.Reg.1.v.10.11.12. filij Sepharuaim, 2.Reg.17.v.31.
units.tr: Examples of those burned to death and devoured by fire: the Sodomites and Gomorrhans (Gen. 19.24-25); Nadab and Abihu (Lev. 10.1-2); the two hundred and fifty men (Num. 16.35); Thamnatha, and the wife of Samson (Judg. 15.6); Saul, dead, and his sons (1 Sam. 31.12); the two captains of fifty with their fifty men (2 Kings 1.10-12); the sons of Sepharvaim (2 Kings 17.31).

units.la: [?]EDERE verba, μεταφορικῶς, pro admittere, Ieremiæ 15.16. Ezech.3.1. Comedere panem, vide PANIS, & BIBERE.
units.tr: [?]To eat words, metaphorically [μεταφορικῶς], for to admit (Jer. 15.16; Ezek. 3.1). To eat bread: see BREAD; and to drink: see DRINK.
