units.la: ESSATIO, (κῶμος, 1.Pet.4.3.) est assidua cibi cuiusl bet etiā nimis, & sæpius quàm necesse sit & expetant vires naturales, sumptio: quę vel in cœtu aliorum fit, vel seorsim à nobis, ob immoderatam voluptatem, quam ex cibo capius. Vide Sobrietas.
units.tr: Feasting [κῶμος, 1 Pet. 4.3] is the constant taking of any food, even too much, and more often than the natural powers require, which is done either in company with others or apart from us, on account of the immoderate pleasure which we gain from the food. See Sobriety.

units.la: COMESSATIONES damnantur, Prouer. 21.17. & 23. v.20.21. & 7. Lucæ 21.34. Rom.13.13. Galat.5 21. Quot mala pariant: 0.21.17. & 23.21. & 28.7. Esa.5.11. Poena: Phil.3.19. Gal.5 21. ide Amos 6.3. &c. V. EBRIETAS dānatur. Comessationis & ebrietatis exempla: Noë, Gen.9.21. Loth.19.33. Esau, 25.33. Israelitæ, Exodi 16.3. & 17.3 & 32.6. Numer.11.4. Iudic.7.6. Philisthæi, 16.23 filij Heli, 1.Sam.2.15. Amnon, 2.Sam.13.v.28. Ela.1 Reg.16. v.8.9. Israelitæ, Nehem. 9.25. Aman, Ith.5.9. Iudæi, Esa.22.13. Sacerdotes & Prophetę, 28.7. Herodes, Matth.14.6. Marc.6.21. Dives, Luc.16.19. Vide CONVIVIORVM, à malis celebratorum exempla.
units.tr: COMESSATIONS are condemned: Prov. 21.17; 23.20-21; Luke 21.34; Rom. 13.13; Gal. 5.21. Their evil effects: Prov. 21.17; 23.21; 28.7; Isa. 5.11. Punishment: Phil. 3.19; Gal. 5.21; see also Amos 6.3, etc. See DRUNKENNESS, which is condemned. Examples of comessation and drunkenness: Noah, Gen. 9.21; Lot, Gen. 19.33; Esau, Gen. 25.33; the Israelites, Exod. 16.3; 17.3; 32.6; Num. 11.4; Judg. 7.6; the Philistines, Judg. 16.23; the sons of Eli, 1 Sam. 2.15; Amnon, 2 Sam. 13.28; Elah, 1 Kings 16.8-9; the Israelites, Neh. 9.25; Haman, Esth. 5.9; the Jews, Isa. 22.13; the priests and prophets, Isa. 28.7; Herod, Matt. 14.6; Mark 6.21; the rich man, Luke 16.19. See FEASTS, examples of banquets celebrated for evil ends.

units.la: MITAS, Est blanda alterius ad nos inuitatio ex communi quadam nostra erga omnes homines charitate: & illius qui ad nos accedit plena suavitatis retentio & tractatio, (Huic vitium contrarium est Inhumanitas, per quam abigimus eos, qui nos adeunt, vel exceptos durè habemus. De qua infrà) Act.16.15.
units.tr: HUMANITY is a friendly invitation extended to others out of a common love we bear towards all human beings, and the gentle welcome and courteous treatment of the one who comes to us. (Its opposite vice is inhumanity, by which we drive away those who approach us, or treat them harshly once received. Of this more below.) Acts 16.15.

units.la: MITAS, Vide MANSVETVDO.
units.tr: HUMANITY: see MEEKNESS.

units.la: COMMINATIO Dei, est denunciatio futurorum malorum, quibus Deus vel suos castigare, vel impios punire se vindicaturum ostendit. Estque vel conditionalis, quae differtur aut auertitur, si resipiscentia consequatur: vt quae Nineuitis pernunciata fuit. Vel absoluta, vt quae Dauidi per Nathan facta fuit: 2. Sam. 12. 14. Filius ille qui natus est tibi omnino morietur.
units.tr: THE THREATENING of God is the announcement of future evils by which God shows that he will either chastise his own people or avenge himself by punishing the wicked. It is either conditional, which is deferred or averted if repentance follows, as was announced to the Ninevites; or absolute, as was made to David through Nathan: 2 Sam. 12.14: "The son who is born to you will certainly die."

units.la: COMMINATIO: Comminationes Dei non inanes, 2. Reg. 9. & 17, 23. Non contemnendae: Deu. 29. 19. &c. Psalm. 139. 7.
units.tr: THE THREATENINGS of God are not empty: 2 Kings 9; 17.23. They are not to be despised: Deut. 29.19; Ps. 139.7, etc.

units.la: COMMOTIO: Commotionis exempla: Herodes & omnis Hierosolyma, Matth. 2. 3. & 21. 10. Vendentes & ementes, Marc. 11. 15. Iudaei, Actor. 13. 50. & 14. 2. & 17. v. 5. 8. 13. & 21. 27. Iudaei gentes, Actor. 14. v. 2. 5. Domini Pythonissae, 16. 19. Plebs Magistratus Philippensis, v. 22. Ciuitas, Ephesus: 19. v. 29. Thessalonica: 17. 5.
units.tr: AGITATION: examples of agitation: Herod and all Jerusalem, Matt. 2.3; 21.10. Those who sell and buy, Mark 11.15. The Jews, Acts 13.50; 14.2; 17.5, 8, 13; 21.27. The Jews and the Gentiles, Acts 14.2, 5. The masters of the Pythoness, Acts 16.19. The crowd and the magistrates of Philippi, Acts 16.22. The city of Ephesus, Acts 19.29. Thessalonica, Acts 17.5.

units.la: COMMVNE (κοινόν) pro profano, Deu. 20. 6. Ezechiel 48. 15. Matthaei 15. 11. Marc. 7. 2. Actor. 10. 14. Hebr. 10. 29. vnde verbum κοινῶν pro polluere, Matth. 15. 11.
units.tr: COMMON (κοινόν) is used for profane, Deut. 20.6; Ezek. 48.15; Matt. 15.11; Mark 7.2; Acts 10.14; Heb. 10.29. Hence the verb κοινῶν [koinoun] is used for to defile, Matt. 15.11.

units.la: COMMVNIO Sanctorum, (1. Ioh. 1. 3.) significat omnes sanctos Christo capiti vniri, (A) per Spiritum ipsius, & ex capite eos ceu membra transfundi dona (B.) tum quae eadem singulis ad salutem necessaria sunt (C.) tum quae varia accommodata sunt, quae omnibus simul requiruntur ad aedificationem Ecclesiae. (D)
units.tr: THE COMMUNION of saints (1 John 1.3) signifies that all the saints are united to Christ their head (A) through his Spirit, and that from the head the gifts are poured into them as members: (B) those gifts which are the same for each and necessary for salvation (C), and those various gifts which are suited to different people, all of which are required together for the building up of the Church (D).

units.la: (A) Christo vniri, Ioh. 15. 4. 5. 6. 7. Manete in me, Rom. 8. 9. Siquis Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est eius, 1. Ioh. 4. 13. 1. Cor. 6. 17. Qui agglutinatur Domino, vnus Spiritus est, 1. Cor. 12. 21. Multa membra sunt, vnum corpus. (B) per Spiritum, 1. Cor. 12. 13. Per vnum spiritum nos omnes in vnum corpus baptizati sumus, Eph. 3. 16. Vobis vt corroboremini per Spiritum suum in interiorem hominem, vt inhabitet Christus per fidem in cordibus vestris. (C) 1. Cor. 12. 11. &c. Eph. 4. 4. ad 17. Roman. 8. 32. ad finem vsque, 1. Cor. 1. 30. (D) Phil. 4. 6. 2. 4. Ne sua quisque bona quaerat, sed alterius, &c. Eph. 4. 11. &c.
units.tr: (A) Union with Christ: John 15.4-7, "Abide in me"; Rom. 8.9, "If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his"; 1 John 4.13; 1 Cor. 6.17, "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit"; 1 Cor. 12.12, "There are many members, but one body." (B) Through the Spirit: 1 Cor. 12.13, "By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body"; Eph. 3.16-17, "that you may be strengthened through his Spirit in the inner man, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith." (C) 1 Cor. 12.11, etc.; Eph. 4.4-17; Rom. 8.32 to the end; 1 Cor. 1.30. (D) Phil. 2.4, "Let each one look not to his own interests, but to the interests of others," etc.; Eph. 4.11, etc.

units.la: Instrumenta externa, ministri mysteriorum Dei dispensatores, 1. Cor. 4. 1. Euangelium potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Roman. 1. 16. Sacramenta, Baptismus, Tit. 3. Rom. 6. 5. Gal. 3. 27. Quicunque in Christo baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Coena D. 1. Cor. 10. 16. Panis & poculum communio corporis & sanguinis Christi sunt. Bene huius communionis participes, Rom. 8. 32. ad finem vsque. Non tandem glorificabuntur, 1. Cor. 15. 42. &c. Phil. 3. 20. 21. Caeterum miserationis.
units.tr: The external instruments, the ministers and stewards of the mysteries of God: 1 Cor. 4.1. The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes: Rom. 1.16. The sacraments: baptism, Titus 3; Rom. 6.5; Gal. 3.27, "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." The Lord's Supper, 1 Cor. 10.16, "The bread and the cup are a communion in the body and blood of Christ." Those who participate well in this communion: Rom. 8.32 to the end. They will at last be glorified: 1 Cor. 15.42, etc.; Phil. 3.20-21. Otherwise, the rest are of pity

units.la: miserrimi, ut palmites à vite excisi, & in ignem coniiciendi. Ioh.1.51.6.
units.tr: most wretched, like branches cut off from the vine and cast into the fire: John 15.1-6.

units.la: COMMVNICATIO idiomatum, Vide CHRISTVS.
units.tr: COMMUNICATION of properties: see CHRIST.

units.la: COMMVNICATIO Spiritus Sancti, 2.Cor.13.13. V.SPIRITVS.
units.tr: COMMUNICATION of the Holy Spirit: 2 Cor. 13.13. See SPIRIT.

units.la: COMPASSIO, sympathia seu commiseratio: est virtus per quam commouemur ad condolendum aliis, etiam hostibus, ob ipsorum calamitates, eosque consolando, & aliis modis lenire vel tollere studemus, quantum iustitia permittit. Christus cum fletu commiseratus est miserabilem Iudæorum interitum, Rom.12.15.
units.tr: COMPASSION, sympathy or commiseration: it is the virtue by which we are moved to grieve with others, even enemies, over their calamities, and we strive to comfort them and to relieve or remove their distress in other ways, as far as justice allows. Christ wept with tears and had compassion on the wretched destruction of the Jews. Rom. 12.15.

units.tr: COMPASSION, or commiseration, common to the faithful: 1 Cor. 12.26-27; Heb. 13.3; 1 Pet. 3.8; 1 John 3.17; Jude 23; Ps. 3.13. Examples of compassion or commiseration: Abraham, Gen. 14.14; Melchizedek, v. 18; Reuben, Gen. 37.21; Joseph, Gen. 43.30; 45.1; the midwives, Exod. 1.17; Pharaoh's daughter, Exod. 2.6; Moses, Exod. 32.12-13, 32; Num. 12.13; Gideon, Judg. 8.5; the Israelites, Judg. 21.15; Boaz, Ruth 2.8-9; Samuel, 1 Sam. 6.1; David, 1 Sam. 30.23-24; Shobi and Machir, 2 Sam. 17.27-29; the boys' mother, 1 Kings 3.26; Obadiah, 1 Kings 18.4; Elijah, 1 Kings 17.19; Elisha, 2 Kings 4; 6.23; 8.12; Jehosheba, 2 Chron. 22.11; Azariah, Berechiah, etc., 2 Chron. 28.15; Nehemiah, Neh. 1.4; 2.3; Amnon (Amiob), Job 2.11; Job, Job 29.11-16; 30.25; Esther, Esth. 7.3; Isaiah, Isa. 21.3; 22.4; Jeremiah, Jer. 4.31; 9.1; Lam. 2.11; Ebed-melech, Jer. 38.7, 9; Baruch, Jer. 45.3; the Lord, Jer. 48.32; Amos 7.3; Ezekiel, Ezek. 3.14; 19.4; Darius, Dan. 6.18; the disciples, Matt. 15.23; Jesus Christ, Matt. 8.3; 9.2, 36; 14.14; 15.32; 20.34; 23; Mark 1.41; 6.37; 8.2; Luke 7.13; 19.41; John 5.6; 11.33-35; 19.26; the master of the household, Matt. 18.27; the Samaritan, Luke 10.33; the widows, Acts 9.39; Paul, Acts 17.16; Rom. 9.3; 2 Cor. 2.7-8; 12.21; Gal. 4.19; Phil. 3.18; Philemon v.; the jailer, Acts 16.33; the faithful of Thessalonica, Acts 20; the faithful of Caesarea, Acts 21.12; the barbarians, Acts 28.2; the Hebrews, Heb. 3.3.

units.tr: Those who are said to "confess their sins" among the Hebrews: see the Elders of the Fathers, etc.

units.tr: Examples of those taken as hostages or bail: Adoni-bezek, Judg. 1.6; Zebah and Zalmunna, Judg. 8.12; the brothers of Ahaziah, 2 Kings 10.13-14; Ahaziah, 2 Chron. 22.9; Zedekiah, Jer. 39; 52.8; Christ, Luke 22.54; Paul, Acts 23.27; 26.21.

units.la: DE CAPTIVORVM hominum exempla.
units.tr: Examples of captive men.

units.la: DENUNCIATORES mittuntur à Iosaphat Rege per vniversum Iudam,2. Paral. 17. 7. Concionatorum, Pastorum, Prophetarum officium,1. Sam.12.23.Esai,58.1. & 61.1. Ierem.1.5.Ezech.3.v.19 12.& 33.v.2.7.Actor.3. 18. Vide Pastor, Propheta,& Minister.
units.tr: HERALDS are sent by King Jehoshaphat throughout all Judah, 2 Chron. 17.7. The duty of preachers, pastors and prophets: 1 Sam. 12.23; Isa. 58.1; 61.1; Jer. 1.5; Ezek. 3.19; 12; 33.2, 7; Acts 3.18. See MINISTER, PROPHET and PASTOR.

units.la: Concordia συμφωνία, est animi sensus, & orationis ipsius multorum inter se consensio, nihil Dei praeceptis contrarium, & ab iis alienum fovens. Alias coiuratio esset(Isa.8.12.)Quae fuit Pilati & Herodis in Christum consensus. A Deo datur:Rom.15.56. Deus det vobis ut eodem animo inter vos mutuò affecti sitis, secundum Christum Iesum: ut concordi ore glorificetis Deum,&c.
units.tr: Concord [συμφωνία, symphonia] is the agreement of minds and of speech among many people with one another, fostering nothing contrary to God's precepts and foreign to them. Otherwise it would be a conspiracy (Isa. 8.12). Such was the agreement of Pilate and Herod against Christ. It is given by God: Rom. 15.5-6, "May God grant you to be of the same mind with one another, according to Christ Jesus, that with one accord you may glorify God," etc.

units.la: CONCORDIA fratrum commendatur, Psalmo 133 1.Prov.19.Eccl.25.2.Matt.5.9 Rom.12.16.& 15 6.1.Cor.1.10.2.Corinth.13.11. Ephes. 4.3 Philip.1.27.& 2.2.& 4.2.2.Thess.3. Tit.3.2.Hebr.10.24.& 12 14.1.Petr. 3.8. Concordia exempla: Abraham & Loth,Gen.13.8. Apostoli,Act.1.14.Fideles,2.44.46.& 4.32.(Vide Charitas.)
units.tr: CONCORD among brothers is commended: Ps. 133.1; Prov. 19; Eccles. 25.2; Matt. 5.9; Rom. 12.16; 15.6; 1 Cor. 1.10; 2 Cor. 13.11; Eph. 4.3; Phil. 1.27; 2.2; 4.2; 2 Thess. 3; Titus 3.2; Heb. 10.24; 12.14; 1 Pet. 3.8. Examples of concord: Abraham and Lot, Gen. 13.8; the apostles, Acts 1.14; the faithful, Acts 2.44-46; 4.32. (See CHARITY.)

units.la: CONCUBINA: Concubinae Davidis, custodia perpetua incestae,2.Sam.20.3. Concubinae Salomonis trecentae,1.Reg.11. Concubina Levitae: Iud.19.1.&c.
units.tr: CONCUBINE: David's concubines were kept in perpetual confinement as incest, 2 Sam. 20.3. Solomon had three hundred concubines, 1 Kings 11. The Levite's concubine, Judg. 19.1, etc.

units.la: CONCUPISCENTIA. I. Spiritualis, quae in novo homine est (qui sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt cum affectibus et concupiscentiis, Gal.5.24.)bona est. Spiritu incedite,(Gal.5.16.)&quod concupiscit caro, ne perficite. Nam caro concupiscit adversus spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus carnem. Haec autem inter se opposita sunt.
units.tr: CONCUPISCENCE. I. Spiritual, which is in the new man (those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, Gal. 5.24), is good. "Walk in the Spirit" (Gal. 5.16), and "do not fulfil the desires of the flesh." For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to one another.

units.la: II. Naturalis,in omni homine a Deo indita, est necessaria & inculpabilis:ut sitire, esurire, sanitatem expetere, &c. Quum vero ob naturae prauitatem omnes animi facultates ita vitiatae sint, ut in omnibus actionibus eminent perpetua quaedam ataxia & intemperies, ideo vitiosas etiam contendimus,non quatenus naturales,sed quia inordinatae sunt,Genes.8.21.Sensus & cogitatio humani cordis in malum prona sunt ab adolescentia sua.
units.tr: II. Natural, implanted in every human being by God, is necessary and blameless: such as thirsting, hungering, desiring health, etc. But since, on account of the corruption of nature, all the faculties of the soul are so vitiated that in all actions a certain constant disorder and intemperance stands out, we therefore also maintain that these are sinful, not insofar as they are natural, but because they are disordered: Gen. 8.21, "The intention and thought of the human heart is inclined to evil from its youth."

units.la: III.Carnalis,qua secundum carnis corruptionem (Iac.1.14.quicquid ad delitias,voluptates, luxum,superbiam,& spectat, rebus necessariis & sufficientibus non contentum, concupiscimus,sive illud licitum sit,sive non.Concupiscentia igitur a Dei voluntate vel minimum aberrans,etsi illi non assentiamur ( nec enim omnia peccata sunt paria ) a Deo damnatur,Rom.7.7. Qui ex tota cogitatione &c.diligendus est: Matt.22.37. Intelligentia carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum:Rom.8.7.
units.tr: III. The carnal desire, which arises from the corruption of the flesh (James 1:14), is whatever we crave beyond what is necessary and sufficient, reaching after luxury, pleasures, delights, pride and the like, whether that thing is lawful or not. Desire that strays even slightly from the will of God is therefore condemned by God, even if we do not assent to it (for not all sins are equal), Rom. 7:7. We ought to love with our whole thought, &c., Matt. 22:37. The mind of the flesh is enmity against God, Rom. 8:7.

units.la: NCVPISCENTIA pro fonte omnium malorum appeti- tuum, Iacob. 1. 15. damnatur Exodi 20. 27. Deut. 5 21. Ioh. 7. 1. Psalm. 62. 11. Prou 23 5. Matth. 5. 28. Rom. 7. 7. & 13. 9. Corinth. 10 6. Galat. 5. 17. Colos. 3. 5. eius partes, 1. Ioann. 2. 16. mala, Matt. 5. 28. Marci 4. 19. Iacob. 1. 15. Concupiscê- ti peccatum per Legem cognoscitur, Rom. 7. v. 7. 8. poena, Corinth. 10. v. 5. 6. Concupiscentiam crucifigere, fræna- re & mortificare iubemur, Rom. 6. v 12. & 8. v. 8. 12 & 13. 14. Galat. 5. 16. Ephes. 4 22. & 5. 3. Coloss. 3. 5. Tit. 2. 12 1. Petr. 2. 11. & 4. v. 3. 6. Hebr. 12. 1. 1. Thessalon. 5. 23. eam in sanctis etiam & baptizatis, atque adeo in vere rena- tis hominibus, quatenus adhuc sunt caro, peccati ra- tionem habere, suo exemplo docet Apostolus, Rom. 7. 7.
units.tr: CONCUPISCENCE, as the source of all evil appetites, is condemned, James 1:15; Exod. 20:17; Deut. 5:21; John 7:1; Ps. 62:11; Prov. 23:5; Matt. 5:28; Rom. 7:7 and 13:9; 1 Cor. 10:6; Gal. 5:17; Col. 3:5. Its parts are 1 John 2:16. Its evils are Matt. 5:28; Mark 4:19; James 1:15. Concupiscence is recognised as sin through the Law, Rom. 7:7-8. It is a punishment, 1 Cor. 10:5-6. We are commanded to crucify, restrain and mortify concupiscence, Rom. 6:12; 8:8, 12-14; Gal. 5:16; Eph. 4:22 and 5:3; Col. 3:5; Titus 2:12; 1 Pet. 2:11 and 4:3, 6; Heb. 12:1; 1 Thess. 5:23. That concupiscence has the nature of sin even in saints and the baptized, and so in men truly regenerate, insofar as they are still flesh, the Apostle teaches by his own example, Rom. 7:7.

units.la: Concupiscere, i. cupere puro mentis affectu, & in bonum finem, Psalm. 45. 12. & 84. 3. & 119. v. 20. 40. 174.]
units.tr: To desire (concupiscere) is to long for something with a pure affection of the mind and for a good end, Ps. 45:12; 84:3; 119:20, 40, 174. ## CONDONATION

units.la: CONDONATIO
Iniuriarum est animi lenitas, quæ non modo non reuocat iniuriam sibi factam, sed eam lubenter etiam ei, qui veniam non deprecatur, ignoscit, propter Dei præ- ceptum. Vide Iniuria.
units.tr: Forgiveness of injuries is a gentleness of mind, which not only does not call back the injury done to oneself, but gladly pardons even the one who does not ask for pardon, on account of God's precept. See Injury.

units.la: CONFESSIO, pro fidei doctrina, Hebr. 3. 1. & 4. 14. Con- sessio fidei & externa spei nostræ professio, necessaria, Psal. 19 10. &c. Roman. 10. v. 9. 10. 2. Corinth. 4. 13. 1. Tim. 6. 12. 2. Tim. 2. v. 12. 13. Hebr. 3. 10. 23. 1. Pet. 3. 15. 1. Ioan. 4. 15. Confessionis fidei exempla: Iethro, Exodi 18. 11. Danielis socij, Dan. 3. 17. Petrus, Matth. 16. 16. Apostoli, Ioan. 6. 69. Martha, Ioan. 21. 27. Eunuchus Candaces reginæ Aethiopum, Act. 8. 37.
units.tr: CONFESSION, for the doctrine of faith, Heb. 3:1 and 4:14. The confession of faith, an outward profession of our hope, is necessary, Ps. 19:10, &c.; Rom. 10:9-10; 2 Cor. 4:13; 1 Tim. 6:12; 2 Tim. 2:12-13; Heb. 3:10, 23; 1 Pet. 3:15; 1 John 4:15. Examples of confession of faith: Jethro, Exod. 18:11; Daniel's companions, Dan. 3:17; Peter, Matt. 16:16; the Apostles, John 6:69; Martha, John 11:27; the eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, Acts 8:37.

units.la: CONFESSIO veritatis est cultus Dei, quū veritatem cœlestem, ex Scriptura sancta cognitam, aperte & intrepide profite- antur, pro ratione nostri officij, ad illustrandam Dei gloriā, et promouendam aliorum salutem, Rom. 10. v. 10. 2. Tim. 1. 8. 1. Pet. 3. 15.
units.tr: Confession of the truth is the worship of God, when with boldness and without fear people openly profess the heavenly truth known from holy Scripture, according to the measure of their office, to illustrate the glory of God and to promote the salvation of others, Rom. 10:10; 2 Tim. 1:8; 1 Pet. 3:15.

units.la: CONFITERI Christum, necessarium, vtile, honorificum, Matth. 10. 32. Marc. 8. 38. Luc. 9. 26. non omnibus credenti- bus datum, Ioan. 12. 42. Confessionis Christi exempla: Zachari- as, Lucæ 1. 68. Simeon, 2. v. 27. 28. Magi, Matth. 2. 11. Ioannes Baptista, Ioan. 1. 29. Andreas, v. 41. Philippus, v. 45. Nathanael, v. 49. Petrus, Matt. 16. 16. Samaritana, Ioan. 4. v. 19. Samaritani, v. 42. Nicodemus, Ioan. 3. 2. Petrus & cæteri Apostoli. Actor. 2. v. 22. 23. & 10. 42. Petrus & Ioannes, 3. v. 13. 14. 15. & 4. v. 8. 9. 10. 12. & 5. verf. 29. 30. Stephanus Actor. 7. v. 51. 52. Paulus, Actor.13.v.22.23. & 12.v. 3. & 24.25. & 26. 22.23. Author Epistolae ad Hebraeos, Hebr. 4. v.14. 15. pollos, Actor.18.28. Ioannes Apostolus,1. Ioan.2.1.
units.tr: To confess Christ is necessary, useful and honourable, Matt. 10:32; Mark 8:38; Luke 9:26. It is not given to all believers, John 12:42. Examples of confession of Christ: Zechariah, Luke 1:68; Simeon, 2:27-28; the Magi, Matt. 2:11; John the Baptist, John 1:29; Andrew, v. 41; Philip, v. 45; Nathanael, v. 49; Peter, Matt. 16:16; the Samaritan woman, John 4:19; the Samaritans, v. 42; Nicodemus, John 3:2; Peter and the other Apostles, Acts 2:22-23 and 10:42; Peter and John, 3:13-15 and 4:8-10, 12; and 5:29-30; Stephen, Acts 7:51-52; Paul, Acts 13:22-23, 12:3, 24:25 and 26:22-23; the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, Heb. 4:14-15; Apollos, Acts 18:28; the Apostle John, 1 John 2:1.

units.la: Confiteri peccata sua, Hebraeis dicuntur, qui se modis omnibus peccatores esse profitentur, & veniam à Dei misericordia petunt, Matth.3. 6. vt apparet ex Psalm. 32. v.5. Dan.9 v.3.&c.
units.tr: To confess one's sins is said in Hebrew of those who profess themselves sinners in every way and seek pardon from God's mercy, Matt. 3:6, as appears from Ps. 32:5; Dan. 9:3, &c.

Confessio priuata Deo facta commendatur, Iob. 13. 15 Psal. 32. vers.3.&c. Proverb. 28.13.1. Ioann. 1.ver.8.9.10.1.R 8.46.&c.
units.tr: The confession of sin, made in the name of the whole Church, is commended, Lev. 16:21; 1 Kings 8:46-47; 2 Chron. 6:36. It was not the kind of confession Satan later introduced into the Church, but one in which all and each stood before God as guilty, as appears from Lev. 16:21. Mention is made of this confession in Heb. 10:3, which was an annual and public profession, in which the people acknowledged themselves guilty, however ancient and old the sins being repeated were, together with all their forefathers: Aaron, Num. 12:11; the Israelites, Num. 21:7; Judg. 2:4 and 10; 1 Sam. 7:6 and 12:18-19; 2 Chron. 12:6; Ezra 9:6-7; Neh. 9:2, 33; Ps. 106:6; Dan. 9:5. Confession of a sin committed in some particular matter is commanded, Num. 5:7. Private confession made to God is commended, Job 13:15; Ps. 32:3, &c.; Prov. 28:13; 1 John 1:8-10; 1 Kings 8:46, &c.

units.la: CONIVGIVM, Est legitima viri unius & unius foeminae secundum Dei institutum coniunctio, cum utriusque consensu in eam inem suscepta, ut in perferendis huius vitae molestiis sese mutuo iuvent, honeste casteque viuant, & sobolem gignant, ad legitimam humani generis propagationem.
units.tr: MARRIAGE is the lawful joining of one man and one woman, according to God's institution, entered into with the consent of both, so that they may mutually help each other in bearing the troubles of this life, live honourably and chastely, and beget offspring for the lawful propagation of the human race.

units.la: CONIVGIVM instituitur, Gen. 2. 24. confirmatur & sanctitur, 9. 1. omnibus honorabile est, Hebr. 13. 4. continere se non valentibus, necessarium, 1. Corinth. 7. ver. 2. 9. taque non spernendum, Matth. 19. 12. Vide MATRIMONIVM.
units.tr: MARRIAGE is instituted, Gen. 2. 24; it is confirmed and sanctified, Gen. 9. 1; it is honourable among all, Heb. 13. 4; for those who cannot contain themselves it is necessary, 1 Cor. 7. 2, 9; and therefore it is not to be despised, Matt. 19. 12. See MATRIMONY.

units.tr: The bond of marriage is the closest and indissoluble tie: Gen. 2. 24; Matt. 5. 32 and 19. 5; Mark 10. 11; Luke 16. 18; 1 Cor. 7. 10. No one but God can dissolve it, Matt. 19. 6. It is said that a man leaves his father and mother for his wife, Gen. 2. 24; Matt. 19. 5. This is not to be understood absolutely [κατὰ π] but comparatively, that is, that he should rather do that than desert his wife. Spouses are mutually bound, 1 Cor. 7. 3, 4; they have mutual care, 1 Cor. 7. 33. Newlyweds are exempt from military service in the first year, Deut. 24. 5. One must not marry unbelievers, Deut. 7. 3; Exod. 34. 16. Otherwise it will be unhappy, as Solomon found by experience, 1 Kings 11. 3, 4. The prohibition of marriage is diabolical, 1 Tim. 4. 3. The duties of spouses: Eph. 5. 22 and 1 Pet. 3. 6, 7, 8. The spiritual marriage between God and his Church: Song of Songs 1. 2, 3, etc.; Isa. 50; Jer. 31. 22; Ezek. 16. 7, 8; Hos. 2. 1, 2, 20; Matt. 9. 15; 22. 2; 25. 5; Mark 2. 19; 2 Cor. 11. 2; Rev. 19. 7; 21. 9. It is confirmed by an oath, Ezek. 16. 8, so that (Eph. 5. 26, 27). See Spiritual Spouse, Christ.

units.la: ¶ Coniugium esse sacramentum afferunt ( sed falso Pontificij ex Ephes. 5. 32. item conferre gratiam & sanctificationem, 1.Thess.4.4. cuius denique rei sit sacramentum. Vide Ephes.5.32.& Matrimonium.
units.tr: ¶ The Papists assert that marriage is a sacrament, but falsely, appealing to Eph. 5. 32; likewise that it confers grace and sanctification, 1 Thess. 4. 4. Finally, of what thing it is the sacrament. See Eph. 5. 32 and Matrimony.

units.la: CONSCIENTIA, συνείδησις, est cogitatio seu iudicium mentis damnans, aut excusans nos: prout facta nostra bona sunt, aut mala. Unde fit ut alia dicatur bona, alia mala. Ro. 2.
units.tr: CONSCIENCE (συνείδησις) is the thought or judgment of the mind, either condemning or excusing us, according as our deeds are good or bad. Hence it is that one conscience is called good and another bad. Rom. 2.

units.la: Bona, est integrum mentis nostrae ex vera charitate dicantis, & factum nostrum examinantis iudicium, de eo tum scopo, tum modo in nostris cum proximo communiter spectato & adhibito, mala est huic contraria. Heb. 9.14. Sanguis Christi purgabit conscientiam vestram ab operibus mortuis, ad serviendum Deo vivo.
units.tr: A good conscience is the sound judgment of a mind that proceeds from true charity and examines our deed, both as to its aim and as to its manner, as generally considered and practised in our dealings with our neighbour. A bad conscience is contrary to this. Heb. 9. 14: The blood of Christ will purge your conscience from dead works, to serve the living God.

Haec enim vis est conscientiae, ut opus natura sua medium, si bona fuerit, bonum reddat: sin mala, malum. Propter conscientiam Dei sustinere molestias, 1. Petr. 2.19. nihil aliud est Petro, quàm quòd iniuste afflicto sit religio Deum offendere, cuius voluntate intelligit hoc onus sibi impositum.
units.tr: CONSCIENCE is to be valued highly: 2 Cor. 1. 12; 2 Cor. 12. 19; 1 Tim. 1. 19; Heb. 10. 22; Heb. 13. 18; 1 Pet. 3. 16, 17, 21; 1 John 1. 7; 3. 19, 20. Examples of good conscience: David and Hanani, 1 Chron. 12. 17, etc.; the Virgin Mary, Luke 1. 46; Zacchaeus, 19; Paul, Acts 18. 6; 23. 1; 24. 16; Rom. 9. 1; 1 Cor. 4. 4; 2 Cor. 1. 12; 2. 17; 4. 2; 7. 2; 1 Thess. 2. 3, 4; Heb. 13. 18. Its fruits: Prov. 12. 2; 28; 11. 3; 20. 7; 28. 1. Consciences subject to the command of God alone, Rom. 6. 17; 14. 8, 9, 10: their freedom must be preserved for them, 1 Cor. 7. 35; 14. 40; 2 Cor. 1. 24; Gal. 5. 13; Col. 2. 16, 20; 2 Thess. 3. 4; 1 Tim. 4. 1; Titus 1. 15; James 4. 12. How it is to be strengthened: Heb. 13. 9. A seared conscience: 1 Tim. 4. 2. A doubtful conscience: nothing is to be undertaken, Rom. 14. 2. The conscience of an idol: Paul speaks of it in a certain manner of speaking, 1 Cor. 8. 7, meaning the silent judgment of those who thought themselves free to eat what had been offered to idols, and therefore could not eat with a good conscience. For this is the power of conscience: that a deed, indifferent in its own nature, if done in good conscience, is made good; but if in bad conscience, bad. To bear grief for the sake of conscience toward God, 1 Pet. 2. 19, means nothing else to Peter than that a man, unjustly afflicted, should be careful not to offend God, whose will he understands this burden to be laid upon him.

units.la: Consolatio communis in omni cruce, Quia crux à diuina prouidentia Patris clementissimi proficiscitur. Heb. 12.5. &c. Rom.8.28. Ps. 119.71. Ps. 94.12. Parit patientiam, Rom.5. 3. Iacob,1.2.3. Momenta-nea est, 2.Cor.4.17. 1.Pet.1.6. Deus cruci modum imponit: 1.Cor.10.13. Nos à charitate Dei separare non potest: Rom.8.39. Cruce probatis vitæ corona parata est, Iacob, 1.12. 2. Non potest electos euertere, 2.Cor.4. 1.Cor.10.13. Spiritus Dei super crucem ferentibus quiet, 1.Pet,4.14. Per hanc oportet nos conformes fieri imagini Filij Dei: Rom.8.28. 1.Pet.4.13. Cruci sancti semper subiecti, Iacob.5.11. Matt.5.12. Hanc perferentes non damnantur in hoc mundo, 1.Cor.11.32. In cruce consolatio ... escit, 2.Cor.1.5. Crucis læta catastrophe, Luc.6.21. Matt.5.4. Per quam nos in Regnum Dei intrare oportet, Act.14. Gaudiū cœlorū multis partibus dolores huius vitæ su-perat, Ioh.16.22. Tandem Deus ab omni malo liberabit Electos: Ps.34.20. (V. Afflictiones non metuendæ.)
units.tr: Common consolation in every cross: because the cross comes from the divine providence of the most merciful Father. Heb. 12:5, etc.; Rom. 8:28; Ps. 119:71; Ps. 94:12. It produces patience, Rom. 5:3; James 1:2-3. It is momentary, 2 Cor. 4:17; 1 Pet. 1:6. God sets a limit to the cross, 1 Cor. 10:13. It cannot separate us from the love of God, Rom. 8:39. For those who are proved by the cross, the crown of life is prepared, James 1:12. It cannot overthrow the elect, 2 Cor. 4; 1 Cor. 10:13. The Spirit of God rests upon those who bear the cross, 1 Pet. 4:14. Through it we must be conformed to the image of the Son of God, Rom. 8:28; 1 Pet. 4:13. The saints are always subject to the cross, James 5:11; Matt. 5:12. Those who endure it are not condemned in this world, 1 Cor. 11:32. In the cross consolation [...], 2 Cor. 1:5. The joyful outcome of the cross, Luke 6:21; Matt. 5:4. Through it we must enter the kingdom of God, Acts 14. The joy of heaven surpasses in many respects the sorrows of this life, John 16:22. Finally God will free the elect from every evil, Ps. 34:20. (See: Afflictions not to be feared.)

units.la: Consolatio, est beneficium Dei, quo nos adversus perturbationem tristitiam, quam miseria, cui in hac vita subiicimur, ad-versitatis, potenter corroborat, malo cuique quod vel ferimus vel formidamus bonum aliquod opponendo, ut nos illius considerationE dolorem vel metum mitigantes, animas nostras per patientiam in spe & silentio possideamus, Ps. 86.17 & 94.19. & 119.76.77. Esai.51.12. & 52.9. & 66.13. 2.Cor.1 3.1. Cor.10.13.
units.tr: Consolation is a benefit of God, by which he powerfully strengthens us against the disturbance and sadness that the misery of adversity, to which we are subject in this life, brings; by setting against whatever evil we either bear or fear some good, so that by considering it we may mitigate our grief or fear, and possess our souls in patience, hope and silence, Ps. 86:17; 94:19; 119:76–77; Isa. 51:12; 52:9; 66:13; 2 Cor. 1:3; 1 Cor. 10:13.

units.la: Consolationis argumenta communiter in omni miseria sup-peditant tum Attributa Dei, tum Opera eius, Esai.40.
units.tr: The arguments for consolation, in every misery, are supplied in common both by the attributes of God and by his works, Isa. 40.

units.la: Consolatione distincta nobis opus est. 1. Aduersus peccatum, pauores ingentes pariens. 2. Aduersus quamuis afflictionem aliam.
units.tr: Consolation must be distinguished for us: 1. against sin, which produces very great terrors; 2. against any other affliction.

units.la: Consolatione aduersus peccatum, ac proinde & Satanæ potestate præbet efficacissimã. 1.Misericordia, gratia dilectio Dei Patris, 2. Filii Dei, 1. Chr. Seruator, Domin9 & Mediator no-ster. 3. Sp. S. & eiusdem donatio. 4. Fœdus gratiæ. 5. Obsignatio eiusdem fœderis per Sacramenta Baptismi,& Cœnæ L. mini. 6. Donum perseuerantiæ in Christo. 7. Exem magnorum peccatorum qui gratiam & remissionem i- quitatum suarum obtinuerunt à Deo:vt Dauid.Manas Mulier peccatrix, filius perditus, Publicanus in tem Zachæus, Afflictus per 38.annos,Mulieres quædam gra calamitatibus oppressæ,Adultera mulier, Latro in cr Petrus Christi discipulus, Iudæi qui Christum crucif runt,Paulus ante apostolatum.
units.tr: Consolation against sin, and therefore also against the power of Satan, is supplied most effectively: 1. by the mercy, grace and love of God the Father; 2. of the Son of God, Christ the Saviour, our Lord and Mediator; 3. of the Holy Spirit and his gift; 4. the covenant of grace; 5. the sealing of this same covenant through the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; 6. the gift of perseverance in Christ; 7. examples of great sinners who obtained grace and the forgiveness of their iniquities from God: such as David, Manasseh, the sinful woman, the lost son, the publican in the temple, Zacchaeus, the man afflicted for 38 years, certain women oppressed by calamities, the adulterous woman, the thief on the cross, Peter the disciple of Christ, the Jews who crucified Christ, Paul before his apostleship.

units.la: Consolatio aduersus afflictiones peccatum consecutas, communis est,vel peculiaris. Afflictio quæcunque ne est patienter ferenda. 1. A manu Patris nostri cæle proficiscitur. 2. Eam promeriti sumus peccatis nost 3. Ad gloriam Dei facit. 4. Confert ad electorum bon & salutem.5.Parit patientiam.6.Est momentanea.
units.tr: Consolation against afflictions that follow sin is common, or particular. Any affliction whatever is to be borne patiently: 1. it proceeds from the hand of our heavenly Father; 2. we have deserved it by our sins; 3. it serves the glory of God; 4. it contributes to the good and salvation of the elect; 5. it produces patience; 6. it is momentary.

units.la: Consolatione peculiari sanat Scriptura peculiariter gentes afflictiones. 1. Hereses & Schismata. 2. Scand & peccata in mundo passim grassantia.3. Antichristi v machinationes. 4. Contemptus pietatis. 5. Calamit patriæ. 6. Prosperitas impiorum.7. Dolores in mor 8. Morbi diuturni. 9.Odia mundi. 10.Bella adu.Eccles 11.Tyrannis multiplex. 12. Paupertas & solitudo. 13. manitas multorum & malignitas. 14. Pericula ingru tia, 5. Exilia. 16. Persecutiones variæ pro nomine C sti. 17. Mors. 18. Iudicium nouissimum.]
units.tr: By particular consolation Scripture heals particular afflictions of the faithful: 1. heresies and schisms; 2. scandals and sins spreading everywhere in the world; 3. the machinations of Antichrist; 4. contempt of piety; 5. calamities of the fatherland; 6. the prosperity of the wicked; 7. pains in death; 8. long-lasting sicknesses; 9. the hatred of the world; 10. wars against the Church; 11. manifold tyranny; 12. poverty and loneliness; 13. the rashness and malice of many; 14. impending dangers; 15. exiles; 16. various persecutions for the name of Christ; 17. death; 18. the last judgment.

units.la: Cor vnum & anima vna, pro summa tum in doctrina, tum in voluntate consensione, Actor. 4.32. Cordi inscriptum habere opus Legis Roman.2.15. est habere turpis honesti, iusti & iniusti discrimen, quod est aequitatis omnis, rectarum legum norma, hominis menti insculpta. In corde psallere Domino, Ephes. 5.19. pro animo vel serio cordis affectu. Cordis lapidei nomine, Ezech. 11.19. & 36.26, summa ingenij & cordis humani duritiei denotatur, quam adumbrabant Tabulae lapideae, ad quas alludit Paulus 2. Corinth.3.3. Cor autem lapideo opponitur cor carneum, non quod in carne versatur (vt accipi solet hoc epitheton, quando carni spiritui opponitur) sed e contrario, quod vi spiritus dei factum est mollius; vt in eo tanquam nouis Tabu-
units.tr: One heart and one soul, for the greatest agreement both in doctrine and in will, Acts 4:32. To have the work of the Law written on the heart, Romans 2:15, is to have the distinction between what is shameful and what is honourable, and between the just and the unjust. This is the standard of all fairness and of right laws, engraved on the human mind. To sing in the heart to the Lord, Ephesians 5:19, means with a sincere and earnest disposition of the heart. The name "stony heart", Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26, denotes the utmost hardness of wit and of the human heart, which the stone tables foreshadowed, and to which Paul alludes in 2 Corinthians 3:3. But the stony heart is opposed to the fleshy heart. This does not mean a heart that dwells in the flesh, as this epithet is usually understood when flesh is set against spirit. On the contrary, it means a heart made softer by the power of God's Spirit, so that the grace of the Gospel may be engraved on it, as on new tables,

Corde creditur ad iustitiam Rom.10 10.
units.tr: "To have heart and heart" is said of the Hebrews, as "double-hearted" is said of the Greeks, James 1:8. It describes a man of double mind, or a dissembler, who says one thing with his words and feels another within. Or rather, especially in James, it describes one who is uncertain of mind, now leaning this way and now that, and who does not labour to be established in true religion. "With the heart one believes unto righteousness", Romans 10:10.

units.tr: CORE, son of Izhar. With his companions he rises against Moses, Num. 16, and is swallowed up by the earth, vv. 32, 33. See CHORE.

units.la: CORINTHVS vrbs Achaiæ maritima: Act.18 1.1.Cor.1.2. vt Paulus ibi quinquennium docuit sermonem Dei, Act.18.11.
units.tr: CORINTH, a seaport city of Achaia: Acts 18:1; 1 Cor. 1:2. Here Paul taught the word of God for a year and a half, Acts 18:11.

units.la: CORINTHII recipiunt Euangelium, Actor.18. v.8.9.10.11. factiones sunt diuisi, 1.Corinth.1.v.11.12 sunt epistola Pauli 2.Corinth.3.2. & Christi, ver.3. gloria Pauli, 2. Corinth.1.1. Apostolatus Pauli sigillum, 1.Cor.9.2.
units.tr: The CORINTHIANS receive the Gospel, Acts 18:8–11. They are divided into factions, 1 Cor. 1:11, 12. They are Paul's epistle, 2 Cor. 3:2, and Christ's, v. 3. They are Paul's glory, 2 Cor. 1:12. Paul's apostleship is the seal of it, 1 Cor. 9:2.

units.la: CORNELIVS Centurio, & eius pietas, Act.10.v.1.2. videt visionem v.3 4. Petro obuiam venit v.25. accidens ad pedes eius & adorans eum erigitur, v.26. 27. baptizatur cum tota domo, v.48. Eius attentio.v.33.
units.tr: CORNELIUS the centurion, and his piety, Acts 10:1, 2. He sees a vision, vv. 3, 4. He comes to meet Peter, v. 25. Falling at Peter's feet and worshipping him, he is raised up, vv. 26, 27. He is baptised with his whole household, v. 48. His attentiveness, v. 33.

units.tr: HORN. The crown of the ark, Exod. 25:11, 25–27; 30:3, 4; 37:2; 1 Kings 14:27. The heavenly crown, Rev. 4:4, 10; 6:2; 12:1; 14. The mystical crown, Rev. 9:7. The royal crown, 1 Chron. 20; Ps. 21:4; Jer. 13:18; Ezek. 21:26; Zech. 6:11–14. The crown of thorns, Matt. 27:29; John 19:2, 5. A crown means a moulding, Jer. 52:22; Ezek. 43:17, 20. For the round of the year, Ps. 65:12. For a circle of men, 1 Sam. 23:26; 1 Chron. 5:54. A garland or wreath of flowers, Acts 14:13; 1 Cor. 9:25. For a multitude, Isa. 28:1, 3. For glorious ornament, Job 19:9; 31:36; Prov. 4:9; 12:4; 14:24; 16:30; 17:6; 27:2; Rev. 3:11; Isa. 28:5; 61:3, 10; 62:3; Lam. 5:16; Ezek. 16:12; 23:42; 24:13, 23; Phil. 4:1; 1 Thess. 2:10. Mystically, a horn stands for the glory, power and strength of Christ, 1 Sam. 2:10; Luke 1:69. It stands for the strength of the Church, which is Christ's body and members, Deut. 33:17; 1 Sam. 2:10; Ps. 99:25; Lam. 2:3. It stands for the power of the wicked outside and inside the Church, Ps. 22:22; Dan. 7:7, etc.; Rev. 5:6; 12:3; 13:1, 11; 17:3, 7. [2.16.] See 1 Kings 22:11. ## BODY

units.la: CORPVS.

Corpus pro hominis parte non regenerata, Roman.8.10. 1. Corinthh.9.27.hoc est,pro veteri homine Spiritui repugnante.Pro toto homine συνεδοχικῶς, Rom. 12.1.vbi alludit Apostolus ad veterem ritum, ut ex epithetis sequentibus apparet,& ex 1 Thess.5.23. Corpus animale,1.Corint.15.44.dicitur,cui anima vitales facultates praeper: imbecillas tamen illas & temporarias, unde fit ut sit corruptioni obnoxium & sordidum, praesertim quum ab anima destitutum seritur, id est, conditur humo quod ψυχικὸν erat:Sicut contra, Corpus spirituale dicitur, quod divinae illius virtutis particeps, tanto excellentiorem vitam vivit,quanto Deus anima praestat:unde fit,ut eiusmodi corpus sit aeternum, gloria & splendore insigne,ab omni denique imbecillitate liberum. Corpus carnis, pro humana natura,Col.1.22.pro massa ex omnibus vitiis conflata,2.11.
units.tr: Body, for the part of man that is not regenerate, Rom. 8:10; 1 Cor. 9:27; that is, for the old man who resists the Spirit. For the whole man, by synecdoche, Rom. 12:1, where the Apostle alludes to the old rite, as appears from the epithets that follow and from 1 Thess. 5:23. "Animal body", 1 Cor. 15:44, is the body to which the soul supplies vital powers, but these powers are weak and temporary. Hence it is subject to corruption and is filthy, especially when it is sown destitute of the soul, that is, buried in the earth, being what was psychic. Conversely, "spiritual body" is the body which, partaking of that divine power, lives a life as much more excellent as God surpasses the soul. Hence such a body is eternal, distinguished by glory and splendour, and finally free from all weakness. "Body of flesh" means human nature, Col. 1:22; or a mass compounded of all vices, 2:11.

Hebraismus,pro,morti obnoxium.Corpus peccati, 6.6.pro,caro, in qua peccatum ipsum haeret, ut eleganter explicatur 1. Petr.4.ver.1.2.Corpus lucidum,Matt.6.v.22.23.in Scriptu-ris dicitur luce oculorum,id est, recto cernentis iudicio illustratum: Corpus tenebricosum contra dicitur, quod in tenebris positum est,vitiosis scilicet affectibus, luminibus mentis officientibus. Corpus non minus quam anima Deo subiectum,1.Cor.6.20.
units.tr: Body of Christ, [mystical, Rom. 12:5; 1 Cor. 6:15; 10:17; 12:13, 27; Eph. 1:23; 4:4, 12, 16; 5:23, 30; Col. 1:18, 24; 2:19; 3:15]. Body, for the truth foreshadowed by the legal shadows, Col. 2:17. To be guilty of the body of the Lord is said of one who has despised it, 1 Cor. 11:27, as the Apostle himself explains in v. 29. To discern the body of the Lord, 1 Cor. 11:29, is to take account of its dignity, so as to distinguish it from other things. Therefore one approaches the holy Supper with the greatest reverence, not as to profane food, but trembling as to the mysteries of the most precious thing of all. "Body of death", Rom. 7:24, is a Hebraism meaning liable to death. "Body of sin", 6:6, means the flesh, in which sin itself clings, as is elegantly explained in 1 Pet. 4:1, 2. "Bright body", Matt. 6:22, 23: in Scripture this is said of the light of the eyes, that is, of a mind illumined by right judgment in seeing. A "dark body", on the contrary, is said of what is placed in darkness, that is, of vicious affections hindering the lights of the mind. The body is subject to God no less than the soul, 1 Cor. 6:20.

units.la: CORPORIS creatio, Gen.2.7. quatenus habenda cura sit, Coloss.2.23.1.Cor.16.15.19 & 9.26.Rom.6.12. & 12.6. mortale Gen.3.29.Heb.9.27.Resurrecturum, Phil.3.21.1.Cor.15.53. Corpora nostra, membra Christi, 1.Corint.6.15. Corporalis exercitatio commendatur, 1 Tim.4.8. Sic vocat Paulus, non illam immodicam, ac multo etiam minus superstitiosam illam, aut impiam potiùs : sed rigidam tamen, & domandæ carni vtilem victus rationem.
units.tr: The creation of the body, Gen. 2:7; how far its care is to be taken, Col. 2:23; 1 Cor. 16:15, 19; 9:26; Rom. 6:12; 12:6. It is mortal, Gen. 3:19; Heb. 9:27. It will rise again, Phil. 3:21; 1 Cor. 15:53. Our bodies are members of Christ, 1 Cor. 6:15. Bodily exercise is commended, 1 Tim. 4:8. Paul calls thus not that immoderate, and much less superstitious, or rather impious, exercise, but a rigid rule of living, useful for taming the flesh.

units.la: CORPVS Christi dicitur cœleste, 1.Corinth.15.47. aut è cœlo: vbi duo notanda veniunt: Vnum, considerari eo loco Corpus Christi in gloria, non in humilitate: siquidem antea, si ex sua natura, seorsim à diuinitate æstimetur, ψυχικὸν & χοϊκὸν erat, sicut & cæterorum hominum, excepto peccato. Alterum, quòd dicitur è cœlo, id per communicationem idiomatum esse intelligendum, vt Ioan.3.13. Idcircò verè sic loquitur Apostolus, vt ipsam Christi carnem sciamus Dei inhabitantis virtute hanc gloriam esse assecutam, quam cum suis membris tandem aliquando communicabit. Corpori honor habendus, & in sanctificatione possidendum, 1.Thess.4.4.
units.tr: The body of Christ is called heavenly, 1 Cor. 15:47, or from heaven. Two things are to be noted here. First, the body of Christ is considered in that place in its glory, not in its humility. For previously, if it is judged by its own nature apart from the divinity, it was psychic and earthly, as were the bodies of other men, except for sin. Second, that it is said to be from heaven is to be understood by communication of properties, as in John 3:13. Therefore the Apostle speaks truly, so that we know that the flesh of Christ itself, by the power of God dwelling in it, attained this glory, which at length it will one day communicate to its members. The body is to be honoured and possessed in sanctification, 1 Thess. 4:4.

units.tr: Fraternal correction is commended, Lev. 19:17, 18; Prov. 1:20; 9:7; 10:17; 12:1; 13:1; 15:31; 17:10; 24:25; 25:12; 27:5; 28:23; 29:1; Eccl. 7:6; Hos. 4; Matt. 18:15; Luke 17:3; Gal. 2:11; 6:1; 1 Thess. 5:14; 2 Tim. 2:25; 4:2; 1 Tim. 5:1, 20. It is to be applied in due time, Prov. 29:1. It is to be received, Prov. 13:18; 15:5, 12, 31, 32; 17:10. Its usefulness: Prov. 19:25; 21:11; 27:5; 28:23; 29:1; Eccl. 7:6. To whom it is useful: Prov. 9:8; David, Ps. 141:5. How harmful is contempt of it: Prov. 10:17; 13:18; 12:1; 15:5, 12, 32; 29:1. See ADMONITION.

units.la: CORVVS ex arca Noe emittitur, Gen. 8.7. eo non vescebantur Iudæi, Leuit. 11.15. Deut. 14.14. Corui pascunt Eliam, 1. Reg. 17.6. Coruis esca à Deo paratur, Iob. 39.3. Psal. 147.9.
units.tr: The RAVEN is sent out from Noah's ark, Gen. 8:7. The Jews did not eat it, Lev. 11:15; Deut. 14:14. Ravens fed Elijah, 1 Kings 17:6. Food is provided for ravens by God, Job 39:3; Ps. 147:9.

units.la: COTURNICES coelitus pluunt, Exod. 16. 12. Num. 11.31. &c.
units.tr: Quails rain down from heaven, Exod. 16.12; Num. 11.31, etc.

units.tr: Cozbi the harlot is killed, Num. 25.8, 15.

units.la: CRAPVLA damnatur, Vide COMESSATIO, & EBRIETAS.
units.tr: Gluttony is condemned. See COMESSATIO and EBRIETAS.

units.la: CRAS, pars temporis proxima, pro toto, synecdoche, id est, posthac, vel in posterum, Ge. 30.33. Exodi 13.14. Deut. 6. 20. Iosh. 4.6. & 22 24. Vide Prou. 3 28. Eccles. 10.11.
units.tr: CRAS (tomorrow), a part of time put for the whole, a synecdoche, that is, henceforth or in future, Gen. 30.33; Exod. 13.14; Deut. 6.20; Josh. 4.6 and 22.24. See Prov. 3.28; Eccl. 10.11.

units.la: CREATIO
units.tr: CREATION

units.la: CREATIO, est opus Dei Patris Filij & Spiritus. S. A quo ex nihilo, B. tantum verbi sui omnipotētis virtute, C. sex diedrum spatio, D. res vniuersas creauit, E. quas etiam sustentat & regit potentissime, F. ad nominis sui gloriam, G. & mundi Incolarum vsum, ac salutem Electorum, H.
units.tr: CREATION is the work of God the Father, Son and Spirit, who created all things out of nothing, by the power of his all-powerful word alone, in the space of six days. He also sustains and governs them most powerfully, to the glory of his name, for the use of the inhabitants of the world and the salvation of the elect.

units.la: A, Gen. cap. 1. integrum. Psal. 33. 6. Ioh. 1.1. Col. 1.16. B, Gen. 31. C. Psal. 33 6. D, Gen. 2.1. 2. E, ibid. F, Matth. 6. 25. &c. Iohann. 5.17. Actor. 17.26. &c. Hebr. 1.3. Ex perpetuitate creaturarum intelligitur Creator æternus, ex magnitudine omnipotēs, ex ordine & dispositione sapiens, ex gubernatione bonus: Aug. in Ioh.
units.tr: A, Gen. ch. 1 entire. Ps. 33.6; John 1.1; Col. 1.16. B, Gen. 31. C, Ps. 33.6. D, Gen. 2.1, 2. E, ibid. F, Matt. 6.25, etc.; John 5.17; Acts 17.26, etc.; Heb. 1.3. G, Prov. 16.4; Ps. 148 entire; Rom. 1.20; Acts 14.17; Rev. 4.11. H, Gen. 1.28; Acts 17.26; Ps. 8.7; Heb. 2.7, 8. From the perpetuity of creatures the Creator is understood to be eternal, from their greatness omnipotent, from their order and arrangement wise, and from their governance good: Augustine, on John.

units.la: CREATIO: Creatio cœli & terræ, Gen. 1.1. Creatio noua, Esa. 43 19.2. Cor. 5.17. Gal. 6.15 Eph. 2 10. Iac. 1,18. 1. Pet. 1. 23. Apoc. 21.5. Vide REGENERATIO.
units.tr: CREATION: the creation of heaven and earth, Gen. 1.1. New creation, Isa. 43.19; 2 Cor. 5.17; Gal. 6.15; Eph. 2.10; Jas 1.18; 1 Pet. 1.23; Rev. 21.5. See REGENERATION.

units.la: CREATVRA, est res omnis, quæ neque à seipsa est, neque semper fuit, sed & aliquando, & à Deo producta est.
units.tr: A CREATURE is every thing which is neither from itself nor has always existed, but was at some time produced by God.

units.la: CREATVRA, κτίσις, interdum significat creationem mundi, Marc. 10.6. interdum res creatas, 13.19. Rom. 8,21. interdum omnes conditos homines, seu, quod idem est, totum genus humanum, Marc. 16 15. aut omnes gentes, vt habetur Matth. 28.19 Lucæ 24. 47. Noua creatura, 2. Cor 5.17.
units.tr: CREATURE [κτίσις] sometimes means the creation of the world, Mark 10.6; sometimes created things, Mark 13.19; Rom. 8.21; sometimes all created men, or, which is the same, the whole human race, Mark 16.15; or all nations, as in Matt. 28.19; Luke 24.47. New creature, 2 Cor. 5.17.

units.la: Creaturæ omnes à Deo conditæ, Genesis 1.1. Deo subditæ, 14. 22. Iob. 38.8. Prou. 20. 12. Creaturæ mutæ, tellæs à Deo citātur, Genesis 31 verf. 48.51. Deut. 4. 26. & 30.19. Iosu. 24.27. Esai. 1 2. Mich. 6. 2. ad audiendum Dei verbum excitantur, Ieremiæ 22. 29. ad exultationem & gratam beneficiorum Dei agnitionem inuitantur, Psal. 96.11. & 98. 8. Esa. 44. 23. & 49.13. Apoc.12.12. Vanitati subiectæ: Rom.8. 10.
units.tr: All creatures were created by God, Gen. 1.1, and are subject to God, Gen. 14.22; Job 38.8; Prov. 20.12. Dumb creatures: the earth is called by God, Gen. 31.48, 51; Deut. 4.26 and 30.19; Josh. 24.27; Isa. 1.2; Mic. 6.2, and are roused to hear God's word, Jer. 22.29; they are invited to exult and to acknowledge God's benefits with gratitude, Ps. 96.11; 98.8; Isa. 44.23; 49.13; Rev. 12.12. Made subject to vanity: Rom. 8.10.

units.la: CREDERE in Christum, vide FIDES. Credere toto corde, Actor. 8.27. non est perfecte omni ex parte Christo credere, sed ex pio animo & syncera mente Christum amplecti. Hic enim est Scripturæ mos, vt toto corde fieri dicat quod syncere & ex animo significat, vt Psalmo 12. 3. & 11 1. & 119.10. & 138.1. [Credere Deo, Deum, in Deum, Christo, in Christum, in Filium Dei, Euangelio, Dei & Christi seruis: locutiones obseruatu dignæ. Credere homini phrasis variæ significationis. Credo, i. certus sum de re quapiam, Deuteron. 28. 66. Iob. 24. 22. Credo, i. committerem quampiam fidei alicuius amici vel serui, Gen.39. v. 4 23. Leu. 6. 2.1. Par. 9. v. 26. 29. Nehe. 13. 13. Ioan. 2. 24. Rom. 2. 1. Tim. 1. 11. Credo, i. existimo, Gen.21 7. Deut. 2. 21. Iob. 15 22. Act. 9.26.]
units.tr: BELIEVE in Christ: see FAITH. To believe with the whole heart, Acts 8.27, is not to believe Christ perfectly in every respect, but to embrace Christ with a pious spirit and a sincere mind. For it is Scripture's manner to say that something is done with the whole heart when it means sincerely and from the soul, as in Ps. 12.3; 11.1; 119.10; 138.1. [To believe God, God in God, Christ in Christ, in the Son of God, the gospel, the servants of God and of Christ: these expressions are worth noting. To believe a man is a phrase of varying meaning. "I believe," that is, I am certain of some matter, Deut. 28.66; Job 24.22. "I believe," that is, I would entrust something to the faith of some friend or servant, Gen. 39.4, 23; Lev. 6.2, 1; 1 Chron. 9.26, 29; Neh. 13.13; John 2.24; Rom. 2.1; 1 Tim. 1.11. "I believe," that is, I think, Gen. 21.7; Deut. 2.21; Job 15.22; Acts 9.26.]

units.la: CREDVLITAS nimia damnatur, Pro.14.15. Ecc.7.22. 2. Tim 3.14. 1. Ioh. 4.1. Credulitatis exempla: Laban, Gen.31. v. 1.2. Putiphar, 39.19. Iosua, Iof. 9 14.15. Dauid, 1. Sam. 25. 12. Hanon 2. units.tr: Excessive credulity is condemned, Prov. 14.15; Eccl. 7.22; 2 Tim. 3.14; 1 John 4.1. units.la: CRESCERE in scientia iubemur, Ephes. 4. v. 14 15. Coloss. 1. 10 1. Petr. 2.2. V. Luc. 1.88. & 2.40. Gen. 1.22. & 8.17.
units.tr: We are commanded to grow in knowledge, Eph. 4.14, 15; Col. 1.10; 1 Pet. 2.2. See Luke 1.80 and 2.40; Gen. 1.22 and 8.17.

units.la: CRESCENS Discipulus Pauli in Galatiam proficiscitur, 2 Tim. 4.10.
units.tr: CRESCENS, a disciple of Paul, sets out for Galatia, 2 Tim. 4.10.

units.la: CRETENSIS, eorum Ecclesiæ fundatæ à Paulo, Tito superstruendæ commendantur, Tit. 1 v. 5. eorum mores perstringuntur, v. 12. CRETA, Græciæ insula, Tit. 1.5.
units.tr: The Cretans, whose churches were founded by Paul, are commended to Titus for building up, Titus 1.5; their manners are censured, v. 12. CRETE is an island of Greece, Titus 1.5.

units.la: CRISPVS, Archisynagogus Corinthi, cum tota familia Deo Christo credit, Act 18.8. baptizatur à Paulo, 1. Cor. 1.14.
units.tr: CRISPUS, ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, with his whole household, believes in God and Christ, Acts 18.8; he is baptized by Paul, 1 Cor. 1.14.

units.la: CRVDELITAS, Est sævitia animi, per quam pœna maior quam delicti ratio postulat, ab eo qui punit, exigitur eo ipso, quòd puniens ipso hominis cruciatu & acerbitate per se delectetur.
units.tr: CRUELTY is savageness of mind, by which the one who punishes exacts a penalty greater than the reason of the offence requires, in that the punisher takes pleasure in the very torment and bitterness inflicted on the man.

units.tr: CRUELTY is condemned, Deut. 25.2, 3; Prov. 11.17; 12.10; Isa. 47.6; 52.4; Zech. 1.15; 2 Tim. 3.3; Jas 2.6; 5.6. It is the companion of avarice, Jas 5.4. Its punishment: Judg. 9.56, 57; 2 Chron. 23.15; Matt. 25.41, 42; 2 Thess. 1.6; Jas 2.13, 14; 5.5. The cruel are treated cruelly. Example: Adoni-bezek, Judg. 1.7. units.la: RVX Ecclesiæ, sunt omnis generis afflictiones, quæ piis inferuntur, Deo disponente, præcipuè propter nomen Christi: vt probentur, & innotescant veri Christiani, ac Deus in ipsis celebretur.
units.tr: The cross of the Church is every kind of affliction which is inflicted on the pious by God's disposing, chiefly for the name of Christ, so that true Christians may be proved and made known, and God may be glorified in them.

Luc.9.23.Philipp.3 18. libenter ferenda est.V de AFFLICTIO,pro po crucis Dominicæ ligno,Matth.27 32.Marci 15 21.Lucæ 23 26.Philip. 2.8.Hebr.12.2.[pro mortis à Christo perpessæ efficacia & dignitate,1.Corin. 1.v.17.18. Gal.2.19.20.& 5.24.& 6.12.14. Philip.3.18.] Consolatio crucis suo loco.
units.tr: CROSS for the doctrine of the gospel, Gal. 5.11; for the preaching of the gospel, or of Christ crucified, Gal. 6.12; as an argument for evangelical preaching, 1 Cor. 1.17; by synecdoche, for mockery, Heb. 6.6; for affliction borne for Christ's name, [μετα παθῶς], Matt. 10.38; 16.24; Mark 8.34; Luke 9.23; Phil. 3.18, is to be borne willingly. See AFFLICTION. For the wood of the Lord's cross, Matt. 27.32; Mark 15.21; Luke 23.26; Phil. 2.8; Heb. 12.2. [For the efficacy and dignity of the death suffered by Christ, 1 Cor. 1.17, 18; Gal. 2.19, 20; 5.24; 6.12, 14; Phil. 3.18.] The comfort of the cross has its own place.

units.la: RVCI FIGERE Christum, Hebr. 6.6.metaphoricè, est Christum quasi rursus crucifixum, omnium ludibrio exponere. Crucifigi vetus homo dicitur, Roman.6 6. qua loquendi formula idem declaratur, atque si peccatum diceretur mortuum,aut nos peccato mortuos esse cum Christo, nisi quod illud ὁμοιωματι θεου est, & mortis genus explicat, cuius participatione mortificamur peccato. Crucifixus mundo dicitur,Gal.6.14.quem mundus despicit:Et mundus eidem crucifixus,ibid.qui mundum vicissim nihili facit.
units.tr: To crucify Christ again, Heb. 6.6, is metaphorically to expose Christ, as it were crucified anew, to the mockery of all. The old man is said to be crucified, Rom. 6.6. By this form of speech the same thing is declared as if sin were said to be dead, or we to be dead to sin with Christ, except that the former is [ὁμοιωματι θεου] and explains the kind of death by whose participation we are mortified to sin. He is said to be crucified to the world, Gal. 6.14, because the world despises him; and the world is crucified to him, ibid., because in turn he makes the world nothing.

units.la: CVLPA remissa,poena remittitur, Psalm. 32.1.Esai.1.18.& 44. 22.& 53.5.Ierem.31.v.31.34.& 50.20.Ezec.18.v.24.27. Oseæ 14.3.Mich.7.19.Roman.3.24.1.Cor.1.30.Eph.1.7.1. Timot. 2.6 1.Petr.2 24. ¶ At Pontifici,remissa culpa,pœnam non remitti contendunt,& nituntur hisce testimoniis, sed falsò,Numer.20 v.12.24.& 27.v.12.13.14 2. Samu.12.ver.9.10. Respondendum est per distinctionem:Poena,aut est pœna supplicij,id est, pœna peccati, de qua loquitur Apostolus Roman.6.23. aut poena castigationis, vel probationis, qua intelligantur dicta, Psalmo 94.2. & 118.18. & 119.; Prou.3.v.11.12.Hebr.12.v.5 6.7.8,1.Corinth.11.32.Iac.1.&; Petr.1 7.Apoc.3.19.De hac posteriore intelligendi sunt loci illi oppositi:nempe de poena castigationis & probationis,quae tantùm abest vt poenae peccati rationem & non mereatur,vt contrà summi erga pios amoris certissimum sit documentum : non autem intelligendi sunt de poenis supplicij,siue pro peccatis admissis, quae Deus pro sua misericordia remisit.
units.tr: When guilt is remitted, punishment is remitted, Ps. 32.1; Isa. 1.18; 44.22; 53.5; Jer. 31.31, 34; 50.20; Ezek. 18.24, 27; Hos. 14.3; Mic. 7.19; Rom. 3.24; 1 Cor. 1.30; Eph. 1.7; 1 Tim. 2.6; 1 Pet. 2.24. ¶ But the Papists contend that, guilt being remitted, punishment is not remitted. They rest on these testimonies, but falsely: Num. 20.12, 24, 27; 27.12, 13, 14; 2 Sam. 12.9, 10. It must be answered by distinction. Punishment is either the punishment of penalty, that is, the punishment of sin, of which the Apostle speaks in Rom. 6.23; or the punishment of chastisement or trial, by which the sayings in Ps. 94.2; 118.18; 119; Prov. 3.11, 12; Heb. 12.5–8; 1 Cor. 11.32; Jas 1.2–3; 1 Pet. 1.7; Rev. 3.19 are to be understood. Those opposing passages are to be understood of the latter, namely of the punishment of chastisement and trial, which is so far from having the character of a penalty for sin, or being deserved, that on the contrary it is a most certain proof of God's highest love towards the pious. But they are not to be understood of punishments of penalty, whether for sins committed, which God has remitted in his mercy.

units.la: CVLICEM excolare,Matth.23 24.
units.tr: To polish the cup: Matthew 23:24.

units.tr: Voluntary worship, how much it is worth: Colossians 2:23. The true worship of God [Exodus 10:26; Numbers 3:7; Joshua 22:16; 1 Chronicles 23:2 and 29:35]. 2 Chronicles 13:11. Besides the outward work, it also requires the inward affection of the person: Deuteronomy 5:19; 6:5; 10:12; 11:13; 26:16; 28:47; 30:2; Joshua 22:5; 1 Kings 12:20; Ecclesiastes 7:31; Isaiah 29:13 and 64:11; Matthew 15:8 and 22:36; John 4:23. See GOD, to be worshipped.

units.tr: Immoderate desires are condemned: 1 Thessalonians 4:4–5 [1 Timothy 3:3; 2 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:7; 1 Timothy 6:10]. See CONCUPISCENCE.

units.tr: CARE: see anxiety.

units.la: CVRIOSITAS,περιεργία,Est vel nimia & solicita rerum alienarum percontatio, & in iis scrutandis narrandisve occupatio, quae non alterius iuuandi gratia fit. Bernard. super Cantica,Doctrina Spiritus non curiositatem acuit,sed charitatem accendit.
units.tr: CURIOSITY, περιεργία [periergia]. It is either an excessive and eager inquiry into other people's affairs, and an occupation in searching out or telling them, which is not done for the sake of helping another. Bernard on the Song of Songs: The teaching of the Spirit does not sharpen curiosity but kindles love.

units.tr: Curiosity is to be avoided: Exodus 19:12, 21; John 21:21–22; Acts 1:7 and 19:19; Romans 12:3; Deuteronomy 29:29; Proverbs 25:27; Ecclesiastes 3:22; 1 Corinthians 2:2; 2 Corinthians 12:2; Ephesians 6:14; Colossians 2:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:1; 2 Thessalonians 2:2 and 3:11; 1 Timothy 1:4; 5:13; 6:3, 16, 20; [illegible]; Titus 2:12; Hebrews 9:5, 10:27 and 11:5. Examples of curiosity: Genesis 3:5–6; Dinah, Genesis 34:1–2; the men of Beth-shemesh, 1 Samuel 6:19; [?]ias, 2 Chronicles 26:16; the scribes and Pharisees, Matthew 12:38–39; the Pharisees and Sadducees, Matthew 16:1; Herod, Luke 9:9 and 23:8; the Pharisees; Peter, John 21:20; the apostles, Acts 1:7; the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, Acts 17:18–21; the Ephesians, Acts 19:19; Agrippa, Acts 25:22–23; the Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians 3:11; the younger widows, 1 Timothy 5:11–13. RUNNING, said of the inward and spiritual course and progress: Psalm 19:32; Proverbs 18:10; Song of Songs 1:4; Romans 9:16; 1 Corinthians 9:24–26; Galatians 2 and 5:7; Philippians 2:16; Hebrews 12:1. On the progress and efficacy of God, who is powerful and gracious: Psalm 147:15; 2 Thessalonians 3:1.

units.tr: Chariot, as a leader: 2 Kings 2:11. Elijah is carried up into heaven in a fiery chariot with fiery horses, ibid.; Elisha sees him, verse 12. Zechariah sees four chariots, Zechariah 6:1. War chariots: [?]Micah 1:19; 4:3; 2 Samuel 8:4 and 10:18; 1 Kings 10:26; Isaiah 21:7. Fiery chariots are seen in the air by Elisha's servant, 2 Kings 6:17. Chariots of Pharaoh, Exodus 14:7.

units.tr: Cyprus: the Jews did not eat of it, Leviticus 11:18; Deuteronomy 14:16. Cyprus, an island lying off Cilicia and Syria, where Paul and Barnabas first preached the gospel, Acts 13:4. Some Cypriots preaching the gospel, Acts 11:20.

units.la: NE,insigne Libyæ oppidum,Actor.2.10. Cyrenæi alteres cum Stephano, Act. 6.9. Euangelizantes, Act.11.20. Cyrenæus quidam Christi crucem tollens,Matt.27.32. NIVS,Syriæ Præses:eo Prouincia administrante, descriptio facta est,Luc.2.2.
units.tr: Cyrene, a famous town of Libya, Acts 2:10. Cyrenians, the others with Stephen, Acts 6:9. Those who preached the gospel, Acts 11:20. A certain Cyrenian who bore Christ's cross, Matthew 27:32. Cyrenius, governor of Syria; while he was administering the province, the registration was made, Luke 2:2.

units.la: vs Rex Persarum,Dei Spiritus impulsu captiuum populum Babylone Ierosolymam dimittit, 2.Paral.36.v.22.23.24. templum instaurent iubet, 1.Esdr.1.3. suis, vt populo renti faueant, præcipit,1.Esdr.1.4.ob id Minister liberationis populi, & Pastor Dei appellatur,Esa.44.28.prosperitas est Deo est, 45.v.1.3. vere Deum non cognouit, v.4.5. reddit vasa quondam à Nabuchodonosor ablata, 1. Eld.1.7. 14.Dan.1.2.
units.tr: Cyrus, King of the Persians: at the impulse of the Spirit of God he sends the captive people from Babylon to Jerusalem, 2 Chronicles 36:22–24. He orders the temple to be restored, Ezra 1:3. He commands his people to favour the returning people, Ezra 1:4; for this reason he is called the minister of the people's liberation and the shepherd of God, Isaiah 44:28. His prosperity is from God, 45:1, 3. He did not truly know God, verses 4–5. He returns the vessels once taken away by Nebuchadnezzar, Ezra 1:7; Daniel 1:2.

units.tr: Kiriath-sepher (also Debir), a town in the tribe of Judah, Joshua 11:21. It is taken by Joshua, 10:38. Given to the sons of Aaron, 13:15. (Debir: oracle.)

units.la: DAEMONIACI sunt, quorum mentes & sensus omnes ab uno spiritus ita occupauit, vt neque ratione, neque communi vtantur, & in proprium exitium indomiti rapiuntur. Matt.4.24.Marc.5.1.&c.
units.tr: Those are demoniacs whose minds and all their senses are taken over by one spirit, so that they use neither reason nor common sense, and are carried headlong to their own destruction. Matthew 4:24; Mark 5:1, etc.

units.la: DAGON, Deus Philistæorum, Iudic.16.23.ante arcam Dei cecidit, 1.Sam.5.3.&c. Vide IDOLORVM catalogum, vbi describitur eius forma.
units.tr: DAGON, god of the Philistines: Judges 16:23. He fell before the ark of God, 1 Samuel 5:3, etc. See the catalogue of IDOLS, where his form is described.

units.la: DALILA, Samsonis amasia, Iudic.16.4. eum prodit, v.5. (Delilah.i.situla vel paupertas.)
units.tr: DELILAH, Samson's mistress: Judges 16:4. She betrays him, verse 5. (Delilah, that is, a bucket or poverty.)

units.la: DALMATIA, regio, pars Illyrici, vbi Titus prædicauit Euangelium, 2.Tim.4.10.
units.tr: DALMATIA, a region, part of Illyricum, where Titus preached the gospel: 2 Timothy 4:10.

units.la: DAMARIS, Atheniensis mulier, Christo credit, Act.17.34.
units.tr: DAMARIS, an Athenian woman, who believed in Christ: Acts 17:34.

units.la: DAMASCVS Syriæ ciuitas, eius ruina prædicitur, Esai.7.17.1.Ier.49.23. Amos 1.5. vastatur ab Assyriis, 2.Reg.16.9. Paulus deducitur, & ab Anania docetur: Act.9.
units.tr: DAMASCUS, a city of Syria. Its ruin is foretold: Isaiah 7:8; Jeremiah 49:23; Amos 1:5. It is laid waste by the Assyrians, 2 Kings 16:9. Paul is let down and is taught by Ananias: Acts 9.

units.tr: ETERNAL DAMNATION, which is prepared for the Devil and for all the ungodly: Job 10:22 and 36:12; Isaiah 24:21, 30:33 and 66:24; [Matthew 3:12, 5:29, 8:12, 29, 13:50, 18:8, 22:13, 33, 25:30, 41; Mark 9:47; Luke 3:17, 16:23, 25; John 10:27; 2 Thessalonians 1:8; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; Revelation 19:20 and 20:10, 21:8]. Damnation of a harlot, a Hebraism for "to be condemned" as a harlot: Revelation 17:8.

units.la: DAMNARI quis dicitur, Scripturæ Sacræ consuetudine, cuius honesto exemplo possit improbitatis, aut vitij alicuius coargui, Matt.12.v.41.42.Rom.2.27.
units.tr: A person is said to be condemned, in the usage of Holy Scripture, when by an honourable example he can be convicted of some wickedness or vice: Matthew 12:41–42; Romans 2:27.

units.la: DAMNVM illatum proximo, quomodo resarciendum, Exod. v.5.6.Levit.6.5.V.Pro.22.3.Act.27.10.
units.tr: A loss inflicted on a neighbour, and how it is to be made good: Exodus 5:5–6; Leviticus 6:5. See also Proverbs 22:3; Acts 27:10.

units.la: DAN (id est, causam agens, vel indicans) filius Iacob ex Bilha, Gen.30.6. eius benedictio,49.16. Tribus Dan quærit sibi possessionem, Iud.18.1. pugnat contra Lesem, & expugnat, Iosu.19.
units.tr: DAN (that is, judging, or the one who judges), son of Jacob by Bilhah: Genesis 30:6. His blessing: 49:16. The tribe of Dan seeks a possession for itself, Judges 18:1. It fights against Leshem and conquers it, Joshua 19.

units.la: DAN vrbs, quæ & Lais, Iudic.18.29.
units.tr: DAN, a city, also called Laish: Judges 18:29.

units.la: DANIEL (i.Iudex Dei) vnus de quatuor adolescentibus Dan.1.6. Balthasar nominatur, v.7. cibis regiis vesci noluit, v.8. omnium Regis interpretatur, 2.v.29.30.31.(significatio. Vide BESTIA) à Rege adoratur, v.46.ad summum honorem euehitur, v.48.&5.29.&6.2. Scripturam arcanam interpretatur, 5.17. edicti Regij minis neglectis, in cultu Dei perseuerat, 6.10.ob id in lacum leonum mittitur.
units.tr: DANIEL (i.e. judge of God), one of the four youths; Dan. 1.6. He is named Belteshazzar, v.7. He refuses to eat the king's food, v.8. He interprets the dream of the king of all, 2.29-31 (for the meaning, see BEAST). He is worshipped by the king, v.46, and raised to the highest honour, v.48; 5.29; 6.2. He interprets the mysterious writing, 5.17. Ignoring the threats of the royal edict, he persists in the worship of God, 6.10, and for this he is thrown into the lions' den.

units.tr: of Israel is anointed, 5.3. He takes the citadel of Zion, v.7. He orders the idols burned, 1 Chron. 14.12. He brings back the ark, 2 Sam. 6.3. Quiet in the kingdom, 7.1. He is forbidden to build the Temple, v.5. 1 Chron. (...) of the people, whom he makes tributary to himself, 2 Sam. 8.v.1.2; 2 Sam. 18.2 and 19.19; 2 Sam. 8.v.6.14. He consecrates to God the vessels that he had received from the Gentiles, 2 Sam. 8.11. He blesses the people, 1 Sam. 16.2. He commits adultery with Bathsheba, 2 Sam. 11. He exposes Uriah to death, v.15. He takes Bathsheba, the wife of the dead man, to himself in marriage, v.27. He is charged by the prophet with murder and adultery, 12.9. Admonished, he repents, v.13. Absalom: he orders (his son) to be recalled, 14.21. He flees from his face, 15. He prays to God against Ahithophel, v.31. He is reviled by Shimei, 16.7. He gives the goods of Mephibosheth to Ziba, v.4. He weeps for Abner dead, 18.33. Restored to the kingdom, he returns to Jerusalem, 19.15. He buries the bones of Saul and Jonathan, 21.12. He orders the people to be numbered, 2 Sam. 24.2; 1 Chron. 21.2. For the penalty of this deed, one of three penalties is proposed to him to choose; he acknowledges his guilt, v.17. He builds an altar, v.26. He prepares what is necessary for the building of the Temple, 22.2. He commends its building to Solomon, v.6 and 28.2. He assigns the duties (?) to the Levites, 23.4. He distributes the sons of Aaron, the priests, into orders, 24.19. He instructs the singers, 2 Chron. ... He orders Solomon to be anointed king, 1 Kings 1.34. His stepmother's words, 2, v.1.2.3.4. He dies, v.10. 1 Chron. 29.28. Years of his reign, 1 Kings 2.11; 1 Chron. 29.27.

Seruus Dei,Psal.89.21.Act.4.25.& Christus Matt 22.43.Marc.12.37.Luc.20.44.Act.2.34. Spiritu sancti afflatu locutus est, 2.Sam.23.2. Matt.22.43. units.tr: Chosen by God, Ps. 78:70. Pleasing to God, Acts 7:46 (22). Called a man of God, 2 Chron. 8:14; Neh. 12:24. A prophet, Acts 2:30. A servant of God, Ps. 89:21; Acts 4:25; and Christ, Matt. 22:43; Mark 12:37; Luke 20:44; Acts 2:34. He spoke by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, 2 Sam. 23:2; Matt. 22:43; Acts 4:25; Heb. 3:7. He was a type of Christ, Acts 2:25. He had wives, 2 Sam. 5:13, and sons, v. 14. Zeal, Ps. 69:10.

units.la: Dauid spiritualis,qui est Christus,promittitur,Ieremias Ezech.34.24. & 37.24. Dauidis filius appellatur Christus, Matt.1.1. & 15.22.& 22.45.Marc.12.35. Luc.20.41. Act. & 13.22 2.Tim.2.8.Apoc.5.5.
units.tr: David, that is Christ, the spiritual David, is promised: Jer. 30:9; Ezek. 34:24; 37:24. Christ is called the son of David: Matt. 1:1; 15:22; 22:45; Mark 12:35; Luke 20:41; Acts 13:22; 2 Tim. 2:8; Rev. 5:5.

units.la: [DAVID, Christus Dauidis F. proprium nomen loco pronymici,Psal.132.10.Esai.37.35.& 55.3.Ier.30.9.& 33.22. Ezech. 34. v.23.24. & 37.24,25. Ose. 3.5. Amos,9.11.Actor.15.16.
units.tr: DAVID: Christ, the son of David, used as a proper name in place of a pronoun. Ps. 132:10; Isa. 37:35; 55:3; Jer. 30:9; 33:22; Ezek. 34:23–24; 37:24–25; Hos. 3:5; Amos 9:11; Acts 15:16.

units.tr: A prophetess who judges Israel, Judg. 4:4. She urges Barak to deliver the country, v. 6, and goes with him to battle, v. 9. Her song of thanksgiving for the victory won, Judg. 5, etc.

units.la: POLIS, regio decem urbium, Iudææ propinqua: Matt. Marc.5.20.
units.tr: DECAPOLIS, a region of ten cities, near Judea: Matt. 4:25; Mark 5:20.

units.tr: NEM: sometimes taken for an indefinite number, as in Gen. 15 and 31:41; Ps. 68:18 and 91:7; Matt. 18:24; 1 Cor. 4:15 and 14; Rev. 2:10.

units.la: MARE, pro decimas exigere, Heb.7.5. pro decimas sol-vere, Matt.23.23. Luc.18.12.
units.tr: (To) TITHE: to exact tithes, Heb. 7:5; to pay tithes, Matt. 23:23; Luke 18:12.

units.la: MAE præcipiuntur, Exod.22.29. Decimæ pro Leuitis peregrinis, pupillis & viduis, tertio anno separandæ, Deut.14.28.29.2.Paral.31.v.4.5. offeruntur. Exempla: Abraham, Gen.14.20. Heb.7.4. Iacob, Gen.28.20. Israelitæ, 2.Paral.31.5. Iuda, Nehem.13.12. Pharisæus, Luc.18.12. Decimæ, Levirum hæreditas, Num.18.v.21.24. Deut.10.9.&14.29. decimæ à populo vt à Leuitis edendæ, Deut.12.v.17.18.&[illegible, ~2 letters]2.
units.tr: TITHES are commanded, Exod. 22:29. Tithes are to be set apart every third year for the Levites, strangers, orphans and widows, and offered, Deut. 14:28–29; 2 Chron. 31:4–5. Examples: Abraham, Gen. 14:20; Heb. 7:4. Jacob, Gen. 28:20. The Israelites, 2 Chron. 31:5. Judah, Neh. 13:12. The Pharisee, Luke 18:12. Tithes as the Levites' inheritance, Num. 18:21–24; Deut. 10:9; 14:29. Tithes to be eaten by the people as by the Levites, Deut. 12:17–18.

units.la: ORVM in Ecclesia seruetur oportet, 1 Cor 14.40.
units.tr: Good order must be kept in the Church, 1 Cor. 14:40.

units.la: RIONES super populum à Mose constituuntur, Deut.
units.tr: OFFICERS over the people are appointed by Moses, Deut.

DEDICATION of the Temple or of the altar: Num. 7:10–11; 84, 88; 1; 3:8; 26, 63, 65; 2 Chron. 7:5, 9; 15:8; 1 Esd. 6:16–17; 2 Esd. 12:27; 3 Esd. 7:7; Ps. 30:1; Mic. 4:56–57, 59; 2 Macc. 2:12, 20. See ALTAR, WALL, TEMPLE.

units.la: LERE, Eph.4.19. pro, omnem doloris sensum abiicere: est, omne σωωτηρίας iudicium amittere, & mentem di ἀδόκιμον, Rom. 1.28.vt veluti scirrho cancrum gi-nte, aut quasi cauterio amputata conscientia, 1.Tim.4. turpissima quæuis & aliena prorsus à natura hominis one aliqua præditi præcipitem ruere.
units.tr: (To be past feeling, Eph. 4:19): to cast off every sense of pain, that is, to lose all judgment of salvation [σωτηρίας] and to have a reprobate mind [ἀδόκιμον], Rom. 1:28; as if the cancer were gnawed by a scirrhus, or the conscience cut away by a cautery, 1 Tim. 4:2, so that they rush headlong into all the most shameful things, and into everything utterly alien to human nature, being endowed with some [...].

units.tr: DELIGHTS: God Almighty is Job's delight, Job 22:26. Delights with men, Prov. 8:31. The delights of the godly are the Law of God. Delight in a chastened son, Prov. 29:17. The widow who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives, 1 Tim. 5:6. False teachers immersed in pleasures, 2 Pet. 2:13. The delights of harlots who go out with great Babylon, Rev. 18:3, 7, 9. See Ezek. 28:12, etc.; Luke 7:25; 2 Sam. 2:2.

units.tr: DEMAS, Paul's helper, Col. 4:14; Philem. v. 24. Held captive in the present age, 2 Tim. 4:10; he deserted Paul. Ibid. (i.e. the common people).

units.tr: DEMETRIUS, a silversmith, Acts 19:24. Fearing for the loss of his trade through Paul's teaching, he stirs up a riot at Ephesus, Acts 19:26–28. (Gr. i.e. Cerealis.)

units.la: DEMETRIVS vir pius,3.Ioan.v.12.
units.tr: DEMETRIUS, a godly man, 3 John v. 12.

units.la: DEPOSITVM:eius lex,Exod.22.7.Depositum Pauli,1.Tim. 20. sunt dona quæcunque ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem ti depositum Deus commiserat seruo suo.
units.tr: DEPOSIT: its law, Exod. 22:7. Paul's deposit, 1 Tim. 6:20. These are all the gifts that God committed as a deposit to his servant for the edification of the Church.

units.la: DERBE,ciuitas Lycaoniæ , Act.14.6.Illic Paulus & Barnabas angelizarunt,v.21.Gaius Derbæus,c.20.v.4.
units.tr: DERBE, a city of Lycaonia, Acts 14:6. Paul and Barnabas preached the gospel there, v. 21. Gaius of Derbe, Acts 20:4.

units.tr: Examples of DERISION: the taskmasters mock and trample the Israelites, Exod. 1:12. The men of Succoth mock Gideon, Judg. 8:6. Goliath mocks David, 1 Sam. 17:42. Nabal mocks David, 1 Sam. 25. Michal mocks David, 2 Sam. 6:16. Elijah mocks the Baalites, 1 Kings 18:27. The boys of Bethel mock Elisha, 2 Kings 2:23–24. The Israelites mock the king's messengers, 2 Chron. 30:6, 10. They mock the prophets, 2 Chron. 36:15–16; 1 Esd. 1:50. Sanballat and Tobiah the Ammonite mock the Israelites, Neh. 4:1–3. The younger men mock Job, Job 30:1. They mock Jeremiah, Jer. 20:7–8; Lam. 3:14. The minstrels mock Christ, Matt. 9:24. The chief priests, scribes and soldiers mock him, Matt. 27:41–42; Mark 15:20; Luke 22:63. Herod mocks him, Luke 23:11. Certain Jews mock the apostles, Acts 2:12–13. The Athenians mock Paul, Acts 17:32. See examples of ILLUSION and MOCKERY.

units.la: DESCENDERE & Ascendere , Vide ASCENDERE.Descendere ad inferos, proprie quidem sepulchro condi significat translatiuè verò de iis dicitur , qui summis vel animi corporis doloribus ita opprimuntur,ut sint vltimo ea pro poximi, vt Gen.37.35 & 42.38. 1.Sam.2.9.Pf.30.4.& 49. Vide Pf.16.7.[& 88. Deicendere de Deo humanitus dicitur, Gen.11.7 & 18.21. Exod 3.8. Act.7.15. Spiritus S. descendit, Ioann.1.v.32.33. filius Dei descendit, Ioan.6.33.&c. ob.4.9.
units.tr: DESCEND and ASCEND. See ASCEND. To descend to the underworld properly means to be laid in a tomb; figuratively it is said of those so overwhelmed by great sorrows of mind or body that they are almost dead: Gen. 37:35; 42:38; 1 Sam. 2:6; Ps. 30:4; 49. See Ps. 16:7 [and 88]. Said of God in human terms: to descend, Gen. 11:7; 18:21; Exod. 3:8; Acts 7:15. The Holy Spirit descended, John 1:32–33. The Son of God descended, John 6:33, etc. Obad. 4, 9.

units.la: SCRIPTIO orbis vniuersi. Luc.2.1.
units.tr: ENROLLMENT of the whole world. Luke 2:1.

units.la: CERTVM, ex vulgi consuetudine pro regione saltuosa, Matt.3.1.in qua habitabat Zacharias, Lucæ 1.40.& in qua esse domum Ioab legitur, 1. Reg.2.34.cuius deserti sex lapida numerantur, Ios.15.61.62.
units.tr: DESERT, in common usage a wooded region, Matt. 3:1, in which Zachariah lived, Luke 1:40; and in which Joab's house is read to lie, 1 Kings 2:34. Its six miles are counted, Josh. 15:61–62.

units.la: DESPERATIO est, peccata sua maiora æstimare, quàm meri- ta Filij Dei, & misericordiam Dei in Filio Mediatore placatam repudiare, ideoque non expectare beneficia creditis promissa, sed horribili sensu iræ Dei, & metu futuræ abiectionis in pœnas æternas cruciari, & Deum tanquam crudelem & tyrannū exhorrescere atq. odisse, Gen.4.13. 17.18.19. Desperationis exempla: Cain, Gen.4.v.13 14. Israe- læ, Exod.14.11. Achitophel, 2.Sam.17.23. quatuor leprosi, 2.Reg.7.4. Saul, 1.Par.10.4. Saulis Armiger, v.5. Iudas, Mat. 5.V.2.Sam.2.26.
units.tr: DESPAIR is to value one's sins above the merits of the Son of God, and to reject the mercy of God appeased in the Son as Mediator. Therefore one does not look for the benefits promised to believers, but is tormented by a horrible sense of God's wrath and by fear of being cast into eternal punishments, and so dreads and hates God as cruel and a tyrant. Gen. 4:13; 17–19. Examples of despair: Cain, Gen. 4:13–14; the Israelites, Exod. 14:11; Ahithophel, 2 Sam. 17:23; four lepers, 2 Kings 7:4; Saul, 1 Chron. 10:4; Saul's armour-bearer, v. 5; Judas, Matt. 27:5; 2 Sam. 2:26.

units.la: DESPERATIO cauenda, 2.Cor.2.7.1.Thess.4.13. Iob.7.16. Eph.
units.tr: DESPAIR is to be avoided, 2 Cor. 2:7; 1 Thess. 4:13; Job 7:16; Eph.

units.la: DISPARACTIO, Vide OBTRECTATIO.
units.tr: DISPARAGEMENT: see DETRACTION.

units.la: DETRACTIO pia, Ex.35.21.29. Num.6.21.1.Reg.8.38. 2.Chr.29.31. impia, turpis, crudelis, 2.Reg.23.10. Pr.7.14. Act 23.12.14.21.]
units.tr: DETRACTION: godly (Exod. 35:21, 29; Num. 6:21; 1 Kings 8:38; 2 Chron. 29:31); impious, base, cruel (2 Kings 23:10; Prov. 7:14; Acts 23:12, 14, 21).

units.la: DEUS est A spiritus B simplicissimus, C infinitus, D æternus, E immutabilis, F omnipotens, summe G sapiens, H bonus, I clemens, K misericors, L iustus, M sanctus, N verax, O liberator, P Pater, Filius & Sp.sanctus, Q conditor cœli ac terræ, & omnium quæ in illis continentur: R Redemtor, & S sanctificator electorum suorum.
units.tr: GOD is (A) spirit, (B) most simple, (C) infinite, (D) eternal, (E) unchangeable, (F) almighty, (G) supremely wise, (H) good, (I) merciful, (K) compassionate, (L) just, (M) holy, (N) true, (O) deliverer, (P) Father, Son and Holy Spirit, (Q) creator of heaven and earth and of all that is contained in them, (R) Redeemer, and (S) sanctifier of his elect.

Vt voca- tur Deus, soli Deo tribuitur, qui essentia unus, ac solus esse eritur, Deu.4.v.35.39.& 6.4.& 32 39. 1.Sam.2.2.2.
