Vide Dei nomen HOMINIBVS interdum tribuitur quod Dei est. Trinitas personis, Vide IN DEO personæ tres.
units.tr: What is attributed to God alone in Scripture is at times also communicated to others, and figuratively ascribed to them. That God is called one, and that he alone is and there is none besides him, is attributed to God alone, Deut. 4:35, 39; 6:4; 32:39; 1 Sam. 2:2; 2 Sam. 7:22; 22:32; 1 Kings 8:60; 18:39; 2 Kings 5:15; 19:15, 19; 1 Chron. 17:20; 2 Chron. 6:14; Ps. 86:10; 2 Macc. 7:38; Isa. 37:20; 42:8, 10; 44:8, 24; 45:21; 46:9; 64:4; Dan. 3:96; Joel 2:27; Mark 12:29; John 17:3; 1 Cor. 8:4, 6; Eph. 4:6; 1 Tim. 2:5. The name of God is also given to others, Exod. 7:1; 22:8; 1 Sam. 28:13; Ps. 47:10; 82:6. See the name of God. What belongs to God is sometimes attributed to men. See GOD, THREE PERSONS in God.

units.tr: 2. God is not an acceptor of persons, Deut. 10:17; 2 Chron. 19:7; Job 34:19; Isa. 11:3; Matt. 22:16; Mark 12:14; Luke 20:21; Acts 10:34; Rom. 2:11; Gal. 2:6; Eph. 6:9; Col. 3:24; 1 Pet. 1:17. He does not judge men by their race or country, whether he embraces or rejects them. His judgment concerns not the men themselves but the external qualities clinging to them: birth, dignity, wealth, and finally their nation or people. He is an helper (Adiutor) of his own, Gen. 15:1, 14; 28:15; 31:24; 35:5; 39:21; 45:5; Exod. 2:25; 14:16; Deut. 32:36, 43; Ps. 19:15; 25:15; 28:8; 30:1; 33:20; 37:39; 46:1; Isa. 41:13; 50:7; Zech. 2:5; 9:15. He is eternal (aeternus): he has no beginning or end, but is himself the beginning and end. Gen. 21:33; Exod. 15:18; Job 19:25; 36:26; Ps. 90:2; 92:93; 102:13; Isa. 41:4; 43:10; 44:6; 48:12; 57:15; 63:16; Lam. 5:19; Dan. 6:26; 7:9; Rom. 16:26; Heb. 1:10; Rev. 1:8, 17; 4:8; 11:17; 16:5. Alone is the Most High (Altissimus), Ps. 18:14. He is the Author (Autor) and fountain of all good things, John 3:27; James 1:17; author of miracles, Ps. 72:18; 136:4; Eccl. [...]; Acts 19:11; others also do miracles, Deut. 34:12; Eccl. 31:48, 4, 15. Author of patience, Rom. 15:5; of peace, Rom. 16:20; 1 Cor. 14:33; 2 Cor. 13:11; Phil. 4:9; 1 Thess. 5:23; 2 Thess. 3:16.

3. God alone is blessed, 1 Tim. 1:11; 6:15; others too are blessed, Gen. 13; Ps. 1:1; 32:1–2; 41:1; 119:1; 127:1; Matt. 5:1, etc.; 16:17; 24:46; Luke 1:45; 14:14; James 1:1. To bless (Mark 14:61; Rom. 1:25; 2 Cor. 1:31). Beneficent: Matt. 5:45; Acts 14:17. God alone is good, and to whom ... Ps. 18:27; 73:1; 68; Lam. 3:25; Nah. 1:7; Matt. 19:17; Luke 18:19. Goodness is attributed to others, Gen. 1:31; 3:6; 49:15; Num. 14:7; 1 Sam. 29:9; 2 Sam. 18:27; 1 Chron. 28:8; Ps. 111:10; 147; Prov. 18:22; 22:1; Eccl. 7:2; Jer. 7:3; Matt. 7:17; Mark; Luke 6:45.

units.tr: 4. God is love, 1 John 4:8, 16, which is far more than if the Apostle had said that God loves us in the highest degree and infinitely, when he says that God is love itself, of which the love of God is a most certain ... 1 John 2:5, by which God is loved. Clement and long-suffering, Gen. 15:16 & 18:21; Exod. 34:6-7; 2 Chron. 30:9 & 36:15; Neh. 9:31; Ps. 7:12 & 86:5, 13 & 33:8 & 111:4 & 116:5 & 136:1 etc. & 145:8; Isa. 30:18 & 55:7 & 5:2; Jer. 31:20; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Mal. 3:17; Luke 6:35 & 12:45 & 13:8 & 15:28; Acts 13:18 & 14:16; Rom. 2:4; James 5:11; 2 Pet. 3:9. See the goodness of God. God is called the head of Christ, 1 Cor. 11:3, inasmuch as Christ is God manifested in the flesh, and therefore Mediator. The Apostle calls him head, however, to whose glory those things that are subject to him are to be referred. Creator, Gen. 1:1 & 14:19; Exod. 20:11 & 31:17; Neh. 9:6; Job 12:9; Ps. 89:12 & 100:3 & 102:26 & 115:16 & 135:6 & 136:5; Isa. 37:16 & 40:26 & 42:5 & 45:12 & 48:13 & 66:2; Jer. 10:12, 16 & 27:5 & 32:17 & 51:15; Amos 4:13; Zech. 12:1; Acts 4:24 & 7:50 & 14:15 & 17:24; Eph. 4:9; 1 Pet. 4:19; Rev. 4:11 & 10:6 & 14:7. He is the Creator of souls, Gen. 2:7; Num. 16:22; Ps. 33:15; Zech. 12:1; Eccl. 12:7; Heb. 12:9. He made all things for himself, Prov. 16:4. He is the comforter of his own, Ps. 71:23 & 81:17 & 94:19; Isa. 12:1 & 49:15, 51:3, 12 & 52:9 & 57:18 & 66:13; Jer. 31:13, 16; Micah 4:6; Nahum 1:7; Zech. 1:17. He is the Keeper of his own, see Ps. 121; he is the helper of his own.

units.tr: God is Faithful and true: that is, it is wrong to doubt his faithfulness, Exod. 34:6; Num. 23:19; Deut. 7:9 & 9:5 & 2:4; Josh. 21:45 & 23:14; 1 Sam. 15:29; 2 Chron. 6:14; Ps. 86:5 & 119:65 & 145:17; Isa. 40:7; Jer. 10:10; Dan. 9:4; John 3:33 & 8:26; Rom. 3:4 & 9:28; 1 Cor. 1:9 & 10:13; 1 Cor. 1:18; 1 Thess. 1:9 & 5:24; 2 Thess. 1:1-2 & 2:16 & 3:2; 2 Tim. 2:13; Titus 1:2; 1 John 1:9 & 5:20; Heb. 10:23; 1 Pet. 4:19; Rev. 3:7, 14 & 6:10. Fountain of life, Ps. 36:10 & 42:3. He alone is Strong, 1 Sam. 2:2; 2 Sam. 23:3; Neh. 1:5 & 9:31; Job 9:4, 19 & 12:13; Ps. 7:12; Isa. 28:2 & 49:26; Jer. 34; Rev. 18:8. Strength is ascribed to others also, Gen. 32:2 & 49:14; Ps. 54:5; Song 3:7; Isa. 19:14; Jer. 9; Matt. 12:29; Mark 3:27; Luke 11:21; Heb. 11:34; 1 Pet. (cf.). He is the strength of his own, Ps. 43:2 & 118:14; Isa. 45; Joel 3:16; Hab. 3:19; Zech. 9:13. The sword of the glory of the people of God, Deut. 33:29; the glory of the virtue of the godly, Ps. 89:18. Glory is to be ascribed to him alone, Ps. 115:1; Isa. 42:8; 1 Tim. 1:17. It is also ascribed to others, 2 Kings 14:10; 2 Chron. 17:5; Ps. 150:9; Luke 14:10; John 5:44.

units.tr: 7. God is a consuming fire, Deut. 4:24 & 9:3; Heb. 12:29. He alone is immortal, 1 Tim. 1:17 & 6:16. He is contained in no place; he is present everywhere, immense, uncircumscribed and incomprehensible, 1 Kings 8:27; 2 Chron. 2:6 & 6:18; Job 11; Ps. 139:7, 10; Isa. 6:3 & 66:1; Jer. 23:24; Amos 9; Matt. 5:35; Acts 7:48 & 17:29. Invisible, Exod. 33:20; Deut. 4:12, 15; John 1:18 & 5:37 & 6:46; Col. 1:15; 1 Tim. 1:17 & 6:16; 1 John 4:12. Yet he was seen and appeared to holy men: to Abraham, Gen. 16:10 & 18:1; to Jacob, Gen. 32:30; to Moses, Exod. 2:2 & 33:11; Deut. 34:10; Num. 12:8; to Isaiah, Isa. 6; and to some others, not indeed according to his essence, which is incomprehensible and invisible, but according to certain images or (as Athanasius puts it) a majesty far weaker than he is in himself and through himself, adapted to their capacity. See examples of appearances. Judge of the whole world, rendering to each one his reward according to his deeds, Gen. 15:1 & 31:49; Deut. 10:17; Judg. 11:27; 1 Sam. 2:10; 1 Chron. 17:2; 2 Chron. 6:23; Job 34:11 & 36:31; Ps. 7:9, 12 & 9:5, 1, 6 & 62:13 & 75:8 & 82:8 & 96:10, 13 & 98:9, 13; Prov. 24:12; Isa. 3:11 & 11:3 & 24:1 & 45:23 & 63:4; Jer. 11:20 & 17:10 & 25:14 & 29:23 & 32:19; Ezek. 7:22, 30 & 33:20; Joel 3:12; Matt. 16:27 & 25:31; Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:5-6 & 3:6; 1 Cor. 4:4 & 5:13; Eph. 6:8; Col. 3:24; 2 Thess. 1:6 & 2:12; 2 Tim. 4:8; Heb. 12:23; James 4:1; 1 Pet. 1:17 & 2:23 & 4:17; 2 Pet. 2:4; Rev. 18:8 & 22:12. Most just Judge, Lev. 18:28; Deut. 8:20 & 10:17-18 & 4; John 23:15; 1 Sam. 12:25; 2 Chron. 12:6 & 19:7 & 26:19; 1 Esdr. 9:15; Neh. 9:33; Job 9:19 & 34:17, 19 & 36:22; Ps. 11:7 & 62:12 & 116:3 & 119:156 & 145:17; Prov. 16:11; Jer. 24:2 & 45:21; Jer. 12:1; Lam. 1:18; Dan. 9:14; Zeph.; Acts 10:34; Heb. 6:10; Rev. 16:5 & 19:2. He alone is Just and True, Ps. 116:11; Rom. 3:4. Other people are also just, Gen. 7:2 & 23.

units.tr: God is the Lawgiver, Isa. 33:22; the only Lawgiver, James 4:12. He is said to speak in the prophets, Heb. 1:1, because the prophets, moved by the divine Spirit, spoke, 2 Pet. 1:21. But in the Son he speaks, for the Son speaks and truly is God, both bodily [σωματικῶς] or essentially [οὐσιωδῶς], as he is, 1 John 1:5.

units.tr: God is the Portion of his people, Lam. 3:24. The Shepherd of the Church, or of the sheep, Ps. 23:1; 77:21; 78:52; 79:13; 80:1; 95:7; 100:3; Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34:13, 15; Jer. 31:10; Zech. 9:5. God is Father, Matt. 23:9; Eph. 5:20; Col. 1:12; 2:2; 3:17; Heb. 12:9; 1 John 3:1. God alone is the true Father, Isa. 63:16; Matt. 23:9. This is not meant in terms of the order and reason of nature and of our birth, but in terms of the source and foundation of our trust and life. In this sense we are forbidden to call anyone our father on earth, Matt. 23:9, because God alone is Father in this way, and men are not. Otherwise, by reason of procreation, those from whom we have been born are commonly called fathers, Exod. 20:12; Heb. 12:9, etc. God the Father is a farmer, John 15:1. The Father of lights, the fount and author of light or knowledge, James 1:17; 3:15. The Father of all, Eph. 4:6. The Father of all the faithful who obey him, Deut. 32:6; Ps. 103:13; Prov. 1:7; Jer. 3:4, 14, 19; James 1:6; Matt. 6:9; 18:14; 23:9; Luke 11:2; John 20:17; 8:15; 1 Cor. 8:6; 2 Cor. 1:3; 6:18; Eph. 3:14; 4:6; 1 Thess. 1:1; 3:2; 2 Thess. 1:1-2; 2:16. Our Father, Isa. 63:16; Matt. 6:9; 23:9; Luke 11:2; Gal. 1:4; 1 Thess. 3; 2 Thess. 2:16. Father of spirits, Heb. 12:9. The ancient Father of the household, Ps. 104:28. God of spirits and of all flesh, Num. 16:22. God is patient; see God merciful and patient. God is perfect, Matt. 5:48. God alone forgives sins, Luke 5:21; others also forgive, but only as ministers of God, Matt. 11; John 20:23. God alone is holy, Rev. 15:4; others also are holy, 1 Pet. 3. Three persons are represented and declared in God, Gen. 1; 18:2; 19:24; Exod. 3:6, 15, 16; 4:5; Ps. 33:6; Isa. 3; 34:16; 48:16; 61:1; Zech. 2:8; 3:2; Matt. 3:16; 28:19; Luke 4:18; John 3:35; 14:16; 15:26; 16:3; 1 John 5:7. God is placable, Exod. 32:14. God is powerful, 1 Tim. 6:15; others are powerful, Exod. 18:21; Ps. 112:2; Acts 8:27; 18:24. First and last, Isa. 41:4; 44:6; 48:12.

units.tr: 13. God is the Sanctifier of his people, Lev. 20:7; 21:23; 22:32; Ezek. 36:25; 37:28. Holy, Lev. 11:44-45; 19:2; 20:7, 26; 21:8; Joel 2:19; Ps. 145:17; Isa. 5:16; 8; 40:25; 41:14, 16; Jer. 3:12; Hab. 3:3; 1 Pet. 1:16; Rev. 8; 6:10; 15:4. God alone is Holy, 1 Sam. 2:2; Rev. 15:4. Holiness is attributed to others, Exod. 3:5; 12:16; 22:31; 28:2; 29:31; 30:29; 35:2; Lev. 11:44; Num. 16:5; Deut. 6:7; Joel 5; Matt. 22:26; 2 Kings 4:9; Judith 8:29; Ps. 5:8; Matt. 7:6; Rom. 2, etc. Holy One of Israel, Isa. 10:17; 12:6; 17:7; 29:23; 30:11-12; 31:1; 37:23; 43:3, 14-15; 45:11; 47:4; 48:17; 49:7; 54:5; 55:5; 60:9; Jer. 51:5. Wise, Job 9:4; 12:13; 21:22. God alone is Wise, Rom. 16:27; 1 Tim. 1:17. Wisdom is also attributed to others, Luke 11:49; Acts 7. The wisdom of God is shown in the making of the world, 1 Cor. 1:21. The wisdom of God is described, Jer. 51:15; Dan. 2:20-21. It is eternal, Prov. 8:22; it is ordained, Ps. 47:5; Isa. 40:28; it is manifold, Eph. 3:10. Saviour alone, Isa. 43:11. Saviour of his people, Isa. 49:26; Dan. 6; Hos. 13:4, 14; Zech. 8:7; 1 Tim. 1:1; 2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:11; Jude 25. He saves and delivers on account of his own, Ps. 106:8. Searcher of hearts, 1 Sam. 16:7; 1 Kings 8:39; 1 Chr. 28:9; 2 Chr. 6:30; Job 16:19; 42:2; Ps. 7:10; 44:22; Jer. 11:20; 17:10; 20:12; Luke 16:15; Acts 1:24; 15:8; 1 Cor. 4:5; 2 Thess. 2:4; Heb. 4:13; 1 John 3:20. Others also know the secret thoughts of the heart, but only as far as they are disclosed to them, and when, 1 Sam. 9:19; 2 Kings 5:26. Knows, hears and sees all things, Exod. 3:19; Num. 12:2; Deut. 31:21; 1 Sam. 2:3; 16:7; 2 Chr. 16:9; Job 14:6; 22:11; 28:24; 31:4; 42:2; Ps. 10; 33:13; 38:10; 90:8; 131:8; Prov. 5:21; 15:3, 11; 22; Isa. 29:15; 40:27; 48:4; Jer. 1:5; 7:11; 17; 23:24; 32:19; Ezek. 11:5; Matt. 6:4; 21:2; Mark 2:8; 14:13; Luke 2:10; John 1:47; 13:21; 16:30; 21:17; Acts 8; Rom. 8:27; 1 Thess. 2:4; 1 John 3:20; Heb. 4:23; Rev. 2. units.tr: God alone is to be served, Deut. 6:13; 10:20; 1 Sam. 7:3; Matt. 4:10; Luke 4:8. Others also are to be served after God, Gen. 25:23; 29:20; 47:25; 1 Tim. 6:2. God is always like himself, Num. 19; Deut. 8:20; Ps. 110:4; 102:27-28; Hos. 13:4; Mal. 3:6; Luke 17:26; Heb. 1:12. God is incomprehensible to us, yet he expresses himself to us by comparisons with our actions. Thus he is likened to an eagle, Exod. 19:4; to a drunken man and a sleeping man, Ps. 78:65; to a roaring lion, Isa. 31:4; to a mother, Isa. 46:3; 49:15; 66:13; to a swimmer, Isa. 25:11. God is Spirit, John 4:24; God of spirits, Num. 16:22; 27:16; Heb. 12:9. Bridegroom of the Church, Isa. 54:5; Jer. 3:1, 14; Hos. 2:16, 19-20; Matt. 9:15, whom he has joined to himself by an oath, Ezek. 16:8; Heb. 6:17. God is sweet to the pious, Ps. 25:8; 31:20; 34:9; 36:5; 100:5; 145:9; 1 Pet. 2:3.

units.tr: 28. The joy of God in helping his Church: Jer. 31.41. Zeph. 3.17. The glory of God, for his mercy: Rom. 9.23. How great the glory of God is: Ps. 8.2 & 108.5. Ezek. 10.18 & 11.23. How greatly it is to be valued: 1 Sam. 2.30. It is not to be transferred to another: Isa. 42.8 & 48. Acts 10.26 & 14.15. Rev. 19.10 & 22.9. It is the end of our election: Eph. 1.6, 12. It is the end of good works: Matt. 16.1. 1 Cor. 10.31. Eph. 1.6, 14. 1 Pet. 2.12 & 4.10. To give glory to God, Rom. 4.20, is to acknowledge God and praise him as supremely good and true: John 3.33. This manner of speaking is taken in this way, Luke 17.18, but a little differently, John 9.24. Josh. 7.19. In these places there is a formula, used when someone was pressed to acknowledge his fault before God, as if it had been said: "Consider that you are before God, who knows the matter so well; therefore reverence his majesty and show this honour, to confess the whole matter openly rather than lie before him." To glorify God as God, Rom. 1.21, is said of one who worships God with that worship which befits his eternal power and divinity. To change the glory of God, Rom. 1.23, is to embrace something else in place of the glorious God. The grace of God, Acts 15.40. Saving for all, Titus 2.11. It surpasses all things, Ps. 4.7, 8. It is free, Exod. 33.19. Isa. 53.1. John 15.16 & 9. Acts 16.6. Rom. 9.15, 18, 23. It anticipates people, Jer. 41.2. Isa. 65.1. Matt. 9.13. Acts 9.3 & 10.5 & 12.6. Rom. 4.17 & 5.6, 8, 10 & 10.20 & 11.6, 35. Gal. 2.20 & 4.9. Eph. 2.1, 4, 5. Col. 1.13. 1 Tim. 1.16. 2 Tim. 1.9. Titus 3.4, 5. Heb. 6.18 & 11.6. 1 Pet. 1.13 & 2.9, 10. 1 John 4.10, 19. Jude 1, 24. God's grace is more effective than Adam's fall, Rom. 5.15. God's grace is to be ascribed to all, Acts 21.19. 1 Cor. 4.4 & 15.10. Eph. 2.5, 8.

units.tr: 29. God's inheritance: see ISRAEL, and the INHERITANCE of God. God's enemies: see the WICKED. ¶ The ignorance of God, how harmful it is: Job 18.21; Matt. 15.14; 1 Cor. 14.38 and 15.34; Eph. 4.18. The ignorance of God, while in the world, is the cause of persecution, Acts 14.6; its punishment, John 16.3 and 2 Thess. 1.8.

units.tr: God's image is restored in the godly, Eph. 4.24. All things are subject to God's command, Ps. 91. God's indulgence toward his own, Gen. 18.16; 28.13; 42.3; Exod. 33.11; Num. 12.8; Deut. 32.10; Josh. 10.12 and 24; Judg. 6.39–40; 2 Sam. 7.14–15; 1 Kings 3.5 and 17.4 and 19.5; 2 Chron. 30.18–19; Mal. 3.17; Luke 15.28 and 22.35; Acts 9.15 and 10.5; Rom. 8.15–16; Heb. 6.17. See God merciful and God patient. God's enemies: see the Wicked. God's invocation: see God to be worshipped, God to be invoked, INVOCATION and PRAYER. God's wrath is to be feared, Ps. 6.1 and 8.1 and 90.9; Isa. 63.6 and 64.9; Jer. 10.24; Zeph. 1.15; Col. 6; Heb. 10.30–31. See WRATH. God's judgments are true: see God the avenger. The end of God's judgments, Isa. 26.9; Zeph. 3.8. God's righteousness, Ps. 89.15. God's righteousness, as the imputation of Christ's righteousness, by which God holds the faithful as righteous, Rom. 1.17; 3.21–22; 10.4; so that they may be holy and blameless before him, Col. 1.22. God's righteousness is commended by the sins of men, Rom. 3.5, but only accidentally, namely through God's goodness, and in those who are themselves sanctified and to whom sins are forgiven. Sins therefore do not, in themselves and properly, illustrate God's glory, but (as they say) accidentally, namely through God's goodness, that is, to those to whom sins are forgiven and who are themselves sanctified. God's righteousness is eternal, Ps. 111.3 and 119.147; it is most excellent, Ps. 36.7; therefore it is to be sought before all things, Matt. 6.33; Luke 12.31. God's righteousness is contrary to the righteousness of men, Rom. 10.3.

units.tr: How great is God's majesty, Exod. 40.35; Job 11.8; Ps. 9.3; 1–3; Isa. 40.17 and 45.7; Eph. 4.6. It is incomprehensible, 1 Kings 27; Isa. 6.2 and 66.1. To search into it too deeply is dangerous, Prov. 25.27. God's hand: see God powerful, and POWER and HAND. God's curse upon creatures, Gen. 3.14, 17; 4.11; Lam. 2.7; Dan. 9.1; Mal. 2.2; Matt. 11.21 and 5.41. It consumes all things, Deut. 28.18; Lev. 26.16; Jas. 5.2. God's commandments: see COMMANDMENTS. God's mercy, Deut. 31; Neh. 9.31, is eternal, Ps. 103.17; 106.1; 136.1; 138.8; Jer. 33.11; it is immense, Exod. 20.6; Deut. 5.10; 2 Sam. 15 and 24.14; 2 Kings 20.5; 1 Chron. 16.34 and 21.13; 2 Chron. 5.13 and 21.7; Neh. 9.17, 19; Ps. 17.7; 25.6; 33.5; 36.6, 8; 51.3; 57.11; 78.38; 86.5, 13; 89.34; 100.5; 103.11; 106.1, 45; 108.5; 119.156; 130.1, 7; 136.1; 138.8; 145.8; Isa. 1.9; 54.10; 55.7; 63.7; Jer. 24.6; 3.18; 33.11; Lam. 3.22, 32; Hos. 14.5; Joel 2.13; John 3.10 and 4.11; Amos 7.3, 6; Mic. 7.18; Hab. 3.2; Mal. 3.17; Luke 1.50, 78 and 15.20; Rom. 9.29; Eph. 2.4; 1 Pet. 1.3. It is free and gratuitous, Exod. 33.19. (See God merciful and GRACE of God.) God's mercy is to be desired above all things, Ps. 65; always to be proclaimed, Ps. 89.1; 92.3; 101.1. It is at hand for those to whom it is ready, Deut. 6.25 and 7.9; Judg. 2.18; Neh. 1.5; Ps. 103.17; Prov. 28.13; Jer. 3.1, 12 and 18.8; Ezek. 18.32 and 33.11, 15; Dan. 4.24 and 9.4; Amos 5.15; Gal. 6.16. It is sweet, Ps. 109.21.

units.tr: God's Nature is described, Exod. 34.6–7. One is born of God, 1 John 5.1, who by faith is joined to Christ, the true Son of God, in whom they are also freely held as sons of the same kingdom and co-heirs. God's name is wonderful, Ps. 8.1, 10; eternal, Ps. 135.13; good, Jas. 2.7; exalted, Josh. 7.9; Isa. 12.4; dreadful to the nations, Mal. 1.14; holy, Ps. 33.21; 99.3; 106.47; 111.9; 138.2; Isa. 57; Ezek. 36.21 and 39.7; Amos 2.7; Luke 1.49; terrible, Ps. 99.3 and 111.9; a most strong tower, Prov. 18.10; not to be taken in vain, Exod. 20.7; Deut. 5.11; to be feared, Ps. 86.10. The name of God in Jerusalem, 2 Kings 21.4, 7 and 23.27; 1 Chron. 6.6 and 12.13 and 33.4, 7. The name of God is given to the city of Jerusalem, Ezek. 48.35. See GOD from the beginning. How much the glory of God's name is to be prized, Josh. 7.9; by the oath, Deut. 6.13 and 10.20. See OATH. The name of God joined with a plural verb, to indicate the mystery of the most holy Trinity, Gen. 1.26 and 20.13; 2 Sam. 7.23; Job 25.1. Sometimes it is taken as an adjective and means the same as greatest, vehement or huge, as in Gen. 30.8; Ps. 37 and 68.16 and 80.11; 1 Sam. 14.15. A plural noun is also added, as in Josh. 24.19. "Holy ones" is said in the plural for the singular, "Most holy" in the superlative degree. Likewise Ps. 58.12 says "Judges" in the plural form for "Judge." God's works are to be admired, Ps. 139.14; Mark 12; Rev. 15.3. They are good, Gen. 1.31; 1 Tim. 4.4. They are unsearchable, Eccl. 8.17 and 11.5. They are magnificent, Ps. 92.6 and 111. They are perfect, Deut. 32.4; Eccl. 3.14. They are terrible, Ps. 66.3. Nothing is to be added to or taken from God's works, Eccl. 3.14.

units.tr: God's patience, 1 Pet. 3.20, for "patient God," by Hebraism. How terrible is God's visible presence, Gen. 1.8, 10; 28.17; Judg. 6.22 and 13.22; Ps. 97.5; Isa. 6.5; Ezek. 1.2; Matt. 17.6; Mark 6.9; Luke 5.8; Rev. 1.17. God's helpful presence removes all fear, Num. 14.9; Deut. 7.11, 20.1 and 31.8; Josh. 1.9; Ps. 23.4 and 27.1; Isa. 43.5; Jer. 8.8, 42.11 and 46.28; Hab. 1.12; Zeph. 3.16; Hag. 2.5; Acts 18.9–10. It sanctifies a place, Gen. 28.17; Ezek. 3.25. God's fullness, Eph. 3.19, is not that by which God himself is full, that is, full divinity (for who could grasp that?), but that vast beneficence of God in Christ, of which he makes us partakers and co-heirs. God's promise, for the Holy Spirit, Acts 1.4. God's universal promises, Matt. 7.7; Luke 11.10, are also "Amen" in Christ, that is, they are supported and fulfilled in Christ alone, 2 Cor. 1.20; they are most certain. 2 Kings 15.12; Ezra 1.1; Neh. 9.8; Isa. 37.33, 37 and 55.10–11; Luke 1.70; Rom. 3.4; Heb. 6.17. One is to trust them, 2 Chron. 20.20. Everything is to be expected from them, 2 Sam. 7.21. They are the foundation of the prayers of the godly, Gen. 28.3–4 and 32.9–10; Exod. 32.13; Deut. 9.27–28; 2 Sam. 7.29. God's promises are conditional, Deut. 19.8 and 28.1 etc., 33.4; Lev. 26.1 etc.; 1 Sam. 2.30; Ezek. 18.1 etc., 33.17, 15, 19; Mark 16.16; John 3.16, 36 and 6.47 and 8.31 and 13.17 and 15.7, 14; Rom. 8.17; Col. 1.23; Heb. 3.14; 2 Pet. 1.4; Rev. 2.1 etc., 3.1 etc., 21.7. It is proper to God to announce future things, Isa. 44.7.

units.tr: 35. The kingdom of God: for the doctrine of the Gospel and its preaching, Matt. 21.43; Mark 4.26; Luke 8.1, 10; 9.2, 11, 60; 6; 13.18, 20; 16.16; Acts 28.31; 1 Cor. 4.20; Col. 4. For the time when the Gospel began to be revealed, Mark 9. For the restoration of the Church through the Messiah, Matt. 12.28; Mark 1.14; 13.43; Luke 10.9, 11; 11.20; 21.31; 23.51; Acts 1.3; 8.12. For the Church, John 3.3, 5. It does not mean Christ himself, as some of the ancients explain, nor eternal life, which we strive for, but the Church, in which God reigns. For Christ there discusses by what means we obtain the right of citizenship in God's city, namely by free adoption through the Holy Spirit, by which we are regenerated in Christ himself

units.tr: The Kingdom of God is eternal, inward and spiritual: Gen. 49; Exod. 15.18; Num. 24.17; 1 Sam. 2.10; 7.9, 10; 1 Chron. 11 and 29.2, 4; Psalms 2, 6, 9, 8, 22.28, 45.7, 1, 110.1, etc.; 145.1; Isa. 9 and 11.1, etc.; 32.16; 40.9; 4.3; 7; 14.27; 9.24, 25; Hos. 3.5; Mic. 4.1, 4, 5; 1 Chron. 9.9; Matt. 13.1, etc.; Luke 1.33; 12.31, 32; 22.29; 2.9. The fruits of the kingdom of God are said to be borne (Matt. 21.43) by those who prove by their life that they are citizens of the heavenly kingdom and who produce those fruits, not of the flesh but of the Spirit, of which Gal. 5.22. To see the kingdom of God (John 3.3) is to enter the kingdom of God, as is explained in the same place, verse 5. The kingdom of God is to be sought first (Matt. 6.33; Luke 12.31). It is within us (17.21). Violence is done to the kingdom, and violent men take it by force (Matt. 11). That is, it is broken into and plundered by a kind of onslaught. The metaphor is taken from camps, or from a citadel which is plundered by invading enemies. See Kingdom.

units.tr: The Word of God is to be proclaimed in the Church (1 Thess. 2.13; 4.11). It is to be proclaimed with confidence (Acts 4.13; Eph. 6.19; Phil. 1.14; Col. 4.4). It is to be proclaimed entire (Exod. 10; 25.40; Deut. 4.2; Prov. 30.6; Jer. 23.28; 26.2; Acts 27; 2 Cor. 4.2; 2 Tim. 2.15; Rev. 22.18, 19). It is to be urged in season and out of season (2 Tim. 4.2). It is to be heard with reverence (2 Kings 22.19; Ps. 95.8; Isa. 50.10; 66.2, 5; Hag.; Luke 10.39). It is in the mouth of the ministers (Jer. 1.9). It will condemn the ungodly (John 12.48). All things, however hidden, will be made manifest (Heb. 4.13). It purifies and sanctifies (John 15.3; 17.17). It profits not only when heard but when received in faith (Gen. 3.11; 4.4, 5; 19.17, 26; Ps. 95.8; Isa. 50.10; 55; Jer. 6.8; 7.22; Ezek. 33.31; Matt. 7.24; 13.9, 20; 4.9, 23; 6.20; Luke 6.47; 8.8, 12, 13, 14, 21; 9.41; 11.28; 14.35; John 12.48; 13.17; 17.6; Acts 4.4, 13; 13.7, 8; 4.2; James 1.21, 22, 23; Rev. 1.3; 2.7, 11, 17; 13.9). It is not to be only heard and spoken, but also believed and carried out in deeds (Deut. 5.17, 27; 31.12; Isa. 29.13; Ezek. 33.31; Matt. 5.19; 7.24; 15.28; 28.20; Luke 6.47; 11.28; 12.47; John 13.17; Heb. 4.21, 22).

Ioan. v. 18. vt traditiones suas partim inutiles, partim absurdas & blasphemas, ac cum norma sacrarum literarum apertè & ex diametro pugnantes stabilire possint. Vide TRANDITIONES. Citant etiam libros quosdam, qui interciderunt, quorum tamen fit mentio in veteri Testamento de quibus vide Librorum quorundam sacrorum nomina, &c.
units.tr: The Papists contend that the whole word of God was not handed down in writing, citing John 14:26, 20:21 and 21:25, 1 Cor. 11:34, 2 Thess. 2:15, 2 John v. 12 and 3 John v. 18. They use this to establish their traditions, some of which are useless, some absurd and blasphemous, and which clearly and directly contradict the norm of the sacred letters. See TRADITIONS. They also cite certain books that have perished, though mention of them is made in the Old Testament. On these see the Names of Certain Sacred Books, etc.

units.tr: God's truth is eternal: Ps. 100:5, 117:2, 119:90. It is not to be held back in unrighteousness, Rom. 1:18. It is always to be proclaimed, Ps. 89:1, 92:3. It is unconquered, 36:6, 57:11, and most excellent, 108:5. The truth of God, Rom. 3:7, means his faithfulness and constancy, and so, as I may put it, God's veracity. God's ways are unsearchable, Job 36:23; Rom. 11:33. God's power is made perfect in weakness, 2 Cor. 12:9; see Ps. 8:3 and Matt. 21:16. How it is conspicuous: Rom. 1:20. God's life, Eph. 4:18, means the life by which God lives in his people, Eph. 2:1, and which he commands and approves.

We must obey God's will. Examples: David, 2 Sam. 12:20, 23, 26; Christ, Matt. 11:26, 26:39; Mark 14:36; Luke 10:21, 22:42; John 4:34, 8:29, 17:4, 18:11; Peter, Acts 11:17; Paul, Acts 18:21; Paul's companions, Acts 21:14. We must submit to God's will, Rom. 1:10; 1 Cor. 4:19, 16:6; Eph. 6:6; James 4:15; 1 Pet. 3:17, 4:19; 1 John 5:14. To obey God's will is God's gift, Heb. 13:21. No one can resist God's will, Gen. 50:19; Num. 23:12; 2 Sam. 20:6; Job 9:4; Isa. 46:10; Dan. 4:32; Rom. 9:19. That is, no one can ever prevent, or has ever prevented, what God has once decreed from coming to pass. God's voice is dreadful, Exod. 19:18, 20:19; Job 37:4–5; Ps. 29:3–5; Heb. 12:26.

units.la: Hanc figurâ Scripturæ familiarem, qua membra humana & humanæ passiones ac effectus Deo tribuuntur, vocant Antropopathian: de quo dicendi genere notetur regula: Membra corporea & humanæ passiones, seu affectus Deo tributa semper incorporaliter significât, & vt plurimum secundum effectum sui generis intelligi debent : quæ fi-gura, vt dictum est, vulgò ἀνθρωποπάθεια vocatur. Potest e-tiam vel ad metaphoram, vel ad metonymiam referri, vt causa pro effectu quasi ponatur. Huc pertinent & illæ re-gulæ : Scriptura sæpe de Deo loquitur secundum captum hominis. Parabolis adhuc secundum fidei tempus de Deo Prophetæ tunc loquebantur, non quomodo Deus erat sed quomodo populus capere poterat. Nam & cùm oculi describuntur,quòd omnia videat, exprimitur : & quando auris,quòd omnes audiat,proponitur:&c. Item, Scriptura per corporalia,spiritualia docet: & invisibilia per visibilia demonstrat.
units.tr: This figure, which is familiar in Scripture, by which human members, human passions and human effects are attributed to God, they call anthropopathy [ἀνθρωποπάθεια]. Concerning this manner of speaking, let this rule be noted: bodily members and human passions or affections attributed to God always signify something incorporeal, and for the most part must be understood according to the effect proper to them. This figure, as has been said, is commonly called anthropopatheia [ἀνθρωποπάθεια]. It may also be referred to metaphor or metonymy, so that the cause is put for the effect. To this belong also these rules: Scripture often speaks of God according to the capacity of man. The prophets, still in the time of faith, spoke of God in parables, not as God was but as the people could grasp him. For when eyes are described, it is expressed that he sees all things; and when an ear is set forth, that he hears all; and so on. Likewise, Scripture teaches spiritual things through corporeal ones, and shows invisible things through visible ones.

units.la: Huc pertinent etiam illæ passiones humanæ, seu affectus, quos Deo tribuit Scriptura: vt sunt Ira ( vide De ira:&,Ira ) Odium, Malach.1.2. Roman. 9.13. Pœnitenti Gen.6.6. 1. Sam.15.11. Ier.18.8.& reliqui his similes affectus,qui μεταμελητικῶς de effectu sunt intelligendi. Dei enim ira,ipsum iræ effectum,videlicet,pœnas:odium, reiectionem, abominationem & abiectionem:pœnitentia, dispensationis mutationem subitam denotat.Quò pertinet illud dictum, Pœnitentia Dei est οἰκονομίας, id est dispensatio mutatio. Item Pœnitentia Dei non est post errorem, sed pœnitentia Dei dicitur,rerum sub eius potestate constitutarum hominibus inopinata mutatio: alioqui certè Deus pœnitere posse negatur, 1.Sam.15.29.Ideóque notanda hoc loco aurea illa regula, Ταῦτα ἀνθρωπινῶς μὲν λέγονται θεοπρεπῶς δὲ νοεῖσθαι.
units.tr: To this also belong those human passions or affections which Scripture ascribes to God: such as anger (see On Anger, and Anger), hatred, Mal. 1:2; Rom. 9:13; repentance, Gen. 6:6; 1 Sam. 15:11; Jer. 18:8, and the other affections like these, which are to be understood as referring to the effect, in a manner akin to repentance [μεταμελητικῶς]. For God's anger denotes the very effect of anger, namely punishments; hatred denotes rejection, abomination and abasement; repentance denotes a sudden change of dispensation. To this belongs the saying: God's repentance is a change of dispensation [οἰκονομίας]. Likewise, God's repentance is not after an error, but is called God's repentance because it is an unexpected change, for men, of things established under his power; otherwise it is certainly denied that God can repent, 1 Sam. 15:29. Therefore this golden rule is to be noted here: These things are said in a human way, but are to be understood in a manner worthy of God [Ταῦτα ἀνθρωπινῶς μὲν λέγονται θεοπρεπῶς δὲ νοεῖσθαι].

units.tr: 42. All glory is to be given to God: Rom. 11:36; Eph. 3:21; 1 Tim. 1:17; 1 Pet. 4:11; Rev. 1:6, 4:11, 5:13. All things are to be ascribed to God: Acts 17:28; Rom. 11:36; 1 Cor. 8. From the most idiomatic Hebrew usage, God is said to be with those in whom some divine excellence shines forth, John 3:2. But (to add these remarks to the passage cited) if Nicodemus had known Christ well, he would have said not only that God is with Christ, as it were of him as Saviour [σωτῆρον], but that God is in him, as the Apostle says, 2 Cor. 5:19.

units.la: 43. [ Deus est (vt paucis superius dicta repetamus) Iehovah Elohim,vnus essentia,tribus personis:Pater,Filius,Spiritus Sanctus. A Deo Patre & Filio procedit Spiritus Sanctus donorum omnium ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ pertinentium author.
units.tr: [43. God is (to repeat briefly what was said above) Jehovah Elohim, one in essence, three in persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. From the Father and the Son proceeds the Holy Spirit, the author of all the gifts that pertain to the building up of the Church.

units.la: praepositio, cum genitivo casu constructa, non tantùm instrumentalem causam denotat,vt 1.Cor.11.12,Gal.5. 6.& multis aliis in locis : sed etiam efficientem, vt ex testimoniis sequentibus patebit,in quibus διά genitivo casui iunctum,vero Deo accommodatur,(nisi velimus Patrem etiam instrumentum constituere)Rom.11.36.Patri, Hebr. 2.10. Filio, Ioan.1.3.1.Cor.8.6. Col.1.16. in posteriori vet sus parte Spiritui Sancto, Rom.5.5. quod eò dicitur, vt scia mus Filium & Spiritum Sanctum non instrumentalem, sed efficientem causam esse cum Patre, tum in creado, tum in conseruando: quod & ipsum rursum ita accipiendum est, vt nec duas, aut tres causas, id est, Deitates constitua mus, cum Filius & Spiritus Sanctus sit <bl>ὁμοούσιος</bl> vnus cum Patre: nec rursus in personarum distinctione inæqualitatem aut separationem aliquam imaginemur. Vanum est igitur cauillum Arianorum, imò impium, qui locum illum Ioann.1.3. ita accipiunt, quasi præpositio <bl>διά</bl> non causam efficientem, sed instrumentalem duntaxat declaret: quod fi sum esse ex authoritate sacræ Scripturæ conuincitur, quod tum Patri, tum Filio, tum Spiritui Sancto tribuit, iam visum est.
units.tr: The preposition, construed with the genitive case, denotes not only an instrumental cause, as in 1 Cor. 11.12, Gal. 5.6 and in many other places, but also an efficient cause, as will be clear from the following testimonies, in which through [διά], joined with the genitive, is applied to the true God (unless we wish to make the Father also an instrument): to the Father, Rom. 11.36; to the Son, Heb. 2.10; John 1.3; 1 Cor. 8.6; Col. 1.16; and in the latter part of the verse to the Holy Spirit, Rom. 5.5. This is said so that we may know that the Son and the Holy Spirit, together with the Father, are the efficient cause, not an instrumental one, both in creating and in preserving. This too must in turn be understood in such a way that we do not posit two or three causes, that is, deities, since the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father; nor again should we imagine any inequality or separation in the distinction of persons. Therefore the cavil of the Arians is empty, nay impious, who take the passage John 1.3 as if the preposition through [διά] declared not an efficient but merely an instrumental cause. That this is false is proved from the authority of Holy Scripture, which ascribes it to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike, as has now been shown.

units.la: Similiter etiam phrasin, ἐξ οὗ, nunc Patri, 1. Corint.8. nunc Filio, Eph.4.16. Colos.2.19. nunc Spiritui Sancti Ioan.3.v.5.6. accommodat. Ac ne quem constructio cui diuersis casibus moueat, & διὰ ὧν & διὰ οὗ, de Patre scriptum habemus, Hebr.2.10. Quòd verò locum Ioannis attinet Ioann.1.3. nemo illum sapientius explicare potest, quàm Paulus, qui pro διὰ οὗ, Ioan.1.3. ponit ἐν ἀυτῷ, Coloss.1.16. quod vni vero Deo tribuitur, Act.17.28. Quin etiam διὰ universa constructione eodem prorsus sensu vsurpatum legimus, διὰ τὸ πάθημα, & διὰ τὸ παθημάτων propter perpessionem, & per perpessiones. Adde etiam quod peccata, nunc διὰ τὸ ὄνομα, Act.10.43. nunc διὰ τὸ ὄνομα, 1.Ioan.2.12. remitti dicantur, διὰ causam finalem interdum significat, & ponitur pro εἰς, ad, vel ἐν, in Roman.6.4.2. Corinth.9 12.2.Petr.1.3 in fine versus, Roman 4.11.& 7.4.1. Timoth.2.15.& 4.14.1. Thessal. 4.14. Hebr. 9.V.Causa.
units.tr: Similarly he applies the phrase from whom [ἐξ οὗ] now to the Father, 1 Cor. 8.6; now to the Son, Eph. 4.16; Col. 2.19; now to the Holy Spirit, John 3.5, 6. And so that anyone may not be troubled by the construction with different cases, we have through whom [διὰ ὧν] and through which [διὰ οὗ] written about the Father, Heb. 2.10. As for the passage in John 1.3, no one can explain it more wisely than Paul, who, for through which [διὰ οὗ] in John 1.3, puts in him [ἐν αὐτῷ], Col. 1.16, which is attributed to the one true God, Acts 17.28. Indeed we read that through [διά] is used in the whole construction in exactly the same sense: on account of the suffering [διὰ τὸ πάθημα] and on account of sufferings [διὰ τὸ παθημάτων], that is, because of the sufferings, and through the sufferings. Add also that sins are said to be forgiven sometimes on account of his name [διὰ τὸ ὄνομα], Acts 10.43, and sometimes for the sake of his name [διὰ τὸ ὄνομα], 1 John 2.12. Through [διά] sometimes signifies a final cause, and is put for to [εἰς] or in [ἐν], Rom. 6.4; 2 Cor. 9.12; 1 Pet. 1.3 at the end of the verse; Rom. 4.11 and 7.4; 1 Tim. 2.15 and 4.14; 1 Thess. 4.14; Heb. 9.5. Cause.

units.la: DIABOLVS, qui & Satan, statim ab orbe condito Apostat mendacij homicidij author, Ioann.8.44.2. Petr.2.4.1. Ioan 3 8.Iudæ v.6.vide ANGELORVM lapsus, &c. Dicitur autem homicida à principio, Ioann.8.44.non ipsius Satanæ sed conditi hominis respectu, siue à primo homine cum dito, antequam humanum genus propagaretur. Accusator est fidelium, Apocal.12.v.9.10. Caput impiorum, mundi huius Princeps, Ioan.12 31.& 14.30.& 16.11. Eph.2.& 6.12.2. Tim.2 26.Heb.2.14.1.Ioā.4.4. Deus seculi huius 2.Cor.4.4. colitur ab impiis, Apoc.13.4. confertur armatis homini omini, Matth.12. 29. Luc. 11.21. Balenæ, Esaiæ 27. 1. Leoni rugienti, 1. Petr.5.8. vt fulgur è cœlo cadit, Luc. 10. 18. vocatur Draco magnus, & Serpens antiquus, Apocal. 12. 9. generis humani hostis est, Genes.3.1. Matth. 13.39. 1. Petr.5. imperium mortis habere dicitur, Hebr.2.14. quia ab ipso exortum est peccatum, quod mors est consecuta, & ipse nos quotidie ad peccandum solicitat, vt nos in æternæ mortis exitium secum trahat. Iudam ingreditur, Luc.22. 3. Ioann. 13. 27. in malis efficaciter operatur, Ephes.2.2.2. Thess.2.9. Tentator est, Marc. 1.13. Luc.4.2. Actor.5.3. 1. Cor. 7.5.1. Thess.3.5. Matt.4.3.
units.tr: DEVIL, who is also Satan, from the very founding of the world an apostate, author of lies and of murder, John 8.44; 2 Pet. 2.4; 1 John 3.8; Jude v. 6. See ANGELS, fall of, etc. He is called a murderer from the beginning, John 8.44, not with respect to Satan himself but with respect to the human being created, or from the first man whom he deceived before the human race was propagated. He is the accuser of the faithful, Rev. 12.9, 10. The head of the impious, the prince of this world, John 12.31; 14.30; 16.11; Eph. 2 and 6.12; 2 Tim. 2.26; Heb. 2.14; 1 John 4.4. The god of this age, 2 Cor. 4.4; he is worshipped by the impious, Rev. 13.4; he is compared to a strong man armed, Matt. 12.29; Luke 11.21; to a whale, Isa. 27.1; to a roaring lion, 1 Pet. 5.8; he falls from heaven like lightning, Luke 10.18; he is called the great dragon and the ancient serpent, Rev. 12.9; he is the enemy of the human race, Gen. 3.1; Matt. 13.39; 1 Pet. 5. He is said to have the power of death, Heb. 2.14, because sin, which death followed, arose from him, and he daily urges us to sin, so as to drag us with him to the ruin of eternal death. He enters into Judas, Luke 22.3; John 13.27; he works effectively in evil men, Eph. 2.2; 2 Thess. 2.9. He is a tempter, Mark 1.13; Luke 4.2; Acts 5.3; 1 Cor. 7.5; 1 Thess. 3.5; Matt. 4.3.

units.la: Diabolus cum suis angelis in terram deiectus, Apocal.12. 9. deo subiectus, 1. Sam.16.14. & 18.10. 1. Reg.22, ver.20.23. Iob.1.v.6.7.12 & 2.v.1. 6. Matth. 8. v.31.32. Marc.5. v.12.13. Luc.8. v.31.32. & 22.31.2. Thess. 2. v. 9. 11. non plus potest, quàm Deus illi permittat, 1. Regum 22. 22. 2. Paral. 18.20. Iob.1.12. & 2.6. Matth.8.31. Marc.5.12. Ephes.2.2.2. Timoth, 1.26. Apoc.20, 7. tribuntur illi potestatum ac principum appellatio, Eph.6.12. ab effectu Diabolorum, ex quibus intelligitur, quæ sit illorum vis ac potestas, minimè id quidem quasi vel sit infinita illorum potentia, vel quod possunt suapte vi possint, vel quod ita illis laxet habenas Deus, vt eorum audacia ad amplificandam suam gloriam vtatur. Diabolus superatur à Christo, Matth. 12. 29. Luc. 11. 22. Coloss.2.15. Hebr.2.14.1. Ioann.3.8. à Deo, Roman.16.20. a fidelibus, Iacob.4.7.1. Petr.5.9.1. Ioann.2. v.13.14. transformatur in Angelum lucis, 2. Corinth. 11.14. colaphis cædit Paulum, 2 Cor.12.7
units.tr: The devil, cast down to earth with his angels, Rev. 12.9; subject to God, 1 Sam. 16.14 and 18.10; 1 Kings 22.20, 23; Job 1.6, 7, 12 and 2.1, 6; Matt. 8.31, 32; Mark 5.12, 13; Luke 8.31, 32 and 22.31; 2 Thess. 2.9, 11. He cannot do more than God permits him, 1 Kings 22.22; 2 Chron. 18.20; Job 1.12 and 2.6; Matt. 8.31; Mark 5.12; Eph. 2.2; 1 Tim. 1.26; Rev. 20.7. The title of powers and princes is ascribed to him, Eph. 6.12, from the effect of the devils, from which it is understood what their force and power is: not indeed as if their power were infinite, or as if they could act by their own strength, or as if God so loosened their reins that their audacity was used to enlarge his own glory. The devil is overcome by Christ, Matt. 12.29; Luke 11.22; Col. 2.15; Heb. 2.14; 1 John 3.8; by God, Rom. 16.20; by the faithful, James 4.7; 1 Pet. 5.9; 1 John 2.13, 14. He is transformed into an angel of light, 2 Cor. 11.14; he strikes Paul with blows, 2 Cor. 12.7.

units.la: DIABOLI, siue Satanæ Angelus, pro ipso Satana, 2. Corinth. 2.7. astutia eius, Genes.3.v.4.5.1. Paralip.21.1. Iob.1.11.& 2. 4. Matth.4.3.& 13.19. Marc.4.15. Luc.8.12. Act.16.17.2. Cor. 2.11.& 11.ver.3.14. Ephes.6.11 1. Petr.5.8. Apoc.12. 12. casus horrendus, Lucæ 10.18. Apocal.12 9. Filij eius, Matth.13.38. Ioann.8.v.41.44. Act.13.10.1. Ioan.3.ver.8.10. quos gignere dicitur, non substantiæ, sed qualitatis corruptæ & imitationis respectu, alioquin & viperæ homines gignerent, Matth.3.7. eius iudicium. Matth.25.41.1. Tim.3.6.2. Pet.2.4. Iudæ v.6. nequitia, Matt.13.19. Marc.4.15. Luc.4.35.& 8.12.& 22.31. Ioan.13.2.1. Thess.2.18. Apoc.12. v.13. 15. potestas ac tyrannica dominatio, Matt.12.29. Marc. 3.27. Luc.12.21. resistendum ei est, Ephe.4.27. Iac.4.7.1. Petri 5.9. Diabolis non permittitur suam de Christo proferre sententiam, Marçi 1.34.Luc. 4. 41. eò quòd non diaboli munus sit prædicare Euangelium. Quamobrem Paulus quoque ægrè fert Pythonis testimonium, [eíque silentium indicit:] Act.16.18. Diabolicus spiritus,pro diabolico,per Hebraismum,Lucæ 4.33 diabolis seu dæmonibus immolare nefas, Leuitici 17, 7.Deut.32.17.2.Paral.11.15.Psalm.106.37.1. Cor.10, 20. diabolo seu Satanæ tradi,1.Cor.5,5.1. Tim.1 20. Vide SATANAE tradi.
units.tr: DEVIL's, or Satan's, angel: for Satan himself, 2 Cor. 2.7; his cunning, Gen. 3.4, 5; 1 Chron. 21.1; Job 1.11 and 2.4; Matt. 4.3 and 13.19; Mark 4.15; Luke 8.12; Acts 16.17; 2 Cor. 2.11 and 11.3, 14; Eph. 6.11; 1 Pet. 5.8; Rev. 12.12; his dreadful fall, Luke 10.18; Rev. 12.9; his sons, Matt. 13.38; John 8.41, 44; Acts 13.10; 1 John 3.8, 10, whom he is said to beget not with respect to substance but with respect to corrupt quality and imitation, otherwise vipers too would beget men, Matt. 3.7; his judgment, Matt. 25.41; 1 Tim. 3.6; 2 Pet. 2.4; Jude v. 6; his wickedness, Matt. 13.19; Mark 4.15; Luke 4.35 and 8.12 and 22.31; John 13.2; 1 Thess. 2.18; Rev. 12.13, 15; his power and tyrannical dominion, Matt. 12.29; Mark 3.27; Luke 12.21. One must resist him, Eph. 4.27; James 4.7; 1 Pet. 5.9. The devils are not permitted to pronounce their own sentence about Christ, Mark 1.34; Luke 4.41, because it is not the office of the devil to preach the Gospel. Therefore Paul too took it badly that the testimony of the Pythoness was given, and [enjoined silence on her:] Acts 16.18. Diabolical spirit, for diabolical, by Hebraism, Luke 4.33. It is an unlawful thing to sacrifice to devils or demons, Lev. 17.7; Deut. 32.17; 2 Chron. 11.15; Ps. 106.37; 1 Cor. 10.20. To be delivered to the devil or to Satan, 1 Cor. 5.5; 1 Tim. 1.20. See delivered to Satan.

units.la: Diabolos esse Spiritus essentiales, sensu & intelligentia præditos, non autem affectus, aut perturbationes malas, probatur,Iob.1.6.& 2.1.Matth.8.29.& 12.45.& 25.41. Ioan. 8.44.2.Petr.2.4.1.Ioann.3. v. 8. 10. Iudæ v. 6. 9. vnum esse Deum credunt,Iac.2.19. [Christum agnoscunt & formidant,]Matth.8.29.Marc.1.24.& 3.11.& 5.7.Lucæ 4. v.34.41. & 8.28. Actor.19.15.diaboli eiiciuntur, Vide MIRACVLA, ¶ diabolos & impios damnatos aliquando seruatum iri, colligunt nonnulli ex Coloss.1.20.sed perperam. Vide INFERI. Eo enim loci agitur de vniuersa Ecclesia, quæ per Christum reconciliari dicitur, quam alibi mundum, simili dicendi genere appellat Apostolus,2.Corinth.5.19.vide & Ephes.1.10.vbi etiam τὰ πάντων[?],id est, omnium nomine intelligendum est totum Ecclesiæ corpus, quod postea in duas veluti partes diuiditur: nempe in ea quæ sunt in cœlis,& in ea quæ sunt in terris:per illa simpliciter intelligūtur fideles ante Christi aduentum mortui: per hæc verò quos Christus viuos deprehendit, vel qui sunt eius aduentum consecuti, quorum rursus duas species facit Apostolus, quæ tamen in vnum corpus coaluerint, Iudæos nimirum & Gentes.Nihil ergo eo loci de diabolis & damnatis aliquando saluandis.
units.tr: That the devils are essential spirits, endowed with sense and understanding, and not evil affections or passions, is proved by Job 1.6 and 2.1; Matt. 8.29 and 12.45 and 25.41; John 8.44; 2 Pet. 2.4; 1 John 3.8, 10; Jude v. 6, 9. They believe that there is one God, James 2.19; [they acknowledge and dread Christ,] Matt. 8.29; Mark 1.24 and 3.11 and 5.7; Luke 4.34, 41 and 8.28; Acts 19.15. The devils are cast out; see MIRACLES. Some gather from Col. 1.20 that the devils and the impious damned will at some time be saved, but wrongly. See HELL. For the passage there treats of the whole Church, which is said to be reconciled through Christ, which the Apostle elsewhere calls the world in a similar manner of speaking, 2 Cor. 5.19; see also Eph. 1.10, where of all things [τὰ πάντων?], that is, in the name of all, must be understood as the whole body of the Church, which is afterwards divided, as it were, into two parts: namely, into those in heaven and those on earth. By the former are simply understood the faithful who died before Christ's coming; by the latter, those whom Christ found alive, or who came after his coming, of whom the Apostle again makes two kinds, which nevertheless have grown together into one body, namely Jews and Gentiles. Therefore there is nothing in that place about devils or the damned at some time to be saved.

units.la: Diabolus, vir nefarius,& aliorum aduersarius. 1. Reg.21 13.Ps.109.10. Diabolus,pestis,Lues formidanda,Haba.3.5. DIACONI,1.Tim.3. 8. Philip. 1.1. proprie sunt qui pauperum curam habebant,& ærario Ecclesiastico præerant:sicut διακονεῖν,Rom.15.25.pro, pecuniam in vsus pauperum collectam distribuere capitur. Diaconi quales esse debeant, Act.6.3.1. Timot.3.v.8.10.12.Diaconorum duæ species,Roman.12.8.1. Cor.12.28.Diaconi septem eliguntur,Act.6.5.diaconi episcopis adiunguntur,Philip.1.1.
units.tr: Devil: a wicked man and adversary of others. 1 Kings 21:13; Ps. 109:10. Devil: a plague, a pestilence to be feared, Hab. 3:5. DEACONS, 1 Tim. 3:8; Phil. 1:1. Properly, they are those who had charge of the poor and presided over the church's treasury. Likewise διακονεῖν [diakonein], Rom. 15:25, is taken to mean distributing money collected for the use of the poor. What deacons should be like: Acts 6:3; 1 Tim. 3:8, 10, 12. There are two kinds of deacons: Rom. 12:8; 1 Cor. 12:28. Seven deacons were chosen: Acts 6:5. Deacons are joined to the bishops: Phil. 1:1.

units.la: DIACONIA (ἡ διακονία) interdum non illi modò conuenit, qui collatam pecuniam administrat & distribuit, sed in genere omnibus qui in pauperum vsus aliquid submini[strant]. [illegible, ~6 letters]rant:qua in significatione postrema accipitur, 2. Cor.9. ,interdum pro officiis erga Sanctos collatis accipitur, vt poc.2.19. Prεterea ν διακονία altera species est functio- i Ecclesiasticarum, Rom.12.7, qua se abdicarūt Apostoli, t.6.v.2.3.4, vbi prophetiæ, i.alterius, & quidem potioris functionum Ecclesiasticarum speciei nomine comprehen- untur, quæ ad docendi munus pertinent. Interdum ta- en Diaconia, multò ampliore & latiore significatione pitur, ita vt omnia munera Ecclesiastica comprehendat, samque adeò Apostolicam functionem, quia nimirum publicè ac priuatim nos oportet Deo ministrare, vt Act.6. & 12.25. Rom.11.13.
units.tr: DIACONIA (ἡ διακονία) [hē diakonia] sometimes applies not only to the one who administers and distributes the money collected, but in general to all who provide something for the use of the poor. In this sense it is taken in the last passage, 2 Cor. 9. Sometimes it is taken for services rendered to the saints, as in Rev. 2:19. Besides, ἡ διακονία [hē diakonia] is another kind of ecclesiastical function, Rom. 12:7, by which the apostles excused themselves from serving tables, Acts 6:2–4, where prophecy, that is, another and indeed the more important kind of ecclesiastical function, is comprehended under the name of this office, which pertains to the duty of teaching. Sometimes, however, diaconia is used in a much broader and wider sense, so that it embraces all ecclesiastical offices, and even the apostolic function itself, since we must indeed minister to God both publicly and privately: Acts 6 and 12:25; Rom. 11:13.

units.la: Similem in hæc duo Ecclesiasticarum functionum ge- ra distributionem adhibet Apostolus, Phil.1.1. 1.Tim.3. .8.nominans Episcopos, quos Rom.12.6. Prophetas ap- llac, quibus nimirum sermonis ministerium commissum : cæteras autem nomine diaconorum imtelligens. Sic quitur & Petrus, 1. Petr. 4.11. Deinde Apostolus Paulus c duo perpetua in Ecclesia functionum genera, ad quæ oostolorum exemplo, Actor.6.v.2.3.4. Ecclesiasticas fun- ones reuocauit idem Paulus, Rom.12.v.6.7.&c. (nam a- temporaria merito omittit) singula rursus in suas spe- s distribuit: nempe Prophetas in Doctores & Pastores, aconos in eos qui eleemosynas distribuunt, in Guber- tores, & in eos qui curandis ipsis pauperibus Ecclesiæ iuiebant, quales erant fere viduæ, de quibus seorsim agi- 1.Tim.5.9. Postremò ν διακονία dupliciter accipitur vno odem in loco apud Paulum, Rom.12,7. Priore quidem o munus ipsum declarat: Posteriore vero ipsam mune- functionem.
units.tr: The apostle Paul uses a similar division of ecclesiastical functions into these two kinds in Phil. 1:1 and 1 Tim. 3:8, where he names the bishops, whom in Rom. 12:6 he calls prophets, to whom the ministry of the word was committed, and understands the rest under the name of deacons. Peter also follows this pattern: 1 Pet. 4:11. Then the apostle Paul, following the example of the apostles in Acts 6:2–4, reduced the ecclesiastical functions to these two perpetual kinds of office in the Church, as well as the same Paul in Rom. 12:6–7, etc. (for he rightly omits the temporary ones). He again divided each kind into its own species: namely, prophets into teachers and pastors; deacons into those who distribute alms, into governors, and into those who attended to the care of the poor in the Church, such as the widows, of whom he treats separately in 1 Tim. 5:9. Lastly, ἡ διακονία [hē diakonia] is taken in two ways in one and the same passage of Paul, Rom. 12:7. In the former sense it denotes the office itself; in the latter, the act of performing the office.

units.la: Diadema, insigne regium, 2. Sam.1.10. & 12.30. 2. Reg.11. 1.Par.20.2. & 2.Par.23.11. Esther, 1.11. & 2.17. & 6.8. Dia- ma, nobilitatis nota, Iob 29.14. Diadema diuinum Esai. 3. mysticum, Cant.3.11. Diademata apocalyptica, Apoc. 3. & 13.v.1 & 19.12.]
units.tr: Diadem: the royal insignia, 2 Sam. 1:10; 12:30; 2 Kings 11:12; 1 Chr. 20:2; 2 Chr. 23:11. Esther 1:11; 2:17; 6:8. Diadem: a mark of nobility, Job 29:14. The divine diadem, Isa. 3. A mystical diadem, Song 3:11. The diadems of the Apocalypse: Rev. 3; 13:1; 19:12.

units.la: dea magna Ephesiorum, Act.19.v.26.27.33.34. Vide OLORVM catalog.
units.tr: Great goddess of the Ephesians, Acts 19:26–27, 33–34. See the catalogue of OLORVM.

units.la: CITAS damnatur, Eph.5.4.
units.tr: CITAS is condemned, Eph. 5:4.

units.la: RE, Hebræorum more, pro iubere, Matth.8.8. & 16.12. rc.10.49. Luc.7.7. & 9.54. 2. Corint.4.6. Dicere in cor- apud se, aut intra se, pro cogitare, Psal.14. Matth.9.11. le LOQVI.
units.tr: RE: in the Hebrew manner, for to command, Matt. 8:8; 16:12; Mark 10:49; Luke 7:7; 9:54; 2 Cor. 4:6. To say in one's heart, or within oneself, for to think: Ps. 14; Matt. 9:11. See LOQVI.

units.la: [Dicere, quando ad Deum refertur, significat, Compellô, Denuntio, Notum facio, Significo, vel conceptis & diserte verbis, vel hoc sensu, summa, aut sententia. Dicit, népe Deus Pater, Ps. 2.7. & 110.1. Vide DEVS Pater, Dicit Dei Filius, aduentum in carne, & tunc vocatur Iehouæ Angelus Iehoua. Quum enim de Iehouæ disertis verbis in V.T. primo occurrit, id ita plerique interpretantur, iuxta Apostolum, Hebr. 1.1. vt Patrem per Filium loquutum esse affirmat, Gen. 31.11. Iudic. 13.3. &c. Pro. 8.3. Zach. 1.9. &c.
units.tr: [To say, when referred to God, means: to address, to proclaim, to make known, to signify, either in set and express words or in this sense, in substance or meaning. Dicit [he says], namely God the Father: Ps. 2:7; 110:1. See DEVS Pater. Dicit: the Son of God, in the flesh, and then he is called the Angel of Jehovah, Jehovah. For when Jehovah is first mentioned in express words in the Old Testament, most interpreters take it, in line with the apostle, Heb. 1:1, that the Father is affirmed to have spoken through the Son: Gen. 31:11; Judg. 13:3, etc.; Prov. 8:3; Zech. 1:9, etc.]

units.la: Aliquoties dicere significat Præcipere ac potenter vel vt aliquid fiat, quod de Deo essentialiter consideratio intelligitur, Gen. 1.v.3.6. &c. Psal. 33.9. & 105.31. & 148.5. Iob 11. Dicit Spiritus S. vel interno motu, vel per Sanctos Dei homines, qui eius impulsu loquuntur, teste Petro. Dicunt Angeli boni, i. variis modis olim reuelarunt hominibus Dei voluntatem. Dicunt, i. colloquuntur Spiritus beati coelis, Apoc. 4.8. & 5.v.5.9. &c.
units.tr: Sometimes dicere means to command and to effect powerfully that something be done, which in relation to God is understood essentially: Gen. 1:3, 6, etc.; Ps. 33:9; 105:31; 148:5; Job 11. Dicit the Holy Spirit, either by inward motion or through the holy men of God who speak at his impulse, as Peter testifies. Dicunt the good angels, that is, they formerly revealed God's will to men in various ways. Dicunt, that is, the blessed spirits converse in heaven: Rev. 4:8; 5:5, 9, etc.

units.la: Quando vero tribuitur hominibus, quòd dicant aut loquantur, idem est ac si dicas, quòd voce efferunt. Præterea dicere, non raro significat, hominum respectu, Affirmare, Cogitare, Deliberare apud se, Præcipere, Renuntiare, Respondere, Significare: quæ quum ex contextu, facile dignoscantur, ad duo referri commodè possunt: nempe, dicere apud se, tum dicere alij, vel homini, vel Deo. Dicere, mortuis figuratè tribuitur, Iob. 28.22. Esai. 38.18. Dicere, creaturis ratione carentibus, & inanimatis, tribuitur, Num. 30. Iudic. 9.v.8.10 14. Iob 28.14. & 38.35. & 39.28. Esai. 28.15. 45.9. Rom. 9.20. 1. Cor. 12.v.15.16.21.]
units.tr: When, however, it is attributed to men that they dicant or speak, it is the same as saying that they utter it with the voice. Besides, dicere, with respect to men, often means to affirm, to think, to deliberate within oneself, to command, to renounce, to answer, to signify. Since these are easily distinguished from the context, they can conveniently be referred to two things: namely, to say within oneself, and to say to another, either a man or God. Dicere is attributed figuratively to the dead: Job 28:22; Isa. 38:18. Dicere is attributed to creatures lacking reason and to inanimate things: Num. 30; Judg. 9:8, 10, 14; Job 28:14; 38:35; 39:28; Isa. 28:15; 45:9; Rom. 9:20; 1 Cor. 12:15, 16, 21.

units.la: DICTIONVM Latinarum Græce declinatarum catalogus. de VOCABVLA.
units.tr: Catalogue of Latin words declined in the Greek manner. Concerning the entry VOCABVLA.

units.la: DIDRACHMVM, (hoc est, sicli Sanctuarii dimidium, quod pendebant olim Israelitæ ex Lege scripta, Exo. 30.13. Qui tuplex autem sit, & quantum valeat siclus, Vide SICLVS. soluunt Iudæi Romanis, Matt. 17.24.
units.tr: DIDRACHMA (that is, half a shekel of the sanctuary, which the Israelites once paid according to the written Law, Exod. 30.13. For what kind of double coin it was and what the shekel was worth, see SHEKEL.) The Jews paid it to the Romans, Matt. 17.24.

units.la: DIES, pro cœlestis vitæ claritate, Rom. 13.12. pro veritatis Christi & Domini: quum dies alicuius Hebræorum idtisimo nihil aliud declaret, quàm spacium quo vixerit aliquis, aut insigne quippiam ipsi vel facere, vel ferre contigerit: dies Christi & Domini nihil aliud significat, quàm aduentum ipsius in carnem, Luc. 17.22. Ioan. 8.56. Signif secundum ipsius adventum ad iudicium cum gloria & maiestate, Luc.17.24.26. Rom.2.16. 1.Cor.5.5.2. Corint.1.14. Philip.1.v.6.10 2.Thess.2.2.2. Pet.3.10. Dies Domini incer- tus, Matth.24.44. 1.Thessal.5.2.2. Pet.3.10. Apoc.3.3. &16.15. Dies Domini qualis impiis futurus, Soph.1.14.15.
units.tr: DAY, for the brightness of heavenly life, Rom. 13.12; for the truth of Christ and the Lord. Since the day of any Hebrew, in the most simple sense, means nothing more than the span of time a man has lived, or some notable thing that happened to him or that he did, the day of Christ and the Lord means nothing other than his coming in the flesh, Luke 17.22, John 8.56. It signifies his coming to judgment with glory and majesty, Luke 17.24, 26; Rom. 2.16; 1 Cor. 5.5; 2 Cor. 1.14; Phil. 1.6, 10; 2 Thess. 2.2; 2 Pet. 3.10. The day of the Lord is uncertain, Matt. 24.44; 1 Thess. 5.2; 2 Pet. 3.10; Rev. 3.3 and 16.15. What the day of the Lord will be like for the impious, Zeph. 1.14, 15.

units.la: [Dies artificialis, est spatium illud horarum a recedente ad accedentem. Naturalis, spatium 24.horarum, quo proRsus fertur circa terram. Dies nonnunquam tempo- ubreue seu longum curriculum significat. Dies Domini, seu indicta quam in praesenti vita frequenter exercet, impios iniens, pios probans. Aliquando dies extremi iudicij. des hominis, vitae spatium, seu molestum, seu commo- am, Dies, pro anni spatio, 1.Sam. 1.3.&2.19. Psalm.61.7. o tempore seu duratione regni, 1.Reg.14.15.16.20.22.cap. 2.Reg.1.8.10.12.13.14.15.20.21.24.25.cap.
units.tr: [The artificial day is the space of hours from the setting of the sun to its rising again. The natural day is the space of 24 hours, in which the sun is carried all the way round the earth. Sometimes "day" signifies a brief or a long course of time. The day of the Lord, or the judgment which he frequently exercises in the present life, condemning the impious and approving the godly. Sometimes it is the day of the last judgment. The day of a man is the span of his life, whether troublesome or pleasant. Day, for the space of a year, 1 Sam. 1.3 and 2.19; Ps. 61.7. For the time or duration of a reign, 1 Kings 14.15, 16, 20, 22; 2 Kings 1.8, 10, 12–15, 20, 21, 24, 25.]

units.la: Dis Christi & Hominis. Vide Christus, Homo.
units.tr: The day of Christ and of man. See CHRIST, MAN.

units.la: Dominicus, 1. Cor. 16 2. Apocal.1.10. pro eo die, qui a paulo dicitur una Sabbathorum, 1.Cor.16.2. ut Act.20.7. assumtus est autem hic dies pro prioris seculi Sabbatho: primo, quia cum Dominica resurrectio sit alterius spiritua- lis mundi velut altera creatio (ut loquuntur Prophetae, Es.65.17. & 66.22. Apocal.21.1.,&c.) Spiritu Sancto procul- ambio dictante, placuit Apostolis, pro prioris seculi Sab- batho, siue die septimo, assumere noui huius mundi pri- mum diem, in quo non illa corporalis & corruptibilis primo veteris mundi die creata, sed coelestis illa & aeterna nobis illuxit. Ille autem veteris Sabbathi dies a crea- tione mundi ad Domini resurrectionem usque stetit, qui postea in diem Dominicum mutatus ab Apostolis est. Ac quod, euanescente paulatim Iudaici Sabbathi ceremonia, die soliti sint Christiani solennes conuentus agere, non accepte colligitur ex Act.20.7 1.Cor.16.2. Secundo, ut dies quem Dominicum a resurrectione Dominica voca- ius, reuocaret in memoriam Dominicae resurrectionis mysterium, & beneficium, Tertio, ut credentes sentirent, ex Legis iugo liberatos & exemptos. Quarto, ut esset dis- crimen inter nos fideles & Iudaeos, Legi etiamnum, sed astres re, addictos.
units.tr: DOMINICAL: Rev. 1.10; for that day which Paul calls the first day of the week, 1 Cor. 16.2, as in Acts 20.7. This day was taken in place of the Sabbath of the former age, for these reasons. First, since the Lord's resurrection is, as it were, a second creation of another, spiritual world (as the prophets speak, Isa. 65.17, 66.22; Rev. 21.1, and so on), with the Holy Spirit dictating, it pleased the apostles to take in place of the Sabbath of the former age, or seventh day, the first day of this new world, on which that bodily and corruptible light which was created on the first day of the old world did not shine on us, but rather that heavenly and eternal one did. That day of the old Sabbath stood from the creation of the world until the Lord's resurrection, and afterwards was changed by the apostles into the Lord's day. And that, as the ceremony of the Jewish Sabbath gradually faded away, Christians were accustomed to hold their solemn assemblies on that day, is rightly gathered from Acts 20.7 and 1 Cor. 16.2. Second, so that the day which, from the Lord's resurrection, is called the Lord's, might recall to memory the mystery and benefit of the Lord's resurrection. Third, so that believers might feel themselves freed and exempted from the yoke of the Law. Fourth, so that there might be a distinction between us faithful and the Jews, who are still bound to the Law, though in shadows.

units.la: Dies irae, Soph.1.15. Rom.2.5. Dies iudicii soli Patri co- nitus, Mat.24.36.Mar.13.32. Luc.17.v.24.30. Act.1.7.1.Thes. 1.2.Pet.3.10. Apoc.3.3.&16.15. Dies iudicij indies expectan- tis, Matth.24.44.&25.13. Marc.13.33. Rom.2.16.1.Thess.5.2.
units.tr: The day of wrath, Zeph. 1.15; Rom. 2.5. The day of judgment, known to the Father alone, Matt. 24.36; Mark 13.32; Luke 17.24, 30; Acts 1.7; 1 Thess. 5.2; 2 Pet. 3.10; Rev. 3.3 and 16.15. The day of judgment, daily expected, Matt. 24.44 and 25.13; Mark 13.33; Rom. 2.16; 1 Thess. 5.2.

units.la: Iac.5.8. 2.Pet.2.9. Dies iudicii à Deo præscriptus, Act.1 31.Dies mali, Gen.47.9. Eph.5.16. ex Hebræorum idioti mo dicuntur tempora difficultatum & asperitatis pleni vita denique aspera & calamitosa: sicut contra dies boni Psal.34.13.1.Pet.3.10.dicuntur beata ac felix vita. Dies natalis olim solennis habitus,Matt.14.6.Marc.6.21.Dies novi mus,pro die iudicii, Ioann. 6.v.39.40.44.54.&12.48. Dies Pentecostes,Act.2.1.&20.16.1.Cor.16.8.Dies salutis,pro tempore Euangelij, 2.Cor.6.2. Dies septimus à Deo sanctificatus,Gen.2.3.Exod.20.11.Dies visitationis,1.Pet.2.12.Dies visitationis, Luc.21.22.Dies urbis Ierusalem, Hebræorum more dicitur tempus illud, quo Dominus singulari beneficio iam dignatus erat, nisi ipsum non eminus vocantem, iam præsentem contemsisset, Luc.19.42. Dies pro anno Num.14.34.Ezech.4.6.Dies ex Cilicum idiotismo prodicio,1.Cor.4.3.
units.tr: James 5.8; 2 Pet. 2.9. The day of judgment, prescribed by God, Acts 17.31. Evil days, Gen. 47.9; Eph. 5.16: by the idiom of the Hebrews, times full of difficulties and hardship are so called, and finally a harsh and calamitous life; just as, on the other hand, good days, Ps. 34.13; 1 Pet. 3.10, denote a blessed and happy life. Birthday, once celebrated with solemnity, Matt. 14.6; Mark 6.21. The last day, for the day of judgment, John 6.39, 40, 44, 54 and 12.48. The day of Pentecost, Acts 2.1; 20.16; 1 Cor. 16.8. The day of salvation, for the time of the Gospel, 2 Cor. 6.2. The seventh day, sanctified by God, Gen. 2.3; Exod. 20.11. The day of visitation, 1 Pet. 2.12; Luke 21.22. The day of the city of Jerusalem: in the Hebrew manner, that time is called in which the Lord had now deigned to honour it with a singular kindness, but which it despised, when he, though calling it from afar, was already present, Luke 19.42. A day for a year, Num. 14.34; Ezek. 4.6. A day, in the idiom of the Cilicians, is a day of trial, 1 Cor. 4.3.

units.la: Dies nonnunquam significat commodum quoddam tempus, aut occasionem: quandoquidem dies actionibus denata est,& nox quieti: omniaque interdiu rectius agunt. Ioann 9.4.&11.9.Rom.13.13. Metaphoricè pro Dei cognitione ac tempore gratiæ accipitur, Rom.13.12.1.Thess.5.2.Pet.1.19.Significat etiam tempus continuum & æternum, Esa.61.7. Dies,pro iudicio aliquoties ponitur,præsertim apostolo,quam etiam humanam vocat, 1.Cor.4.3 quoniam in iudiciis agendis certa dies utrique parti constituitur. Dies Christi, seu extrema totius mundi,& aduentus illius gloriosi, Philipp. 1.v.6.10.&2.16. Dies tem Christi est pus illud quod Euangelistæ indicant præfixum fuisse periculo vocationis & passionis Christi.
units.tr: Day sometimes signifies a convenient time or an opportunity, since the day is given to actions and the night to rest, and all things are done more rightly by day, John 9.4 and 11.9; Rom. 13.13. Metaphorically it is taken for the knowledge of God and the time of grace, Rom. 13.12; 1 Thess. 5.2; 1 Pet. 1.19. It also signifies a continuous and eternal time, Isa. 61.7. Day is sometimes put for judgment, especially the apostle's, which he also calls human, 1 Cor. 4.3, since in conducting trials a fixed day is set for each party. Day of Christ, that is, the last day of the whole world and his glorious coming, Phil. 1.6, 10 and 2.16. Day of Christ is that time which the evangelists indicate was fixed for the peril of Christ's calling and passion.

units.la: DIES distincti,Gen.1.14.Dies nouissimi, pro extrema mundi senecta 2.Pet.3.3.
units.tr: DAYS distinguished, Gen. 1.14. The last days, for the final old age of the world, 2 Pet. 3.3.

units.la: DIERVM discrimen per Christum sublatum, Rom.14.5.6 4.10.Col.2.v.16 17.Dierum longitudo quibus promissa xod.20.12.Deut.5.v.16 33 & 6.v.2.3.&11.v.9.21.
units.tr: The distinction of days abolished through Christ, Rom. 14.5, 6; Col. 2.16, 17. The length of days, for which a promise was made, Exod. 20.12; Deut. 5.16, 33; 6.2, 3; 11.9, 21.

units.la: DIFFIDENTIA, Contumacia,Eph.2.2.&5 6.Infidelitas. man.4.20.Vide INCREDVLITAS.
units.tr: DIFFIDENCE, obstinacy, Eph. 2.2 and 5.6; unbelief, Eph. 4.20. See UNBELIEF.

units.la: DIGITVS pars manus & pedis hom. Digitus Dei, Vide digitus,Digiti seni in Gigantis cuiusdam manibus & pedibus,2.Sam.21.20.probro afficiens Israelem,à Ionathan cutitur,v.21.Digiti contra parietem scribentes,Dan.5.5 digiti mystici,Cant.5.5.
units.tr: FINGER: a part of the hand and foot of a man. The finger of God: see FINGER. Six fingers on the hands and feet of a certain giant, 2 Sam. 21.20, reproaching Israel, which Jonathan struck down, v. 21. Fingers writing against the wall, Dan. 5.5. Mystical fingers, Song 5.5.

units.la: DILECTA, Ecclesia Christi sponsa, Cant.2.7.&35.8.
units.tr: BELOVED: the Church, the bride of Christ, Song 2.7 and 3.5.

units.la: [ Dilectus, Christus Filius Dei, sponsus Ecclesiæ, sæpius appellatur. 1. Ab Ecclesia in Cant. 2. A Prophetis & apostolis, Ps.45.1.Esai.5. 1. Matth.12.18.Eph.1.6.2.Pet.1.17.
units.tr: [The Beloved, Christ the Son of God, the bridegroom of the Church, is called so most often: 1. by the Church in the Song; 2. by the prophets and apostles, Ps. 45.1; Isa. 5.1; Matt. 12.18; Eph. 1.6; 1 Pet. 1.17.]

units.la: A Deo Patre, Matth.3.17.& 17.5. Luc.20.13. Dilectus Dei populus in Christo adoptatus, ex Iudaïs, deinde ex Iudæis Gentibus simul collectus, Psal.60.7. Ier.11.15. Rom.1.7. Col.3.12. 1.Thess.1.4.Iud.3. Dilectus filius matris charis. Gen.31.1. Dilectus, 1. Charissimus in Christo, Rom.16.v.5. 1.Cor.15.58.1.Tim.1.2. Tit.1.4. Philem.3.]
units.tr: By God the Father, Matt. 3.17 and 17.5; Luke 20.13. The beloved people of God, adopted in Christ, first from the Jews and then gathered together with the Gentiles, Ps. 60.7; Jer. 11.15; Rom. 1.7; Col. 3.12; 1 Thess. 1.4; Jude 3. The beloved son of a mother, dear, Gen. 31.1. Beloved: 1. most dear in Christ, Rom. 16.5; 1 Cor. 15.58; 1 Tim. 1.2; Titus 1.4; Philem. 3.]

units.la: DILECTIO Dei. Vide DEI dilectio. Dilectio proximi præcipitur. Vide AMOR, & CHARITAS.
units.tr: The love of God: see LOVE OF GOD. Love of one's neighbour is commanded: see LOVE and CHARITY.

units.la: DILEMMA, syllogismus utrinque vinciens: Dilemmatum usus scripturæ familiaris, Matt.21.25.Mar.11.30.Luc.6.9. & 20.4. Joan.8.5.& 18.23. Act.5.v.38.39.& 25.11.
units.tr: DILEMMA, a syllogism binding on both sides. The use of the dilemma is familiar in Scripture: Matt. 21.25; Mark 11.30; Luke 6.9 and 20.4; John 8.5 and 18.23; Acts 5.38, 39 and 25.11.

units.la: DILIGENTIA commendatur, Prov. 22.29. Exempla: Servi Isaac, Gen. 24.56. Ioseph, Gen.39.2.21 & 41.40. Dan.1.19. Ionathan & Achimaas 2. Sam. 17.18. Vide contrarium vitium ACEDIAM, & NEGLIGENTIAM. ] 1. Tim.3.5. Matt.25.21.
units.tr: DILIGENCE is commended, Prov. 22.29. Examples: Isaac's servant, Gen. 24.56; Joseph, Gen. 39.2, 21 and 41.40; Dan. 1.19; Jonathan and Ahimaaz, 2 Sam. 17.18. See the contrary vice, SLOTHFULNESS and NEGLIGENCE. 1 Tim. 3.5; Matt. 25.21.

units.la: DILIGERE & non diligere animam suam, id est vitam, Hebræis qui dicantur. Vide ANIMAM diligere.
units.tr: To love and not to love one's soul, that is, one's life: so it is said in the Hebrew idiom. See LOVE THE SOUL.

units.la: DILUVIUM a Deo immittitur, Gen.7.17. Diluuium deinceps non metuendum, 9.11. in eius rei fidem signi loco datur a Deo Arcus cœlestis, v. 12. 13. Nobis exemplo esse debet: Matt.24.37. c.2.Pet.3.6.
units.tr: The FLOOD is sent by God, Gen. 7.17. The flood is not to be feared thereafter, 9.11; as a sign and pledge of this, God gives the rainbow, vv. 12, 13. It ought to be an example to us: Matt. 24.37; 2 Pet. 3.6.

units.la: DIVIVM, pro afflictione & clade graviss. Psa.32.6. Nahum. 3.
units.tr: DIVISION, for the most grievous affliction and slaughter: Ps. 32.6; Nahum 3.

units.tr: DINAH, daughter of Jacob by Leah, is born, Gen. 30.21; she is ravished by Shechem, 34.2. Not restraining herself at home [1 Tim. 5.13; Titus 2.5] (that judgment).

units.tr: DIONYSIUS the Areopagite believes in Christ, Acts 17.34.

units.tr: CHURCH DISCIPLINE: see CHURCH and EXCOMMUNICATION. Discipline of the household: see PARENT.

units.tr: DISCIPLE (feminine), Acts 9.36.
