(Hezron. i. atrium, sagitta, [illegible, ~1 letter]SE pro fieri, Hebræorum more: Iudic. 11.8. Psalm. 31.3. & 1.3. Mat. 19.5. Luc. 3.5. pro agnosci & aperte conspici, 1. Cor. 5.28. pro significat, Mat. 15. 38.1. Cor. 10.4. μετονυμικῶς & sa-cramentaliter, pro repræsentare & adumbrare, Gal. 4.24. [illegible, ~1 letter]n priore versus parte, pro in pretio haberi: & contrà, non [illegible, ~1 letter]esse, pro nullo loco censeri, 1. Cor. 1.28. [De signo Sacram. [illegible, ~1 letter]licitur quod fit res significata, cuius est signum Symbo-[illegible, ~1 letter]um, & quam certissime repræsentet, Matt. 26.26. & 1. Cor. 11.24.]
units.tr: HEZRON, son of Perez, grandson of Judah, in the genealogy of Christ: Matt. 1.3; 1 Chr. 2.5; Ruth 4.18. (Hezron, i.e. court, arrow, ...) ESSE, meaning "to become," in the Hebrew manner: Judg. 11.8; Ps. 31.3; Ps. 1.3; Matt. 19.5; Luke 3.5. It means "to be known and clearly seen": 1 Cor. 5.28. It means "to signify": Matt. 15.38; 1 Cor. 10.4, metonymically [μετονυμικῶς] and sacramentally. It means "to represent and foreshadow": Gal. 4.24. In the former part of a verse it means "to be held in esteem," and conversely "not to be" means "to be counted of no account": 1 Cor. 1.28. [On the sign of a sacrament: it is said that what is done is the thing signified, of which it is the sign and symbol, and which it most certainly represents: Matt. 26.26; 1 Cor. 11.24.]

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letter]SE in carne, quid significet. Vide In carne esse. Esse in fe[illegible, ~1 letter]le [illegible, ~1 letter]imaritudinis, Act. 8.23. Hebræis ἐμφατικῶτερον est, quàm si diceretur, Fel esse in aliquo. Esse sub peccato, Rom. 3 9. est [illegible, ~1 letter]reos peccati siue fontes esse. esse in luce, pro regeneratum [illegible, ~1 letter]esse, 1. Ioan. 2.9.
units.tr: ESSE in the flesh: what it means. See To be in the flesh. To be in the gall of bitterness, Acts 8.23. For the Hebrews it is more emphatic [ἐμφατικώτερον] than if one said "to have gall in someone." To be under sin, Rom. 3.9, is to be guilty of sin, or to be sources of sin. To be in the light is to be regenerate, 1 John 2.9.

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letter]S THER regina efficitur, Esther. 2. 17. Regem & Aman
units.tr: ESTHER becomes queen, Esther 2.17. She receives the king and Haman

units.la: conuiuio excipit,5.4.pro sua & populi vita Regem orant 3. (.i.abscondita,vel demoliens.)
units.tr: at a banquet, 5.4. For her own life and the life of her people she begs the king, 3. (Esther, i.e. hidden, or destroying.)

units.la: Est & Non in sermonibus Pauli non fuit, neque in prophetionibus Dei, 2.Corin.1.v.17.18.19.20.
units.tr: Yea and Nay were not in the preaching of Paul, nor in the prophecies of God, 2 Cor. 1.17–20.

units.la: Est,est,Non,non,loco iuramenti dicendum,Matth.5.37. 5.12.
units.tr: "Yea, yea; Nay, nay" is to be said in place of an oath, Matt. 5.37; 5.12.

units.la: Esvrire iustitiam,Psalm.107.9. Esa.55,1.Matth.5.6. Luc.6.21. Apocal.21.6. & 22.17. Esurientes cibandi, Rom. 12.20.
units.tr: To hunger after righteousness, Ps. 107.9; Isa. 55.1; Matt. 5.6; Luke 6.21; Rev. 21.6 and 22.17. The hungry are to be fed, Rom. 12.20.

units.la: Esvrit Christus,Matt.4.2. Vide Christvs verus homo. Esurienti Eliæ ministrat Angelus, 1.Regum 19.5.
units.tr: Christ hungered, Matt. 4.2. See Christ, true man. An angel ministers to the hungry Elijah, 1 Kings 19.5.

units.la: Et,pro quia,1.Corint.8.4. 2. Corinth 5.6.Coloss.1.24.& Hebr.4.13.1.Ioan.3.20.pro, vt:Marci 9.49. interdum non est copulatiua, sed illatiua potius: verum cum interrogatione semper,Matth.5.14. Marc.10.26.pro,id est:2.Cor. Galat.1.4.Ephes.1.3. Coloss.1.3.Apocal.21.22.
units.tr: "And" for "because," 1 Cor. 8.4; 2 Cor. 5.6; Col. 1.24; Heb. 4.13; 1 John 3.20. For "that," Mark 9.49; sometimes it is not copulative but rather illative, though always with an interrogation: Matt. 5.14; Mark 10.26. For "that is": 2 Cor. ...; Gal. 1.4; Eph. 1.3; Col. 1.3; Rev. 21.22.

units.la: Et hai in Dauidem fidelitas, 2.Sam.15.v.19.20.21.(Hora tempus siue paratus.)
units.tr: HAI (Hebrew, "as the Lord lives"): the faithfulness of David, 2 Sam. 15.19–21. (Hora, i.e. time, or ready.)

units.la: Eva ,Vide, Heva.
units.tr: EVA. See HEVA.

units.la: Evangelivm pro historia per Euangelistas conscripta cùm dicitur, Euangelium secundum Matthæum, Marcum,&c.vt interpretatur Lucas, Act.1.1. pro Euangelij doctrina,seu salutis doctrina, non ab hominibus excogitata,sed è cœlo,(Ioan.1.18.)ad nos allata,Marci 16.15. Rom.1.6.sicut prædictum fuit Esai.52.7.vt mutua sit interdem & verbum prædicatum relatio, Rom. 10.17. pro doctrinæ illius salutiferæ annuntiatione, Rom.1.vers.1.9. 15.19.1.Corint.4.15.& 9.14. 2.Cor. 8.18. Phil.2.22. & 4. Coloss.1.5.1. Thess.3.2.2.Thess.2.14.2.Tim.1.1.& 2.8.
units.tr: GOSPEL, when it is said of the history written by the Evangelists, "the Gospel according to Matthew, Mark," etc., as Luke explains, Acts 1.1. It means the doctrine of the Gospel, or the teaching of salvation, not devised by men but brought to us from heaven (John 1.18), Mark 16.15; Rom. 1.6, as was foretold, Isa. 52.7. The relation between the preached word and the gospel is sometimes mutual, Rom. 10.17. It means the proclamation of that saving doctrine: Rom. 1.9; 15.19; 1 Cor. 4.15; 9.14; 2 Cor. 8.18; Phil. 2.22; 4; Col. 1.5; 1 Thess. 3.2; 2 Thess. 2.14; 2 Tim. 1.1; 2.8.

units.la: Evangelivm Crux interdum dicitur, Galat.5.11.& à tro λόγω, id est sermo,per excellentiam dicitur,Actor. 36 37.
units.tr: GOSPEL is sometimes called the cross, Gal. 5.11; and by excellence it is called "the word" [ὁ λόγος], Acts 36, 37.

units.la: Evangelivm Christi, Marci 1.1.Roman.1 9.& 15.19. Cor.2.12.& 10.14.Gal.1.7.1. Thess.3.2.2. Thess.1.1.8. Dei, Roman.11.2.Cor.11.7.1.Thess.2.v.8.9.1. Petr.4.18. Regni Dei, Marc.1.14. Ministri Euangelij aliquando suum illud vocant,Rom.2.16.& 16.25.2.Cor.4.3.2.Thess.2.14.2. Timoth.2.8.Euangelium gloriæ Dei nomine significatum,1. Timoth.1.11. & potentia Dei,Rom.1,16.Euangelio lacti comparatur, Petri 2,2.(vide 1.Cor.3.2.)Euangelio vocatur lex fidei,Rom.3.26.quod quomodo intelligendum sit, Vide Lex.Euangelium luciferi vocabulo significatum, 2.Petr.1.19.mortuo præd rædicatum dicitur, 1.Petr.4.6. vbi per mortuos intelligi debent ij, qui tum quidem cùm prædicaretur illis Euangelium, viui erant, nunc verò cùm illud dicitur, sunt mortui. Euangelium dicitur odor mortis ad mortem, 2. Cor.2.16. ex quorundam sententia in eorum videlicet exilium, qui mortem Christi tantùm vt mortem considerabant, quibus ipsa crucis prædicatio erat vel stultitia, vel offendiculum, 1.Corinth.1.23. aliis verò odor vitæ ad vitam, qui vitam in hac morte propositam amplectebantur. Euangelium præputij μετανυμικὸς vocatur, Galat.2.7. Euangelium inter gentes annuntiandum: sicut Euangelium Circumcisionis, ibid. quod inter circumcisos annuntiandum est: neque tamen duplex est Euangelium in se, sed populorum genera erant duo, quibus annuntiabatur: num circumcisorum, alterum incircumcisorum. Euangelium Regni, pro felici de Regno cœlorum nuntiatione, Matthæi 24.14.
units.tr: GOSPEL OF CHRIST, Mark 1.1; Rom. 1.9; 15.19; 2 Cor. 2.12; 10.14; Gal. 1.7; 1 Thess. 3.2; 2 Thess. 1.8. OF GOD, Rom. 11.2; 2 Cor. 11.7; 1 Thess. 2.8, 9; 1 Pet. 4.18. OF THE KINGDOM OF GOD, Mark 1.14. Ministers of the gospel sometimes call it "their own," Rom. 2.16; 16.25; 2 Cor. 4.3; 2 Thess. 2.14; 2 Tim. 2.8. The gospel is signified by the name "gospel of the glory of God," 1 Tim. 1.11, and "power of God," Rom. 1.16. The gospel is compared to milk, 1 Pet. 2.2 (see 1 Cor. 3.2). The gospel is called the law of faith, Rom. 3.26; how this is to be understood, see LAW. The gospel is signified by the word "light," 2 Pet. 1.19. It is said to be preached to the dead, 1 Pet. 4.6, where by the dead must be understood those who, when the gospel was preached to them, were alive, but now are dead. The gospel is said to be a savour of death unto death, 2 Cor. 2.16: according to some opinions, this is to their exile, namely of those who considered the death of Christ only as death, to whom the very preaching of the cross was either foolishness or a stumbling block, 1 Cor. 1.23; but to others it is a savour of life unto life, who embraced the life proposed in this death. The gospel of the uncircumcision [μετανυμικὸς] is so called, Gal. 2.7: the gospel to be preached among the Gentiles, just as the gospel of the circumcision, ibid., is to be preached among the circumcised. Yet the gospel is not twofold in itself, but there were two kinds of people to whom it was preached: the circumcised and the uncircumcised. The gospel of the kingdom is the joyful announcement of the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 24.14.

units.la: Euangelium vocatur spiritus, 2.Cor.3.6. sicut Lex litera, primò, propter veteres ceremonias temporarias, & in rebus crassis ac corporeis positas. Secundò, & quidem potissimum, quia materia, argumentum, Minister denique Euangelij est Iesvs Christus, non iam docens quid facere, quid fugere oporteat (quod legis officium est) sed seipsum in æternam vitam gratis offerens credentibus, nec offerens nodò, sed etiam re ipsa insinuans. Euangelium stulta prædicatio vocatur à Paulo, 1.Corint.1.21. per concessionem hominum hypothesi, vt in sequenti versu stultitiam & infirmitatem Dei vocat. Vide quiddam in Iosephi Maria, &c.
units.tr: The Gospel is called spirit (2 Cor. 3:6), as the Law is called letter: first, because of the old temporary ceremonies, which were set in gross and bodily things. Second, and chiefly, because the matter and subject of the Gospel, and finally its Minister, is Jesus Christ, who no longer teaches what must be done or avoided (which is the office of the Law), but offers himself freely to believers for eternal life, not merely offering but actually bestowing himself. Paul calls the Gospel foolish preaching (1 Cor. 1:21), by way of concession to human opinion, since in the following verse he calls it the foolishness and weakness of God. See something in Iosephi Maria, etc.

units.la: EVANGELIVM est æternum, Apoc.14.6. arcanum, Ephes.1. & 3.3. & 6.19. Col.1.26. & 4.3. 1.Tim.3.9.
units.tr: The Gospel is eternal (Rev. 14:6), a hidden mystery (Eph. 1 and 3:3 and 6:19; Col. 1:26 and 4:3; 1 Tim. 3:9).

units.la: EVANGELII effecta: Fides, 1.Tim.4.6. illustratio vitæ, 2.Corinth.4.6.2.Timot.1.10. pax, Ephes.6.15. reconciliationis ministerium, 2.Corint.5.18. Regnum Dei stabilire, Matt.3. & 4.23. & 9.35. & 24.14. Mar.1.14. Luc.16.16. Col.4.11. regimen vitæ, Galat.6.16. salutis collatio, Act.13.26. & 28.28. Rom.1.16. Spiritus administratio, 2.Cor.3.8. vitæ collatio. Act.5.20. Philip.2.15.
units.tr: The effects of the Gospel: faith (1 Tim. 4:6); the illumination of life (2 Cor. 4:6; 2 Tim. 1:10); peace (Eph. 6:15); the ministry of reconciliation (2 Cor. 5:18); the establishing of the kingdom of God (Matt. 3, 4:23, 9:35, 24:14; Mark 1:14; Luke 16:16; Col. 4:11); the rule of life (Gal. 6:16); the bestowing of salvation (Acts 13:26, 28:28; Rom. 1:16); the administration of the Spirit (2 Cor. 3:8); the bestowing of life (Acts 5:20; Phil. 2:15).

units.la: EVANGELII subiectum Christus, & eius gloriæ illustratio. Rom.1.3. 2.Corin.4.4. hinc fit, vt testimonium Christi non minetur, 1.Cor.1.6. & 2.1.2. Tim, 1.8. Dicitur virtus Dei. Rom.1.16. 1.Cor.1.v.18.24.
units.tr: The subject of the Gospel is Christ, and the illumination of his glory (Rom. 1:3; 2 Cor. 4:4). Hence it does not threaten the testimony of Christ (1 Cor. 1:6; 2:1; 2 Tim. 1:8). It is called the power of God (Rom. 1:16; 1 Cor. 1:18, 24).

units.la: EVANGELIVM quibus manifestum, Matth.11.25.& 13 11. cæ 10.21. omnibus & palam in toto orbe annuntiandi. Matt.10.27.& 24 14 & 28.19. Marci 13.10 & 16.15. Luc. 23.& 24.47. Tit. 2. 11. vbiqʒ annuntiatum, Col. 1.23. lumninis obnoxium, Rom. 3.8. quibus opertum, 2.Cor. per Prophetas promissum, Rom. 1.2. afflictionibus promouetur, Philip. 1.v.12.13. à paucis recipitur, Esaiæ 53.1. Matth. 14.Rom.10.16.& 11.v.3 9. Euangelij certitudo, 1.Corinth. 1.Gal.1.8.1.Pet.3.12.2.Pet.1.16.
units.tr: The Gospel is revealed to some (Matt. 11:25; 13:11; Luke 10:21), and is to be announced to all, openly, throughout the whole world (Matt. 10:27; 24:14; 28:19; Mark 13:10; 16:15; Luke 23 and 24:47; Titus 2:11). It has been announced everywhere (Col. 1:23); it is exposed to the light (Rom. 3:8); it is hidden from some (2 Cor.); it was promised through the prophets (Rom. 1:2); it is advanced by afflictions (Phil. 1:12–13); it is received by few (Isa. 53:1; Matt. 14; Rom. 10:16; 11:3, 9). The certainty of the Gospel: 1 Cor. 1; Gal. 1:8; 1 Pet. 3:12; 2 Pet. 1:16.

units.la: Euangelij confirmatio ex donis Spiritus Sancti, 1.Cor. v.5.9 ex Pauli constantia, Philip.1.7. (vide supra, Evangelium afflictionibus promouetur) ex multitudine, Cor. 1.6. ex Prophetarum orationibus, 2. Petr.1.19. Euangelij doctrina, lac & cibus, 1.Cor.3 2. Hebr.5.12.1.Pet.2.2. Euangelij doctrina noua videtur, Marci 1.27. Act. 17.v.19. noua tamen non est, Ioan.8 25. Actor.2.16.& 3.18.& 10. & 13.32. Roman.12.& 16.25. Ephes.1.9.& 3.verf.8.9.2.Tim. 19.1.Ioann.12.& 2.7. Euangelij afflictiones Paulo dicitur, 2.Tim.18. quia Euangelium dicitur quodammodo affligi in iis à quibus annuntiatur, nisi (quod simplicius accipiamus pro ipsius annuntiatione, qua sit crux coniuncta. Euangelij encomia, Vide EVANGELII effecta.
units.tr: The Gospel is confirmed by the gifts of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 1:5, 9); by Paul's constancy (Phil. 1:7; see above, "the Gospel is advanced by afflictions"); by the multitude of believers (1 Cor. 1:6); by the prayers of the prophets (2 Pet. 1:19). The teaching of the Gospel is milk and food (1 Cor. 3:2; Heb. 5:12; 1 Pet. 2:2). The teaching of the Gospel seems new (Mark 1:27; Acts 17:19), yet it is not new (John 8:25; Acts 2:16, 3:18, 10, 13:32; Rom. 12, 16:25; Eph. 1:9, 3:8–9; 2 Tim. 1:9; 1 John 1:2, 2:7). The afflictions of the Gospel are attributed by Paul to the Gospel (2 Tim. 1:8), because the Gospel is in some sense said to be afflicted in those by whom it is announced; unless we understand it more simply of the very announcement of it, to which the cross is joined. Praises of the Gospel: see the effects of the Gospel.

units.la: Euangelij definitio ab effectis sumta habetur, Rom.1. cuius sensus est: Euangelium est organum Dei vere potens & efficax ad seruandum, quamobrem etiam vocatur Virtus Dei, Esa.53 1.Euangelij finis, Rom.1.16.& 15.13. Corint.1.9.& 2.7.2.Corin.3.18.& 10.v.4.5 6.1.Thess.1.4.3. Tit.2.v.11.12.2 Petri 1.4. scopus, est Filius Dei, Romani 3 Actor.4.12.1.Ioan.2.12. Vide EVANGELII subiectum. Euangelij hostes duplices, Matth.7.6. Euangelij patrocinium ab omnibus suscipiendum, 2.Tim.4.16.Philem.v.13.14. 19.20.22.Hebr.13.3.
units.tr: The definition of the Gospel is taken from its effects (Rom. 1): its sense is that the Gospel is the instrument of God, truly powerful and effective for saving; for this reason it is also called the power of God (Isa. 53:1). The end of the Gospel (Rom. 1:16; 15:13; 1 Cor. 1:9; 2:7; 2 Cor. 3:18; 10:4–5; 6:1; 1 Thess. 1:4; 1 Tim. 3; Titus 2:11–12; 2 Pet. 1:4). Its goal is the Son of God (Rom. 3; Acts 4:12; 1 John 2:12); see the subject of the Gospel. The enemies of the Gospel are twofold (Matt. 7:6). The protection of the Gospel is to be undertaken by all (2 Tim. 4:16; Philem. 13–14, 19–20, 22; Heb. 13:3).

units.la: Euangelij praedicatio quanti æstimanda, Rom.10.15. Cor.4.4.Gal.3.v.2.5.Apoc.1.20.Euangelij prædicatio confertur messi, Matt.9.37.Luc.10 2.Ioan.4.35. fermento, Ioan.13.21. Euangelij prædicatio, cultus Deo gratus, Ioan.4. Roma.1.9.& 15.16. Euangelij admiranda propagatio, Act. 41.& 4.v.4.31 32.& 5.v.14.25.28.42.& 6.v.1.2.& 10.44. 11.v.19.20.21.24.& 11.26.& 13.v.42.43.44. Euangelij Potentia, 2.Cor.3.ver.6.7.Ephes.3.8. Colossi.1.27.& 4. Heb.6.18. Euangelium Lege præstantius. Esa.54.1. Rom. 1.Cor.3.v.7.8 Galat.4.v.24.26.27.Heb.2 1 & 7.19. & 12. 8.22.23.Euangelij puritas retinenda, Rom. 6. 7. Gal.2. 5.v.8.9. Iudæ v. 3. Euangelij thesaurus in vasis fictilibus absconditus,2.Cor.4.7. Euangelij veritas,pro eius genuina puritate,Gal.2.5. Euangelij vis, quanta in arcanis patefa-iendis,Luc.2.35.
units.tr: The preaching of the Gospel is to be valued highly (Rom. 10:15; 1 Cor. 4:4; Gal. 3:2, 5; Rev. 1:20). The preaching of the Gospel is compared to a harvest (Matt. 9:37; Luke 10:2; John 4:35), to leaven (Matt. 13:33). The preaching of the Gospel is a worship pleasing to God (John 4; Rom. 1:9; 15:16). The propagation of the Gospel is admirable (Acts 4:1, 4:31–32; 5:14, 25, 28, 42; 6:1–2, 10:44; 11:19–21, 24, 26; 13:42–44). The power of the Gospel (2 Cor. 3:6–7; Eph. 3:8; Col. 1:27, 4; Heb. 6:18). The Gospel is more excellent than the Law (Isa. 54:1; Rom. 1; 1 Cor. 3:7–8; Gal. 4:24–27; Heb. 2, 7:19, 12:22–23). The purity of the Gospel is to be retained (Rom. 6–7; Gal. 2, 5:8–9; Jude 3). The treasure of the Gospel is hidden in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 4:7). The truth of the Gospel, for its genuine purity (Gal. 2:5). The force of the Gospel, how great it is in disclosing mysteries (Luke 2:35).

units.la: EVANGELII & Legis discrimen, Ioann. 1.17. Rom.6.14.& 7. 2.Cor.3.ver.7.8.9.10.11.Gal.4.v.24 26.Hebr.8.13.& 9.v.
units.tr: The difference between the Gospel and the Law (John 1:17; Rom. 6:14; 7; 2 Cor. 3:7–11; Gal. 4:24–26; Heb. 8:13; 9).

units.la: 1.Euangelij pro toto noui Testamenti ministerio accepi munus proprium esse prædicare pœnitentiam salutarem seu μετάνοιαν, atque adeò totam ad Deum conversionem per fidem,non autem Legis, his rationibus & testimoniis confirmatur, contra eos qui non rectè perpendentes discrimen Legis & Euangelij, vim Legis & virtutem mortis & resurrectionis Christi (vt interim taceam magnam eos Christo iniuriam facere, in cuius solius nomine pœnitentia est prædicanda) falsò illud Legi adscribunt.
units.tr: First: it is established that, for the whole ministry of the New Testament, the proper task received is to preach saving repentance, or metanoia [μετάνοιαν], and thus the whole conversion to God through faith, and not the Law. This is confirmed by these reasons and testimonies, against those who, not weighing rightly the difference between Law and Gospel, falsely ascribe that to the Law, along with the power of the Law and the virtue of the death and resurrection of Christ (to pass over for the moment that they do great wrong to Christ, in whose name alone repentance is to be preached).

units.la: Primò, quia eius est inuitare ad pœnitentiam, cuius est rem veniæ facere. Atqui id nō Legis (quæ perpetuò sine ulla summi rigoris ἀπαραιτήτου clamat damnatoriam illam sententiam, Maledictus quisquis, &c.Deu.27.26.Gal.3.10.) sed Euangelij est, vtpote quod manu quasi ducit ad Medium animarum nostrarum Christum,qui perfectè Legem implevit,& nostram in se transferens culpam,vere pœnitentes à reatu absoluit, ideoq; in nomine suo vult prædicari pœnitentiam,Lucæ 24.v.46.47.
units.tr: First, because it belongs to the one who makes forgiveness available to invite to repentance. But this is not the office of the Law, which without any mercy, [ἀπαραιτήτου] cries out its condemning sentence, "Cursed is whoever…" (Deut. 27:26; Gal. 3:10). It is the office of the Gospel, which, as it were, leads by the hand to Christ, the Mediator of our souls, who perfectly fulfilled the Law and, transferring our guilt to himself, absolves truly penitent people from the debt; therefore he wills that repentance be preached in his name (Luke 24:46–47).

units.la: Secundò à fine:Finis prædicationis pœnitentiæ est,vt sit aliquis gratiæ locus. Atqui gratiam & remissionem peccatorum annuntiare,Euangelij: damnationem verò, Legis: ideóque ministerium mortis vocatur ab Apostolo ipsa Lex,2.Cor.3.7.hoc est,Lex facit,vt ex agnitione peccati intelligamus nos morte dignos esse.
units.tr: Second, from the end: the purpose of preaching repentance is that there may be a place for grace. But to announce grace and the forgiveness of sins belongs to the Gospel, while to announce damnation belongs to the Law; therefore the Law itself is called by the Apostle "the ministry of death" (2 Cor. 3:7), that is, the Law brings it about that, through the recognition of sin, we understand that we deserve death.

units.la: Hæc peccati agnitio ex Lege petita & excitata duplicem pro diuersis subiectis operatur dolorem. Nam interdum ita vulnerat conscientiam, vt tamen illa peccatum非 non oderit, sed solo pœnæ metu excrucietur, sicut in Cain,Esau,Saule, Iuda apparet. Interdū verò sic afficitur animus, iudicij diuini terroribus, vt tamen seipsum erigit & fulciat spe misericordiæ & remissionis peccatorum propter Christum,fide apprehensum: & quoniam verè odit peccatum, resipiscat etiam & in viam iustitiæ ingediatur. In illis, id est, impiis, terrores illi & compunctiones cordis ex agnitione peccati, & sensu irae diuinae sunt veluti inferorum atrium, & certissimum ad desperationem iter: In electis vero (vt iam dictum est) illi scientiae pauores, quos vulgò Contritionem cordis vocant, occasionem prebent verę conuersionis & resipiscentiae. Sic enim agnito peccato, incipiunt de remedio cogitare & quaerere ac oblatum Christum per fidem ample&ti, Spiritu ipsius aguntur, vt iustitiae viuant. Atqui haec demum est Christiana illa & salutaris poenitentia, quae μετάνοια est, resipiscentia dicitur. Vnde liquet manifeste resipiscentiam hanc, μετάνοιαν, ad Euangelium proprissime, non ad Legem pertinere.
units.tr: This recognition of sin, derived and aroused from the Law, produces a twofold sorrow according to the different subjects. For sometimes it so wounds the conscience that it nonetheless does not hate sin, but is tormented only by fear of punishment, as appears in Cain, Esau, Saul and Judas. But at other times the mind is so affected by terrors of divine judgment that it nonetheless raises and sustains itself with hope of mercy and forgiveness of sins through Christ, apprehended by faith; and since it truly hates sin, it also repents and enters the way of righteousness. In the first, that is, the ungodly, those terrors and pangs of heart from the recognition of sin and the sense of divine wrath are like the courtyard of hell and a most certain road to despair. In the elect (as has already been said), those fears of knowledge, which are commonly called contrition of heart, provide the occasion of true conversion and repentance. For thus, once sin is recognized, they begin to think about the remedy and to seek and embrace Christ offered through faith, and are driven by his Spirit so that they live in righteousness. But this at last is that Christian and saving repentance, which is metanoia [μετάνοια], and is called repentance (resipiscentia). Hence it is plain that this repentance, metanoia [μετάνοιαν], pertains most properly to the Gospel, not to the Law.

units.la: Tertiò, à Baptismi natura: quia cùm Baptismus sit stabilis quaedam poenitentiae concio, docente id Paulo Roman. 6. v. 3. 4. Gal. 3. 27. cuiuscunque Baptismus sacramentum, eiusdem etiam erit officij, poenitentiam praedicare, cuius est symbolum, Luc. 3. 3. Actor. 2. 38. & Atqui Baptismum non Legis, sed Euangelij sacramentum esse, vel ex ipsa Baptismi institutione patet, Matth. 28. 19. Mar. 16. 16. Deinde sigillum, & id cuius illud sigillum eodem pertinere nemo sanus, vt opinor, dissitebitur. qui fidei sigillum, quae per Euangelij praedicationem in bis infunditur & ingeneratur, est & dicitur Baptismus Matt. 28 19. Marc. 16. 16. Actor. 2. 41. & 8. v. 37. 38. & 10. v. 48. & 16. v. 14. 15. 30. 32. 33. 34. & 18. 8. quod ipsum & de circumcisione, cui succedit Baptismus, affirmare Paulus dubitat, Roman. 4. 11. Quare cùm fides & Baptismus, est poenitentiae symbolum, Luc. 3. 3. Actor. 2. 38. & 19. 4. res coniunctissimae, Euangelicæ propriæ, liquere arbitrari poenitentiam non ad Legem, sed ad Euangelium pertinere.
units.tr: Third, from the nature of Baptism: since Baptism is a certain abiding proclamation of repentance, as Paul teaches (Rom. 6:3–4; Gal. 3:27), whoever's Baptism is a sacrament will also have the office of preaching repentance, of which it is the sign (Luke 3:3; Acts 2:38). But that Baptism is a sacrament of the Gospel and not of the Law is clear from the very institution of Baptism (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:16). Further, it is a seal, and no sane person, I think, will deny that the thing of which it is the seal belongs to the same [Gospel]: Baptism is the seal of faith, which is poured into and engendered in people through the preaching of the Gospel, and is called Baptism (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:16; Acts 2:41; 8:37–38; 10:48; 16:14–15, 30, 32–34; 18:8). Paul hesitates to affirm this of circumcision, to which Baptism succeeds (Rom. 4:11). Therefore, since faith and Baptism are the sign of repentance (Luke 3:3; Acts 2:38; 19:4), most closely joined and proper to the Gospel, it is plain that repentance pertains not to the Law but to the Gospel.

units.la: Quarto, quia nemo serio resipiscit, nisi qui seipsum aliquando odit ex animo, & iustitiam ex praescripto verbi Dei volens amplectitur. Hoc nemo vlla ex parte praestare vult, aut potest, nisi qui est regeneratus: Nemo regeneratur à Deo, nisi in Christo: Christum nemo amplectitur, cuius iustitia gratis imputata iustificetur, & eius participatione sanctificetur, nisi qui fide eum amplectitur: Fides vera & salutaris in neminem cadit, nisi eum qui promissionibus Euangelicis de gratuita Dei misericordia & remissione peccatorum, absque vllis operibus meritis ritis innititur, illisque acquiescit. Quemadmodum igi-fides est Euangelij propria, ita pœnitentiæ etiam præ-paratio ad Euangelium, & non ad Legem pertineat necef-sit.
units.tr: Fourth, because no one repents in earnest unless he at some time hates himself from the heart and willingly embraces righteousness according to the prescription of the Word of God. No one is willing or able to do this in any respect unless he has been regenerated; no one is regenerated by God except in Christ; no one embraces Christ, by whose righteousness, imputed freely, one is justified, and by whose participation one is sanctified, unless he embraces him by faith; true and saving faith falls upon no one except him who relies upon the Gospel promises of God's free mercy and the forgiveness of sins, without any works or merits, and rests in them. Just as faith is proper to the Gospel, so the preparation for repentance must of necessity pertain to the Gospel, and not to the Law.

units.la: Quinto, quia vera pœnitentia, seu resipiscentia absque re-generatione esse nequit. Atqui nemo nisi per Euange-lium, Spiritu Sancto intus per fidem agente & operante, regeneratur, quam regenerationem externo quasi signo significat Baptismus, Tit.3.5. Ergo neque pœnitentiæ prae-dicatio alterius quam Euangelij est propria.
units.tr: Fifthly, because true repentance, or repentance that returns to God, cannot exist without regeneration. But no one is regenerated except through the Gospel, with the Holy Spirit working and acting inwardly through faith. Baptism signifies this regeneration by an outward sign (Titus 3:5). Therefore the preaching of repentance also belongs to the Gospel and to no other teaching.

units.la: Sexto, quia fides & pœnitentia salutaris indissolubili nexu cohærent: quomodo. n.quis vere resipiscat, nisi idem credat etiam de venia, quam nobis offert Euangelium, con-fidat? Atqui fides per Euangelium annuntiatur, & per illud tanquam medium infunditur & ingeneratur à Spiritu Sancto, utpote quæ in Euangelicas promissiones soluere-rumbit, & animos sensu iræ & iudicij diuini perculsos terret, sed potius Euangelicis promissionib. solatur ac sæpe misericordiæ ac veniæ peccatorum, ne succumbant vt Caino, Iudæ, &c. contigit) erigit. Lex autem ex fide non est, Gal.3.12. hoc est, non pronunciat iustum eum cui dedit, sed qui fecerit, quod ipsa præcipit. Quare liquet, eisdem esse prædicare pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum, cuius est annunciare fidem, vnicum illud salutis ac Christi apprehendendi instrumentum.
units.tr: Sixthly, because saving faith and repentance are joined by an indissoluble bond. For how can anyone truly repent unless he also believes and trusts the same concerning the pardon that the Gospel offers us? But faith is announced through the Gospel and, as through a means, is poured into us and engendered by the Holy Spirit. Faith does not terrify souls struck by the sense of wrath and divine judgment, as happened to Cain, Judas, and others, but rather comforts them with Gospel promises and raises them up, lest they sink down. "The Law is not of faith" (Gal. 3:12); that is, it does not pronounce just the one to whom it gives itself, but the one who does what it itself commands. Therefore it is clear that preaching repentance and the remission of sins belongs to the same office as proclaiming faith, which is the one instrument of salvation and of laying hold on Christ.

units.la: Septimò, quia Legis prædicatio, nisi Euangelio tanquam dulcissima Legis θεωρία temperetur & mitigetur, perpetuo talem efficit timorem, qui certum sit ad desperationem & mortem iter, 2. Cor. 7.10. ac proinde Lex salutarem illam pœnitentiam, quæ ex dolore secundum Deum fit, & salutem sibi adhuc iam habet, 2.Cor.7.10. prædicare non potest.
units.tr: Seventhly, because the preaching of the Law, unless it is tempered and softened by the Gospel as the sweetest contemplation [θεωρία] of the Law, always produces a fear that leads surely to despair and death (2 Cor. 7:10). Consequently the Law cannot preach that saving repentance which arises from godly sorrow and already has salvation for itself (2 Cor. 7:10).

units.la: Octavo, quia impossibile est Legem se præstantiorem producere effectum. Atqui si Legis munus esset prædicare pœnitentiam salutarem, & Lex eam in nobis operaretur, produceret effectum se præstantiorem: Lex enim ipsa neminem unquam iustificauit, nec iustificabit, sed perpetuo & sine ulla intermissione & remissione suum illum rigorem vrget: pœnitentia autem salutaris, quæ resipiscentiam vocamus, salutem efficit, teste Paulo, 2. Cor.7.10.
units.tr: Eighthly, because it is impossible for the Law to produce a more excellent effect. But if the office of the Law were to preach saving repentance, and the Law were to work it in us, it would produce an effect more excellent than itself. For the Law itself has never justified anyone, nor will it justify, but it presses its rigour constantly and without any interruption or relaxation. Saving repentance, which we call repentance unto life, brings about salvation, as Paul testifies (2 Cor. 7:10).

units.la: Nono, quia Ioannes Baptista prædicabat pœnitentiam,
units.tr: Ninthly, because John the Baptist preached repentance,

units.la: Matt.3.v.2.8.atqui Ioannes Baptista erat ξαφχ noui Testamenti, & Euangelij potissimùm præco.
units.tr: (Matt. 3:2, 8). But John the Baptist was the beginning [ἀρχή] of the New Testament and above all the herald of the Gospel.

units.la: Decimò, quia ipse etiam Christus, qui est Euangelij subiectum & scopus, Act.4.12. Roman.1.3.1.Ioan.2.12. prædicaut poenitentiam, Matthæi 4.17. eamque Discipuli in toto terrarum Orbe prædicarent, in mandatis de Lucæ 24.47. cum alioqui Euangelij prædicationem singulariter & seriò demandârit, Marci 16.15. quod Apostolos fecisse liquet ex Mat.6.11. Luc.9.6. Act.17.30. & 21.& 26 20.2.Petri 3.9.
units.tr: Tenthly, because Christ himself, who is the subject and aim of the Gospel (Acts 4:12; Rom. 1:3; 1 John 2:12), preached repentance (Matt. 4:17), and commanded his disciples to preach it throughout the whole world (Luke 24:47), although he especially and earnestly enjoined the preaching of the Gospel (Mark 16:15). That the apostles did this is clear from Matt. 6:11, Luke 9:6, Acts 17:30, 21:26, 20:2, and 2 Peter 3:9.

units.la: Vndecimò, quia inseparabili vinculo coniuncta est poenitentia salutaris, & promissio gratiæ ac remissionis peccatorum. At promissio gratiæ ac remissionis peccatorum per Christum Mediatorem Fide apprehensum, est Euangelij proprium.
units.tr: Eleventhly, because saving repentance is joined by an inseparable bond to the promise of grace and of the remission of sins. But the promise of grace and of the remission of sins, laid hold of through faith in Christ the Mediator, belongs to the Gospel alone.

units.la: Duodecimò, idem manifestè euincitur ex collatione omnium locorum, ubi hæ phrases & verborum formæ, Euangelizare, & prædicare poenitentiam, inter se permutantur, Marci 6.12. Lucæ 9. 6. Nam quod Lucas dixit Euangelizare, Marcus illud ipsum explicans dixit, prædicare resipiscerent homines: quasi dicat, Euangelium esse prædicationem poenitentiæ & remissionis peccatorum in nomine Christi, Luc.24.47.
units.tr: Twelfthly, the same is plainly proved from comparing all the passages where these phrases and forms of words, to preach the Gospel and to preach repentance, are used interchangeably (Mark 6:12; Luke 9:6). For what Luke called preaching the Gospel, Mark, explaining it, called preaching that men should repent. It is as if he said that the Gospel is the preaching of repentance and of the remission of sins in the name of Christ (Luke 24:47).

units.la: Decimotertiò, quia tutissimum est in docendo & tradendis dogmatibus doctrinæ cœlestis sequi phrasin Scripturæ sacræ. At Scriptura sacra poenitentiæ salutaris prædicationem adeò non excludit à doctrina ministerij Euangelij propria, ut expresse illam ad Euangelium referat, ut patet ex Esaiæ 61.1. Ezech.33.11. Matt.3.2. & 9.13. Mar.16.16. Luc.4.18. & 24.v.46.47. Act.5.3. & 11.18. & 14.15. & 17.30. & 21.& 26.20.2. Petri.3.9.
units.tr: Thirteenthly, because it is safest, in teaching and in handing down the doctrines of heavenly teaching, to follow the phrasing of holy Scripture. But holy Scripture so little excludes the preaching of saving repentance from the teaching of the ministry of the Gospel that it expressly refers it to the Gospel, as is evident from Isaiah 61:1, Ezek. 33:11, Matt. 3:2 and 9:13, Mark 16:16, Luke 4:18 and 24:46–47, Acts 5:31, 11:18, 14:15, 17:30, 20:21, 26:20, and 2 Peter 3:9.

units.la: Decimoquarto & postremò, quia Spiritus Sanctus per Euangelium arguere dicitur incredulitatis peccatum, Ioan. 16.9. Atqui quemadmodum non in Lege, sed in Euangelio patefit, incredulitatem in Filium Mediatorem (quem audire iubemur, Matth.17.5.) esse peccatum, ita etiam per Legem arguitur incredulitas in Filium, quâ Lex irrat esse peccatum, sed per Euangelium, quod illum aut dum & honorem illi deferendum præcipit, Psalm.2. 6 11.12. Esaiæ 53.11. Quare quum incredulitas in Filium ignota sit, vel maximè eam, ut peccatum, arguere proinde poenitentiam etiam de ea prædicare non potest. [illegible, ~10 letters]que tamen interim, dum pœnitentiæ salutaris prædica-[illegible, ~8 letters]nem Euangelij ministerio adscribimus, Legem penitus [illegible, ~6 letters]illimus, & sic Antinomis fauemus. Nam fatemur Legem [illegible, ~6 letters]onstrare peccata ipsi nota, Roman. 3. 20. ad quorum [illegible, ~6 letters]enitentiam nos inuitet Euangelium. Et agnoscimus Le-[illegible, ~5 letters]m Dei, quam vsitatè Decalogum appellamus, normam [illegible, ~3 letters]è vitæ Christianæ. Sed hæc duo præcipua doctrinarum [illegible, ~3 letters]nera distincta esse volumus, ne quo modo confundan-[illegible, ~3 letters]r, ac quadruplicem hanc inter illa differentiam const-[illegible, ~3 letters]imus. Differunt enim Lex & Euangelium. Primò, notitia, [illegible, ~3 letters]oman. 2. 15. Ioannis 1.18. Secundò forma promissionum, [illegible, ~3 letters]euteron. 27.26. Matthæi 19.17. Luc. 10.28. & Roman. 4.16. [illegible, ~3 letters]ò, effectibus, qui Legi & Euangelio attribuuntur di-[illegible, ~3 letters]rsi, 2. Corinth 3. ver. 6. 7. 8. 9. Quartò, appellatione ad ob-[illegible, ~3 letters]ta diuersa, seu ad diuersos hominum gradus, 2. Timot. 2. [illegible, ~3 letters]. Esaiæ 61, 1. Lucæ 4.18. Gal. 5. v 22, 23. 1. Tim. 1. 9. V. EVAN-[illegible, ~3 letters]ELII & Legis discrimen.
units.tr: Fourteenthly and lastly, because the Holy Spirit through the Gospel is said to convict of the sin of unbelief (John 16:9). Just as unbelief in the Son, the Mediator (whom we are commanded to hear, Matt. 17:5), is revealed to be sin not in the Law but in the Gospel, so unbelief in the Son is also convicted by the Law, not as sin, since the Law does not so convict it, but through the Gospel, which commands us to acknowledge the Son and to render him honour (Ps. 2:6, 11–12; Isa. 53:11). Therefore, since unbelief in the Son is unknown to the Law, it cannot convict it as sin and so it cannot preach repentance for it either. Yet meanwhile, while we ascribe the preaching of saving repentance to the ministry of the Gospel, we utterly exclude the Law, and so we favour the Antinomians. For we confess that the Law shows sins known to us (Rom. 3:20), to repentance from which the Gospel invites us, and we acknowledge the Law of God, which we commonly call the Decalogue, as the rule of Christian life. But we want these two principal offices of doctrine to be kept distinct, so that they are not confused in any way, and we set out this fourfold difference between them. For the Law and the Gospel differ. First, in knowledge (Rom. 2:15; John 1:18). Second, in the form of promises (Deut. 27:26; Matt. 19:17; Luke 10:28; Rom. 4:16). Third, in the effects attributed to Law and Gospel (2 Cor. 3:6–9). Fourth, in the different address, or in the different grades of men (2 Tim. 2:15; Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18; Gal. 5:22–23; 1 Tim. 1:9). See DIFFERENCE between the GOSPEL and the LAW.

units.la: EVANGELIO omnia posthabenda, Matth. 13. 46.
units.tr: All things are to be counted as secondary to the GOSPEL (Matt. 13:46).

units.la: EVANGELISTAE dantur Ecclesiæ à Christo, Ephes. 4. 11.
units.tr: EVANGELISTS are given to the Church by Christ (Eph. 4:11).

units.la: EVANGELIZARE absolutè positum, pro prædicare, 1. Corinth. 9. 16.
units.tr: EVANGELIZE, used absolutely, means to preach (1 Cor. 9:16).

units.la: EVANGELIZARI passiuè, pro Euangelium annuntiari, aut Euangelij prædicatione dignari, Esa. 61. 1. Matth. 11. 5. Luc. 8. 18.
units.tr: To be EVANGELIZED, in the passive, means that the Gospel is announced, or that one is found worthy of the preaching of the Gospel (Isa. 61:1; Matt. 11:5; Luke 8:18).

units.la: EVANGELIZANTI debetur necessaria vitæ sustentatio, Matth. 10. 9. Marc. 6. 8. Luc. 9. 3. & 10. 7. Roman. 15. 26. 1. Corinth. 9. v. 7. 11. 13. Galat. 6. 6. 1. Tim. 5. 17. 2. Tim. 2. 6. Vide ECCLESIA.
units.tr: To the one who EVANGELIZES is owed the necessary support of life (Matt. 10:9; Mark 6:8; Luke 9:3, 10:7; Rom. 15:26; 1 Cor. 9:7, 11, 13; Gal. 6:6; 1 Tim. 5:17; 2 Tim. 2:6). See CHURCH.

units.la: EVTVCHVS, Romæ sancto Paulo familiaris fuit. 2. Tim. 4. 21.
units.tr: EUTYCHUS was a familiar of St Paul at Rome (2 Tim. 4:21).

units.la: EVCHARISTIA: ¶ Eucharistiam sub vna tantum, panis nimirum, specie, Ioannis 6. 58. datam esse à Christo, Luc. 24. 30. 31. ab Apostolis, Act. 2. 42. & 20. 7. vociferantur Pontificij, quorum in utroque loco aiunt panem Syrios vertisse, Eucharistiæ nomine. ¶ Item in Eucharistia substantiam panis non remanere post consecrationem, sed esse verum Christi corpus & sanguinem, probare nituntur verbis institutionis, Matt. 26. 26. Mar. 14. 22. Luc. 22. 19. item Ioannis 6. 51. ¶ Eucharistiam præterea in publicis supplicationibus circumferendam esse, eò quòd id præfiguratum sit, Iosu. 6. v. 6. 7. 11. &c. 1. Sam. 4. 3. 2. Sam. 6. v. 4. 5. 6. itemque demum adorandam esse. Psal. 22. v. 28. 30. & 99. 5. Ioh. 6. 38. quæ quid sunt aliud, quàm mere blasphemiæ in Filium Dei, & manifestæ profanationes sacrosanctæ Cœnæ Do-minicæ?
units.tr: EUCHARIST: The Papists cry out that the Eucharist was given by Christ under one kind only, that of bread, namely (John 6:58), and by the apostles (Luke 24:30–31; Acts 2:42, 20:7), and they say that in each of these places the Syrian translators rendered bread by the name of Eucharist. Likewise they strive to prove from the words of institution (Matt. 26:26; Mark 14:22; Luke 22:19), and also from John 6:51, that the substance of the bread does not remain after consecration but is the true body and blood of Christ. Moreover, they maintain that the Eucharist is to be carried about in public processions, because this was prefigured (Josh. 6:6–7, 11; 1 Sam. 4:3; 2 Sam. 6:4–6), and finally that it is to be adored (Ps. 22:28, 30, 99:5; John 6:38). What are these things but mere blasphemies against the Son of God and manifest profanations of the most holy Lord's Supper?

units.la: {Εὐδοξία}, Latinis beneuolentia, pro Euangelio, Lucæ 2.14. gratuito & infinito illo Dei in electos amore, quos ante tempora æterna in Filio dilexit, Ephes. 1.4. sic.5.9. pro mutua hominum inter se amicitia, qua alij aliorum commodis studeant, Roman. 10.1. pro charitate, qua homines ipsum Deum diligunt, Phil. 1.15.
units.tr: Eudokia [εὐδοξία], in Latin benevolence, is used for the Gospel (Luke 2:14), for that free and infinite love of God toward the elect, whom he loved in the Son before eternal times (Eph. 1:4), and so also in Eph. 5:9. It is used for the mutual friendship of men among themselves, by which some seek the advantage of others (Rom. 10:1), and for the charity by which men love God himself (Phil. 1:15).

units.la: EVILA, Regio ad Orientem vergens, quam circuit Phison. Fluuius de Paradiso egrediens, in ea aurum preciosum nascitur &c. Gen.2.11.
units.tr: EVILA: a region facing east, which the Pishon river encircles, flowing out of Paradise; gold is found there, and so on. Gen. 2.11.

units.la: EVILMERODAC, i.Itultus amaré contritus, Rex Babylonis. Reg.25.27.
units.tr: EVIL-MERODACH: i.e. foolish, crushed by bitterness; king of Babylon. 2 Kings 25.27.

units.la: EVNICE, bona seu læta victoria, mater Timothei, Iudæa fi-lis, Actor.16.1.2. Tim.1.5.
units.tr: EUNICE: a good or joyful victory; mother of Timothy, a Jewish daughter. Acts 16.1, 2; 2 Tim. 1.5.

units.la: EVNVCHVS, Aulicus, vel (vt nonnulli putant gynecæi custos ab εὐνή 1. cubile, & ἔχω, custodio. Eunuchi nomen priè muneris & actionis est: eorum videlicet, qui in necæo adhibebantur, quasi fœminarum cubilis custodes [Gen.37.36. vel etiam rerum præfecti ita nominabantur. Actor.8.27. In prima significatione, ] cùm plerunque ligerentur castrati, hinc factum vt de castratis quibus diceretur promiscue, [& de castratis fit sermo, Deut.23. qui ab Ecclesia Iudaica, vel potius ab administratione rum politicarum & Ecclesiasticarum arcebantur,] Eunuchus Candaces Reginæ, Scripturam sacram legit, Actor. 28. baptizatur à Philippo, v.38. Eunuchorum diuersa ge-ra, vt sunt spadones, thlibiæ, & castrati, Matth.19.12. cum ierui Eunuchi vocati, Gen.39.1.1.Sam.8.15.Dan.11. [Eunuchus spiritu, Matt.19.12. [v.Esa.56..3.4.
units.tr: EUNUCH: a courtier, or (as some think) a keeper of the women's chamber, from eunē [εὐνή], bed, and echō [ἔχω], I guard. The name is properly one of office and function, namely of those who were employed in the bedchamber, as it were guardians of the women's quarters [Gen. 37.36]. Or also those in charge of property were so called [Acts 8.27]. In the first sense, since eunuchs were mostly castrated men, it came about that the name was applied loosely to castrated men [and there is talk of castrated men in Deut. 23], who were excluded from the Jewish Church, or rather from the political and ecclesiastical administration. The eunuch of Queen Candace read Holy Scripture [Acts 8.28]; he is baptized by Philip [v. 38]. There are different kinds of eunuchs, such as spadones, thlibiae and castrati [Matt. 19.12], and servants called eunuchs [Gen. 39.1; 1 Sam. 8.15; Dan. 11]. [Eunuchs of the spirit, Matt. 19.12; see Isa. 56.3, 4.]

units.la: EVPHRATES fluuius è Paradiso terrestri manat, Gen.2. terræ Chananæ terminus est, Deut.1.7.Ios.1.4. (i.fer siue fructificans).
units.tr: EUPHRATES: a river flowing out of the earthly Paradise [Gen. 2]; it is the boundary of the land of Canaan [Deut. 1.7; Josh. 1.4]. (i.e. bearing or fruitful.)

units.la: EVTYCHVS adolescens, præceps è fenestra ruens, mi-tur, Actor.20.9. excitatur à Paulo, v.12. (i.bene fo-natus).
units.tr: EUTYCHUS: a young man who, falling headlong from a window, is picked up dead [Acts 20.9]; he is restored by Paul [v. 12]. (i.e. fortunate.)

units.la: EXACTIO, Vide TRIBVTVM.
units.tr: EXACTION: see TAX.

units.la: EXALTANTES se humiliabuntur, Luc.14.11.&18.14. Matth.23.12. Iob.22.29. Pro.29.23. Iacob.4.6.1. Pet.5.5.
units.tr: Those who exalt themselves will be humbled [Luke 14.11; 18.14; Matt. 23.12; Job 22.29; Prov. 29.23; James 4.6; 1 Pet. 5.5].

units.la: EXASPERANDVS Deus non est, 1.Sam.12.14.
units.tr: God is not to be provoked [1 Sam. 12.14].

units.la: EXAVDIRE quando dicatur Deus per ignem, 1. Reg.18.4.
units.tr: When God is said to hear by fire [1 Kings 18.24].

units.la: audit Deus afflictos clamantes, Exodi 22. 27. Exau-di: Moses pro Israel orantem, 32.14. Num. 14. 20. Deuter. 19.
units.tr: God hears the afflicted when they cry out [Exod. 22.27]. Hears: Moses praying for Israel [32.14; Num. 14.20; Deut. 9].

units.la: EXAECATIONIS nostrae causa, peccatum, Esai. 59. 9. Vide EXAECITAS.
units.tr: The cause of our blindness is sin [Isa. 59.9]. See BLINDNESS.

units.la: EXANDESCENTIA, θυμός, est prima sanguinis ebullitio, quae iuriae nobis illatae vindictam iam cogitat, Gal. 5. 20. Eph. 4. 31. Col. 3. 8. Exempla, in Nazarethanis contra Christum, Luc. 4. 28. &c. In Ephesiis contra Paulum, Act. 19. 27.
units.tr: EXASPERATION, thymos [θυμός], is the first boiling of the blood, which already plans vengeance for an injury done to us [Gal. 5.20; Eph. 4.31; Col. 3.8]. Examples: the people of Nazareth against Christ [Luke 4.28, etc.]; the Ephesians against Paul [Acts 19.27].

units.la: EXCELSA, erecta & aedificata à Salomone, 1. Reg. 11. 7. Ieroboamo, 12. 31. vniuersa Iudaea, 14. 23. Israelitis, 2. Reg. 17. Ierem. 7. 31. & 19. 5. Manasse, 2. Reg. 21. 3. Ioram, 2. Paral. 21. 11. sublata ab Ezechia, 2. Reg. 18. 4. Esa 36. 7. Iosia, 2. Reg. 23. 13. 2. Paral. 34. 3. Asa, 14. 3. Iosaphat, 17. 6. Israelitis, 1. 1. à populo, contra suorum fidelium Regum exemplum, tenta: ab Asa, 1. Reg. 15. 14. Iosaphat, 22. 44. 2. Paral. 20. à Regibus non omnino malis pessime tolerata: à Ioas, 2. Reg. 12. 3. Amasia, 14. 4. Azaria, 15. 4. Ioathan, v. 35. in excelsis, ante aedificationem Templi, immolat populus, 1. 2. eg. 3. 2. Excelsorum Sacerdotes occiduntur à Iosia, 2. 2. Reg. 23. 20.
units.tr: HIGH PLACES: built and erected by Solomon [1 Kings 11.7]; by Jeroboam [12.31]; throughout all Judaea [14.23]; by the Israelites [2 Kings 17; Jer. 7.31; 19.5]; by Manasseh [2 Kings 21.3]; by Joram [2 Chron. 21.11]; removed by Hezekiah [2 Kings 18.4; Isa. 36.7]; by Josiah [2 Kings 23.13; 2 Chron. 34.3]; by Asa [14.3]; by Jehoshaphat [17.6]; by the Israelites [1 Kings 1]. Tried by the people against the example of their faithful kings; by Asa [1 Kings 15.14]; by Jehoshaphat [22.44; 2 Chron. 20]. Tolerated very badly by kings who were not altogether wicked: by Joash [2 Kings 12.3]; by Amaziah [14.4]; by Azariah [15.4]; by Jotham [v. 35]. The people sacrificed on high places before the building of the Temple [1 Kings 3.2]. The priests of the high places were slain by Josiah [2 Kings 23.20].

units.la: EXCESSVS, exitus è vita mortali, Lucae 9. 31. Ecstasis, Actor. 10. 10. & 11. 5. festinatio praeceps, Psal. 31. 23. & [6. 11.]
units.tr: EXCESS: a departure from mortal life [Luke 9.31]. Ecstasy [ekstasis ἔκστασις] [Acts 10.10; 11.5]; headlong haste [Ps. 31.23; 6.11].

units.la: COMMVNICARE idem est apud Christianos, quod Iudaeis Synagoga moueri, Ioann. 9. 22. & 12. 42. & 16. 2. nemo nomen expungi è populo Dei, vt explicatur Luc. 6. 22. sicut Latinis dicebantur, Capitis diminutionem patiuntur, qui ex albo à Censoribus expungebantur.) Quae poena omnium maxime formidabilis est in Dei Ecclesia, sed ita demum Censores Dei fuerint instrumenta: id est, ex Dei verbo quispiam legitimo verae Ecclesiae iudicio damnetur: alio-quin praestat ex impiorum consortio exci, quam inter eos numerari, Psal. 1. 1. v. 1. 2.
units.tr: To be excommunicated among Christians is what being cast out of the synagogue was for the Jews [John 9.22; 12.42; 16.2]: that a name is struck off from the people of God, as explained in Luke 6.22. Just as among the Latins those who were struck off the roll by the censors were said to suffer loss of civic rights. This punishment is the most dreadful of all in the Church of God, but the censors are instruments of God only when someone is condemned by the word of God through the lawful judgment of the true Church; otherwise it is better to be cut off from the fellowship of the ungodly than to be numbered among them [Ps. 1.1, 2].

units.la: COMMVNICATIO in Ecclesia necessaria est, Matthaei 18. 17. 1. Cor. 5. v. 3. 4. 5. 6. 2. Thess. 3. 14. 1. Tim. 1. 20. Tit. 1. 10. excommunicatio legitima quanti sit apud Deum momen-ti, Matt. 18. 18. abusus, 3. Ioan. 10. Excommunicationis finis & scopus: primus, vt excommunicatus pudore victus, ad poenitentiam excitetur, & deflectat à malo, 1. Corin. 5. 5. 2 Cor. 2. 7. 2. Thess. 3. 14. 1. Tim. 1. 20. Secundus, ne contagio ad reliquos serpat, 1. Cor. 5. v. 6. 7. Excommunicationis ius erat olim non penes vnum quempiam (vt patet 1. Corinth. 5.4.) siue Episcopum, siue ab Episcopo delegatum, sed penes Pastorem & eorum coetum, quos peculiari appellatione Gubernatores vocat Apostolus, 1. Corinth. 12.28. & Presbyterium, 1. Tim. 4.14. (vide ECCLESIAE significata, & SENIORES: & PRESBYTERI.) quibus Ecclesiasticae disciplinae cura committebatur, quamuis cuiuscunque tota Ecclesia: alioquin quomodo excommunicatorum familiarem consuetudinem vitasset?
units.tr: Excommunication is necessary in the Church [Matt. 18.17; 1 Cor. 5.3–6; 2 Thess. 3.14; 1 Tim. 1.20; Titus 1.10]. How great the weight of lawful excommunication is before God [Matt. 18.18]; its abuse [3 John 10]. The aim and purpose of excommunication: first, that the excommunicated person, overcome by shame, may be roused to repentance and turn from evil [1 Cor. 5.5; 2 Cor. 2.7; 2 Thess. 3.14; 1 Tim. 1.20]; second, that contagion may not creep on to the rest [1 Cor. 5.6, 7]. The right of excommunication was formerly not in the hands of any one person (as is clear from 1 Cor. 5.4), whether a bishop or one delegated by a bishop, but in the hands of the minister and his assembly, whom the Apostle calls by the special name of governors [1 Cor. 12.28] and the presbytery [1 Tim. 4.14] (see CHURCH, signification of; and ELDERS and PRESBYTERS). To them the care of ecclesiastical discipline was committed, although it belonged to the whole Church; otherwise how could one have avoided familiar dealings with the excommunicated?

units.la: Excommunicationis & separationis exempla: Adam & Eua Genes. 3.24. Leprosi utriusque sexus, Num. 5.v. 1.2.3. Maria, 12.15. Core, Dathan, & Abiro, 16.v.24.25.26.27. Achan Iosu. 7.vers. 24.25. Ananias etiam & Saphira sunt speciales quaedam & tristissimum excommunicationis exemplum. Act. 5.1. &c. Iudaei, 13.46. Corinthius incestuosus, 1. Corinth. 5.5. Pseudoapostoli, Galat. 1.vers. 8.9. Hymenaeus & Alexander, 1. Timoth. 1.20. Phigellus & Hermogenes, 2. Tim. 1.15.
units.tr: Examples of excommunication and separation: Adam and Eve [Gen. 3.24]. Lepers of both sexes [Num. 5.1–3]. Miriam [12.15]. Korah, Dathan and Abiram [16.24–27]. Achan [Josh. 7.24, 25]. Ananias and Sapphira are also a particular and most sorrowful example of excommunication [Acts 5.1, etc.]. The Jews [13.46]. The incestuous Corinthian [1 Cor. 5.5]. The false apostles [Gal. 1.8, 9]. Hymenaeus and Alexander [1 Tim. 1.20]. Phygellus and Hermogenes [2 Tim. 1.15].

units.la: EXCVSATIO, Excusationis legitimae exempla: Dauid 1. Sam. 1.29. Achimelech, 22.15. Christus, Matth. 12.3. Excusationis modestae exempla: Fratres Iosephi, Genesis 42.10. Ruben, Gad, & dimidia Tribus Manasse, Iosue 22.vers. 22.23. Gedeon, Iudic. 8. vers. 1.2.3. Anna, 1. Sam. 1.15. Daniel, Dan. 6.22. Excusationis peccati exempla: Adam & Eua Genes. 3.v.12.13. Iuda, 44.16. Iudaei, Ierem. 2.35. Excusationis ineptae exempla: Sara, Genesis 18.15. Saul, 1. Sam. 13.v.11.12.13.&15.v.15. 20. vocati ad coenam magnam, Luc. 14.16. Excusationis ironicae exemplum: Paulus, Act. 23.
units.tr: EXCUSE. Examples of lawful excuse: David [1 Sam. 21.29]; Ahimelech [22.15]; Christ [Matt. 12.3]. Examples of modest excuse: the brothers of Joseph [Gen. 42.10]; Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh [Josh. 22.22, 23]; Gideon [Judg. 8.1–3]; Hannah [1 Sam. 1.15]; Daniel [Dan. 6.22]. Examples of excuse for sin: Adam and Eve [Gen. 3.12, 13]; Judah [44.16]; the Jews [Jer. 2.35]. Examples of foolish excuse: Sarah [Gen. 18.15]; Saul [1 Sam. 13.11–13; 15.15, 20]; those invited to the great supper [Luke 14.16]. Example of ironic excuse: Paul [Acts 23].

units.la: EXEMPLVM est narratio rei gestae aut tanquam gestae, similitudine quadam instituto nostro conueniens. Vt Cham patrem ignominia affecit, ideoque maledictus est. Igitur qui parentes ignominiose tractant maledicentur.
units.tr: An EXAMPLE is a narrative of a deed done, or as if done, suited to our purpose by some resemblance. Thus Ham dishonoured his father and was therefore cursed. Therefore those who treat their parents dishonourably will be cursed.

units.la: Quatenus exempla V. T. in N. T. locum habeant.
units.tr: How far the examples of the Old Testament have a place in the New.

units.la: 1. Quae articulos fidei confirmant, apte in suo genere applicanda sunt, vt Diluuium nouissimi iudicij ideam habet. 2. Pet. 3.6.
units.tr: 1. Those which confirm the articles of faith are to be applied aptly within their own kind; thus the Flood has the idea of the last judgment [2 Pet. 3.6].

units.la: 2. Quae bonos mores informant, in N. T. vim habet probationis, Heb. 13.2.
units.tr: 2. Those which shape good morals have the force of proof in the New Testament [Heb. 13.2].

units.la: 3. Exempla poenarum valent ad deterrendos peccat. 1. Cor. 10.10.11.
units.tr: 3. Examples of punishments serve to deter from sin [1 Cor. 10.10, 11].

units.la: 4. Quae typo aliquo Christum respexerunt, non debent longius euagari quam deceat. Vt hostiae hominibus Deum placent. lacabant: Ergo multò magis hostia Christi: rectè. Sed impiissimè dixerit, Ergo in N. T. Sacerdotes Deo hostias offerre debent. Nam Christus ũpis finem imposuit. Gal. 2.1.2.3.4.
units.tr: 4. Those which looked to Christ under some type ought not to wander further than is fitting. For example, the sacrifices pleased God for men: Jacob's sacrifices; therefore much more so the sacrifice of Christ. This is rightly said. But it would be most impiously said: therefore in the New Testament priests ought to offer sacrifices to God. For Christ put an end to the types [Gal. 2.1–4].

units.la: 5. Quæ confirmant res N.T. in genere, singula etiam in suo genere valent. Vt Arca Noachi, Ecclesia in hoc mundo fluctuantem notat. Serpens æneus, Christi morte, &c. Unde scrutatio Scripturarum à Christo commendatur. Ioh. 5.39.
units.tr: 5. Those which confirm things of the New Testament in general also have force in their particulars, each in its own kind. Thus the Ark of Noah signifies the Church tossed by the waves in this world; the brazen serpent signifies the death of Christ, etc. Whence the searching of the Scriptures is commended by Christ [John 5.39].

units.la: Quæ verò moribus obsunt, nihil concludunt: nec in exemplum trahenda sunt, vt Dauidis adulterii, & similia.
units.tr: But those which are harmful to morals prove nothing, nor are they to be drawn into example, such as David's adultery and the like.

units.la: 2. Specialia facta, etiam honesta, non sunt imitanda: quia destituimur mandato Dei, quod illic extat.
units.tr: 2. Particular deeds, even honourable ones, are not to be imitated, because we lack the command of God, which is set out there.

units.la: 3. Specialia facta, quibus inest aliqua crudelitatis species, aut turpitudo, non imitamur, vt Israelitæ ex Ægypto referunt vasa aurea mutuata: Israelitæ in Madian nec infantibus quidem parcere debuerunt. Hoc mandato D. excusantur.
units.tr: 3. Particular deeds which have some appearance of cruelty or baseness we do not imitate; for example, the Israelites carrying off gold vessels they had borrowed from Egypt, and the Israelites in Midian, who ought not to have spared even the infants. These are excused by the command of God.

units.la: 4. Quæ iam completa sunt, non sunt in pristinũ vsum revocanda. Sic tota lex cæremonialis completa est in Christo, Qui finis est Legis, ad iustitiã cuiuis credenti: Rom. 10. 4.
units.tr: 4. What has already been fulfilled must not be brought back into former use. Thus the whole ceremonial law has been fulfilled in Christ, who is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes: Rom. 10. 4.

units.la: EXEMPLAR nostrum Christus, Ioann. 13.15. Philip. 2. 5. &c. 1. Petri 2.21. Exemplar vitæ & doctrinæ Paulus. Philip. 3. 17.
units.tr: Our EXEMPLAR is Christ: John 13.15; Phil. 2.5, etc.; 1 Pet. 2.21. Paul is the example of life and doctrine: Phil. 3.17.

units.la: V. Matt. 11.29. Deus: Leuitic. 11.44. Matt. 5.44. &c.
units.tr: See Matt. 11.29. God: Lev. 11.44; Matt. 5.44, etc.

units.la: EQVIAE Saræ celebrātur, Genes. 23. 2. Iacobi 50. 10. Mosis Deut. 34. 8. Abneri, 2. Sam. 3.31.
units.tr: FUNERALS: The funeral of Sarah is celebrated, Gen. 23.2; of Jacob, Gen. 50.10; of Moses, Deut. 34.8; of Abner, 2 Sam. 3.31.

units.la: EXERCITVS cœli, pro Angelis, Luc. 2. 13. pro Sole & Luna cũ reliquis syderibus, Act. 7.42. vt apparet ex Deut. 17.3. [Exercituum Deus, exercitus hominum. Vocatur autem Deus, exercituum Dominus & Deus, quòd creaturæ omnes imperio eius pareant, quomodo, quoties, quibus locis, & quantum vult, ad nominis eius gloriam & electorum salutem.]
units.tr: HOST of heaven, meaning the angels: Luke 2.13; meaning the sun and moon with the other stars: Acts 7.42, as appears from Deut. 17.3. [The God of hosts, the host of men. God is called the Lord and God of hosts because all creatures obey his command, how, when, in what places, and as much as he wills, for the glory of his name and the salvation of the elect.]

units.la: EXHORTARI posse, Dei donum est. Rom. 12. 8. Exhortandi inuicem sumus per singulos dies ad fidem in Christum, Heb. 3. 13. Col. 3. 16.
units.tr: To be able to EXHORT is a gift of God: Rom. 12.8. We must exhort one another every day to faith in Christ: Heb. 3.13; Col. 3.16.

units.la: EXHORTATIO pars Prophetiæ, 1. Corinth. 14. 3. Exhortationes doctrinam sequi debent, Rom. 6. v. 11. 12. & 8. v. 11. 12, 1. Corinth. 9. 24. piis sunt necessariæ, 2. Corint. 6. 1. & 13. 10. Ephes. 4. 25. Philip. 4. 1. 1. Thess. 2. 12. & 3. 2. 1. Tim. 4. 12. & 6. 2. 2. Tim. 3. 16. & 4. 2. Tit. 1. 9. & 2. v. 1. 15. Heb. 3. 12. & 13. v. 16. 22. 1. Petr. 1. 13. 2. Petr. 3. 1. 1. Ioan. 2. 12. & 4. 7. & 5. 19. Exhortationum bonarum exempla: Dominus Deus omnipotens, Genes. 4. v. 6. 7. Loth. 19. 7. Rebecca, 27. v. 9. 43. Ruben, 37. 42. soror Mosis, Exodi 2. v. 7. 8. Iethro, 18. 21. Abigail, 1. Sam. 25. v. 24. 25. 26. 32. Abner, 2. Sam. 2. 21. Aggæus & Zacharias, 1. Esd. 5. 1. Abdemelech. Ierem. 38. v. 9. 10. Vide CONSILII boni exempla: & PRAEDICATIO. Exhortationis pij regis ad populum exempla: Iosaphat, 2. Paral. 20. v. 20. 21. Ezechias, 32. 7.
units.tr: EXHORTATION is a part of prophecy: 1 Cor. 14.3. Exhortations ought to follow doctrine: Rom. 6.11–12; 8.11–12; 1 Cor. 9.24. They are necessary for the godly: 2 Cor. 6.1; 13.10; Eph. 4.25; Phil. 4.1; 1 Thess. 2.12; 3.2; 1 Tim. 4.12; 6.2; 2 Tim. 3.16; 4.2; Titus 1.9; 2.1, 15; Heb. 3.12; 13.16, 22; 1 Pet. 1.13; 2 Pet. 3.1; 1 John 2.12; 4.7; 5.19. Examples of good exhortations: the Lord God Almighty, Gen. 4.6–7; Lot, 19.7; Rebekah, 27.9, 43; Reuben, 37.42; the sister of Moses, Exod. 2.7–8; Jethro, 18.21; Abigail, 1 Sam. 25.24–26, 32; Abner, 2 Sam. 2.21; Haggai and Zechariah, Ezra 5.1; Abdemelech, Jer. 38.9–10. See the examples of good counsel and PREACHING. Examples of the exhortation of a godly king to the people: Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20.20–21; Hezekiah, 32.7.

units.la: EXIRE & introire, Vide INGREDI & EGREDI. Exitus pro morte, Luc. 9. 31.
units.tr: GOING OUT and coming IN: see GOING IN and GOING OUT. Exit for death: Luke 9.31.

units.la: EXORCISTAE vocabantur, qui Dæmones eiiciebant, addita per Dei nomen obtestatione, quam vulgò Coniurationem vocant. Vide ADIVRARE. Exorcistæ tempore Pauli, Act. 19. 13. quos fidei expertes diabolus vulnerat.
units.tr: EXORCISTS were those called who cast out demons, adding an invocation of the name of God, which is commonly called conjuring. See ADJURE. Exorcists in the time of Paul: Acts 19.13, whom the devil wounds, being strangers to faith.

units.la: EXPIATIONIS aqua, dicitur aqua peccati, Num. 8. 7. eò quòd adhiberetur ad expiandum peccatum, quę quomodo confici deberet, præscribitur, 19. 1. &c. [Expiationis hostia, Exod. 29. 36. Leuit. 1. 4. & 16. 30.] Expiatio iuramenti & aliorum peccatorum, Leuit. 5. 1. &c. Num. 5. 6. Sanctuarij, Tabernaculi, Altaris, Leui. 16. v. 14. 16. 18. Expiationum dies 23. 27. Expiationum festum, 16. v. 29. 30.
units.tr: EXPIATION water is called the water of sin, Num. 8.7, because it was used to expiate sin; how it was to be prepared is prescribed, 19.1, etc. [Expiatory sacrifice: Exod. 29.36; Lev. 1.4; 16.30.] Expiation of an oath and of other sins: Lev. 5.1, etc.; Num. 5.6. Of the sanctuary, the tabernacle, and the altar: Lev. 16 v. 14, 16, 18. Days of expiation: 23.27. The feast of expiation: 16 v. 29–30.

units.la: EXPLORATORES terræ Chanaan, Numer. 13. 3. Deuter. 1. 22, Exploratores mittuntur Ierichunta, Ios. 2. 1. &c. Rahab meretricis hospitio excipiuntur, v. 4. ab ea occultantur, v. 6. per fenestram funę salui demittuntur, vers. 15. [Heb. 11. 31.] Rahab hospitam ex incendio urbis Ierichuntinæ liberant, 6. v. 23. Exploratores terræ promissionis moriuntur omnes, præter Caleb & Iosue, Num. 14. v. 36. 37. V. horum constantiam v. 6. &c. Exploratur Hai, Ios. 7. 2.
units.tr: EXPLORERS of the land of Canaan: Num. 13.3; Deut. 1.22. Explorers are sent to Jericho: Josh. 2.1, etc. They are received into the lodging of the harlot Rahab, v. 4; she hides them, v. 6; they are let down safely through the window by a rope, v. 15. [Heb. 11.31.] Rahab and her household are rescued from the burning of the city of Jericho, 6.23. All the explorers of the promised land die, except Caleb and Joshua: Num. 14 v. 36–37. See their constancy, v. 6, etc. Ai is explored: Josh. 7.2.

units.la: EXPOSTVLATIO: Expostulationis exempla: Pharao, Genesis 12. 18. Abimelech, 20. 9. Iacob, 29. 25. & 31. 36. Dauid, 1. Sam. 20. 1. Psalm. 82. 2. Ioab, 2. Sam 14. 31. Nehemias, Nehe. 13. 11. Dominus Deus omnipotens, Ierem. 2. 5. quidam ex Circumcisione,
units.tr: EXPOSTULATION. Examples of expostulation: Pharaoh, Gen. 12.18; Abimelech, 20.9; Jacob, 29.25 and 31.36; David, 1 Sam. 20.1; Ps. 82.2; Joab, 2 Sam. 14.31; Nehemiah, Neh. 13.11; the Lord God Almighty, Jer. 2.5; certain men of the circumcision,

units.la: cumcisione, Actor. 11.3. Expostulationis futilis exemplum, Laban, Genes.31.v.26.27. maligna exemplum, Israelitæ, Exod. 14.11.
units.tr: Acts 11.3. Example of a futile expostulation: Laban, Gen. 31.26–27. Example of a malicious one: the Israelites, Exod. 14.11.

units.la: EXPROBRATIO maligna damnatur & prohibetur, Leuitic. 19.33. Iudic.8.15. Prou. 14.31. & 17.5. Luc.6.22. Exprobratio laudata, vtilis, necessaria, Matt.11.20. Marc.16.14.]
units.tr: Malicious REPROACH is condemned and forbidden: Lev. 19.33; Judg. 8.15; Prov. 14.31; 17.5; Luke 6.22. Reproach that is praised, useful and necessary: Matt. 11.20; Mark 16.14.

units.la: EXPROBRATIONIS maligne & impie exempla: Hebræus, Exo. 2.14. [Succothani, Iud.8.15.] Phenenna, 1. Sam. 1. 6. Goliath, 1.Sam.17. v.10.25.26.45. Sennacherib, 2. Reg. 19. v. 4 16. 22. 23. Dauidis & Christi, à Dauide præfigurati, hostes. Psal.35.7 & 42.11. & 69.10. & 89.52. Dei & Ecclesiæ inimici, Psal.44.17. & 79.12. & 102.9. Soph.2.8. Luc.6.22.] Principes Sacerdotum, Matt.27.42. Marc. 15.31. populus, Luc.23.35. Pharisæi, Ioann.9.34. Exprobrationis beneficiorum exempla: Dominus Deus, Iudic.6.9. & 10. v.11.12.13. Vir Dei, 1, Sam.2.27. Samuel 10. v.17.18. & 12.v 7.8.9.& 15.17. Nathan, 2.Sam.12.7. Ahia, 1. Reg.14.7. Iehu Propheta, 16.
units.tr: EXAMPLES OF REPROACH, malicious and impious: the Hebrew, Exod. 2.14. [The men of Succoth, Judg. 8.15.] Peninnah, 1 Sam. 1.6. Goliath, 1 Sam. 17 v. 10, 25–26, 45. Sennacherib, 2 Kings 19 v. 4, 16, 22–23. The enemies of David, prefigured by David, and of Christ: Ps. 35.7; 42.11; 69.10; 89.52. Enemies of God and the Church: Ps. 44.17; 79.12; 102.9; Zeph. 2.8; Luke 6.22. The chief priests: Matt. 27.42; Mark 15.31. The people: Luke 23.35. The Pharisees: John 9.34. Examples of reproach for benefits: the Lord God, Judg. 6.9 and 10 v. 11–13; a man of God, 1 Sam. 2.27; Samuel, 10 v. 17–18; 12 v. 7–9; 15.17; Nathan, 2 Sam. 12.7; Ahijah, 1 Kings 14.7; Jehu the prophet, 16.

units.la: 2. Exprobrationis vitiorum exempla: Iehu, 2. Reg. 9.22. Prophetæ, Esaiæ 3.13. & 57.4. Ezech. 16.14. Dominus Deus Israel, 34.3. Abd.v.11. Mich.6.4. Christus, Matth.8.26. & 11. 20.& 14.31. & 15.16.& 16.8.& 17.17. Marc.14.48. & 16.14. Lucæ 24.25. Ioan.3.10. & 4.48. & 5.40. & 6.v.26.36. & 7. 19. Petrus, Actor. 3. v.13.14. & 4.v.10.11.& 5.30. Ioannes Baptista, Matth.14.4. Stephanus, Actor. 7.51. Paulus & Barnabas, 13.46. Paulus, 2. Cor.12.11. & 13.3. Gal.1.9. & 3.1. Apostolus: Heb,5.12.
units.tr: 2. Examples of reproach for vices: Jehu, 2 Kings 9.22; the prophets, Isa. 3.13; 57.4; Ezek. 16.14; the Lord God of Israel, 34.3; Obad. v. 11; Mic. 6.4. Christ: Matt. 8.26; 11.20; 14.31; 15.16; 16.8; 17.17; Mark 14.48; 16.14; Luke 24.25; John 3.10; 4.48; 5.40; 6.26, 36; 7.19. Peter: Acts 3.13–14; 4.10–11; 5.30. John the Baptist: Matt. 14.4. Stephen: Acts 7.51. Paul and Barnabas: Acts 13.46. Paul: 2 Cor. 12.11; 13.3; Gal. 1.9; 3.1. The Apostle: Heb. 5.12.

units.la: XTERIOREM hominem quid vocet Paulus, Vide Homo,
units.tr: What Paul calls the outward man: see MAN.

units.la: XTERORVM nomine, Marci 4.11.1. Corinth.5.12. intelliguntur, quicunque non accensentur fidelium cœtui.
units.tr: By the name of OUTSIDERS, Mark 4.11; 1 Cor. 5.12, are understood all those who are not counted in the assembly of the faithful.

units.la: XTERIORES tenebræ, Vide Tenebrae.
units.tr: OUTER darkness: see DARKNESS.

units.la: XVLVM & profugorum reditus tempus, Num.35.32. Exulum exempla: Adam & Eua, Genes. 3.24. Cain, 4 16. Abraham, 12. 1. Dauid, 2, Sam. 15.v.13.14.16. Elias, 1. Regum 19. 3. Israelitæ, 2.Reg.17. v.5.6. Ose. 9.v.3.4. Ioseph, Maria & Christus, Matth.2.14.
units.tr: EXILE, and the time of the return of fugitives: Num. 35.32. Examples of exiles: Adam and Eve, Gen. 3.24; Cain, 4.16; Abraham, 12.1; David, 2 Sam. 15 v. 13–14, 16; Elijah, 1 Kings 19.3; the Israelites, 2 Kings 17 v. 5–6; Hos. 9 v. 3–4; Joseph, Mary and Christ, Matt. 2.14.

units.la: Paulus & Barnabas: Act.13. v.50.51. Aquila, Priscilla, & fideles Iudæi, Act.18. v.2. Pij in hoc mundo peregrinantes, 2. Cor.5.6. Heb.11.v.13.14. Gen.47.9.
units.tr: Paul and Barnabas: Acts 13 v. 50–51. Aquila, Priscilla, and the faithful Jews: Acts 18.2. The godly, wandering as pilgrims in this world: 2 Cor. 5.6; Heb. 11 v. 13–14; Gen. 47.9.

units.la: ZECHIAS filius impij Achaz, pius Rex Iuda, 2.Regum 18.1, 2,Paral. 28.27. vir admodum pius est, 2.Reg. 18.5. instaurat Templum, 2. Paralip.29 3. Phase celebrari iubet, 30.1. Populum vt Deo fidat hortatur, 2, Paral. 32. 7. pro Vrbis liberatione Dominum deprecatur, 2.Reg.19,15.2.Paral. 32. 20.Esai.37.16. liberationis signum illi datur, v. 30. ægroti Deum orat,2.Reg.20.3.Esa.38. 2. vitæ integræ fuit, v.3. 2 Reg.20. 3. reprehenditur, v. 13.14.Esa. 39. v. 1. 5.&c. signum recuperandæ sanitatis & prorogatæ vitæ accipit, Esa. 38. eius conualescentis scriptum, v. 9.10. &c. moritur, 2.Reg. 20.21.2.Par.32.33. gloria eius quanta, 2,Par.32.27.
units.tr: HEZEKIAH, son of the impious Ahaz, a pious king of Judah: 2 Kings 18.1–2; 2 Chron. 28.27. He was a very pious man: 2 Kings 18.5. He restores the Temple: 2 Chron. 29.3. He orders the Passover to be celebrated: 30.1. He exhorts the people to trust in God: 2 Chron. 32.7. He prays to the Lord for the deliverance of the city: 2 Kings 19.15; 2 Chron. 32.20; Isa. 37.16. A sign of deliverance is given to him: v. 30. He prays to God when sick: 2 Kings 20.3; Isa. 38.2. He was of blameless life: v. 3; 2 Kings 20.3. He is rebuked: v. 13–14; Isa. 39 v. 1, 5, etc. He receives a sign of recovered health and of prolonged life: Isa. 38. A writing of his after his recovery: v. 9–10, etc. He dies: 2 Kings 20.21; 2 Chron. 32.33. How great his glory was: 2 Chron. 32.27.

units.la: EZECHIEL Propheta: tempus Prophetiæ eius Ezech. 1. cum aliis captiuus vehitur in Babylonem, ibidem. vocati & mittitur,2.1. iubetur volumen comedere,3.1. adducitur in spiritu in Ierusalem,8.3. Reditus captiuorum aperiti ei.: 11.17. &c. Vxoris mors ipsi non deflenda: 24.18. D gloriam in templum redeuntem vidit: 43.2. (Iehezkel. fortitudo Domini.)
units.tr: EZEKIEL the prophet. The time of his prophecy is Ezek. 1. He is carried with the other captives into Babylon, ibid. He is called and sent, 2.1. He is ordered to eat the scroll, 3.1. He is carried in the Spirit to Jerusalem, 8.3. The return of the captives is revealed to him, 11.17, etc. His wife's death is not to be mourned by him, 24.18. He sees the glory of God returning into the temple, 43.2. (Yehezkel: strength of the Lord.)

units.la: F
units.tr: F

units.la: ABER ferrarius & ærarius primus, Tubacain, Gen.4.22.Faber ferrarius deficit Israel,1.Sam.13.19.Faber lignarius erat Ioseph putatiuus Christi pater, Luc. 3.23 Mariæ Virginis sponsus,Matth. 13.55.Marc. 6.3.
units.tr: The first worker in iron and bronze was Tubal-cain, Gen. 4.22. A blacksmith failed Israel, 1 Sam. 13.19. A carpenter was Joseph, the supposed father of Christ, Luke 3.23, and the betrothed husband of the Virgin Mary, Matt. 13.55; Mark 6.3.

units.la: FABULAE profalsis & inutilibus doctrinis, 2. Tim. 4.4. e passim amplectuntur homines,ibid. Fabulæ, seu Mythologiæ, reconditam doctrinam continentes à nonnullis in aliorum institutionem propositæ: Iudic. 9.7.2. Reg. 14.9. Sam.14.6. Fabula: Fabula de Diana Ephesina, Act.19. Vide DIANA, fabulæ Iudaicæ, 1.Tim.1. 4.Fabulæ vitandæ, ibid. Tit.1.14.2.Pet.1.16. in Fabulam fuerunt aliis, Iudæi inobedientes,Deut.28.37.1. Reg.9.7.
units.tr: FABLES, from false and useless doctrines, 2 Tim. 4.4, which men everywhere embrace, ibid. Fables, or myths, containing hidden teaching, were put forward by some for the instruction of others: Judg. 9.7; 2 Kings 14.9; 1 Sam. 14.6. Fable: the fable of Diana of Ephesus, Acts 19. See DIANA. Jewish fables, 1 Tim. 1.4. Fables to be avoided, ibid.; Titus 1.14; 2 Pet. 1.16. Disobedient Jews became a fable to others, Deut. 28.37; 1 Kings 9.7.

units.la: FACERE nomen,pro acquirere,Gen.11. 4.&12.2.Deut. 8.1 Facere,pro ponere,aut statuere,Matth.12.33. pro eligere, designare,Mar.13.24. ¶Facere,pro sacrificare Pontificij[detorquent ad missaticum sacrificium, sed impie, contra mentem Spiritus S. ]Levit.15.v.15. 30.Num.6. v.16.&8.12.&9.v.2.4.10.14.Iudic.13.16.Luc.22.9.
units.tr: To MAKE a name, that is, to acquire, Gen. 11.4 and 12.2; Deut. 8.1. To make, that is, to place or appoint, Matt. 12.33. To choose or designate, Mark 13.24. ¶ To make, that is, to sacrifice. The Papists twist this to the sacrifice of the Mass, but wrongly, against the mind of the Holy Spirit: Lev. 15.15, 30; Num. 6.16; 8.12; 9.2, 4, 10, 14; Judg. 13.16; Luke 22.9.

units.la: FACIENDA aliis, quæ nobis fieri volumus, Matth.7.12. Luc. 6.31.Verba fœderis facietis, ut secundetis quicquid factu celtis,Deut.29.9. Matth.7.24. Rom.2.13. Iacob.4.22. factor. IAT tibi Deus, hæc & hæc addat, modus adiurandi apud Hebræos, 1. Sam. 3. 17. Fecit nos Deus pater noster: Deut. 6. 6.
units.tr: Do to others what you want done to you, Matt. 7.12; Luke 6.31. "You shall do the words of this covenant, that you may prosper in whatever you do," Deut. 29.9. Matt. 7.24; Rom. 2.13; James 1.22. A doer. "God do so to you, and more also": a manner of swearing among the Hebrews, 1 Sam. 3.17. "God our Father made us," Deut. 6.6.

units.la: FACIES, Hebræorum more, pro, externa, species, & quasi vultus rerum quarumlibet, Math. 16. 3. Facies Dei præcedebat Israelitas, Exodi, 33. v. 14. 17. iuxta faciem non iudicat Deus, 2. Sam. 16. 7. vt faciem suam ostendat nobis Deus, orandum, Numer. 6. 25. Facie ad faciem locutus est Moses Deus, Exod. 33. 23. Deut. 5. 4. & 34. 10. Facie ad faciem quando Deum simus cogniturí, 1. Cor. 13. 12. Vide 1. Ioan. 3. 2. In Faciem cadere Hebræis, est pronos adorare, Matt. 17. 6. Facierum panes qui vocantur. Vide PANES facierum.
units.tr: FACE, in the Hebrew manner, means the outward appearance, and as it were the countenance, of any things whatever, Matt. 16.3. The face of God went before the Israelites, Exod. 33.14, 17. God does not judge according to the face, 2 Sam. 16.7. God is to be prayed to, that he would show us his face, Num. 6.25. Moses spoke with God face to face, Exod. 33.23; Deut. 5.4 and 34.10. We shall know God face to face, 1 Cor. 13.12; see 1 John 3.2. To fall on the face, among the Hebrews, is to worship prostrate, Matt. 17.6. The bread of the faces, which is called: see SHOWBREAD.

units.la: FACIES Dei, id est, diuinæ maiestatis, gloriæ, præsentiæ, potentiæ, indignationis, beneuolentiæ, designatio peculiaris, quæ ex contextu consideratione facile discernitur, Gen. 8. Exod. 33. 11. Num. 6. 25. Iudic. 5. 5. 3. Sam. 13. 12. 1. Paral. 16. 11. 30. Nehem. 1. 4. Psal. 10. 11. 1. Cor. 13. 12. Apocal. 22. 4. facies Dei Patris, Matt. 18. 10. Apocal. 6. 16. facies Christi, filij Dei in carne manifestandi & manifestati, Esai. 50. vers. 6. 7. Dan. 10. 6. Malac. c. 3. Matth. 17. 2. & 26. v. 39. 67. 2. Corint. 4. 6. 2. Thess. 1. 9. Apoc. 1. 16. & 10. 1. facies Iehouæ, arca testimonij, 1. Sam. 2. 18 & 21. 6. Psalm. 24. 6. & 42. 3. & 95. 2. & 114. 7.]
units.tr: The FACE of God is the particular designation of the divine majesty, glory, presence, power, anger, or goodwill, which is easily distinguished from the context: Gen. 8; Exod. 33.11; Num. 6.25; Judg. 5.5; 1 Sam. 13.12; 1 Chr. 16.11, 30; Neh. 1.4; Ps. 10.11; 1 Cor. 13.12; Rev. 22.4. The face of God the Father, Matt. 18.10; Rev. 6.16. The face of Christ, the Son of God, to be and having been manifested in the flesh, Isa. 50.6–7; Dan. 10.6; Mal. 3; Matt. 17.2; 26.39, 67; 2 Cor. 4.6; 2 Thess. 1.9; Rev. 1.16; 10.1. The face of Jehovah, the ark of the testimony, 1 Sam. 2.18 and 21.6; Ps. 24.6; 42.3; 95.2; 114.7.

units.la: Facies, Os, vultus, conspectus, præsentia, status externus, sermo, actio, conditio hominis, Gen. 2. 7. & 16. 8. Esa. 3. 15. & 30. 6. & 37. 6. Marc. 12. 14. Ioan. 7. 24. 2. Cor. 5. 12. & 10. v. 1. 7. facies mystica, Cant. 2. 14. facies, 1. superficies orbis, cœli, terræ, maris, &c. Gen. 1. 2. & 4. 6. Iob. 37. 22. Esai. 19. 8. Ezech. 37. 2. Matt. 16. 3. Act. 17. 26.
units.tr: Face: the mouth, countenance, sight, presence, outward state, speech, action, or condition of a man, Gen. 2.7 and 16.8; Isa. 3.15 and 30.6 and 37.6; Mark 12.14; John 7.24; 2 Cor. 5.12 and 10.1, 7. Mystical face, Song 2.14. Face, 1, the surface of the globe, of the heavens, of the earth, of the sea, etc.: Gen. 1.2 and 4.6; Job 37.22; Isa. 19.8; Ezek. 37.2; Matt. 16.3; Acts 17.26.

units.la: Facies animalium variorum, Ezech. 11. 19. Dan. 7. 8. Ioel 2. 3. &c. Apoc. 9. 7. facies Serpentis, Draconis, Satanæ, Apoc. 12. 14. facies Afflictionis variæ, Esai. 19. 16. Ier. 42. 17. & 48. 44. Thren. 5. 10. facies arcus, gladij, prælij, Iob. 19. 29. Psal. 60. 6. Esai. 21. 15. facies rerum artificialium, Exod. 28. 27. 1. Reg. 6. 3. Ezech. 40. 15. &c. facies venti, ignis, frigoris, Psal. 18. 45. & 88. 3. & 14. 7. 17. Mich. 1. 4.]
units.tr: The faces of various animals: Ezek. 1.10; Dan. 7.8; Joel 2.3, etc.; Rev. 9.7. The face of the Serpent, the Dragon, Satan: Rev. 12.14. The faces of various afflictions: Isa. 19.16; Jer. 42.17 and 48.44; Lam. 5.10. The face of a bow, sword, battle: Job 19.29; Ps. 60.6; Isa. 21.15. The faces of artificial things: Exod. 28.27; 1 Kings 6.3; Ezek. 40.15, etc. The face of wind, fire, cold: Ps. 18.45 and 88.3 and 14.7, 17; Mic. 1.4.

units.la: AGILITAS nimia, Vide CREDVLITAS.
units.tr: Excessive AGILITY. See CREDULITY.

units.la: ACTIO, i. vociferatio, Amos. 6. 7. [
units.tr: ACTION, that is, shouting: Amos 6.7.

units.la: ACTOR, Creator, Iob. 4. 17. & 32. 22. Prou. 14. 31. & 17. 5. Esai. 17. 7. & 29. 16. & 45. 9. & 51. 13. Ose. 8. 14. Benefactor, Redemptor, Deut. 32. 6. 15. factor, obseruator, homo reipsa præstans
units.tr: ACTOR, Creator: Job 4.17 and 32.22; Prov. 14.31 and 17.5; Isa. 17.7 and 29.16 and 45.9 and 51.13; Hos. 8.14. Benefactor, Redeemer: Deut. 32.6, 15. Doer, one who observes, a man who in deed performs

units.la: quod ei præscriptum & præceptum est, Rom.2.13. Iaco 1.v.22.23.25.& 4.11. ]
units.tr: what is prescribed and commanded to him: Rom. 2.13; James 1.22, 23, 25; 4.11.

units.tr: Actions [ἔργα], Rom. 8.13. Works, Jer. 25.14; Rom. 3.27; 1 Tim. 5.25; James 1.25. Deeds, the works of God: Ps. 64.10 and 143.5.
