Sam.8.5.rebelles sunt,Deut.9.24 Ægyptum repetere constituunt,Num.14.4.id facere prohibentur , Deut.17.16. a Deo reiecti sunt, Psalm.106.40, siccis pedibus Iordanem transeunt,Ios.3.17.
units.tr: ISRAEL, or the Israelites, the patronymic of all the posterity of Jacob, are called the inheritance of the Lord: Deut. 4:20; 9:26, 29; 14:2; 32:9; 2 Sam. 21:3; 1 Kings 8:31, 53; Ps. 47:5; 78:71; 106:5, 40; 135:4; Isa. 19:25; 47:6; Zech. 2:12. See INHERITANCE of God and HERITAGE of God. Israel is the people of God: 2 Sam. 7:24; 1 Chron. 17:22; Isa. 51:19. The sceptre of God's inheritance: Jer. 51:19. The vineyard of the Lord: Ps. 80:9; Isa. 5:1; Jer. 2:21; Matt. 21:33; Mark 12:1; Luke 20:9. They multiply in Egypt, Exod. 1:7; Ps. 105:24; for this reason they are oppressed, Exod. 1:13; Acts 7:18, 19. They are slaughtered by the Philistines, 1 Sam. 31:1; 1 Chron. 10:1. They celebrate the Passover, Josh. 5:10; Exod. 12:2. They go out of Egypt with their wealth, Exod. 12:36; Ps. 105:37. They are chosen by God, Deut. 7:6; 14:2; 10:15. They break the covenant, Ps. 78:56. They are dreadful to all, Josh. 5:1. They are most excellently instructed, Deut. 18:14, etc. They murmur against Moses, Num. 14:2; 16:41. Forgetting God, they are oppressed, Judg. 3:7, 8; 10:7; 13:1. They desire flesh, Num. 11:4. They importunately ask for a king, 1 Sam. 8:5. They are rebels, Deut. 9:24. They resolve to return to Egypt, Num. 14:4. They are forbidden to do this, Deut. 17:16. They are rejected by God, Ps. 106:40. They cross the Jordan on dry feet, Josh. 3:17.

units.la: ISRAELITARVM contumacia, Exod.32.9.&33 3.Deut 9.v. 13.Num.14.11.dignitas ac præstantia,Exo.19 6.Deut.4.7 & 7.6.& 26.19.& 33 29.2.Sam.7 23.1.Par.17.21.Psalm.147. 20.idololatria eorum prędicta,Deut.31.16.&c.damnatur, & describitur , 32.16.&c.ludic.2.11. & 8.33.& 10.6.Neh.9. 18.Psal.78.58.& 106.v.19.28.37.38.Ezech.23 3. ingratitudo eorum,Neh.9.26.Psal.106.7.pedes non attriti, Deuter.8. 4.nec vestimenta consumta,ibid.votum eorum, Numer. 21.2.
units.tr: The obstinacy of the Israelites: Exod. 32:9; 33:3; Deut. 9:13; Num. 14:11. Their dignity and excellence: Exod. 19:6; Deut. 4:7; 7:6; 26:19; 33:29; 2 Sam. 7:23; 1 Chron. 17:21; Ps. 147:20. Their idolatry is foretold: Deut. 31:16, etc.; it is condemned and described: Deut. 32:16, etc.; Judg. 2:11; 8:33; 10:6; Neh. 9:18; Ps. 78:58; 106:19, 28, 37, 38; Ezek. 23:3. Their ingratitude: Neh. 9:26; Ps. 106:7. Their feet were not worn down: Deut. 8:4; nor were their garments consumed, ibid. Their vow: Num. 21:2.

units.la: ISRAEL , pro tota Ecclesia , Psalm. 125. 5. Galat. 6. 16. pro Iacobo Isaaci filio , Roman. 9 6. in priore parte versus:in posteriore metonymice , pro gente ipsa Israelitarum.
units.tr: ISRAEL, for the whole Church: Ps. 125:5; Gal. 6:16. For Jacob, son of Isaac: Rom. 9:6 in the first part of the verse; in the latter part, by metonymy, for the Israelite nation itself.

units.la: ISRAELIT IS semen perpetuum,Ierem.31.v.37.38.&c.
units.tr: The ISRAELITES are a perpetual seed: Jer. 31:37, 38, etc.

units.la: ISRAELITAE veri quinam censendi , Rom.an.9.8.Galat. 6.16.
units.tr: Who are to be regarded as the true Israelites? Rom. 9.8; Gal. 6.16.

units.la: ISRAEL seu Israelitæ,pro decem Tribubus apostatis,1.Reg. 12.16.1.Paral.10.1.7.quæ separant se à domo Dauid, 1.Reg. 12.v.3.9.(6.secundum verba Ahiæ Prophetæ,11.29. Vitulum à Ieroboamo novo suo Rege conflatum adorant, 1. Reg.12.30.non tamen omnes, 2. Paral.11.16.vincunt Iudam,28.8.eorum captivitas prædicitur,1.Reg.14.15. Ose. 11.5.Amos,6.8.& 7.17. Israelitarum ab Assyrijs oppressio, 2.Reg.13.22.eorum deportatio , 18.11. iuxta illud Deut.4.26.idololatria 1.Reg.12.28.& 14.15.2. Reg.17.7 Ierem.3.v.6.20.& 11.v.10.13.Ezech.20.v.30.31. Ose.1.2.& 3.1.& 6.10.& 8.4.& 9.1.& 10.1.& 11.2.& 13.1. Amos 5.26. Initas,Esa.28.1.Ier.5.11.& 7.1.& 13.12. Amos 2.6.& 5.12. conversio,Ierem.31.9.liberatio,Ose 11.11.Israelitæ secundum carnem vocantur, 1. Cor.10.18.qui externis sacrificiis & ceremoniis adhuc vacabant, quæ seorsim à Christo & per se æstimata,dicuntur sanctificationes & iustificationes carnis,Heb.10.v.10.11.eò quòd ad animum usque non pertingant.
units.tr: ISRAEL, or the Israelites, meaning the ten apostate tribes: 1 Kings 12.16; 1 Chron. 10.1, 7. They separated themselves from the house of David, 1 Kings 12.3, 9 (6), according to the words of the prophet Ahijah, 11.29. They worship the calf made by Jeroboam, their new king, 1 Kings 12.30, though not all of them, 2 Chron. 11.16. They conquer Judah, 28.8. Their captivity is foretold, 1 Kings 14.15; Hos. 11.5; Amos 6.8 and 7.17. The Israelites are oppressed by the Assyrians, 2 Kings 13.22; they are carried into exile, 17.11, according to that saying in Deut. 4.26. Idolatry: 1 Kings 12.28 and 14.15; 2 Kings 17.7; Jer. 3.6, 20 and 11.10, 13; Ezek. 20.30, 31; Hos. 1.2; 3.1; 6.10; 8.4; 9.1; 10.1; 11.2; 13.1; Amos 5.26. Iniquity: Isa. 28.1; Jer. 5.11 and 7.1 and 13.12; Amos 2.6 and 5.12. Conversion: Jer. 31.9. Liberation: Hos. 11.11. They are called Israelites according to the flesh, 1 Cor. 10.18, who were still devoted to external sacrifices and ceremonies, which, when considered apart from Christ and in themselves, are called sanctifications and justifications of the flesh, Heb. 10.10, 11, because they do not reach the mind.

units.la: [Quæ de Israele in scripturis S. dicta ocurrunt ad sequentes sectiones referri posse videntur.
units.tr: [What is said of Israel in the Holy Scriptures may seem to be referred to the following sections.

units.la: 1. Voce illa denotatur persona Iacobi Patriarchæ, cuius vt & posterorum Deus frequenter appellatur Deus.
units.tr: 1. By this word is denoted the person of the patriarch Jacob, whose God, as well as that of his posterity, is often called God.

units.la: 2. Israelis nomine , Iacobi patriarchæ posteri omnes intelliguntur: duplici nomine consideranti, nempe secundum carnem & secundum spiritum, tum ante, tum post exhibitum in carne Messiam:qui Israel, domus Israel, filij ij Israel, populus Israel, Israelitæ appellantur.
units.tr: 2. By the name Israel are understood all the posterity of the patriarch Jacob, considered in a twofold respect, namely according to the flesh and according to the spirit, both before and after the Messiah was revealed in the flesh. They are called Israel, the house of Israel, the sons of Israel, the people of Israel, Israelites.

units.la: 3. Israel, Iudæi seu Israelis posteri in tota tribu Iudæ, in parte tribus Beniamin & Simeonis, qui sub Roboamo & sequentibus Dauidis successoribus in verę religionis professione permanserunt, distinctæ à decem tribubus, quæ sub Ieroboamo regnum constituerunt quod Israelis dictum est. At nomen Iudæorum, post reditum ex Babylone tributum est Israelitis, qui apud Prophetas ita designatur. Quæ autem in Novo Testamento de Israele dicta occurrunt, quamuis ad Iudæos potius, quam ad Israelitas decem tribuum referri videantur, tamen sectione secunda includuntur: quum Iudæis e Babylone redeuntibus multi Israelitæ decem tribuum admixti sunt, & duodecim tribuum Israel, ad quas Christus missus est, mentio fiat ab Euangelistis & Apostolis, totúsque Dei populus ex Israelis seu Iacobi Patriarchæ posteris, & Gentibus, in Messiam exhibitum credentibus & creduturis, compositus sit.
units.tr: 3. Israel means the Jews, or the posterity of Israel, in the whole tribe of Judah, in part of the tribes of Benjamin and Simeon, who under Rehoboam and the later successors of David remained in the profession of the true religion. They are distinguished from the ten tribes, which under Jeroboam formed a kingdom that was called Israel. But the name of Jews was given to the Israelites after the return from Babylon, and this is how they are designated by the prophets. The things said of Israel in the New Testament, although they seem to refer to the Jews rather than to the Israelites of the ten tribes, are nevertheless included in the second section. For when the Jews returned from Babylon, many Israelites of the ten tribes were mixed with them, and the Evangelists and Apostles mention the twelve tribes of Israel, to which Christ was sent. And the whole people of God is composed of the posterity of Israel or of the patriarch Jacob, and of the Gentiles, who believe and will believe in the Messiah revealed.

units.la: 4. Tribus omnes populi Israelitici, hoc nomine sæpius à tribu Iuda distinguuntur.
units.tr: 4. All the tribes of the Israelite people are often distinguished by this name from the tribe of Judah.

units.la: 5 Israel, Tribus Iuda, 2. Samuel. 15. 17. & 1. Reg. 12. 17. Speciatim vero ciues Ierosolymitani, 2. Paral. 31. 15.
units.tr: 5. Israel: the tribe of Judah, 2 Sam. 15.17; 1 Kings 12.17. Specifically, the citizens of Jerusalem, 2 Chron. 31.15.

units.la: 6. Israel, decem tribus quæ regnum constituerunt à domo Dauidis separatum, & sub Ezechia funditus ab Assyriis euersum.
units.tr: 6. Israel: the ten tribes, which constituted a kingdom separated from the house of David, and which under Hezekiah were utterly overthrown by the Assyrians.

units.la: 7. Israel, terra, regio, termini, fines Israel, Chanaan in qua Israelis posteri habitarunt.
units.tr: 7. Israel: the land, region, borders and territory of Israel, Canaan, in which the posterity of Israel dwelt.

units.la: 8. Locus in terra Chanaan, Iosue 11. 16. & 2. Sam. 17. 25.
units.tr: 8. A place in the land of Canaan, Josh. 11.16; 2 Sam. 17.25.

units.la: Israelita, quidam ex posteris Iacobi patriarchæ, Leuitic. 24. 10. Numer. 25, v. 8. 14. Iudic. 7. 11. 1. Sam. 14. 22. & 17. 11. & 31. 7. In novo Testamento Israelitæ nomine Iudæus intelligitur, tum Christi discipulus, tum eiusdem quoquo modo aduersarius, Ioann. 1. 47. Act. 2. 22. & 3. 12. & 5. 35. & 13. 16. & 21 28. Rom. 9. v. 4. 6. & 11. 1. 2. Cor. 11. 22. Israelitis mulier, Leuiti. 24. 10.]
units.tr: An Israelite: a certain one of the posterity of the patriarch Jacob, Lev. 24.10; Num. 25.8, 14; Judg. 7.11; 1 Sam. 14.22; 17.11; 31.7. In the New Testament, Israelite is understood as Jew, whether a disciple of Christ or in some way his adversary: John 1.47; Acts 2.22; 3.12; 5.35; 13.16; 21.28; Rom. 9.4, 6; 11.1; 2 Cor. 11.22. An Israelite woman, Lev. 24.10.]

units.la: ISSACHAR (id est, viri merces) Iacobi ex Lea filius, Genes. 30. v. 17. 18. benedicitur. 49. 14. Deuter. 33. 18. eius genealogia, Genes. 46. 13. 1. Paral. 7. 1. sors, Iosue 19. 17. [Hoc nomine etiam Issacharis tribus designatur, Genes. 49. 14. Deut. 27. 12. & 33. 18. Iudic. 5. 15. & 10. 1. 1. Paral. 12. 40. & 27. 18. 1. Paralip. 30. 18. Ezech. 40, versi. 25. 26. 33. Significat etiam sortem seu regionem Issacharitarum in terra Chanaan, Iof.17.11.1.Reg.4.17.]
units.tr: ISSACHAR (that is, man of hire), son of Jacob by Leah, is blessed, Gen. 30.17, 18; 49.14; Deut. 33.18. His genealogy: Gen. 46.13; 1 Chron. 7.1. His lot: Josh. 19.17. This name also designates the tribe of Issachar: Gen. 49.14; Deut. 27.12 and 33.18; Judg. 5.15 and 10.1; 1 Chron. 12.40 and 27.18; 2 Chron. 30.18; Ezek. 40.25, 26, 33. It also signifies the lot or region of the Issacharites in the land of Canaan, Josh. 17.11; 1 Sam. 4.17.]

units.la: ITALIA, regio & patria Romanorum, ab Italo rege sic dicta. Act.18.2.&27.1.6. Heb.13.24.
units.tr: ITALY, the region and homeland of the Romans, so called after King Italus. Acts 18.2; 27.1, 6; Heb. 13.24.

units.la: ITER sabbathi, pro itinere duorum milliarium, Actor. 1.12. Itineris filiorum Israel dux Deus fuit, interdiu & noctu, Exodi 13.21. itineris Iacob comes Deus, Genes. 28.15.
units.tr: ITER (a journey) of a Sabbath, meaning a journey of two miles, Acts 1.12. God was the guide of the journey of the sons of Israel, by day and by night, Exod. 13.21; God was the companion of Jacob's journey, Gen. 28.15.

units.la: IVBAL, Lameth & Ada alter filius, citharae & organorum musicorum inuentor, Gen.4.21.
units.tr: JUBAL, the other son of Lamech and Adah, the inventor of the lyre and of musical instruments, Gen. 4.21.

units.la: IVBILAEVS annus, & eius lex, Leuit.25.v.10.11.&c. Vide Solemnitas.
units.tr: The JUBILEE year and its law, Lev. 25.10, 11, etc. See Solemnity.

units.la: IVDA (ex Iehouae & celebrandi verbo, Iehuda dictus) Iacobi ex Lea filius nascitur, Gen.29.35. ducit vxorem, 38.2. nurū suam incestu contaminat, v.10. benedicitur, 49.8. Deut.33.7. eius genealogia, Gen.46 12.1. Paral.2 3.
units.tr: JUDAH (named from the verb meaning to praise or celebrate in Jehovah, Jehuda) is born as son of Jacob by Leah, Gen. 29.35. He takes a wife, 38.2. He defiles his daughter-in-law by incest, v. 10. He is blessed, 49.8; Deut. 33.7. His genealogy: Gen. 46.12; 1 Chron. 2.3.

units.la: IVDA Tribus sola Dauidem sequitur, 2.Sam.2.10.&20.1.1. Reg.12.20. eius idololatria, 14.22. Amos 2.4. Mich.1.9. V.
units.tr: The tribe of Judah alone follows David, 2 Sam. 2.10 and 20.1; 1 Kings 12.20. Its idolatry, 14.22; Amos 2.4; Mic. 1.9. See.

units.la: IVDAEI. Ne fornicetur cum idolis, monetur, Ose.4.15. eius captiuitas praedicitur, Ier.4.7.
units.tr: JUDAEANS. They are warned not to commit fornication with idols, Hos. 4.15. Their captivity is foretold, Jer. 4.7.

units.la: [IVDA, Heb. Iehuda, patriarchae Iacobi filius, cuius varia historia a 29.cap. Gen. ad 50. describitur multis locis, sicut & in sequentibus libris. V. Testamenti, & Matth.1.v.2.3. Luc.3.33. Heb.7.14.
units.tr: [JUDAH, Heb. Iehuda, son of the patriarch Jacob, whose varied history is described in many places from Genesis chapter 29 to 50, as also in the following books of the Old Testament; and Matt. 1.2, 3; Luke 3.33; Heb. 7.14.

units.la: 2. Hoc nomine designantur posteri Iudae patriarchę, qui tribum inter duodecim tribus constituerunt, Num.2.3. Deut.27.12. Iudic.1.2.1. Sam.15.4.
units.tr: 2. By this name are designated the posterity of the patriarch Judah, who formed the tribe among the twelve tribes, Num. 2.3; Deut. 27.12; Judg. 1.2; 1 Sam. 15.4.

units.la: 3. Regnum Iudae, quod ex tribu Iehudae, parte item trib. Beniaminis & Simeonis constitutum est. Huius etiam regni subditi. Vide libros Regum, Paralip. Prophetarum maiorum & minorum: in quibus regni Iudae frequens mentio.
units.tr: 3. The kingdom of Judah, which was formed from the tribe of Judah and likewise from part of the tribes of Benjamin and Simeon. Also the subjects of this kingdom. See the books of Kings and Chronicles, and the Prophets, major and minor, in which the kingdom of Judah is frequently mentioned.

units.la: 4. Iudaei, seu populus ex captiuitate in Iudaeam reversus, & quorum patres regibus Iudae, seu Dauidis successoribus subditi fuerant. V. Esdram, Nehem. Agg. Zachariam & Malachiam.
units.tr: 4. The Jews, or the people who returned from captivity to Judea, and whose fathers had been subject to the kings of Judah, that is, to the successors of David. See Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.

units.la: 5. Tribus Iudę fors seu regio, 1.Reg 13.v.1.12.21.2.Reg. 23.17.Luc.1 65.
units.tr: 5. The lot or region of the tribe of Judah, 1 Kings 13.1, 12, 21; 2 Kings 23.17; Luke 1.65.

units.la: 6. Iudas, nomen discipuli Christiani, Actor.9.11. Iuda Iohannae filius, Luc.3.16. Iosephi F. Luc.3.30.]
units.tr: 6. Judas, the name of a Christian disciple, Acts 9.11. Judas son of Joanna, Luke 3.16. Judas son of Joseph, Luke 3.30.]

units.la: IVDAEA, (quae & Chananęa & Palęstina) aliās est tota terra duodecim tribuum: aliās duae tantum tribus Iuda & Beniamin hoc nomine designatur. (V.Iudaei paulo inferius.)
units.tr: JUDAEA (also Canaan and Palestine) is at one time the whole land of the twelve tribes; at another time only the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin are designated by this name. (See Jews a little further below.)

units.la: opponitur Christianismo: Gal. 1.13.14.&c. vtriusque Paulus fuit obseruantissimus: illius quidem vt hostis Christi, huius vero vt fidelis eiusdem præco.
units.tr: It is opposed to Christianity: Gal. 1.13, 14, etc. Paul was most zealous in both: in the former as an enemy of Christ, in the latter as his faithful herald.

units.la: Iacobi frater, Marc.6.3. Iudæ v.1. Ioh.14.22.
units.tr: Brother of James, Mark 6.3. Jude, v. 1; John 14.22.

units.la: Iscariotes (id est, vt nonnulli coniectant, Hebraeis Isch-Keryot, hoc est, vir Keriot, seu Keriothites, ab vrbe in Tribu Iuda sic vocata oriundus, cuius sit mentio Ios.15. 25.) Apostolus eligitur, Matth.10.4. Marc.3.v.14.19. Lucae 22.3. Ioan.12.4. fur erat & latro, v.6. marsupium eleemosynarum habebat, 12.6.&13.29. Christi proditor appellatur, Mar.10.4 & 26.48. Mar.14.44. à Satana possidetur, Luc.22.3. Christum osculo prodit, Matt.26.v.48.49. Mar.14.v.44.45. Luc.22.v.47.48. Ioan.18.3. peccatum agnoscit, Matt.27.3. pretium turpissimæ negotiationis abiiciens, laqueo sibi mortem conscivit, v.5. suspensus crepuit medius, Act.1.18. Iudæ horrenda conditio, Matth.26.24. Marc.14.21. Lucae 22.22. eius perfidia multo ante cognita & praedicta, Psal. 41.10. Ioan.13.18.
units.tr: ISCARIOT (that is, as some conjecture, in Hebrew Ish-Kerioth, meaning a man of Kerioth, or a Keriothite, sprung from the town so called in the tribe of Judah, which is mentioned in Josh. 15.25). He is chosen as an apostle, Matt. 10.4; Mark 3.14, 19; Luke 6.16; John 12.4. He was a thief and a robber, v. 6; he had the purse of alms, 12.6 and 13.29. He is called the betrayer of Christ, Mark 10.4 and 26.48; Mark 14.44. He is possessed by Satan, Luke 22.3. He betrays Christ with a kiss, Matt. 26.48, 49; Mark 14.44, 45; Luke 22.47, 48; John 18.3. He acknowledges his sin, Matt. 27.3. Casting away the price of his most shameful bargain, he took his own death by a noose, v. 5; hanging, he burst asunder in the middle, Acts 1.18. The dreadful condition of Judas: Matt. 26.24; Mark 14.21; Luke 22.22. His treachery was known and foretold long before, Ps. 41.10; John 13.18.

units.la: Galilæus Pseudopropheta, seditionis autor, Act.5.37. hic & eius assectæ pereunt, ibid.
units.tr: A Galilean pseudo-prophet, author of a sedition, Acts 5.37. He and his followers perish, ibid.

units.la: qui & Barsabas: Hic & Silas ab Apostolis cum multa commendatione Antiochiam missi, Actor.15.vers. 22.25.
units.tr: Also called Barsabbas. This man and Silas were sent by the Apostles to Antioch with great commendation, Acts 15.22, 25.

units.la: verus quis, Rom.2. v.28.29. Iudaei vnde oriundi, Ezech.16 ver.3.4. Apostatae sunt, Ezec.2.3. Filij Prophetarum & pacti, Act.3.25 hoc est, ij quibus peculiariter destinati fuerunt prophetae, & quibus foedus est sancitum. Quo pertinet illud Rom.9.4. vel, posteritas Prophetarum, Abraham, &c. ac filij foederis, id est, semen illud Abrahae foedere comprehensum, Hebraismus. Hypocrite, Roman. 2.v.17.23. incredduli, & cognitionis Dei expertes, Ioan.7.v.28.&8.55. inexcusabiles, Ezech.2.v.5.&3.7. Ioan.15.v.22.24. interfectores Prophetarum, Matth.23.34. Luc.11.49. Act.7.52. 1.Thess.2.15. persecutores Euangelij, Act.13.46.1. Thess.2.14. primi in Ecclesia, Act.11.19.&13.v.26.46. proditores Christi,3.v.13.&7.52. non omnes reiecti, Rom.11.2. Legis transgressores, Ioan.7.19. (i. confessor verae de Deo doctrinae.)
units.tr: Who is a true Jew, Rom. 2.28, 29. The Jews from whom they originated, Ezek. 16.3, 4. They are apostates, Ezek. 2.3. Sons of the prophets and of the covenant, Acts 3.25; that is, those to whom the prophets were especially sent and with whom the covenant was ratified. To this belongs Rom. 9.4, or, the posterity of the prophets, of Abraham, etc., and sons of the covenant, that is, that seed of Abraham comprehended in the covenant: a Hebraism. Hypocrites, Rom. 2.17, 23. Unbelievers and strangers to the knowledge of God, John 7.28; 8.55. Inexcusable, Ezek. 2.5; 3.7; John 15.22, 24. Killers of the prophets, Matt. 23.34; Luke 11.49; Acts 7.52; 1 Thess. 2.15. Persecutors of the Gospel, Acts 13.46; 1 Thess. 2.14. First in the Church, Acts 11.19; 13.26, 46. Betrayers of Christ, Acts 3.13 and 7.52. Not all rejected, Rom. 11.2. Transgressors of the Law, John 7.19 (that is, confessors of the true doctrine concerning God).

units.la: Christum crucifixerunt, Luc.24.20. Act.2.v.23.36.&3.15.&4.10.&5.30.&10.39. 1. Thess.2.15. hostes suos interficiunt, Esth.9.5. signum petunt, Matth.12.38. &16. 1.Marc. 8.11. Ioann.2.18.1.Cor.1.22.
units.tr: They crucified Christ: Luke 24.20; Acts 2.23, 36; 3.15; 4.10; 5.30; 10.39; 1 Thess. 2.15. They kill their enemies: Esth. 9.5. They seek a sign: Matt. 12.38; 16; Mark 8.11; John 2.18; 1 Cor. 1.22.

units.la: IVDAEORVM adoptio, Rom. 9.4. apostasia, Ezech. 9.9. cæcitas, Esa.42.19. ceremoniæ, vmbra erant futurorum, Exo. 13.v.9.14. Num. 15 38. Deut. 6.8. Ezech. 20.20. 1. Corint. 10. 1.2. Corint. 3.13. Heb. 7.17. & 8.5. & 9. v.1.10.23. & 10. 1. consuetudines quædam certæ, Genes. 32.32. Iudic. 11.40. Ruth. 4.7.2. Paral. 35.25. excidium prædicitur, Matt. 23.38. Luc. 13. 35. generatio, cui similis, Matt. 11.17. Luc. 7.32. gloriatio inanis, Ezech. 33.24. Matth. 3.9. Ioan. 8.39. Rom. 2.17. idololatria, V. IDOLOLATRIA. ignorantia remissibilis, Luc. 23. 34. Act 3.17. incredulitas, Roman. 10.21. invidia in gentes.
units.tr: JEWS: adoption, Rom. 9.4. Apostasy, Ezek. 9.9. Blindness, Isa. 42.19. Ceremonies were shadows of things to come: Exod. 13.9, 14; Num. 15.38; Deut. 6.8; Ezek. 20.20; 1 Cor. 10.1–2; 2 Cor. 3.13; Heb. 7.17; 8.5; 9.1, 10, 23; 10.1. Certain customs: Gen. 32.32; Judg. 11.40; Ruth 4.7; 2 Chron. 35.25. Destruction is foretold: Matt. 23.38; Luke 13.35. A generation like the one: Matt. 11.17; Luke 7.32. Empty boasting: Ezek. 33.24; Matt. 3.9; John 8.39; Rom. 2.17. Idolatry: see IDOLATRY. Ignorance that can be forgiven: Luke 23.34; Acts 3.17. Unbelief: Rom. 10.21. Envy towards the Gentiles.

units.la: Vid. INVIDIA: & ZELVS malus. obstinatio, Esa. 48 4. & 65. 2. Ierem. 5.7. & 6.10. & 7.27. & 17.1. & 25. v.3.4. & 44.17. Ezech 3.7. Actor. 7.51.
units.tr: See ENVY, and ZEAL, evil. Obstinacy: Isa. 48.4; 65.2; Jer. 5.7; 6.10; 7.27; 17.1; 25.3–4; 44.17; Ezek. 3.7; Acts 7.51.

units.la: Peccatum duplex, Iere. 2.13. præstantia & prærogatiua, Psal. 76. v.1.2. Matt. 10.6. & 15.24. Luc. 24.47. Ioan. 4.22. Act. 3. v.25.26. & 11.19. & 13. v.26.46. Rom. 3. v.1.2. & 9.4. Eph. 1. 12. & 2.12. purificationes, Ioan. 2 6. reiectio, Esa. 50. 1. Matt. 8.12. Luc. 13. v.28 30. religioni eorum multi adhærent, Esth. 8.17. sævitia in Paulum, 2. Corin. 11.24. superstitiones, Gen. 32.32. Matt. 15.2. Marc. 7. v.2.3.4. Zelus, Vide ZELVS præpotterus.
units.tr: Sin is twofold: Jer. 2.13. Pre-eminence and prerogative: Ps. 76.1–2; Matt. 10.6; 15.24; Luke 24.47; John 4.22; Acts 3.25–26; 11.19; 13.26, 46; Rom. 3.1–2; 9.4; Eph. 1.12; 2.12. Purifications: John 2.6. Rejection: Isa. 50.1; Matt. 8.12; Luke 13.28–30. Many cling to their religion: Esth. 8.17. Savagery against Paul: 2 Cor. 11.24. Superstitions: Gen. 32.32; Matt. 15.2; Mark 7.2–4. Zeal: see ZEAL, headstrong.

units.la: IVDAEORVM & Gentium æqualitas, Roman. 3. 28. & 11. 32. Gal. 3.14. Ephes. 2.14. Col. 3.11. Iudæorum & aliarum gentium collatio, Ierem. 2. v.10.11. Iudæorum & Gentium coniunctio, Zach. 8.23. Ioan. 10.16. Iudæorum & Gentium discrimen, Rom. 3.1.1. Cor. 1.22. Ephes. 2.11.
units.tr: Equality of Jews and Gentiles: Rom. 3.28; 11.32; Gal. 3.14; Eph. 2.14; Col. 3.11. Comparison of Jews and other nations: Jer. 2.10–11. Union of Jews and Gentiles: Zech. 8.23; John 10.16. Distinction between Jews and Gentiles: Rom. 3.1; 1 Cor. 1.22; Eph. 2.11.

units.tr: To JUDGE, meaning to govern: Judg. 3.10; 4.4; 10.2; 12.7–8, 11, 13; 15.20; Heb. 10.30. Meaning to condemn: Gen. 15.14; Matt. 7.1; Rom. 2.3; 14.13. In the first part of the verse, and in the latter part, meaning to exercise judgment in settling some matter: so also 2 Thess. 2.12; Heb. 11.7. Also a familiar form of speech, meaning to expose the sins of others by the example of one's own virtue: Matt. 12.27, 41–42. To be judged means to be condemned: 1 Cor. 10.29; 1 Pet. 4.6; meaning to undergo a trial: 1 Cor. 6.1. THE SAINTS WILL JUDGE the world: Matt. 19.28; Luke 22.30; 1 Cor. 6.2; Jude 14. Christ indeed will be judge of the living and the dead, but with the love he bears towards his own, he will join them to himself. Hence he said, Matt. 19.28 and Luke 22.30, "You will sit", etc., and the Apostle, of the elect, that they will go to meet Christ in the air: 1 Thess. 4.17. By the name "world" must be understood the company of the wicked, whom the elect, with Christ presiding, will condemn at the last judgment; by the name "angels" are meant evil spirits. II. Others explain it thus: the rule of the external judgment will be not so much the Law as the Gospel, according to John 12.48 and Rom. 2.16; for which reason Christ asserts that the Apostles will judge the twelve tribes of Israel, Matt. 19.28; Luke 22.30, and Paul asserts that the elect, who have embraced Christ by faith and believed the Gospel, will judge the world, 1 Cor. 6.2. For although the wicked are also condemned by the voice of the Law, yet this is shown not by the Law but only by the Gospel, and this is what makes the distinction between the condemned and the saved, since all men are by nature children of wrath and no one in this life has conformed to the Law: Eph. 2.3; Ps. 14.1; 53.3; Rom. 3.12. But this is the voice of the Gospel alone, which the Apostles preached and the elect believed, and not the voice of the Law; the Gospel will indeed be the norm of the final judgment, according to John 3.36; 12.48; Rom. 2.16. III. Others briefly thus: the Apostles will judge the twelve tribes of Israel, that is, the faith of the Apostles will take away from the Israelites every excuse at the last judgment, so that the word "judge" is taken in the same sense as in Matt. 12.41–42. IV. Others thus: the saints are said to judge the world, because God will set all his adversaries before himself and before the whole assembly of the Church at the last judgment, which God promises he will do, Joel 3.2, where they think that by the valley of Jehoshaphat (which took its name from the notable victory mentioned in 2 Chron. 20) the sight of the whole Church is to be understood.

units.tr: JUDGMENTS OF GOD: Exod. 6.6; 7.4; Ps. 105.7; Isa. 26.8–9; Ezek. 5.8, 10, 15; 16.41; 25.11; 30.19. Judgments in the Old Testament are very often called the ordinances, laws, commandments, precepts and statutes of God, delivered to the people by the hand of Moses, pertaining to external worship and the various duties of life: Exod. 15.25; Lev. 18.4, etc.; Num. 36.13; Deut. 4.1, etc.; Josh. 24.24–25; Ezek. 5.6, etc.; Dan. 9.5. Judgments: wonders, conspicuous signs of power: 1 Chron. 16.14.

units.tr: JUDGMENT for equity: Luke 11.42. For reform and amendment: John 12.31; 1 Pet. 4.17. For the manner of conducting affairs: Rom. 11.33. Whence "to judge" is not rarely taken to mean "to govern" (see JUDGE). For the authority which Christ holds in heaven and on earth: John 16.11, as he himself seems to explain, Matt. 28.18, namely, lifted up above all the heavens; Phil. 2.9. For the punishment with which Christ was afflicted: Acts 8.33. For the very penalties of judgment: Matt. 5.22. For God's vengeance and punishment of sinners: 1 Pet. 4.17. For supreme power and authority, by which what is just and equal is decreed, and by its just sight: John 5.27, 30; 9.39. For what is equal and just: Luke 11.42. For a settled state: Matt. 12.18, because, namely, by Christ the true religion was to be proclaimed among the Gentiles, superstitions being cast out; wherever this happens, the Lord is said to reign and to judge there, that is, to preside over affairs and to govern.

units.tr: Judgment ought to be equal: Lev. 19.35; Deut. 25.1; 27.19; Amos 5.15; Mic. 6.8; Zech. 7.9; 8.16; John 7.24; 8.15. Judgment ought to be preceded by deliberation and examination of the cause: Gen. 3.11; 11.5; 18.21; Exod. 3.7–8; 23.1; Deut. 13.6, 8; 17.9; 19.18; Josh. 7.18; 22.13, etc.; Judg. 20.3, 12; Prov. 18.13; Eccl. 11.7. Premature and rash judgments are to be avoided: Ps. 41.1; Matt. 7.1; Luke 6.37; 12.57; 13.2; John 7.51; Rom. 2.1; 11.2–4; 14.3–4, 10, 13; 1 Cor. 4.3, 5; James 4.11–12.

units.la: IVRAMENTVM Legitimum, est species invocationis Dei, qua petitur, vt Deus sit testis animi iurantis, quod non velit in ea re de qua iurat, fallere, & puniat iurantem si fallat, sancita à Deo vt sit vinculum veritatis inter homines, & testimonium quòd Deus sit author & defensor veritatis. Heb.6.16.Exod.23.13.2.Cor.1.23.
units.tr: A lawful oath is a kind of invocation of God, by which it is asked that God be witness to the mind of the one swearing, that he does not wish to deceive in the matter about which he swears, and that God punish the swearer if he deceives. It was ordained by God to be a bond of truth among men and a testimony that God is the author and defender of truth. Heb. 6.16; Exod. 23.13; 2 Cor. 1.23.

units.la: Huic contraria sunt Iuramentum temerarium, ex levitate, hoc est, nulla necessitate, aut nulla graui de causa datum: de quo, Mat.5.34. Iacob.5.12. Et periurium, de quo suo loco.
units.tr: Opposed to this are the rash oath, given out of levity, that is, without any necessity or grave cause (on which see Matt. 5.34; James 5.12), and perjury, on which see in its place.

units.la: Iuramentum est cultus diuini species,Esaiç 45.23 & 48.1.ideo synecdochicè pro toto Dei cultu sumitur,Psal.63. 12.Ier.4.2.Vide Esa.45.23 Rom.14.11.Philip.2 v.10.11.per Dei nomen iurandum, Deut 6.13.& 10.20. Iosu.23.7.Esai. 65 16 Ier.5 7.& 12.16.non per idolorum nomina, Exo.23. 13.Iurare,pro iuramento dare, Gen 50.24 25.
units.tr: An oath is a species of divine worship (Isa. 45.23; 48.1), and so by synecdoche it is taken for the whole worship of God (Ps. 63.12; Jer. 4.2). See Isa. 45.23; Rom. 14.11; Phil. 2.10, 11. Swearing is done by the name of God (Deut. 6.13; 10.20; Josh. 23.7; Isa. 65.16; Jer. 5.7; 12.16), not by the names of idols (Exod. 23.13). To swear (iurare) means to give an oath (Gen. 50.24, 25).

units.la: IVSTIFICARE, pro iustum se approbare, Luc.10.29.
units.tr: JUSTIFY, to approve oneself as just: Luke 10.29.

units.la: IVSTIFICARE, pro iustum declarari, Matt.12.37.
units.tr: JUSTIFY, to be declared just: Matt. 12.37.

units.la: Ivstr-
units.tr: Justi-

units.la: IVSTIFICANDI verbum multipliciter vsurpatur in sacra Scriptura, quæ multiplex acceptio & significatio hoc loco explicanda venit.
units.tr: The verb to justify is used in many ways in Holy Scripture, and this manifold acceptance and meaning must be explained here.

units.la: Primo, cùm iustificatio non semper consideretur absolutè in eo cui inest iustitia, sed etiam comparatè alterius alicuius ratione, quando tum demum incipit iustus esse aliquis, cùm ipsius iustitia patefit: inde factum est, vt iustificare accipiatur etiam, pro iustitiam vel suam, vel alienam declarare, & sese aut alium quempiam iustum censere ac agnoscere, vt Matthæi 11.19. Lucæ 7.v.29 35.& 10.9.& 18.&c.
units.tr: First: since justification is not always considered absolutely in the one in whom justice inheres, but also comparatively, with reference to the judgment of someone else, a person then at last begins to be just when his justice is made manifest. Hence it came about that to justify is also taken to mean to declare one's own or another's justice, and to judge and acknowledge oneself or someone else as just, as in Matt. 11.19; Luke 7.29, 35; 10.9; 18, etc.

units.la: Secundo: Iam verò quia in iudiciis, qui insons declaratur, is etiam liberatur, & iudicio eximitur: hinc quoque factum est, vt iustificare & condemnare opponantur, id est, vt iustificare nihil aliud declaret, quàm absolui, vt Matt. 12.37. Act. 13.ver 38.39. Ro.5.16.& 8.30.&c. & aliis in locis, in quibus fideles dicuntur non condemnari.
units.tr: Second: Now since in judicial proceedings the one who is declared innocent is also freed and released from judgment, hence it also came about that to justify and to condemn are set against each other; that is, to justify means nothing other than to be absolved, as in Matt. 12.37; Acts 13.38, 39; Rom. 5.16; 8.30, etc., and in other places where the faithful are said not to be condemned.

units.la: Tertio: Neque id verò duntaxat in re forensi dicitur, sed in genere iustificari à re aliqua, significat, ab ea re prorsus liberum & immunem fieri, ac declarari, Rom.6.7.
units.tr: Third: This is said not only in a legal matter, but to be justified from some thing signifies to be made wholly free and immune from that thing, and to be declared so: Rom. 6.7.

units.la: Quarto: Deniq; quia iustitiæ nomine interdum vniuersalis quidam virtutum omnium concentus declaratur, interdum verò virtus illa, qua suum cuique reddimus, denique nonnunquam Dei bonitas in eo præcipuè apparens, quod nobis quantumuis indignis præstet quicquid vltrò pollicitus est: pro varia iustitiæ significatione, variè quoque dicitur iustus aliquis vel fieri, vel declarari. Sic dicitur Christus iustificatus Spiritu, 1 Timoth. 3.16. id est, diuinam illam naturam, quæ in sese est integerrima, & perfectissima, ipsámque adeò integritatem & perfectionem hominibus esse patefactam per diuinam illam virtutem in Christo corporaliter habitantem, Coloss. 2.9. quæ toties, ac præsertim in carnis ipsius resurrectione sese exeruit: Sic Iacobo dicimur ex operibus iustificari, Iac. 2.21. id est iusti declarari, (vnde Abraham ex operibus iustificatus dicitur) quia is demum iustus est, qui iustitiam facit: & contrà, Operibus neminem iustificari testatur Apostolus, Roman. 3.20. hoc est, iustum censeri & absolui, vt integrum & ἀνέγκλητον coram Deo, vt ipse explicat, Coloss. 1.22. Item qui iustus est, debet laborare, vt adhuc iustificetur, id est, cui datum est velle ac facere, is quotidie debet donum Dei in semetipso excitare. rare, vt magis ac magis in studio pietatis ac innocen- tiæ proficiat, Iustificari, pro, iustum pronuntiari apud tribunal Dei, Roman.2.13. Iustificamur fide in Christum, Actor.13.39. Rom.4.6. & 5.1. Gal.2.16. non ex operibus Legis, 3.10.
units.tr: Fourth: Finally, since by the name of justice sometimes a certain universal harmony of all the virtues is meant, sometimes that virtue by which we render to each his own, and sometimes God's goodness, appearing especially in this, that he grants to us, however unworthy, whatever he has freely promised; according to this varied meaning of justice, someone is also variously said to be made just or declared just. Thus Christ is said to be "justified in the Spirit" (1 Tim. 3.16 [ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι]), that is, that divine nature which in itself is most entire and most perfect, and that integrity and perfection itself was made manifest to men through that divine power dwelling bodily in Christ (Col. 2.9), which showed itself so often, and especially in the resurrection of his flesh. So we are said to be justified by works, according to James (2.21), that is, declared just (whence Abraham is said to have been justified by works), because he is just who does justice. And conversely, the Apostle testifies that no one is justified by works (Rom. 3.20), that is, to be accounted just and absolved, as whole and "unaccused" [ἀνέγκλητον] before God, as he himself explains (Col. 1.22). Likewise, he who is just ought to labour that he may still be justified; that is, to him to whom it has been given to will and to do, he ought daily to stir up God's gift in himself, so that he may advance more and more in the pursuit of piety and innocence. To be justified means to be pronounced just before the tribunal of God (Rom. 2.13). We are justified by faith in Christ (Acts 13.39; Rom. 4.6; 5.1; Gal. 2.16), not by works of the Law (Gal. 3.10).

units.la: Iustificatio proprie, est actio Dei iudicialis gratuita, qua electos accusationi & maledictioni Legis in seipsis obnoxios, per fidem, propter Christum, imputatione iustitiæ illius, iustos iudicat, ad laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ, & ipsorum salutem.
units.tr: Justification, properly speaking, is God's gracious judicial act, by which He declares the elect, who in themselves are liable to the accusation and curse of the Law, to be righteous through faith, on account of Christ, by the imputation of His righteousness, to the praise of the glory of His grace and their salvation.

units.la: Iustificatio, pro peccatorum remissione, & iustitiæ imputatione, Roman.5.18. ex Christi gratia proficiscitur, 3.24. & 4.6. Iustificatio vera, Esa.53.11. Iustificationis nomen large acceptum, Tit.3.7, ita vt complectatur quicquid à Christo consequimur, tum per imputationem, tum per Spiritus nos sanctificantis efficaciam, vt simus perfecti & integri. Sic capitur & Rom.8.30. Iustificationis finis quis, 7.4. causa efficiens quæ, nempe Christus. Gal.2.20.
units.tr: Justification, taken for the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of righteousness, Rom. 5.18, proceeds from the grace of Christ, Rom. 3.24 and 4.6. True justification, Isa. 53.11. The name of justification is taken broadly, Tit. 3.7, so that it embraces whatever we obtain from Christ, both by imputation and by the efficacy of the Spirit who sanctifies us, so that we may be perfect and whole. Rom. 8.30 is also understood in this way. What is the end of justification? Rom. 7.4. What is the efficient cause? Namely, Christ, Gal. 2.20.

units.la: ¶Iustificationem, qua quis ex iusto fit iustior, adscribi bonis operibus contendunt Pontificij, ex Eccles.18.22. Rom.2.13. Iac.2.v.21.24. Apoc.22.11. & hanc secundam vocant iustitiam. ¶Docent præterea iustificationem impij non fidei solum, sed aliis etiam virtutibus adscribi passim in sacris literis, vtpote spei, Rom.8.24. charitati, Exo.20.6. Prou.10.12. Luc.7.47. 1 Cor.13.4. Galat.5.6. 1.Pet.4.8. 1.Ioan.4.v.7.8.9. timori, Eccles.1.v.27.28. pœnitentiæ operibus, Sapien.11.24. Ezech.18.v.21.22. Mat.3 v.2.8. Hebr.6.16. & 10.35. & 11.26. Iac.2.24. Apoc.20.v.7 8. & 22.12.
units.tr: The Papists contend that justification, by which a man becomes more righteous from being righteous, is ascribed to good works, from Ecclus. 18.22, Rom. 2.13, Jas. 2.21, 24, Rev. 22.11, and they call this the second righteousness. They further teach that the justification of the ungodly is ascribed not only to faith but also to other virtues, scattered throughout the Sacred Letters: to hope, Rom. 8.24; to charity, Exod. 20.6, Prov. 10.12, Luke 7.47, 1 Cor. 13.4, Gal. 5.6, 1 Pet. 4.8, 1 John 4.7–9; to fear, Ecclus. 1.27–28; to the works of repentance, Wisd. 11.24, Ezek. 18.21–22, Matt. 3.2, 8; Luke 7 in the example of Magdalene, Luke 15 in the example of the prodigal son, and Luke 18 in the example of the publican. To good works, Matt. 5.12, 10.42, 16.27, 25.34, Rom. 2.6, 1 Cor. 15.28, 2 Cor. 5.10, 2 Tim. 4.8, Heb. 6.10, 10.35, 11.26, Jas. 2.24, Rev. 20.7–8, 22.12.

units.la: Iustitia, pro ea iustitia, quæ nobis per Christi gratiam communicatur, Rom.3.v.21.22. ex fide comparatur, Hebr. 11.7. nulla eam præcedunt merita, Ge.15.6. Esa.45.25. & 53. v.8.11. Ierem.23.6. & 33.16. Dan.10.7. &c. Abac.2.4. zachar. 9.11. Act.10.43. & 13.39. Rom.1.17. & 3.v.21.22. & 5.v.1.18. & 10.v.4.10. 1. Corint.1.30. Gal.2.16. & 3.11. & 5.5. Philip.3.9. Tit.3.7. 1. Petri.3.18. Hæc iustitia Christo in solidum tribuenda est, vt stent dicta illa, Ro.3.v.10.20. & 4.2. 1.Cor. 4.4. Gal.2.21.
units.tr: Righteousness, in the sense of that righteousness which is communicated to us through the grace of Christ, Rom. 3.21–22, is obtained by faith, Heb. 11.7; no merits precede it, Gen. 15.6, Isa. 45.25, 53.8, 11, Jer. 23.6, 33.16, Dan. 10.7, etc., Hab. 2.4, Zech. 9.11, Acts 10.43, 13.39, Rom. 1.17, 3.21–22, 5.1, 18, 10.4, 10, 1 Cor. 1.30, Gal. 2.16, 3.11, 5.5, Phil. 3.9, Tit. 3.7, 1 Pet. 3.18. This righteousness must be ascribed wholly to Christ, so that those sayings stand: Rom. 3.10, 20, 4.2, 1 Cor. 4.4, Gal. 2.21.

units.la: Quomodo autem iustitia ipsis etiam hominibus tri-buitur, de fructibus tantùm & testimoniis iustitię ex gra-tia in nobis creatæ, (non autem de causa efficiente, mulṯ minus de illa Christi iustitia, gratis nobis imputata, cuius vnius merito coronamur) accipiendum est, vt Lucæ 1.6. Iustitia pro beneficentia, 2.Corin.9.10. ¶ Iustitiæ nomiṉ interdum Hebræi speciatim eleemosynam intelligunt, vt verterunt etiam Græci, Deut.24.13. Dan.4.27. pro leg̱ & regula recte viuendi, Romanor.6.19. pro perfectione Hebr.5.13. Iustitia vera quæ, Philipp.3.9. commendatur Proverb.21.3. Ephes.5.9.1.Tim.6.11.2.Tim.2.22. Tit.1.8.&2.12.
units.tr: But how righteousness is also attributed to men themselves must be understood of the fruits and testimonies of righteousness created in us by grace only, not of its efficient cause, much less of that righteousness of Christ which is imputed to us freely and by whose merit alone we are crowned, as in Luke 1.6. Righteousness is taken for beneficence, 2 Cor. 9.10. The Hebrews sometimes understand by the name of righteousness specifically alms, as the Greeks also translated, Deut. 24.13, Dan. 4.27. It is taken for the law and rule of right living, Rom. 6.19; for perfection, Heb. 5.13. What true righteousness is, is commended in Phil. 3.9, Prov. 21.3, Eph. 5.9, 1 Tim. 6.11, 2 Tim. 2.22, Tit. 1.8 and 2.12.

units.la: Iustitiæ & æquitatis exempla: Abraham, Gene.13.9. Moses, Num.27.vers.5.6.7. Samuel,1.Sam.15.33. Dauid,26.23.&30.24.2.Sam.24.24. Harbona Eunuchus, Esther 7.9. Deus, Ierem.51.49. Rex Darius, Dan.6.24. quidam Rex, Matt.18.34. (Vide AEQVITATIS & iustitiæ exem-pla.) Iustitia Pharisaica damnatur, Matt.5.20. Lucæ 16.15. & 18. 14. Iustitiæ Pharisaicæ exempla: Legisperitus, Luc.10.29. Princeps quidam, 18.22. ¶ Iustitia in Christo triplex consideranda: Una essentialis, quatenus Dei est quæ cùm sit ipsamet Deitas, distinguenda est omni-no etiam in Christi persona ab ea iustitia, quæ est qualitas assumtæ humanitati, vt subiecto inhærens. Altera est perfectissimæ sanctitatis & integritatis habi-tus, quo plenissimè perfudit illam à se assumtam hu-manitatem ab ipso conceptionis ex Spiritu Sancto mo-mento. Tertia est huius habitus effectum, quo factum est, vt Legem perfectissimè pro nobis, pro quibus etiam & natus est, & Legi sese subiecit, præstaret, obediens fa-ctus Patri pro nobis vsq; ad mortem, & quidem mortem crucis.
units.tr: Examples of righteousness and equity: Abraham, Gen. 13.9; Moses, Num. 27.5–7; Samuel, 1 Sam. 15.33; David, 26.23 and 30.24, 2 Sam. 24.24; Harbonah the eunuch, Esth. 7.9; God, Jer. 51.49; King Darius, Dan. 6.24; a certain king, Matt. 18.34. (See the examples of equity and righteousness.) The righteousness of the Pharisees is condemned, Matt. 5.20, Luke 16.15, 18.14. Examples of Pharisaic righteousness: the lawyer, Luke 10.29; a certain ruler, 18.22. The righteousness in Christ is to be considered threefold. The first is essential, in so far as it belongs to God; since it is the Deity itself, it must be distinguished altogether, even in the person of Christ, from that righteousness which is a quality of the assumed humanity, inhering in it as its subject. The second is the habit of most perfect holiness and integrity, with which He most fully endowed that humanity He had assumed, from the very moment of conception by the Holy Spirit. The third is the effect of this habit, by which it came about that He rendered the Law most perfectly on our behalf, for whom He was both born and subjected Himself to the Law, becoming obedient to the Father for us even unto death, and indeed the death of the cross.

units.la: Ex his autem illa, cùm sit essentialis, per se maneat o-portet: de alterius imputatione, quæ corruptioni nostræ opponitur, agitur Rom.8.in initio capitis. De tertia verò, partim quatenus in ea versatur nostrorum peccatorum expiatio, agit Apostolus Rom.5.vsque ad versum 11. cuius imputatione per gratiam, aboleri reatum naturali propa-gatione contractum, idem Apostolus docet, v.17. ¶ Iustitia Dei passiue, vt Augustinus interpretatur, pro illa iustitia, qua Deus iustos facit, Psal.32.1.&71.2. Rom.1.17.&3.21. Actiua enim Dei iustitia dicitur, qua iudicat & punit no-centes. centes. Iustitia Dei, pro eo quod præscribit Deus, Iac.1. 20. Iustitiam facere, Hebræis est iuste & recte viuere Psal. 15.2. Mat.6.1. ¶Iustitiæ lex Paulo, Rom.9.31. est ea iustitiæ norma, quæ in Lege Dei præscribitur, & est vera, si quis Legē præstando, possit eam adipisci. Iustitiæ liberum esse, Paulo, Roman.6.20. est, nullo iustitiæ imperio teneri, sed peccati iugo prorsus mancipatum esse.
units.tr: Of these, the essential righteousness, since it is essential, must remain in itself. Concerning the imputation of the second, which is opposed to our corruption, the Apostle treats in Rom. 8 at the beginning of the chapter. But concerning the third, partly insofar as the expiation of our sins is involved in it, the Apostle treats in Rom. 5 up to verse 11; by its imputation through grace, the same Apostle teaches, v. 17, that the guilt contracted by natural propagation is abolished. The righteousness of God passive, as Augustine interprets it, is that righteousness by which God makes men righteous, Ps. 32.1, 71.2, Rom. 1.17, 3.21. For the righteousness of God is called active, by which He judges and punishes the guilty. The righteousness of God is what God prescribes, Jas. 1.20. To do righteousness, in Hebrew idiom, is to live justly and rightly, Ps. 15.2, Matt. 6.1. The law of righteousness, for Paul, Rom. 9.31, is that norm of righteousness which is prescribed in the Law of God, and it is true if anyone could attain it by fulfilling the Law. To be free from righteousness, for Paul, Rom. 6.20, is to be held by no authority of righteousness, but to be wholly enslaved to the yoke of sin.

units.tr: RIGHTEOUSNESS: the Law and fear of God, the rule of piety, equity and temperance; in short, every thought and action agreeing with that Law: Gen. 18.19, Deut. 4.5, 9.4–6, Job 29.14, Ps. 7.9, Prov. 11.4–6, 18, Eccles. 7.16, Isa. 1.21, Jer. 22.3, 15, Ezek. 18.19–20, etc., 33.12, etc., Dan. 6.22, Hos. 10.12, Matt. 5.20, Luke 1.75, Rom. 10.5, Eph. 5.9, 1 Tim. 6.11. Righteousness is also almsgiving, Matt. 6.1. Right, Neh. 2.20, Isa. 54.17. The law of nations, implanted by God in the very nature of men: the law of nature, Rom. 1.32. The profession of the Christian religion, Matt. 5.10, 1 Pet. 3.14. The saving knowledge of God, Dan. 12.3, Mal. 3.3. The manner of life, Isa. 57.12.

units.tr: 3. By righteousness, various attributes of God are signified. (1) The prosperous administration and right governance, Ps. 85.14, 94.15, Isa. 32.1, 16–17, 11. (2) Equity, Ps. 85.11–12, 89.15, 97.2, 48.11, 99.4; and this under the kingdom of the Messiah, as the following testimonies show, Isa. 11.4, 33.5, 40.14. (3) Judgment, Judg. 5.11, Job 37.23, Ps. 36.7, 50.6, Isa. 5.16, 28.17, Amos 5.24, Mic. 6.5, 2 Pet. 2.5. (4) Omnipotence, Ps. 97.6, Isa. 28.29. (5) The truth of the promises, joined with the highest clemency and kindness, Ps. 5.9, 31.2, 40.10–11, 48.11, 51.16, 71.2, 15–16, 19, 24, 88.12, 89.17, 98.2, 103.17, 143.1, 145.7, Isa. 45.23, Jer. 9.24, Hos. 2.19, Mic. 7.9, Rom. 3.5, Eph. 6.14.

4. Righteousness, namely that by which we stand before the judgment of God unto eternal life, Gen. 15.6, Rom. 1.17, 3.21–22, 25–26, 4.3, 5, 6, 9, 11, 13, 22, 5.17, 9.30, 10.3–4, 10, 14, 17, 1 Cor. 1.30, Gal. 2.21, 3.6, 21, 5.4, Phil. 3.9, Heb. 11.7, Jas. 2.23, 2 Pet. 1.1, 3.13.
