Filij Samuelis, 8.3. Absalom, 2. Sam.16,v.1.2.3 4. Filius prodigus, Luc.15.v.11 12. ¶ Liberorum procreatio donum Dei est, Gen.1.28.& 4.v.1.25.& 16, 2, & 20.v.17.18. & 25 21.& 29.v.30.31.& 30.22,& 48.9.Ruth.4.13.1.Sam.1.v. 19.27.& 2.21.Psal.113 9.& 127.4.Esa.66.9.
units.tr: Examples of children's stubbornness and disobedience towards their parents: Ham, Gen. 9:22. Esau, Gen. 26:34-35 and 28:8-9. Simeon and Levi, Gen. 34:30. The sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, 1 Sam. 2:22-24. The sons of Samuel, 1 Sam. 8:3. Absalom, 2 Sam. 16:1-4. The prodigal son, Luke 15:11-12. ¶ The begetting of children is a gift of God: Gen. 1:28; 4:1, 25; 16:2; 20:17-18; 21:21; 29:30-31; 30:22; 48:9. Ruth 4:13. 1 Sam. 1:19, 27; 2:21. Ps. 113:9; 127:4. Isa. 66:9.

units.la: LIBERATIONEM, seu libertatem per Christum, Græcis ἀπολύτρωσιν duplicem constituit Paulus,Eph.1.cap. Vnam qua redimimur,persoluto pretio, Christi videlicet sanguine, vt à seruitute peccati & mortis manumittamur, v.7.vt fusiùs explicatur Rom.7.capite. Alteram,qua in iustam libertatem prorsus vindicemur,Ephes1.14. Nos enim quamuis liberos, retinet tamen aliquatenus per vim peccatum in aliqua seruitutis specie, vt quod volumus,non faciamus, Galat.5.17.& mors etiam nexos in vinculis tenet, in diem illum iudicio extremo destinatum,quo nos Christus,vt à se redemptos,liberali sua manu afferet. Non pugnant igitur inter se duæ istæ liberationes:sed illa quidem peracta est,hanc verò, quæ illius est complementum, speramus, vt Lucæ 21.28.Roman.8.23.Eph.4 30.cuius est arrhabo Spiritus Sanctus, ex quo nos manumissos esse didicimus per fidem, vt nos tandem in iustam libertatem ex malæ fidei possessoris potestate asserendos esse non dubitemus.Illam igitur docendi causa ἀπολύτρωσιν ἐλευθερώσεως vocare licebit,cuius passim meminit Apostolus,vt Rom.6.22.& 8.2. Hæc verò dicitur ἀπολύτρωσις τῆς ἀξιώσεως,i.ad verbum, Liberatio vindicationis,siue assertionis.
units.tr: Paul sets out a twofold liberation (in Greek apolytrōsis) through Christ. The first is that by which we are redeemed, the price having been paid, namely the blood of Christ, so that we are set free from the bondage of sin and death (Eph. 1:7), as is explained at more length in Rom. 7. The second is that by which we are fully vindicated into true liberty (Eph. 1:14). For although we are free, sin still holds us to some extent in a kind of bondage, so that we do not do what we want (Gal. 5:17), and death also keeps us bound in chains until that final day of judgment, when Christ will bring us, redeemed by himself, into his generous hand. These two liberations, then, do not contradict each other. The first has been accomplished, but the second, which completes the first, we hope for (Luke 21:28; Rom. 8:23; Eph. 4:30). The Holy Spirit is the pledge of it, and through him we have learned by faith that we have been set free, so we do not doubt that we shall at last be asserted into true liberty, released from the power of a possessor of bad faith. For the sake of teaching, therefore, it will be permissible to call that liberation the redemption of freedom (apolytrōsis eleutherōseōs), which the Apostle mentions everywhere (Rom. 6:22; 8:2). The second is called apolytrōsis tēs axiōseōs, that is, word for word, liberation of vindication, or of assertion.

units.la: LIBERTAS pro liberatione à Legis ceremoniis,1. Corint. 9.v.1.19.pro primo gradu ad vivificationem,2. Cor.3 17. id est,pro conditione illa Filiorum Dei, quibus exemtum est velamen cordis,seruitutis nimirum illa misera cæcitatis,& iugum illud tenebrarum, quod vnius hominis peccato nobis impositum, Lex non modò grauabat, sed etiam altero iugo adgrauabat.Denique hoc ipsum est,quod Propheta ait,Cor lapideum tollere,& carneum dare, cor illuminare, cor convertere, lucem videre,& similia omnia, quibus illa gratiæ Dei per Christum vis significatur,illa inquam nos reddens liberos, & ad tantam aspiciendam lucem Euangelii idoneos.
units.tr: Liberty is taken for release from the ceremonies of the Law (1 Cor. 9:1, 19), and for the first step towards quickening (2 Cor. 3:17), that is, for that condition of the sons of God from whom the veil of the heart is taken away. This is the wretched blindness of slavery, and that yoke of darkness which, imposed on us by the sin of one man, the Law not only weighed down but also burdened with a second yoke. Finally, this is what the Prophet means when he says: to take away the stony heart and give a fleshly one, to enlighten the heart, to convert the heart, to see the light, and all similar things, by which the power of God's grace through Christ is signified, that grace which, I say, makes us free and fit to look upon so great a light of the Gospel.

units.la: Libertas vera per Christum,Ioan.8.v.32 36.Gal.4.31 & 5.13.Rom.6.18 & 8.2.20.1.Petr.1.18 & 2.16.2. Petr.2.19.ex cognitione veritatis,Ioan.8.32.& conscientia bona,1. Timoth.3.13 per fidem,Gal.3.25. Libertas Christiana charitati subiecta est,1.Cor.8.v.1 9. inter ædificationis & charitatis. ritatis terminos consistere debet, Roman. 14. v.19.20.21. 1.Corinth. 6. 12. in rebus mediis ad infirmorum fratrum conscientiam attemperanda est, 1.Cor. 11 29. Libertas spiritualis, 7. 22. cum seruitute carnali non pugnat, Ephes. 6.5.1.Petr.2.16. Libertare Christiana non abutendum, Rom. n.14.v 15 16.1.Corinth. 6. 12 & 10 23.& 8.v.8.9. Galat.5.13.1.1 et.2.16.abusus eius coercetur, 1.Corin.8.8. quomodo ea vsus sit Paulus, 9.v.15. 18.21. nempe vt non offenderet quenquam, ibid.& 2.Cor.11.12. Libertas prava & improbanda, Iob.11.12.Ierem.34.15. Ose.7.16.2. Pet.2. 18.19.Libertatis lex quae dicatur, Iac.1 25. Vide Lex libertatis.
units.tr: True liberty through Christ (John 8:32-36; Gal. 4:31; 5:13; Rom. 6:18; 8:2, 20; 1 Pet. 1:18; 2:16; 2 Pet. 2:19) comes from the knowledge of the truth (John 8:32) and a good conscience (1 Tim. 1:13), and through faith (Gal. 3:25). Christian liberty is subject to charity (1 Cor. 8:1-9); it must remain within the bounds of edification and charity (Rom. 14:19-21; 1 Cor. 6:12). In things indifferent it must be adjusted to the conscience of weaker brothers (1 Cor. 10:29). Spiritual liberty does not clash with carnal servitude (1 Cor. 7:22; Eph. 6:5; 1 Pet. 2:16). Christian liberty must not be abused (Rom. 14:14-15; 1 Cor. 6:12; 10:23; 8:8-9; Gal. 5:13; 1 Pet. 2:16). Its abuse is restrained (1 Cor. 8:8). Paul used it thus (1 Cor. 9:15, 18, 21), namely so as not to offend anyone (ibid.; 2 Cor. 11:12). Perverse and reprehensible liberty (Job 11:12; Jer. 34:15; Hos. 7:16; 2 Pet. 2:18-19). What is called the law of liberty (James 1:25). See "Law of liberty".

units.la: LIBERTAS Loquendi, (παρρησία, subseruit veritati.)
units.tr: FREEDOM OF SPEECH (parrhēsia, which serves the truth)

units.la: Est animi nostri, atque conscientiae integritas, quae neque nobis ipsis, neque aliis quicquam eorum, quae significanda sunt, simulare aut dissimulare propter Dei praeceptum vult, neque etiam potest, Act. 4.13.2.Cor. 3.12. Eph. 6.19.
units.tr: It is the integrity of our mind and conscience, which by God's command wills neither to feign nor to conceal, either toward ourselves or toward others, anything that must be made known, and indeed cannot do so (Acts 4:13; 2 Cor. 3:12; Eph. 6:19).

units.la: LIBERUM esse iustitiae, est non tubesse imperio iustitiae, Roman. 6. 20. nec iustitiam vllum ius in quempiam habere.
units.tr: To be free from justice is not to be under the rule of justice (Rom. 6:20), nor for justice to have any right over anyone.

units.la: LIBERUM ARBITRIUM hominis, est voluntas eius eligens aut repudians id, quod intellectus eligendum aut repudiandum esse dictat.
units.tr: The free will of man is his will choosing or rejecting what the intellect dictates is to be chosen or rejected.

units.la: Arbitrium ante lapsum erat liberum omnibus modis, scilicet, a seruitute cum peccati, tum miseriae peccatum comitantis: a coactione: quia ad bonum vel ad malum inclinare, aut alterutrum eligere, & stare aut labi suis viribus, poterat Adamus.
units.tr: Before the Fall, the will was free in every way: free, that is, from the bondage both of sin and of the misery that accompanies sin, and free from compulsion. Adam was able to incline to good or to evil, to choose either, and to stand or fall by his own powers.

units.la: Post lapsum, Arbitrium in non renatis, Est tum liberum, scilicet ab omni coactione, sed tantum ad malum in omnibus rebus tam spiritualibus quam civilibus & externis. Nihil enim nisi peccare possunt: Rom. 7.18. Libertas enim ad bonum per peccatum amissa est: Et quicquid ex fide non est, peccatum est: Rom.14.23. Tum seruum & captiuum in bonis & sanctis rebus, atque in primis ad salutem & vitam aeternam spectantibus. Vide Gen.6.5. Psal. 14.1.2 3. 4.Matth.7.18.Rom.7.18.
units.tr: After the Fall, the will in the unregenerate is free, that is, free from all compulsion, but only towards evil in all things, both spiritual and civil and external. For they can do nothing but sin (Rom. 7:18). The freedom to good was lost through sin, and whatever is not of faith is sin (Rom. 14:23). The will is then a slave and captive in good and holy things, and above all in those that concern salvation and eternal life. See Gen. 6:5; Ps. 14:1-3; Matt. 7:18; Rom. 7:18.

units.la: In Renatis liberum partim ad bonum, partim ad malum. Ad bonum singulari Spiritus S. beneficio, qui incohat, continuat & perficit in iis conuersionem ad Deum & bona opera. Nec Renati sunt otiosi, sed acti a Spiritu S. agunt. Deut.30.6.Rom.6.18.Phil.2.13. Ad malum: quia regeneratio in hac vita incohatur tantum: unde semper manent peccati reliquiae quae agnitionem in mente non nihil obscurant, & voluntatem inclinant, ut non illico faciamus quae volumus: Rom. 7.18.19.
units.tr: In the regenerate, the will is free partly towards good and partly towards evil. Towards good, by the singular benefit of the Holy Spirit, who begins, continues, and completes in them their conversion to God and good works. Nor are the regenerate idle, but acted upon by the Holy Spirit they act (Deut. 30:6; Rom. 6:18; Phil. 2:13). Towards evil, because regeneration is only begun in this life. Hence the remnants of sin always remain, which somewhat obscure knowledge in the mind and incline the will, so that we do not at once do what we want (Rom. 7:18-19).

units.la: Post hanc vitam Arbitrium, Beatorum liberum erit tantum ad bonum: ita ut nihil nisi bonum velle possint. Cum enim Deus erit omnia in omnibus, 1.Cor.15.28. Regeneratio perfecta erit. Matth.22.30. 1.Ioh.3.2.
units.tr: After this life, the will of the blessed will be free only towards good, so that they can will nothing but good. For when God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), regeneration will be complete (Matt. 22:30; 1 John 3:2).

units.la: Damnatorum servuum ad malum erit tantum: quia semper in regno satanae manebunt. Matth.25.46.
units.tr: The will of the damned will be a slave only to evil, because they will always remain in the kingdom of Satan (Matt. 25:46).

Free will was given to Adam at the beginning, because he was created in the image of God (which is a participation in divine wisdom, justice, integrity, truth and innocence), Gen. 1:27; 5:1; 9:6; Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:9. But he lost it for himself and his posterity (Eccl. 7:29; John 8:34; Rom. 5:12). Hence all men are declared to be without free will: Gen. 6:3, 5; 8:21; Deut. 12:8; 29:4; 30:6; 1 Kings 8:58; Ps. 51:12; 62:10; 94:11; 119:18, 34, 36; Prov. 16:9; Isa. 26:19; 55:1; 60:2; Jer. 13:23; 17:9; 24:7; 30:21; 31:18, 33; 32:29-30; Heb. 8:10; Ezek. 11:19; 36:26; Hos. 13:9; Matt. 16:17; John 1:5, 13; 3:6, 27; 6:44; 8:34; 15:4-5; Rom. 6:18, 20; 7:15, 19; 8:6-7; 9:16; 12:2; 14:4; 1 Cor. 1:31; 2:14; 4:7; 12:3, 6; 15:10; 2 Cor. 3:5; 6:17; Eph. 1:18; 2:3, 5; 4:17-18, 22; 6:13; Gal. 5:22; Phil. 1:6; 2:13; Col. 1:21; 1 Thess. 5:23; 2 Tim. 2:1; Titus 3:5; Heb. 12:15; 13:21; James 1:17-18; 1 Pet. 2:9; 2 Pet. 1:3; 2:19. (See MERITS are overthrown.) ¶ But on the contrary the Papists contend that free will remained even after the Fall, from Gen. 4:7; Deut. 30:19; Josh. 24:15; Ps. 27:9; Wis. 9:10; Matt. 24:37; 1 Cor. 3:9; 7:37, etc. ¶ That it cooperates with the grace of God: 1 Sam. 7:3; 1 Chr. 12:14; Ps. 10:17; 73:13; Prov. 16:1, 5, 9; Eccl. 2:26; Isa. 1:6, 17-18; 40:3; 46:8; 56:6-7; Jer. 3:1, 12, 22; 4:3-4, 14; 7:3; 18:8, 11; 25:5; 26:13; 32:15; Ezek. 18:21-22, 27-28, 30-31; 33:14-16, 19; Zech. 1:3; Mal. 3:7; Matt. 3:2-3; 11:33; 12:28; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4; John 1:12, 23; 7:37; Acts 3:19; 8:22; 9:6; 10:35; Rom. 10:13; 1 Cor. 3:9; 15:10; 2 Cor. 7:1; Eph. 5:14; Phil. 2:12-13; 4:13; Col. 1:29; 1:9-10; 1 Tim. 4:16; 2 Tim. 2:21; Heb. 4:16; 12:12-13; James 4:8; 1 Pet. 1:22; 1 John 3:3; Rev. 3:20.

units.la: LIBERALITAS, Est ea animi virtus, per quam pecunias nostras damus quibus oportet, & quo modo oportet
units.tr: Liberality is that virtue of the mind by which we give our money to those to whom we ought, and in the way we ought

units.la: non spe recipiendi totidé aut alterius mercedis: sed solius præcepti & gloriæ Dei respectu, & affectu proximi subleuandi. Huic opponuntur Prodigalitas & Auaritia.
units.tr: not in hope of receiving as much back or some other reward, but with respect only to the command and the glory of God, and out of affection for relieving our neighbour. Its opposites are prodigality and avarice.

units.la: LIBERALITAS commendatur, Prouerb. 11. 26. & 28. 16. Tit. 3. 13. Liberalitatis bona, Prou. 28. 27. Liberalitatis exempla: Rex Sodomorum, Gen. 14. 21. Rebecca, 24. 18. Iacob, 33. 10. Moses, Exo. 2. 17. Israelitæ, 36. 5. Dauid, 1 Sam. 30. 26. 2. Sam. 9. 7. Sobi & Naas, 17. 28. Berzellai, 19. 32. Regina Saba, 1 Reg. 10. 10. quidam Princeps ex Tribu Ephraim, 2 Par. 28. 15. units.tr: There are two Libyas; one is Cyrenaica (Acts 2.10). The part of Libya that lies around Cyrene. After this, Libya of the Ethiopians, reaching as far as the southern ocean.

units.tr: The tree of life, Gen. 2.9; 3.22; Prov. 3.18; 11.30; 13.12; 15.4; Rev. 2.7; 22.2, 14. Water made sweet by a piece of wood thrown into it, Exod. 15.25. The hewers of wood among the Israelites, Deut. 29.11; Josh. 9.23. The parable of the trees, Judg. 9.8 etc. Gathering wood on the Sabbath was forbidden, Num. 15.32-35. "Lignum" for "tree," a Hebraism, Rev. 2.7; 22.2. John calls the tree of life that divine power which will nourish us in that blessed and everlasting immortality, and likewise Paradise, the place appointed for our blessedness. The tree planted in that most pleasant garden was a type of these things; from it we fell in Adam, who was a living natural being. Paul also, in the manner of an anagogical sense, sets up two Adams opposed to one another, 1 Cor. 15.45 etc.

A good tongue is praised, Prov. 15.4; 18.21. The tongue is governed by God, Prov. 16.1 (?). The tongue must be governed and restrained, Lev. 19.16; Job 21; Ps. 34.13-14; 52.4; 141.3; Prov. 4.24; 10.19; 11.9; 12.13-14, 19; 13.2-3; 15.2; 16.27; 17.20, 27; 18.21; 21.23; 25.28; 26.20; 30.11; Eccles. 5.2; Matt. 12.36; Luke 6.45; 1 Cor. 15.33; 1 Pet. 2.1 and 10; James 1.19-20; 3.5, 8; 4.11. (See on the restraint of the tongue.) The tongue can be restrained only with difficulty, James 3. The tongue of angels stands for something singular and outstanding, 1 Cor. 13.1. (See the entry on the tongues of angels.) The tongue is more harmful than it seems, Prov. 18.21; James 1.26; 3.5 etc. The division of tongues arose from pride, Gen. 11.8. The outstanding gift of tongues was given to the apostles, Acts 10.46; 1 Cor. 12.7, 10, 28. See [loquacity].

units.la: LIS, Est, vel in iudicio vel extra iudicium, duorum vel plurium inter se de re eadem animosa, & vindictæ nec iuris quærendi gratiâ facta, disceptatio & quæstio.
units.tr: A dispute, or quarrel, is a contest and inquiry between two or more people about the same matter, carried on with hostility and for the sake of revenge rather than of seeking justice; it takes place either in court or outside it.

units.la: LITERA, pro externa ceremonia, & à spirituali suo fine separata, Roman. 2. verf. 27.29. Vetustas literæ, pro lege, 7.6. pro verbi Dei prædicatione ad animum vsque non penetrante, 2 Corinth.3.6. literam vocare solet paulus non raro legem ipsam nudam, & à Christo separatam, hoc est tanquam mortuum quoddam scriptum in sese, quod ad salutem nihil prosit carnis nostræ vitio, quia videlicet morbum duntaxat indicare potest in visceribus nostris labentem, sanare verò non item. Quin etiam quia lex illa extra Christi Spiritum considerata, peccatum in nobis irritat, vt fiat supra modum peccans & morti nos dedat, Roman.7.13. idcirco dicit paulus, litteram occidere, 2 Corinth.3.6. & Mosis ministerium vocat ministerium mortis & condemnationis, ibid. versic.7.& Legem quoque peccati virtutem, 1 Corinth.15.56. quæ quidem de vniuersa lege Mosis accipienda sunt, quatenus extra Christum consideratur. Huic autem literæ idem Paulus opponit Spiritum, id est, Sancti Spiritus efficaciam, 2 Corinth.3.6. quæ tum Christi iustitiam, tum etiam legem ipsam in cordibus nostris insculpsit: qua ratione dicitur Spiritus viuificare quos lex occidit: Et Euangelium ministerium, ministerio Mosis ex illa hypothesi oppositum, dicitur non esse literæ, sed Spiritus, 2 Cor.3.v.6.&c. Interdum autem hæc literæ & Spiritus antithesis peculiariter spectatur in ceremoniis, vt Rom. 2.v.27.29.& sæpe alibi. Tunc igitur γράμμα, hoc est, litteram vocat paulus externum signum, ab ipsius signi fine, siue à virtute seiunctum, quam vocat Spiritum: quoniam externa ceremonia est res per se mortua, & inutilis, nisi coniungatur veritas, quasi illius vita. Itaque Circumcisio per literam (vt & hoc addatur) seu carnis (de qua agitur Rom.2.v.27.29.) est pelliculæ abscissio. Circumcisio autem per Spiritum, siue cordis, est spiritualis finis illius ceremoniæ: vera nempe pietas, iustitia, cæteraque virtutes, quibus vere demum populus Dei à profanis gentibus discernitur.
units.tr: "Letter" means an external ceremony, separated from its spiritual purpose, Rom. 2.27, 29. "The old letter" means the law, Rom. 7.6; it means preaching of God's Word that does not penetrate to the mind, 2 Cor. 3.6. Paul often calls the letter the bare law itself, separated from Christ; that is, a kind of dead writing in itself, which by the fault of our flesh does nothing for salvation, since it can only indicate the disease that is wasting away in our inner parts, but cannot heal it. Indeed, because that law, considered apart from the Spirit of Christ, stirs up sin in us so that we sin beyond measure and hand ourselves over to death, Rom. 7.13, therefore Paul says that "the letter kills," 2 Cor. 3.6, and he calls the ministry of Moses "the ministry of death and condemnation," ibid. v. 7; and he calls the law "the power of sin," 1 Cor. 15.56. These things are to be understood of the whole law of Moses, insofar as it is considered apart from Christ. Paul sets the Spirit against this letter, that is, the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, 2 Cor. 3.6, which has engraved both the righteousness of Christ and the law itself in our hearts. For this reason the Spirit is said to make alive those whom the law kills. And the gospel ministry, set against the ministry of Moses on that hypothesis, is said not to be of the letter but of the Spirit, 2 Cor. 3.6 etc. Sometimes this antithesis of letter and Spirit is looked at particularly in ceremonies, as in Rom. 2.27, 29, and often elsewhere. Then Paul calls the external sign "letter" (γράμμα), that is, cut off from the purpose or power of the sign itself, which he calls the Spirit; for an external ceremony is in itself a dead and useless thing unless truth is joined to it as its life. Thus circumcision "by the letter" (to add this too), or "of the flesh" (of which Rom. 2.27, 29 speaks), is the cutting away of the foreskin. But circumcision "by the Spirit," or of the heart, is the spiritual end of that ceremony: namely true godliness, righteousness and the other virtues, by which at last the people of God is truly distinguished from the profane nations.

units.la: LONGANIMITAS, sive lenitas, μακροθυμία, Est cum durissima quæque & toleratu difficillima, nobis iniuste illata, non tantum patienter, sed etiam cum gaudio ad extremum vsque spiritum, totaque vita propter Dei voluntatem perferimus. Cuius effecta sunt perseverantia in bono, & constantia ad finem vsque.
units.tr: LONGANIMITY, or gentleness [μακροθυμία]. It is when we bear with patience, and even with joy, to the last breath and throughout our whole life for the sake of God's will, the hardest and most difficult things that are unjustly inflicted on us. Its effects are perseverance in good and constancy to the end.

units.la: LONGANIMITAS commendatur, Gal.5.22. Col.1 11. Longanimitatis exempla: Abraham diu expectauit prolem ex Sara, tandem centenarius suscepit, Gen.21.5. Deus, Exo.34.6. fideles 1.Per.3.15. Iob, Iob 13.15. Abacuc. Abac.2, 3. Paulus, 2.Cor 6.v.4.5.6. Simeon, Luc.2.25.
units.tr: LONGANIMITY is commended (Gal. 5.22; Col. 1.11). Examples of longanimity: Abraham waited a long time for a child by Sarah, and at last at a hundred years old received him (Gen. 21.5); God (Exod. 34.6); the faithful (1 Pet. 3.15); Job (Job 13.15); Habakkuk (Hab. 2.3); Paul (2 Cor. 6.4–6); Simeon (Luke 2.25).

units.la: [LONGITUDO Geometrica, Gen.6.15. & 13.17. Exo.c.25 10. & 26.2.27.1. Ezec.à c,40. ad finem Zach.2.2. & 5.2. Longitudo mystica, Eph.3.18. Longitudo, spatium dierum, Deut. 30.20. Ps.91.16. Prou.3.v.2.16.]
units.tr: [LENGTH. Geometrical length (Gen. 6.15; 13.17; Exod. 25.10; 26.2; 27.1; Ezek. 40 at the end; Zech. 2.2; 5.2). Mystical length (Eph. 3.18). Length, a span of days (Deut. 30.20; Ps. 91.16; Prov. 3.2, 16).]

units.la: LOQVACITAS, Est linguæ garrulitas ambulatoria de nugis non congruenti tempore philosophans. Ratio vero ipsa, siue natura docet frenandam esse linguam, quia binas aures dedit, vnam tantum linguam, eamque duplici vallo, nimirum dentium & labiorum coercitam ne temere exiret. Itaque vectes & frenu est illi iniiciendum, Eccle.28.28.
units.tr: LOQUACITY is the chattering of the tongue, wandering about and philosophising on trifles at an unsuitable time. Reason itself, or nature, teaches that the tongue must be restrained, since she gave us two ears and only one tongue, and has hemmed it in with a double wall, namely of teeth and lips, so that it may not rush out rashly. Therefore bars and a bridle must be put on it (Ecclus. 28.28).

units.la: LOQVACITAS damnatur, Prou.29.20, Colos.4.6. (Vide MVLTILOQVIVM vitiosum,) Loquacitatis exempla: Eua, Genes.3. 2. Dalila Samsonis vxor, Iudi.14.v.16.17, & 16.v.16.17. Vxor Iob, Iob 2.v.9.10.
units.tr: LOQUACITY is condemned (Prov. 29.20; Col. 4.6). (See Vicious Talkativeness.) Examples of loquacity: Eve (Gen. 3.2); Delilah, wife of Samson (Judg. 14.16–17; 16.16–17); the wife of Job (Job 2.9–10).

units.la: LOQVI in tempore prudentia est, Prou. 25.11. Loquendum non statim, nec temerè, 13.3. & 17.v.27.28. Iac.1.19. Loquenda sunt vera, honesta, & quæ auditoribus prodesse queat, Exo.22.28. Psalm.14.1. &c. Prou.13.2. & 24.26. Eccles.5.2. & 7.17. Mar.5.37. & 12.36. Eph.4.29. & 5.3. Col.3.8. 1.Pet.3.10. loquendi tempus & opportunitas, Prou.15.23. & 25.11. Eccles.8.6. quomodo loquendum, Iob.6.29. Prou.15.4. & 16.v.20.22. & 29.11. Eccles.4.14. & 5.16. & 6.5. Coloss.4.6. loquendi formulæ ex comparatione, Osee.6.6. Matth.9.13. & 12.7. Luc.14.26. 1.Petri 2.19. loqui coram insipientibus intempestiuum, Prou.23.9. loqui ad cor, est blandè & suauiter alloqui ac consolari, Genesis 34.3. & 50.21. Iudic.19.3. Ruth.2.13.2. Sam.19.7. Esa.40.2. Osee.2.14. hoc est, loqui quæ sint ei cordi. loqui in corde, est cogitare, Psalm.4.5. & 14.1. & 35.15. & 53.2. loqui, pro polliceri, Lucæ 1.v.55.70. Hebraismus.
units.tr: SPEAKING. Prudence is needed in speaking at the right time (Prov. 25.11). One should not speak at once, nor rashly (Prov. 13.3; 17.27–28; James 1.19). Things spoken must be true, honourable, and such as can benefit the hearers (Exod. 22.28; Ps. 14.1, etc.; Prov. 13.2; 24.26; Eccl. 5.2; 7.17; Mark 5.37; 12.36; Eph. 4.29; 5.3; Col. 3.8; 1 Pet. 3.10). The time and opportunity for speaking (Prov. 15.23; 25.11; Eccl. 8.6). How one should speak (Job 6.29; Prov. 15.4; 16.20–22; 29.11; Eccl. 4.14; 5.16; 6.5; Col. 4.6). Forms of speech by comparison (Hos. 6.6; Matt. 9.13; 12.7; Luke 14.26; 1 Pet. 2.19). To speak before fools is unseasonable (Prov. 23.9). To speak to the heart is to address and comfort kindly and gently (Gen. 34.3; 50.21; Judg. 19.3; Ruth 2.13; 2 Sam. 19.7; Isa. 40.2; Hos. 2.14), that is, to speak what is dear to someone's heart. To speak in the heart is to think (Ps. 4.5; 14.1; 35.15; 53.2). To speak, for to promise (Luke 1.55, 70). A Hebraism.

units.la: LOQVTIONIS Dei cum homine, & hominis cum Deo exempla: Cum Adam & Eua, Genes.3. v.9.10.11. Cain, 4. versi. 6.7. Noe, 6.13. & 7.1. & 8.15. & 9.1. Abrahamo, 12.1. & 13.14. & 15.1. & 17.1. & 18.13. Abimelech, 20.3. Isaac, 26.v.2.24. Iacobo 28.13. & 35.1. & 46.2. Laban, 31.24.29. Mose, Exod.3. 4. & 4.ver.11.12. Mose & Aarone, 6.13. Aarone & Maria, Numer.12.4. Iosua, Iof.1.1. & 4.1. & 7.10. Gedeone, Iudi, 6.39. & 7.2. Israelitis, 10.v.10.11. & 20.23. Samuele, 1 Sam.3.v.10.17. & 8.7. & 15.10. & 16.1. Dauide, 23.4 2.Sam.2.1. Nathã, 7.4. Salomone, 1 Reg.3.5. & 9.v.2.3. & 11.11. Semeia, 12.22. Ahija, 14.5. Elia, 1 Reg.17.2.8.9. & 18.1. & 19.9. & 21.18. Manasse, 2 Paral 33.10. Esaia, Esa.7.3. & 38.4. Ieremia, Ierem.1. 4. Ezechiele, Ezech.2.1.
units.tr: Examples of God speaking with man, and man with God: with Adam and Eve (Gen. 3.9–11); with Cain (Gen. 4.6–7); with Noah (Gen. 6.13; 7.1; 8.15; 9.1); with Abraham (Gen. 12.1; 13.14; 15.1; 17.1; 18.13); with Abimelech (Gen. 20.3); with Isaac (Gen. 26.2, 24); with Jacob (Gen. 28.13; 35.1; 46.2); with Laban (Gen. 31.24, 29); with Moses (Exod. 3.4; 4.11–12); with Moses and Aaron (Exod. 6.13); with Aaron and Miriam (Num. 12.4); with Joshua (Josh. 1.1; 4.1; 7.10); with Gideon (Judg. 6.39; 7.2); with the Israelites (Judg. 10.10–11; 20.23); with Samuel (1 Sam. 3.10, 17; 8.7; 15.10; 16.1); with David (1 Sam. 23.4; 2 Sam. 2.1); with Nathan (2 Sam. 7.4); with Solomon (1 Kings 3.5; 9.2–3; 11.11); with Shemaiah (1 Kings 12.22); with Ahijah (1 Kings 14.5); with Elijah (1 Kings 17.2, 8–9; 18.1; 19.9; 21.18); with Manasseh (2 Chron. 33.10); with Isaiah (Isa. 7.3; 38.4); with Jeremiah (Jer. 1.4); with Ezekiel (Ezek. 2.1).

units.la: [LOQVITVR Deus, Gen.18.33. & passim hæc formula occurrit. loquitur Pater, Hebr.1. & 5.5. loquitur Filius ante & post incarnationem. loquitur Spiritus S. Matt.10.20. Ioh.16.13. Act.6.10. & 28.25. loquitur S. Angelus, 2 Reg.1.3.15. Dan.8.9.10. cap. Luc.1.19. Act.8.26. & 10.7. Apoc.17.1. & 21.v.9.15. loquitur Angelus malus, Ioan.8.44. loquitur bestia mystica, Apoc.13.v.5.11.15.]
units.tr: [GOD SPEAKS (Gen. 18.33), and this formula occurs throughout. The Father speaks (Heb. 1; 5.5). The Son speaks before and after the incarnation. The Holy Spirit speaks (Matt. 10.20; John 16.13; Acts 6.10; 28.25). A holy angel speaks (2 Kings 1.3, 15; Dan. 8.9–10; chapter; Luke 1.19; Acts 8.26; 10.7; Rev. 17.1; 21.9, 15). An evil angel speaks (John 8.44). The mystical beast speaks (Rev. 13.5, 11, 15).]

units.la: LOQVVTIONIS Angelorum cum hominibus & hominum cum Angelis exempla: Cum Agar, Gen.16.ver.8.9. Loth 19.12. Agar, 21.17. Abraham, 21.11. Balaam, Num.22.ver.32. &c. Israelitis, Iudic.2.4. Gedeone, 6.20. Manue, 13.13. cum Propheta Dei, 1 Reg.18. Elia, 19.7. God, 1 par.21.18. [Cum Zacharia, Luc.1.13. &c. cum Maria eodem, c.v.30. &c. cum IoseIosepho Matt. 1.20. & 2.20. cum pastoribus Bethlehemi-ticis, Luc. 2.10. cum Christo, Luc. 22.43. cum mulieribus, Matt. 28.5. cum Maria Magdal. Ioann. 20.13. cum Apostolis, Actor. 1.11. & 5.20. cum Philippo, Actor. 8.26. cum Cornelio, Actor. 10.3. cū Petro, Act. 12.8. cum Paulo, Act. 27.24. cum Ioanne, multi{?}vicibus, in Apocalypsi.
units.tr: Examples of angels speaking with men and men with angels: with Hagar (Gen. 16.8–9); with Lot (Gen. 19.12); with Hagar again (Gen. 21.17); with Abraham (Gen. 21.11); with Balaam (Num. 22.32, etc.); with the Israelites (Judg. 2.4); with Gideon (Judg. 6.20); with Manoah (Judg. 13.13); with a prophet of God (1 Kings 18); with Elijah (1 Kings 19.7); with Gad (1 Chron. 21.18). [With Zechariah (Luke 1.13, etc.); with Mary, the same chapter, v. 30, etc.; with Joseph (Matt. 1.20; 2.20); with the shepherds of Bethlehem (Luke 2.10); with Christ (Luke 22.43); with the women (Matt. 28.5); with Mary Magdalene (John 20.13); with the apostles (Acts 1.11; 5.20); with Philip (Acts 8.26); with Cornelius (Acts 10.3); with Peter (Acts 12.8); with Paul (Acts 27.24); with John, many times, in the Apocalypse.]

units.la: Loquitur creatura ratione carens Num. 22.28. Iudic. 9.12. Iob. 28.14. & 40.22. Dan. 7.v.8. 11.20. 2 Petr. 2.16. Apoc. 10.v.3.4. ] Gen. 3.1.4.
units.tr: A creature lacking reason speaks (Num. 22.28; Judg. 9.12; Job 28.14; 40.22; Dan. 7.8; 11.20; 2 Pet. 2.16; Rev. 10.3–4)] Gen. 3.1, 4.

units.la: LORICA hominis, 1 Sam. 17.v.5. 38.2 Par. 26 14. Nehem. 4.16. Ierem. 46.4. Ezech. 23.24. & 38.4. Lorica Dei, Esai. 59. 17. Lorica filiorum Dei, Ephes. 6.14. 1 Thess. 5.8. Lorica satellitum Antichristi, Apoc. 9.v.9 17. ]
units.tr: A man's BREASTPLATE (1 Sam. 17.5, 38; 2 Chron. 26.14; Neh. 4.16; Jer. 46.4; Ezek. 23.24; 38.4). The breastplate of God (Isa. 59.17). The breastplate of the sons of God (Eph. 6.14; 1 Thess. 5.8). The breastplate of the soldiers of Antichrist (Rev. 9.9, 17).

units.la: LOTH filius Aran, Genes. 11.27. vir dives, 13.5. captivus abducitur, 14.12. ab Abrahamo liberatur, v. 16. ab Angelis eripitur ex incendio Sodomorum, 19.vers. 15.17. vxor eius in statuam commutatur, v. 26. Luc. 17.32. cum filiabus incestum committit, Gene. 19.v.33.34. iustus dicitur, 2 Pet. 2.7. (Lot, 1. absconditus). Crucians animā ob impios: ibid.
units.tr: LOT, son of Haran (Gen. 11.27). A rich man (Gen. 13.5). He is taken captive (Gen. 14.12) and is freed by Abraham (v. 16). He is snatched by angels from the burning of Sodom (Gen. 19.15–17). His wife is turned into a statue (v. 26; Luke 17.32). He commits incest with his daughters (Gen. 19.33–34). He is called righteous (2 Pet. 2.7). (Lot, that is, hidden.) Tormenting his soul over the wicked (ibid.).

units.la: LOTIO pedum, Genes. 18.4. & 19.2. Ioan. 13.v.4. 14.1. Timot. 5.10.
units.tr: WASHING OF FEET (Gen. 18.4; 19.2; John 13.4–5, 14; 1 Tim. 5.10).

units.la: LVCAS Medicus Antiochenus, scripsit Euangelium, & acta Apostolorum. Colos. 4.14. Lucas Pauli adiutor, 2 Tim. 4. 11. Philem. v. 24.
units.tr: LUKE, a physician of Antioch, wrote the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles (Col. 4.14). Luke, companion of Paul (2 Tim. 4.11; Philem. 24).

units.la: LVCEO metaphoricè de vitæ sanctimonia cum sincerę veritatis professione coniuncta, dictum, Matt. 5.16. Ioann. 5. 35. Philip. 2.15. Item, de illustri illa cognitione Filij Dei, mundo potenter & gratiosè sese patefacientis, Ioan. 1.15. & 1 Ioan. 2.8.
units.tr: TO SHINE is used metaphorically of holiness of life joined with the sincere profession of truth (Matt. 5.16; John 5.35; Phil. 2.15). Likewise, of that illustrious knowledge of the Son of God, which reveals itself powerfully and graciously to the world (John 1.5; 1 John 2.8).

units.la: LVCERNA, Lux æterna Ecclesiæ, 2 Sam. 22,29. Apocal. 21.23. Lux piorum, verbum Dei Psalm. 119.10.5. Prou. 6.23.2. Pet. 1.19. Lux Ecclesiæ in ministerio & vitæ puritate, Ioan. 5.35. Lux populi, seu laudatus princeps, subditis merito charus: quo sublato malorum tenebræ suboriuntur, 2. Sam. 21.17, Psalm. 18.29. Dei benignitas & veritas Domui Dauidis seu regno Iudæ clementer affulgens, 1 Reg. 11.36. & 15.4.2. Reg. 8.19.2. Par. 21.7. gratiosa Dei præsentia, hominem fouens, Iob. 29.3. gloria Ecclesiæ sub Euangelio, Psal. 132.17. Anima hominis, Prou. 20.27. Oculus, Matt. 6. 22. Iudicij diuini designatio, Sophon. 1.12. Opus, studium, Prou. 21.4. Prosperitas Iob. 18.6. & 21.17. & 29.3. Lucernæ tabernaculi septem, Exod. 25.37, quando, & cur accensæ, Ex.27.208. Leuitic.24.3.1. Sam.3 3. Earum dispositio, forma, oleum, Exod.25.37. & 27.20. Num.8.2.3.
units.tr: LAMP. The eternal light of the Church (2 Sam. 22.29; Rev. 21.23). The light of the pious is the word of God (Ps. 119.105; Prov. 6.23; 2 Pet. 1.19). The light of the Church in the ministry and purity of life (John 5.35). The light of the people, or a praised prince, justly dear to his subjects, when he is removed the darkness of evils rises (2 Sam. 21.17; Ps. 18.29). The goodness and truth of God graciously shining on the house of David or the kingdom of Judah (1 Kings 11.36; 15.4; 2 Kings 8.19; 2 Chron. 21.7). The gracious presence of God, cherishing man (Job 29.3). The glory of the Church under the Gospel (Ps. 132.17). The soul of man (Prov. 20.27). The eye (Matt. 6.22). The designation of divine judgment (Zeph. 1.12). Work, zeal (Prov. 21.4). Prosperity (Job 18.6; 21.17; 29.3). The seven lamps of the tabernacle (Exod. 25.37): when and why they were lit (Exod. 27.20–21; Lev. 24.3; 1 Sam. 3.3). Their arrangement, form, and oil (Exod. 25.37; 27.20; Num. 8.2–3).

units.la: LVCIFER, aurora, matutinum tempus, Iob. 11.17. Astera mos poli antarctici, Iob.38.32. Rex Babylonis, in summa dignitatem euectus, & inter alios principes, sicut stella matutina in cœlo fulgens, Esai.14.12. Aurora mystica et multitudo filiorum Dei, Psalm. 110.3. Illustris doctrina Euangelij, 2 Petr.1.19.
units.tr: LUCIFER: dawn, the morning time (Job 11.17). The Star of the southern pole (Job 38.32). The king of Babylon, raised to the highest dignity and shining among the other princes like the morning star in the heavens (Isa. 14.12). The mystical dawn and the multitude of the sons of God (Ps. 110.3). The bright teaching of the Gospel (2 Pet. 1.19).

units.la: LVCIVS, Christi discipulus & doctor in Ecclesia Antiochena, Act.13.1. Rom.16.21.
units.tr: LUCIUS, a disciple of Christ and a teacher in the church at Antioch (Acts 13.1; Rom. 16.21).

units.la: LVCRVM eximium, Matt. 18.15. 1. Cor.9.20. Philip.1.21. & 3.7.8. Lucrum damnosum, 1 Tim.3.8. Tit.1.v.7.11.1.Pet.5.2.
units.tr: LUCRE, a remarkable gain (Matt. 18.15; 1 Cor. 9.20; Phil. 1.21; 3.7-8). Shameful gain (1 Tim. 3.8; Titus 1.7, 11; 1 Pet. 5.2).

units.la: LVCVS: Luci plantatio, Deut.16.21. Luci Gentium excindi iubentur, Exod.34.13. id quod Iosias praestitit, 2 Reg. 23.6.
units.tr: GROVE: the planting of a grove (Deut. 16.21). The groves of the nations are commanded to be cut down (Exod. 34.13), which Josiah carried out (2 Kings 23.6).

units.la: LVDERE: Ludunt coram vitulo Israëlitæ, Ehod.32.6. Ludit Dauid coram arca, 2 Sam.6.12. &c. Ludere pro ludentium modo gestire, 6.5.
units.tr: TO PLAY: the Israelites play before the calf (Exod. 32.6). David plays before the ark (2 Sam. 6.12, etc.). To play, meaning to exult in the manner of those who dance and play (2 Sam. 6.5).

units.la: LVGERE. Luctus, siue lugentium exempla: Abraham luget Sarram, Gen.23.2. Iacob Iosephum, 37.v.33.34. Filij Iacob Patrem, 50.10. Israelitæ transgressionem, Exod.33 4. Numeri 14.39. Mosis obitum, Deut.34.8. Filię Israel filiam Iephte Iudic. 11. v.39.40. populus Bethsamiticus cæsos, 1 Sam. 6.19. Samuel Saulem, 15.35. Israelitæ Samuelem, 28. Dauid Saulem & Ionatham, 2 Sam.1.17. Israel Abiam 1 Reg.14.v.17.18. Ephraim filios suos, 1 Paral.7.22. Iuda Ierusalem Iosiam, 2 Paral.35.24. Aman, Esth.6.12. Rachel (id est, tota illa vicinia Bethlehemitica, in qua Rachel Iacobi coniux in partu mortua sepultaque fuit) suos filios Ierem 31 15. Matt.2.18 Sacerdotes calamitatem, Ioel.1.8. (Vide FLETVS & mortuus.)
units.tr: TO MOURN. Mourning, or examples of those who mourn: Abraham mourns Sarah (Gen. 23.2). Jacob mourns Joseph (Gen. 37.33-34). The sons of Jacob mourn their father (Gen. 50.10). The Israelites mourn their transgression (Exod. 33.4; Num. 14.39). They mourn the death of Moses (Deut. 34.8). The daughters of Israel mourn the daughter of Jephthah (Judg. 11.39-40). The people of Beth-shemesh mourn those who were slain (1 Sam. 6.19). Samuel mourns Saul (1 Sam. 15.35). The Israelites mourn Samuel (1 Sam. 28). David mourns Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam. 1.17). Israel mourns Abijah (1 Kings 14.17-18). Ephraim mourns his sons (1 Chron. 7.22). Judah and Jerusalem mourn Josiah (2 Chron. 35.24). Haman (Esth. 6.12). Rachel (that is, the whole neighbourhood of Bethlehem, where Rachel, the wife of Jacob, died in childbirth and was buried) mourns her sons (Jer. 31.15; Matt. 2.18). The priests mourn the calamity (Joel 1.8). (See WEEPING and DEAD.)

units.la: Luctus mortuorum qualis tempore Christi, Matt.9.2. Lugentes beati, 5.4. Luget Dauid Amnomem filium, 2.Sa. 13.37. Lugendi non sunt mortui, 1 Thess.4.13. Lugenti bus consolatio promittitur, Lucæ.6 21. V. Esa.6.3. Apoc.21.4. Eccl.7.2.
units.tr: The mourning of the dead as it was in the time of Christ (Matt. 9.2). Blessed are those who mourn (Matt. 5.4). David mourns his son Amnon (2 Sam. 13.37). The dead are not to be mourned (1 Thess. 4.13). Consolation is promised to those who mourn (Luke 6.21). See Isa. 6.3; Rev. 21.4; Eccl. 7.2.

units.la: LVMBI mentis succingendi, Luc.12 35.1.Pet.1.13.
units.tr: LOINS: to gird up the mind (Luke 12.35; 1 Pet. 1.13).

units.la: [LVMEN, proprie lux à Deo creata, vel artificio humano accensa, tenebras exteriores illustrans, naturale & artificiale lumen frequenter dictum occurrit. Vide 1.cap.Gen. Esai.13.10. Ier.31.35. Ezech.32.7. Matth.10.27. & 24.29. Luc. 8.16. Act.16.29. Eph.5.13. Apoc.21.11. Figurate, lumen esse occuoculus & videndi facultas, Iudic.16.28. Psal.38.11. Luxcæle stis, Act.12.7. & 22.v.9.11.&26.13. Apoc.21.11. Christus redemptor, electis via ad felicitatem, veritas ad salutem, vita ad gloriam æternam, Esai.60.v.1.3. Luc.2.32. Ioann 1 8. &12.35. Apoc.21.23. Deus Israelitas illuminans & sanctificans. Esai.10.6.17. Doctor veritatis, Rom.2.19. Lætus rerum successus, ex Dei benegnitate fluens: pax & prosperitas gloriosa, Iob.22.28. & 25.3. & 29 3. Psalm.47.&36.10.&89 16.&112.4. Esai.58.8. Lux spiritualis, seu cognitio veritatis in verbo Dei patefactæ, Psal 119.105. Esai.2.5.&50.10. Ioann.8.12. Act.26.13. 1 Petr 2.9.1.Ioan 2 v.8,10. Lux naturalis in conscientia, Iob.24 13. Intelligentia seu sapientia carnis quam animalis homo veritati divinæ opponit, Esai.50.11. Mentis iudicium, Ratio, Matth.6.23. Luc.11.35. Regnum cæleste, in quo lux gratiæ, gloriæ, & vitæ æternæ, Coloss.1.12. Spes liberationis, Amos.8 9 Vita humana pace quadam externa fruens, Pro.20 21. Ierc.25.10. Dona spiritualia nobis in Christo communicata, Iacob 1.17.
units.tr: [LIGHT, properly the light created by God, or kindled by human skill, illuminating the outer darkness; it is frequently called natural and artificial light. See Gen. 1; Isa. 13.10; Jer. 31.35; Ezek. 32.7; Matt. 10.27; 24.29; Luke 8.16; Acts 16.29; Eph. 5.13; Rev. 21.11. Figuratively, light means: the eye and the faculty of seeing (Judg. 16.28; Ps. 38.11); heavenly light (Acts 12.7; 22.9, 11; 26.13; Rev. 21.11); Christ the Redeemer, the way to happiness for the elect, the truth for salvation, the life for eternal glory (Isa. 60.1-3; Luke 2.32; John 1.8; 12.35; Rev. 21.23); God illuminating and sanctifying Israel (Isa. 10.6, 17); the teacher of truth (Rom. 2.19); the joyful outcome of affairs, flowing from the kindness of God: peace and glorious prosperity (Job 22.28; 25.3; 29.3; Ps. 47; 36.10; 89.16; 112.4; Isa. 58.8); spiritual light, or knowledge of the truth revealed in the word of God (Ps. 119.105; Isa. 2.5; 50.10; John 8.12; Acts 26.13; 1 Pet. 2.9; 1 John 2.8, 10); natural light in the conscience (Job 24.13); the understanding or wisdom of the flesh, which the natural man sets against divine truth (Isa. 50.11); the judgment of the mind, reason (Matt. 6.23; Luke 11.35); the heavenly kingdom, in which is the light of grace, glory and eternal life (Col. 1.12); the hope of deliverance (Amos 8.9); human life enjoying a certain outward peace (Prov. 20.21; Jer. 25.10); spiritual gifts communicated to us in Christ (James 1.17).]

units.la: LVMINARIA in cœlo, Genes. 1 v.14 16. Psalm.136.7. Ezech. 32.8. fideles Phil.2.15. Lapas in tabernaculo, Exod 25.v.6.
units.tr: LIGHTS in the heavens (Gen. 1.14-16; Ps. 136.7; Ezek. 32.8). The faithful (Phil. 2.15). Lamps in the tabernacle (Exod. 25.6).

units.la: LVNA creatur, Genes.1.16. Lunam adorantes occidebantur, Deuter.17.v.3 5. V.c.4.v.19. Luna coram Deo splendida non est, Iob.25.5. Luna cursum intermisit: Iosue 10.12.13.
units.tr: THE MOON is created (Gen. 1.16). Those who worshipped the moon were put to death (Deut. 17.3-5; cf. 4.19). The moon is not bright before God (Job 25.5). The moon halted its course (Josh. 10.12-13).

units.la: LVNAE officium, Gen.1.16.18. Psal.104.19.&c.&148.3. Lunæ & aliis stellis sacrificat populus, Ier.44.17. &c. Lunæ gloria alia quàm Solis, 1 Cor.15.41.
units.tr: THE OFFICE OF THE MOON (Gen. 1.16, 18; Ps. 104.19, etc.; 148.3). The people sacrifice to the moon and to other stars (Jer. 44.17, etc.). The glory of the moon is other than that of the sun (1 Cor. 15.41).

units.la: LVNATICI, sunt qui ad lunæ crescentis aut decrescentis motum, habent peius aut melius: quales sunt qui mo bo comitiali, aut cerebri naturali defectione laborant, Mat.4.24.&17.15.
units.tr: THE MOON-STRUCK are those who, according to the motion of the waxing or waning moon, are worse or better; such are those who suffer from epilepsy or from a natural failing of the brain (Matt. 4.24; 17.15).

units.la: LVNATICI à Deo sanantur, Vide MIRACVLA.
units.tr: THE MOON-STRUCK are healed by God. See MIRACLES.

units.la: LVPANARIA quæ erant in domo Iehouæ destruxit Iosias, 2. Reg.22.7
units.tr: BROTHELS, which were in the house of Jehovah, were destroyed by Josiah (2 Kings 23.7).

units.la: LVPVS animal carniuorum, Ierem.5 6. Abac.1 8. Ezec.22. 27. Mat.10.16 homo crudelis, prædæ inhians, avarus, Gen. 49 27. Soph.3 3 homo moribus efferis, profanus, sed Euangelij voce ad Christum tandem convertendus, Esai 11.6. & 65.25. Seductor, mendacij doctor, sinceræ doctrinæ & disciplinæ aduersarius, Ioann.10 12. Act.20.29.
units.tr: WOLF: an animal of prey (Jer. 5.6; Hab. 1.8; Ezek. 22.27; Matt. 10.16); a cruel man, greedy for plunder and avaricious (Gen. 49.27; Zeph. 3.3); a man of savage manners, profane, yet at last to be turned to Christ by the voice of the Gospel (Isa. 11.6; 65.25); a seducer, a teacher of falsehood, an adversary of sound doctrine and discipline (John 10.12; Acts 20.29).

units.la: LVTERES ænei in Templo Salomonis, 1 Reg.7.38.
units.tr: BRONZE LAMPSTANDS in the Temple of Solomon (1 Kings 7.38).

units.la: LVX, Gen.1.3. Est qualitas cœlestis primo die creata, quæ rebus externè adueniens vi sua eas calefacit, adiuuatq; ut oriantur & viuant, & illustrat ut dignoscatur
units.tr: LIGHT (Gen. 1.3). It is a heavenly quality created on the first day, which, coming to things from outside, warms them by its power, helps them to rise and live, and illuminates them so that they may be discerned.

units.la: Lux pro doctrina Euangelij, Actor.26.23. pro Filio Dei, Ioan.1.8. pro lucis ipsius creatore, v.5. pro vi illa rationis & intelligentiæ in hominum animis accensa, v.4. pro cognitione gloriæ Dei, 2 Corinth.4.6. pro cælesti gloria & spirituali Angelorum intelligentia, 2. Corint.6.14. pro vitæ sanctimonia, Matth.5.16. Lux est Christus, Esa.9.1.& 42.6.& 49.6.& 60.v.1 19. Ioan.1.5. & 8.12.& 9.5.& 12.verf. 35 46, 1 Ioan.1.5. & 2.8. Lux sunt & Christiani, Prov.4. 18.Matth.5.14.15.16.Rom.2.19.Ephes.5.8.Philip.2.15, idque quibus de causis, Vide Fideles. Lux sunt Gentes post Christum cognitum, Ephes.5.8. in luce incedere, 1 Ioan. 1.7. dicuntur fideles, quatenus ipsis radij illius lucis, quæ ibidem esse, & in qua esse dicitur Deus, ad æternam beatitudem contendentibus prælucent. Lucis opera, omnis bonitas, Ephes.5.9. societatem cum illa habere, 1.Ioann.1.7.
units.tr: Light for the teaching of the Gospel (Acts 26.23); for the Son of God (John 1.8); for the very Creator of light (v. 5); for that power of reason and understanding kindled in the minds of men (v. 4); for the knowledge of the glory of God (2 Cor. 4.6); for the heavenly glory and spiritual understanding of the angels (2 Cor. 6.14); for the holiness of life (Matt. 5.16). Christ is the light (Isa. 9.1; 42.6; 49.6; 60.1, 19; John 1.5; 8.12; 9.5; 12.35, 46; 1 John 1.5; 2.8). Christians are also lights (Prov. 4.18; Matt. 5.14-16; Rom. 2.19; Eph. 5.8; Phil. 2.15), and see FAITHFUL for the reasons why. The Gentiles after Christ was known are lights (Eph. 5.8). To walk in the light (1 John 1.7) is said of the faithful, insofar as the rays of that light, in which God is said to be and in which he dwells, shine before those who strive towards eternal blessedness. The works of light are all goodness (Eph. 5.9). To have fellowship with it (1 John 1.7).

units.la: Luxus siue Luxuria, ἀσωτία, Est nimia cultus restitusque corporis nostri cura, vel etiam sumptus in eo nimius. Hęc autem varijs ex causis oriri potest, vel ex ambitione, vel ex turpi libidine atque placendi studio. Est etiam luxus, cum quis corpus alimentis onerat vltra necessitatem; Eph.5.18.
units.tr: LUXURY, or wantonness, [ἀσωτία], is an excessive care for the dress and adornment of our body, or also excessive expense on it. This may arise from various causes: from ambition, or from base lust and a desire to please. There is also luxury when someone burdens the body with food beyond need (Eph. 5.18).

units.la: Luxuria damnatur, Galat.5.19. Luxuriæ exempla: Antiquior mundus, Gen.6.1 Sodoma & aliæ ciuitates circumiacétes 19.13. Sichem, 34.2. Stupratores vxoris Leuitæ peregrini, Iudic.19.25. & 20.46. Abner,2. Sam.3.8. Herodiadis filia, Matt.14.7. Mar.6.22. Prodigus filius, Luc.15.13. Luxuria & superfluitas in vino; Eph.5.18.
units.tr: Luxury is condemned (Gal. 5.19). Examples of luxury: the world before the Flood (Gen. 6.1); Sodom and the neighbouring cities (Gen. 19.13); Shechem (Gen. 34.2); the foreign men who violated the Levite's wife (Judg. 19.25; 20.46); Abner (2 Sam. 3.8); the daughter of Herodias (Matt. 14.7; Mark 6.22); the prodigal son (Luke 15.13). Luxury and excess in wine (Eph. 5.18).

units.la: Lyza, quæ Bethel, ciuitas Chananææ in tribu Beniamin, Gen. 28.19.& 35.6 Ios.18.13. (1.amygdala)
units.tr: Lyza, which is Bethel, a city of Canaan in the tribe of Benjamin (Gen. 28.19; 35.6; Josh. 18.13). (1. almond tree)

units.la: Lycaonia prouincia, Asiæ minoris: Act.14.6.
units.tr: Lycaonia, a province of Asia Minor (Acts 14.6).

units.la: Lydia purpuraria credit in Christum, Act.16.14.
units.tr: Lydia, a seller of purple, believes in Christ (Acts 16.14).

units.la: Lysanias Abytenes tetrarcha: Luc.3.1.
units.tr: Lysanias, tetrarch of Abilene (Luke 3.1).

units.la: Lysias Tribunus, ciuis Romanus pretio pretiato factus, Act 22.28. paulum è manibus Iudæorū liberat, 23.10. puerū de insidiis paulo structis admonentem benignè audit, v.19. ad Felicem præsidem de paulo scribit, versi.26.27.
units.tr: Lysias, a tribune, made a Roman citizen for a large sum (Acts 22.28). He rescues Paul from the hands of the Jews for a time (Acts 23.10). He kindly hears a boy who warns him of a plot laid against Paul (v. 19). He writes to the governor Felix about Paul (vv. 26-27).

units.la: Lystra oppidum Lycaoniæ. Eò confugiunt paulus & Barnabas, Act.14.v.6.&c. Lystrenses Paulo & Barnabæ sacrificare volunt, v.13.18. V.2.Tim.3.11. Ibi Apostoli, sanato Claudo, dij vocantur &c. Act.14.10.&c.
units.tr: Lystra, a town of Lycaonia. Paul and Barnabas flee there (Acts 14.6, etc.). The Lystrans want to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas (vv. 13, 18). See 2 Tim. 3.11. There the Apostles, after healing a lame man, are called gods (Acts 14.10, etc.).

units.la: M
units.tr: M

units.la: MAACHA,filia Tholmai Regis Geffur vxor Dauidis mater Absalonis, 1.Par. 3.2.(i. attrita.)
units.tr: MAACHA, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, wife of David and mother of Absalom, 1 Chron. 3:2. (i.e. crushed.)

units.la: MAACHA filia Absalom, mater Abiam Regis Iuda, 1 Regum 15.2.appellatur Machaia,vel Michæa,2 Paral. v.20.21. 22.& 15.16. [ Aliarum multarum huius nominis mulierum & mentio, in lib.Sam.Reg.& Paral. virorum item.Sed ista omnia non sunt tanti momenti,vt describi necesse sit.]
units.tr: MAACHA, daughter of Absalom, mother of Abijam, king of Judah, is called in 1 Kings 15:2 Maachah or Michaiah, 2 Chron. 11:20-22 and 13:1-2. [Many other women and men of this name are mentioned in the books of Samuel, Kings and Chronicles. But none of these is of such importance that it must be described.]

units.la: IACEDA,vrbs in tribu Iuda à Iosua capitur,Iof.10.28. eius eo modo, quo Rex Ierichuntis, à Iosua tractatur,ibid. (Makiedah, i.fœtor verticis.)
units.tr: JEDA? Not this; see: IACEDA, a town in the tribe of Judah, taken by Joshua, Josh. 10:28. It was dealt with by Joshua in the same way as the king of Jericho, ibid. (Makkedah, i.e. stench of the head.)

units.la: MACEDONIA prouincia Græcorum:in eam vt euangelizet adducitur Paulus,Act.16.v.9.10.mittit eleemosynas pauperibus Ierosolymitanis,Rom.15 26.2.Corinth.8.2.Macedonum laus,2.Cor.8.v.1.2.3. zelus,11 9.
units.tr: MACEDONIA, a province of the Greeks. Paul is brought into it to preach the gospel, Acts 16:9-10. The Macedonians send alms to the poor of Jerusalem, Rom. 15:26; 2 Cor. 8:2. The praise of the Macedonians, 2 Cor. 8:1-3. Their zeal, 2 Cor. 9:2.

units.la: MACERIAM inter Gentes & Iudeos diruit Christus,Ephe. 2.14.
units.tr: Christ destroys the dividing wall between Gentiles and Jews, Eph. 2:14.

units.la: MACHIRITARVM possessio.Deut.3.15.Iof.17.v.1.3.
units.tr: The possession of the Machirites, Deut. 3:15; Josh. 17:1, 3.

units.la: MACVLA, peccatum, vitium, latens in corde, vnde erumpunt peccata externa,Iohu,22.17.Iob.31.7,Pf.15. 2. Cant, 4.7.Eph.5.27.1.Tim.1,14.2.Pet.2.13 Apoc.14.15.Vulnus alicui inflictum,Leuitic,24.19.22. Vitium in animali offerendo,Exod,12.5.Leui.1.10.& 9 3.& 14.10,Vitium in corpore hominis,lepra, Leui.13.31.&c. Vitium seu defectus corporis,Dan.1.4. Conuicium, Prou 9 7.
units.tr: SPOT, sin, a fault lying hidden in the heart, from which outward sins break forth: Job 22:17; Job 31:7; Ps. 15:2; Song 4:7; Eph. 5:27; 1 Tim. 1:14; 2 Pet. 2:13; Rev. 14:5. A wound inflicted on someone, Lev. 24:19-22. A blemish in an animal offered in sacrifice, Exod. 12:5; Lev. 1:10; 3:1; 4:3; 14:10. A blemish in the human body, leprosy, Lev. 13:31, etc. A defect or deformity of the body, Dan. 1:4. Reproach, Prov. 9:7.

units.la: MADIAN, filius Abraham ex Cetura,Gen.25 2.ab eo orti Madianitæ,qui ab Israelitis Dei iudicio cœduntur vnà cum Regibus eorum, Num.31.7. opprimunt Israelem, Iudic. 6.1.irruit in eos Gedeon,7.1.&c.mutuis sese vulneribus interficiunt,v.22.(i.Iudicium,seu contradictio.)
units.tr: MIDIAN, son of Abraham by Keturah, Gen. 25:2. From him sprang the Midianites, who were slain by the Israelites, together with their kings, by the judgment of God, Num. 31:7. They oppressed Israel, Judg. 6:1; Gideon attacked them, Judg. 7:1ff. They killed one another with mutual wounds, Judg. 7:22. (i.e. judgment, or contradiction.)

units.la: MAGDALVS, vrbs Ægypti, ad quam Israelitæ,cum exiissent de AEgypto,peruenerunt, priùs quàm mare transirent:Exod.14.2.Vbi Iudei quidam, Babyloniorum impetum declinantes, habitarunt.Hier.44.1. Est alia Magdalus siue Magdala in tribu Iuda:vnde Magdalena(de qua V.Maria.)Matth.15.39.
units.tr: MAGDALA, a town of Egypt, which the Israelites reached when they had come out of Egypt, before they crossed the sea, Exod. 14:2. There some Jews, avoiding the attack of the Babylonians, settled, Jer. 44:1. There is another Magdalus or Magdala in the tribe of Judah, from which comes Magdalene (of whom see Mary), Matt. 15:39.

units.la: MAGIA, Est pactio cum diabolo, vt illius ope cognoscantur vel efficiantur res non necessariæ, vel ad explendas malas cupiditates, vel ad ostentationem, vel ad vitæ commoditatem spectantes: vel vt ab ipso accipiantur, quæ à solo Deo petenda & expectanda sunt. Deut.18.11. Vide INCANTATIO.
units.tr: MAGIC is a pact with the devil, by whose help things that are not necessary are known or brought about, whether to satisfy evil desires, for display, or for the convenience of life; or by which things are received from the devil that are to be sought and expected from God alone. Deut. 18:11. See INCANTATION.

units.la: MAGI, id est, diuini, non consulendi, (V. Diuini.)
units.tr: MAGI, that is, diviners, who are not to be consulted. (See Diviners.)

units.la: MAGI Pharaonis virgas suas in colubros mutant, Exodi 7. 12. ranas super terram educunt, 8.7. educere ciniphes seu pediculos non possunt, v 18. Digitum Dei, id est, virtutem Dei in Mose & Aarone operari agnoscunt, v. 19. duo eorum à Paulo commemorantur Iannes & Iambres, 2. Timot. 3. 8. Magi & Arioli à Saule sublati, 1. Sam. 28.3.
units.tr: The magicians of Pharaoh turn their rods into serpents, Exod. 7:12; bring up frogs upon the land, 8:7; they cannot produce gnats or lice, v. 18. They recognise the finger of God, that is, the power of God working in Moses and Aaron, v. 19. Two of them are named by Paul, Jannes and Jambres, 2 Tim. 3:8. Magicians and necromancers were removed by Saul, 1 Sam. 28:3.

units.la: MAGI Persæ, i. Sapientes, Christum adoraturi veniunt, Matt.2.1. V.Magus.
units.tr: THE MAGI of Persia, that is, wise men, come to worship Christ, Matt. 2:1. See Magus.

units.la: MAGISTRI, pro iis, qui ius rigidæ censuræ in alios vsurpant, damnantur, Iacob.3.1. magistri mendaces quales,2. Pet.2.1.
units.tr: TEACHERS: those who claim the right of strict censure over others are condemned, James 3:1. Lying teachers, such as those of 2 Pet. 2:1.

units.la: MAGISTER noster Christus solus, Matthæi 23.10. Ioan. 13.13.
units.tr: Christ alone is our Teacher, Matt. 23:10; John 13:13.

units.la: MAGISTRATVS * Bonus à Deo est, 2. Paral.2.11.Esa.22.20. 21. Magistratum bonorum exempla: Ioseph. Genes.50.v.19. 20. septuaginta Seniores, Numer. 11. 16. Iosua, 27. v.18.19.Deut.31.7 Judices, Iudic.2.v.16.18. Othoniel,3.9. Aod. suæ Ehud,v.15. Gedeon,6.v.14.15.34. Saul,1.Sam.9.v. 15. 16. Dauid, 2, Sam.5.12.1.Paral. 28.4.Salomon,1.Reg. 3.7.&10.9.Iehu, 2.Reg.9. verf.1.2.3.&c. Ioachaz,13.v.4 5.Cyrus,2.Paral.36.22. Nabuchodosor, Dan,2.v.37.38.& 3.29.
units.tr: Good magistrates are from God, 2 Chron. 2:11; Isa. 22:20-21. Examples of good magistrates: Joseph, Gen. 50:19-20; the seventy elders, Num. 11:16; Joshua, Num. 27:18-19; Deut. 31:7; the judges, Judg. 2:16-18; Othniel, Judg. 3:9; Ehud, v. 15; Gideon, Judg. 6:14-15, 34; Saul, 1 Sam. 9:15-16; David, 2 Sam. 5:12; 1 Chron. 28:4; Solomon, 1 Kings 3:7 and 10:9; Jehu, 2 Kings 9:1-3, etc.; Jehoahaz, 2 Kings 13:4-5; Cyrus, 2 Chron. 36:22; Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 2:37-38 and 3:29.

units.la: Magistratus, Dei ministri, Rom.13.v.4. 6. Dij vocantur, Psalm.82.1. Cur sic vocentur, Vide REX.Non sunt asspernandi, Ioan.10.v.34.35.2.Pet.2.10.Iudæ v.8. Vide REX, Magistratus boni quàm necessarij, Iudic.2.19.&8.33.1. Sam.7.13.1. Reg.3.28.2. Paral.29.29.Prou.11.14.Eccles. 10.17.
units.tr: Magistrates are the ministers of God, Rom. 13:4, 6. They are called gods, Ps. 82:1. On why they are so called, see KING. They are not to be despised, John 10:34-35; 2 Pet. 2:10; Jude 8. See KING. Good magistrates are as necessary as they are valuable: Judg. 2:19 and 8:33; 1 Sam. 7:13; 1 Kings 3:28; 2 Chron. 29:29; Prov. 11:14; Eccl. 10:17.

units.la: Magistratus Officia,2.Paral.9.8.&19.6.Psal.82.2.Rom, 13.v.3.4.sunt.
units.tr: The duties of magistrates, 2 Chron. 9:8 and 19:6; Ps. 82:2; Rom. 13:3-4, are these:

units.la: I. Amplecti veram religionem,illi hospitiū præbere, & Dei gloriā ac hominū salutem, quantum in se est,prouocare& promouere. Exempla:Iosua,Num.27.18.19.Ios.3.v.5. 6.7.Saul,1.Sa.10.10.Samuel,12.v.20,21,Dauid,2.Sam.6.v. 20.21.Psal.2.v.10.11.& 24 v.6.7.& 148.11.1.Reg.2.v.1.2.3.1. Paral.16.v.1.2.Salomon,1.Reg.8.v.22 23.24.& 9.25. Ezechias,2.Reg.18.v.3.4.5.2.Par.19.v.25.26.&c.Iosaphat 17. v. 3.4.5.Iosias,2.Reg.23.v.2.3.4.2.Par.34.33.& 35.v.1.&c. Cyrus,36.22.1.Esdr.1.v.1.&c.
units.tr: I. To embrace the true religion, to give it hospitality, and, as far as lies in them, to promote and advance the glory of God and the salvation of men. Examples: Joshua, Num. 27:18-19; Josh. 3:5-7; Saul, 1 Sam. 10:10; Samuel, 1 Sam. 12:20-21; David, 2 Sam. 6:20-21; Ps. 2:10-11 and 24:6-7 and 148:11; 1 Kings 2:1-3; 1 Chron. 16:1-2; Solomon, 1 Kings 8:22-24 and 9:25; Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:3-5; 2 Chron. 19:25-26, etc.; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 17:3-5; Josiah, 2 Kings 23:2-4; 2 Chron. 34:33 and 35:1, etc.; Cyrus, Ezra 1:1, etc.

units.la: II. Abolere idololatriam Gentilium, & ritus honestati aduersantes. Exempla:Asa,1.Reg.15.v.12.13.Iehu, 2.Reg.10.v.25.26.&c. Ezechias, 18.v. 4.5. Iosias,23.verf. 4.5.6.
units.tr: II. To abolish the idolatry of the Gentiles and the rites that oppose decency. Examples: Asa, 1 Kings 15:12-13; Jehu, 2 Kings 10:25-26, etc.; Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:4-5; Josiah, 2 Kings 23:4-6.

units.la: III. Illis sublatis & abolitis, curare vt pura & syncera doctrina tradatur,ac propagetur, veríque cultus & ceremoniae diuinitus institutae obseruentur & exerceantur. Exempla:Rex Assyriorum ,2.Reg.17.v.26.27. Iosaphat.2. Paral.17.v.7.8.Darius,Dan.6.v.25.26.Iosias, 2.Reg.23.21. Exechias,2.Paral.30.1.
units.tr: III. Once these are removed and abolished, to take care that pure and sincere doctrine is taught and spread, and that the true worship and ceremonies instituted by God are observed and practised. Examples: the king of the Assyrians, 2 Kings 17:26-27; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 17:7-8; Darius, Dan. 6:25-26; Josiah, 2 Kings 23:21; Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 30:1.

units.la: IV. In pietate vera & religione sana maiorum exempla imitari,Exempla:Asa,1.Reg.15.v.11 12.Iosaphat,2. Paral.17,v.3.4.Ezechias,2.Reg.18.v.3.4 &c. 2. Paral.29.2.Iosias,2.Reg.22.2.
units.tr: IV. To imitate the examples of our forebears in true piety and sound religion. Examples: Asa, 1 Kings 15:11-12; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 17:3-4; Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:3-4, etc.; 2 Chron. 29:2; Josiah, 2 Kings 22:2.

units.la: V. Esse nutritium Ecclesiarum & Scholarum , Exempla : Pharao hospitium praebet, & alimentum subministrat patri & fratribus Ioseph,Genef.47. v.5.6. Duces populi Israelitici , Numer. 7. v.1.2.&c. Principes Israelitarum , 31.v.49.50. Dauid,1.Paral.29.2. Principes familiarum , v.6.7.Hiram ,1.Reg.5.10. Salomon , 8.64. Asa,15,v.11.15. Ezechias & subditi eius,2. Paralip.31.v.4.5. Cyrus,1.Esd.1.v.6.7. Darius , Dan. 6. v. 3. 4. Abdias domus Regis Achab dispensator,1.Reg.18.13. Abdemelech,Ierem.38.v.7.8.9.10.Magi,Matth.2. 11.iuxta illud Esaiae 49.23.
units.tr: V. To be nursing fathers of the Churches and schools. Examples: Pharaoh gives hospitality and supplies food to the father and brothers of Joseph, Gen. 47:5-6. The leaders of the Israelite people, Num. 7:1-2, etc. The princes of the Israelites, Num. 31:49-50. David, 1 Chron. 29:2. The heads of families, v. 6-7. Hiram, 1 Kings 5:10. Solomon, 8:64. Asa, 15:11, 15. Hezekiah and his subjects, 2 Chron. 31:4-5. Cyrus, Ezra 1:6-7. Darius, Dan. 6:3-4. Obadiah, steward of the household of King Ahab, 1 Kings 18:13. Ebed-melech, Jer. 38:7-10. The magi, Matt. 2:11, according to that saying of Isaiah, 49:23.

units.la: VI. Exemplo pietatis , honestatis & iustitiae subditis praeire,& iisdem de victu prospicere, praesertim famis tempore.Exempla:Ioseph,Gen.47.v.23.24. Dauid non curat irrisionem vxoris suae , sed laetatur , & ludit coram arca Domini , 2.Sam.6.14.1.Paralip.18.14. Saul , 2.Sam. 1.24. Samuel , 1. Sam.12.v.2.3. Salomon, 1. Reg.10.v.6.7. 8.Iosaphat,2. Paralip.19.v.6.7.Rex Niniuitarum , Ion.3. v.6.7.
units.tr: VI. To go before their subjects as an example of piety, honesty and justice, and to provide for them in food, especially in time of famine. Examples: Joseph, Gen. 47:23-24. David does not care about the mockery of his wife, but rejoices and dances before the ark of the Lord, 2 Sam. 6:14; 1 Chron. 15:29. Saul, 2 Sam. 1:24. Samuel, 1 Sam. 12:2-3. Solomon, 1 Kings 10:6-8. Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 19:6-7. The king of the Ninevites, Jonah 3:6-7.

units.la: VII. Ceremonias diuinitus institutas vnà cum subditis sanctè obseruare , & idoneos Ecclesiae Pastores legitimè à Deo & Ecclesia electos ac vocatos praeficere Exempla:Salomon.1.Reg.2.v.26.27.35. Salomon & omnis Israel, 8. v.62.63 64.Rex Assyriorum, 2.Reg.17.v.27.28. Ezechias & populus Iudaicus,2.Paral.30.v.1.2. Ezechias, 31.2.
units.tr: VII. To observe the ceremonies instituted by God holily together with their subjects, and to appoint as ministers of the Church those who are lawfully chosen and called by God and the Church. Examples: Solomon, 1 Kings 2:26-27, 35. Solomon and all Israel, 1 Kings 8:62-64. The king of the Assyrians, 2 Kings 17:27-28. Hezekiah and the Jewish people, 2 Chron. 30:1-2. Hezekiah, 31:2.

units.la: IIX. De rebus agendis & administrandis, os Domini consulere, hoc est, ministerium verbi, eique obtemperare, Exempla:Iosua consulit Eleazarum, Num.27.v.20.21.22.Saul obtemperat Samueli, 1.Sam.10.v.8.9. David consulit Dominum.23.10. monitis Gad obtemperat. 2. Sam. 24.18.Iosaphat & Achab consulunt Michæam,1. Reg.22.v.5.7.Rex Iuda,Israel & Edom, Elisæum,2.Reg.3.11.Ezechias Esaiam,19.2.Sedechias Ieremiam, Ierem. 38.14.
units.tr: VIII. In matters to be done and administered, to consult the mouth of the Lord, that is, the ministry of the Word, and to obey it. Examples: Joshua consults Eleazar, Num. 27:20-22. Saul obeys Samuel, 1 Sam. 10:8-9. David consults the Lord, 1 Sam. 23:10; he obeys the admonitions of Gad, 2 Sam. 24:18. Jehoshaphat and Ahab consult Micaiah, 1 Kings 22:5-7. The kings of Judah, Israel and Edom consult Elisha, 2 Kings 3:11. Hezekiah consults Isaiah, 19:2. Zedekiah consults Jeremiah, Jer. 38:14.

units.la: IX. In publicis calamitatibus subditos ad seriam poenitentiam & orationem edictis cohortari, Exempla: Iosaphat,2.paral.20.v.3.4.18.19.20.Ezechias,32.v.6.7. Rex Niniuitarum,Iob.3.v.6.7.
units.tr: IX. In public calamities, to exhort their subjects by edicts to serious repentance and prayer. Examples: Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20:3-4, 18-20. Hezekiah, 32:6-7. The king of the Ninevites, Jonah 3:6-7.

units.la: X. Extruere & reparcire ædificia, in quibus verus Dei cultus exercetur, Exempla: Dauid instituit ædificare domum Domino,sed prohibetur,2.Sam.7.v.2.5.Salomon,1.Reg.5.v.4.5.& 6.2.Iosias ,2.Reg.22.v.3.4.5.Cyrus,2.Paral.36.22.Darius,1.Esdr.6.v.1.2.3.
units.tr: X. To build and repair buildings in which the true worship of God is practised. Examples: David resolves to build a house for the Lord, but is forbidden, 2 Sam. 7:2-5. Solomon, 1 Kings 5:4-5 and 6:2. Josiah, 2 Kings 22:3-5. Cyrus, 2 Chron. 36:22. Darius, Ezra 6:1-3.

units.la: XI. Viros pios ac bonos ad gubernationem idoneos præfectos ordinare & constituere,Exempla:Moses, Exod.18.v.21.22.Dauid.2 Sam.8.v.14.15.16.17.18.& 10.v.13.Salomon,1.Reg.2.v.34.35.& 4.v.2.3.& 11.28.Iosaphat, 2. Paral.19.v.4.5.11.Dauid prolixè describit,quos & quales in aula sua ferret, Ps.101. v.4.5.6.7.
units.tr: XI. To appoint and establish as governors men who are pious and good and fit for the task. Examples: Moses, Exod. 18:21-22. David, 2 Sam. 8:14-18 and 10:13. Solomon, 1 Kings 2:34-35; 4:2-3; 11:28. Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 19:4-5, 11. David describes at length whom and what sort of men he would have in his court, Ps. 101:4-7.

units.la: XII. Prius cognoscere causam,quàm sententiam ferre, & in rebus ambiguis propter aliquot probabiles causas decidere,Exempla:Israelitæ,Iudi.20.v.3.&c. Iosua,Iosaphat 9.v.19.20 Salomon,1.Reg.3.v.23.24.
units.tr: XII. To learn the cause before pronouncing sentence, and in doubtful matters, for some probable reasons, to decide. Examples: the Israelites, Judg. 20:3ff. Joshua, Josh. 9:19-20. Jehoshaphat. Solomon, 1 Kings 3:23-24.

units.la: XIII. Inire fœdus, & colere amicitiam & pacem cum vicinis gubernatoribus. Exempla: Abimelech cum Abraham,Gen.21.27.Dauid cum Hanon,1.Para.19.2. Salomon cum Hiram,1.Reg.5.v.4.5.cum Pharaone,3.v.1.2. cum vicinis Regibus,2.Paral.9.v.23.24.
units.tr: XIII. To enter into covenant and to cultivate friendship and peace with neighbouring rulers. Examples: Abimelech with Abraham, Gen. 21:27. David with Hanun, 1 Chron. 19:2. Solomon with Hiram, 1 Kings 5:4-5; with Pharaoh, 3:1-2; with neighbouring kings, 2 Chron. 9:23-24.

units.la: XIV. Dimicare pro libertate,vel defendenda, vel recuperanda,& tueri authoritatem ac regnum aduersus sedi-tiosos ac hostes publicos. Exempla : Quinque Reges Sodomorum,Gen. 14.8. Adod.siue Ehud,Iudic.3.28.Samgar, v.31. Debora & Barach, 4.14. Gedeon,7.v.22.23 Iephthe, Tephthe, ii. v.32. 33.Ioab,2.Sam.10.12.Dauid,20.6.Ezechias,2.Reg.18.v.7.8.
units.tr: XIV. To fight for liberty, either to defend or to recover it, and to maintain authority and the kingdom against seditious men and public enemies. Examples: the five kings of Sodom, Gen. 14:8. Ehud, Judg. 3:28. Shamgar, v. 31. Deborah and Barak, 4:14. Gideon, 7:22-23. Jephthah, v. 32-33. Joab, 2 Sam. 10:12. David, 20:6. Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:7-8.

units.la: XV. Supplicia de hostibus sumere, & innocentibus parcere:Exempla:Iosua,Iof.8.26.Samuel, 1.Sam.15.v.33.34. Saul parcit Cinæo,v.6.Salomon,1.Reg.1.52.
units.tr: XV. To take punishment upon enemies, and to spare the innocent. Examples: Joshua, Josh. 8:26. Samuel, 1 Sam. 15:33-34. Saul spares the Kenite, v. 6. Solomon, 1 Kings 1:52.

units.la: Magistratus boni præmia à Deo promissa & præstita. Exempla:Iosuæ,Iof.3.7.Dauidi,1.Reg.2.v.44.45.Salomoni, 9.4.Ieroboamo, 11.v.30.31.38.Ezechiæ, 2.Reg.18.7.Iosaphato,2.Paral.17.v.3.5.
units.tr: The rewards of good magistrates promised and bestowed by God. Examples: Joshua, Josh. 3:7; David, 1 Kings 2:44-45; Solomon, 9:4; Jeroboam, 11:30-31, 38; Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:7; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 17:3, 5.

units.la: MAGISTRATVS impij mala opera.
units.tr: The wicked deeds of a magistrate

units.la: I. Rapere sibi ius dominandi, sine Dei, & eorum penes quos est potestas, voluntate. Exempla:Abimelech,Iudic. 9.v.5.6.Absalom,2.Sam.15.v.10.11.Adonias,1.Reg.1.v.5.6. Zambri,16.v.9.10.Phacee,seu Pekach,2.Reg.15.25. Osea, v.30.Vide Eccles.7.v.6.7.
units.tr: I. Seizing the right to rule for oneself, without the will of God and of those in whose power the authority lies. Examples: Abimelech, Judg. 9.5, 6; Absalom, 2 Sam. 15.10, 11; Adonijah, 1 Kings 1.5, 6; Zimri, 16.9, 10; Pekah, or Pekach, 2 Kings 15.25; Hoshea, v. 30. See Eccles. 7.6, 7.

units.la: II. Idololatricos cultus instituere,Idolis templa ædificare,& sanctificare. Exempla:Salomon, 1.Regum 11.7.Ieroboam,12.v.26.27.Ochosias,1.Reg.22.54. Vide IDOLOLATRIA.
units.tr: II. Instituting idolatrous worship, building temples to idols and consecrating them. Examples: Solomon, 1 Kings 11.7; Jeroboam, 12.26, 27; Ahaziah, 1 Kings 22.54. See IDOLATRY.

units.la: III. Ob veritatis confessionem, & pœnitentiæ concionem,odisse & persequi Dei Ministros. Exempla:Ieroboam,virum Dei, 1.Reg.13.4.Baasa Iehu & Prophetam, 16.7.Achab Eliam,18.10.&c. Michæam.22.v.8.27.Asa videntem,2.Paral.16.v.7.10.Amasias Prophetam, 2.Paral. 25.v.15.16.17.Sedechias Principes, & Phassur Ieremiam, Ierem.20.2.&37.15.&38.6. Nabuchodonosor Sidrach, Misach,& Abdenagonem,Dan.3.19. (Plura exempla vide in,CONFESSIO fidei:CONSTANTIA:IMPIOS verbum Dei ferre non posse:INCARCERATIO:VERITAS odium parit: & , PROPHETARVM & Ministrorum verbi Dei in hoc mundo præmia.)
units.tr: III. Hating and persecuting the ministers of God because they confess the truth and preach repentance. Examples: Jeroboam against the man of God, 1 Kings 13.4; Baasha against Jehu and the prophet, 16.7; Ahab against Elijah, 18.10, etc.; Micaiah, 22.8, 27; Asa against the seer, 2 Chron. 16.7, 10; Amaziah against the prophet, 2 Chron. 25.15, 16, 17; Zedekiah and the princes, and Pashhur, against Jeremiah, Jer. 20.2, 37.15, 38.6; Nebuchadnezzar against Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, Dan. 3.19. (More examples see under CONFESSION OF FAITH; CONSTANCY; THE IMPIOUS CANNOT BEAR THE WORD OF GOD; IMPRISONMENT; TRUTH BEGETS HATRED; and THE REWARDS OF PROPHETS AND MINISTERS OF THE WORD OF GOD IN THIS WORLD.)

units.la: IV. Imitari,vel etiam superare maiorum & antecessorum suorum idololatriam. Exempla : Nadab,1.Regum 15.26.Homri,16.v.25.26. Ochosias,22.v.53.54.Ioram,2. Reg.3.2.Ioachaz,13.2.&23.v.30.&c. Zacharias,15.9,Manahen,v.18.Achaz,16.2.Manasses,21.2.Amon,v.20.Ioachim, 24.9 Sedechias,v.19.
units.tr: IV. Imitating, or even surpassing, the idolatry of their forefathers and predecessors. Examples: Nadab, 1 Kings 15.26; Omri, 16.25, 26; Ahaziah, 22.53, 54; Joram, 2 Kings 3.2; Jehoahaz, 13.2, and 23.30, etc.; Zechariah, 15.9; Menahem, v. 18; Ahaz, 16.2; Manasseh, 21.2; Amon, v. 20; Jehoiakim, 24.9; Zedekiah, v. 19.

units.la: V. Verbo Dei & legi naturæ , aliisque scriptis legibus contraria promulgare,& innocentes interficere.Exempla: Pharao,Exodi 1.v.15.16.Ieroboam,1.Regum 12.v.27.28.Achab,22.v.26.27.Nabuchodonosor,Dan.3.5.Darius,6.v.7.8.
units.tr: V. Promulgating things contrary to the word of God, to the law of nature and to other written laws, and killing the innocent. Examples: Pharaoh, Exod. 1.15, 16; Jeroboam, 1 Kings 12.27, 28; Ahab, 22.26, 27; Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 3.5; Darius, 6.7, 8.

units.la: (Vide EDICTORVM tam bonorum quàm malorum exempla.)
units.tr: (See examples of edicts, both good and bad.)

units.la: Magistratus peccata puniuntur in subditis, Exempla: Saulis homicidium, 2.Sam.21 1. Davidis superbia, 12.10. & 24.v 15 17. Salomonis idololatria, 1.Re.11.v.30 31 32.33. peccata Ioram, 2.Paral.21.v.12.13. impius Achaz, 28.19 Achab, 1.Reg.20.42. (Vide MULTITVDO ob vnius peccatum, &c.) Magistratus impij & iniqui exempla: Magistratus [Ithi-lippensium,] Actor 16.22. Gallion Tribunus, 18.17. Tribunus, 22.24. Magistratus potestas à Deo, Ioannes 19. 11. Magistratuum timor à Deo, Iof. 4. 14. Magistratus malus malo populo iustâ Dei irâ cedit, 1.Reg.12. 26.&c. Iob.34.30. Prov.28.2. Esa.3.4.&29.10. Ezech.14.9. 10. Ofeæ 13.11.2. Thess.2 11. Magistratus mali arguuntur: Psalm.82.2. Esa.1.23. Ierem.5.v.5.28. Ezech.22.27. Mich.3 11. Soph.3.3. Magistratus avari quàm noxij, Prov.29.4. Magistratui etiam profano parendum, Ierem.27.8. Matth.17. 27.&22.21.&23.3. Luc.20.25. Rom.13.1. Tit.3 1,1. Pet.2.13. suo tamen omnipotenti Deo seruato illibato honore Dan.3.v.14.15.16.17.18.&6.v.9 10. Actor.4 9.&5.29. (Vide MANDATIS impiis & inhonestis non esse parendum.) Magistratus Deum timentes, Exodi 18.25. Deut. 1.15. impij, Prov.29.v.8.10.12. Magistratibus non debent trahendum, Exod.22.28. parendum, Rom.13.1 &c. Tit.3 1.1.Pet.2.13. Magistratui tributū soluit Christus Mat.17,24.
units.tr: The sins of magistrates are punished in their subjects. Examples: the murder committed by Saul, 2 Sam. 21.1; the pride of David, 2 Sam. 12.10 and 24.15, 17; the idolatry of Solomon, 1 Kings 11.30, 31, 32, 33; the sins of Joram, 2 Chron. 21.12, 13; the ungodly Ahaz, 28.19; Ahab, 1 Kings 20.42. (See MULTITUDE, on the sin of one man, etc.) Examples of ungodly and unjust magistrates: the magistrates of Philippi, Acts 16.22; Gallio, the proconsul, 18.17; the tribune, 22.24. The power of a magistrate is from God, John 19.11; the fear of magistrates is from God, Josh. 4.14. A wicked magistrate yields to a wicked people through the just wrath of God, 1 Kings 12.26, etc.; Job 34.30; Prov. 28.2; Isa. 3.4 and 29.10; Ezek. 14.9, 10; Hos. 13.11; 2 Thess. 2.11. Wicked magistrates are rebuked: Ps. 82.2; Isa. 1.23; Jer. 5.5, 28; Ezek. 22.27; Mic. 3.11; Zeph. 3.3. Greedy magistrates are as harmful as they are: Prov. 29.4. Even to a profane magistrate obedience is owed: Jer. 27.8; Matt. 17.27, 22.21, 23.3; Luke 20.25; Rom. 13.1; Titus 3.1; 1 Pet. 2.13; yet with the honour of the almighty God kept whole and inviolate, Dan. 3.14–18 and 6.9, 10; Acts 4.9 and 5.29. (See that impious and dishonourable commands are not to be obeyed.) Magistrates who fear God: Exod. 18.25; Deut. 1.15; impious magistrates: Prov. 29.8, 10, 12. Magistrates are not to be reviled, Exod. 22.28; they are to be obeyed, Rom. 13.1, etc.; Titus 3.1; 1 Pet. 2.13. Christ paid tribute to the magistrate, Matt. 17.24.

units.la: MAGNANIMITAS, Est fortitudo excelsi animi, per quam redu-arduas, difficiles, & periculo plenas aggredimur. Exercetur in suscipiendis rebus arduis, tum in contemnēdis periculis, difficultatibus, etiam morte ipsa: item in defensione innocentiæ aduersus iniustas calumnias. Cum hac pugnant Præsumptio, & Pusillanimitas.
units.tr: MAGNANIMITY, is the strength of a lofty spirit, by which we undertake difficult, arduous and dangerous tasks. It is exercised in taking up hard tasks, in despising dangers and difficulties, even death itself, and likewise in defending innocence against unjust slanders. Presumption and Pusillanimity are opposed to it.

units.la: MAGNANIMITAS suadetur exemplis: Elisæi ad Regem Israëlis 2.Reg 3 v.13.14. Azariæ Sacerdotis, & cum eo octoginta virorum fortissimorum ad Oziam Regem, 2. Paral. 26. 18. Nehemiæ, Neh. 2. 20. & 6. 11. Esther Esth. 4.16. Ioannis Baptistæ, Matth.3.7.&14.4.Mar. 6.18. Luc.3.7. Discipulorum Ioannis, Mar.6.29. Iosephi Arimathæi, Mar.15.43.Luc.23.52. Cœci nati, Ioan.9.3. Petri & Ioannis, Actor.5.29. Stephani, 7.51. Pauli, 13,v.1 46.&21.13.
units.tr: MAGNANIMITY is commended by examples: Elisha to the king of Israel, 2 Kings 3.13, 14; Azariah the priest, with eighty very brave men, to King Uzziah, 2 Chron. 26.18; Nehemiah, Neh. 2.20 and 6.11; Esther, Esth. 4.16; John the Baptist, Matt. 3.7, 14.4; Mark 6.18; Luke 3.7; the disciples of John, Mark 6.29; Joseph of Arimathea, Mark 15.43; Luke 23.52; the man born blind, John 9.3; Peter and John, Acts 5.29; Stephen, 7.51; Paul, 13.46 and 21.13.

units.la: MAGNIFICA Dei erga Israelem, 1.Sam.12.24. Erga Christum 2.Pet.1.17. MAGNIFICORVM hominum exempla : Abraham, Genef. 12.v.1.2.& 24.35. Iosua, Ios.4.14. Samuel, 1.Sam.2, 21. Salomon, 1.Reg.10.23.1 Paral.29.25.2 Paral. 1.1. & 9.22. Iosaphat, 17.12. Nabuchodonosor, Dan.4.19. &c. Christus, Act. 5.31.
units.tr: The magnificent deeds of God toward Israel, 1 Sam. 12.24; toward Christ, 2 Pet. 1.17. Examples of magnificent men: Abraham, Gen. 12.1, 2 and 24.35; Joshua, Josh. 4.14; Samuel, 1 Sam. 2.21; Solomon, 1 Kings 10.23, 1 Chron. 29.25, 2 Chron. 1.1 and 9.22; Jehoshaphat, 17.12; Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 4.19, etc.; Christ, Acts 5.31.

units.la: MAGNIFICENTIA, est quæ magnos, & non vulgares vel mediocres, sumptus, quando, & in quibus rebus oportet, lubenter ad Dei gloriam facit : quemadmodum Dauid & Solomo in exornando Hierosolymitano Dei templo. Hæc verè regia est virtus, non priuatorum hominum. Vti frugalitas in priuatis laudatur potius, quàm in Regibus.
units.tr: MAGNIFICENCE is that which, when and where it is fitting, gladly spends great and uncommon sums, not ordinary or moderate ones, for the glory of God, as David and Solomon did in adorning the temple of God at Jerusalem. This is truly a royal virtue, not the virtue of private persons. Thrift is praised in private persons rather than in kings.

units.la: MAGNIFICENTIA Deo danda, Deut. 32.39. Magnificantium Deum exempla: Dauid, 2.Sam.7.22. Psalm.34.4. & 68.35. Esaias, Esa.33.5. Nabuchodonosor, Dan.4.34. Turba, Matth. 15.31. Maria virgo, Luc,1.46. Populus 4.15. Paralyticus & turba: 5.:5.26. Naimitæ 7.16. Samaritanus leprosus, Luc. 17,15. Cœtus illuminatus, 18.43, Fideles Act.10.46. Iudæi & Gentiles, 19.16.17. Discipuli & Seniores, 21.20. (V.LAVDANTIVM Deum exempla.)
units.tr: MAGNIFICENCE is to be given to God, Deut. 32.39. Examples of those who magnify God: David, 2 Sam. 7.22; Ps. 34.4 and 68.35; Isaiah, Isa. 33.5; Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 4.34; the crowd, Matt. 15.31; the Virgin Mary, Luke 1.46; the people, Luke 4.15; the paralytic and the crowd, Luke 5.25, 26; the people of Nain, 7.16; the Samaritan leper, Luke 17.15; the crowd that saw the light, 18.43; the faithful, Acts 10.46; Jews and Gentiles, 19.16, 17; the disciples and elders, 21.20. (See PRAISING GOD, examples of.)

units.la: MAGNVS Deus proprie dicitur, frequenter apud Prophetas, nominatim in Psalmis. Magnus, magna, magnum, quicquid de nominib. & attributis diuinis profertur. Magnus Deus Pater, Ioan. 10.29. & 14.28. magnus Filius Dei in carne manifestandus & manifestatus, Dan.12.1. Matth.12.6. Luc.1.32. & 7.16. Heb.4.14. & 10.21. & 13.20. De homine dicitur magnus, maior, maximus, ætate, dierum numero, tempore, dignitate, efficacia, magnus, magna, magnum, De expansione, mensura, mole, proceritate, statura. Magnus numero, ordine, potentia varia. Sexcenta in has significationes dicta occurrunt. Maiores natu, 1. Seniores, non tam ætatis quàm dignitatis respectu, Genef.50.7. Exod.19.7. Leuitic. 9. Deut.5.23. Iosu.24.1 Iudic.11.5.
units.tr: GREAT is properly said of God, frequently among the Prophets and especially in the Psalms. Great, greatly, greatest: whatever is said of the divine names and attributes. The great God the Father, John 10.29 and 14.28; the great Son of God, to be manifested and manifested in the flesh, Dan. 12.1; Matt. 12.6; Luke 1.32 and 7.16; Heb. 4.14, 10.21, 13.20. Of man it is said great, greater, greatest, with respect to age, number of days, time, dignity, efficacy; great in extent, measure, bulk, height and stature. Great in number, in rank, in power, in various ways. Six hundred instances occur in these senses. Elders (maiores natu), i.e. seniors, not so much with respect to age as to dignity: Gen. 50.7; Exod. 19.7; Lev. 9; Deut. 5.23; Josh. 24.1; Judg. 11.5.

units.la: MAGOG filius Iaphet, Gen.10.2.1Par.1.5. Magog & Gog, tecti & derectti hostes Ecclesiæ, Ezec.38.2.&39.6. Apoc.20.8. MAGVS, Leuit.19.31. &20.6. 1.Sam.28.v.3.9.2. Par.33.6. Act. 8.9.& 13.v.6.8. Magi Chaldæorum Dan.1.20. & 2,2. &c. Magi apud Persas nomen est honestum, ac significat homines tum sapientia tum religione claros: cùm verò significat deditos artibus magicis, sumitur in malam partem. Matth.2.v.1.7.16. V.Magia, & magi.
units.tr: MAGOG, son of Japheth, Gen. 10.2; 1 Chron. 1.5. Gog and Magog, covered and uncovered enemies of the Church, Ezek. 38.2 and 39.6; Rev. 20.8. MAGUS: Lev. 19.31 and 20.6; 1 Sam. 28.3, 9; 2 Chron. 33.6; Acts 8.9 and 13.6, 8. The magi of the Chaldeans, Dan. 1.20 and 2.2, etc. Among the Persians "magus" is an honourable name, meaning men distinguished both for wisdom and for religion; but when it means those devoted to magic arts, it is taken in a bad sense. Matt. 2.1, 7, 16. See MAGIC, and magi.

units.la: MAIESTAS & gloria Dei, Exo. 40,35. propria nō scrutāda, Pr. 25.27. [Esa.2.10. Maiestas Christi, Matth.25.31. Maiestas Magistratuum, Iud.v.8. Maiestas idoli ex hypothesi idolola-trarum, Act.19 27.]
units.tr: The majesty and glory of God, Exod. 40.35; one's own (glory) is not to be sought out, Prov. 25.27. [Isa. 2.10. The majesty of Christ, Matt. 25.31. The majesty of magistrates, Jude v. 8. The majesty of an idol, on the supposition of idolaters, Acts 19.27.]

units.la: MAIOR in Ecclesia quis, Matth.5.19. & 18.1. &c.
units.tr: Who is greater in the Church? Matt. 5.19, 18.1, etc.

units.la: MALACHIAS (angelus siue nuntius meus) Propheta vlti-mus concludens vetus Testamentum: Malach.1.1. Rom.9.13. Matt.11.14. & 17.11. Luc.1.16.
units.tr: MALACHI (my angel or messenger), the last of the Prophets, closing the Old Testament: Mal. 1.1; Rom. 9.13; Matt. 11.14, 17.11; Luke 1.16.

units.la: MALALEEL filius Cainā gignitur, Genes. 5.12. anno ætati suę lxxv. Iared primogenitum gignit, v.15. quot anno vixerit, v.17. (.i. laudans Deum.)
units.tr: MAHALALEEL is begotten by Cainan, Gen. 5.12, in the 75th year of his age. He begets Jared, his firstborn, v. 15; how many years he lived, v. 17. (i.e. praising God.)

units.la: MALCHON idolum, V. Idolorum catalogus.
units.tr: MALCHON, an idol. See the catalogue of idols.

units.la: MALCHVS Pontificis seruus à Petro auricula truncatur, Mat 26.51. Marc.14.47. Luc.22.50. Ioann.18.10. à Christo vin-cto sanatur, Luc.22.51. (.i. rex aut regnum, aut confi-liarius.)
units.tr: MALCHUS, servant of the high priest, has his ear cut off by Peter, Matt. 26.51; Mark 14.47; Luke 22.50; John 18.10; and is healed by Christ, who was bound, Luke 22.51. (i.e. a king or kingdom, or a counsellor.)
