Vide Duritiei & indurationis exempla.
units.tr: OBSTINACY is to be avoided: Deut. 10.16; Ps. 95.8; Prov. 21.29; Rom. 2.5; 2 Tim. 3.13; Heb. 3.8, 13, 15. Punishment of obstinacy: Isa. 1.20; Jer. 19.15; Zeph. 3.1, 2, 3. Examples of obstinacy and transgression: Cain, Gen. 4.6. Pharaoh, Exod. 7.13, 22; 8.15, 19, 32. The Hebrews, 2 Kings 17.14; 2 Chr. 24.19, 21; 30.8. Zedekiah, 36.13. The Jews, Jer. 5.3; 44.10, 17; John 19.15; Acts 7.51. The Israelites, Ezek. 2.4; Zech. 7.11, 12; Bar. 2.7, 8; Amos 4.6, 7 etc. Jerusalem, Matt. 23.37; Luke 13.34. The chief priests, Matt. 27.4; Luke 23.10; John 11.47. See examples of hardness and hardening.

units.la: OBSTINATI neque legis concionibus, neque poenis moventur, nisi accedente singulari Dei efficacia. Exempla: Pharao tot miraculis à Moïse, digito Dei editis non movetur, sed magis induratur. Exodi 7.v.13.22. & 8.v.15 19.32. & 9.v.7 12.34. & 10.20.27. Saul innocentia Davidis toties demonstrata non conuertitur, quia Deus ipsius cor non mutat, sed indurat, iusto suo iudicio, 1 Sam.17.18.19.&c. cap.Iudæi, Ierem.2.v.29.30. & 5.3 & 6.v.28.29. & 7.v.25.26. & 15.7. & 35.v.14.15. Israelitæ, Amos 4.v.7.8.9 10. Agg.2.18. Obstinatorum interitus, Ezech.6 4.11.
units.tr: Obstinate people are moved neither by sermons of the Law nor by punishments, unless the singular efficacy of God is added. Examples: Pharaoh, moved by so many miracles wrought by Moses through the finger of God, is not moved but rather hardened: Exod. 7.13, 22; 8.15, 19, 32; 9.7, 12, 34; 10.20, 27. Saul, though David's innocence was so often demonstrated, is not converted, because God does not change his heart but hardens it by his just judgment: 1 Sam. 17.18, 19 etc. The Jews, a chapter of its own: Jer. 2.29, 30; 5.3; 6.28, 29; 7.25, 26; 15.7; 35.14, 15. The Israelites: Amos 4.7, 8, 9, 10; Hag. 2.18. The destruction of the obstinate: Ezek. 6.4, 11.

units.la: OBTRECTATIO, Est is animus, qui aliorum bona opera, vel peruersa interpretatione iis vitio vertit, & in mala commutat, vel debitam illis gloriam maligna æstimatione imminuit.
units.tr: Detraction is that disposition which takes offence at the good works of others, either by a perverse interpretation turning them into evil, or by malicious estimation diminishes the glory due to them.

units.la: OBTRECTATORVM consortia fugienda, Prou.24.21. Obtrectatorum merces, Psalm.109.v.20 29. & 120.3. Prouerb.24.22. Obtrectationis & detractionis exempla: Filij Laban, Genes.31.1. Vxor Putipharis, 39.v.14.17. Maria & Aaron, Numer.12.v.1.2. Exploratores terræ, 14.36. Multitudo, 16.41. Filij Belial, 1 Samu.10 27. Doeg Idumæus, 22 9. Philistæi, 29 4. Principes Ammonitarum, 2 Samu. 10.3. Absalom 15 3 Siba, 16.3. Regum cum sociis, 1 Esdr. 4.13. Aman Eth. 3.8. principes Iuda, Ieremiæ 38. 4. quidam Chaldæi, Dan. 3 8. &c. Danielis hostes, 6 13. Pharisæi, Matth. 9.11. Iudæ, 11. v. 18. 19. Luc. 19.7. & 23.5. Ioan. 7.12. & 8 48. & 9. v. 16. 24.28. Domini famulę Pythonissæ, Act. 16.20. Iudæi Thessalonicenses, 17.7. Epicurei & Stoici Philosophi, v. 18. Iudæi Corinthij, 18.13. & 19.9. Iudæi Asiatici, 21. 28. Barbari, 28. 4. Vide Accusationis & falsò accusatorum exempla.
units.tr: The company of detractors is to be shunned: Prov. 24.21. The wages of detractors: Ps. 109.20, 29 & 120.3; Prov. 24.22. Examples of detraction and slander: the sons of Laban, Gen. 31.1. Potiphar's wife, Gen. 39.14–17. Miriam and Aaron, Num. 12.1, 2. The spies of the land, Num. 14.36. The multitude, Num. 16.41. The sons of Belial, 1 Sam. 10.27. Doeg the Edomite, 1 Sam. 22.9. The Philistines, 1 Sam. 29.4. The princes of the Ammonites, 2 Sam. 10.3. Absalom, 2 Sam. 15.3. Ziba, 2 Sam. 16.3. The kings with their allies, 1 Esd. 4.13. Haman, Esth. 3.8. The princes of Judah, Jer. 38.4. Certain Chaldeans, Dan. 3.8 etc. Daniel's enemies, Dan. 6.13. The Pharisees, Matt. 9.11; Matt. 11.18, 19; Luke 19.7 & 23.5; John 7.12 & 8.48 & 9.16, 24, 28. The servant girl who was a soothsayer, Acts 16.20. The Jews of Thessalonica, Acts 17.7. The Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, Acts 17.18. The Corinthian Jews, Acts 18.13 & 19.9. The Jews of Asia, Acts 21.28. The barbarians, Acts 28.4. See examples of accusation and of falsely accused persons.

An opportunity offered must not be let slip: Ps. 32.6; Eccl. 9.10; Isa. 55.6 & 65.12; Jer. 13.16 & 21.12; Hos. 10.12; Matt. 25.10, 13; Luke 13.24, 25 & 17.22 & 19.26; John 7.34 & 8.21 & 12.35, 36; Rom. 2.4 & 11.25 & 12.10 & 13.11; 2 Cor. 6.1, 2; Gal. 6.10; Heb. 2.1 & 3.13, 15 & 4.16 & 12.17; 1 Pet. 3.9. (See: the eye is commanded to be plucked out.)

units.la: Occasus, vel plaga occidentalis Hebraeis interdum a mari sumit denominationem, propter Mediterraneum scilicet mare, quod est ab occidente Chanaan, Gen. 12 8. ideoque & ventus occidentalis, ventus maris appellatur, Exod. 10. 19. Ezech. 42.19. & 47.20. & 48.2. &c. Dan. 8.4.
units.tr: The west, or western region, the Hebrews sometimes take their name from the sea, namely the Mediterranean, which lies to the west of Canaan: Gen. 12.8. Hence also the west wind is called the wind of the sea: Exod. 10.19; Ezek. 42.19 & 47.20 & 48.2 etc.; Dan. 8.4.

units.la: Occisi, V. Mors violenta.
units.tr: The slain: see Violent death.

units.la: Ochosias, filius Achab, Rex Israel constituitur, 1 Reg. 22. 40. idolis seruit, v. 54. matris hortatu, 2 Paral. 22.3. læsus i-dolum consulit, 2 Reg. 1 2. ob id ab Elia reprehenditur, ver. 16. moritur, versi. 17 (Achaziahu. i. apprehendens dominum.)
units.tr: Ahaziah, son of Ahab, is made king of Israel: 1 Kings 22.40. He serves idols: v. 54. At his mother's urging: 2 Chr. 22.3. Injured, he consults an idol: 2 Kings 1.2. For this he is rebuked by Elijah: v. 16. He dies: v. 17. (Ahaziah, i.e. holding the Lord.)

units.la: Ochosias, filius Ioram, regnum Iuda obit, 2 Reg. 8 25.2. Paral. 22.1. impius est, 2 Reg. 8 27. à Iehu occidi iubetur, 9.27. 2 Paral. 22.9.
units.tr: Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, obtains the kingdom of Judah: 2 Kings 8.25; 2 Chr. 22.1. He is impious: 2 Kings 8.27. He is ordered to be killed by Jehu: 2 Kings 9.27; 2 Chr. 22.9.

units.la: Ocvlvs interdum, ex Hebraeorum idiotismo pro toto hominis ingenio ponitur, & tunc mentis ipsius iudicium significat, Matth. 6.22. Luc. 11 34. eò quòd oculi sunt præcipui mentis indices. Oculus simplex & rectus, Matth. 6. 22. Luc. 11.34. Oculus malus, pro invidia, Matth. 20. 15. Marc. 7 22. Deuter. 15.9. Oculus nequam, Genes. 6.2. Proverb. 6 13. Eccles. 4 8. Matth. 6.23. Marc. 7.22. Luc. 11 34. Ioan. 2 16. Oculus allegorice & hyperbolice erui iubetur. Matth. 5.29. Sensus est. Si effugere vis æternum illud exitium, omnes occasiones, quibus ad obscœnas cogitationes impelli mentem senseris, vita etiam cum charissimarum rerum iactura: quamobrem etiam oculi dextri & manus
units.tr: The eye is sometimes, by Hebrew idiom, put for a person's whole disposition, and then signifies the judgment of his mind, Matt. 6.22; Luke 11.34, because the eyes are the chief indicators of the mind. A single and right eye: Matt. 6.22; Luke 11.34. An evil eye, for envy: Matt. 20.15; Mark 7.22; Deut. 15.9. A wicked eye: Gen. 6.2; Prov. 6.13; Eccl. 4.8; Matt. 6.23; Mark 7.22; Luke 11.34; John 2.16. The eye is commanded to be plucked out, allegorically and hyperbolically: Matt. 5.29. The sense is this: if you wish to escape that eternal destruction, you must give up all occasions by which you sense your mind is being driven to obscene thoughts, even at the cost of your dearest possessions, which is why mention is made also of the right eye and of the right

units.la: [Edge of text partly lost in binding shadow; the final words "manus" run into the margin.] manus dextræ fit mentio, quòd dextræ partes sint chariores, cùm istis alioquin partibus etiam sinistris non minùs quàm dextris homines abutantur.
units.tr: [Edge of text partly lost in binding shadow; the final words "manus" run into the margin.] the right hand is mentioned because the right parts are dearer, although men otherwise abuse the left parts no less than the right.

units.la: Oculus insatiabilis est, Eccl. 1.8. oculum eruenti, oculus eruendus, Exodi 21.24. Leuit. 24.20, Deut. 19.21. Matth. 5.38. oculi aperiuntur Adamo & Euæ. Genesis 3.7. Balaamo, Num. 22.31. Cæco nato, Ioan. 9.10. aliis cæcis, Vide MIRACVLA. Aperiri dicuntur autem oculi Hebræis, cum videndi visus restituitur, Ioan. 9.10. quemadmodum & clausi dicuntur oculi cæcorum, qui videndi visu carent, & luci non sunt peruij. oculi eruntur: Samsoni, Iudic. 16.21. Sedechiæ, 2 Reg. 25.7. oculi dextri Iabeditarum ab Ammonita pro fœderis signo petuntur, 1 Sam. 11.2. Horrendum dictu.
units.tr: The eye is insatiable: Eccl. 1.8. The eye of the one who plucks out an eye, the eye to be plucked out: Exod. 21.24; Lev. 24.20; Deut. 19.21; Matt. 5.38. Eyes are opened to Adam and Eve: Gen. 3.7. To Balaam: Num. 22.31. To the man born blind: John 9.10. To other blind men: see MIRACLES. Eyes are said to be opened among the Hebrews when the power of seeing is restored, John 9.10, just as the eyes of the blind are said to be closed, since they lack the power of sight and are not open to the light. Eyes are put out: of Samson, Judg. 16.21; of Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25.7. The right eyes of the men of Jabesh are demanded by the Ammonites as a sign of covenant: 1 Sam. 11.2. Horrible to say.

units.la: Ocvlvs fidei, 2 Cor. 4.18. Oculus mentis, vel intellectus, Num. 24.3. Deut. 29.4. Esa. 6.9. Luc. 24.29. 31. Actor. 26.18. Eph. 1.18. In oculis tuis, vel coram te, pro apud te, vel tibi, Hebraismus, Mat. 21.42. Num. 11.15.
units.tr: The eye of faith, 2 Cor. 4.18. The eye of the mind or understanding, Num. 24.3; Deut. 29.4; Isa. 6.9; Luke 24.29, 31; Acts 26.18; Eph. 1.18. "In your eyes," or "before you," meaning "with you" or "to you," is a Hebraism: Matt. 21.42; Num. 11.15.

units.la: Ocvlorvm custodia quantopere sit necessaria ad vitandum peccata, Genes. 3.6. & 6.2. & 34.2. [& 38.15. & 39.7.2. Samu. 11.2. & 13.1. Iob. 31.1: Psalm. 119. 37. Prouer. 23. v. 26. 33. Matt. 5.28. 2 Petr. 2.14. (Oculus non vidit quæ parauit D. 1 Cor. 3.9.)
units.tr: How necessary the guarding of the eyes is for avoiding sin: Gen. 3.6; 6.2; 34.2; [38.15; 39.7]; 2 Sam. 11.2; 13.1; Job 31.1; Ps. 119.37; Prov. 23.26, 33; Matt. 5.28; 2 Pet. 2.14. (Eye has not seen what God has prepared, 1 Cor. 2.9.)

units.la: Ocvlvs membrum externum nobilissimum in capite animantis. Pro. 20.12.2. Oculus Spiritualis, Cor, Mens, Psal. 13.4. & 36.2. & 69.24. Esa. 6.10. & 29.v.10.18. & 32.3. & 33.15. & 35.5. & 43.8. & 44.18. Ier. 5.21. Zach. 11.17. Matth. 6.22.23. & 13.15. Ioan. 12.40. Act. 26.18. & 28.27. Rom. 11.v.8.10. Eph. 1.18.1 Ioan. 2.11. Apoc. 3.18. (Oculus fui cæco, Iob. 29.15. Vilurus sum D. 19.27.)
units.tr: The eye is the most noble external member in the head of a living creature: Prov. 20.12. Spiritual eye: heart, mind: Ps. 13.4; 36.2; 69.24; Isa. 6.10; 29.10, 18; 32.3; 33.15; 35.5; 43.8; 44.18; Jer. 5.21; Zech. 11.17; Matt. 6.22-23; 13.15; John 12.40; Acts 26.18; 28.27; Rom. 11.8, 10; Eph. 1.18; 1 John 2.11; Rev. 3.18. (I was eyes to the blind, Job 29.15. I will be eyes to ..., Deut. 19.27.)

units.la: Oculi Filij Dei, Zac. 3.9. in carne manifestati, Luc. 6.20. Ioann. 6.5. & 11.41. & 17.1 Apoc. 1.14. & 2.18. & 5.6. & 19.12. 6 8. oculi idolorum, Psal. 115.5. & 135 16.
units.tr: The eyes of the Son of God, Zech. 3.9, manifested in the flesh: Luke 6.20; John 6.5; 11.41; 17.1; Rev. 1.14; 2.18; 5.6; 19.12; 6.8. The eyes of idols: Ps. 115.5; 135.16.

units.la: ED Propheta, 2 Paral. 28.9. eius de dimittendis Iudæ captiuis comminatio, ibid. v. 11. (i. tenens aut erigens.)
units.tr: ODED the prophet, 2 Chron. 28.9; his threat concerning the release of the captives of Judah, ibid. v. 11. (That is, holding or raising up.)

units.la: ODIVM μῖσος, est tanta cordis atque affectus nostri auersio à persona proximi, vt ne vultum quidem eius iam ferre, & iucundè intueri possimus, propter iniuriæ nobis illatæ recordationem.
units.tr: HATRED [μῖσος] is such a turning away of the heart and affection from the person of our neighbour that we can no longer bear to look at his face or regard him with pleasure, because of the memory of an injury done to us.

units.la: ODIVM proximi prohibetur, Leuit.19.17. Prou.15.17. Matt. 5.v.23.24. 1 Ioan.2.v.9.11.& 3.15. & 4.20. Odium rixas generat, Prou.10.12. Odium malì præcipitur. Ps.97.10.& 139.21. Amos 5.15.& 6.8. Rom.12.9. Odium Christi quàm exitiale, Ioan.15.23. Odium Euangelij causa, Matth.10.22. Marc.13.13. Luc.21.17. Ioan.16.2. Odium reprobationis nota & signum, 1 Ioan.3.13. Odij exempla: Abimelech & socij eius, Gen.26.27. Esau, 27.41. Chananæi, 34.30. Fratres Ioseph, 37.v.4.5. Ægypti, Exo.1.12. Madianitæ, Num.25.v.17.18. Israelitæ, Iudi.11.v.6.7. cæci & claudi, 2 Sam.5.8. Amnô, 13.v.15.22. Razon, &c.1 Reg.11.25. Achab, 22.8. Hostes Iudæ, 1 Eldr.4.1. Aman, Esth.7.6. Hostes Dauidis, Ps.18.18.& 25.19.& 44.8.& 69.v.5.15. Iudæi, Amos 5.10. Mundus, Ioan.7.7.& 15.18. Vide DISSENSIO.
units.tr: Hatred of a neighbour is forbidden: Lev. 19.17; Prov. 15.17; Matt. 5.23-24; 1 John 2.9, 11; 3.15; 4.20. Hatred generates quarrels: Prov. 10.12. Hatred of evil is commanded: Ps. 97.10; 139.21; Amos 5.15; 6.8; Rom. 12.9. How deadly is hatred of Christ: John 15.23. Hatred for the sake of the Gospel: Matt. 10.22; Mark 13.13; Luke 21.17; John 16.2. Hatred is a mark and sign of reprobation: 1 John 3.13. Examples of hatred: Abimelech and his companions, Gen. 26.27; Esau, 27.41; the Canaanites, 34.30; the brothers of Joseph, 37.4-5; the Egyptians, Exod. 1.12; the Midianites, Num. 25.17-18; the Israelites, Judg. 11.6-7; the blind and the lame, 2 Sam. 5.8; Ammon, 13.15, 22; Rezon, etc., 1 Kings 11.25; Ahab, 22.8; the enemies of Judah, 1 Esd. 4.1; Haman, Esth. 7.6; the enemies of David, Ps. 18.18; 25.19; 44.8; 69.5, 15; the Jews, Amos 5.10; the world, John 7.7; 15.18. See DISSENSION.
[Hatred of God: Deut. 1.27; 9.28; 16.22; Ps. 5.6; 115; Prov. 6.16; Isa. 1.14; Jer. 12.8; 44.4; Amos 5.15; 6.8; Zech. 8.17. Hatred of the Messiah: Ps. 45.8; Heb. 1.9; Rev. 2.6.]

units.la: ODORATVR Deus sacrificium pii, Gen.8.21. [1 Sam.26.19.] Equus bellum, Iob. 39.28. Idola nihil adorantur, Deuter.4.28.
units.tr: God smells the sacrifice of the godly: Gen. 8.21. [1 Sam. 26.19.] A horse smells the battle: Job 39.28. Idols smell nothing: Deut. 4.28.

units.la: OFFENDICVLA necesse est venire, Matth.18.7. Vide HAERESES. Offendiculum fratri non obiiciendum, Rom.14.13. sine offendiculo sit Christianus, 1 Corinth. 9.12. Vide Scandalum.
units.tr: It is necessary that stumbling-blocks come: Matt. 18.7. See HERESIES. A Christian must not put a stumbling-block before a brother: Rom. 14.13. A Christian should be without offence: 1 Cor. 9.12. See SCANDAL.

units.la: OFFENSIONES vitandæ, & quomodo, Rom.3.8.& 6.v.1.14.& 16.17. 1 Cor.9.22. 2 Tim.2.19. 1 Cor.10.32. 2 Cor.6.3.
units.tr: Offences are to be avoided, and how: Rom. 3.8; 6.1, 14; 16.17; 1 Cor. 9.22; 2 Tim. 2.19; 1 Cor. 10.32; 2 Cor. 6.3.

units.la: OFFERENDVM Deo, non Dæmonibus, Leu.17.7. offerendam non est hostia vitiosa, Deut.17.1. offerendarum pecudum armentorum, &c. titus, Leuit.1.1 &c. ¶ Offerendum esse pro defunctis, contendunt Pontificij ex 2.Mach.12.13.
units.tr: Offering is to be made to God, not to demons: Lev. 17.7. A faulty victim must not be offered: Deut. 17.1. The rites of offering herds and flocks, etc., Lev. 1.1 etc. The Papists contend, from 2 Macc. 12.13, that offering is to be made for the dead.

units.la: OFFICIVM subditorum, (Vide SVBDITI.) & aliorum V suis locis.
units.tr: The duty of subjects (see SUBJECTS), and of others, in their own places.

units.la: OG, Rex Basan, Israeli cum valido exercitu se opponit. Num.21.33. vincitur, v.35. & cæditur, v.33. Deut.3.3. eius lectus ferreus, v.11. (. panis subcinericius.)
units.tr: Og, king of Bashan, sets himself against Israel with a strong army: Num. 21.33. He is defeated, v. 35, and struck down, v. 33; Deut. 3.3. His iron bed, v. 11. (That is, a cake baked in the ashes.)

units.la: OLDA prophetissa, Vide HOLDA.
units.tr: OLDA the prophetess: see HOLDA.

units.la: OLEVM lapidi à Iacobo extructo suffunditur, Genes.28.18. & 35.14. Oleum Tabernaculi lucernæ. Exod.27.20. olei vsus,Psal.104. 15. oleum mulierem Eliam pascentem non deficit,1 Reg.17.16.Oleum quondam sanitatis restituendæ signum, non autem medicamentum ægrotis adhibebatur,Marc.6.13. Iac.5.14.Olei sancti confessio, Exo.30.25. Oleum allegorice significat gratiam Spiritus Sancti.Mat. 25.4.[Oleum lætitiæ,quo Messias unctus est,Ps.45.8 & 89. 21.Heb.1.9. Oleum mysticum, Cant. 1.3.Oleum pro sermone dulci ac bene composito,Psal.141.5. Pro.21.20.] oleū dat Deus diligentibus se, Deut. 11.14.oleo non unguntur inobedientes, 28.40. oleo ungitur Rex Saul, 1 Sam.10.1. ungatur infirmus à Presbyteris,Iac.5.14. uncti ab Apostolis sanantur,Mar.6.13.
units.tr: Oil is poured on the stone that Jacob set up: Gen. 28.18; 35.14. The oil of the Tabernacle for the lamp: Exod. 27.20. The use of oil: Ps. 104.15. The oil did not fail the widow feeding Elijah: 1 Kings 17.16. Oil was once a sign of restoring health, but it was not applied to the sick as a medicine: Mark 6.13; James 5.14. The confection of holy oil: Exod. 30.25. Allegorically, oil signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit: Matt. 25.4. [The oil of gladness with which the Messiah was anointed: Ps. 45.8; 89.21; Heb. 1.9. Mystical oil: Song 1.3. Oil for sweet and well-composed speech: Ps. 141.5; Prov. 21.20.] God gives oil to those who love him: Deut. 11.14. The disobedient are not anointed with oil: Deut. 28.40. King Saul was anointed with oil: 1 Sam. 10.1. Let the sick be anointed by the elders: James 5.14. The anointed ones were healed by the Apostles: Mark 6.13.

units.la: OLEA Christus,Rom.11.17.Oleaster populus Gentium,ibi, Olea arbor preciosa semper habita:Osc.14.6.
units.tr: The olive is Christ: Rom. 11.17. The wild olive is the Gentile people, ibid. "The olive, a tree always held precious": Hos. 14.6.

units.la: OLERA amara dulcescunt, V.MIRACVLA. Oleribus vescitur infirmus,Rom.14.v.2. (V.Herba.)
units.tr: Bitter herbs are made sweet; see MIRACLES. The weak eat herbs, Rom. 14.2. (See HERB.)

units.la: OLIVARVM reliquiæ relinquendæ adveniς, pupillis & viduis, Deut.24.20.Columba ad Noë folium oliuæ retulit: Gen.11.
units.tr: The remnants of the olives are to be left for the strangers, the orphans and the widows: Deut. 24.20. The dove brought Noah an olive leaf: Gen. 11.

units.la: OLLA: Ollæ carnium, Exodi 16.3. Ollæ fractæ symbolo Ierosolymæ incendium significatur, Ezechiel. 24.4.
units.tr: Pots of meat: Exod. 16.3. Broken pots are a sign signifying the burning of Jerusalem: Ezek. 24.4.

units.la: OMER,vel Gomer,mensura, & eius quantitas, Exodi 16.36. Homer decima est Ephæ:v.37. (Omer.i,fasciculus, manipulus spicarum.)
units.tr: The omer, or gomer, a measure, and its quantity: Exod. 16.36. The homer is the tenth part of the ephah: v. 37. (Omer means a sheaf, a handful of ears of grain.)

units.la: OMNIS:Omnes pro multis, 1 Corint.14.31.Philipp.2 21.pro quibusuis indefinitè, 2 Reg.8. 9. Matth.4.23. & 7.8.& 5.11, & 13.47.Actor.1.18.& 10.12.Ioann.12.32.1 Timoth.2.4.Omnis interdum quantitatem discretam denotat, & est idem quod totus, Marci 2.13. Omne, pro perfecto & cumulato,Rom.15.13. non enim omnis generis gaudium & pacem, se perfectam & cumulatam suis exoptat Apostolus.Sic capitur hæc pericula & 1 Cor.13.2.Ephes.1.3. Omnis,nota universalis. (Vide NOTA universalis.) Omnes qui sub cœlo sunt, hyperbole Hebræis familiaris, Deuter. 2.25.Act.2.5 Omnes sistemur ad Tribunal Christi,Rom.14.10.2 Corinth.5.10.omnia à Deo, Act. 17.26.2 Corint.5.18.omnia in primitiva & nascenti Ierosolymorum Ecclesia communia erant. Act.2.44. & 4.v.32.24.omnia in Christo condita,Ioan.1.3.Colo.1.16. Hebr.1.& 2. 10.omnia piis à Deo data, 1 Corinth. 3.22. omnia in Dei gloriam,10.31. & Christi nomine facienda, Coloss. 3.17. omnia per Christum instaurata, Ephes.1.10. omnia mundis, Tit. 1. 15. omnia rebus spiritualibus, & vitæ spirituali postponenda. Matth.18.8. Lucæ 14.24. & 17.33. Ioann.2.5. omnia Deo possibilia, Matth.19.26. Marc.10.27. Luc.1.37. omnia credenti possibilia, Marci 9.23. omnia probanda, 1 Thessal.5.21. omnia Christo subiecta, Matth. 11.27. & 28.18. Ioann.16.15. 1 Cor.15.27. Hebr.2.8. omnia Deo tribuenda, Roman.15.18. 1 Cor.3.v.6.7.10. 2 Cor.3.5. & 4.7. Iac.1.17. omnia ad ædificationem fiant, 1 Cor.14.v.26.40.
units.tr: ALL: "All" for many: 1 Cor. 14.31; Phil. 2.21. For any whatever, indefinitely: 2 Kings 8.9; Matt. 4.23; 7.8; 5.11; 13.47; Acts 1.18; 10.12; John 12.32; 1 Tim. 2.4. "All" sometimes denotes a discrete quantity and is the same as "whole": Mark 2.13. "All," for perfect and abundant: Rom. 15.13; for the Apostle does not wish for every kind of joy and peace, but for perfect and abundant joy and peace. So these are understood in 1 Cor. 13.2; Eph. 1.3. "All" is a universal mark (see UNIVERSAL MARK). "All who are under heaven" is a hyperbole familiar to the Hebrews: Deut. 2.25; Acts 2.5. We must all be made to stand before the judgement seat of Christ: Rom. 14.10; 2 Cor. 5.10. All things are from God: Acts 17.26; 2 Cor. 5.18. All things were common in the primitive and newborn Church of Jerusalem: Acts 2.44; 4.32. All things were created in Christ: John 1.3; Col. 1.16; Heb. 1–2; 10. All things are given by God to the pious: 1 Cor. 3.22. All things are to be done for the glory of God: 1 Cor. 10.31, and in the name of Christ: Col. 3.17. All things are restored through Christ: Eph. 1.10. All things are clean to the clean: Titus 1.15. All things are to be placed after spiritual things and spiritual life: Matt. 18.8; Luke 14.24; 17.33; John 2.5. All things are possible with God: Matt. 19.26; Mark 10.27; Luke 1.37. All things are possible to the believer: Mark 9.23. All things are to be tested: 1 Thess. 5.21. All things are subject to Christ: Matt. 11.27; 28.18; John 16.15; 1 Cor. 15.27; Heb. 2.8. All things are to be ascribed to God: Rom. 15.18; 1 Cor. 3.6-7, 10; 2 Cor. 3.5; 4.7; James 1.17. All things are to be done for building up: 1 Cor. 14.26, 40.

units.la: OMNIPOTENS Deus, Genesis 17.1. & 35.11. & 48.3. Exodi 15.2. Num.11.23. (V.Deus.)
units.tr: Almighty God: Gen. 17.1; 35.11; 48.3; Exod. 15.2; Num. 11.23. (See GOD.)

units.la: ONAGER Deo curæ est. Ps.104.v.10.11. eius natura describitur, Iob.39 v.8.9.
units.tr: The wild ass is a concern of God: Ps. 104.10-11. Its nature is described: Job 39.8-9.

units.la: ONAN, filius Iuda, nascitur, Genes.38.4. propter nequitiam à Deo interficitur, v.10. (.i.dolor.)
units.tr: Onan, son of Judah, is born: Gen. 38.4. On account of his wickedness he is slain by God: v. 10. (That is, sorrow.)

units.la: ONESIMVS à Paulo inter vincula gignitur Christo, Philem. v.10. fidelis frater est, Col.4.9. (.i.vtilis G.)
units.tr: Onesimus is begotten to Christ by Paul while in chains: Philem. 10. He is a faithful brother: Col. 4.9. (That is, useful, Greek.)

units.la: ONESIPHORVS, vir pius, 2 Tim.1 16. eius constantia & charitas, v.16.17.18. (.i. vtilitatem afferens. G.)
units.tr: Onesiphorus, a pious man: 2 Tim. 1.16. His steadfastness and love: vv. 16–18. (That is, bringing profit, Greek.)

units.la: ONOCROTATVM non comedebant Iudæi, Leuit.11.18. Deut. 14.18.
units.tr: The Jews did not eat the pelican: Lev. 11.18; Deut. 14.18.

units.la: ONVS Christi leue, ideóque ferendum, Matth.11.v.29.30. onus suum quisque portabit, Rom.14.12. Gal.6 5. onus & infirmitas fratris ferenda, v.2. onus graue imponunt populo Scribæ & Pharisæi, Matth.23.4. Onus, pro afflictione, qua aliquis puniendus prædicitur, Esa.13.1. & 17.1. & 19.1. & 21.v.1.11.13. & 22.1, & 23.1 & 30.6. Ierem.23. v.33.34. 36.38. Ezec.12.10. Nah.1.11. Abac.1.1. Zach.9.1. & 12. onus cui ferendo non sumus, V. Lex, onera alij aliorum portare iubemur, Rom.15.7. Gal.6.2. Ephes.4.32. Colos.3.13. onera quæ ferri nequeunt, à Iurisperitis hominibus imponuntur, Mat.23.4. Luc.11.46. onerati ad Christum vocantur, Matt.11.28.
units.tr: Christ's burden is light, and therefore to be borne: Matt. 11.29–30. Each shall bear his own burden: Rom. 14.12; Gal. 6.5. The burden and weakness of a brother are to be borne: v. 2. The scribes and Pharisees lay heavy burdens on the people: Matt. 23.4. "Burden" for affliction, by which someone is foretold to be punished: Isa. 13.1; 17.1; 19.1; 21.1, 11, 13; 22.1; 23.1; 30.6; Jer. 23.33–34, 36, 38; Ezek. 12.10; Nah. 1.11; Hab. 1.1; Zech. 9.1; 12. A burden which we are not able to bear: see LAW. We are commanded to bear one another's burdens: Rom. 15.1; Gal. 6.2; Eph. 4.2; Col. 3.13. Burdens which cannot be borne are laid on people by lawyers: Matt. 23.4; Luke 11.46. Those burdened are called to Christ: Matt. 11.28.

units.la: POLIAB, alter Tabernaculi artifex, Exo.31.6. à Deo sui artificij peritiam accipit, ibid.
units.tr: POLIAB, the other craftsman of the Tabernacle, receives the skill of his craft from God, Exod. 31.6, ibid.

units.la: POLLA, meretrix, soror Poliabæ, Ezech.23.4. (Ahalibah.i.tabernaculum meum in ea.
units.tr: POLLA, a harlot, sister of Poliab, Ezek. 23.4. (Aholibah, that is, my tabernacle is in her.)

units.la: OPERARIVS mercede sua dignus est, Matth. 10.10. Luc.10.7. Iac.5.14. operandum manibus, Vide LABOR. Operarij dolosi:2 Cor.11.13.
units.tr: A WORKMAN is worthy of his wages, Matt. 10.10, Luc. 10.7, Jas. 5.14. For working with the hands, see LABOUR. Deceitful workers: 2 Cor. 11.13.

units.la: OPES à Deo sunt, Genes.12.7. & 13. versi.14.15. & 15.18. & 26.3. Iob.1.10.& 42.12 Prou. 22. 2. Eccles.5.18. opes nimiæ non appetendæ, Prouerb.23.v.4.5 & 30.8. Eccles 5.9. Iopes statim & derepente cum dolo, mendacio, fœnore & rapinis parte inutiles, Prouer.13.11.& 20.21.& 21.6.& 22.16. & 28, versi.18.29. opes interdum suis dominis ruinam adferunt, Eccles.5.12. opibus affluere, vanitas, 2.1. Vide DIVITIAE.
units.tr: RICHES are from God, Gen. 12.7, 13.14-15, 15.18, 26.3, Job 1.10, 42.12, Prov. 22.2, Eccl. 5.18. Excessive riches are not to be desired, Prov. 23.4-5, 30.8, Eccl. 5.9. Riches gained suddenly and at once through deceit, lying, usury and plunder are partly useless, Prov. 13.11, 20.21, 21.6, 22.16, 28.18, 29. Riches sometimes bring ruin to their owners, Eccl. 5.12. To abound in riches is vanity, 2.1. See RICHES.

units.la: OPHIR, nomen proprium nepotis Eber, Genef.10.29. à quo locus etiam auri optimi feracissimus ophir denominatus est, 1 Reg.9.28 & 10.11 & 22.49 1 Paral. 29.4.2. Paral.8.v.18.[i.palatium.]
units.tr: OPHIR, the proper name of a grandson of Eber, Gen. 10.29, from whom the very fertile region of the finest gold was also named Ophir, 1 Kings 9.28, 10.11, 22.49, 1 Chron. 29.4, 2 Chron. 8.18. [That is, a palace.]

units.la: φθαλμοδουλία, Col.3.22. Ephes.6.6. est fucata & simulata animi nostri summissio & obedientia, quæ vel pœnæ metu, vel spe prædij à nobis ei præstatur, cui parendum est, non autem ipsius Dei metu, neque in vera cordis simplicitate.
units.tr: [φθαλμοδουλία] eye-service, Col. 3.22, Eph. 6.6, is a feigned and pretended submission and obedience of mind, which we render to one whom we must obey, either from fear of punishment or hope of reward, and not from fear of God himself, nor in true simplicity of heart.

units.la: OPHNI, V.I. PHINEES.
units.tr: OPHNI: see PHINEHAS.

units.la: OPINIO quorundam de Ioanne Baptista, Luc.7.33. opiniones de Christo variæ, Matth.16.14. Marc.6.15.& 8.28. Luc.9.ver.8.19, Ioann.7.12.& 10.v.20.21. opiniones & cogitationes hominum frequenter sunt erroneæ, Leuit.10.1. Num. 15.39. Deuter.12.8.& 29.19.1 Sam.15.9.2.Sam.6,6. Prouer. 12.15.& 14.12 & 21.2. Esaiæ 5.21.& 7.12.& 14.13.& 55.8. Matt. 3.14.& 16.22. Marc.8.32. Ioan.11.4.& 13.8. V.Intentio.
units.tr: The opinion of some about John the Baptist, Luke 7.33. Various opinions about Christ, Matt. 16.14, Mark 6.15, 8.28, Luke 9.8, 19, John 7.12, 10.20-21. The opinions and thoughts of men are often mistaken, Lev. 10.1, Num. 15.39, Deut. 12.8, 29.19, 1 Sam. 15.9, 2 Sam. 6.6, Prov. 12.15, 14.12, 21.2, Isa. 5.21, 7.12, 14.13, 55.8, Matt. 3.14, 16.22, Mark 8.32, John 11.4, 13.8. See INTENTION.

units.la: OPITVLATIONES, pro Diaconorum functionibus, 1 Cor. 12.28.
units.tr: HELPS, for the functions of deacons, 1 Cor. 12.28.

units.la: OPPRESSIO bonorum in mundo piis destinata, Ioann.16. 33.1 Thess.3.3.1 Petr. 2.21. & 4.19. oppressio bonorum in mundo perpetua. Exempla: Abel, Gene.4.8. Angeli à Loth hospitio excepti, 19.v.4.9. Iacob, 27.41. vniversus Israel, Exodi 1.12. filij Gedeon, Iud.9.5. Dauid.1 Sam.18.11. Elias, 1 Re.19.2 Elisæus 2 Reg.6.31. Zachariæ filius, 2 Paralip. 24.21. Mardochæus, Esth.3.6 Ieremias, Ier.20.2. Sidrach, Misach, Abdenago Dan.3.ver.19 20. Daniel.6.16 & 14.29, Ioannes Baptista, Matth.14.10. Christus.27.v 28.44. Mar. 15.19. Luc.23.11. Ioan.19.1. Apostoli, Actor, 5.v.18 40. Stephanus, 6.12.& 7.v.57.58. Iacobus Apostolus, 12.2. Paulus & Barnabas 13.50. Paulus, 14.19. & 16.19. Paulus cum Sila v.23.24 (Vide AFFLICTIO:&, TRIBVLATIO:&, BONORVM per malos oppressorum.)
units.tr: The OPPRESSION of the good in the world is appointed for the pious, John 16.33, 1 Thess. 3.3, 1 Pet. 2.21, 4.19. The oppression of the good in the world is perpetual. Examples: Abel, Gen. 4.8; the angels received and entertained by Lot, 19.4-9; Jacob, 27.41; all Israel, Exod. 1.12; the sons of Gideon, Judg. 9.5; David, 1 Sam. 18.11; Elijah, 1 Kings 19.2; Elisha, 2 Kings 6.31; the son of Zechariah, 2 Chron. 24.21; Mordecai, Esth. 3.6; Jeremiah, Jer. 20.2; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, Dan. 3.19-20; Daniel, 6.16, 14.29; John the Baptist, Matt. 14.10; Christ, Matt. 27.28, 44, Mark 15.19, Luke 23.11, John 19.1; the apostles, Acts 5.18, 40; Stephen, Acts 6.12, 7.57-58; the apostle James, Acts 12.2; Paul and Barnabas, Acts 13.50; Paul, Acts 14.19, 16.19; Paul with Silas, Acts 16.23-24. (See AFFLICTION, TRIBULATION, and the good oppressed by the wicked.)

units.la: OPRESSORES pauperum à Deo punientur, Prouerb. 22.v. 22.23, Amos 5.12. &c. (Vide Pauperes)
units.tr: OPPRESSORS of the poor will be punished by God, Prov. 22.22-23, Amos 5.12, etc. (See POOR.)

units.la: OPTIO eligendi hanc vel illam castigationem, à Deo piis interdum datur, 2 Sam. 24.12. 1 Paralip. 21.12. V. Iof. 24.15. Deut. 30.19.
units.tr: CHOICE of undergoing this or that chastisement is sometimes granted by God to the pious, 2 Sam. 24.12, 1 Chron. 21.12. See Josh. 24.15, Deut. 30.19.

units.la: OPVS: Opus pro operis vel mercenarij mercede, Leuitici. 19.13. Esa. 61.8.2. Corint. 5.10. Ephes. 6.8. per metonymiam ex Hebraeorum idiotismo. Sic & Apocal. 14.13. opera ponuntur pro praemio quod ipsa bona opera consequitur, Capitur & pro effectu, Iac. 1.4. opus idem Deo & hominibus diuersa ratione tribuitur: Deo & Sauli, 1. Paral. 10. v. 4 14. Deo & Israelitis, 2 Paral. 11.4. Deo & Sabaeis, Iob. 1.v.15.21. opus idem Prophetis & Diabolo tributum diuersa ratione, Esaiae. 6.10.2 Cor. 4.4. Fides quomodo dicatur opus, Ioan. 6.29. Vide FIDES.
units.tr: WORK: work is used for the work or the wages of a labourer, Lev. 19.13, Isa. 61.8, 2 Cor. 5.10, Eph. 6.8, by metonymy after the Hebrew idiom. So also Rev. 14.13: works are put for the reward which good works themselves obtain. It is also taken for the effect, Jas. 1.4. The same work is ascribed to God and to men in different ways: to God and to Saul, 1 Chron. 10.4, 14; to God and to the Israelites, 2 Chron. 11.4; to God and to the Sabeans, Job 1.15, 21. The same work is ascribed in different ways to the prophets and to the devil: Isa. 6.10, 2 Cor. 4.4. How faith is called a work, John 6.29. See FAITH.

units.la: [OPVS, Opera Dei, quae in creatione & conseruatione rerum, iudiciis & misericordiis eius conspiciuntur, pro coniextus ratione facile distingui possunt. Opus Opera Dei Patris, Ioan. 4.34. &5 20. & 6.29. & 9.v.4 37.38. &14.10. & 17.4. Heb. 2.7. Opus, Opera Filij Dei, Christi Dei-hominis, Matth. 11. 2. Luc. 24.19. Ioan. 5.36. & 7.3.21. & 10.v.25.32. & 14 v.11.12. &15.24. &17.4. Phil. 2.30. Hebr. 1.10. Apoc. 2.26. Opus, Opera Spiritus S. eidem communia cum Patre & Filio, sunt Opera creationis & conseruationis rerum: Sanctificationis item, nempe bona Opera, quae in electis efficit, de quibus vide Bona Opera.]
units.tr: [WORK, the works of God, which are seen in the creation and preservation of things, in his judgements and mercies, can easily be distinguished according to the context. Works of God the Father, John 4.34, 5.20, 6.29, 9.4, 37-38, 14.10, 17.4, Heb. 2.7. Works of the Son of God, Christ God-man, Matt. 11.2, Luke 24.19, John 5.36, 7.3, 21, 10.25, 32, 14.11-12, 15.24, 17.4, Phil. 2.30, Heb. 1.10, Rev. 2.26. Works of the Holy Spirit, which he has in common with the Father and the Son, are the works of creation and preservation of things; likewise sanctification, namely the good works which he effects in the elect, on which see GOOD WORKS.]

units.la: Opus, Opera hominis, bona, mala indifferentia, quae ex locorum circunstantiis facile discernuntur. Opus, Opera S. Angelorum, Ezech. 1.16. Diaboli, Ioann. 8.41.2. Thess. 2.9.1 Ioan. 3.8.
units.tr: Works of man, good, evil or indifferent, which are easily distinguished by the circumstances of places. Works of the holy angels, Ezek. 1.16. Of the devil, John 8.41, 2 Thess. 2.9, 1 John 3.8.

units.la: OPERA BONA
units.tr: GOOD WORKS

units.la: Sunt actiones quae operante Spiritu sancto a regeneratis per fidem secundum Legem Dei fiunt, ad gloriam Dei, fidei & Electionis nostrae confirmationem, & proximi aedificationem.
units.tr: These are actions which regenerate people perform through faith, according to the Law of God, by the working of the Holy Spirit, to the glory of God, to confirm their faith and election, and to edify their neighbour.

units.la: OPERA bona commendantur, Matth. 3.10. Luc. 3.9. Matth. 5.16 & 7.17. & 12.33. Rom. 2.7. Eph. 2.10. 1. Tim. 6.18. Tit. 2. 14. & 3. v. 8.14. Heb. 6.10. & 10.24. 1. Pet. 2.11. 2 Pet. 1.10. Opera bona sunt testimonia pietatis, 1 Tim. 2.10. Opera bona remunerantur, & quare, Vide MERCES. Ad hoc probandum, ut merita operum stabilire possint, abutuntur Papistae his locis, Psal. 119.112. Proverb. 11.18. Eccles. 36.18. Esaiae. 3.10. Matt. 5.12. & 10.42. & 12.37. & 16.27. & 25.34. Luc. 1.30. Ioh. 4.14. Rom. 2.6. 1. Cor. 15.28. 2. Cor. 5.10. 2. Timoth. 4.8. Heb. 6.10, & 10.35. & 11.26. Iac. 2.24. Apoc. 20 v. 7.8. v.7.8.& 22.12. Sed quomodo & quare remunerentur bona opera, Vide MERCES & meritum.
units.tr: Good works are commended: Matt. 3.10, Luke 3.9, Matt. 5.16, 7.17, 12.33, Rom. 2.7, Eph. 2.10, 1 Tim. 6.18, Titus 2.14, 3.8, 14, Heb. 6.10, 10.24, 1 Pet. 2.11, 2 Pet. 1.10. Good works are evidences of piety, 1 Tim. 2.10. Good works are rewarded, and why, see REWARD. To prove that the merits of works can be established, the Papists abuse these passages: Ps. 119.112, Prov. 11.18, Eccl. 36.18, Isa. 3.10, Matt. 5.12, 10.42, 12.37, 16.27, 25.34, Luke 1.30, John 4.14, Rom. 2.6, 1 Cor. 15.28, 2 Cor. 5.10, 2 Tim. 4.8, Heb. 6.10, 10.35, 11.26, Jas. 2.24, Rev. 20.7-8, 22.12. But how and why good works are rewarded, see REWARD and MERIT.

units.la: Opera carnis quæ, Gal.5.19. quæ mala ex eis proveniant, Iacob.4.1. Opera Dei, Hebraismus, pro operibus diuinis, Ioan.6.28. Opera mala Deo displicent, & poenam merentur, Gen. 3.11. &4.7. & 6.v.3.5.6.7. & 7.4,& 9.6.&11.4. & 17.14. & 18.20. & 19.v.11.24.26.& 20.3.& 42. 21. & 44.16. Exod. 3.9 & 8.9.10 11 12.14.20.21,22.capitib & 31.13 & 32.v.9 27.28.33. Leu t.10.12.opera mortua, Heb. 9 14. ¶ Opera præparatoria his dictis nituntur probare Pontificij, Act.3.19. & 10.35 ad ea evertenda locus appositus. Rom.3.24 & 11.35. Ephes. 2 9. Adferunt præterea pro operum meritis & hæc testimonia, Gen.4.v.4.7.& 5, 24. & 6.v.8.9. & 8.v.20.21. & 20.7. & 22.16. & 26.v.4.5.& 29.32. Exod.1.20. & 20.1. &c. & 23.v.22.25. Leuit. 11.vers. 43.44.45.
units.tr: The works of the flesh, Gal. 5.19; what evils proceed from them, Jas. 4.1. The works of God, a Hebraism for divine works, John 6.28. Evil works displease God and deserve punishment: Gen. 3.11, 4.7, 6.3, 5-7, 7.4, 9.6, 11.4, 17.14, 18.20, 19.11, 24, 26, 20.3, 42.21, 44.16; Exod. 3.9, 8.9-12, 14, 20-22, chapters 12, 31.13, 32.9, 27-28, 33; Lev. 10.12. Dead works, Heb. 9.14. ¶ The Papists try to prove preparatory works by these sayings: Acts 3.19, 10.35; the passage cited to overturn them is Rom. 3.24, 11.35, Eph. 2.9. They also bring forward these testimonies for the merits of works: Gen. 4.4, 4.7, 5.24, 6.8-9, 8.20-21, 20.7, 22.16, 26.4-5, 29.32; Exod. 1.20, 20.1 etc., 23.22, 25; Lev. 11.43-45.

units.la: Opera superogationis (quæ vocant) jeuertuntur, Rom. 11.35. opera tenebrarum 13.12. hoc est, vita illa, quam agere solent, qui lucis conspectum fugiunt. Vide Ephes.5.12. 1 Thess.5.5.6 7.8. opera bona dicuntur vocationem & electionem firmam efficere, 2 Pet. 1. 10. non quòd spes nostra, vocatio & electio vllis nostris operibus nitatur, vt testatur Apostolus Rom.3.27 & 4.2. sed quatenus sunt fidei nostræ testimonia, ac proinde nostræ in Christo reconciliationis, dicuntur vocationem & electionem firmam efficere, nostri videlicet respectu. Vide quiddam 1. Tim.6.19. (Vide & ELECTIO) Operum bonorum finis, gloria Dei, Matt 5.16 1 Petr. 2.12. opera à nobis proximo exhibita tanquam sibi facta reputat Deus, siue bona sint, siue mala, Esa.37.23. Ierem.1.19. Zach.2.8. Matt.25.40. Act. 9.5.1.Cor.8.12.
units.tr: Works of supererogation (as they call them) are overturned: Rom. 11.35. Works of darkness, Rom. 13.12, that is, the life which those who shun the sight of light are accustomed to lead. See Eph. 5.12, 1 Thess. 5.5-8. Good works are said to make the calling and election sure, 2 Pet. 1.10, not because our hope, calling and election rest on any of our works, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 3.27, 4.2, but insofar as they are testimonies of our faith, and therefore of our reconciliation in Christ; they are said to make the calling and election sure, namely with respect to us. See also 1 Tim. 6.19. (See also ELECTION.) The end of good works is the glory of God, Matt. 5.16, 1 Pet. 2.12. Whatever is shown by us to the neighbour, God regards as done to himself, whether good or evil: Isa. 37.23, Jer. 1.19, Zech. 2.8, Matt. 25.40, Acts 9.5, 1 Cor. 8.12.

units.la: ORANDVM vbiquè locorum, Psal.103.22. Ierem.23.24. Ioan. 4.23.1. Corinth.1.2.1. Tim.2.8. cum fiducia, 1 Paral. 17.25. Matth.21.21 Mar.11.24. Ioan.14.13. & 16.24. Iac 1.6.1 Ioan. 5.14.15. orandum in nomine IESV, Ioan.14.13.&15.16.&16. vers. 23. 26.1 Ioan. 5.14. orandum in Spiritu Sancto, Iudæ vers.20. orandum Spiritu, 1 Corinth.14.15. orandum indesinenter, Psalmo. 119.62. Matth.7.7. Luc.11.9. & 18. 1.& 21 36. Matt.24.42. & 25.13. Marc.13.33. Act.6.4.& 10.2. Rom.12,12. Eph.6.18. Coloss.4.v.2.3. Thessal.3.19. & 5.17. 2 Thess.3.1,1, Tim.5.5 2. Tim.1.3.1. Petr.4.7. & 5.9. orandum pro ægrotis, Iac.5.14. Exempla: Abraham pro Sodo
units.tr: PRAYER is to be made in every place: Ps. 103.22, Jer. 23.24, John 4.23, 1 Cor. 1.2, 1 Tim. 2.8; with confidence, 1 Chron. 17.25, Matt. 21.21, Mark 11.24, John 14.13, 16.24, Jas. 1.6, 1 John 5.14-15; in the name of Jesus, John 14.13, 15.16, 16.23, 26, 1 John 5.14; in the Holy Spirit, Jude 20; in the Spirit, 1 Cor. 14.15; without ceasing, Ps. 119.62, Matt. 7.7, Luke 11.9, 18.1, 21.36, Matt. 24.42, 25.13, Mark 13.33, Acts 6.4, 10.2, Rom. 12.12, Eph. 6.18, Col. 4.2-3, 1 Thess. 3.10, 5.17, 2 Thess. 3.1, 1 Tim. 5.5, 2 Tim. 1.3, 1 Pet. 4.7, 5.9. Pray for the sick, Jas. 5.14. Examples: Abraham for Sodom, Gen. 18.23; Lot for Zoar, 19.19; Abraham for Abimelech, 20.17; Moses for the Hebrew idolaters, Exod. 32.11; Aaron for the people struck by God, Num. 16.48; Samuel for Saul, 1 Sam. 15.11. See PRAYER for others; and the prayers of others are to be sought for oneself.

units.la: mitis , Genef. 18. 23. Loth pro Segor. 19.' 19. Abra-ham pro Abimelech. 29.17. In our prayer we ought to doubt nothing, Matt. 7.7; 21.22; Mark 11.24; Luke 11.9; John 14.13; 16.24; James 1.6. Our prayers, proceeding from faith, avail also for our brothers, 2 Cor. 1.11. units.la: ORATIO Ideam generalissimam habet ex doctiss. Theologi sententia,in gratiam studiorum hic subiectam , Orationis seu precationis naturam explicant eius 1. Definitio,2.Requisita,3.Effecta.
units.tr: PRAYER. The general idea of this, according to the opinion of a most learned theologian, is set out here for the benefit of students. They explain the nature of prayer or supplication under three heads: 1. definition; 2. requisites; 3. effects.

units.la: 1. Definitio est nominis & rei , vbi multa nomina vocabula,& phrases occurrunt.
units.tr: 1. The definition concerns the name and the thing, where many names, terms and phrases occur.

units.la: 2. Requisita externa & interna. Externis contine- Causa efficiens & finalis,Efficiens triplex,Procreans,Impellens pellens, Corrumpens. Procreans, Spiritus S. Impellens, Dei voluntas declarata mandato, promissis, minis: Necessitas nostra: Intercessio Christi Pontificis: Exempla: Prophetarum, Christi, Apostolorum. Corrumpens, impellenti quasi contraria, luxus, discordia finalis, Dei gloria & nostra salus. Interna requisita respicit Subiectum, nempe recipiens in se, Ecclesia militans in terris: ad se Deus unus: & subiectum occupans indeterminatum, atque determinatum personale ac reale. Sequitur forma communis interna, quae est in reverentia, ardore, fiducia: nec non externa in gestibus & voce. Dein forma propria, & ex utraque natae variae precum formulae. Sequuntur connexa, nempe locus & tempus.
units.tr: 2. The requisites are external and internal. Among the external ones are the efficient and final causes. The efficient cause is threefold: producing, impelling, and corrupting. The producing cause is the Holy Spirit. The impelling cause is God's will as declared by command, promises and threats; our necessity; and the intercession of Christ our High Priest. Examples: the prophets, Christ, the apostles. The corrupting cause, which is contrary to the impelling one, is luxury and discord. The final cause is the glory of God and our salvation. The internal requisites concern the subject, namely the recipient, the Church militant on earth; the one God, to whom prayer is addressed; and the object, which is indeterminate or determinate, personal or real. There follows the common internal form, which consists in reverence, ardour and trust, as well as the external form in gestures and voice. Then comes the proper form, and from both arise the various formulas of prayer. Connected with these are the place and the time.

units.la: 3. Effecta precum sunt quadruplicia. 1. medicina sterilium, & aegrotorum corporum. 2. pauperum victus. 3. afflictarum animarum solatium, & praesidium in adversis. 4. Vis Orationis in omnes creaturas & in Creatorem ipsius.
units.tr: 3. The effects of prayers are fourfold: 1. a remedy for barren and sick bodies; 2. sustenance for the poor; 3. comfort for afflicted souls and protection in adversity; 4. the power of prayer over all creatures and over the Creator himself.

units.la: Sicut Pietas & conversio promovent effecta precationis, eadem impediunt impietas & impoenitentia. Ad superiorem ideam innumera Scripturae Sacrae testimonia & exempla referuntur, quae libro peculiari consignata sunt, & Theologiae candidatis ante aliquot annos maximo cum fructu communicata.}
units.tr: Just as piety and conversion advance the effects of prayer, so impiety and impenitence hinder them. Innumerable testimonies and examples of Holy Scripture are referred to the above idea; these have been recorded in a separate book and, some years ago, were communicated with great profit to candidates for theology.

units.tr: The earth's orb is immovable, Ps. 93.1; 96.10. The future world, that is, the renewed one, Heb. 2.5.

units.tr: ORDER: for ecclesiastical discipline, Col. 2.5. Order is to be kept in the Church, 1 Cor. 14.30-31, 40. Example of ecclesiastical order: the synod of Jerusalem, Acts 15.13. Political order is to be kept and cherished, Rom. 13.1; Titus 3.1; 1 Pet. 2.13. Those who disturb it are to be avoided, 2 Thess. 3.6. Orders of the Levites: see LEVITAE.

units.la: ORNATVS κοσμιότης, est vestitus cultúsque corporis, qualis nos pro ratione personæ decet, moderatio: nequid sordidum vel lasciuum vel affectatum in eo insit vel appareat.1 Tim.2.9.1.Pet.3.3.5. Peccatur in eo genere variis modis, quibus offenduntur fratres : vt in vestium nimia pretio, nitore, forma, ornamentis, mollitie. Quum hic in vestitu nostro neque sordes, neque quicquam præter decorum esse debeat. (Vide Mulierum curiosus ornatus: & cultus.)
units.tr: ORNAMENT [κοσμιότης] is the clothing and care of the body that suits each person's station, a moderation which admits nothing dirty, wanton or affected in it or on show (1 Tim. 2.9; 1 Pet. 3.3, 5). People sin in this matter in various ways, by which their brothers are offended: by excessive expense on clothes, by their sheen, cut, trimmings or softness. Our dress ought to have nothing squalid in it and nothing beyond what is seemly. (See the immoderate adornment and dress of women.)

units.la: ORNATVS Aaronis & Filiorum. Vide AARON.

units.la: Os, oris, pro sermone & locutione, Num.23.16. Matth.18.16. pro voce, atque adeo tacito etiam testimonio, id est, cùm res ipsa per se loquitur, 21.16. Os hominis à Deo, Exod. 4 11. os ex abundantia cordis loquitur. Matth.12.34 Luc.6 45. os gladij, Hebræorum more, pro acie, seu cuspide, quod ea parte quasi mordeat, vel ahuriat sanguinem, Luc. 21.24. os aperire, pro vouere, ludic.11.36. alias, dicendi initium facere, aut se ad loquendum præparare, Matth 5.2. Os Domini interrogare, i. eius consilium sciscitari, piùm & sanctum, Ioh.9.14. Esai.30.2.
units.tr: MOUTH (os, oris) is used for speech and utterance (Num. 23.16; Matt. 18.16), and for voice, and even for silent testimony, that is, when the thing speaks for itself (Matt. 21.16). The mouth of a man is from God (Exod. 4.11). The mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart (Matt. 12.34; Luke 6.45). The mouth of the sword, in the Hebrew manner, means the edge or point, because it bites, as it were, or drinks blood on that part (Luke 21.24). To open the mouth means to vow (Judg. 11.36); otherwise, to begin speaking, or to prepare oneself to speak (Matt. 5.2). To ask at the mouth of the Lord, that is, to seek his counsel, is devout and holy (John 9.14; Isa. 30.2).

units.tr: [The mouth of Christ: Song 1.1; Isa. 11.4; 49.2; 53.7, 9; Matt. 5.2; John 19.29; 2 Thess. 2.8; 1 Pet. 2.22; Rev. 1.16; 2.16; 3.16; 19.15, 21.] The mouth of a man, that is, his face or appearance (1 Sam. 21.13); the brow (Ezek. 16.12). The mouth of a fish (Matt. 17.27). Of a four-footed beast (Num. 22.28; Deut. 25.4; Job 40.18; Dan. 6.22; 7.5; Amos 3.12; 1 Cor. 9.9; 1 Tim. 5.18; Heb. 11.33). The mouth of the mystical beast (Rev. 13.2, 5-6). The mouths of the mystical horses (Rev. 9.17-19). The mouth of a lion.

units.la: Impij & violenti, Psalm. 22. 22. x 58 7. os serpentis, draconis, i. Satanæ, Apoc. 12. 15. & 16. 13. os idolorum, Psalm. 115. 5. & 135 v. 16. 17. Ierem. 51. 44. os gladij, cuspis & acies, Exod. 17. 13. Num. 21. 24. 1 Sam. 15. 8. os putei, Gen. 29. 2. &c. putei item mystici. Psal. 69. 16. os sacci, Genes. 42. 27. os sepulchri, Esai. 5. 14. os ipeluncæ. Ios. 10. 18. Dan. 6. 17. os terræ, Genes. 4. 11. Numer. 16. 30. Apocal. 12. 16. Os vulvæ. Prov. 30. 16.]
units.tr: Of the wicked and violent (Ps. 22.22; 58.7). The mouth of the serpent or dragon, that is, of Satan (Rev. 12.15; 16.13). The mouths of idols (Ps. 115.5; 135.16-17; Jer. 51.44). The mouth of the sword, the point and edge (Exod. 17.13; Num. 21.24; 1 Sam. 15.8). The mouth of a well (Gen. 29.2, etc.), and likewise of the mystical well (Ps. 69.16). The mouth of a sack (Gen. 42.27). The mouth of a tomb (Isa. 5.14). The mouth of a cave (Josh. 10.18; Dan. 6.17). The mouth of the earth (Gen. 4.11; Num. 16.30; Rev. 12.16). The mouth of the womb (Prov. 30.16).

units.la: os Agni Paschalis nullum frangendum, Exod. 12. 46. Num. 9. 12. Ioan. 19. 36.
units.tr: No bone of the Paschal lamb is to be broken (Exod. 12.46; Num. 9.12; John 19.36).

units.la: os. A Ioseph ex Ægypto per Moysen translata sepeliuntur, Exod. 13. 19. Ios. 24. 32. ossa Saulis & filiorum eius sepulta, 1 Sam. 31. 12. 13. 2 Sam. 21. 12. &c. ossa cuiusdam servi Dei a Iosia servantur. 2 Reg. 23. 18. ossium eiiciendorum commi- natio, Ezech. 6. 5.
units.tr: Bones. The bones of Joseph were carried up out of Egypt by Moses and buried (Exod. 13.19; Josh. 24.32). The bones of Saul and his sons were buried (1 Sam. 31.12-13; 2 Sam. 21.12, etc.). The bones of a certain servant of God were preserved by Josiah (2 Kings 23.18). A threat to cast out the bones (Ezek. 6.5).

units.la: ossium aridorum visio Ezechieli patefacta, Ezech. 37. versu 2. &c.
units.tr: The vision of dry bones was revealed to Ezekiel (Ezek. 37.2, etc.).

units.la: OSANNA, V. Hosanna, pro Hosianna.
units.tr: HOSANNA: see Hosanna, for Hosianna.

units.la: OSCVLVM sanctum & pudicum charitatis symbolum. Genes. 29. 13. & 45. 14. 15. & 48. 10. & 50. 1. Exod. 4. 27. Luc. 15. 20. Actor 20. 37. Rom. 16. 16. 1 Cor. 16. 20. 2 Corinth. 13. 12. 1 Thess. 5. 26. 1 Petri 5. 14. [osculum mysticum, Cant. 1. 1.] Oscula saluandi ritus orientalibus familiaris, cuius & Apostolus locis citatis meminit. Osculi sancti & minime fatigati exempla: Isaac, Genes. 27. 27. Iacob, 29. 11. Laban. 31. 55. Esau. 33. 4. Ioseph, 45. 15. & 50. 1. Aaron, Exod. 4. 27. Moses 18. 7. Noemi, Ruth. 1. 9. orpha, v. 14. Samuel, 1 Sam. 10. 1. David & Ionathas, 20. 40. 41. Dauid, 2 Sam. 14. 33. & 19. 39. Absalom, 15. 5. Elisæus, 1 Reg. 19. 20. Mulier peccatrix, Luc. 7. 38. Pater Acolasti, 15. 20. Fideles, Actor. 20. 37. osculum fictum, periculosum, Prov. 27. 6. osculum proditioni præ- textum, aut osculum proditorium: Exempla: Ioab, 2 Sam. 20. v. 9. 10. Iudas Iscariotes, Matth. 26. 49. Marc. 14. 45. Luc. 22. 47.
units.tr: KISS, a holy and chaste symbol of love (Gen. 29.13; 45.14-15; 48.10; 50.1; Exod. 4.27; Luke 15.20; Acts 20.37; Rom. 16.16; 1 Cor. 16.20; 2 Cor. 13.12; 1 Thess. 5.26; 1 Pet. 5.14). [The mystical kiss, Song 1.1.] The custom of greeting with a kiss was familiar to the East, and the Apostle mentions it in the passages cited. Examples of holy and unfeigned kissing: Isaac (Gen. 27.27); Jacob (29.11); Laban (31.55); Esau (33.4); Joseph (45.15; 50.1); Aaron (Exod. 4.27); Moses (18.7); Naomi (Ruth 1.9); Orpah (v. 14); Samuel (1 Sam. 10.1); David and Jonathan (20.40-41); David (2 Sam. 14.33; 19.39); Absalom (15.5); Elisha (1 Kings 19.20); the sinful woman (Luke 7.38); the father of the prodigal (15.20); the faithful (Acts 20.37). A feigned kiss is dangerous (Prov. 27.6). A kiss used as a pretext for betrayal, or a treacherous kiss. Examples: Joab (2 Sam. 20.9-10); Judas Iscariot (Matt. 26.49; Mark 14.45; Luke 22.47).

units.la: SEE, Ela filius, occiso Rekach regnum Israelis vsurpat. 2 Reg. 15. 30. Assyriorum Regi tributarius est. 17. 3. ab eo in carcerem coniicitur, v. 4. (1. Saluator, vel saluatus.)
units.tr: HOSEA, son of Elah, who after killing Pekah seized the kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 15.30). He was tributary to the king of the Assyrians (17.3), and was cast into prison by him (v. 4). (That is, saviour, or saved.)

units.la: SEAS, Vide Hosea.
units.tr: HOSEA: see Hosea.

units.la: TENTATIO (quæ ὑπερηφανία, Marc. 7. 22. videtur nominari posse) est intolerabilis honoris alicuius eximij adexti vel adipiscendi iactatio & beatus, per quem qui in ea dignitate est seipsum immodice & importune ostentat. vel etiam adeptum munus egregium ad aliorum iniu-riam & contumeliam nimia superbia & effreni licentia exercet, 1 Pet 5.5. Sic Roboam alienauit à se Israelem 1. Reg.12.14. Ostentator est, qui opes magnas præter dignitatem, & quibus in rebus minime opus est, expenditaut qui suas opes superbe ad sui ipsius non ad gloriam Dei ostentat. Qualis fuit Ezechias, Isa.39.2.6.
units.tr: OSTENTATION (which may be called pride, hyperēphania [ὑπερηφανία], Mark 7.22) is the unbearable boasting of some outstanding honour that a man has or seeks to win, and a showing-off by which he who holds the office displays himself immoderately and tiresomely. It is also when a man, having obtained an eminent office, uses it to the injury and insult of others, with excessive arrogance and unbridled licence (1 Pet. 5.5). So Rehoboam alienated Israel from himself (1 Kings 12.14). He is a show-off who spends great wealth beyond his station, and on things where there is no need at all, or who proudly displays his wealth for his own glory and not the glory of God. Hezekiah was such a man (Isa. 39.2, 6).

units.la: Ostivm sermonis. [1 Corint.16.9. Col.4.3. Apoc.3.8.] Vide Verbvm Dei. Ostia carceris aperta. Vide Miracvla, Ostium Christus, Ioan.10.v.17.&c. Ostium fidei Act.14.27. Ostium in cælo Apoc.4.1. [Ostium mysticum, Cantic.5.6. & 8.9. Apoc.3.20.] V. Ioan.14.2.
units.tr: A door for the word (1 Cor. 16.9; Col. 4.3; Rev. 3.8). See the Word of God. Prison doors opened. See Miracles. Christ is the door (John 10.7, etc.). A door of faith (Acts 14.27). A door in heaven (Rev. 4.1). [A mystical door, Song 5.6; 8.9; Rev. 3.20.] See John 14.2.

units.la: Othoniel, Caleb ex fratre nepos, ob captam Cariat-sepher ciuitatem, Axam auunculi filiam vxorem ducit, Iudic.1.13 Israelem iudicat, 3.9. moritur, v.11. (Athniel.i.tempus meum Dei.)
units.tr: Othniel, nephew of Caleb through his brother, who after taking the city of Kiriath-sepher married Achsah, his uncle's daughter (Judg. 1.13). He judged Israel (3.9) and died (v. 11). (Athniel, that is, my time of God.)

units.la: Otium vitandum, Prou. 6. v. 6.9.&10 v.4.26.& 12.11.& 14.4. & 20.4. & 28.19 & 31.27. Eccl.11 6. Eph.4.28.1 Thess.4.11.2 Thess.3.10. Tit.3.14. (Vide Acedia: & Negligentia.)
units.tr: Idleness is to be avoided (Prov. 6.6-9; 10.4, 26; 12.11; 14.4; 20.4; 28.19; 31.27; Eccl. 11.6; Eph. 4.28; 1 Thess. 4.11; 2 Thess. 3.10; Titus 3.14). (See Sloth and Negligence.)

units.la: Ovis: Ouem comedunt Iudæi, Deut.14.4 Oues errantes ante conuersionem, 1 Pet.2.25. Oues, benedicti Dei, Matt.25.33. Oues Christi, vocem eius audiunt, Ioan.10.4. Quiū caulæ multiplicantur obedientibus Dei præceptis, Deut.28.4. Ouinm parabolam proponit Michæas, 1 Reg.22.17. Ouis perditæ parabola. Matt 18 11.12.&c. Lucæ 15.4 (Vide Parabolarvm catalogus) de Ouibus oblatio, Leuit.3.6. Oues μεταφορικῶς, pro mansuetis & fraudis nesciis homi-nibus, Matt.7.15. Ouile Ecclesia Christi ex Iudæis & Gentibus, Ioan.10.16. [Oves Dei, Ps.79.13.& 95.7.& 100.3. Ezech.34.5.&c. Zach.13.7. Heb.13.20. Ouile Christi, Ioan 10 16.[1 Pet.2.25.]
units.tr: SHEEP. Jews eat the sheep (Deut. 14.4). Sheep that wander before conversion (1 Pet. 2.25). Sheep, the blessed of God (Matt. 25.33). Christ's sheep hear his voice (John 10.4). When the folds are multiplied by obedience to God's commands (Deut. 28.4). Micaiah sets forth the parable of the sheep (1 Kings 22.17). The parable of the lost sheep (Matt. 18.11-12, etc.; Luke 15.4). (See the catalogue of parables.) Concerning offering of sheep (Lev. 3.6). Sheep, metaphorically, for gentle people who know no deceit (Matt. 7.15). The fold of the Church of Christ from Jews and Gentiles (John 10.16). [The sheep of God, Ps. 79.13; 95.7; 100.3; Ezek. 34.5, etc.; Zech. 13.7; Heb. 13.20. The fold of Christ, John 10.16; 1 Pet. 2.25.]

units.la: Oza & Ahio, filij Aminadab, 2 Sam.6.3. Oza temere De-arcæ manum imponit, v.6.1. Paral. 13.9.ob id à Deo.punitur, 2 Sam.6.7.1 Paralipom.13 10. (Oza.i. robustus Domini.)
units.tr: Uzza and Ahio, sons of Abinadab (2 Sam. 6.3). Uzza rashly laid his hand on the ark of God (v. 6; 1 Chron. 13.9), and for this was punished by God (2 Sam. 6.7; 1 Chron. 13.10). (Uzza, that is, strong of the Lord.)

units.la: Ozias Rex, Vide Vzias, & Azarias. (Oziel fortitudo mea Deus.)
units.tr: Uzziah the king; see Azariah and Uzziah. (Uzziel, God is my strength.)

units.la: PABVLVM, Gen.42.27. Iudic.19.21. Dan.4.21. Pabulum ignis, Leuit.3.11.
units.tr: FODDER: Gen. 42.27; Judg. 19.21; Dan. 4.21. Fuel for fire (Lev. 3.11).

units.la: PACATVS, Iob.8.6. Hebr.12.11.
units.tr: CALM: Job 8.6; Heb. 12.11.

units.la: PACIFICI beati, Matth.5.9. pacificus Salomon, 1 Paral.22.9. Moses, Exo.2.13. Dauid, Ps.120.7. Christus, Col.1.20. Eph.2.
units.tr: PACIFICI, blessed are the peacemakers, Matt. 5.9. Solomon is peaceable, 1 Chron. 22.9. Moses, Exod. 2.13. David, Ps. 120.7. Christ, Col. 1.20; Eph. 2.

units.la: PACIFICORVM hostiæ, Leu.3. & 7.18.19. cap.14. Apostoli &c. Esa.52.7. 2. Cor.5.19.20.
units.tr: PACIFICORUM hostiae (peace offerings), Lev. 3; 7.18, 19; ch. 14. The Apostles, etc. Isa. 52.7; 2 Cor. 5.19, 20.

units.la: PACTVM salis, 2 Paral. 13.5. pactum cum quibus non ineundum, V. FOEDVS.
units.tr: PACTUM salis (a covenant of salt), 2 Chron. 13.5. A covenant not to be entered into with certain people; see COVENANT.

units.la: Pacta sunt seruanda. exempla. Iosua, Iof.6.25. Dauid, 1 Samu. 24.v.22.23.1 Reg.2.8. Michæas, 2 Paral. 18.13. V. FOEDVS:& IVRAMENTVM.
units.tr: Covenants are to be kept. Examples: Joshua, Josh. 6.25; David, 1 Sam. 24.22, 23; 1 Kings 2.8; Micaiah, 2 Chron. 18.13. See COVENANT and OATH.

units.la: PAEDAGOGVS ad Christum, Vide LEX Pædagogi, 1 Corinth. 4.15.
units.tr: PAEDAGOGUE to Christ: see LAW (the schoolmaster), 1 Cor. 4.15.

units.la: Παιδευτὴς, Vide IMPVDICITIA: &, CONCVBITVS illiciti.
units.tr: Paideutes [Παιδευτής]: see IMPURITY; and ILLICIT intercourse.

units.la: PAEDOBAPTISMVS, V. BAPTISMVS infantium.
units.tr: PAEDOBAPTISM: see BAPTISM of infants.

units.la: PALAESTINI: eorum excidium prædicitur, Ierem.47.4. Ezec.25.15. Palæstina, regionis nomen, quæ terra Chanaan, vel terra sancta dicitur, quam Israelitæ tenuerunt. V. Gen. 2134. Amos,6.2.
units.tr: PHILISTINES: their destruction is foretold, Jer. 47.4; Ezek. 25.15. Palestine is the name of a region, which is called the land of Canaan or the holy land, and which the Israelites held. See Gen. 21.34; Amos 6.2.

units.la: PALLIVM Eliæ Elæi & Elisæi, 1 Reg.19.19.2 Reg.2. v.8.13. V. Mat.5.40.
units.tr: PALLIUM (mantle) of Elijah, of Elisha, 1 Kings 19.19; 2 Kings 2.8, 13. See Matt. 5.40.

units.la: PALMA, arbor tereti & procero stipite, orbibus ordine in eo scandentibus, omnium arborum rectissima: V. Cant.7.7. Hier.10.5. Diutissime viget & viuit, vt apparet ex Ps.92.12. Apud Veteres victoriæ fuit insigne in certaminibus, vt apparet ex Apoc.7.9. Iustus vt palma florebit, Psal.92 13. Acceperunt ramos palmarum venientes obuiam Christo &c. Ioh.12.13. V. Apoc.7.9.
units.tr: PALM, a tree with a slender and tall trunk, with rings arranged in order on it as it rises, the straightest of all trees; see Song 7.7; Jer. 10.5. It flourishes and lives for a very long time, as appears from Ps. 92.12. Among the ancients it was an emblem of victory in contests, as appears from Rev. 7.9. "The righteous shall flourish like the palm," Ps. 92.13. Those coming to meet Christ received branches of palms, etc., John 12.13. See Rev. 7.9.

units.la: PALMES, Ioan.15.v.4.6. palmes spiritualis Ps. 80. 12. Ezech. 17.v.6.7.9.& 19.11.& Ioan.15,v.2.5.]
units.tr: PALM branch (vine branch), John 15.4, 6. A spiritual branch, Ps. 80.12; Ezek. 17.6, 7, 9; 19.11; John 15.2, 5.

units.la: PALMAS dant in faciem Christi, Matt.26.67.
units.tr: They gave blows in the face of Christ, Matt. 26.67.

units.la: PALMVS Dei, Esai.40.12.] V.Exo.18.16.
units.tr: The hand of God, Isa. 40.12. See Exod. 18.16.

units.la: ALPAT in meridie inobediens, Deut.28.29. Esa.59 10. Iob. 5.14.
units.tr: Stumbling at noon, not obedient, Deut. 28.29; Isa. 59.10; Job 5.14.

units.la: AMPHILIA regio Asiæ, Act.2.10 & 13.13.& 14.24. (tota dilecta.)
units.tr: AMPHILIA, a region of Asia, Acts 2.10; 13.13; 14.24. (All of it beloved.)

units.la: ANIS, pro quolibet cibi genere, Genes.3.19. & 18.5.& 21.14. & 31.54.37.25. & 43.25. Exod.2.20.&18.12. Deuter.8.3.pæ

synecdochen. Sic Prouerb.25.21. Roman.12.20. Inde sunt phrases Hebraeis familiares: Panem edere, pro cibum capere, Marc.3.20. & 7.2. panem frangere, ibidem pro capere cibum, Act.2.46. panis fractio, pro mutuo conuictu & conuiuiis, quae inter Iudaeos celebrantur, 2, 42. (Vide FRACTIO.) panis item capitur pro eo cibi genere, quod panem vocamus, Marc.8.4. panis hominem fulcit, Genes.3.19. Eccles.11,6. Ephes.4.28. 1 Thessal.4.11. 2 Thessal.3.10. Tit.3.14. panes facierum (quos Latine propositionis, vel propositivos vertunt) Hebraeis ideo sic dicuntur, Exod.25.30. Leuit.24 v.5.7. Matth.12.4. Marc 2.26. Luc.6.4. Heb.9.2. quod coram Domino appositi tota hebdomade manerent in aurea mensa, huic cultui consecrata, sicut edixit Dominus Leuitic.24.5. appositivos non inepte vocaueris. Panes multiplicantur, (Vide MIRACVLA) panis Evangelij, Iudaeorum erat, Matt.15.26 &c. Marc.7.27. panis laicus, vt vocant, 1 Sam.21.4. panis vitae, hoc est, panis vivificus, (Hebraismus) caro Christi, Ioann.6.v.35.51. panis vnius & calicis participatio, 1 Corinth.10.16. panes primitiarum multiplicati, 2 Regum 4.42. pane & aqua cibatur Elias, 1 Reg.19.v.6.8. pane solo non viuit homo, Deut.8.3. Matt.4.4. Luc.4.4. panibus obedientium sibi benedixit Deus, comeduntq; in saturitate, Leu.26.5. panes pluit Deus e coelo, Exo.16.13. panibus quinque, quinque hominum millia saturati. Matt.14.v.17.21. septem, quatuor millia 15.v.34.38. panum oblatio, Leu.2.4.
units.tr: (a synecdoche). So Prov. 25.21; Rom. 12.20. From this come phrases familiar to the Hebrews: to eat bread, meaning to take food, Mark 3.20; 7.2; to break bread, meaning in the same place to take food, Acts 2.46; the breaking of bread, meaning the mutual fellowship and feasts celebrated among the Jews, Acts 2.42 (see BREAKING). Bread is also taken for that kind of food which we call bread, Mark 8.4. Bread sustains a man, Gen. 3.19; Eccl. 11.6; Eph. 4.28; 1 Thess. 4.11; 2 Thess. 3.10; Titus 3.14. The "bread of the faces" (which they translate in Latin as "of the presence" or "of setting forth") is so called by the Hebrews, Exod. 25.30; Lev. 24.5, 7; Matt. 12.4; Mark 2.26; Luc. 6.4; Heb. 9.2, because they were set before the Lord and remained for a whole week on the golden table consecrated to this worship, as the Lord commanded in Lev. 24.5. One may not inaptly call them "the setting-forth loaves." Loaves are multiplied (see MIRACLES). The bread of the Gospel was for the Jews, Matt. 15.26, etc.; Mark 7.27. Lay bread, as they call it, 1 Sam. 21.4. Bread of life, that is, life-giving bread (a Hebraism), the flesh of Christ, John 6.35, 51. The participation in the one bread and cup, 1 Cor. 10.16. The multiplied first-fruit loaves, 2 Kings 4.42. Elijah is fed with bread and water, 1 Kings 19.6, 8. Man does not live by bread alone, Deut. 8.3; Matt. 4.4; Luke 4.4. God blessed with bread those who obeyed him, and they ate to the full, Lev. 26.5. God rains bread from heaven, Exod. 16.13. With five loaves, five thousand men were satisfied, Matt. 14.17, 21; with seven, four thousand, 15.34, 38. The offering of bread, Lev. 2.4.

units.la: [PANIS vocula[?] ita distinximus.
units.tr: [We have distinguished the little word PANIS thus.]

units.la: 1. Frequenter quemuis cibum, vel tenuem, vel lautum significat: vt ex contextuum circumstantiis apparet. Quando autem cum adiecto legitur (vt Gen.18.6. Exo.12. v.8 39. & alibi panem purum vt plurimum significat.
units.tr: 1. It frequently signifies any kind of food, whether plain or rich, as appears from the circumstances of the contexts. When it is read with an adjective (as in Gen. 18.6; Exod. 12.8, 39, and elsewhere), it usually signifies unleavened bread.

units.la: 2. Panis afflictionis, oppressionis, tribulationis, lacrymarum, Deut.16.3. 1 Reg.22.27. Psal. 42.4. & 80.6. & 127. Esai. 30.20.
units.tr: 2. Bread of affliction, of oppression, of tribulation, of tears: Deut. 16.3; 1 Kings 22.27; Ps. 42.4; 80.6; 127.2; Isa. 30.20.

units.la: 3. Panis impietatis & mendacij, i. pessimis artibus comparatus, Prou.4.17. & 23.3.
units.tr: 3. Bread of wickedness and falsehood, that is, obtained by the worst arts: Prov. 4.17; 23.3.
4. Bread from heaven, the manna: Exod. 16.4, 8, 12, 15, 32; Neh. 9.15; Ps. 78.24, 25; 105.40; John 6.31.

units.la: 5. Panes propositionis, seu facierum, qui coram facie Dei i. mensa in tabernaculo, apponebantur, Exo.25.30. Num 4.7. 1 Sam.21.v.4.6. Matt.12.4. Heb.9.2.
units.tr: 5. The bread of the setting-forth, or of the faces, which were placed before the face of God, that is, on the table in the tabernacle: Exod. 25.30; Num. 4.7; 1 Sam. 21.4, 6; Matt. 12.4; Heb. 9.2.

units.la: 6. Panis Dei, panis vitæ, panis cœlestis, nempe Christus, Ioan. 6. v. 32. 33. 35. 41. 48. 50. 51. 58. panis mysticus, 1 Cor. 10. 17. panis regni Dei, Luc. 14. 15. panis sapientiæ diuinæ, Prou. 9. 5. Esai. 55. 2.
units.tr: 6. The bread of God, the bread of life, the heavenly bread, namely Christ: John 6.32, 33, 35, 41, 48, 50, 51, 58. The mystical bread, 1 Cor. 10.17. The bread of the kingdom of God, Luke 14.15. The bread of divine wisdom, Prov. 9.5; Isa. 55.2.

units.la: 7. Panis sacer, 1. Cuius vsus erat, præsertim in rebus sacris, Exo. 29. 23. 32. &c. Num. 6. 15. Ezech. 44. 7.
units.tr: 7. Holy bread. 1. Its use was especially in sacred things: Exod. 29.23, 32, etc.; Num. 6.15; Ezek. 44.7.

units.la: 8. panis sacramentalis in Cœna Domini, Matt. 26. 26. 1 Cor. 10. v. 16. 17. & 11. v. 23 26. 27. 28 ]
units.tr: 8. The sacramental bread in the Lord's Supper: Matt. 26.26; 1 Cor. 10.16, 17; 11.23, 26, 27, 28.

units.la: PARABOLA, Græcis παραβολὴ passim in Euangelio, non tam comparationem, aut collationem declarat, quales adhiberi à plerisque Scriptoribus solent, ad ea illustranda, quæ alioquin videri possent obscurius dicta, quam allegoricam orationem: quæ non facile ab omnibus intelligatur. Matth. 15. 15. Marc. 12. 1. & alibi sæpe: & quod cæteri Euangelistæ παραβολὴν vocant, Ioannes παροιμίαν vocare solet, vt & Ioann. 10. 6. est autem paræmia oratio obscurior, & quasi deflexa à communi itinere & loquendi formula. Capitur item parabolæ vox pro similitudine, Mat. 13. 3. Hebr. 11. 19. pro typo, seu exemplari, Hebr. 9. 8. pro eo quod Latinis prouerbium dicitur, Luc. 4. 23. Parabolæ Salomonis, 1 Reg. 4 32. Parabolæ, id est, comparationes & allegoricæ orationes continuis metaphoris expressæ, Iudic. 9. 8. 2 Sam. 12. 1. & 14. 5. 1 Reg. 20. 39. & 22. 17. 2 Reg. 14. 9. 2. Paral. 18. 16. & 25. 18. Ezech. 5. 1. & 12. 3. & 17. 3. Matth. 11. 16. & 13. 31. &c. & 21. 28. & 22. verf. 2. 23. & 25. 14. Marc. 13. 28. & 12. 1 Luc. 7. 41. & 12. 16. & 13. versi. 6. 21. & 14. ver. 7. 16. 28. 31. & 15. v. 4. 8. 11. & 16. 1. & 18. 10. & 20. 9. & 21. 29. Ioann. 10. 1. units.tr: PARABLE. The Greek parabolē, found throughout the Gospel, signifies not so much a comparison or collation, such as most writers are wont to use to illustrate things which might otherwise seem spoken too obscurely, but an allegorical discourse which is not easily understood by all: Matt. 15.15; Mark 12.1, and often elsewhere. And what the other Evangelists call parabolē, John is accustomed to call paroimia (proverb), as also John 10.6. Now paroimia is a more obscure discourse, and as it were turned aside from the common road and form of speaking. The word parable is also taken for a likeness, Matt. 13.3; Heb. 11.19; for a type or pattern, Heb. 9.8; for what the Latins call a proverb, Luke 4.23. The parables of Solomon, 1 Kings 4.32. Parables, that is, comparisons and allegorical discourses expressed by continuous metaphors: Judg. 9.8; 2 Sam. 12.1; 14.5; 1 Kings 20.39; 22.17; 2 Kings 14.9; 2 Chron. 18.16; 25.18; Ezek. 5.1; 12.3; 17.3; Matt. 11.16; 13.31, etc.; 21.28; 22.2, 23; 25.14; Mark 13.28; 12.1; Luke 7.41; 12.16; 13.6, 21; 14.7, 16, 28, 31; 15.4, 8, 11; 16.1; 18.10; 20.9; 21.29; John 10.1. A catalogue of parables: the parable of the waters flowing out of the house, Ezek. 47.1; of the great eagle, 17.3; of the trees anointing a king over themselves, Judg. 9.8; of the two baskets of figs, Jer. 24.1; of the thistle and the cedar, 2 Kings 14.9; 2 Chron. 25.19; of the linen girdle, Jer. 13.1; of the great supper, Matt. 22.2; Luke 14.16; see Rev. 19.9; of the rich man and the poor man who had one little ewe, 2 Sam. 12.1; of the rich man whose fields were abundant, Luke 12.16; of the two debtors, 7.41; of the unjust steward called to account by the Lord, 16.1; of the drachma, 15.8; of the leaven, Matt. 13.33; Luke 13.20, etc.; of the potter, Jer. 18.2; of the fig tree, Matt. 24.32; Mark 13.28; Luke 13.6; 21.29; of the prodigal son, 15.11; of the two sons of the same mother, 2 Sam. 14.5; of two sons, one obedient and the other disobedient, Matt. 21.28; of the grain of mustard seed, Matt. 13.31; Mark 4.31; Luke 13.19; of those invited to the wedding, Matt. 22.6; of the unjust judge, Luke 18.2.
