units.la: Christus suis seorsim Discipulis edisserebat, Marci 4.v.10.11. Luc.9.v.9.10. in parabolis cur loquutus sit Christus, Matth.13.v.13 34.
units.tr: Christ explained things privately to his disciples (Mark 4:10–11; Luke 8:9–10). Why Christ spoke in parables: Matthew 13:13–34.

units.la: Vsvs parabolarum seu similitudinum. 1. Sapientia diuina, cum norit quanta caligo in hominis animum per peccatum sit inducta subinde similibus vtitur, ad perspicuè patefaciendam nobis suam voluntatem. 2. Deinde non ad intelligentiam modò, sed & ad memoriam plurimùm valet similitudo: quia firmius hærent, quæ pluribus sensibus percipiuntur. 3. Ad excitandum & persuadendum magna vis similitudini inest. Christus iā moriturus Iohanni dixit: Ecce mater tua: item mulieri Ecce filius tuus: qua ratione cor ipsum ad officium præstandum rapitur. Itaque parabolarum ea vis est, vt rem illustrent, si bene intelligantur: attentionem excitent, ac rem altius memoriæ figant. Si tamen non applicentur aut explicentur, interdum rudioribus & incredulis sensum obscurant & occasionem dubitandi præbent, iusto Dei iudicio, variósque sensus excogitandi, Matt.13 4. Accuratè inspiciendæ sunt parpartes, inter quas fit collatio. Neque enim necesse est in aliis omnibus partibus simile conuenire. Videndum igitur quatenus collationes cuiusuis generis sint applicandæ: ne arrepto earum scopo minus primario, primarium negligamus: ac ita à vero ipsius loci sensu aberremus, aut in errorem incidamus, si ea vrgeamus, quæ applicanda non sunt. 5. Sapientia diuina quum à rebus terrenis res cœlestes nobis commendat, cauendum ne quorundam incogitantiam imitati prætextu similitudinis terrenæ (qua se Deus ingenij nostri modulo accommodat) res cœlestes extenuemus. Nam vocabula ab homine, aut ab aliis rebus ad Deum translata sunt multò significatiora, quam cum res humanas denotarent. Rem enim ipsam, ac potentes actiones indicant. Sic benedicere & maledicere Dei (quod non est amplius verbale, vt apud homines) significat idem, quod potenter benefacere aut malefacere alicui. &c.
units.tr: The use of parables or similitudes. (1) Divine wisdom, knowing how deep a darkness sin has brought upon the human mind, sometimes makes use of likenesses so as to reveal its will to us clearly. (2) Moreover, a likeness helps not only understanding but also memory greatly, since things perceived through several senses cling more firmly. (3) A likeness has great force for stirring and persuading. Christ, about to die, said to John, "Behold your mother," and to the woman, "Behold your son" (John 19:26–27), by which means the heart itself is drawn to perform the duty. Thus parables have this power: if they are rightly understood, they illustrate the matter, arouse attention, and fix the thing more deeply in the memory. If, however, they are not applied or explained, they sometimes darken the meaning for the simpler and the unbelieving and give occasion for doubt, by the just judgment of God, and for devising various senses (Matt. 13:4). The parts between which the comparison is made must be examined with care, for it is not necessary that everything else should agree in every part. We must therefore consider how far the comparison of each kind is to be applied, lest, seizing on a secondary purpose, we neglect the primary one, and so stray from the true sense of the passage, or fall into error by pressing points that ought not to be applied. (5) When divine wisdom commends heavenly things to us from earthly things, we must beware lest, imitating the carelessness of some, we belittle heavenly things under the pretext of earthly likeness, by which God accommodates himself to the measure of our understanding. For words transferred to God from man or from other things are much more significant than when they denote human matters, since they indicate the thing itself and powerful actions. Thus to bless and to curse, said of God (which is no longer merely verbal, as among men), means the same as to act powerfully for good or for ill toward someone, etc.

units.la: parabola, Dictorium, proverbiũ Sarcasticum, 2. Chron. 7.21. ps.69. 12. Esai.14.4. Ierem.24.9. Ezech.18.2.3. Mich.2. 4. Habac.2.6.
units.tr: Parable: a saying, a taunt, a sarcastic proverb (2 Chron. 7:21; Ps. 69:12; Isa. 14:4; Jer. 24:9; Ezek. 18:2–3; Mic. 2:4; Hab. 2:6).

units.la: PARACLETVS, παράκλητος promittitur, Ioan.14 16. & 15.26, & 16,7, παράκλητος aduocatus dicitur Christus, 1 Ioan.2,1, hoc est, nostro quidem respectu, patronus, vt qui nostram in se causam recipiat, qui & Mediator respectu patris dicitur, tum expiationis merito, tum quod personam quodammodo deprecatoris sustineat, cùm non nisi eius nomine Patrem precemur. Idemque Iudex est & Dominus, habita aduersariorum nostrorum ratione, ad patris dexteram considens: estque totum hoc munus vni Christo adeò proprium, vt absque insigni scelere transferri ad nullum alium, siue in cœlis, siue in terris possit, ne persona quidem ipsa Spiritus Sancti excepta, vt qui παράκλητος paracletus, diuersa prorsus ratione dicatur, Ioan. 14.16. & 15.26. & 16.7. quatenus videlicet nos ad veritatis illius cognitionem adductos, eaque refocillatos solatur, & hos ipsos clamores ad patrem per Filium deferendos docet. Rom.8.26. Gal.4 6.
units.tr: THE PARACLETE [παράκλητος] is promised (John 14:16; 15:26; 16:7). Christ is called Advocate [παράκλητος] (1 John 2:1), that is, with respect to us, a patron, since he takes our cause upon himself. He is also called Mediator with respect to the Father, both by the merit of his atonement and because he in some measure sustains the role of intercessor, since we pray to the Father only in his name. He is also Judge and Lord, having regard to our adversaries, sitting at the right hand of the Father. This whole office belongs so exclusively to Christ alone that it cannot be transferred to anyone else, whether in heaven or on earth, not even to the person of the Holy Spirit himself, who is called Paraclete [παράκλητος] in a quite different sense (John 14:16; 15:26; 16:7). That is to say, he comforts us, having been led to the knowledge of that truth, and refreshes us by it, and teaches us that these very cries are to be carried to the Father through the Son (Rom. 8:26; Gal. 4:6).

units.la: PARADISVS voluptatis à Deo plantatur, Genes.2,8, paradisus [tertium cælum, mansio electorum] locus beatitudinis, seu beatis destinatus, Luc.23.43. 2 Cor.12.4, Apoc.2.7. è paradiso voluptatis eiicitur Adam, Genes.3,23.
units.tr: Paradise of pleasure was planted by God (Gen. 2:8). Paradise [the third heaven, the dwelling of the elect] is a place of blessedness, or destined for the blessed (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:4; Rev. 2:7). Adam was cast out of the paradise of pleasure (Gen. 3:23).

units.la: PARALYTICI sunt, quos dissolutio neruorum debilitauit, vt membtorum vsu destituantur: quos feré apoplexia tandé enecat. Paralysis, seu hemiplexia, quum hoc malum alteram tantùm corporis partem incurrit: nam cùm totum corpus afficitur, apoplexia dicitur.
units.tr: Paralytics are those whom a loosening of the nerves has weakened, so that they are deprived of the use of their limbs, and whom apoplexy at last generally kills. Paralysis, or hemiplegia, occurs when this malady strikes only one side of the body; when the whole body is affected, it is called apoplexy.

units.la: PARALYTICI à Christo sanantur. (Vide MIRACVLA) Mat. 4.24.
units.tr: Paralytics are healed by Christ (see MIRACLES; Matt. 4:24).

units.la: [PARDVS, figuratè sumitur pro viro crudeli & effero, ad Christum conuerso, mansuefactóque virtute Spiritus S. Esai.11,6.]
units.tr: [The leopard is used figuratively for a cruel and savage man, converted to Christ and tamed by the power of the Holy Spirit (Isa. 11:6).]

units.la: PARENTES honorandi & timendi, Exo.20.12. Leu.19 3. Deu. 5.16. & 27.16. Prou.23.22. Martth.15.4. & 19.19. Marc.7.10. & 10.19. Luc.18.20. Ephef.6.2. Col.3.20. Parentes non irri-dendi, Prou.30.17. non percutiendi, nec eis maledicen-dum, Exo 21.15.17. Leu.20.9. Parentes Christi secundùm carnem, Luc.2.27. & 8 56.
units.tr: Parents are to be honoured and feared (Exod. 20:12; Lev. 19:3; Deut. 5:16; 27:16; Prov. 23:22; Matt. 15:4; 19:19; Mark 7:10; 10:19; Luke 18:20; Eph. 6:2; Col. 3:20). Parents are not to be mocked (Prov. 30:17), nor struck, nor cursed (Exod. 21:15, 17; Lev. 20:9). Christ's parents according to the flesh (Luke 2:27; 8:56).

units.la: PARENTVM amor, Christi amori cedere debet, Matt.10.37. Luc.14.26. parentum in liberos, in matrimonio obeundo authoritas, 1 Corint.7.36. exempla: Isaac, Gen.28.1. Manue, Iudic.13.2. (Vide MATRIMONIVM.)
units.tr: Love for parents must give way to love for Christ (Matt. 10:37; Luke 14:26). The authority of parents over their children in arranging marriage (1 Cor. 7:36). Examples: Isaac (Gen. 28:1); Manoah (Judg. 13:2). (See MARRIAGE.)

units.la: Parentum erga liberos officia. Primò, Liberos recté educare, & eos pro donis habere. exempla, Iacob, Genef. 33.5. Ioseph, 48.9. Secundo, Diligere liberos, exempla: Iacob, Genef.42. ver.36.37. Dauid, in quo magna storga paterna elucet, 2 Sam.12. ver.16.17. altera Meretrix, 1 Reg.3.26. Tertiò, pietatem eos docere, Exod.12.27. & 13. versic. 8.14. Deuteron.4.10. & 6. vers.7. 20. & 11.19. & 32.46. Iofu. 4.v.6.7.21.22.24. psal.78.v.4 5.6. Esai.38.19. Ioel,1 3. Ephe. 6.4. exempla: Dauid, 1. Paralipom.28.9. mater Lamuelis, proverb.31 ver.1. 2. Quartò, Eos corrigere, & peccata eorum arguere, 1 Sam.3.13. Prouerb.13.24. & 23.23. & 29.17. Hebr. 12. 7. exemplum: Iacob, Genef. 34 30, Quintò, In eis corrigendis & arguendis moderatione vti, Ephe.6.4. Coloss.3.21. Sextò, Orare pro liberorum felicitate, & peccatis amoliendis. Exempla: Dauid, 2 Samu.12.16. 1 paral.29. 19. Iob, Iob.1.5. Septimò, Tradere liberis facultates. Exempla: Abraham, Genef.24.36. & 25.v.5,6. Iofaphat,2 paralip. 21.3. Octauò, Illis prospicere de matrimonio. Exempla: Abraham, Gen. 24. v.2.3. Agar.21.21. Isaac, 28.1 Hemor, 34. 4. Iudas, 38.6. Manue & vxor eius, Iudic.14.v.3. &c. (Vide MATRIMONIVM.)
units.tr: The duties of parents toward children. (1) To bring up children rightly and to regard them as gifts. Examples: Jacob (Gen. 33:5); Joseph (Gen. 48:9). (2) To love their children. Examples: Jacob (Gen. 42:36–37); David, in whom a great paternal affection shines (2 Sam. 12:16–17); the other, the harlot (1 Kings 3:26). (3) To teach them piety (Exod. 12:27; 13:8, 14; Deut. 4:10; 6:7, 20; 11:19; 32:46; Josh. 4:6–7, 21–22, 24; Ps. 78:4–6; Isa. 38:19; Joel 1:3; Eph. 6:4). Examples: David (1 Chron. 28:9); the mother of Lemuel (Prov. 31:1–2). (4) To correct them and rebuke their sins (1 Sam. 3:13; Prov. 13:24; 23:23; 29:17; Heb. 12:7). Example: Jacob (Gen. 34:30). (5) To use moderation in correcting and rebuking them (Eph. 6:4; Col. 3:21). (6) To pray for the happiness of their children and for the removal of their sins. Examples: David (2 Sam. 12:16; 1 Chron. 29:19); Job (Job 1:5). (7) To leave their children property. Examples: Abraham (Gen. 24:36; 25:5–6); Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 21:3). (8) To provide for them in marriage. Examples: Abraham (Gen. 24:2–3); Hagar (Gen. 21:21); Isaac (Gen. 28:1); Hamor (Gen. 34:4); Judah (Gen. 38:6); Manoah and his wife (Judg. 14:3), etc. (See MARRIAGE.)

units.la: PARENTIBVS honorem deferre, est illis benefacere, Matth. 15.v.5.6. Marc.7. v.10.11.12. parentibus filij nequam molestiam
units.tr: To render honour to parents is to do them good (Matt. 15:5–6; Mark 7:10–12). Wicked children bring trouble upon their parents (see CHILDREN).

units.la: lestiam afferunt, Vide FILII. parentibus manus violentas inferentes, morte digni, Exodi 21.15. parentibus non maledicendum, aut, mortem subeundum, 21.17. Leuitic. 20.9. Matth.15.4. Marc.7.10. parentibus non nocendum, Proverb.28.24. parentibus obediendum, Vide OBEDIENTIA.
units.tr: Those who lay violent hands on their parents are worthy of death (Exod. 21:15). Parents are not to be cursed, nor is death to be incurred by doing so (Exod. 21:17; Lev. 20:9; Matt. 15:4; Mark 7:10). Parents are not to be harmed (Prov. 28:24). Parents are to be obeyed (see OBEDIENCE).

units.la: PARIO, de muliere frequenter, item de quadrupedibus & auibus dictum. 2. De Deo magna exequente, Esai.49.21. Soph.2.2.3. De Ecclesia. Esai.4.9. 21.21. & 54.1. & 66.7.8. Mich.5.3. Gal.4.27. Apoc.12.14.5.13. 4. De conatu bono vel malo, Esai.26.18. & 37.3. Iob.15.35. Psal.7.15. Esai.33.11. & 59.4. Iacob.1.15.
units.tr: PARIO (to bring forth). It is said frequently of a woman, and also of four-footed beasts and birds. (2) Of God accomplishing great things (Isa. 49:21; Zeph. 2:2–3). Of the Church (Isa. 4:9; 21:21; 54:1; 66:7–8; Mic. 5:3; Gal. 4:27; Rev. 12:14; 5:13). (4) Of a good or evil endeavour (Isa. 26:18; 37:3; Job 15:35; Ps. 7:15; Isa. 33:11; 59:4; James 1:15).

units.la: PAROEMIA, Ioan.10.6. V. Parabola.
units.tr: PAROEMIA (proverb) (John 10:6). See Parable.

units.la: Παρρησία, pro orationis perspicuitate & verborum euidentia, 2 Cor.3.12. pro libera professione, Heb.10.35.
units.tr: Parrhesia [παρρησία]: for clarity of speech and plainness of words (2 Cor. 3:12); for open profession (Heb. 10:35).

units.la: PARS Dei, Israel, Ecclesia, Deut.32.9. Ierem.12.10. Zach.2.12. pars Ecclesiæ, Deus, Num.18.20. Iosu.22.27. Psa.16.5. & 73.26. Ierem.10.16. & 51.19. Threu.3.24.
units.tr: The portion of God: Israel, the Church (Deut. 32:9; Jer. 12:10; Zech. 2:12). The portion of the Church: God (Num. 18:20; Josh. 22:27; Ps. 16:5; 73:26; Jer. 10:16; 51:19; Lam. 3:24).

units.la: Pars portio rei, beneficium Dei, latus materiæ oppositum, pars loci, pars populi.
units.tr: Pars (part) means a portion of a thing, a benefit of God, the side opposed to the matter, a part of a place, a part of a people.

units.la: PARSIMONIA auget opes, Prou.13.11. Vide Frugalitas.
units.tr: Thrift increases wealth (Prov. 13:11). See Frugality.

units.la: parthi, Act.2.9. Participatio, coagmentatio, Psal.122.3. communio, 1 Cor.10.16. Consortium, 2 Cor.6.14.
units.tr: Parthians (Acts 2:9). Participation, joining together (Ps. 122:3); fellowship (1 Cor. 10:16); partnership (2 Cor. 6:14).

units.la: PARTICVLA vniuersalis, Vide NOTA vniuersalis: & OMNIS.
units.tr: The particle "universal": see the note on UNIVERSAL and ALL.

units.la: parturio, de muliere dicitur, 2. de ineffabili generatione sapientiæ æternæ, Pro.28.25. 3. de Ecclesia, Esai.66.7.8. 4. de sollicitudine & charitate vehementi in Dei seruo, Gal.4.19. 5. de opere bono vel malo, Prou.1.c.31. P.-7.15. 6. de ciuitate populosa, Esai.23.4. 7. de creaturis liberationem expectantib. Rom.8.22.
units.tr: To travail (parturio) is said of a woman. (2) Of the ineffable generation of eternal wisdom (Prov. 8:25). (3) Of the Church (Isa. 66:7–8). (4) Of the anxious and fervent love in God's servant (Gal. 4:19). (5) Of a good or evil work (Prov. 1:31; Ps. 7:15). (6) Of a populous city (Isa. 23:4). (7) Of creatures awaiting their liberation (Rom. 8:22).

units.la: PARTVS dolores, pro iudicio illo horrendo, subsecuturo afflictiones & oppressiones inauditas, Matth.24.8. quæ illud præcedant, vt partus dolores ipsum eni-xum.
units.tr: The pains of childbirth (partus dolores): of that dreadful judgment which will follow, with unheard-of afflictions and oppressions, which will precede it as labour pains precede the actual birth (Matt. 24:8).

units.la: PARVI, dicti fideles, non ætatis, sed τῷ τεληοφοεφοσιώνς ratione, Matth.18.6. parui, per concessionem, Apostoli à Christo dicti, homines nimirum coram mundo viles & abiecti, 19.42. Paruulus, vel puerulus, pro quopiam ita sese demittẽte, vt puerum decet, 18,5. Paruorum nomine omnes pij continentur, v.10. Parvuli in Christo, 1 Cor.3.1. paruulis legendum Deuteronomium, Deut.31.12.
units.tr: The faithful are called "little ones", not by age, but by reckoning of perfection (Matt. 18:6). The apostles were called "little ones" by Christ, by way of concession, that is, men who are base and abject in the eyes of the world (Matt. 19:42). A "little child" (paruulus) or "small child" means someone who humbles himself as a child should (Matt. 18:5). All the godly are included under the name of little ones (v. 10). Little children in Christ (1 Cor. 3:1). Deuteronomy is to be read to little ones (Deut. 31:12).

units.la: Paruus, qualitate, quantitate, numero, stabura. parum item, qualitatiue, quantitatiue, & de temporis momento dictum.
units.tr: Small (paruus) in quality, quantity, number, or stature. Little (parum) is likewise said qualitatively and quantitatively, and of a moment of time.

units.la: PASCHA, fuit Sacramentum veteris Testamenti, quo fideles comesto agno paschali admonebantur tum præteritæ ereptionis corporalis in Ægypto à cædæ primogenitorũ, tum futuræ spiritualis liberationis per Christum. Exod. 12.1.2. Num.9.1.11.1 Cor.5.7.c. Ioh.1.29.1.Pet.1.19.
units.tr: PASCHA was a sacrament of the Old Testament, by which the faithful, eating the paschal lamb, were reminded both of the past bodily deliverance in Egypt from the slaughter of the firstborn and of the future spiritual liberation through Christ. Exod. 12.1.2. Num. 9.1.11. 1 Cor. 5.7 etc. John 1.29. 1 Pet. 1.19.

Numer.9.12, Ioan.19.36, 1 Corint. 5.7. & sacramentum, carne agni vt signo constans, Exod. 12, v.8, 11, & Christo, vero agno, vt re significata, 1 Cor.5. v.7,8, & 10,3, à solis circumcisis edendum, Exod.12, v.43, 44,48, commendatur, Leuit.23 5, Num.9, v 3 4. Deut.16 2. non vbique celebrandum, v.5,6, celebratur, Exod.12,18, Iosu.5,10 2, Reg. 23, verf. 21,22,2 Paral.35 1,1, Esdr. 6,19. Matth.26,19, Marc.14 12, Luc.22.15, pascha, pro Agno paschali, qui erat figura ipsius phasc: μα πανυμικῶς, figura Sacramentis peculiari, qua rei nomen suo signo tribuitur, Marc.14,12, Luc.22,7. Simili ratione Christus etiam ipse, à paulo pascha nostrum vocatur, 1, Cor.5,7.
units.tr: The Passover of the Jews was instituted in Exod. 12, verses 1, 2, 3. It is a sacrifice (vv. 6, 21, 26, 27), a eucharistic sacrifice (vv. 14, 42), and a type of the sacrifice of Christ (v. 46; Num. 9.12; John 19.36; 1 Cor. 5.7). It is a sacrament, consisting in the flesh of the lamb as a sign (Exod. 12, vv. 8, 11), and in Christ, the true Lamb, as the thing signified (1 Cor. 5.7, 8; 10.3). It was commended to be eaten only by the circumcised (Exod. 12, vv. 43, 44, 48; Lev. 23.5; Num. 9.3, 4; Deut. 16.2). It was not to be celebrated everywhere (vv. 5, 6), yet it was celebrated (Exod. 12.18; Josh. 5.10; 2 Kings 23.21, 22; 2 Chron. 35.1; Ezra 6.19; Matt. 26.19; Mark 14.12; Luke 22.15). The word pascha is used for the paschal lamb, which was a figure of the Passover itself, by a sacramental figure in which the name of the thing is given to its sign [συνωνυμικῶς] (Mark 14.12; Luke 22.7). By a similar figure, Christ himself is called our Passover by Paul (1 Cor. 5.7).

units.la: PASCIT Dauid populum Israel, 2 Sam. 5. 2.& 7.8 [psal.78, v.27,28,29, pascit Deus aues, Luc.12.24, pascit Ecclesiam suam, Gen.48,15. Nehem.9,21, Esai.49,9, Ezech.34,v.13. 14,15.16. pascit Christus oues suas,1. units.tr: David fed the people of Israel (2 Sam. 5.2; 7.8; Ps. 78.27, 28, 29). God feeds the birds (Luke 12.24). God feeds his Church (Gen. 48.15; Neh. 9.21; Isa. 49.9; Ezek. 34.13, 14, 15, 16). Christ feeds his sheep, the Church of God (Song 1.7; 2.16; 6; Isa. 40.11; Ezek. 34.23; Mic. 5.4; 7.14; Zech. 11.4, 7, 9). He feeds through his servants, the watchmen of the flock (Song 1.8; Acts 20.28; 1 Pet. 5.2; John 21.15, 16, 17; Rev. 12.5).

units.la: Pasci dicuntur fideles in communione sanctorum, Esa. 11,6,7,& 65,25, Soph.2,7, & 3,17, Corui pascunt Eliam,1, Reg.17,4,6.]
units.tr: The faithful are said to be fed in the communion of the saints (Isa. 11.6, 7; 65.25; Zeph. 2.7; 3.17). Ravens fed Elijah (1 Kings 17.4, 6).

units.la: PASSER auicula, citra, Dei prouidentiam non cadit, Matth. 10,29, Deo authore nidificat, psal.104,17. solitudinis impatiens est,102,8.
units.tr: The sparrow, a little bird, does not fall without God's providence (Matt. 10.29). It builds its nest by God's authority (Ps. 104.17). It is impatient of solitude (Ps. 102.8).

units.la: PASSIONES & affectus peccati, Romau.7,7, &c. passiones huius vitæ, Rom.8,18, passionibus Christi communicare 1 Pet.4,13, in passionibus exultandum, Col.1,11,1 Pet.1,6.
units.tr: Passions and affections of sin (Rom. 7.7 etc.). The passions of this life (Rom. 8.18). We are to share in the sufferings of Christ (1 Pet. 4.13), and to rejoice in our sufferings (Col. 1.11; 1 Pet. 1.6).

units.tr: The true Pastor is Christ (John 10.11, 14). (See CHRIST.) The Shepherd of shepherds, the Pastor of pastors (Heb. 13.20). See 1 Pet. 5.4.

units.la: PASTORIS & Mercenarij discrimen, Ioan. 10. v. 11,12. Pastoris vox duplex, Tit. 1,9, sc. ad regendos dociles, & refractarios refutandos
units.tr: The difference between a minister and a hireling, John 10:11-12. The twofold voice of the minister, Titus 1:9, namely to rule the docile and to refute the refractory.

units.tr: Ministers are called kings, princes and leaders (Jer. 6:3 and 12; 10; [25:34-36; 49:19]; Nahum 3:18; Zech. 11:3, 5), God's servants and for this reason honoured with the name of the place (Zech. 13:7; 1 Cor. 3:9), and stewards of God's mysteries (1 Cor. 4:1; Titus 1:7). See the MINISTERS, Jelogia. They ought to be apt to teach (1 Tim. 3:2), and they ought to lead by the example of their life (Matt. 5:13-16; Luke 8:16; 1 Tim. 4:12; Titus 2:7; Heb. 13:7; 1 Pet. 5:3). Ministers are the glory of their disciples (2 Cor. 1:14). They are ambassadors of Christ (2 Tim. 2:3) and his ministers (Acts 1:25; 1 Cor. 3:5; 2 Cor. 3:6; 6:4; Col. 1:25). They are ministers of reconciliation (2 Cor. 5:18-19), of the Spirit and not of the letter (2 Cor. 3:6), a good odour of Christ (2 Cor. 2:15). They are called fathers of the flock over which they preside, as a mark of honour (2 Kings 6:21; 1 Cor. 4:14-15; 2 Cor. 6:13; 12:14; Gal. 4:19; 1 Thess. 2:11; 1 Tim. 1:2; 2 Tim. 4:2; Titus 1:3; Philem. 10; 1 John 2:1, 28; 3:7; 4:4; 5:21). They are elders (Acts 20:17; 1 Tim. 5:17; 1 Pet. 5:1). In what sense ministers are called priests (Rom. 15:16; Phil. 2:17). What kind of ministers ought to be chosen (1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6-7; 2:7); their perfect pattern is described in the same places. They ought to be loved by their own people (Gal. 4:15; Phil. 2:29; 1 Thess. 5:12-13). Ministers who sin publicly are to be rebuked openly (1 Tim. 5:20). Good ministers are sent by God (Jer. 3:15; 23:4; Matt. 9:38; Luke 10:2; Acts 20:28; Rom. 10:15; Eph. 4:11-12). They ought to be teachable (2 Tim. 2:4) and learned (Titus 1:9; 2 Tim. 2:15). Ministers and ministers of the Word are exposed to the slanders of many. Examples: Paul (1 Cor. 2:1; 2 Cor. 10:2; 1 Tim. 1:15); John (3 John 10). What they ought to teach (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:15; 2 Cor. 4:5; Gal. 1:8-9; 1 Pet. 4:11). They do not speak of themselves (Jer. 1:9; Ezek. 2:8; 3:17; 33:7). Without God they can do nothing (1 Cor. 3:7, 9-10). With what care ministers, teachers and other rulers ought to look after those committed to their faith (Prov. 27:23-24; Ezek. 34:4; Matt. 18:2; 24:45; Luke 15:4; John 10:11; 13:1; 17:9, 11; 8:8; Acts 20:22, 28, 31; Rom. 9:2-3; 12:7-8; 1 Cor. 4:14; 2 Cor. 11:28-29; Gal. 4:19).

units.la: PASTORUM aduentus laetus, Esai 52,7. Rom. 10,15, Nahum. 15. Pastorum ambitio valde noxia, 1. Thes. 2.6.2. Thes. 2.4.
units.tr: The coming of ministers is welcome (Isa. 52:7; Rom. 10:15; Nahum 1:15). The ambition of ministers is very harmful (1 Thess. 2:6; 2 Thess. 2:4).

units.tr: (1 Tim. 3:6; 1 Pet. 5:2-3). The weapons of ministers are spiritual (2 Cor. 10:4). Their greed is condemned (Isa. 56:11; 1 Thess. 2:5; 1 Tim. 3:3; Titus 1:11; 1 Pet. 5:2). How great the authority of ministers is (2 Cor. 10:5-6, 8; 13:8, 10; Titus 2:15; Philem. 8).

units.tr: The condition of ministers (Ezek. 2:6; Luke 10:3; John 21:18). Lawful marriages of ministers (1 Cor. 9:5; 1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6). The consolation of ministers (Rom. 1:12; 2 Tim. 3:9, 11; 1 Pet. 5:4). The constancy of ministers comes from God (Jer. 1:8, 18; Ezek. 3:8-9). Examples: Isaiah (Isa. 50:7; 62:1); Habakkuk (Hab. 2:1); Paul (Phil. 2:17; 2 Tim. 1:12). See CONSTANCY, examples. The dignity and excellence of ministers (Jer. 1:10-11; Matt. 11:10-11; Luke 7:28; Acts 1:8; 2 Cor. 4:7; 5:18; Phil. 2:29; 1 John 4:6). The reputation of ministers must be kept whole (1 Tim. 3:7). The confidence of ministers (Matt. 5:19; 2 Cor. 3:12; 13:6). The children of ministers are to be well brought up (1 Tim. 3:4; Titus 1:6; 1 Sam. 2:22). The enemies of ministers perish (Jer. 20:11). How harmful the ignorance of ministers is (Hos. 4:9). The wages of ministers (1 Cor. 3:8; 1 Thess. 3:8; 1 Pet. 5:4). The warfare of ministers (Jer. 19:2; 2 Cor. 6:7; 10:4; Eph. 6:12; Phil. 2:25; 1 Tim. 1:18; 6:12; 2 Tim. 2:3; 4:7). The death of ministers in Christ's cause is a confirmation of the godly (Phil. 2:17). The morals of ministers are prescribed (2 Cor. 6:4; 1 Tim. 2, etc.). The office of ministers (Isa. 40:9; 49:9; 52:7; 58:1; 61:1; 62:11; Jer. 1:10; Ezek. 3:17; 33:2; Hos. 8:1; Mic. 3:8; Matt. 5:13-14; John 4:38; Acts 6:4; 20:28, 31; 26:28; Rom. 15:16; 1 Cor. 3:2; 4:1-2; 2 Cor. 1:18; 2:2; 5:19-20; 6:1; 11:2; 12:14; 13:7; Gal. 4:12, 19; Eph. 3:14; 4:11-12; 6:19; Phil. 3:1; Col. 1:18; 4:4; 1 Thess. 2:5; 5:12; 1 Tim. 2:7; 4:11; 5:1, 7; 2 Tim. 2:15; 4:25; Titus 1:1, 11; 3:8; Heb. 13:17; 1 Pet. 4:11; 5:1; 2 Pet. 3:1; 1 John 2:26; 5:13; Jude 5). Rebuking people of different ages and sexes is the duty of prudence (1 Tim. 5:1-3, etc.). The work of ministers (1 Thess. 1:2). Prayers (Eph. 3:14; 1 Pet. 5:10). Ornaments (1 Tim. 4:11). Patience (2 Tim. 2:24; 4:2). Prudence (1 Tim. 3:2). The consideration to be shown to ministers (Matt. 10:12; Mark 6:10; Luke 10:7; 1 Cor. 9:4, 9, 11, 14; Gal. 6:6; Phil. 4:14; 1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 5:17-18; Heb. 13:7). The true reception of ministers (Luke 10:42; 2 Cor. 7:15; Gal. 4:14; 1 Thess. 2:13). The temptations of ministers. Examples: Isaiah (Isa. 49:4); Jeremiah (Jer. 20:9). The triumph of ministers (2 Cor. 2:14; 1 Thess. 2:2; 2 Tim. 4:8); victory (Jer. 1:19). The life of ministers is dear to the Church (Acts 9:25; 19:30-31; 21:12; 1 Cor. 16:10; Phil. 2:29).

units.la: lip.2.29. Pastorum vitia, priuatorum vitiis multò gra- uiora, Ierem. 23. 15. Pastorum vocatio à Deo, Esai.49.1. Hebr.5.4. Vide PASTORES à Deo mittuntur. Pastorum vxores quales esse debeant 1 Timoth.3.11.
units.tr: The vices of ministers are much more serious than the vices of private persons (Jer. 23:15). The calling of ministers by God (Isa. 49:1; Heb. 5:4). See MINISTERS, sent by God. What the wives of ministers ought to be like (1 Tim. 3:11).

units.la: ASTORIBVS fidelibus interdum stultitia à mundo obiici- tur, Vide INSANIA.
units.tr: Sometimes folly is objected to faithful ministers by the world. See MADNESS.

units.la: PASTORES mali, populi seductores, Ierem.12.10.& 14.v.13, 14.& 23 14.& 50.6. Ezech.13 10. Matt.15.14.& 23.13. Exempla: Pontifices.27.20. Mar.15.14. Pastores mali seipsos intrudunt, Ierem.23.21. & 27.15. Ezech.13 6. maledicuntur, Ierem.23 1. seriò obiurgantur, 5.31.& 6.14. & 12.10. Thren. 2.14. Mich.3 5. Zach.10.3. Pastores mali conferuntur mutis canibus, Esa.56.v.10.11. Pastores laceranles & deglubentes gregem, Ierem.23.1 Ezech.34.v.2.3.
units.tr: Evil ministers, seducers of the people (Jer. 12:10; 14:13-14; 23:14; 50:6; Ezek. 13:10; Matt. 15:14; 23:13). Examples: the high priests (Matt. 27:20; Mark 15:14). Evil ministers thrust themselves in (Jer. 23:21; 27:15; Ezek. 13:6). They are cursed (Jer. 23:1). They are sharply rebuked (Jer. 5:31; 6:14; 12:10; Lam. 2:14; Mic. 3:5; Zech. 10:3). Evil ministers are compared to dumb dogs (Isa. 56:10-11). Ministers who tear and flay the flock (Jer. 23:1; Ezek. 34:2-3).

units.la: PASTORVM malorum descriptio, Esai.56.10. Pastorum socordium poena, Ezech.3.20.
units.tr: A description of evil ministers (Isa. 56:10). The punishment of negligent ministers (Ezek. 3:20).

units.la: PASTORIBVS malis moribus præditis, & veram nihilomi- nus doctrinam annuntiantibus, obediendum, Mat.23.2. &c. Pastoribus impiè docentibus obedientes perituri, Ier. 14 16.& 20.6.
units.tr: Ministers of evil morals, yet proclaiming true doctrine, are to be obeyed (Matt. 23:2, etc.). Those who obey ministers who teach impiously will perish (Jer. 14:16; 20:6).

units.la: PASTORES ouium, filij Iacob, Genes.46.32. Pastoribus nuntiatur Christus natus, Luc.2.8
units.tr: Shepherds of sheep, the sons of Jacob (Gen. 46:32). To shepherds the birth of Christ is announced (Luke 2:8).

Ephes.4.6. idque quo sensu intelligendum sit, Vide DEVS pater est, &c. Pater gloriæ, pro patre glorioso, vel gloriæ pleno, per Hebraismum, Ephes. 17. Vide 1 Cor.2.8. patri etiam tribuitur Seruatoris nomen. 1 Tim.1 1 Vide DEVS SERVATOR.
units.tr: FATHER: among the Hebrews, for grandfather, and indeed for ancestors themselves, as appears from Exod. 2:18 and Num. 10:29; for author (John 8:44; James 1:17); absolutely, for the first person of the most holy Trinity (Luke 10:21); remains in the Son Christ (John 17:23); bears witness of the Son (Matt. 3:17; 17:5; John 5:32; 17:5; 1 John 5:7); the union of Father and Son (John 17:21-22). No one is to be called father, because there is one Father, who is in heaven (Mal. 1:6; Matt. 23:9; Eph. 4:6); and in what sense this is to be understood, see GOD is Father, etc. Father of glory, for a glorious father, or one full of glory, by Hebraism (Eph. 1:7). See 1 Cor. 2:8. The title of Saviour is also given to the Father (1 Tim. 1:1). See GOD THE SAVIOUR.

units.la: PATRES, id est, maiores, in Mose baptizati, 1 Corinth.10.v. 1.2. Vide sensum loci in BAPTIZARE. Non semper inimandi, psal.78.8.& 95.9. Heb.3.9. Ierem. 16. 12. Ezec.20.18. Amos 2.4. Zach.1.4. Act.7. v. 51.52. Patres pro filiis non occidendi, & contrà, Vide FILII. Patres veteris Testamenti, fide præditi, Rom.4.v.3.16.18. Gal.3 6. Heb.11.v.4. 7.1 Pet.1.12. Vide & Act. 15.11. non adepti sunt promissiones, Heb.11.v.13 39. hoc est, idem ipsam promissam, metonymicè, aut promissionis præstationem.
units.tr: FATHERS, that is, ancestors, baptized in Moses (1 Cor. 10:1-2). See the sense of the passage under BAPTIZE. They are not always to be imitated (Ps. 78:8; 95:9; Heb. 3:9; Jer. 16:12; Ezek. 20:18; Amos 2:4; Zech. 1:4; Acts 7:51-52). Fathers are not to be killed for their children, and conversely; see CHILDREN. The fathers of the Old Testament, endowed with faith (Rom. 4:3, 16, 18; Gal. 3:6; Heb. 11:4, 7; 1 Pet. 1:12; see also Acts 15:11), did not obtain the promises (Heb. 11:13, 39), that is, the very same promised thing, by metonymy, or the fulfilment of the promise.

units.la: Huius loci duplex sensus erui potest (Vide & 1 Pet.1.12.) Aut respectu Christi & Messiæ promissi, in quo omnes Dei promissiones sunt Etiam & Amen, 2 Cor.1.17. quem Patres non assecuti esse dicuntur, eò quòd in nostra usque tempora ipsius in carne adventus dilatus sit, quamuis ex fide descriptione, Heb.11.1. per fidei aspectum fuerit illis Messias visibilis, & viderint illum venturum eminùs (id quod & de Abrahamo affirmat Christus, Ioan.8.56.) aut terræ Chanaan respectu, qua Patres nunquam potiti sunt. Erat autem illis hæc regio, paternæ Dei beneuolentiæ, cœlestisque hæreditatis, nascituræ denique ex ipsis Ecclesiæ typus ac figura, ut inuictam eorum fidem esse oportuerit, qui de rebus ipsis non dubitarint, quarum tamen promissa pignora nunquam sintadepti. Patres pietatem filios docere debent, Vide PARENTES.
units.tr: Two senses of this passage can be drawn out (see also 1 Pet. 1.12). Either it refers to Christ, the promised Messiah, in whom all God's promises are "Yea and Amen" (2 Cor. 1.17). The Fathers are said not to have attained him, because his coming in the flesh was deferred until our own times, although through faith, the description of which is in Heb. 11.1, the Messiah was visible to them, and they saw him coming from afar (which Christ also affirms of Abraham, John 8.56). Or it refers to the land of Canaan, which the Fathers never possessed. Yet this region was for them a pledge of the paternal goodwill of God and of the heavenly inheritance, and finally a type and figure of the Church to be born from them. So their faith must have been invincible, since they did not doubt the things themselves, whose promised pledges they never obtained. Fathers ought to teach piety to their sons; see PARENTS.

units.tr: The anxiety of the Fathers under the Law, 1 Pet. 3.19. The sins of the Fathers are not to be passed over. Examples: Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 29.6; his messengers, 3 Kings 7; Josiah, 4 Kings 21.4; Nehemiah, Neh. 1.6; the Levites, Neh. 9.16, 32, 34; David, Ps. 78.8 and 106.6; Isaiah, Isa. 43.27; Jeremiah, Jer. 2.5, 3.25, 14.20, 16.19, Lam. 5.7; Daniel, Dan. 9.8; Zechariah, Zech. 1.4; Christ, Luke 6.26 and 11.47; Stephen, Acts 7.39, 51–52; parricides, 1 Tim. 1.9. Those who are said by the Hebrews to fill up the measure of the Fathers; see MEASURE OF THE FATHERS, etc. The care of the father of a household, Prov. 27.23, etc. [The word PATER is used in Scripture in the following senses.]

units.la: 1. Pater, Deus Pater, prima in Diuinis persona: Pater æternus æterni Filij, nempe Iesu Christi, Domini nostri.
units.tr: 1. Father: God the Father, the first person in the Godhead, the eternal Father of the eternal Son, namely Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: 2. Christus Pater futuri seculi, Esai.9.5.6.
units.tr: 2. Christ is the Father of the age to come, Isa. 9.5–6.

units.la: 3. Deus, Pater eorum quos creauit in suam gloriam, sibi gratis adoptauit in filios.
units.tr: 3. God is the Father of those whom he created for his own glory, and freely adopted as sons for himself.

units.la: 4. Pater naturalis, vir ex vira hominem generans, secundùm naturæ ordinem.
units.tr: 4. A natural father: a man who begets a man from a woman, according to the order of nature.

units.la: 5. Non modò nomen Patris, verùm etiam aui, abaui, proaui, ataui, &c. Pater sæpius indicat: & patrum nomine maiores vt plurimùm intelliguntur, sexcentis locis.
units.tr: 5. Not only the name of father but also grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, etc. The word "father" often indicates this, and by "fathers" ancestors are usually understood, in six hundred places.

units.la: 6. Pater, auctoritatis, dignitatis, potestatis vel ciuilis vel Sacræ respectu, Iudic.18.19.1 Sam.24.12.2 Reg.2.12. 5.13.&6.21.&13.14. Act.22.1.
units.tr: 6. Father, with respect to authority, dignity or power, whether civil or sacred: Judg. 18.19; 1 Sam. 24.12; 4 Kings 2.12, 5.13, 6.21, 13.14; Acts 22.1.

units.la: 7. Pater, auctor, doctor, institutor alicuius artis, v scientiæ, Gen.4.20.21.1 Par.4.14.
units.tr: 7. Father, author, teacher, founder of some art or science: Gen. 4.20–21; 1 Chron. 4.14.

units.la: 8. Pater, Creator, nempe Deus, Iob.38.28. Malac.2.10.
units.tr: 8. Father, Creator, namely God: Job 38.28; Mal. 2.10.

units.la: 9. Pater multarum Gentium, Abraham: quòd Gentes per fidem Christo, semini mulieris promisso, adhærentes inter Abrahæ pasteros deputentur, Gen.17.v.4.5. Rom.4. v.1.11.12.16.17.18. Iacob.2.21.
units.tr: 9. Father of many nations: Abraham, because the Gentiles who cling to Christ, the promised seed of the woman, are reckoned among Abraham's offspring: Gen. 17.4–5; Rom. 4.1, 11–12, 16–18; Jas. 2.21.

units.la: 10. Iudæorum Pater, Abraham, de quo gloriati sunt, Matth.3.9. Ioan.4.12. & 8.v.39.53.56.
units.tr: 10. Father of the Jews: Abraham, in whom they boasted, Matt. 3.9; John 4.12, 8.39, 53, 56.

units.la: 11. Pater, adiutor, protector, Iob.29.16. Esa.12.21. Ier.2.27. Thren.5.3.
units.tr: 11. Father, helper, protector: Job 29.16; Isa. 12.21; Jer. 2.27; Lam. 5.3.

units.la: 12. Pater putatiuus, Luc.2.v.48. Ioan.6.42.
units.tr: 12. Putative father: Luke 2.48; John 6.42.

units.la: 13. Pater dicitur aliquid, cui adhæremus, ut filius adhæret patri, Iob.17.14.
units.tr: 13. Father is said of something to which we cling, as a son clings to his father: Job 17.14.

units.la: 14. Pater impiorum & mendacij, Ioan.8.v.38.41.44.
units.tr: 14. Father of the wicked and of lies: John 8.38, 41, 44.

units.tr: Fatherhood: the family or the Church, Eph. 3.15.]

units.la: PATI, pro supplicio mortis affici, Luc. 22.15. pati pro Christo, Dei donum est, Phil.1.29. & honorificum, Matth.5.11. 1 Pet.3.14.& 4.v.14.16. V.Act.5.41.
units.tr: PATI, to undergo the punishment of death, Luke 22.15. To suffer for Christ is a gift of God, Phil. 1.29, and an honour, Matt. 5.11; 1 Pet. 3.14; 4.14, 16. See Acts 5.41.
PATIBULUM (the gibbet or cross-beam): Gen. 40.22; Num. 25.4; Deut. 21.22; Josh. 8.29, 10.27; Esth. 2.23, 6.4, 7.10, 9.13.]

units.la: PATIENTIA, ὑπομονή Col.1.12. Iac.1.14: est virtus animi, per quam omnia sensui & carni aduersa & dura, iniuste nobis illata, æquo tamen animo, nullo manente in ipsum affligentem nostro odio, toleramus, propter Dei præceptum. Itaque qui propter sua scelera iustas pœnas luunt, eásque patienter ferunt, proprie patientes dici non debent: & cum tam præclaræ virtutis nomine donantur, lata significatione patientia tunc accipitur.1 Pet.4.15.
units.tr: PATIENCE, ὑπομονή [hypomonē] (Col. 1.11; Jas. 1.4), is a virtue of the mind by which we bear with an even mind all things hard and adverse to sense and flesh, which are unjustly inflicted upon us, while no hatred toward the one who afflicts us remains in us, for the sake of God's command. Therefore those who pay just penalties for their own crimes and bear them patiently should not properly be called patient; and when they are given the name of so excellent a virtue, patience is then taken in a broad sense. 1 Pet. 4.15.

units.la: : Patriæ tres Christo tribuuntur ab Euangelistis: Nazareth, educationis, Matt.2.23. Marc.6.1. Luc.4.16. Bethlehem, ortus, 2.4. &c. Capernaum, incolatus, vbi plurima signa edidit, vt exprobrat Luc.10.13. &c. Huc pertinet illud Theophylacti: Bethlehem genuit: Nazareth educauit: Capernaum incolam habuit Christum. Patria cedit Abraham, Deo obsecutus, Gen.12.1. Act.7.v.3.4. Patria fidelium coelestis, Heb.11.v.13 14.16. & 13.14. Vide &2 Cor.5.6.
units.tr: Three homelands are attributed to Christ by the Evangelists: Nazareth, of his upbringing, Matt. 2.23; Mark 6.1; Luke 4.16; Bethlehem, of his birth, Matt. 2.4, etc.; Capernaum, of his residence, where he performed very many signs, as Luke 10.13 reproaches, etc. To this belongs the saying of Theophylact: Bethlehem brought him forth, Nazareth raised him, Capernaum had Christ as its inhabitant. Abraham gave up his homeland, obeying God, Gen. 12.1; Acts 7.3–4. The heavenly homeland of the faithful, Heb. 11.13–14, 16, 13.14. See also 2 Cor. 5.6.

units.la: Baptizare se missum esse negat, 1 Corint.1.17. non simpliciter & absolutè, cum Apostoli etiam baptizare iussi sint, Matth.28.19. & Paulus ipse baptizarit, 1 Cor.1.v.14. 16. sed κατὰ τι, Intelligit enim Paulus, & vult significare, se non peculiariter & præcipuè baptizandi, sed euangelizandi munus à Deo accepisse. Est ergo quædam species hyperboles è vulgo petita, quando absolutè negatur, quod tamen κατὰ τι negari oportuerit. (Similis est loquendi forma, Ierem.7.21.) contumeliis affectus, Act.17.18. & 26. 24. ab auaritia alienissimus, Actor 18 3. & 20.33. 1 Cor.9.12. 2 Cor.12.v.13.14. 2 Thess.3.8. olim blasphemus, 1 Tim.1.13
units.tr: He denies that he was sent to baptize (1 Cor. 1:17). He does not mean this simply and absolutely, since the apostles were also commanded to baptize (Matt. 28:19), and Paul himself baptized (1 Cor. 1:14, 16). He means it in a certain respect [κατὰ τι]. Paul intends to say that he had received from God the office not chiefly and particularly of baptizing, but of preaching the gospel. This is therefore a kind of hyperbole taken from common usage, when something is denied absolutely that ought to have been denied only in part. (A similar form of speech is at Jer. 7:21.) Reviled (Acts 17:18; 26:24). Most free from covetousness (Acts 18:3; 20:33; 1 Cor. 9:12; 2 Cor. 12:13-14; 2 Thess. 3:8). Formerly a blasphemer (1 Tim. 1:13).

units.tr: PEACOCK: it exults over others, and in the variety of its colour and plumage, which shines in its tail like certain fictitious eyes. When, however, it looks at its bristling scales of feet, the splendour of its crest and starred tail collapses. Did you give the exulting peacocks their wings? (Job 39:16; 1 Kings 10:22.)

units.tr: POOR: who are the true poor (Prov. 19:1, 22; Matt. 5:3; Luke 6:20). The poor are always in the world (Matt. 26:11; Mark 14:7; John 12:8). The poor in spirit are blessed (Matt. 5:3; Luke 6:20). God chooses the poor (1 Cor. 1:26-28; James 2:5). They are not to be despised (Prov. 17:5; 28:27; 29:7; James 2:2-5). The poor are commended (Deut. 15:11; 24:19; Prov. 21:13; 31:9; Isa. 1:17; Matt. 25:40; Luke 14:13; Rom. 12:13; 1 Cor. 16:1; 2 Cor. 9:4; James 1:27; 5:4). The poor of this world are called people who are needy and humble; and, if you look at the judgement of the world, the most abject of men. The poor in spirit (Matt. 5:3) are those whose spirits are subdued, who attribute nothing to themselves before God, and who submit themselves to God. The oppression of the poor is condemned (Prov. 22:22-23; 23:10-11; Isa. 1:23; Jer. 22:13; Ezek. 22:29; Amos 4:1; 5:11; 8:4; Mal. 3:5; Matt. 23:14; Mark 12:40; James 5:4). Account is to be taken of them (Lev. 19:9-10; Zech. 7:10; Gal. 2:10). Examples: the Church of Jerusalem (Acts 4:34), the Church of Antioch (Acts 11:29), Achaia (2 Cor. 9:2), Job (29:12; 31:16, 20).

units.tr: Paul uses this word throughout his prayers in three senses: first, peace of conscience with God; second, mutual love and concord among the godly; third, God's protection and blessing in every way. It is taken for εἰρήνη [eirēnē], that is, that tranquillity and serenity of mind (Rom. 5:1), which elsewhere (Phil. 4:7) is called the peace of God. It is so understood also at Luke 2:14 and 2 Pet. 3:14. True peace (John 14:27); peace from God (Num. 6:26; 1 Chron. 14:6; Isa. 26:12; 45:7; Prov. 16:7; Lev. 26:6); through Christ (Rom. 5:1). Peace in heaven (Luke 19:38), on earth (Luke 2:14). Peace in the time of the Messiah (Isa. 2:4; 11:6; 26:12; 66:12; Mic. 4:3; Zech. 9:10). Peace is to be loved and sought (Ps. 34:15; Zech. 8:19; Mark 9:51; Luke 10:5; 12:58; Rom. 12:18; 14:19; 1 Cor. 7:15; 14:33; 2 Cor. 13:11; Gal. 5:22; Eph. 4:3; Col. 3:15; 2 Tim. 2:22; Heb. 12:14; 1 Pet. 3:11). To be especially cultivated by the ministers with the flock (1 Thess. 5:13). Peace is to be sought in Christ (John 16:33). Peace left to us by Christ (John 14:27). No peace for the wicked and impious (Isa. 48:22; 57:21). For whom peace is promised (Ps. 119:165; Isa. 54:13). "Peace be with you": the greeting of the Hebrews (Gen. 43:23; Judg. 19:20; 1 Sam. 25:6; John 20:19, 21). "Go in peace": a formula for "happily and quietly," which the Hebrews use towards those departing (1 Sam. 1:17; Luke 7:50; Mark 5:34). See PEACEMAKERS.

units.tr: Some peace is temporal, some eternal (Gen. 13:6, 8; 26:22; 45:24; Lev. 26:6; Num. 6:26; Ecclus. 25:2; 28:15, 19; Jer. 29:8; Matt. 5:9; Mark 9:51; Luke 14:32; Acts 9:31; Rom. 12:18; 1 Cor. 14:33; Eph. 4:3; 2 Tim. 2:22; Heb. 12:14; James 3:18; 1 Pet. 3:11; Rev. 6:4). Internal peace, such as that between God and his friends and faithful (Isa. 2:4; 9:5; 11:6-7; 66:12; Hos. 2:14, 20; Mic. 4:3; Zech. 9:10; Luke 2:14; 24:36; John 14:27; 16:33; 20:19; Acts 10:36; Rom. 5:1; Eph. 2:14; Phil. 4:7). The Israelites are warned not to make peace with the Moabites (Deut. 23:6). Peace is to be offered to a besieged city (Deut. 20:10). False prophets promise peace and mercy (Jer. 6:14; 8:11; 14:13; 23:16-17; Ezek. 13:10, 16; Mic. 3:5; 1 Thess. 5:3). False peace (Luke 23:12; Gen. 6:1-2; 2 Chron. 19:2).

units.la: PECCATORES, pro omnino vitiosis & peccato addictis: & eorum miseria conditio, Psalm. 1. v.1.5. & 3.8. & 7. 10 & 9.v.17.18. & 10.v.3.4.15 18. & 37 v.20.34. Ioann.9.31.1 Timoth.1.9.1. Petr.4.18. peccatores, pro iis, in quibus peccatum regnat, Rom.5.8. pro iis, qui à foedere alieni sunt, Galat.2.15. pro peccato obnoxiis, quales sunt omnes homines. V. HOMO.
units.tr: SINNERS: those wholly given to vice and addicted to sin, and their wretched condition, Psalm 1.1, 5; 3.8; 7.10; 9.17-18; 10.3-4, 15, 18; 37.20, 34; John 9.31; 1 Timothy 1.9; 1 Peter 4.18. Sinners: those in whom sin reigns, Romans 5.8; those who are estranged from the covenant, Galatians 2.15; those liable to sin, which is the case with all men. See MAN.

units.la: Peccatores in bonam partem, Matth.9.13. pro iis, qui sensu peccatorum saucij, misericordiam Dei amplectuntur, peccatores mortui censentur, Osea 13.1. peccatores speciatim dicti publicani, Matt.9.10. V. PUBLICANI. peccatores quomodo tractandi, 2 Cor.7.12. Gal.2.14.1 Thess. 5.14.2 Thess.3.v.6.15.1 Tim.5.20. Tit.1.13. & 2.13. Iudæ.v.22. V. IMPII.
units.tr: Sinners in a good sense, Matthew 9.13: those who, wounded by a sense of their sins, embrace the mercy of God. Dead sinners are reckoned as those in Hosea 13.1. Sinners specifically called tax collectors, Matthew 9.10. See TAX COLLECTORS. How sinners are to be dealt with, 2 Corinthians 7.12; Galatians 2.14; 1 Thessalonians 5.14; 2 Thessalonians 3.6, 15; 1 Timothy 5.20; Titus 1.13 and 2.13; Jude 22. See WICKED.

units.la: PECCARE dicitur is, 1 Ioann. 3. 4. non quisquis labitur, sed quisquis sanctitati non studet. Quod ita esse liquet, cum ex antithesi, ibid. tum ex 1 Ioann.1.8.& 2.1. Non peccare contra dicuntur, non ij qui non labuntur, nec etiam, iustus septies cadit, Prov.24.16. sed qui peccato repugnando, puritati student, seu purificant se. peccare in coelum, dicitur prodigus ille filius, Luc.15.18. hoc est, reus esse, non Deo solo, sed ipso etiam coelo, quacunque patet, teste. peccare sine lege, per se lethale, Rom.2.12. peccare in lege, lethale, ibid.
units.tr: He is said to sin who is not one who merely slips, but one who does not strive for holiness. That this is so is clear from the antithesis in the same place, and from 1 John 1.8 and 2.1. Those are said not to sin who do not stumble, nor even the just man who falls seven times, Proverbs 24.16, but who, by resisting sin, strive for purity or purify themselves. The prodigal son is said to have sinned against heaven, Luke 15.18, that is, to be guilty not only before God but before heaven itself, which is a witness wherever it extends. To sin without law is deadly in itself, Romans 2.12; to sin under the law is deadly, ibid.

units.la: PECCATVM ADAMI, est actus inobedientiæ in Adamo, tanquam indiuiduo singulari, & principio communi omnium, quo legem Dei violando, se, & suos in æternum perdidit. Gen.3. Rom.5.15.16.17.18.19.2 Cor.11.3.
units.tr: THE SIN OF ADAM is the act of disobedience in Adam, as in a single individual and the common origin of all, by which, violating the law of God, he destroyed himself and his own forever. Genesis 3; Romans 5.15-19; 2 Corinthians 11.3.

units.la: PECC. ORIGINALE, est vitiositas hereditaria, qua propter inobedientiam Adami omnes ex eo naturaliter aut propagati aut propagandi, vtriusq; mali, tum culpæ tum pœnæ rei efficiuntur. Psal.51.7. Eph.2.3. Rom 5.12.
units.tr: ORIGINAL SIN is hereditary vitiation, by which, on account of the disobedience of Adam, all who are naturally born or to be born from him are made liable to both evils, to guilt and to punishment. Psalm 51.7; Ephesians 2.3; Romans 5.12.

units.la: PECC. ACTVALE, est iniquitas seu anomica, qua in actionibus nostris à rectitudine Legis aberrantes, reatum & culpæ & pœnæ in dies augemus. Mat.12.34.35. Rom.8.7. Iacob 1.13.14.
units.tr: ACTUAL SIN is iniquity or lawlessness, by which, straying from the rectitude of the Law in our actions, we increase day by day our liability to guilt and punishment. Matthew 12.34-35; Romans 8.7; James 1.13-14.

units.la: Peccatum in genere definiri potest, ἀναμία instinctu satanæ à primoribus nostris parentibus in mundum inuecta, voluntati Dei repugnans, cuius fructus est, ex iusta Dei maledictione, miseria præsentis vitæ & mors æterna.
units.tr: Sin in general may be defined as lawlessness [ἀναμία], brought into the world by our first parents at the instigation of Satan, opposed to the will of God, the fruit of which, by the just curse of God, is the misery of the present life and eternal death.

units.la: PECCATUM, pro hæreditario illo morbo, quem peccatum originale vocant, Iob 14.4, & 15.14.16. Psalm.51.7. Roman. 3.ver.9.23. & 5.12. omnibus hominibus ingenitum est, 5.12.& 6.12. Ephes 2.3. ab Adamo traduce in omnes derivatum, Roman 5.12. effectus eius, Genes.3.16. &c. & 6.5. Eccl. 17.30. Rom.5.v.12 17.& 6.23 & 7.v 8.11 13.17. Gal.5 17. Ephes.2 3. mortem in mundum invexit, Genes.2 17.& 3.19. Roman.5.versi.12.15.1 Corint.15.56. Ephes.2 1. reatus eius, seu formale, ut vocant, tollitur per Christum, Ioann.1.29. Roman.3.ver.23 24.& 5.vers 9 15 17.18.19.& 6.3.& 7.24.& 8.versi.1.2. Galat.3.13. &c. Ephes 2 5. pro corruptione quæ manat à peccato originali, Roman.6.1. pro peccato actuali, Iac.1.15. peccatum sine lege mortuum est, Roman.7.8. Vide MORTVVM peccatum. piis non dominabitur, Roman.6.14. peccatum, pro peccati originalis fructibus, describitur 1 Ioann.3.4.& 5.17. Roman.4.25. Hebr.6.1.ex concupiscentia est, Iac.1.15. causa diluuij est, Genes.6.v.7.17.
units.tr: SIN, for that hereditary disease which they call original sin, Job 14.4 and 15.14, 16; Psalm 51.7; Romans 3.9, 23 and 5.12; it is innate in all men, Romans 5.12 and 6.12; Ephesians 2.3; derived from Adam by descent into all, Romans 5.12. Its effects, Genesis 3.16 etc. and 6.5; Ecclesiasticus 17.30; Romans 5.12, 17 and 6.23 and 7.8, 11, 13, 17; Galatians 5.17; Ephesians 2.3. It brought death into the world, Genesis 2.17 and 3.19; Romans 5.12, 15; 1 Corinthians 15.56; Ephesians 2.1. Its guilt, or what they call the formal element, is taken away through Christ, John 1.29; Romans 3.23-24 and 5.9, 15, 17-19 and 6.3 and 7.24 and 8.1-2; Galatians 3.13 etc.; Ephesians 2.5. For the corruption which flows from original sin, Romans 6.1. For actual sin, James 1.15. Sin without the law is dead, Romans 7.8. See DEAD SIN. It does not rule over the godly, Romans 6.14. Sin, for the fruits of original sin, is described in 1 John 3.4 and 5.17; Romans 4.25; Hebrews 6.1. It arises from concupiscence, James 1.15. It was the cause of the flood, Genesis 6.7, 17.

units.la: peccatum, pro punitione, seu pœna pro peccato infligenda, 19.15. Sic accipiunt nonnulli & Gen. 4.13 pro victima expiatrice, (per metonymiam) & sacrificio pro peccato, Exo.29.14 & 30.10. Deut.9.21 Psal.40.7. Thren 3.39 & 5.7. Ezech.45 19. Ose.4 8.7.2 Cor.5.21. Hebr.9.28. in postrema versus parte. peccatum ignorantiæ, Psalm.19.13. peccatum ignorantia committum, quomodo expiandum, Leuit.5. v.17.18. Num.15.v.20.22. peccatum superbia commissum, quomodo expiandum,15.28. peccatum vltroneum, quomodo expiandum, Leuit.6.v.2 6 peccatum homines miseros reddit, Prou.14.34. Matth.12.31. Marci 3.29. Luc.12. 10. Hebr 6.vers.4.6.& 10.26. 1. Ioan.5.16. peccatum vindictam clamans, Genes.4.10. & 18 20. Exod.22. versi.23.27. Iac.5.4. Vide CLAMOR peccatorum. peccatum contra naturam, quod est commixtio, cum masculis, Genes.19. 5. Leuit.20.13 Iudic.19.22.&c. Roman. 1.27. 1 Corinth. 6, 9.1. Timoth. 1.10. Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, Matth.12.31 Marc.3.29. Luc.11.15.& 12.10. Heb.6.4.6.& 10. 26. 1 Ioan.5.16.
units.tr: Sin, for the punishment or penalty to be inflicted for sin, Genesis 19.15. Some also take it thus in Genesis 4.13; for the expiatory victim (by metonymy), and the sacrifice for sin, Exodus 29.14 and 30.10; Deuteronomy 9.21; Psalm 40.7; Lamentations 3.39 and 5.7; Ezekiel 45.19; Hosea 4.8; 2 Corinthians 5.21; Hebrews 9.28, in the last part of the verse. Sin of ignorance, Psalm 19.13. How a sin committed in ignorance is to be expiated, Leviticus 5.17-18; Numbers 15.20-22. How a sin committed in pride is to be expiated, 15.28. How a voluntary sin is to be expiated, Leviticus 6.2, 6. Sin makes men miserable, Proverbs 14.34; Matthew 12.31; Mark 3.29; Luke 12.10; Hebrews 6.4-6 and 10.26; 1 John 5.16. Sin crying out for vengeance, Genesis 4.10 and 18.20; Exodus 22.23, 27; James 5.4. See CRY OF SINS. Sin against nature, which is intercourse with males, Genesis 19.5; Leviticus 20.13; Judges 19.22 etc.; Romans 1.27; 1 Corinthians 6.9; 1 Timothy 1.10. Sin against the Holy Spirit, Matthew 12.31; Mark 3.29; Luke 11.15 and 12.10; Hebrews 6.4-6 and 10.26; 1 John 5.16.

units.la: PECCATI corpus quid apud Paulum significet, (Vide CORPVS) peccati & eius effectuum exempla: in Adamo & Eua, Genesis 3.versi.6.7.10.16.&c. Caino 4.versi 10 11. Sodomitis,18 ver.20.21.& 19.24. pharaone, Exod.10.16. Israelitis, Iudic.2.versi.11.14. Rechabet Bahana, 2 Sam.4.v.10.11. Dauide 243. &c. 2 Paral.17.16. Iudæis, Ieremiæ 44. ver. 22.Paralytico,Matth.9.2.Languido, Ioan.5.14. Adultera, 8.11.peccati cognitio necessaria,Ierem.3.2.peccati cognitio per Legem,Roman.7.7.peccati finis,mors,6.21. peccati origo, Gen.2.17. & 3.6 Rom. 5. 12. 1 Corinth. 15. 21. peccati remissio, Vide Remissio. & paulò inferius peccati seruitus quàm periculosa,Ioan.8.34. Rom.6.20.peccati stipendia mors,v.23.
units.tr: The body of sin, what it signifies in Paul (see BODY). Examples of sin and its effects: in Adam and Eve, Genesis 3.6-7, 10, 16 etc.; in Cain, Genesis 4.10-11; in the Sodomites, Genesis 18.20-21 and 19.24; in Pharaoh, Exodus 10.16; in the Israelites, Judges 2.11-14; in Rechab and Baanah, 2 Samuel 4.10-11; in David, 2 Samuel 24.3 etc.; 2 Chronicles 17.16; in the Jews, Jeremiah 44.22; in the paralytic, Matthew 9.2; in the invalid, John 5.14; in the adulteress, John 8.11. Knowledge of sin is necessary, Jeremiah 3.2. Knowledge of sin through the Law, Romans 7.7. The end of sin is death, Romans 6.21. The origin of sin, Genesis 2.17 and 3.6; Romans 5.12; 1 Corinthians 15.21. The remission of sin, see REMISSION. And a little lower: how dangerous the slavery of sin is, John 8.34; Romans 6.20. The wages of sin are death, verse 23.

units.la: Peccato mortuum esse, in tertio & sexto casu quid declaret, Vide Mori peccato,peccato renuntiandum est, Ioann.8.11. Rom.6. ver.4.12.Hebr.12.1. 1 Pet.4.2. 1 Ioan. 3.6. in peccato mori qui dicantur, Vide Mori in peccato.
units.tr: To be dead to sin: what it signifies in the third and sixth case, see To Die to Sin. Sin must be renounced, John 8.11; Romans 6.4, 12; Hebrews 12.1; 1 Peter 4.2; 1 John 3.6. Who are said to die in sin, see To Die in Sin.

units.la: Peccata non sunt æqualia,aut paria, Ezech.4. ver.5.6. & 5.v.5.6.& 16.ver.47.51.52. & 23.1.Matth.10.15.& 11.ver.22. 24.& 23.14.Luc.10.v.12.14.& 12 ver.47.48. & 20.47.Ioan. 19.11.nec pares eorum pœnæ, Matth.5.22. & 10.15. & alibi sæpe id inculcatur. Peccata,quamuis inæqualia sint, qui tamen vnicum Legis apicem violarit, reus violatæ Legis in genere cêsetur,Ezec.18.24.25.Iac.2.10. & quoduis peccatum, quantumuis minutum, mortem æternam meretur sua natura, ne ipso quidem merè originali excepto, Rom.5.14. & 6.13. peccata aliis condonanda, Matth.6.14. Mar.11.25.Luc.17.3.peccata, Syris debita dicta, Matt.6.12. peccata à piis redarguenda, Eph.5.11. peccata Dei benedictio nem quodam modo impediunt, Ierem.5.25. peccata homines à Deo separant,Esaiæ 59.2.
units.tr: Sins are not equal or alike, Ezekiel 4.5-6 and 5.5-6 and 16.47, 51-52 and 23.1; Matthew 10.15 and 11.22, 24 and 23.14; Luke 10.12, 14 and 12.47-48 and 20.47; John 19.11. Nor are their punishments equal, Matthew 5.22 and 10.15; and this is often impressed elsewhere. Although sins are unequal, yet whoever has violated even a single point of the Law is guilty of violating the Law in general, Ezekiel 18.24-25; James 2.10. And any sin, however small, deserves eternal death by its very nature, not even excepting original sin alone, Romans 5.14 and 6.13. Sins are to be forgiven by others, Matthew 6.14; Mark 11.25; Luke 17.3. Sins are called debts by the Syrians, Matthew 6.12. Sins are to be rebuked by the godly, Ephesians 5.11. Sins in some way hinder God's blessing, Jeremiah 5.25. Sins separate men from God, Isaiah 59.2.

units.la: peccata punit Deus. Exempla: Salomon, 1 Reg.11.v.14. Achab & Iezabel, 2 Reg.9. v.7.25.26. 2 paral.22 7. Manasses, 2 Reg.24.v.2.3.4. Amasias, 2 paral.25.20. Iudæi Iere.13.22.& 30.15.Ezech.14.13.& 33.v.25 27.[Sacerdotes,] Malach.2,2. patres,Psalm.106.v.6.7.Iudæi,Esa.3.v.8.9.& 1.v.24.25.
units.tr: God punishes sins. Examples: Solomon, 1 Kings 11.14; Ahab and Jezebel, 2 Kings 9.7, 25-26; 2 Chronicles 22.7; Manasseh, 2 Kings 24.2-4; Amaziah, 2 Chronicles 25.20; the Jews, Jeremiah 13.22 and 30.15; Ezekiel 14.13 and 33.25-27; [the priests,] Malachi 2.2; the fathers, Psalm 106.6-7; the Jews, Isaiah 3.8-9 and 1.24-25.

units.la: Etiam in Sanctis castigat illa Deus.exempla: In Mose & Aarone,Num.20.v.12.13. Mose, 27.ver.12.13 14. Heli Sacerdote,1.Sam.2.v.27.28.&c. Dauide, 2 Sam.12.v.10. &c. Salomone, 1 Reg.11.v.11.12. Roboamo, 2 paral.12. v.7.8. Ioramo,21.16. iustis à iustitia se auertentibus, Ezech,18. 24,Iona,Ion.1.v 3.4.
units.tr: God chastises even the saints. Examples: in Moses and Aaron, Numbers 20.12-13; Moses, Numbers 27.12-14; Eli the priest, 1 Samuel 2.27-28 etc.; David, 2 Samuel 12.10 etc.; Solomon, 1 Kings 11.11-12; Rehoboam, 2 Chronicles 12.7-8; Joram, 21.16; just men who turn away from righteousness, Ezekiel 18.24; Jonah, Jonah 1.3-4.

units.la: Peccata committunt, & labuntur etiam Sancti, exempla:Fratres Ioseph, Genel.37. v.26.27.Moses, Exod.32.32. Dauid,2 Sam.24.1.Iob,Iob.3.v.1.2.3.&c. Ieremias,Ierem.20.v. 20.v.14.15. in Iona etiam exemplum lapsus Sanctorum est, quod munus sibi delegatum à Domino detractárit, Ion.1.v.10.11. quòd indigne tulerit Deum pœnitentibus misericordiam exhibere, Ion. 4.v. 2.3. 10 11. cuius lapsus particeps etiam fuit frater filij prodigi, Luc. 15.28. Paulus, cuius etsi peccata sunt absoluta, Act.22, 16. nihilominus tamen conqueritur habitare in carne sua peccatum, Rom.7.v.15.16,17. &c. & cupit se anathema fieri pro Fratribus suis secundum carnem, quod etiam non caret aliqua labe, Rom.9 3 Petrus, Gal.2.v.11.12.13. Vide ABNEGATIONIS exempla.
units.tr: The saints also commit sins and fall. Examples: the brothers of Joseph, Genesis 37.26-27; Moses, Exodus 32.32; David, 2 Samuel 24.1; Job, Job 3.1-3 etc.; Jeremiah, Jeremiah 20.14-15. In Jonah too there is an example of the fall of the saints, in that he withdrew the office delegated to him by the Lord, Jonah 1.10-11; in that he took it hard that God showed mercy to penitents, Jonah 4.2-3, 10-11. The brother of the prodigal son also shared in this fall, Luke 15.28. Paul, whose sins were forgiven, Acts 22.16, nevertheless complains that sin dwells in his flesh, Romans 7.15-17 etc., and desires to be made accursed for his brothers according to the flesh, which also is not free from some stain, Romans 9.3. Peter, Galatians 2.11-13. See examples of DENIAL.

units.la: Peccata Dei iustitiam commendare, & gloriam Dei illustrare dicuntur, Roman.3. 5.non per se, seu ex peccati natura, sed per accidens: ex Dei videlicet bonitate, idque in iis demum, quibus remittuntur, qui & ipsi sanctifi-cantur. ¶ Peccata solus Deus propria authoritate remittere potest, Exodi 37.7. Psalm.19.13. &32.5. &103.12. Esai. 43.25.& 44.22. & 53.1.&c. Ierem.31.34. & 33.8. Mich.7.18. Matth.9.2. Marc.2.5. Luc 5.20.& 7.48. ¶ remittunt & Ministri Verbi, sed divina authoritate, quatenus sunt Dei Ministri, Matt.18.18. Ioan.20.23. Vide DEVS ¶ Peccata remittuntur per Christum, Esa.43.25. & 53.1. &c. Dan.9. 24.Matth.1.21. & 9 2.& 11,18, & 20.28.& 26.27. Marci.2.5. Luc.1.77.& 5.24.46.Ioan.1.29. Actor.2.38 & 4.12. & 5.31 & 10. v. 35. 43. & 13. 38. Rom.4.25.& 5. 9.1 Cor.6.11 & 15.3.2 Cor.5.21. Galat.1.4. Colossi.1.14.& 2.13. Ephes.1.7.& 5.25.1 Tim.1.15. Tit.2.14. Heb.1 3 & 9.v.12 14. 1 Pet.1.18. & 2.24. & 3.18.& 4.11 Ioan.1.7.& 2.12.& 3 5. Apoc.1.5. ¶Propter vanius aut paucorum peccata puniuntur multi, Gen.3.1.&c. Numer.16.20.&c. Iosh.7.1.&c, Iudic.19.25. 2 Sam. 24.1.&c. Vide MAGISTRATUS. ¶ Peccata non solum non imputantur pijs, sed etiam vere remittuntur, & anima illorum abluitur, ac mundatur, Ps.51.12. Act.2.38. 1 Cor. 6.11.2. Petr.1.9.1.Ioann. 1.9. Peccata sua quinam dicantur confiteri Hebraeis, Vide CONFITERI.
units.tr: Sins are said to commend the righteousness of God and to illustrate the glory of God (Rom. 3:5). This is not in themselves, or by the nature of sin, but incidentally, namely through God's goodness, and that only in those to whom they are forgiven, who are themselves also sanctified. Only God can forgive sins by his own authority (Exod. 37:7; Ps. 19:13; 32:5; 103:12; Isa. 43:25; 44:22; 53:1, etc.; Jer. 31:34; 33:8; Mic. 7:18; Matt. 9:2; Mark 2:5; Luc. 5:20; 7:48). Ministers of the Word also forgive sins, but by divine authority, insofar as they are ministers of God (Matt. 18:18; John 20:23). See GOD. Sins are forgiven through Christ (Isa. 43:25; 53:1, etc.; Dan. 9:24; Matt. 1:21; 9:2; 11:18; 20:28; 26:27; Mark 2:5; Luc. 1:77; 5:24, 46; John 1:29; Acts 2:38; 4:12; 5:31; 10:35, 43; 13:38; Rom. 4:25; 5:9; 1 Cor. 6:11; 15:3; 2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 1:4; Col. 1:14; 2:13; Eph. 1:7; 5:25; 1 Tim. 1:15; Tit. 2:14; Heb. 1:3; 9:12, 14; 1 Pet. 1:18; 2:24; 3:18; 4:11; 1 John 1:7; 2:12; 3:5; Rev. 1:5). Because of the sin or sins of a few, many are punished (Gen. 3:1, etc.; Num. 16:20, etc.; Josh. 7:1, etc.; Judg. 19:25; 2 Sam. 24:1, etc.). See MAGISTRATE. Sins are not only not imputed to the godly, but are truly forgiven, and their souls are washed and cleansed (Ps. 51:12; Acts 2:38; 1 Cor. 6:11; 1 Pet. 1:9; 1 John 1:9). Which sins the Hebrews say must be confessed: see CONFESS. ## The Remission of Sins

units.la: REMISSIO Peccatorum, Est gratuita, eaque pleuissima in Christo per fidem apprehenso omnium peccatorum condonatio, in quorum locum successit eiusdem Christi iustitiæ imputatio.
units.tr: It is a free and most full forgiveness of all sins in Christ, laid hold of by faith, in whose place the imputation of that same righteousness of Christ has succeeded.

units.la: PECCATVM irremissibile, seu in Spiritum S. est peccatum ad mortem, & blasphemia in Spiritum S.Mat.12.31.1 Ioh.5.16. Ad cuius constitutionem tria concurrunt. Primo abnegatio veritatis contra scientiā & conscientiā. Secundo Apostasia universalis à Christo, non autem particulare peccatū aduersus primam, vel secundam Legis tabulam. Tertiò rebellio ex odio veritatis nata, coniuncta cum tyrannica, sophistica, & hypocritica oppugnatione. Dicitur autem peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, non respectu essentiae aut personae diuinae Spiritus, sed respectu officij, id est, gratiae & illuminationis, cuius Spiritus sanctus proprie effector est. Irremissibile verò dicitur tribus causis: Primò propter iustum Dei iudicium, qui non patitur Spiritum suum, qui Spiritus est veritatis, mendacij arguī: Secundò propter impœnitentiam seu respiscendi difficultatem. Tertiò propter veritatem & dignitatem redemptionis per Christum partæ. Nulla quippe alia restat hostia, vbi à Christi hostia discessum est. Heb.6.4.5.6.& 10. 26.29.16.
units.tr: The unforgivable sin, or sin against the Holy Spirit, is the sin unto death and the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Matt. 12:31; 1 John 5:16). Three things concur to make it up: (1) the denial of the truth against knowledge and conscience; (2) a universal apostasy from Christ, and not a particular sin against the first or second table of the Law; (3) a rebellion born of hatred of the truth, joined with a tyrannical, sophistical and hypocritical opposition. The sin is called against the Holy Spirit not with respect to the essence or person of the divine Spirit, but with respect to his office, that is, grace and illumination, of which the Holy Spirit is properly the author. It is called unforgivable for three reasons: first, on account of God's just judgment, who does not suffer his Spirit, which is the Spirit of truth, to be charged with lying; second, on account of impenitence, or the difficulty of repentance; third, on account of the worth and dignity of the redemption obtained through Christ. For no other sacrifice remains where one has departed from the sacrifice of Christ (Heb. 6:4, 5, 6; 10:26, 29; 16).

units.la: PECCATORVM remissio, est modus per quem Deus Pater nos in Filio seruat, vt docet Paulus Rom.4.7.ex illo Dauidis Psalm.32 1. peccatorum remissio promittitur, & quibus, Esa.1.18. & 27.9. & 30.15. & 40.2.& 50.8.& 55.3. Ierem.31 34. Mich.7.19. Actor.3.19. Hebr.10.17. Peccatorum remissio a Deo solo petenda, Matt.6 12. Lucæ.11.4. quia solus peccata remittit: Tribuitur tamen etiam legitimo Verbi Dei Ministro, tanquam instrumento, V. paulò superiùs.
units.tr: The forgiveness of sins is the manner by which God the Father preserves us in the Son, as Paul teaches (Rom. 4.7), from that saying of David (Ps. 32.1). That forgiveness of sins is promised, and to whom, see Isa. 1.18; 27.9; 30.15; 40.2; 50.8; 55.3; Jer. 31.34; Mic. 7.19; Acts 3.19; Heb. 10.17. Forgiveness of sins is to be sought from God alone (Matt. 6.12; Luke 11.4), because he alone forgives sins. Yet it is also attributed to the lawful minister of God's Word, as an instrument; see a little above.

units.la: Peccatorum remissio in Ecclesia, Esa.33.24. Ierem.31.8. Zach.13.1. peccatorum remissio hominem beatum efficit, Psalm.32.v.1.2. Rom.4.v.6.8. Esaiæ.30 26. peccatorum remissio nunquam est sine resipiscentia, vt patet ex Marci.1.4. Peccatorum remissio in futurum seculum reiicitur, Matth.12.32. aut quia peccatorum remissio, quam quisquam in ipso mortis articulo consequitur, proprie respicit futurum seculum: aut quia remissionis peccatorum plenum fructum non percipient fideles, nisi ab extremo illo iudicij futuri die. Impii econtrà, eo die corpore & anima plene cruciatibus immergentur, quibus nullus nec modus, nec finis erit. Apparet igitur & remissionem & condemnationem in futurum seculum non simpliciter reiici, sed secundùm quid, quatenus videlicet Dominus eo demum die penitus sua iudicia reuelabit & exequetur.
units.tr: Forgiveness of sins in the Church: Isa. 33.24; Jer. 31.8; Zech. 13.1. The forgiveness of sins makes a man blessed (Ps. 32.1–2; Rom. 4.6–8; Isa. 30.26). The forgiveness of sins is never without repentance, as is clear from Mark 1.4. Forgiveness of sins is denied in the age to come (Matt. 12.32); either because the forgiveness of sins which anyone obtains at the very moment of death properly looks to the age to come, or because the faithful will not receive the full fruit of the forgiveness of sins until that last day of the future judgment. The wicked, on the contrary, on that day will be fully plunged into torments in body and soul, for which there will be neither measure nor end. It appears therefore that both forgiveness and condemnation are not absolutely denied in the age to come, but only in a certain respect, namely insofar as the Lord will at last, on that day, fully reveal and execute his judgments.

units.la: Sic loquitur Paulus, Rom.2.5. 1 Cor.1.8.& 5.5.2 Cor.5. 10.29. 10.2 Tim.4.8. Petrus, 1 Petr.1.5. Erit ergo sensus, Nō remittetur, &c. Matt.12.32. hoc est, declarabitur & in hoc seculo, & in futuro, peccata illi non esse remissa: aut, ut sit μάνωσις Hebraica; Non remittetur: hoc est, certò, absque ulla venia punietur, tum in praesenti, tum in futura vita: quia μάνωσις est illa, Matt. 24.22. non seruaretur, pro, periret. Peccatorum sensus, & ex illo orta tristitia, primus est ad salutem gradus, 2. Cor.7.10.
units.tr: Paul speaks thus (Rom. 2.5; 1 Cor. 1.8; 5.5; 2 Cor. 5.10; 2 Tim. 4.8), and Peter (1 Pet. 1.5). The sense will therefore be: "It shall not be forgiven," etc. (Matt. 12.32); that is, it will be declared that those sins have not been forgiven, both in this age and in the future one. Or, taken as a Hebraism [μάνωσις]: "It shall not be forgiven," that is, it will certainly be punished, without any pardon, both in the present life and in the future. For the word is that of Matt. 24.22, "would not be saved," in place of "would perish." The sense of sin, and the sorrow arising from it, is the first step to salvation (2 Cor. 7.10).

units.la: PECCATIS alienis non communicandum. Prouer.29.24. Ephes.5. 7.1 Tim.5.22. In peccatis esse, 1 Cor.15. 17. & sanctificatum non esse, nec peccatorum remissionem consecutum esse.
units.tr: One must not share in the sins of others (Prov. 29.24; Eph. 5.7; 1 Tim. 5.22). To be in sins (1 Cor. 15.17) is not to be sanctified, nor to have obtained the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: PECCARE varia respicit, dicitur enim quis peccare Deo, in Deum, in Dominum, in Christum, in Spiritum S. in coelum, in proximum, in seipsum.
units.tr: To sin has various objects: for one is said to sin against God, against the Lord, against Christ, against the Holy Spirit, against heaven, against one's neighbour, against oneself.

units.la: PECCATVM Diuisiones quinque recipit.
units.tr: Sin admits of five divisions.

units.la: 1. Originale & Actuale.
units.tr: 1. Original and actual.

units.la: 2. Regnans non regnans.
units.tr: 2. Reigning and not reigning.

units.la: 3. Contra Conscientiam.
units.tr: 3. Against conscience.

units.la: 4. Remissibile, Irremissibile.
units.tr: 4. Forgivable and unforgivable.

units.la: 5. Per se, per accidens.
units.tr: 5. In itself, and incidental.

units.la: PECCATOR reus coram Deo & morte aeterna dignus, nisi interueniat peccatorum remissio propter mediatorem Christum. Peccator item dicitur homo improbus, Operarius iniquitatis, peccatis deditus & venditus, poenitere nescius, nequam, filius Belialis, Cauteriata conscientia, caecitate, idolentia, stupore, impudentia, malitia desperata percussus. Peccator, reus coram hominibus, quorum leges transgressus est.
units.tr: A sinner is guilty before God and worthy of eternal death, unless the forgiveness of sins intervenes on account of the mediator Christ. A sinner is also called a wicked man, a worker of iniquity, given over and sold to sins, ignorant of repentance, worthless, a son of Belial, with a seared conscience, struck with blindness, insensibility, stupor, impudence, and desperate malice. A sinner is also guilty before men, whose laws he has transgressed.

units.la: PECCVLATVS, est rei publicae furtum, cum quis quae totius sunt Reip. in suū vsum & comodū deriuat. cui annectitur crimen repetundarum. Exod.20.15.
units.tr: Peculatus is the theft of public property, when someone diverts to his own use and profit what belongs wholly to the commonwealth. To this is joined the crime of extortion (Exod. 20.15).

units.la: PECTORALE, V. Rationale.
units.tr: PECTORAL. See Rationale.

units.la: PECVLIVM Dei, populus ipsius, Exo.19.5. Deut.7.6. & 14.2. Malach.3.17. Ioan.1.11. Eph.1.14.1. Petr.2.9. paulus vocat alibi, populum peculiarem, Tit.2.14. Vide & 1.Par.29 3.
units.tr: PECULIAR (people) of God: his own people, Exod. 19.5; Deut. 7.6 and 14.2; Mal. 3.17; John 1.11; Eph. 1.14; 1 Pet. 2.9. Paul elsewhere calls it a peculiar people, Titus 2.14. See also 1 Chron. 29.3.

units.la: PECVNIA non danda ad vsuram, Deut. 23.19. de pecunia deposita apud amicum, Exo.22.7. mutuò data pauperi, v.25. pecuniā non comparatur Spiritus Sancti donum, Act 8. 20. pecuniis confidentes, Marc.10.24. Milites testes resurrectionis Christi pecunia corrupti: Mat.28.12.
units.tr: MONEY not to be lent at interest, Deut. 23.19; on money deposited with a friend, Exod. 22.7; lent to a poor man, v. 25. The gift of the Holy Spirit is not bought with money, Acts 8.20. Those who trust in money, Mark 10.24. The soldiers, witnesses of Christ's resurrection, were bribed with money, Matt. 28.12.

units.la: PECVS: pecoris in terra Aegypti clades, Exod.9.6. pecudis nomen, pro numis, quibus pecudis imago impressa erat, Genes. 33.19. Ios.24.32. Iob.42,11. iuxta quorundam sententiam. Pecudum offerendarum ritus, Leuit. 1. verf. 2.3.4. (V. Bestia) Creatio, Gen.1.24.
units.tr: CATTLE: the plague on the cattle in the land of Egypt, Exod. 9.6. The word for livestock is used for coins which bore the impression of an animal, Gen. 33.19; Josh. 24.32; Job 42.11, according to the opinion of some. The rite of offering animals, Lev. 1, vv. 2, 3, 4. (See Beast.) Creation, Gen. 1.24.

units.la: Pediculi in hominibus, Exo.8.17. in bestiis. v.18. magi non potuerunt pediculos producere v.18.
units.tr: Lice on men, Exod. 8.17; on beasts, v. 18. The magicians could not produce lice, v. 18.

units.la: Pedes calceati praeparatione Euangelii (quae sit calceorum instar) Eph.6.15.
units.tr: Feet shod with the preparation of the gospel (which is like shoes), Eph. 6.15.

units.la: Pedum lotio, Vide Lotio. Ad pedes Christi sedet Maria, Lucae.10.39. pedes Christi vngit peccatrix, 7.38. pedes dolet Asa, 1 Regum 15.23. pedes Sanctorum seruat Deus, 1 Sam.2.9. Psal.91.11.12. pedes pro aduentu, Esai.52.7. Roman. 10.15. pedes Elitai ab eius hospita apprehenduntur, 2 Reg. 4.27. pedes Israelitarum in deserto non attriti, Deut.8.4. pedes lauare ex itinere fessis hospitibus antiquitus in more positum fuit, Gen. 18.4. & 19.2. Iud.19.21. Vide Lotio pedum. Pedibus Dei appropinquantes docentur ab eo Deut.33.3. pedes Discipulorum a Christo lauantur, Ioan.13.5. &c. V. Pes. & Eccl.5.1. Disponit D. pedes nostros &c. 2. Sam.22.34.
units.tr: Washing of feet. See Washing. Mary sits at the feet of Christ, Luke 10.39; a sinful woman anoints the feet of Christ, 7.38. Asa was diseased in his feet, 1 Kings 15.23. God keeps the feet of his saints, 1 Sam. 2.9; Ps. 91.11–12. Feet for the coming (of messengers), Isa. 52.7; Rom. 10.15. Elisha's feet are seized by his hostess, 2 Kings 4.27. The feet of the Israelites did not wear out in the wilderness, Deut. 8.4. Washing the feet of weary travellers who came as guests was an ancient custom, Gen. 18.4; 19.2; Judg. 19.21. See Washing of feet. Those who draw near to God's feet are taught by him, Deut. 33.3. The disciples' feet are washed by Christ, John 13.5, etc. See Feet. Also Eccl. 5.1. The LORD makes our feet..., 2 Sam. 22.34.

units.la: Peleg (id est diuisio) filius Eber, Genes.10.25. ratio appellationis, ibid.
units.tr: Peleg (that is, division), son of Eber, Gen. 10.25; the reason for the name, ibid.

units.la: Pentapolis, Syriae regio ad Orientem Iudaeae a quinque ciuitatibus, Sodoma, Gomorrha, Adama, Seboim, & Segor, sic dicta, igne & sulphure euersa, Gen.13.10. & 19.25. & 10.19. Sap.10.6. V. Segor, &c.
units.tr: Pentapolis, a region of Syria to the east of Judea, named from five cities: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Zoar. It was so called because it was overthrown by fire and brimstone, Gen. 13.10; 19.25; 10.19; Wisd. 10.6. See Zoar, etc.

units.la: Pentecoste, erat dies festus magnus die quinquagesimo a feria paschatis, quo quae libet familia duos panes ex primitiis frugum offerebat, ad memoriam promulgatae Legis: Ex.23.16. Leuit.23.15.16.17.
units.tr: Pentecost was a great feast day on the fiftieth day after the feast of Passover, on which every household offered two loaves from the first fruits of the harvest, in memory of the giving of the Law: Exod. 23.16; Lev. 23.15–17.

units.la: Pentecostes, [Act.2.1. & 20.16. 1 Cor.16.8.] Vide Solennitas. Pentecostes festum, Exod.23.16. Leuit.23.15. Deut. 16.9.16.
units.tr: Pentecost, [Acts 2.1; 20.16; 1 Cor. 16.8.] See Solemnity. The feast of Pentecost, Exod. 23.16; Lev. 23.15; Deut. 16.9, 16.

units.la: Penuel siue Peniel, locus in quo Iacob cum Angelo tota nocte colluctans, Israelis nomen obtinuit: Gen.32.30. Ierobo-ham aedificauit Penuelem: 1 Reg.12.25. Penuel pater Gedoz-eorum: 1 Chron.4.4. Vide phanuel.
units.tr: Penuel or Peniel, the place where Jacob wrestled with the angel all night and received the name Israel: Gen. 32.30. Jeroboam built Penuel, 1 Kings 12.25. Penuel, the father of the Gedorites, 1 Chron. 4.4. See Phanuel.

units.la: Penuria rerum inobedientibus, Deut 28.48. & 32.24. V. Pro.28.27. Marc.12.44. Phil.4.11.12.
units.tr: Want of things for the disobedient, Deut. 28.48; 32.24. See Prov. 28.27; Mark 12.44; Phil. 4.11–12.

units.la: Percutiens hominem ad mortem moriatur, Leuit.24.17. 21. patrem, aut mulierem praegnantem, moriatur, Exo.21. v.15.23. Seruum, multatur. v.26. Bos percutiens v.28. Deus ferit erit & sanat: Deut.32.39. percussio in maxillam ignomi-niosa, Iob.16.10. Matt.5.29. & 26.68. Luc.22.64. Act.23.2.3. Ioh.18.22.23.1. Reg.22.24.
units.tr: Striking: one who strikes a man so that he dies shall die, Lev. 24.17, 21. One who strikes a father or a pregnant woman shall die, Exod. 21.15, 23. A slave who is struck is to be punished, v. 26. An ox that gores, v. 28. God wounds and heals, Deut. 32.39. A blow to the cheek is a disgrace, Job 16.10; Matt. 5.29; 26.68; Luke 22.64; Acts 23.2–3; John 18.22–23; 1 Kings 22.24.

units.la: percussio Dei immediata vel mediata, Angeli boni vel mali, Hominis boni vel mali aliarum creaturam.
units.tr: God's striking, whether immediate or mediate; the striking of good or evil angels; of a good or evil man against other creatures.

units.la: PERDITIO 2 Petr.2.v.13. & 37.16. Abyssus, locus perditionis, Iob.28.22. Ps.88.12. prou.15.11. & 29.20. Animi aegritudo, Mich.6 13. Calamitas grauiss. Deuter.32.35. Iob.21.30. prou.6.15. & 24 22. Ierem.18.17. & 49.8. Consumptio, destructio, exilium, desolatio, vastatio, Iob.31.v.3.12. Prou.11.10. Thren.2.8. Ioel.3 19. Abd.v.12. Mich 1.7. & 6 16. profusio inutilis, Matt.26.8. Marc.14.4.]
units.tr: PERDITION: 2 Pet. 2.13; and Isa. 37.16. The abyss, the place of perdition, Job 28.22; Ps. 88.12; Prov. 15.11; 29.20. Sickness of the soul, Mic. 6.13. Most grievous calamity, Deut. 32.35; Job 21.30; Prov. 6.15; 24.22; Jer. 18.17; 49.8. Destruction, ruin, exile, desolation, devastation, Job 31.3, 12; Prov. 11.10; Lam. 2.8; Joel 3.19; Obad. v. 12; Mic. 1.7; 6.16. Useless waste, Matt. 26.8; Mark 14.4.

units.la: PERDITO de boue, oue, aut alia re proximi, quid agendum Deut.22.1. &c. Exod.22.9.
units.tr: LOSS of an ox, sheep or other property of a neighbour: what is to be done, Deut. 22.1, etc.; Exod. 22.9.

units.la: PERDERE, pro aeternis supplicijs immergere & cruciare, Mat.10.28. non enim peribit, id est non in nihilum redigetur substantia damnandorum.
units.tr: TO PERISH: to plunge into eternal punishments and torment, Matt. 10.28. For "will not perish" means that the substance of the damned will not be reduced to nothing.

units.la: PEREGRINVS: Peregrinis benefaciendum, Gen.18.2. Exod.22.21. & 23.9. Leuit.19 33. & 23.22. Num.15.14. Deut.10,18. & 14.21. & 24.v.14.17. & 26.11. Ezech.22.29. & 47.21. Zach.7.10. suscipiendi sunt, Exo.23 9. & alendi, Deut.14.29. Iusteis administrandum iuste: Deut.24.17. Psal. Deut.10.18. Ezech.22.7.15. Deut.27.19. peregrini sumus & advenae in hac vita, Gen.15 13. & 23.4. & 47 9.1. Par.29.15. psal.39.13. & 119 19.2. Cor.5.7. Phil.3.20. Hebr.11.13.1. Petr.2 11. peregrinus in aliqua civitate translatitie dicitur, qui ignorat quod caeteri illic norint, Luc.24.38. peregrinamur a Domino, 2 Cor.5.6. peregrinatio est vita Iacob, Gen.47.9. Vide Aduena.
units.tr: FOREIGNER: good is to be done to foreigners, Gen. 18.2; Exod. 22.21; 23.9; Lev. 19.33; 23.22; Num. 15.14; Deut. 10.18; 14.21; 24.14, 17; 26.11; Ezek. 22.29; 47.21; Zech. 7.10. They are to be welcomed, Exod. 23.9, and fed, Deut. 14.29. They are to be dealt with justly, Deut. 24.17; Ps.; Deut. 10.18; Ezek. 22.7, 15; Deut. 27.19. We are strangers and sojourners in this life, Gen. 15.13; 23.4; 47.9; 1 Chron. 29.15; Ps. 39.13; 119.19; 2 Cor. 5.7; Phil. 3.20; Heb. 11.13; 1 Pet. 2.11. Someone is called a stranger in a city in a figurative sense if he does not know what the others there know, Luke 24.18. We are away from the Lord, 2 Cor. 5.6. The life of Jacob is a pilgrimage, Gen. 47.9. See Sojourner.

units.la: PERFECTI, pro, in fide & reliquis regenerationis donis, confirmatis, Hebr.5.14. non qui plenam iam & absolutam sapientiam sint assecuti, sed comparatiue, qui prae reliquis in cognitione rerum diuinarum profecerunt, & sano incorruptoque sunt iudicio, 1 Cor.2.6. Philip.3.15,2. Tim.3.17. Et vocantur Christiani perfecti, tum quod in fide & reliquis regenerationis donis confirmati & certi sint, tum quod ad perfectionem illam futuram contendant, Eph.4.13.
